title: Oral Questions: The Budget
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Budget Officer went looking for the numbers in this budget and could not find them: a $62-billion cut with no programs, an $8-billion savings tied to nothing and $135 billion that they called capital, which is not capital at all. The numbers she could find are even worse. The government will spend more on interest on the debt than on health care for every single Canadian. Instead of hiding what the debt is costing Canadians in mortgages and higher prices, will the minister table the real numbers?

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative leader is losing staff at a quicker rate than he actually built houses as housing minister. Budget 2026 is twofold. On one side, we are going to focus on affordability for Canadians, end homelessness and provide a one-time top-up for the groceries and essentials benefit. On the other side, yes, we are going to invest in Canadians. The productivity mega deduction will supercharge investment in capital across this country. The party opposite is not taken seriously. We are here to build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, it is the Parliamentary Budget Officer they hired who is sounding the alarm bells. The government promised to double homebuilding, and housing starts are down. That promise vanished out of the budget. The $500 billion that they boasted about from their investment summit is not tied to a single real project. Those are her words, and they hired her. This is a government that traffics in announcements and not results. Why does it take the Parliamentary Budget Officer to tell Canadians what the government will not?

Mr. Speaker, the member wishing it so does not make it true. Let us look at the economic fundamentals. We have the best net debt to GDP in the G7, the strongest fiscal position in the G7, and wages outpacing inflation. Our economy is the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7. They are not serious about the economy. Their leader continues with the rhetoric and the empty parking lot press conferences. On this side, we are serious about building a strong economy and a strong Canada for everybody from coast to coast to coast.

Mr. Speaker, over the past few months, I have heard from families in Sackville—Bedford—Preston and across Nova Scotia about how events beyond our borders are impacting the cost of living for families across our province. In this uncertain world, Nova Scotians know their government is stepping up to support them with real targeted supports at the pump, the grocery store and in their daily lives. Could the Secretary of State for Children and Youth outline how budget 2026 will support families across Nova Scotia?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Sackville—Bedford—Preston for his advocacy. Our plan gives Canadians a boost today and a bridge to tomorrow. Families in Nova Scotia will benefit from an increase to the groceries and essentials benefit, and the renewal of the Canada strong pass. We will be making investments in housing and in a national heat pump rebate program, just to name a few. This is real, targeted support for Nova Scotians. Our government will always be there to support families in Atlantic Canada and across the country.

title: Oral Questions: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship
turns: Mr. Speaker, the other day I spoke to Nikki, who waited four years for back surgery. She had to work through the pain because, of course, with this economy, she could not afford to take time off. Six million Canadians have no doctor. Canadians are dying on wait-lists, yet the Prime Minister plans to bring in a record 650,000 new permanent residents, 50% higher than the biggest year under Justin Trudeau. How does the Prime Minister expect to accept so many new people to this country at a time when Canadians cannot get the basic health care they need?

Mr. Speaker, we are here fighting for Nikki and for all the people in this country who deserve and need health care. Conservatives are claiming they care for Canadians and for health care. I have reserved 5,000 spaces in the immigration plan for health care professionals. I prioritized health care professionals with our express entry system. This government has invested $100 million for credential recognition and $5 billion for hospitals. We will continue to make our immigration plan durable, stable and in control.

Mr. Speaker, if it were true that the minister is bringing in 5,000 new doctors, we do not need to have 650,000 new permanent residents to do that. However, it is worse than that. According to the national nurses union, thousands of nurses already here as immigrants cannot get licensed to work. According to the medical association, there are 13,000 doctors who cannot get licensed to work. We proposed a blue seal program that would get them licensed nationwide and serving in our hospitals. Why does the Prime Minister not do that before bringing in a record-smashing 650,000 new permanent residents?

Mr. Speaker, the federal government supports provinces and territories to license newcomers who are medical professionals through our foreign credential recognition program, something the member opposite votes against time and time again. The Conservatives are talking out of both sides of their mouth. They say they care about newcomers who want to use their skills in Canada, yet they undermine them every chance they get.

Mr. Speaker, due to increased demand, average wait times for health care in Canada have increased to 31 weeks, and more than 23,000 Canadians died while waiting for care in 2024-25. Youth unemployment is at 13.7%, and housing starts are down by 10%. Housing is down, unemployment and wait times are up, and yet the minister plans to bring in more than 650,000 new permanent residents next year. How can she possibly justify that as sustainable?

Mr. Speaker, let us talk about youth unemployment for a moment, and talk about the obstruction from Conservative members of Parliament who continually vote against the interests of our youth, including Canada summer jobs, which all of them benefit from in their own riding, and the $8 billion for team Canada strong, which is building new apprentices, building new tradespeople and helping people, like those in the Canadian Construction Association, find the talent they need. These guys are talking out of both sides of their mouth. They do not want to be part of the solution. They are obstructing for the purpose of obstruction, and that is not what Canada needs or wants.

Mr. Speaker, the immigration department warned the Prime Minister that rapid increases in immigration put pressure on health care, but he ignored that warning and he is bringing in close to a million new people next year. When two families are waiting for the same scarce hospital bed, the blame does not belong on a newcomer who came to Canada to build a better life. Will the Prime Minister admit that the blame belongs squarely on him, because he is bringing in too many people too fast for housing and health care to keep up?
Mr. Speaker, the member knows very well that what she is saying is not true—

Mr. Speaker, the information is not accurate. The fact is, the majority of the people who will be coming into permanent residency next year are already people living here, paying taxes, working, helping our children in day cares, feeding people in their homes and helping those in hospital beds. They are already here on temporary status. Which ones would she like to get rid of? Can she please tell us?

Mr. Speaker, let us think about what the minister just said. She just admitted that the 5,000 people she was going to give the spots to are already here and already practising. There are six million people in Canada who, even with those people here, already do not have a doctor. Why would the Prime Minister bring one million more people to Canada? These people also need hospital beds and diagnostic imaging. My question to the minister is this—

Mr. Speaker, one million new people to Canada need hospital beds and access to surgery. My question to the minister is this: Which hospital bed does the Prime Minister plan to give the one million newcomers? Is it the one that does not exist or the one that somebody already here is waiting for?

Mr. Speaker, those are totally fabricated numbers that the member is talking about. Our immigration plan is to maintain control of our system. It is to bring fairness to people who are already in the country. I will quote a physician who is a Hong Konger. He said: The time-limited measure presented in this year’s immigration levels plan gives our Hong Kong community renewed hope. By clearing the backlog for the Hong Kong pathways, Canada will not only honour its commitment, it will also unlock valuable health care manpower that is already here in Canada, contributing to our economy

title: Oral Questions: Agriculture and Agri-Food
turns: Mr. Speaker, inflationary spending in the Liberal budget is driving up input costs and Canadian farmers are struggling. While farmers are struggling, the agriculture minister is lavishing more than $40 million on external consultants. In fact, over the last decade, he has lavished more than $500 million on Liberal consultants. At the same time, he is dismantling the very heart of Canadian agriculture, shutting down research centres across the country. The minister had a choice to give consultants more than $500 million or to keep these seven research centres operating for decades. Why did he choose Liberal lobbyists over Canadian farmers?

Mr. Speaker, Canadian farmers are at the forefront of everything that is happening around the world today. In our budget, we are doing intergenerational rollover for farmers. We are doing amendments to the Canadian Agricultural Loans Act. We are renewing the local food infrastructure fund. Most importantly, which I have been told by many organizations across the country, the productivity mega deduction is so important to move agriculture forward. We will keep investing in agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, when it mattered most, the agriculture minister decided to give his Liberal friends $500 million rather than fund agricultural research. The Liberals chose to give them another $40 million and cut almost 700 jobs in agricultural science and research. The Liberals chose to shut down seven research centres across the country. We are losing our best and brightest and decades of institutional knowledge are being lost. Why did the minister close these research centres and fire frontline scientists? Was it just to ensure that his Liberal lobbyists got paid?

Mr. Speaker, it has been known that we are doing as much research now as we have done in the past. We are doing research in every province in the country and we are going to continue to do research. We are doing more precise research. We have signed an MOU with Saskatchewan. We have been in talks with his home province. We have been in talks with Université Laval. We have been in talks with Guelph University. We are making changes. We are coming into a time when we need more research, not less. That is what we are going to do.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal budget excludes key sectors of our economy. Budget 2026 introduces the new capital gains exemption for up to $15 million for qualifying businesses through the Canada growth incentive and the much-touted productivity mega deduction. These incentives are largely excluding agriculture, fishing and forestry, and they are the backbones of our economy and our major GDP drivers. Can the minister please explain why these sectors were excluded from these incentives despite their importance to Canada's food sovereignty, food security and our rural economy?

Mr. Speaker, I suggest the hon. member read the budget, because the productivity mega tax deduction is directly an incentive for farmers, whether it is buying a combine, buying a sprayer or buying a tractor. I am not sure what he is talking about. We just invested $3.2 billion in the national food security strategy, the largest investment in agriculture and agri-food in our history. We are moving agriculture forward, and we are diversifying our trade. We are going to keep on going, and we are not going to take any lessons from over there.

Mr. Speaker, again, I hope the hon. member has an opportunity to read the budget and really figure out what the benefits are to agriculture. I remember that their platform in the last election did not have anything in it about agriculture. I think it is really important that we call a spade a spade in the House of Commons. If they want to learn more, and if I can get them briefing notes for the budget, I will do that.

title: Oral Questions: Indigenous Affairs
turns: Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister says he wants to fast-track the Pacific link pipeline while promising first nations that they will decide if the project goes ahead. Our representative at the B.C. First Nations Leadership Council said the Prime Minister assured them that we will get consent. Will the Prime Minister approve the pipeline, even if just one of the 129-plus first nations along the pipeline route does not provide consent?

Mr. Speaker, indigenous rights are not an obstacle to building Canada strong. They are part of the foundation on which we will build it. As part of our duty to consult, we heard directly from more than 130 indigenous communities across Alberta and B.C. Where appropriate, accommodations will be made. Further consultations will inform conditions for Pacific link guided by UNDRIP and anchored in the principle of free, prior and informed consent. We will always respect the rights of indigenous people.

Madam Speaker, this is exactly what the Prime Minister claimed, that he provided full, meaningful consultation with indigenous peoples, and he has made different promises to different First Nations. Is he seeking consensus or following UNDRIP commitments while fast-tracking the Pacific link major project designation with only two months of consultation? Will the Prime Minister only approve the pipeline if all the 129-plus nations provide consent?

Madam Speaker, we will continue to work with indigenous communities across Canada, and as part of the work moving forward to ensure that we get these projects over time, the key criteria in this is to ensure that we advance indigenous interests with meaningful participation, meaningful equity and meaningful partnership. We are going to continue to build with first nations communities, and we are going to continue to ensure that we are all moving forward together.

Madam Speaker, let us see if we can make it three for three with the same answer. Last week, the Prime Minister smiled for another photo op with chiefs to announce a new pipeline. Conservatives know we need to unlock our resources and get this pipeline built, but announcements are not results, photo ops are not consultation and Liberals' claiming relationships with chiefs and councils does not make it real. Chief Trevor Mercredi said that using first nation leaders in press conferences does not mean a vote of confidence. Why is the Prime Minister putting crucial major projects in jeopardy by using first nation chiefs as photo ops?

Madam Speaker, let me reiterate what we are saying on this side of the board. Indigenous rights are not an obstacle for building Canada strong; they are part of the foundation on which we will build it. We will continue to work with first nations communities. We will continue to work with indigenous people. On this side of the House, we respect constitutional rights and we respect consultation. We will continue to do so.

Madam Speaker, here is another opportunity for something new. Treaty chiefs are not the only ones calling out the Liberal government. The AFN national chief that said that those at the Major Projects Office “don't know what they are doing when it comes to First Nations” and that it is a pattern for this government and its MPO CEOs to act like they are too good to meet with chiefs. The truth is that treaty rights do not disappear when they become inconvenient for Liberals. Chiefs are tired of the announcements and photo ops, so why did the Prime Minister create a Major Projects Office just to disrespect chiefs and cover his failures on building major projects in this country?

Madam Speaker, on this side of the House we believe in economic reconciliation. That means, when we are advancing projects that are important to this country, that we ensure we are advancing indigenous interests, which means, and I will say it again for the other side so they hear it loud and clear, we are making sure it is meaningful partnership, meaningful equity and meaningful participation in all projects moving forward. Indigenous communities will build together with the government.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Mr. Speaker, interest costs on the national debt are skyrocketing. By 2030, they will chew up 14¢ of every tax dollar, which is $85.5 billion a year and $8,000 for a typical family of four. That is more than we will spend on public health care, and more than we will spend on a whole range of other social programs. It is the fastest-growing expense in the government's budget. What is the government going to do if we face another major crisis like we faced in 2008 and 2020?

Mr. Speaker, the member mentioned “fastest-growing”. Canada has the fastest-growing economy in the G7, as of quarter two results, at 3.3%. That has given us $27.5 billion more in revenue, with a lower deficit than projected in the spring economic update. I am happy to confirm for the member opposite that the Government of Canada is exceeding its fiscal guardrails. We are balancing the operating budget one year ahead of schedule and sticking to our deficit-to-GDP ratio declining path.

Mr. Speaker, in most projections, growth remains anemic, below 1% this year, which is essentially zero. Over the past six months, the government has announced tens of billions of dollars in tax expenditures outside of this place, which we only got the details of yesterday in the budget, so I have a simple question. Will the government commit that in the next six months, it is not going to be making any more major tax expenditure or spending announcements outside of this place, and will instead respect Parliament and announce them here?

Mr. Speaker, what we will commit to is growing the Canadian economy as fast as possible to achieve what we promised Canadians, which is to have the strongest, most resilient economy in the G7. How do we do that? We leverage the strong fundamentals and fiscal firepower this country has to invest in Canadians, to support them with affordability measures like a boost to the groceries and essentials benefit, to move forward with our electricity strategy, to end homelessness and to ensure that we have a growing, prosperous economy that creates good-paying jobs for the future.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance told this House that they had found $60 billion in savings in the expenditure review. His own deputy minister, though, stated that the review was merely an allocation exercise and that there were no actual savings. The costly credit card budget is showing an increase of billions in operating spending, adding to the already crushing debt load on Canadians. Did the finance minister mislead the House, as his deputy and the budget show? If not, where is the $60 billion in savings?

Mr. Speaker, we are at a time when our sovereignty and economic security are being tested. What is the Government of Canada's response to that? It is to realize that our future is in our hands and that to build that future is our responsibility. What we are doing is leveraging fiscal strength with fiscal responsibility to invest in the Canadian economy and to support Canadians with new affordability measures in this budget, like the groceries and essentials benefit and like making certain tax credits and extending them to encourage more investment and more growth. That is exactly what Canadians elected us to do.

Mr. Speaker, not wanting to be left out, the President of the Treasury Board, responsible for spending oversight, also stated that they had found $60 billion in savings. His deputy, though, contradicted him, calling it a “reallocation exercise” and stating there were no actual savings. Here we have the two ministers most responsible for the public purse both claiming $60 billion in savings, yet the costly credit card budget shows an increase of billions in operating spending. Did both ministers mislead the House? If not, where is the $60 billion in savings?

Mr. Speaker, budget 2026 puts Canada's future in our hands. It is in our hands to build this country up. We have a growing economy, with 3.3% second quarter GDP growth. We found $27.5 billion less of a deficit, with a 9% increase in new business investment, and non-U.S. trade is up 56%. We are putting Canada on track to enter an investment supercycle to see our economy go from $3.4 trillion to $4 trillion over the next number of years. That is progress. That is how we build Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister claims his budget will make Canadians masters of their own destiny but with this massive debt binge, the only masters are global bankers and bondholders. The total deficit, projected at $150 billion, undermines our economy. Debt interest payments are now over $1 billion each week, and the fiscal guardrails are far in the rearview mirror. Canada lost over 50,000 private sector jobs just last month. Unemployment is up. When will the Prime Minister finally master his credit card spending so that Canadians will not be mastered by his debt?

Mr. Speaker, I just want to remind my colleagues across the way that Stephen Harper ran deficits in seven of nine fiscal years. In Alberta, we are seeing the plan we are putting in place go to work. We have 40,000 new jobs this year, 4,000 of which are youth jobs. We have the Pacific link pipeline under construction next year. We also have the pathways carbon capture project going. It is an exciting time to be a Canadian. It is an exciting time to be an Albertan. I really hope they get on board.

Mr. Speaker, if I mastered my own finances the same way the Prime Minister masters the budget, I would not qualify for a payday loan at Money Mart. The Prime Minister told Canadians his deficit was only a measly $62 billion but when he includes his so-called investments, it reaches $150 billion. This kind of accounting trickery would not get someone a bank loan from the Prime Minister, but he keeps printing money and driving up inflation. Meanwhile, Canada lost 50,000 jobs just last month. When will the Prime Minister finally get his costly credit card spending under control so that Canadians will not be mastered by his debt?

Mr. Speaker, why does it seem that Conservatives only seem to celebrate when they think Canada is failing? It is as if they are confirming what they really want every day in the House. We are standing up and using the fiscal strength that Canada has to make the country stronger, to support Canadians with real affordability measures. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. We have seen the economy growing, and we are continuing to invest in jobs. In my region alone, 50,000 new jobs have been created by our government. There are billions of dollars of new investment. That is how we build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, let us talk a bit about that 50,000 figure. The member said that there is an aspiration in the budget to, at some point in the next five years, create 50,000 jobs. In today's job report, released today, we hear that 50,000 private sector jobs were already lost in the last month. That is not an aspiration. Those are real concrete numbers reported not by the finance minister but by Statistics Canada. The government whip pretending that things are better than they are does not comfort Canadians at home who are struggling. He should stop pretending that things are better than they are and start fighting for people who matter.

Mr. Speaker, it is not aspirational when I mentioned 50,000 jobs. The new nuclear project at Darlington is 21,700 jobs in my region alone. The Pickering refurbishment project is another 30,000 jobs. Those are real jobs for real Canadians in my region. That is not aspirational. That is not hope. It is real action in the real economy, creating growth and good jobs for the future. That is exactly what we are about on this side.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised to make life affordable and get government spending under control. Instead, the Liberals gave Canadians a costly credit budget that should have been titled masters of debt. One in three Canadians is now skipping meals or eating less because they simply cannot afford groceries. While Canadians struggle to put food on the table, the Liberals continue to borrow billions and billions of dollars more, leaving taxpayers with the bill. How much debt does the Prime Minister intend to pile onto Canadians before he admits that his approach of just throwing it on the tab is no substitute for reasonable fiscal policy?

Mr. Speaker, one of the first things that our government did when elected was to cut taxes for 22 million Canadians. We then entered into a comprehensive expenditure review and found $60 billion in savings over five years from government operations. In the budget, we are leveraging that strength. We are enhancing the groceries and essentials benefit, offering hundreds more dollars per year to Canadian families. Twelve million Canadians are going to get more support this year as a result of the fiscal strength that our government has shown because our economy is growing. We will continue to invest in them.

Mr. Speaker, those programs clearly are not working, or they would not have put $100 million toward food banks that need more money to keep up with the pace of demand because of their policies. Families are already struggling with mortgages, groceries and gas. Half of Canadians say they have had to dip into their savings just to cover basic necessities, yet this year the federal government will spend $60 billion paying interest on the Liberals' debt. That is more than we send to the provinces to deliver health care and nearly twice what families are provided through the Canada child benefit. With interest payments consuming more than 10% of the federal budget, when will the Prime Minister present a credible plan to get Liberal spending under control and reverse—

Mr. Speaker, this budget puts money in the pockets of Canadians, not tomorrow, but today. We are increasing the amount of the Canadian groceries and essentials benefit so that, with this one-time top-up, families of four will receive $2,570. That is real money that they can put toward groceries and can use to ensure that their children have a good start. However, we do not stop there. There is no consumer carbon tax. We have put a pause on the fuel excise tax. There is $10-a-day child care and school meals for up to 400,000 children. They laugh.

title: Statements by Members: Affordability
turns: Mr. Speaker, in response to the Liberals' inflationary spending, the Bank of Canada this week raised interest rates for the first time in three years. This interest rate hike will hit residents in the communities that I represent hard. This increase directly affects mortgage rates. They will go up. I represent one of the eldest ridings in Canada, with many fixed-income seniors already juggling mortgages, credit lines and the need to drive to medical appointments. We are already seeing seniors who used to donate to food banks now standing in line at food banks. The Liberals are ignoring the fact that this affordability crunch is getting worse, with benefits and savings struggling to keep up and seniors just trying to afford to put food on the table.

Mr. Speaker, families in Cowichan—Malahat—Langford and across Vancouver Island are working hard, but the bills keep growing. Parents worry about the grocery checkout. Seniors go without because their pensions cannot cover the basics. The Bank of Canada now forecasts 2027 inflation at 3.1%, up from 2% in the July report. This means mortgage payments will go up and prices will rise faster, on top of the already high cost of living Canadians face. Unless wages and pensions keep pace, their money will buy less food and cover fewer necessities. The people on Vancouver Island need breathing room. They deserve decisions that serve all Canadians rather than the political interests of the Prime Minister and his favoured few. I will keep fighting for lower costs, responsible spending and honest answers. The people of Cowichan—Malahat—Langford have entrusted me to stand up for them. I will honour that trust every day. I call on the government to do the same.

Mr. Speaker, 18 months ago, Canadians elected a new Prime Minister with a new government. From day one, the issue of affordability has been important not only to the Prime Minister, but to every Liberal member of this caucus. At the end of the day, actions speak louder than words. What members will see is that we brought forward programs such as the national food program for our schools, which feeds 400,000 children. The Conservatives said no to that. We brought forward the national dental care program, which provides dental services for seniors on fixed incomes. The Conservatives said no to that. Somewhere within that caucus is a small fraction of Progressive Conservatives. We need those Conservatives to stand up, start speaking on behalf of Canadians and get rid of the far right.

title: Oral Questions: The Budget
turns: Mr. Speaker, there are more reports critical of the budget. Here is what PBO Annette Ryan said: Housing starts are down. Funding is up. And the government is falling behind on its promise to double homebuilding. It also seems to have stepped away from its earlier commitment to build 500,000 new homes per year, yet proposes to approve an additional 200,000 permanent residents to Canada in Budget 2026. The Prime Minister promised in the last election “to build homes at a scale and at a speed not seen since the Second World War.” What happened?

Mr. Speaker, I know it is Wednesday, and we need to remind the Conservatives. Let me quote a great Conservative premier. I think his name is Scott Moe, Premier of Saskatchewan, talking about the budget: “I would say it’s probably the best budget we’ve had in a decade”. That is visionary. I want to talk about the premier-designate of British Columbia. Maybe they will prefer that. “Today's federal budget proves British Columbia is critical to Canada's economic success.” Canadians across the nation understand that we need to build this country, tackle affordability and defend our sovereignty. We are going to build Canada stronger.

Mr. Speaker, the PBO said interest payments “are already the fastest-growing expense in the fiscal framework.” She said interest payments “will rise to $85.5 billion in 2030-31”. That is more than the government spends on public health care. Now the government is not only cutting the Commissionaires; it is now cutting most cadet activities until next spring. The Prime Minister promised, last election, “responsible fiscal management”. How is spending more on interest than public health care, cutting the Commissionaires and cutting cadet activities “responsible fiscal management”?

Mr. Speaker, it is Wednesday, so I have more good news. Let us talk about the Canadian Chamber of Commerce: This is a radical shift, and the government is now focusing on “the kind of business investment and reinvestment Canada needs.” That is exactly what budget 2026 is about: fiscal discipline, visionary investment, defending sovereignty and helping Canadians with affordability. Canadians understand that from coast to coast to coast. We are going to build Canada strong together.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Budget Officer has exposed the Prime Minister's accounting trick, $136 billion of expenses relabelled as investments. The Prime Minister, in fact, has not balanced the operating budget. He created an accounting scheme to make the numbers look better, and then he boasted about balancing the operating budget, but under the original definitions, that budget will remain in a deficit for at least another five years. Why is the Prime Minister telling Canadians that the operating budget is balanced, when he knows it is not?

Mr. Speaker, that leader's office flees to B.C. to work for their premier. By the way, that premier called our budget the best he has seen in a decade. We agree with that B.C. premier. We are going to build Canada strong while looking after the most vulnerable. Our groceries and essentials benefit will be topped up by 50%, and our productivity mega deduction will unleash capital investment in our country like not ever seen before.

Mr. Speaker, the member clearly dodged the question, but let me say this: The finance minister, in fact, said that he did this for transparency. He invented definitions not used anywhere else in the world for transparency, and then used them inconsistently for transparency. Then, the numbers cannot be independently replicated with public information for transparency, but conveniently, this accounting scheme moves $136 billion of expenses to investments and causes the operating budget to be balanced. Does he really think that Canadians are foolish enough to believe his scheme, or does he think that telling the truth does not matter anymore?

Mr. Speaker, budget 2026 is titled “Masters of our destiny”. That leader is master of division in his caucus and in his office. We have a plan to build Canada strong. We have a plan to invest in Canada to unleash capital investment in projects. We are going to invest in major projects, infrastructure and housing. On this side of the House, we have a plan to build our economy strong. They have no plan whatsoever.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are looking to us to build a stronger, more affordable and more independent economy. Our plan is grounded in a simple principle: Hard work leads to greater opportunity and Canadian workers and Canadian labour will be at the heart of building a stronger and resilient economy. However, while we build a stronger economy, we know affordability remains a very real concern. Can the Minister of Finance tell my constituents in Peterborough how budget 2026 is providing greater certainty and support for low- and modest-income workers?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member for Peterborough for her excellent work. In budget 2026, she is right that we announced Canada's worker benefit, which will help lower-income Canadians continue to work and contribute to Canada's economy, while keeping a little extra money in their pocket, which means their families will receive up to $3,100 per year in support. That means increased financial certainty for nearly two million Canadian workers who will benefit. That means an additional 240,000 Canadians will be lifted out of poverty—

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Prime Minister is out of touch, Canadians are out of money and the debt is out of control. More inflation is on the horizon as the Parliamentary Budget Officer calculated that the government is expected to add $730 billion to our national debt over the next five years. That is three-quarters of a trillion dollars more on the national credit card, working out to $40,000 in debt for every single Canadian. That is more handouts to corporate power brokers, more interest to bankers, and more food and housing inflation for Canadians. How does he expect them to pay this bill?

Mr. Speaker, we will take no lessons from the Conservatives. Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have one of the most educated workforces in the world. We are able to build planes, build ships and build cars in this country. We have the critical minerals to power the economy of the 21st century. We have an abundance of energy and we are going to produce even more. We are the only G7 nation with a free trade agreement with all the other G7 nations. This is what is building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, the finance minister is absolutely right that Canadians are very educated. They are educated enough to know that the government is cooking the books. The Prime Minister is dividing his deficits on three credit cards. One he calls operational spending, another he claims is investment and a third goes to Crown corporations. However, Canadians understand that just because the Liberals put their debt on three different credit cards does not mean they do not have to pay the interest. Given that Canadians understand that, when will the Prime Minister get this basic financial lesson?

Mr. Speaker, one thing Canadians understand is that the Leader of the Opposition keeps talking the Canadian economy down. He keeps talking against the industries in this country. We have the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7. We have one of the lowest deficits in the G7. We are the only country with Germany in the G7 to have an AAA credit rating. We are going to build Canada strong and we are going to do it with all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it is the Liberal government that is driving the Canadian economy down. It is doing it with credit card debt, and the interest on it is not free. It comes with interest. What is the biggest expense in this Liberal budget? Is it health care? Is it seniors? No, the fastest-growing expense is interest on the debt. The average family of four will spend $6,000 on federal taxes just for the debt, not for health care and not for our military. How does the Prime Minister expect a family to spend $6,000 when they cannot afford groceries?

Mr. Speaker, this is what the Prime Minister is spending money on: 5,000 new jobs in Churchill Falls, 8,000 new jobs for Contrecoeur, 1,000 new jobs for Nouveau Monde Graphite, 18,000 new jobs at Darlington and 30,000 new jobs at Pickering. Rather than talk down the economy, why do the Conservatives not help us add new jobs to the Canadian economy?

Mr. Speaker, what do a leaky roof, a growing credit card bill and Canada have in common? The longer we ignore the problem, the more expensive it gets. Our economy is barely growing, borrowing is way up, and interest rates are on the rise. The Prime Minister promised to put the brakes on spending, but instead he is racking up crazy credit card debt. If his plan is working, why do 12.5 million Canadians, one in three people, need a grocery assistance benefit just to put food on the table?
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our colleagues here, I want to congratulate the new government of B.C., the premier-elect and his team.

Mr. Speaker, I thank outgoing Premier Eby and his team. To speak directly to the question from the member opposite, this government is focused on delivering on affordability, whether that is through tax cuts on income tax, the groceries and essentials benefit or the fuel excise tax. We have brought down the costs. We have seen rents come down for 24 months in a row. We are delivering on affordability. There is a lot more work to do. We could use some support from the Conservatives rather than them ranting and raving about it.

Mr. Speaker, this is heartbreaking. Right now, in Bradford and in towns and cities across Canada, every shelf in the food bank is bare. Despite the continued generosity of the community, food banks cannot keep up with demand. This is the consequence of Liberal failures that have seen food prices keep soaring, far outpacing what everyday Canadians can afford. People should not have to rely on government or charity just to put a meal on the table. When will the Prime Minister reverse his inflationary policies so that Canadians can afford to eat again?

Mr. Speaker, those same Canadians are asking when the Conservatives are going to change their approach. When are they going to start standing up and supporting the government when we put forward initiatives like the groceries and essentials benefit and the Canada child benefit? We stand up and support a national school food program that serves food in the member's communities, but he still stands up and votes against it time and time again, against the very Canadians who benefit from the support the government is working to deliver.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals can pretend that their expensive programs are working, but the record numbers of Canadians lined up at food banks can tell us that they are not. Food bank usage in Canada has a record 2.35 million visits in a month, and nearly one in five clients is employed. These are working Canadians who used to make ends meet and now cannot because of the government's failed policy. If the Prime Minister thinks life is so affordable, why is a full-time job not enough to feed a family?

Mr. Speaker, we know that Canadians are facing challenges right now. Food is the beginning, but this also extends to the work we are doing to bring down the cost of renting or buying a home, one of the highest expenses that we know Canadians face. We have renewed our child care deals to keep building a program that is saving families thousands of dollars a year. We are making massive investments in students, in training and in the skilled trades. We are investing in the things that are going to build prosperity and build a bright future for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government is costing Canadians more. In 2026, food banks in Alberta have seen more than 230,000 visits. This represents a staggering 9% increase from last year alone. These numbers should alarm every Canadian. Will the Liberals acknowledge that relying on food banks is now the new normal for Canadians, or are they totally out of touch?

Mr. Speaker, when times are uncertain, our government shows up. It is why residents in the member's riding and those across Canada are receiving the groceries and essentials benefit, receiving close to $1,890 this year. That is not all. We are leaning in. We are supporting them with child care and supporting them with dental care. We are investing in Canadians, and that is how we build Canada strong.

title: Statements by Members: Tragedy at CFB Wainwright
turns: Mr. Speaker, the tragedy at CFB Wainwright has shaken Albertans and Canadians. Sergeant Morgan Wong and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark lost their lives in service to Canada, and 39 Canadian Armed Forces members were injured. My deepest condolences go to their loved ones and their fellow soldiers. Military and civilian first responders, paramedics, nurses and medical teams across our region answered the call without hesitation. For military families and frontline workers, all whose lives changed forever, the impact will be felt for years to come. In the face of such loss, Canadians are asking how they can help. One real way is to donate blood, so if able, please give now and in the weeks ahead. For the families who lost, the injured who face a long road to recovery and the first responders who came to help, this tragedy does not end when the headlines fade and the politicians move on. Our gratitude must extend beyond words, and our real support must endure long after today.

Mr. Speaker, our Canadian Armed Forces members know when they enrol that they may be required to make the supreme sacrifice. Private Aidan Goulding, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Hayden Lykkemark and Sergeant Morgan Wong have made that sacrifice. The army trains as it fights. It does this to make sure it is as prepared as possible to face the challenges of conflict. This is inherently dangerous. As we remember these four fallen heroes and the 39 injured in this tragedy at CFB Wainwright, let us please remember that our military personnel do not stop. They are still training and they are still deploying in the service of Canada. It is what they do. The impact this has on the military leadership is often forgotten. They are the ones who need to inform the families and still lead the rest of the team to get back into the fight. We cannot forget the families. Trust me, there is nothing we can tell a family member, a spouse, a parent, a sibling, a child or a friend that removes the pain. The only thing we can do is never forget. Aidan, Shaun, Hayden and Morgan, I will not forget. Canada will not forget. Lest we forget.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today with a heavy heart. On Saturday, a fire at CFB Wainwright took four of our soldiers from us: Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark. Each one was loved, and each one chose to serve. Canada grieves with their families and all who loved them, and we will never forget them. Their comrades in Patricia's infantry, including the 39 injured, are not alone. I thank the Leader of the Opposition, whose riding is home to Wainwright, for going and standing with those families. As a veteran, I feel this loss deeply. May they rest in peace.

Mr. Speaker, on Saturday, four Canadian soldiers tragically lost their lives at CFB Wainwright: Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark. Four lives and four families are forever changed. Across Canada, military families watched the news, desperately waiting for a call or a message of just four words: “I am okay, mom.” For some, that message never came. For those whose loved ones are safe, relief is accompanied by heartbreak for the families who were not so fortunate. Across our country, Canadians are praying for the recovery of those injured and for the families keeping vigil at their hospital bedside. I stand with them in their grief in the difficult days ahead and always. Lest we forget.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Budget Officer, an expert in economics and finance, just issued a scathing report card on the Liberals' fiscal management. She said that the debt-to-GDP ratio will get worse every year until 2031. She said that the Prime Minister will blow past his own benchmark of a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio, and she found that interest on the debt will be the fastest-growing expense in the entire federal budget. With such stark warnings from an expert the government itself hired, will the Liberals finally admit that it is time to reverse course and rein in spending?

Mr. Speaker, I have good news for the House. It is Tuesday. Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have the lowest net debt to GDP in the G7. We have one of the lowest deficits to GDP in the G7. We are the only country, with Germany, in the G7 to have a AAA credit rating. Not only do we have fiscal discipline, but trade is up, employment is up and we are going to build Canada strong. I hope they will get on board.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised the fastest-growing economy in the G7, and it is actually shrinking. He should read his briefing notes. In 2021, the interest on the debt cost $25 billion. This year, it is nearly $60 billion. That will be $83 billion by 2030. That is not money for nurses. It is not money for housing or groceries. It is interest. The minister knows that Canadians cannot even pay their rent, so will he at least get up and acknowledge that Canada is in an affordability crisis that he has created over the last 11 years in that chair?

Mr. Speaker, one thing I will always do is stand up for Canadians and celebrate the workers of this great country. Every day, we are going to fight for Canadians, as we have done. Let us celebrate as well the fact that the IMF projected that Canada would have the second-fastest growth in the G7 in 2027. We are building Canada strong. We are investing in our workers. We are investing in our industries. I just wish the Conservatives would stop talking down the Canadian economy and work with us to build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has a unique opportunity to build a stronger, more independent and resilient country. In a rapidly changing world, that means new jobs, new investments and new opportunities for all Canadians. Can the Minister of Finance and National Revenue please update the House on the next steps in our plan to help Canadians seize these new opportunities?

On November 5, I will be tabling this year's budget, which will outline the next steps in our plan to build a stronger, more resilient and more affordable Canada. This plan will unlock investments, create high-paying jobs across our nation and strengthen our economy and our country for generations to come. On November 5, I will present a plan to build Canada strong and continue to build maîtres chez nous.

Mr. Speaker, last year, the Prime Minister campaigned on a promise to lower the federal debt relative to Canada's GDP. Today, the Parliamentary Budget Officer revealed that was just another broken promise. According to the PBO, debt to GDP will increase under the Liberals for years. Meanwhile, the Liberals are hiding behind creative accounting to fool Canadians. Will the Liberals admit that Canada is facing an affordability crisis after 11 years of their government, or are they totally out of touch?

Mr. Speaker, what I have been hearing from Manitobans is that we are building Canada's future, but the opposition keeps voting against Manitobans. Conservatives voted against $19 million for aerospace jobs in Winnipeg. They voted against supports to help farmers get products to market. They voted against broadband for 10,000 residents in northern Manitoba. Manitobans deserve leaders who vote for them. The opposition needs to get on board.

Mr. Speaker, today's PBO report reveals that the Liberals will blow through a key fiscal anchor that they promised only months ago. The Liberals promised declining deficits to GDP. The PBO confirms the opposite: rising deficits to GDP. This is a complete indictment. The Liberals are failing to follow through on a central pillar of their budgetary policy. In the face of that, how can Canadians have any confidence in their so-called fiscal plan?

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the member will have to change his QP card. In fact, Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. That is the reality. These are the facts. We have the lowest net debt to GDP. We have one of the lowest deficits to GDP. We have a AAA credit rating. Investment is up, trade is up, and employment is up. On this side of the House, we are going to continue to build Canada strong with Canadians across the nation.

Mr. Speaker, today's PBO numbers confirm what Canadians know and feel. Food bank usage is at a record high, and groceries and rent are unaffordable. Canadians are literally paying the price for the Liberal government's fiscal mismanagement. After 11 years, will the Liberals finally acknowledge that Canada is in an affordability crisis courtesy of their policies, or are they totally out of touch?

Mr. Speaker, because today is October 20, I want to make sure that my colleague across the way knows that 3.5 million families in this country are receiving the Canada child benefit today. That is six million children who are benefiting with up to $8,100 this year as a result of a policy that our government put in place, that our government is delivering and that the opposition continues to vote against.

title: Oral Questions: Democratic Institutions
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government's foreign influence registry is in shambles. The deadline to register has passed. This week, the commissioner revealed that only 30 persons or entities have registered, despite an estimated 2,400 that are required to do so, according to Public Safety Canada. That is a pathetic 1% compliance rate. How does the minister explain that?

Mr. Speaker, Canada now has an office dedicated to increasing transparency around foreign influence activities. The office is now fully operational, with Mr. Boegman being at the helm. This is a major step for Canada. The registry will be a tool to hold individuals and entities accountable for conduct of influence on behalf of foreign entities. It will provide more transparency for Canadians, and it is a testament to the principles of protecting Canadians, defending our democracy and upholding the rule of law.

Mr. Speaker, again, the Liberals are all talk and no results. They have had two and a half years to get the registry up and running, and there is a pathetic 1% compliance rate. Canadians deserve to know who is influencing elected officials and other public office-holders on behalf of foreign governments. Compliance is not optional. It is the law. What exactly is the minister doing to enforce the law?

Mr. Speaker, I share the member opposite's assertion that compliance is not optional. It is the law. That is exactly what we have set up. Mr. Boegman is seized with establishing the registry, which is already done. He is in the process of registering and onboarding those who are required to register, and those who do not comply will face the full consequences of the law.

Mr. Speaker, our Prime Minister has been engaging many world leaders and has been ensuring that business investments come into Canada, investments that this country critically needs. It is a testament to his leadership that we have been able to expand them and have a level of investments that we have never seen in Canada before. With respect to the integrity of our electoral system and the protection of Canadians, the transparency registry is on target. It will continue to register and onboard those who are required to register.

Mr. Speaker, protecting Canada's democracy is our collective responsibility in this House. I can assure the member opposite that we have a system that is working. We have a commissioner who is engaged and who is working to ensure that those who are required to register will register. If people do not comply, we have laws in place to hold them accountable.

title: Oral Questions: Artificial Intelligence
turns: Mr. Speaker, at a time when many Canadian families are feeling the pinch of the cost of living crisis, how can the Liberal government justify taking $1.6 billion out of the pockets of Canadians and giving it to Cohere, an AI company valued at more than $36 billion? Is this AI company so strapped for cash that it has to take it from taxpayers who are struggling to put food on their tables and gas in their tanks, or is this just another example of the Liberals giving taxpayer-funded handouts to big corporations and their Liberal friends?

Mr. Speaker, we have a choice. We can either build this strategically important technology here in Canada, or we can buy it from someone else. We choose to build in Canada, support Canadian champions and build safe, sovereign AI. With this company, we are taking an equity position so all Canadians can benefit. This company will create 1,000 jobs and invest $1.7 billion in computing here. This is what it means to build Canada strong and build sovereign, safe Canadian AI.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government recently announced that it purchased a $1.6-billion stake in the artificial intelligence firm Cohere. We soon found out this money was being funnelled to well-connected Liberal insiders. Dominic Barton, the chair of Invest in Canada, and Patrick Pichette, the head of digital transformation Canada, were early investors in Cohere. They also have long-standing ties to the Prime Minister. Having been promoted to these high-profile government roles, they now stand to gain from the Liberal government's so-called investment in Cohere. Why is it that every time the Prime Minister spends millions or billions, a Liberal insider is so easy to find?

Mr. Speaker, we are not going to wait for others to build AI. We are going to build safe Canadian AI. We are going to invest in Canadian companies. We are going to keep the jobs here in Canada. We are going to keep the intellectual property here in Canada. We are going to make sure that Canada has a seat at the table with this safe, sovereign technology. We will not do what the Conservatives would like us to do, which is nothing. We are building in Canada, because that is how we have control over the future.

Mr. Speaker, this AI scandal perfectly illustrates why the government should not be in the business of picking winners and losers. It is a masquerade that is simply about using taxpayer dollars to reward their friends in the Liberal club. It is a hallmark of virtually every Liberal government. Let us take Dominic Barton, for example. As a former global managing director at McKinsey, he benefited from hundreds of millions of dollars in Liberal government contracts. Now, as an early investor in Cohere, he stands to gain once again. Can the Prime Minister please explain why his Liberal friends are doing so well, while so many other Canadians are just barely hanging on?

Mr. Speaker, this is not about what the Conservatives say, picking winners or losers. This is about investing in Canadians. They should try it for a while. Canadians are winners because they build here in Canada. We are one of the few middle powers. There are only four countries that have the capacity to build safe, sovereign companies. Cohere is a Canadian champion. It will put 1,000 jobs here in the next three years. It will invest $1.7 billion, and Canadians now can benefit from this company staying Canadian. The Conservatives should try to build Canada strong for a change.

title: Oral Questions: Automotive Industry
turns: Mr. Speaker, I am not sure I heard when that order would be made, but let us move on. In the deal that we now know between Stellantis and Roshel, it has been reported that it was supposed to be a Chinese electric vehicle maker sharing space with the Canadian defence contractor. This is the deal that the government has known about for some time, including the Prime Minister's Office, the Minister of Defence and four Liberal MPs. Have they forgotten about the espionage that brought down Nortel, or does the minister really want a Canadian defence manufacturer to share space with a Chinese company that answers to Beijing?

Mr. Speaker, we are really into conspiracy theory reality right now. I would like to say to my colleague that, no, that was never the case. That was never on the table. There was always one company the government was negotiating with. That was Stellantis. It needs to protect the jobs. If not, we will go after the money, hundreds of millions of dollars to the government. I have already sent a letter of demand and a notice of default. It now has 25 days to come back to us.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals gave hundreds of millions of dollars to Stellantis. Ten months ago, it defaulted on the agreement. The minister said she was going to sue. She did nothing. In July, four Liberal MPs toured the plant with Roshel. It told them it was going to buy the plant from Stellantis. She did nothing. In September, Roshel announced it was going to buy the plant. She did nothing. She lost the money. She lost the jobs. Why does she still have her job?

The reality is there is a fact my colleague never alludes to, which is the American tariffs that are having an impact on American automakers working also, of course, in Canada, and all our auto workers. Meanwhile, while they are not alluding to the trade war, which is affecting Stellantis, which has affected jobs in Brampton, we will continue to help and work with the Ontario government and Unifor, of course, to make sure we can protect the jobs. We will be meeting on Friday.

Mr. Speaker, I am focused on her failure to keep her own word. She said she was going to sue. She has not sued. Guess what. Stellantis does not believe she is going to sue. The Stellantis workers do not believe she is going to sue. There is probably not a single person in this entire chamber who believes she is going to sue. In fact, if she was going to sue, she would have done it already. Why does she not just step aside? They can appoint another Trudeau-era minister who can stand in this House, pretend to be outraged that the plant is sold and pretend they are going to sue.

Mr. Speaker, I know my colleague seems to love coming back with his oldies and classics, but that is exactly what he was saying on Stelco. Do members know what is going on right now? Five hundred workers are back and will be able to have a job before Christmas. That is first. Second, when it comes to facts, my colleague also mentioned that the contracts the Government of Canada has with Stellantis have clear protections and clear job guarantees. Go back to your CTV interview. Then come back and ask me questions.

Mr. Speaker, for all the public chest-puffing, condemnation, indignation and denial of the news that Stellantis was selling its plant to Roshel, the plan to betray Stellantis workers and their families has been known for months by the Prime Minister, the industry minister and Liberal MPs. On July 14, four Liberal MPs from Brampton met with Roshel and were told of the plan to buy the plant. They knew it was happening, the Prime Minister knew, so did the industry minister, yet they still went months without blocking it. Why did they deceive the workers and families until the point they got caught?

Mr. Speaker, it is clear, as the Minister of Industry has said, that Stellantis is in default and it either hires the workers or we get our money back. Why? Because we stand by our workers. What is the proof? Whether it is federal economic development, where we have over 540 different projects, many in that member's riding, to support industries or the 500 workers at Stelco who are back at work, we stand with our workers.

Mr. Speaker, they say they stand with those workers, but those workers have not been at work since 2023. For months, the Prime Minister did nothing to stop the sale of the plant. The tough act and threats toward Stellantis only started after it became public that, behind the scenes, they were quietly endorsing a plan that would leave thousands of Brampton Stellantis workers and their families without jobs. I have two questions: How many jobs will be saved with the sale? How many billions of Canadian tax dollars does the government expect to shell out this time for what has become a pattern of failed Liberal investments?

Mr. Speaker, it would be wonderful if the opposition would just once condemn the tariffs that are hurting Canadian workers, just once speak out against the tariffs and fight for workers. Whether we are fighting for workers in the case of Stellantis is clear. We stand with the workers. Stellantis will be in default. If it does not pay back the money, Stellantis is in default. It will be sued. We are standing with workers. Whether it is the steelworkers at Stelco, the tool and die makers or the auto parts manufacturers, we will always stand with our workers. We would love the opposition to do—

title: Statements by Members: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, families and seniors across Coast of Bays—Central—Notre Dame are working hard and doing their best to live within their means, yet they are struggling to make ends meet. The Liberal Prime Minister promised Canadians affordability, but the reality is that we have higher costs and growing financial pressure on households. In Newfoundland and Labrador, food security affects more than one in four residents. Food bank usage across our province has increased by 44% since 2019. These are not just statistics. These numbers represent real people making impossible choices between groceries, heating their homes and putting fuel in their vehicles. As Liberals prepare to table their budget, Canadians deserve action, not more spending and debt. The government needs to cut waste and restore fiscal responsibility, instead of spending and making more debt. The government needs to eliminate all taxes on gas and diesel. It is high time that the Prime Minister lives up to the expectations of those who voted for him—

Mr. Speaker, lobster season opens November 10 in southwest New Brunswick. Fishing families along the Bay of Fundy are ready to work, but many are worried about making ends meet. Before setting day, diesel is already up 50% in a year. It is made worse by the Liberals' clean fuel tax that adds 19¢ a litre to diesel and 15¢ a litre to gasoline. Every boat carries hundreds of lobster traps; they have now been hit with a Canadian tariff. Our fishermen are literally paying their own government in Ottawa just to go to work. These men and women work hard, follow the rules and pay their taxes. They are the backbone of coastal communities. They work as hard as ever, pay more and fall further behind. This is a story across Canada, worsened by 11 years of massive deficit spending. It is a government that spends well beyond its means and passes the costs to Canadians. The budget must cut taxes, stop inflationary money printing and end its wasteful spending. Canadians deserve nothing less.

Mr. Speaker, after more than a decade of inflationary Liberal policies, Canadians are concerned with the direction our country is going. News of Canada's inflation rate rising is sad confirmation they have every reason to be. While the Prime Minister promised affordability, Canadians are watching the cost of housing, groceries, fuel, insurance, utilities and everyday living rise to increasingly unsustainable levels. Even though they are working full time at good-paying jobs, they are still struggling to afford necessities. Recent reports of increased food bank usage and people skipping meals because they cannot afford groceries are further confirmation of this sad reality. The Prime Minister is out of touch, his spending is out of control and Canadians are out of money. In today's budget, Conservatives are calling on the Liberals to cut wasteful inflationary spending, keep their promised debt anchors and save Canadians money by reducing the cost of gas, groceries—

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Trump administration has hurled insults at Canada's military and has made unjustified threats against our country, but we have learned this week that the Liberal government has awarded a $12-million security contract for the CRA to an American firm that does business with Donald Trump's ICE instead of to Canada's largest employer of veterans, the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires, a not-for-profit. The difference in price was less than 1%. I think we can all agree that employing Canadian veterans and hiring Canadian companies are important. The question for the Liberals is, why did they not do that in this case?
Mr. Speaker, the member knows full well that politicians are never involved in decisions like that. The CRA process was handled independently by experts. That being—

Mr. Speaker, the member knows that politicians are not involved in decisions like that. That being said, the process resulted in the selection of a qualified Canadian supplier headquartered in Mississauga that employs nearly 8,000 Canadians across the country. Building on this, the CRA has launched a policy direction on prioritizing Canadian suppliers and content in a strategic procurement. Again, the member knows that politicians are never involved in an independent decision by the CRA.

Mr. Speaker, when reached for comment, the minister said that “putting Canadian workers and industries first” was the heart of their buy Canadian policy. This does not look like either of those things. Instead, a $12-million contract went to a firm that does business with Donald Trump's ICE instead of to a not-for-profit Canadian company, the largest employer of Canadian veterans. The question for the Liberals is this. Instead of creating employment opportunities for Canadian veterans and buying Canadian, why did they choose to put an American firm that has close ties to Donald Trump ahead of Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, the member knows better than that. This is a Canadian firm. It employs 8,000 Canadians. We are always going to stand with veterans who have defended our country, including with respect to employment opportunities. The CRA process is independent and does not involve politicians. The member knows that. We are always going to do what is right. This company is Canadian. It employs 8,000 workers across this country.

Mr. Speaker, it is the height of hypocrisy that after all the buy Canadian, support Canadian and defend Canadian sovereignty lectures that have gone on with the Liberals that the Prime Minister would allow an American security company with ties to Donald Trump's ICE, the very agency that has been central to Trump's mass deportation efforts, to replace a hundred-year-old Canadian institution such as the Commissionaires for security services at the CRA over an $80,000 difference in bids. At a time when our veterans are already struggling to transition to civilian employment, why are the Liberals undermining the country's largest veterans employer instead of supporting it?
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what it was like 11 years ago, but on this side of the House, politicians are not involved in those decisions—

Mr. Speaker, they are fired up on the other side today. Let me say this: Politicians are not involved in these decisions. Imagine what it would be like if I could direct the CRA to hire a friend, or something like that. On this side of the House, the CRA had an independent decision. The decision was clear: It is a Canadian company employing 8,000 Canadians. On this side of the House, with the CRA, we are going to do it right. The opposition can continue with the misinformation.

Mr. Speaker, hiring friends is already happening. The Commissionaires is the largest employer of veterans in the country. Taking away the CRA contract and giving it to an American firm is not just a contract that was lost. It is also meaningful employment opportunities and cultural relevance for Canadian veterans to work, after their service, with their friends and their peers. Now it has been lost, and for $80,000. Here is a solution to give the contract back to the Commissionaires and secure Canadian veterans' jobs: How about the Prime Minister not spend $160,000 in catering on his next flight, and use that money to make up the difference that the contract was lost by?

Speaker, the member knows that this is a Canadian company. It employs 8,000 Canadians. The process was independent. There were criteria that were evaluated against. This was an objective, fair and transparent decision. We stand behind the decision.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister tells Canadians to buy Canadian, but his own government is happy to buy American. He fired the veterans guarding the Canada Revenue Agency. The Commissionaires, Canada's largest employer of veterans, lost the contract to Allied Universal, an American firm cashing in on the ICE contract. Allied underbid the Commissionaires by $80,000, which is less than 1%. Why is the Prime Minister choosing an American firm over veterans who served this country?

Mr. Speaker, the member also knows that the decision was objective. It was transparent. This is a Canadian supplier hiring 8,000 Canadians across the country. We stand behind the decision. The criteria were met. The company was hired.

Mr. Speaker, the CRA prioritizes hiring veterans. That is number one. Number two is that, with respect to this decision, it was an independent process. There were selection criteria that were met. This is a Canadian supplier. It hires 8,000 Canadians across this country. We stand by the decision.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires is a wonderful organization that does great work across this country, but this decision was objective. There were selection criteria it was evaluated against. It is a Canadian supplier. It hires 8,000 Canadians across this country.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Mr. Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth than what the member utters in the House. Conservatives like to try to instill doubt. There is no denying that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio and the highest second quarter growth in the G7. That is well-recognized. We are using that strength to focus on what we can control to counteract the headwinds that the country faces. We have seen record numbers in new business investment and foreign direct investment, and further domestic commitments, reaching nearly half a trillion dollars. We have seen the highest level of non-U.S. trade and much—

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada raised its interest rates for the first time since 2023. The government is claiming that inflation and interest rates are like the weather and are completely beyond its control, but we know that is not the truth. We know that sovereign debt accelerates inflation. Canada now spends more on interest than it does on health care or on the military. The interest rate hike means that millions of Canadians will be forced to the financial brink. Will the government commit to achieving its own fiscal anchor of a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio?

Mr. Speaker, Conservatives this Halloween are handing out tricks and calling them treats. Nobody is fooled by this. Let me ask the members opposite to tell us how feeding hungry kids is inflationary, tell us how investing in our defence capabilities is inflationary and tell us how cutting taxes on income, housing and fuel is inflationary. Maybe they need a basic economics tutorial over in the Conservative caucus. It is clear that their leader has no economic credentials. If they need a lesson, please let us know.

Mr. Speaker, the Governor of the Bank of Canada was quite clear: He has raised interest rates because of increasing inflationary pressure. All experts agree that expansive fiscal policy accelerates inflation. In effect, the Governor of the Bank of Canada is hitting the brakes hard while the Minister of Finance continues to accelerate faster and faster. Will the minister commit to some fiscal restraint in the upcoming budget so that Canadians are not pushed over the inflationary cliff?

Mr. Speaker, it is not news to us that the country is facing headwinds and that Canadians are being impacted. That is exactly why we stepped up with a plan to support them. We introduced the groceries and essentials benefit, and it delivered 12 million Canadians a cheque to help with the cost of living. We cut taxes on new business investment and saw an immediate spike of 8.9% in activity. We rapidly signed 20 new trade and security agreements, and we saw the highest level of non-U.S. trade this last summer. We streamlined permitting processes, and we have seen more jobs and shovels in the ground. Those are the results of this government.

Mr. Speaker, in September 2025, the Prime Minister stood in the House and stated, “We are going to have a declining level of debt”, yet the Parliamentary Budget Officer is projecting debt to climb from $1.5 trillion to $2.3 trillion over the next four years. Would the Prime Minister like to explain how debt going from $1.5 trillion to $2.3 trillion is, in his own words, a declining level of debt, or is he using the same math that he used to conclude that affordability is the best it has been in a decade?

Mr. Speaker, this Halloween, Conservatives are doing their very best to try to spook Canadians, but Canadians know that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have a stable democracy and a government that cares about them, a government that is investing in them, is supporting them through affordability challenges, is investing in a stronger economy, is diversifying trade and is laser focused on building the strongest, most resilient economy in the G7. All this member can do is cast doubt on that plan. Every moment of every day in the House, that is all we hear from the Conservatives. When will they start celebrating all that Canada has to offer?

Mr. Speaker, also casting doubt on their plan is the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada's monetary policy report states that there is slack in the labour market. It states that businesses have excess capacity. Normally, this would lead to lower interest rates, yet the Bank of Canada increased interest rates due to persistent inflation. The Prime Minister says the Liberals will focus on what they can control. Will the Prime Minister focus on what he can control, his inflationary spending binge, and do what he promised and deliver a declining level of debt?

Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are always short on details. They keep saying that somehow government spending and investments in the Canadian economy are inflationary, but they never indicate what specifically is inflationary about that spending. Is it inflationary to feed hungry children? Is it inflationary to cut taxes for 22 million Canadians on their income? Is it inflationary to help with the cost of fuel? Is it inflationary to invest in our defence or get major projects built in this country? What is inflationary about those investments in a growing, prosperous Canadian economy?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are paying more at the grocery store and more to keep a roof over their heads. This week the Bank of Canada raised interest rates, meaning higher mortgage payments for families. Meanwhile, the Parliamentary Budget Officer projects annual interest on the federal debt will reach $83 billion by 2031, more than health transfers and more than defence. Debt is rising, interest rates are rising, and Canadians are out of money. With Halloween tomorrow, will the Liberals admit that their costly spending plan is all trick and no treat?

Mr. Speaker, we finally got a Halloween reference in there out of the Conservatives, but they are truly trying to spook Canadians every single day. They simply cannot back up their claims, though, and they do not seem to understand economics. It is not the case that inflation is being driven by the federal government. Everybody out there in the real world knows that inflation is being driven by a U.S. trade war that was not started by the Government of Canada and conflicts in the Middle East, which were not started by Canada. Those are the true causes, and the Conservatives cannot fool anybody.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised to spend less. Instead, the PBO projects another $730 billion in borrowing over five years. By 2031, the federal debt will approach $40,000 per Canadian, with annual interest equivalent to $8,000 per family. Canadians are paying more, getting less and falling further behind. Will the Liberal government finally cut deficit spending and adopt our Conservative plan to lower costs for all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, every single day, this government works our hardest to leverage the fiscal strength that Canada has to invest in the things that Canadians need: jobs for the future, wages that outpace inflation, and higher productivity and growth in the economy. While doing that, we have also enhanced our social safety net with things like the groceries and essentials benefit, tax cuts and the national school food program. We continue to do that work every day because we know that is what builds a stronger Canada. Canadians need a government that supports them.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada just raised its interest rate for the first time in three years, hitting Canadians with higher mortgage and borrowing costs at a time when families are already struggling to make ends meet.
