The cost of fuel, food and homes keeps rising. Families are already going further into debt each month just to make ends meet, and now they have to pay higher interest. We know that inflation and interest are rising due to the Liberal government's massive deficit spending. Why will the Prime Minister not stop his inflationary spending and his taxes that are driving up the cost for struggling Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, we care deeply about housing affordability, and that is why we are working with the provinces to build infrastructure that allows them to build new homes. That drives down the cost to purchase for new homeowners. However, we are not stopping there. We are working with Build Canada Homes. We have 19,000 units under way across the country, and this is ensuring that whether people rent or buy, there is a home for them.

Mr. Speaker, the gap in this country between the haves and the have-nots is growing wider and wider. Liberal inflationary spending and taxes are driving up the cost of living for those who are struggling and padding the pockets of the wealthiest. Canadian families are already the most indebted in the G7. With rising inflation and interest rates, they will now have to pay more for their mortgage, car payments and line of credit. Every single dollar that the Liberal government borrows makes every dollar that Canadians have to borrow more expensive. When will the Prime Minister finally get his spending under control so that Canadians can afford to pay their bills?

Mr. Speaker, of course, that is not how any of that works. If we look at the Bank of Canada's report, it says the inflation is driven by global energy prices. It is undeniable. However, there is good news in my home province of Alberta. There are 67,000 new jobs since the start of the year. We are seeing record production of oil and gas. We are seeing record diesel production up 16%. That is how we tackle affordability. We are making Alberta strong. We are making Canada strong.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, while families across Canada are struggling to put food on their table, the Prime Minister has no problem putting food on his table, most of which we cannot pronounce: truffle risotto, veal blanquette, entrecôte beef with demi-glace sauce, sea bass fillet and desserts like crème brûlée to top of it all off. This adds up to the low price of $175,000. How does the Prime Minister have the nerve to stick this bill to hard-working Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, we see the silliness coming from the Conservative Party. Let me give the member a tangible example. Let us think of my home province of Manitoba: Under the national school program, 29,000 children are being fed in schools. Across Canada, it is 400,000. This Prime Minister is the one who made it a permanent program. On the other hand, the member who just posed the question voted against that. Shame on the Conservative Party of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard this all before. This is not the first time that the Liberals wasted over $175,000 and gave the same shameful excuse for inflight catering. The reality is this trip cost hard-working taxpayers $300 for each meal for each person. Does the silver spoon, Bay Street banker Prime Minister really think that Canadians have the luxury of spending $300 on a meal? Quite frankly, I have had no one in my family ever be able to dream of paying $300 for a meal.

Mr. Speaker, what is quite extraordinary is that it probably took the member a week to come up with that question. The reality is he should be talking about Churchill Falls and Bay du Nord. He should be talking about investments in the Atlantic fisheries fund, things that impact Atlantic Canadians in terms of job and affordability. We are building Canada up in Atlantic Canada, taking the lead. It is time that he and other folks on that side, especially in their Atlantic caucus, join us.

Mr. Speaker, in March, 2.4 million Canadians had to rely on the food bank. The Bank of Canada expects prices to rise through next year. This is an out-of-touch government. Excessive taxation and rising energy costs are making it worse for Canadians. Conservatives would lower costs at the grocery store by scrapping all federal taxes on diesel sales until at least next Canada Day. Why would the government not adopt our plan?

Mr. Speaker, it always shocks me in the House when Conservatives pretend to care about people at food banks, when they vote against every single measure that would take people out of those food banks. When we wanted to feed hungry kids in school, which was the top ask of Food Banks Canada for many years, we implemented a national school food program, which feeds 400,000 kids at school. That literally takes kids out of food bank lineups. What did the Conservatives do? They said no, then they called the program garbage in the House. They should be ashamed of themselves for mentioning—

Mr. Speaker, the Governor of the Bank of Canada projects that rising energy and shipping costs will drive up grocery prices this coming year. With food bank usage at record levels and household budgets already stretched, families cannot afford another increase at the checkout line. Will the Liberal government reverse its course and adopt our Conservative plan to scrap the federal taxes on diesel, which would help bring down the cost of food?

Mr. Speaker, we cut taxes on gas and diesel, and the Conservatives voted against it. This week, the Conservatives have been talking about food banks. They come in the House of Commons and talk about food banks, yet they actually do not listen to Food Banks Canada, the organization responsible for food banks. Here is what it said: “For people relying on food banks, this program [the groceries and essentials benefit, which the Conservatives voted against] will provide direct assistance to low-income households to help cover...costs such as food, rent, or childcare, as we have called for.”

Mr. Speaker, months ago, Food Banks Canada reported that food bank demand reached 2.3 million visits in March. Liberal inflation has only made things worse. In Salmon Arm, my hometown, the food bank now serves 500 clients per month. Many are families, meaning the number could be 7% to 10% of a small city relying on the food bank. Will the government adopt our Conservative plan to lower the cost in grocery stores by scrapping all federal taxes on diesel sales until at least Canada Day 2027?

Mr. Speaker, I sincerely appreciate the hon. member's concern for the ability of families to put food on the table, but it betrays the perspective that the Conservative Party has demonstrated in this House with its voting record over the last number of years. Let us think about the groceries and essentials benefit that we put forward that is going to put almost $1,900 on the table for a family of four, which the Conservatives voted against. Let us think about the middle-class tax cut that we put forward to save money for 22 million Canadians, which they voted against. Let us think about the national school food program, which is actually feeding hungry children in our communities today, which they did not just vote against but called garbage on the floor of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, in British Columbia alone, food banks recorded more than 250,000 visits in March, up 14% in one year. The hon. member across the aisle mentioned children. Over 75,000 of those were children. Diesel drives up the cost of growing, transporting and delivering food, putting even more pressure on grocery bills across Canada. Why will the Liberal government not adopt our Conservative plan to scrap all federal taxes on diesel until at least Canada Day 2027 and give Canadians some relief?

Mr. Speaker, we have been working hard on housing affordability to bring down rents and the cost to buy a home. I would like to point out that in British Columbia, we have made meaningful progress. We have committed 1,100 homes in B.C. through Build Canada Homes. We are investing more than $5 billion in housing-enabling infrastructure. We are working with the province to bring down development charges. In addition, I would like to point out that we have 116 purpose-built rental homes under way in Burnaby, 349 at UBC and the Burke Mountain Community Centre in Coquitlam is under construction. There is lots under way. We care about affordability.

title: Oral Questions: Automotive Industry
turns: Mr. Speaker, last week I was also speaking to auto workers at Stellantis who were out in the cold. The Prime Minister claimed he felt betrayed by the sale of its plant to Roshel. We now find out that the government was intimately involved in brokering the sale, and now the Prime Minister is saying he wants to pivot to Chinese automakers. According to Brian Kingston of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers' Association, “Ask the Europeans how their China auto strategy is working out...104,000 auto jobs lost [since they started it].” Why is the Prime Minister selling out our auto workers to Beijing?

Mr. Speaker, let me set the record straight. Our priority number one has always been to restore operations at the Stellantis plant. It has always been to make sure that the company would respect the undertaking and its obligations to the workers, to the industry and to Canadians. Instead of complaining, the Conservatives should join in and fight for Canadians. At a time like this, workers at Stellantis are expecting every member of this House to fight for them. On this side of the House, we know that every day is a good day to fight for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister called the sale of Stellantis a betrayal of Canadian workers, but records show both the Prime Minister's Office and the labour minister's office were meeting with Roshel in August, September and October. The Liberals' new sales talks were happening, yet thousands of Canadian workers were left in the dark about their future. My question is very simple. When exactly did the minister learn about the proposed sale?

Mr. Speaker, we always welcome investment. We also always make sure we fight for the workers. We have been in discussions with Stellantis for over a year. They have made commitments. Yes, they have made proposals to us. None of those proposals met their commitments. We are making sure they honour their commitments. We have a good record of late of making sure that companies honour their commitments, such as in Hamilton, with Stelco, thanks to the hard work of the Hamilton members on this side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, Roshel is a mid-sized defence manufacturer, yet it is now positioned to purchase a massive Stellantis plant that once employed thousands of Canadian workers. That is an ambitious purchase for a company of its size—

Mr. Speaker, Roshel is a mid-sized defence manufacturer, yet it is now positioned to purchase a massive Stellantis plant that once employed thousands of Canadian workers. It is an ambitious purchase for a company of its size. The Liberals claim they oppose this sale but government officials were meeting with Roshel for months before it was announced. Canadians deserve to know this. Did the Liberal government promise Roshel any future defence contracts or subsidies connected to the purchase of the Stellantis plant?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians want to know where that party was when these tariffs were hitting us. Were they standing up for workers in Brampton, in Hamilton and elsewhere? Canadians know we are standing up for them, and that is why we have been working very hard to make sure that the workers in that plant have a mandate to get those jobs back. We are working very hard. In our view, Stellantis is in breach of its commitments. We will get our money back or there will be jobs back in that plant.

Mr. Speaker, I have now been advised that the Liberal government was actually involved in drafting the press release that Roshel sent out when they said they were purchasing the Stellantis plant. Think about what that means for a minute. On the one hand, they are saying they are outraged and that they are going to do everything they can to prevent the sale, but behind the scenes, they are actually helping to draft the press release that Roshel sent out. This is a master class in deceit and a master class in gaslighting. Either the minister knew the plant was going to be sold and then gaslit Canadians by saying she was outraged and that it should stop and therefore she should resign—

Mr. Speaker, that is an absurd allegation. I will tell members about a press release that we were involved in drafting, which is the press release welcoming $867 million of new investment in Honda, in Alliston, retaining 4,000 workers, 400,000 vehicles a year in that plant, which is one of the best plants in the world. I would hope the member opposite would stand and cheer for that.

Mr. Speaker, if they sought it, I think that the Speaker would find unanimous consent for a 15-minute break so they can to try and get their story straight on this. One cannot actually say, on the one hand, that one is outraged that the plant is going to be sold while, at the same time, department officials are in the background actually helping to draft the press release saying that the plant has been sold. We cannot have our cake and eat it too. Are they opposed to the sale of the Stellantis plant or were they in the background drafting a press release to try and make it look like it was great news for Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, we are on the side of the workers of Brampton. We are on the side of the people who want that plant to have an auto mandate. We are on the side of the workers who have had commitments made to them. We are going to defend the commitments that were made to them. In our view, Stellantis is in breach of its obligations. We are going to make sure that there is an auto mandate or they are going to return the money.

Mr. Speaker, as the government attempts to deflect and obscure, Canadians deserve to know the facts. Will the minister confirm that, in fact, her staff and her officials in her department, along with officials in the Prime Minister's Office, were aware of the proposed sale well before it was announced? Will the minister finally come clean with the House about when she first learned of the proposed sale to Roshel?

Mr. Speaker, this government has sided with auto workers from the beginning, and the minister has said this repeatedly. We know Stellantis is in breach, and we will make sure that those workers have their jobs back, or they will return the money. It is a simple thing. We are on the side of the auto workers.

Mr. Speaker, they are on the side of the Canadian auto workers while they welcome thousands and thousands of Chinese EVs that will hollow out the Canadian automobile industry. This government is turning out to be just like the last. Their favourite game to play is, “Who knew what, when?” When will the minister finally stand up in this House and admit when she learned of the sale of the Brampton plant to Roshel?

Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House, we believe that Canada has the best auto workers in North America. We will do everything in our capacity to make sure that we maintain the integrity of our auto workers, their jobs and an integrated North American auto industry. We will continue to make sure that Stellantis pursues its obligations to keep those auto jobs here in Ontario at that Brampton plant. We will make sure that we create good jobs for auto workers here in Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, it is a fiasco and there is no other way to describe the Stellantis affair. Thousands of Stellantis workers and their families now know that while the Liberals were playing the tough guy with Stellantis, they were betraying the workers and their families by secretly negotiating the sale of the plant to another company. The public chest puffing, the deception and betrayal by the Prime Minister and the industry minister are worthy of an Academy Award. Behind all the smoke and mirrors, one thing is true, Stellantis workers deserve to know the truth. Will the Prime Minister come clean and, for once, tell the truth about what happened in this fiasco?

Mr. Speaker, let me reiterate, we will always stand with our auto workers, whether it is protecting them and fighting for their jobs, knowing that Stellantis is in breach, whether it is making sure that we get great investments like we just got in the Honda plant, or whether it is through federal economic development where we are investing in the parts manufacturers. We will always stand with the workers, not just the auto workers, the steel workers. We are very proud, by the way, to see the Stelco workers in Hamilton back at work. Why? Because we stand with workers.

Mr. Speaker, they are systematically dismantling the auto industry in this country. There are reports of more than a dozen meetings between the company and the Liberals, on selling the plant to Roshel. There are also reports that four Liberal MPs toured the plant with Roshel, discussing the sale. The bottom line is that, privately, the Prime Minister knew the sale was happening and the minister also knew, but in public, they acted shocked, indignant and outraged. Turns out, it was all an act of deceit, because the sale was in the works months ago and the Liberals knew it all along. After this massive betrayal of these workers, will the minister resign?

Mr. Speaker, where was that member and where was that leader when illegal and unjustified tariffs specifically targeted our steel, our forest, our automobile and our aluminum industries? Where was that member? Where was that party? Where was that leader? How dare they ask my colleague to resign? They should all resign.

Mr. Speaker, just because they say the same answer over and over again, it does not make it true. It neither makes it true when they scream that answer, but there is not a single answer for the thousands of Stellantis workers who lost their jobs. Here is another question. The Prime Minister goes to China and floats letting in even more EVs. That means more Chinese electric cars flooding our market and more layoffs, like Stellantis. Europe proves it. Chinese imports cost them 104,000 auto jobs in 2024 and 2025 alone. That is 142 jobs lost a day. Before he signs on the dotted line, will the Prime Minister think of the Canadian auto workers that he is selling out?

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and this government are absolutely clear that our auto workers are some of the best in the world, and our number one job is to make sure that they are fully deployed and that they remain very much a part of a North American integrated market. That is why we are really focused on making sure that we end up with an arrangement with the United States, so that we can continue with those important jobs. We will also ensure that we continue to diversify our economy to ensure that we are opening new opportunities for our workers as well. We will stand by our auto workers every single day.

title: Oral Questions: National Defence
turns: Mr. Speaker, here are the facts. Every prime minister before this one got a deal done with America. Even Justin Trudeau signed a trade deal with Trump. Trudeau also finally ordered the F-35s. Let us be clear. The Royal Canadian Air Force wants the F-35s. The Canadian Armed Forces wants the F-35s. Over 1,000 Canadians who are already working on them want Canada to buy the F-35s, but the Prime Minister would rather play political theatre. Canadians did not elect a performer this time. They were promised a negotiator. Will the Prime Minister quit acting and finally get what our military needs?

Mr. Speaker, we are procuring right across the Canadian Armed Forces family. The member is aware of this. We are rebuilding our bases. We are buying hardware, we are buying materiel, we are supplying kit, and yes, we are looking at a fighter fleet for the Royal Canadian Air Force. We are going to review this procurement approach, as we have, with discipline. We are going to take the time we need to get it right.

Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General confirmed critical ammunition shortages and NATO ammunition requirements not met. The Minister of National Defence told Canadians, “we have progress to make, and we're making it.” Well, I have heard of our soldiers on the front lines in Latvia going on patrol with no ammunition in their rifles, backed by only a few days of artillery shells should tensions erupt. The minister has failed to properly arm our forces and failed to meet our NATO commitments and, most importantly, failed to defend Canada's sovereignty. Will the minister immediately table the required ammunition levels, Canada's NATO requirements and a timeline to meet them, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, some 10 months ago, we stood up Canada's first defence industrial strategy. One of the 10 priorities for the country was to move forward in ammunition production. The member is aware of this. By the way, where was the former Conservative government on ammunition production? There was not a single deal, not a single site, not a single manufacturing installation, no joint ventures, absolutely nothing. We are moving forward. We are making progress. We are looking after our forces.

Mr. Speaker, the government announced $9.2 billion over 13 years for ammunition. That only buys about 7,800 artillery shells a month, if nothing else is purchased. In Ukraine, they are firing about 180,000 a month. At this rate, it will take years to meet our NATO stockpile requirements. My question was about the requirement, not history. The minister failed to answer my question, so I will ask it again. Will he immediately table the required ammunition levels, Canada's NATO requirements and the timeline to meet that plan, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, there is a very good reason why that member does not want to talk about history, and I think we all know what that reason is. We have never moved faster on the procurement for our military of aircraft, subs, radar and ammo. This is the most we have spent, and the fastest we have moved, literally in generations. We could use the Conservatives' support. What would be beneficial is if at committee they would support the supplementary estimates by voting for spending money on our military, something that member refuses to do.

Mr. Speaker, for more than a decade, the Liberal government has been questioning and erasing the very values that define this nation, but in New Brunswick, at CFB Gagetown, it reached a new low. This summer, the Liberal government actually stole Jesus off the cross and came back for the nails. Using building improvements as a cover, it stripped St. Luke's Chapel of its crosses, its altar and its stained glass after nearly 70 years and is refusing to put them back. The congregation was never consulted, and multi-faith spaces already exist on base. We are not making room for others by erasing the faith of those who already serve. Will the minister order that St. Luke's Chapel be fully restored at CFB Gagetown?

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Armed Forces is strengthened by the diversity of traditions, backgrounds and beliefs of all its members. The policies to support diversity are a moral and ethical responsibility of the Royal Canadian Chaplain Service, the chief of the defence staff and CAF leadership, and their commitment to care for all. The spiritual health and well-being of Canadian Armed Forces members are vital to our operational effectiveness. These guidelines do not ban private or personal faith and are meant to be more inclusive for a wide range of spiritual and faith traditions. The member knows this.

title: Routine Proceedings: Petitions
turns: Madam Speaker, I am presenting a petition today on behalf of my constituents who have pointed out that Canada Post and the governing Liberals are taking an axe to long-treasured postal services, eliminating good jobs, eliminating door-to-door delivery and lowering mail delivery standards. As well, they are pointing out that these cuts have not been released publicly and that these cuts are disproportionately going to impact seniors, disabled Canadians, in particular rural Canadians, and remote and indigenous populations. They are calling upon the Government of Canada to stop these postal service cuts and to immediately launch a full, transparent, mandated review of Canada Post that allows all stakeholders to provide meaningful input.

Madam Speaker, if I may, permit me to wish everyone a very happy Thanksgiving as we are about to leave Ottawa for the moment. These petitioners within my riding and across Canada are extremely concerned, and I am very honoured to get this petition in before we have our Thanksgiving constituency week. This is the issue that really troubles so many Canadians, and I give thanks to Jann Arden for making sure people do not forget. We ship live horses out of this country to other countries for slaughter, often for consumption as sushi. It just makes Canadians so desperately upset about the idea of the inhumane treatment of these horses, shipping them on airplanes. The petitioners ask that the Government of Canada please ban the export of horses for slaughter by amending the Health of Animals Regulations to prohibit this practice.

Madam Speaker, I rise to present a petition that was signed by over 3,000 petitioners. The petitioners are concerned with the historically long time that security screening is taking for immigration files. They point out the harms to families, to their careers and to finances that extensively long security screening times are creating. They are calling on CSIS to publish measurable service standards, establish a documented escalation and review process, publish aggregate data and develop an immigration screening backlog reduction plan.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition from Vancouver Islanders. They highlight that indigenous and affordable housing providers, including M’akola Housing Society in British Columbia, are facing the expiration of long-standing federal operating agreements. The expiration of these agreements threatens the affordability of 528 indigenous homes across British Columbia, affecting approximately 1,775 people, including families, elders and persons with disabilities, including 42 homes in Port Alberni. Without continued federal support, these households could face rents that double or triple, putting residents at risk of housing insecurity and displacement. Provinces and territories have been calling on the federal government to renew bilateral agreements under the national housing strategy, provide long-term funding certainty and preserve existing indigenous social and affordable housing, as it is essential to addressing Canada's housing crisis and advancing reconciliation. Petitioners are calling on the government to commit to renewing and adequately funding national housing strategy bilateral agreements before existing agreements expire to ensure that indigenous housing providers and their tenants are protected from unaffordable rent increases resulting from the expiration of federal operating agreements. Lastly, they call on the government to work with indigenous housing providers, provinces and territories to establish a long-term funding framework that preserves existing affordable indigenous housing and provides housing security for current and future tenants.

Madam Speaker, I rise today on a petition like I have not seen before, petition e-7372. This is a petition put forward by a woman whose husband, unfortunately, has succumbed to Alzheimer's. Despite his desire to receive medical assistance in dying in those kinds of cases, the current laws do not accommodate him. His family and friends have seen his situation deteriorate and have thus decided to petition their government to seek changes to the law. The family would like to see clear safeguards and advanced MAID requests that offer people dignity, compassion and choice. I know there are people on both sides of the coin on this who struggle with these issues, but I think here in our Parliament of Canada, we can always discuss what matters most: our family and their future.

Madam Speaker, I am tabling a petition today from Canadians deeply concerned about unemployment in this country. In particular, the petitioners highlight the issue of high youth unemployment. New numbers out today show youth unemployment jumping up to 13% in a context where we have the lowest labour force participation in almost 30 years. The petitioners highlight how alarmingly high youth unemployment is and how training and skills development programs have not kept up with the realities of the labour market. The petitioners highlight concerns about immigration policy and the rising cost of living impacting young people and making things more challenging when it comes to jobs and also to affording essentials. The petitioners call on the government to present a clear plan to reduce youth unemployment, developed in consultation with young Canadians, employers and educators. They want young people to have opportunity, jobs, homes and hope once again. They the government to report Parliament on progress towards job creation, training alignment and youth labour market participation.

title: Oral Questions: Public Safety
turns: Mr. Speaker, under the Liberals, violent crime is up 55%, sexual assaults are up 76%, human trafficking is up 85% and extortion is up a colossal 330%. We have TV ads from the Liberals telling us that we have never had it so good, and it is like the Liberals are buying their own spin. When will the Liberals stop buying their own spin, recognize there is a problem and keep Canadians safe at home?

Mr. Speaker, this government is taking action at a pace that has not been seen before with respect to the criminal justice system. We have a number of pieces of legislation that have already been passed, including reforming bail and sentencing. We have invested with the RCMP, 1,000 new RCMP officers, as well as 1,000 CBSA officers. We will continue to ensure the safety and security of Canadians. I would just invite the member opposite to speak to the chief of the Toronto Police Service and to look at the numbers in Toronto, which demonstrate that our plan is actually working.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the minister just said that they are taking action at a pace that has never been seen before. I think the pace is a bit slower than he might want to acknowledge, because we have never seen so much inaction from a government as we are under the Liberals. Take sexual offences against children, up 121%, and offences related to child sexual abuse and exploitation material, up 195%. While the Prime Minister globe-trots, Canadian children at home are vulnerable. Will this government acknowledge the problem and take action now?

Mr. Speaker, when we do take action, for example, with Bill C-22, the party opposite slow-walks it. The Canadian Centre for Child Protection spoke at the Senate this week, confirming the need for lawful access. If my friend opposite is serious about addressing crimes such as childhood sexual exploitation, he and his party would support the fast passage of Bill C-22.

Mr. Speaker, 911 is there for emergencies, but when that line gets cut, lives are at risk. Bell Canada has already recorded 116 incidents of copper theft in Cambridge this year. Thieves are damaging fibre lines bundled with copper wire, cutting families and businesses off from 911, Internet and wireless services. This is not petty theft; it is a threat to public safety. Stolen copper does not just vanish; it is sold for cash. When will the Liberal government go after the thieves, sellers and buyers who keep this crime paying?

Mr. Speaker, we are on top of this issue. That is why we included the theft of copper in Bill C-14, which has passed and became law in this country on July 15. We are seeing good results from the passage of many pieces of legislation, like our hate crime bill and the bail and sentencing reform bill. Police across the country are laying charges under these new pieces of legislation and combatting crime at the same time.

Mr. Speaker, the deflection in here today is absolutely unreal. The Liberals say, “Conservatives, Conservatives”, but I think they forgot that they have a majority government. Money laundering is not a victimless crime. It is the business model that keeps—

Mr. Speaker, money laundering is not a victimless crime. It is a business model that allows drug traffickers to turn human misery into profit, with $113 billion laundered through Canada annually. Meanwhile, FINTRAC cannot show any tangible outcomes. Can the finance minister please stand and share how many dollars are taken away from criminals and how many—

Mr. Speaker, we are not deflecting anything. We are tackling these issues head-on by creating the financial crimes agency and by making sure all the bills that we have passed address money laundering. Actually, we put forward money laundering provisions in Bill C-2, a bill that the Conservatives would not allow to pass. Many of those initiatives that we have put forward have been delayed by the Conservative Party of Canada. It has been perplexing throughout this whole Parliament, because they have not been on the side of Canadians. We have been making sure that we implement laws that will protect—

Mr. Speaker, it has been a year since the Liberal government gave the Minister of Industry the power to order the removal of Huawei and ZTE technology from Canada's telecommunications network. In that year, the minister has, again, failed to act, and whistle-blowers now say she has no intention of acting. Will that order be made, or is the minister putting the national security and sovereignty of Canadians at risk to appease Beijing in trade talks?
Mr. Speaker, when it comes to our national security, it is always our utmost priority, and we will make sure that is the case in every single case.

title: Oral Questions: Taxation
turns: Mr. Speaker, if only screaming, hollering and the minister's finger in the air could lower grocery prices by Thanksgiving, everyone would be eating for free, but in reality, they are paying more than ever. In fact, today, Canadians are paying 25¢ a litre more for diesel than the U.S. and global averages because of Liberal taxes, a weak Liberal dollar and Liberal laws that prevent us from refining diesel for every Canadian. Will they vote today for our motion to get rid of all the taxes on diesel so that we can save Canadians money and bring home our jobs?

Mr. Speaker, I have some good news. Canadian diesel production is up 16% this year. More good news is that diesel prices have gone down three cents in the last several days. I have even more good news. If the member wants to actually help, he can vote for Bill C-38 and extend the excise tax exemption.

Mr. Speaker, that is good news? Three cents a litre is the good news he announces after prices are up 100% and have risen to the highest place anywhere in the world outside of the Prime Minister's beloved Europe. It is not good news to have three cents off. We need to bring diesel prices down so that we can lower the cost of food, appliances and basic essentials. Everything that we have comes in a truck. Conservatives have a plan to lower the cost and repatriate the production. The Liberals can vote on it today. Will they vote to save Canadians money?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians know that the Leader of the Opposition likes to talk, but now he will have a test. Will he walk the talk? Instead of presenting a motion to oppose, I have a suggestion for him and his entire bench. Why do they not vote for farmers? Why do they not vote for truckers? Why do they not vote for families? Why do they not vote for Canada one day? They could vote for Bill C-38 and extend the suspension of the fuel tax. That is an immediate measure that would help all of Canada. Will they vote for Canada once and for all?

Mr. Speaker, we want to vote to get all taxes off fuel until at least July 1, 2027, and get rid of the worst Liberal taxes on fuel forever. That would be the way to vote for farmers, for truckers and for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, we have the oil, we have the workers and we have the capacity, yet Canadians pay 24¢ per litre more for diesel than Americans do. The government keeps talking about making Canada stronger, while making Canadian energy more expensive for Canadians. A country with the fourth-largest oil reserves in the world should not be paying a premium to fuel itself. Will the Liberals vote for our Conservative motion to save Canadians money today, or will the Prime Minister keep making Canadians pay more?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians can see through the cynicism on the other side of the aisle. The federal government has already reduced the price of gasoline by 25¢ a litre. We are building new energy infrastructure across this country. Rather than talk down Canada, why do the Conservatives not help us build the right Canada for the future?

Mr. Speaker, this Thanksgiving, the same family dinner costs 10% more than it did just a year ago. When diesel goes up, everything goes up. Farmers pay more to grow the food, truckers pay more to move it and families pay more at the till. The government says it wants to lower costs, but here is its chance. Will the Prime Minister vote for our emergency fuel relief plan today and drive costs down for families instead of giving empty promises and false prophecies?

Mr. Speaker, while the other side focuses on caucus revolts, image reboots and finding the leader yet another riding to run in, we are focused on affordability for Canadians. The groceries and essentials benefit will lift 77,000 Canadians out of poverty. On this side of the House, we are going to deliver affordability measures for Canadians. The Conservatives can continue to vote against each and every one of them.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, yet Canadian truckers pay 24¢ more per litre for diesel than Americans do and 31¢ more than the global average. Diesel prices have surged nearly 80% in the past year, driving up costs for truckers, farmers and families. Our Conservative emergency fuel relief plan would cut diesel taxes today and refine more Canadian fuel here at home instead of relying on U.S. refineries. Will the Liberals support our Conservative plan to save Canadians money?

Mr. Speaker, maybe the Conservative Party would join with us in pausing the federal excise fuel tax, which will save Canadians 10¢ a litre when they fill up at the pump. We also cut the consumer carbon tax, saving Canadians 18¢ a litre when they fill up at the pump. The leader has been in the House for 7,600 days. He has produced nothing for Canadians. We are focused on affordability.

Mr. Speaker, last week, hundreds of dump truck drivers hit the roads protesting the rising diesel prices. Diesel powers the trucks that move our goods, the equipment that builds our communities and the farms that put food on our tables. When diesel costs rise, Canadians pay more for everything. Today the Liberals have the opportunity to vote on a Conservative emergency fuel relief plan to cut all taxes on diesel until Canada Day and bring some relief during Thanksgiving. Will the Prime Minister listen to our truckers and finally give relief to Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, with the ongoing global conflicts and supply chain disruptions, we are focused on what we can control: bringing down costs for Canadians so they can get ahead. By suspending the federal fuel excise, we reduced costs by 10¢ per litre on gasoline and four cents on diesel. Lowering the price at the pump is one step to support Canadians, but let us also talk about the Canada groceries and essentials benefit that arrived in bank accounts this week, including in those of almost 1.5 million Canadians who live in British Columbia.

title: Oral Questions: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship
turns: Mr. Speaker, we have been working on immigration since we formed government. The work is continuing, and we will have more to share soon.

Mr. Speaker, Liberals have sent immigration out of control. We now learn that the Prime Minister cannot even keep track of the number of people here in the country. In June, he claimed that the population had gone down, but then Statistics Canada said this month that there are 300,000 more people in Canada than the Prime Minister had said. How can the Prime Minister tell The New York Times that we need an increase in immigration, when he cannot even keep track of the number of people already here?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians have heard the Leader of the Opposition, again and again, saying many things. One thing they know is that the Prime Minister has taken back control of the immigration system in the country. Not only did we do that, but we also ensured that we would have a sustainable level of immigration. We know, on this side of the aisle, that the people who come to our country choose Canada, contribute to our society, build families here and contribute to the greatness of the country.

Mr. Speaker, immigrants themselves are not to blame. They are hard-working, law-abiding and decent people. What is to blame is the Liberal government, which has destroyed the system. The asylum claim backlog is up 2,500% since the government took office. Temporary foreign worker permits are up 135%. The number of temporary residents is up 260%. The Liberals have lost track of 300,000 people. If the Prime Minister cannot even keep count of the number of people here, how can he claim that we need to bring more immigration in?

Mr. Speaker, the member opposite might want to speak to his caucus about not demonizing immigration. In fact, so often we hear from members on the opposition bench about how immigrants are stealing Canadians' jobs. They are forgetting about the hard work immigrants do to build a life here, to contribute to our economies and in fact to build businesses. He should speak to the members of his caucus who continually ask for more temporary foreign workers while ignoring the need for sustainable immigration levels that we can manage, that help our economy grow—

Mr. Speaker, if anyone should be apologizing to immigrants, it is the Liberal government, for completely destroying the system and allowing corporate power brokers to use vulnerable immigrants to drive wages down and rents up. Provinces must deliver the services related to newcomers: health care, jobs and housing. However, the Prime Minister wants to concentrate all the power in his hands, where he has let the system run out of control. Why not allow Alberta, Quebec and the other provinces more control so they can ensure that we protect health care, housing and jobs for all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what we have done with the temporary foreign worker program. We have worked closely with provinces and territories to ensure that flexibilities are there for provinces that need short-term labour availability when there are no Canadians to take the jobs. What does not help is an opposition party that demonizes immigration and demonizes immigrants, making it harder for people to get the workers they need, for people to land in our communities and contribute to their fullest. Enough is enough. They need to stop speaking out of both sides of their mouth.

title: Statements by Members: The Budget
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government's costly credit card budget does not put Canadians first. According to the Parliamentary Budget Officer, debt interest is the fastest-growing expense and will soon hit $85 billion a year, or 26% more than federal health care spending. Housing is out of reach, jobs go to temporary workers and health care is inaccessible. Emergency rooms are overcrowded, and it is not always Canadians receiving the care they pay for. New data from Second Street suggests that in the last five years, health care bodies wrote off over half a billion dollars in losses from non-Canadian residents who never paid. Meanwhile, the government will bring in over 650,000 permanent immigrants in one year, adding more pressure to a crumbling health care infrastructure. Canadians should not be made to compete for jobs, housing and health care in their own country because of Liberal mass immigration. The federal government should put Canadians first. The Conservatives know this. The Liberals need to learn it.

Mr. Speaker, this budget was an opportunity for the government to show Canadians that it understands the financial pressures that families are facing. Instead, it added nearly $765 billion in borrowing over five years. The Parliamentary Budget Officer says that the interest on the federal debt is “the fastest-growing expense”. Soon, Canadians will be paying more to service the debt than they spend on health care transfers. These numbers hit home, because families are struggling with groceries and housing. In rural communities, like Dunnville, food bank demand has increased by over 80% in the last six years. Entire families are reliant on food banks. Canadians deserve a government that is going to respect their tax dollars, and I am not going to stop fighting for financial accountability and affordability in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians expect the government to make life more affordable and put an end to wasteful spending. Instead, this costly Liberal credit card budget has added $765 billion in new debt and an increase of $92.3 billion since the spring economic statement. The Liberals have said they want a target of 100,000 new Red Seal workers by 2031. Despite adding $5.5 billion to team Canada strong, they provided no update on whether they are on track to meet their own targets. As a tradesperson myself, I am concerned that there will be 100,000 potentially new trained tradespeople without jobs or work to go to. The government continues to add to the burden of Canadians with more spending and more debt without providing a plan or even a clear explanation of where taxpayer money is going. Families are losing jobs, struggling to keep food on the table and barely making ends meet. The government's priority should be to address these challenges and save money for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, according to the Parliamentary Budget Officer and her most recent report on budget 2026, the government is hooked on spending. When a government gets addicted to spending, it is Canadians who suffer the consequences, and Canadians are about to get the bill. Over the next five years, the Liberal government will add $765 billion to our national debt. That is $476 billion more than the deficits that it is admitting to. That nearly $500 billion is not tied to a single project, and Canadians want to know where the money is. The interest alone will be $85 billion annually, which is 26% more than is spent on the Canada health transfer. That is $2,000 per person every year, just in interest charges. In housing, starts are down 4%. The promise to double homebuilding has quietly vanished, and the government is adding 200,000 more permanent residents than it did last year. The reality is that, as the Liberal government spends more and borrows more, it delivers less.

title: Oral Questions: International Trade
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister called this the greatest crisis since the Second World War. Then he said Trump is a transformational president. He said integration is subordination and then wanted more integration to “make America great again.” He decried a world of fortresses and then “fortress North America”. He said that we are “at war” and the U.S. wants to break us to own us. Now he has a chat with the President about T-shirts and dress shirts. There is a new deal, the best deal, then no deal beats a bad deal, and now a bad deal beats no deal at all. Every position changes except for one: whatever helps Liberals in December's by-elections. What is the actual plan, or is it just putting his party ahead of the country?

Mr. Speaker, speaking of some positions that never change, there are the attempts of the Conservative Party to connect a series of dots that do not exist. I am surprised the Conservatives continually talk about by-elections. I am not sure it is going to be something they will like to talk about in a few weeks. Some of them, in fact, were caused by members of their own party evacuating the caucus. I understand our friends on the other side want to connect a series of dots. They know very well our government is hard at work to defend workers and businesses in Canada, and we will continue to do that.

Mr. Speaker, “defend workers”? Last month, economist Trevor Tombe told the foreign affairs committee there is no evidence the Liberal countertariffs changed American behaviour, none. What they did was raise prices across the board and slash the income of Canadians earning under $30,000. Liberals are taxing our most vulnerable to punish Washington, and Washington could not be bothered. Beyond the domestic Liberal politics designed to control our national debate, what is the plan beyond “elbows up” to actually level up?

Mr. Speaker, again, we see members of the Conservative Party attempt to attribute a series of motivations in circumstances that do not exist. They know very well. Our government was very clear. When the Americans increased unjustified and illegal tariffs on Canadian businesses and workers, Canadians expected our government to take a strong position, something the opposition would never have done, because they continually find excuses as to why Canada should not have stood up to the Americans and done the right thing to defend workers.

title: Adjournment Proceedings: Labour
turns: Mr. Speaker, my question tonight relates to the Air Canada strike and a decision made by the Minister of Jobs and Families to use section 107, but more fundamentally, it is a question about integrity. I know it is against our rules in the House to accuse a member of lying, and I would certainly never do that. I want to share some of the context around what happened in this case and allow people to draw their own conclusions about what the Minister of Jobs and Families said. In the context of deciding to use section 107 to end a strike at Air Canada, the minister spoke specifically about the transportation of pharmaceuticals and organ tissue as being a motivator for ending that strike. She said in a written statement, not in an off-the-cuff comment, “This nationwide labour disruption is impeding the movement of passengers and critical cargo.” Later in the statement she wrote, “Further, the shipments of critical goods such as pharmaceuticals and organ tissue, over 40% of which are moved by Air Canada, should continue to reach their destinations.” Blacklock's, I believe, was the first one to do an ATIP and identify the fact that there were no records within the Government of Canada to verify claims about how the strike was putting at risk the transport of organs and tissue. I repeatedly asked the minister and officials at committee whether they could present the evidence they had relied on to do this. I also asked whether, if they had been told in some meeting that the transport of organs and tissue was at risk, they could share with us who told them that and when the meeting was. I then asked officials whether officials have any record of this meeting, where it took place and which officials were present. Of course, typically officials or staff of some sort would be present for briefings with the minister. No information was provided, in terms of when and where that meeting took place, so I followed up with this again with an Order Paper question, which is Question No. 1407. I asked in various ways what records the government has with regard to the transportation of organs by air and how those shipments are tracked and managed. In response to this question, the government repeatedly affirmed that it did not collect data. It had no data on those things. I then asked in the same question about the meeting or alleged meeting that took place in which the minister received this information. Again, there were no records of that meeting whatsoever and no record of the information. The best that the government could offer is that “the Minister receives a continuous flow of information, analysis, assessments, and advice from a broad range of sources within and outside government.” At best, taking the most charitable view, maybe the minister was, in private and off the cuff, told by somebody that this was a risk associated with the strike, and used that information as the basis for ending the strike, even though she had no evidence whatsoever to support that claim. Perhaps she made it up herself. Perhaps somebody else made it up and said it to her, but this was clearly a statement that was not true, one that the minister has repeatedly made and doubled down on. Speaking of the integrity of the minister, is she or a representative willing to acknowledge that this was not true? At what point, given the clear evidence in this Order Paper question, are we going to have an acknowledgement of that reality?

Mr. Speaker, I do not accept the member's characterization of the minister's actions. She has explained the concerns she was weighing in her responsibility to Canadians. At committee, the minister said she received briefings about disruptions to critical medical supplies. In the House, she explained why those concerns mattered. Canadians depend on the movement of essential medicines and medical products, including organs for transplant, within Canada and across our borders. For someone waiting for treatment, getting those supplies on time matters. That had to be part of the decision. The member is entitled to question the decision. Canadians are also entitled to hear the context in which it was made. The government believes in collective bargaining. We respect the right to strike. We know that a negotiated agreement gives workers and employers the strongest foundation to move forward together. That is why federal mediators work alongside the parties to help them find common ground. The vast majority of negotiations in federally regulated workplaces conclude without a work stoppage. That reflects the hard work of unions, employers and the people who help them reach agreements. In the Air Canada dispute, negotiations had been under way for eight months. Despite extensive support, the parties remained at an impasse. The minister had a responsibility to protect Canadians' access to essential medicines and medical supplies. People depend on those deliveries for their care. Those needs could not be set aside. That meant weighing the consequences of a disruption alongside workers' rights. The minister directed the Canada Industrial Relations Board to send the dispute to arbitration under section 107 of the Canada Labour Code. As she has explained, the purpose was to help resolve the dispute and protect Canadians. Intervening in a labour dispute is a serious and exceptional step. Our preference was, and remains, an agreement reached by the parties at the table. The concerns flight attendants raised about their own working conditions also deserve action. I have said in this House that nobody should work for free in this country. Flight attendants do important work to keep passengers safe. They deserve to be paid fairly for that work. When allegations of unpaid work were raised, the government launched an investigation into pay practices in the airline sector. We have been working with airlines and unions to examine compliance with the Canada Labour Code. Employers must meet their obligations. Workers deserve certainty. We also want to give workers and employers a better chance of resolving difficult disputes themselves. That is why Bill C-39 proposes earlier support for bargaining and clearer requirements before section 107 can be used. A special mediator would work intensively with the parties. If they could not reach an agreement, a public report would help Canadians understand the outstanding issues and prospects for settlement. A national impact assessment would examine the consequences of a disruption beyond the bargaining table. These changes would make the process more transparent and give the parties further opportunities to reach a deal. Intervention must always remain a last resort. Bringing people together takes work. It means listening to workers, expecting employers to do their part, and taking seriously the consequences for Canadians when talks break down. The government will continue to do that work. Workers deserve fair treatment, and Canadians deserve a government that takes their health and safety seriously.

Mr. Speaker, there is a lot I could say about the unpaid work issue, but that is not the core issue here. The core issue here is the integrity of the government. The minister made a written claim. That claim is not supported by any evidence or by any information the minister received. In response to my question tonight, the parliamentary secretary doubled down on and repeated this claim. The claim that the strike impacted organ transport is not a matter of opinion or philosophy. It is a falsifiable, factual claim. That is, it is either objectively true or objectively not, and whether or not it is true is dependent entirely on the evidence. However, the minister made a claim, that factual claim, as we now know from the Order Paper question, the ATIP and other supporting evidence, entirely without information or evidence. How do they defend that?

Mr. Speaker, the member opposite keeps repeating his allegation. The minister told the committee that she was briefed on risks to critical medical supplies. She has explained why she took those concerns seriously. Canadians depend on essential medicines, medical supplies and organs moving across this country and across our borders. Their needs do not stop because there is a labour dispute. After months of negotiations, the parties at the time were at an impasse. The minister had a responsibility to work toward a resolution and consider the consequences for Canadians. That is why she referred the dispute to the Canada Industrial Relations Board. Nobody should be expected to work for free. We acted on allegations of unpaid work in the airline sector, and employers must meet their obligations. The member is entitled to disagree, but the responsibility to protect Canadians does not disappear because a decision is difficult.

title: Private Members' Business: An Act to Repeal Certain Restrictions on Shipping
turns: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and address the House on the important issue of Canada's natural resources and how those resources can be of great value to all Canadians. If we really want to take a look at how the Government of Canada has been addressing that issue, we have to understand just how important collaborative federalism is, meaning that Ottawa works with our provinces and other stakeholders on doing the things we are doing in order to build that stronger and healthier economy. When we take a look at the legislation before us today, we should also take a look at what has been happening since 1972. We had a great deal of commitment to our environment even back then, including from industries and different stakeholders, including the provinces, indigenous community leaders or the federal government, and an understanding of the dangers of such things as oil spills and protecting the B.C. coastline. It is important that we continue to look at ways to encourage and support that collaborative approach in building a stronger and healthier Canada. It is something the Prime Minister and this government have strived to achieve since the last federal election when Canadians made the decision to elect a new Prime Minister. This is a government that understands the importance of building an economy that works for all Canadians and the benefits of doing so, and in working with other provinces. British Columbia just had an election, as we all know, and I congratulate the new Premier-elect, Lorne Doerkson, on his election. I listened very attentively to what he had to say; there were a lot of common links with what the Prime Minister of Canada has been talking about. We will see that not only are there concerns about the environment, but there are also concerns in regards to how we can actually build that stronger Canada and the important role that British Columbia plays in that. The week before, we saw the people of Alberta, an overwhelming majority, understanding the value of Canada as a federal system and the potential that Alberta, B.C. and every province in Canada has. The way we achieve that potential is to ensure that we have the Prime Minister , ministers, the government as a whole, and I would even extend that to every member of the House of Commons, contributing towards a co-operative federalism that ensures every Canadian and every region of the country benefits. That is what we should be attempting to achieve. However, a great deal of the legislation before us deals with rhetoric. The Conservative opposition's approach to oil and the development of our natural resources, which is to say full steam ahead, that we do not care what the indigenous people of Canada have to say and would not even listen to what provincial governments have to say. Whether individuals advocate for a healthier environment or a healthier economy, the Conservatives like to think that the Conservative spin is going to resolve the issues. I have heard the leader of the Conservative Party talk about dealing with clearing the way and getting pipelines built to the B.C. coast, at times completely ignoring indigenous interests and just saying they should build anyway. However, as a government, I believe there is a responsibility of consultation, both morally and legally, that needs to take place. That is what I mean by collaborative approach. It does not mean that it is not going to happen. In fact, take a look at Stephen Harper. What did Prime Minister Stephen Harper actually accomplish when it came to building pipelines to tidewater? Absolutely nothing. There was not even an inch of pipeline built in the direction of the west coast. It was not until the current leader and Prime Minister Stephen Harper left office a few years later where we started to actually see action on that front. That is the reality. That is a fact. Since the last federal election, the Prime Minister has made a commitment to Canadians that we are going to build, and build Canada strong, that means taking a look at our natural resources and other things across the nation, and how it is that we are going to advance that build. That is why we brought forward not one, but two pieces of legislation dealing with things such as one Canadian economy. Canadians want that, they expect that, and the federal government has delivered that. Now we continue to encourage co-operation among the provinces to continue to take down barriers that prevent trade between our provinces. Part of trade is dealing with pipelines and dealing with the mobility of labour. They are so very important to our nation. Take a look at the projects. Here we are dealing a great deal in the bill that is being proposed by the Conservatives today, with the Province of British Columbia. I will remind members from across the way that the single greatest expenditure between government and the private sector was LNG phase one, under the government of Justin Trudeau. Some 18 months later, we now have an agreement to push forward with LNG phase two. We are talking about billions of dollars of investment that is going to generate billions in terms of future revenue for the federal government, while working with an NDP government in B.C. and a Conservative government in Alberta. In other words, it is a team Canada approach. The political stripe is secondary. What is important is that it be in the interest of Canadians. I believe we have demonstrated that time and time again. I can talk about B.C. as I just did. I can talk about the MOU in Alberta. I can talk about the copper mine in Saskatchewan. I can talk about the port of Churchill in Manitoba and nuclear energy in Ontario. I can talk about the port of Montreal and the expansion there, energy expansion in Atlantic Canada and the list goes on. I can talk about how it is we are using natural resource development and enticing investors to come to Canada as the Prime Minister hosted them back in Toronto, where we saw half trillion dollars, which was previously unheard of.

Madam Speaker, in 2015, the northern gateway pipeline was a conditionally approved 525,000 barrel per day link between the Alberta oil sands and the Pacific coast. In the 2015 election, the Liberals campaigned against this project. They were aided and abetted heavily by environmentalist NGOs, many foreign-funded, that opposed that project. Their then leader, Justin Trudeau, his campaign manager and many of his candidates were vehemently opposed to the northern gateway pipeline. This is what happened in 2015. A pipeline was conditionally approved and the Liberals opposed it. When they formed their government, they failed to champion this approved pipeline. They failed to take any steps to work with anybody toward ensuring that conditions could be met or that the opposition could be worked with to ensure its construction, and they killed it by a ministerial order in the fall of 2016, about 10 years ago. Then they brought in Bill C-48 to ensure that no pipeline could ever be built to the northwest coast. That is the track record of the government. They are opposed to northern shipping because they oppose a pipeline and the increased production to fill the pipeline. The northern route is the best route to world markets. It is the closest way to world prices. It is the least number of shipping days to get to Asian markets. It is the way that Canada could get off the differential with the existing bottlenecks that cause Canadians to take a discount on our prices. Getting to Asian markets, world markets and world prices is how Canada can diversify its trade relationships with Canada's most valuable commodity, by far the biggest source of export revenue and contribution to the Canadian economy. I heard as recently as last week in debate in this House that they claim there was never any shipping traffic and Bill C-48 was just codifying a long-existing de facto ban. That is all nonsense. They deliberately banned shipping traffic with this bill. Bill C-48 prohibits the loading and unloading of tankers off the northwest coast of British Columbia and this bill today would repeal that decision. Let us face it and admit to ourselves that Bill C-48 never had anything to do with environmental policy, certainly not with maritime environmental policy. It had everything to do with ensuring that the northern gateway pipeline would never be built and that the expansion of the oil sands to fill the pipeline would not happen. That was the agenda. We need to go back to that time and hear some of the things members said in this place. We need to hear what Prime Minister Trudeau said when he appeared at the industry committee, I think in 2021, under questioning from the opposition leader. He doubled down, said he supported it and thought it was the right decision to kill northern gateway. He did not say it was because the Liberals did not want shipping traffic off the northwest coast. It was because they did not believe in the project and did not want a northern pipeline. It was not about safety. It was about their opposition to pipelines and the oil and gas industry. So many of the members of the Liberal government and caucus are quite clearly on the record about this. The current Minister of the Environment, on her MP web page, gave herself credit for opposing an expansion of the oil sands. This is not something we dug up deep from the history of the Internet. This is live while she is Minister of the Environment. I questioned her about it at the natural resources committee. I was actually surprised that the Liberals did not have it taken down within the hour when it was aired publicly. It took months before they took it down. We have the Minister of the Environment who proudly opposes an expansion of the oil sands, and today they would have us think that they are aggressively moving forward to ensure that we have an expansion of our exports and that we become an energy superpower. In order to do that, we would have to export far more oil and gas and energy products than we currently do. We would need two or three northern gateways. We would need a doubling of TMX. We would need Keystone XL to be built. We would need an eastern pipeline to Sarnia or all the way to Saint John. These are the things that an energy superpower would need. The most efficient way to get our exports to world markets would be to allow the shipping traffic that is currently banned by this law. If the northern gateway pipeline had been built at 525,000 barrels a day, at today's world prices, that would be nearly $20 billion a year in revenue. Think of the taxation base for public services. Think of all the high-paying jobs. Think of what we would have today economically if that pipeline and other pipelines had been built, if the Liberals had championed Keystone XL to ensure its construction or had not chased TransCanada Energy out of Canada. It literally had to change its name and moved all of its investment activity to Mexico and the United States. The Liberals have an opportunity today. They can stand up and vote for this bill, although we will probably not have the vote today but this week. They can declare whether they want to actually undertake the steps necessary to allow Canada to become an energy superpower. They can repeal Bill C-48, which was calculated to restrict the expansion of the oil sands and our exports. They have a chance to do that now. There is today a private sector proponent that wishes to ship 250,000 barrels a day from Prince Rupert, which is the closest port to, and has the fewest number of shipping days from, Asian markets. This proponent would need a repeal of Bill C-48. The Liberals have a chance, with this bill, to be on the side of Canadian jobs, of Canadian export diversification and of getting us out of our dependence on the United States as an export destination. They have the chance to do it with this bill, and it will be really interesting to see if they will undertake a concrete step in furtherance of the objectives they sometimes talk about. The Liberals speak of Canada as an energy superpower yet have not repealed Bill C-69, which is the “no more pipelines” bill. They will need to support Bill C-264 to remove the shipping ban. These things have to be done. They cannot just say the words “energy superpower”. They will have to change the laws the government passed that prevent Canada from reaching its potential as an energy superpower. This is an important step. Bill C-5, which we supported, gives the Liberals the power to exempt people from the law, but that is not the way to go. They need to change the laws that actually prevent the activity. I want to thank the member for Calgary Signal Hill for bringing this bill to the House. I want to thank my friend James Cumming for his attempt in an earlier Parliament to strip away Bill C-48. It is a long-time policy of the Conservatives to repeal this ban, which is all about reducing Canada's export potential of oil and gas.

Madam Speaker, earlier this month, the Prime Minister announced that Canada would pursue another oil pipeline to the Pacific coast. I agree that Canada should be selling more of its energy to the world, but I have one question: If more oil tankers can be part of a responsible national project on the south coast of B.C., why is the answer automatically “no” when somebody proposes a project farther north? This is what Bill C-264 asks us to reconsider. Let me be clear. I do not want oil splashing up on a beach or destroying an ecosystem; nobody does. We can disagree about how best to protect the environment without pretending that one side cares about it and the other side does not. We ought to be honest about this law, including where it came from. In 2016, Justin Trudeau announced that his government would reject the northern gateway pipeline and introduced a tanker ban for northern B.C. His stated reason was environmental protection. What does the law actually do? It prohibits tankers carrying more than 12,500 metric tonnes of crude oil or certain persistent oils from loading, unloading or stopping at ports and marine installations along the northern B.C. coast. It does not ban every tanker passing offshore, though. It prevents the development of a large crude oil export terminal using those ports. There is an important difference, because oil tankers did not vanish from the Pacific coast when this law was passed. Let us consider Alaska. American tankers have long carried crude oil to destinations farther south, including Washington state. They travel offshore, west of a voluntary tanker exclusion zone established back in 1985. We need to look at the broader picture. We recognize that marine shipping carries risks, and we manage some of those risks through routes, rules and emergency preparedness. Meanwhile, a company proposing a northern export terminal faces a ban regardless of what safeguards it might offer. We manage oil shipping elsewhere. Tankers operate on the St. Lawrence and around Newfoundland. They load Canadian crude oil at Westridge in Burnaby. In the second quarter of this year alone, Trans Mountain reported that 82 vessels were loaded at that terminal. Those waters are not all alike, but that is exactly why we have experts, navigational assessments and environmental reviews. The risks of a particular project ought to be assessed where it would actually operate. This brings me back to the Pacific link project, the new pipeline that was announced. It is proposed to follow a southern route to an export terminal at Roberts Bank outside of the northern moratorium area. It has not been built or finally approved. The federal government says it could carry another million barrels of oil a day toward customers in Asia. I am glad the Liberal government finally recognizes that more buyers for Canadian energy would be a good thing. We have depended heavily on the American market, and we should not put all of our eggs in one basket, nor should we be effectively donating billions of dollars to the United States by selling to it at a discount when higher world prices are available. However, we cannot keep assuming that every new pipeline to the Pacific should end up along some variation of the same southern corridor. There are communities, mountains, already very busy ports and environmental concerns along those routes too. Sometimes, using an existing corridor will be the sensible option. Sometimes, it may not be. Why would we decide today that future engineers, investors and communities would not even be allowed to put another northern option on the table? Here is what really bothers me about the tanker ban: It substitutes a blanket political decision for the hard work of judging individual proposals as they come in. Let us think about how ridiculous that is. A company could come forward with a proposal that uses the safest tankers available, the latest navigation technology, tugboats to escort every vessel and an emergency response system that goes well beyond anything required today. It could offer to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on additional safety measures and demonstrate that it can meet every environmental standard we can throw at it. What would the federal government say? “Sorry, we are not interested.” It does not matter how safe a company can make it, how much technology has improved or what precautions it is prepared to take. The answer was decided back in 2019, and the government is not even going to consider the question. This is the absurdity of this ban in a nutshell. The government did not set a higher environmental standard for companies to meet. It decided that no matter how much companies invest, how safe the technology becomes or how strong environmental protections are, nothing will ever be good enough. They are not being given a tough test to pass. They are being told they are not even allowed to take the test. That strikes me as a rather strange way to govern. We regulate plenty of activities that carry serious risks. Pipelines, railways, ports, factories and even the driving of cars all operate under rules designed to prevent accidents and limit their consequences. We do not simply assume that every project is safe. We demand evidence, impose conditions and, when necessary, refuse permission. At the very minimum, we should at least examine what is being proposed. There is something else worth remembering. Back in 2013, Stephen Harper's Conservative government launched a major effort to improve tanker safety in Canada. It increased tanker inspections, expanded aerial and satellite monitoring, improved our ability to respond to spills and brought in tougher rules for facilities handling oil. These were not just promises. The measures were put into practice, and Transport Canada's own evaluation later confirmed that they helped improve marine safety. The Harper government also recognized that preventing spills was only part of the equation. It changed the law to make sure that if something did go wrong, the people responsible would be held financially accountable. In 2014, the government proposed removing the compensation limit on Canada's ship-source oil pollution fund. The principle was simple: If a tanker causes a spill, the people who suffer the losses should be compensated and the polluter should pay. Further changes were passed in 2018, removing the compensation ceiling on the fund and clarifying the rules for certain economic losses. Today, that fund can provide compensation for claims without a fixed overall limit for each incident. Over the years, we have built a system designed to prevent accidents, respond when they happen and hold those responsible for them financially accountable. Rather than simply banning certain tanker operations outright, should we not be asking whether those protections can be made even stronger? If the existing rules are not good enough for northern B.C., let us identify what is missing. Do we need more tugboats escorting tankers? Do we need better equipment stationed across the coastline? Do we need restrictions on sailing during dangerous weather, perhaps, or tougher financial requirements for companies that want to operate there? If a company wants to build a terminal and ship oil through those waters, it should have to demonstrate that it can operate responsibly. It should be prepared to invest in the necessary safety measures and take financial responsibility if something goes wrong. That brings us back to Bill C-264. Passing this legislation would not approve a single new pipeline or tanker terminal. It would not give an oil company permission to do whatever it wants, and it would not remove Canada's other marine safety or environmental laws. It would simply repeal the existing tanker moratorium, allowing future proposals to be considered under the other laws and approval processes that apply to it. Those reviews should be rigorous.
