If a proposed project cannot meet the required environmental standards, it should not be approved. If the risks are simply too great, the answer should be no. Surely we should be willing to examine the evidence before making that decision. The Prime Minister keeps telling us that he wants to make this country an energy superpower. I would ask him this: How can we seriously talk about opening new markets while maintaining a law that rules out an entire region of potential export opportunities before anyone could even put forward a proposal? We cannot assume that every future pipeline to the Pacific Ocean should have to squeeze into the same southern corridor, nor should we assume that every proposal for a northern terminal would be suitable. We should be making those decisions based on actual proposals. I do not believe that protecting the environment and developing our natural resources must be competing objectives. We should, in fact, be able to walk and chew gum. I think it is perfectly reasonable to take another look at whether the tanker ban still makes any sense. That is why I will be supporting Bill C-264.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to address the House this morning and to express my strong support for Bill C-264. This is a bill that would finally repeal the Liberal tanker ban. This is an opportunity to talk about pipeline policy in this country and to call out the slipperiness of the Liberal government. It is clear that over the last 10 years, the Conservative opposition has won the public debate on pipelines. There is certainly very strong public support for the construction of pipelines and other major national energy projects, and this creates the conditions in which the government faces a political imperative to try to pretend to be more supportive of energy infrastructure projects than it has been in the past. However, while we have won the public debate around the construction of pipelines and other major energy infrastructure, the government continues to obstruct, at a policy level, actual progress on these issues. We have won the public debate, but we have not won the policy battle. That is what Bill C-264 tries to do: complete policy work that certainly reflects the public demand for these kinds of projects to go forward. To understand, though, how the government says one thing and does another when it comes to pipelines, I think it is important to dig into the history. If we look at the history over the last 10 or 15 years as it relates to pipelines, the government has done everything possible to obstruct pipelines and major energy infrastructure from going forward. It has also tried to do so indirectly. Those who are familiar with crime films will recognize the phrase “make it look like an accident.” The government has tried to kill pipelines and make it look like an accident. Let us talk about where we were in 2015 when Justin Trudeau became prime minister. Looking back at the record of the Harper government, in 2015, four major pipelines were constructed and a fifth had been approved, the northern gateway project. The Liberals promised in the 2015 election to kill the northern gateway pipeline. They did two things: first, they killed it directly; and second, they legislated to prohibit energy exports from the northern coast of B.C. This was designed, or intended, to kill the northern gateway project and the opportunities associated with it. This was a decision of the government to kill that project in two ways: first, to kill it directly; and second, to legislate to prevent those energy exports. The Liberal government subsequently passed Bill C-69, adding additional challenges and barriers for pipeline construction, and killed the energy east pipeline. It did so by applying conditions to it that had never been applied previously to other development projects. Even then, the government wanted to say it was a private sector decision to kill the energy east pipeline. It changed the game by piling impossible conditions on the project and then said, “Oh, too bad. The proponents killed it.” This is part of the “kill major infrastructure projects and make it look like an accident” approach of the government, which is to apply legislative and other policy barriers that make it very difficult, if not impossible, for these kinds of projects to move forward. Now we have a different Prime Minister, who has written extensively, in a negative way, about the development of our energy resources, but now that he is Prime Minister, he wants people to think that he is maybe more supportive of these developments. The simple thing he could do is repeal the antidevelopment rules that were put in place by his predecessor. If the Prime Minister is really different from Justin Trudeau, he could simply repeal Bill C-69 and Bill C-48. These are two major anti-energy bills that his predecessor put forward. In particular, he could repeal Bill C-48, which is the bill regarding the tanker exclusion zone. That is the bill that Bill C-264, which we are debating today, would repeal. If the Prime Minister is sincere about getting pipelines built, he could simply vote in favour of this bill, or he could have moved to repeal Bill C-48 earlier. However, the approach the Liberal government has taken has not been, notably, to repeal the barriers that were put in place by his predecessor to prevent energy development. Instead, the Liberals brought us Bill C-5, which was the option for the government to approve, in exceptional circumstances, that some projects would not be subject to the rules that apply to every other project. Instead of simply removing the barriers that prevent development, they created a process in which those barriers that prevent development from moving forward are still in place, but if someone wants to build a project, they could go, cap in hand, to the government to ask It would refer them to this Major Projects Office. That will look at the project, and it will be designated and reviewed by various panels. Maybe at the end of it, they might get exceptional treatment for one project, even though the barriers would remain in place for all the other projects. If we could build major projects with red tape, the government would be all over it, because that is what it has been building: more and more red tape. They try to make it look like the Liberals are really trying, that they are going to add more offices, say that people can send their project here, refer it over here, and then this panel will take a look at it. Then maybe at the end of the day, they might create exemptions to the framework that was designed to prevent these projects from going forward. Conservatives have a much simpler solution, which is to get rid of the red tape and get rid of the laws that prevent these major projects from going forward so that we can build things again. This is what I think the public wants. The public wants major energy projects to go forward. We saw great news out of British Columbia. It is a strong endorsement by the voters of British Columbia for a government that is committed to creating jobs and building opportunity. There is a government now in British Columbia that sees how we can prosper together as a country instead of trying to make B.C. the barrier to exports that the previous NDP government wanted it to be. We see in that result, and in the expression of voters across the country, a desire for these kinds of projects to move forward. The government is slippery and savvy politically. The government knows it does not want to challenge directly this desire for major projects to go forward, so instead, it is just trying to make it look really difficult. The government wants to leave in place these barriers. It wants to add on red tape. It wants to promise that it might allow workarounds in certain situations if things are designated as such. The simple thing that the government can and should do to make it so much easier for major projects in energy, pipelines and other major projects, to go forward, is vote for Bill C-264. It would not add more laws. It would repeal a previous law that was put in place to block development. This is going to be a clear test for the government on Wednesday. When we vote on Bill C-264, we will see whether individual members of the government from energy-producing regions, as well as members from other regions, are prepared to vote in favour of a bill that would clear away red tape and create opportunities for major projects to go forward, or if they will vote to leave that red tape in place as an excuse to say they would like to, but it is just really difficult. It is really difficult because we have a law that makes it difficult. The building of major infrastructure could happen much more easily if we had not had governments for 11 years that tried to prevent it from happening. Let us underline that it is the same people.
You guys have to get over Trudeau.

Madam Speaker, the member for Winnipeg North, who is heckling me right now, has been here for a long time. He is not new. He voted for all these measures. In fact, I asked the Liberal member for Calgary Confederation, who is new, when he was first elected, if he would have voted in favour of C-48, and he said yes, and he is from Calgary. It is the same group of people, and in the cases where there are newer members, they profess to think the same way as the previous ones. The member said we are talking too much about Trudeau. I would be very happy to turn the page on the disastrous years of Justin Trudeau. Does the member know how we can turn the page on the disastrous record of Justin Trudeau? We can vote in favour of this bill, which would repeal a centrepiece part of Justin Trudeau's radical antidevelopment agenda. The Prime Minister can show he is different on Wednesday by voting in favour of Bill C-264. If he were to vote in favour of Bill C-264, I will say that maybe there is some real change, to coin a phrase, but if he were to vote for the Justin Trudeau policy on Wednesday, we will have to conclude that they are doubling down on the same energy policy. Yes, they are trying to nuance it in the communications in light of the fact that we have won the public debate on this issue, but they have not really changed. Again, we will see in the vote on Wednesday.

Madam Speaker, I cannot help but violently agree with my colleague's summation of the best way to turn the page on Justin Trudeau. It is amazing how the Liberals have forgotten that he ever existed, as if they were not here, all along the way, voting in favour of all the terrible policies that caused so much hardship, not just for western Canada and the energy sector, but also for Canadians from coast to coast. We have had the massive inflation crisis, the crime crisis, the drug crisis and, of course, the energy crisis, where Canada has been forced to discount its natural resources because, thanks to Liberal policies, Canada no longer has an ability to get oil to growing markets in Asia where it would pay a premium for what Canada is selling. This would be a wonderful opportunity to show sincere commitment to change by undoing Liberal policies. My colleague used the analogy of crime TV shows and movies, and of making something look like an accident. There is another theme in those types of movies where there are elements of a criminal underworld and the mobsters who run protection rackets. They come by someone's shop and throw a brick through the window. They then come back the next day and say, “Hey, we can make sure that nobody throws bricks through your windows.” That is what the Liberals have done with energy policy. They have thrown bricks through the ability of private sector proponents of projects to get things built. They then come along, after billions of dollars have left Canada for other jurisdictions and, after Canadian energy companies choose to invest in South America, Asia, Africa and even in the Middle East, they say, “Hey, if you work with us, if you jump through new hoops and new hurdles, and allow the government to take ownership positions in energy projects, then you can get something built.” That is what we have seen with the MOU that was imposed on Alberta, forcing the Government of Alberta to agree to an industrial carbon tax and to paying billions of dollars of costs into the pathways project. That is completely unnecessary. We now see a major development in the energy sector that Canada could take advantage of. Strathcona Resources pitches 250,000 barrels of oil per day on an export route to Asia. That is wonderful news. A private sector company is using its own money, not taxpayers' money, to push a project that would allow new exports to Asian markets, getting around the U.S. discount that Canadian producers have to face. There is only one thing standing in the way, and that is Bill C-48, the Liberal shipping ban. For people who have not heard about this before, the ban is a Liberal law that was brought in under the Trudeau government. It was voted for by all the members I see across the way who were there at the time, and it imposed a ban on Canadian energy being shipped off the west coast. This ban does not apply to U.S. tankers. U.S. tankers can come down from Alaska and take inland routes into U.S. refineries in the northwestern United States. This ban only applies to the loading of Canadian energy on Canadian ships leaving Canadian ports. It is a completely self-imposed double standard that means that no oil can flow through that northern route. Why is that important? That northern route is closer to Asia. It is cheaper to ship through that northern route because it is a shorter distance. It is also a deeper water port. Right now, in order to handle the potential expansion of TMX and a southern route in the Vancouver port, they are going to have to dredge along the Second Narrows Bridge because they cannot load the tankers to full capacity. They would be too low and those tankers would not be able to go through that particular waterway. That is not a problem in the northern route. That northern route is already a deep water port. This is a perfect example of the government causing a problem. This is hallmark Liberal politics. The Liberal policy causes a problem. The Liberal policies cause Canadian energy companies to abandon Canadian projects and to move Canadian dollars offshore to invest in other places. What is the solution to bad Liberal policy? It is more Liberal policy, more hoops and hurdles, bigger bureaucracies, and more red tape. The Conservatives have a different approach. We believe we should treat the root cause of the problem. The root cause of the problem right now in the energy sector is not a lack of demand, a lack of expertise or even a lack of capital, since there are Canadian companies with lots of money to invest. It is a lack of confidence in being able to get anything built after 10 years of Liberal policies killing things and blocking things. We now live in a world where private sector investors would rather build pipelines in war zones than in Canada. They would rather deal with bombs and bullets than with bureaucracy. The Liberal solution is to come along and say that we have a new complicated scheme, a new Major Projects Office and new lists and new hurdles. The government is going to take an ownership share, with all the distorting effects that would have, and that is the only way forward. Conservatives believe that, if we were to treat the root cause of the problem, which is to repeal bad Liberal policies, the bill we are debating today would be a huge step along that road. Let us lift the moratorium on Canadian shipping, put Canadian producers and exporters on a level playing field and get our resources to market.

Madam Speaker, it is an honour, as always, to rise in the House to speak on behalf of the residents of Calgary Signal Hill. Bill C-264 puts a tremendous opportunity before the House, which is to get rid of one more of the anti-energy, antidevelopment laws, which were put in place by the Trudeau Liberal government, that remain on the books today and continue to hamper and hinder economic development and business in Canada. First of all, I want to note that the MOU, the memorandum of understanding, between the federal government and the provincial government of Alberta, which was entered into in late 2025, just about a year ago, states that it would “enable the export of bitumen from a strategic deep-water port to Asian markets, including if necessary through an appropriate adjustment to the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act.” That makes clear the position of the government. Let us not go halfway, but all the way. Let us get rid of a law that has no purpose at all in environmental protection, in safety or in maritime shipping issues, but has simply been put in place to keep Alberta oil in the ground. There are several red herrings, if members can pardon the limited pun, in the waters today in respect of this debate. First, the oil tanker ban, Bill C-48, is somehow a logical extension of the voluntary exclusion zone that exists off Canada's west coast and applies to U.S. tanker traffic. Roughly five supertankers a week transit from Valdez, Alaska, to U.S. ports on the southern western coast of the United States. Those tankers stay offshore by agreement. This tanker ban, Bill C-48, covers only interior waters that those tankers do not transit on any regular basis. Second, on indigenous participation, one of the members opposite has suggested over the course of the debate on this bill that Conservatives do not care about indigenous consultation. It is quite the opposite. Under the last Conservative government of Stephen Harper, the Eagle Spirit Energy project was well-developed. That was an indigenous-owned pipeline that would have put in place the opportunity to transport Alberta crude oil to the west coast. That project died with Bill C-48 and other anti-energy Liberal laws. I believe in reconciliation, and true reconciliation comes from working together, particularly as economic partners. There is no effort on the part of this side of the House to limit that consultation and those processes to develop partnerships that would allow economic prosperity for all. Third, with respect to the red herrings is the environment and safety, it has been suggested that we want to cut corners. Nothing could be further from the truth. I am as concerned about environmental protection as any other Canadian. Let me note something from a former Liberal MP, Ms. Martha Hall Findlay, who was pretty succinct on this subject in respect of shipping risk. She stated, “There are risks associated with any kind of transportation with any goods, and not all of them are with oil tankers. All that singling out one part of one coast did was prevent more oil and gas from being produced that could be shipped off that coast”. Our west coast shipping industry, and indeed the Canadian maritime shipping industry writ large, is safe, capable and world-class. Perhaps the members opposite forming government at this point in time do not have confidence in that industry, but I certainly do. The ability for our industry to ship and ship safely is extensive. Last, I want to quote from Greg Ebel, the CEO of Enbridge, Canada's largest crude oil shipper. He said, “The tanker ban is a great example of how things will have to change to allow our country to maximize its economic potential. Let markets and real demand guide routes and capacities while government focuses on enabling the conditions for success”. I could not agree more. As my friends on this side of the House have made clear, Bill C-48 has never been about protecting the environment. It has never been about safety. It is only about keeping oil in the ground. It must be repealed.
Madam Speaker, I would request a recorded division.

title: Oral Questions: Steel and Aluminum Industry
turns: Mr. Speaker, 10 months ago, the industry minister promised that she was going to sue Stellantis and get the jobs back. Did she sue? No. Did she get the jobs back? No. Guess what. The industry minister is now saying that she is going to sue Stelco and get the jobs back. Has she sued? No. Has she got the jobs back? No. When will the minister stop the talk and get results? Does her word to workers actually mean anything?

Mr. Speaker, have the Conservatives ever denounced the American tariffs? No. Have they done anything to prevent them from hurting us? No. That is why we need to make sure we have our eyes wide open when dealing with Stellantis and when dealing with Stelco. When it comes to Stelco, we will do everything to bring the jobs back. There are 11 days left. The clock is ticking, and we will make sure to protect jobs.

Mr. Speaker, did the minister say anywhere in that answer that she was really going to sue? No. It is all talk and no results with the Liberals. She went on a diatribe about a whole bunch of things that the opposition should do in the face of American tariffs. Here is news for the minister: They are the government. They are the one who are supposed to do something about it. I will go back to this: Does the minister's word actually mean anything? At the expiration of her second 15-day notice, will she sue, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, it has been a month since Stelco announced that 350 Hamilton steelworkers would lose their jobs. Here is the Conservative five-point plan to protect the steel industry and its workers: get a steel deal with the U.S., which the Prime Minister promised a year and a half ago; end illegal foreign steel dumping; get rid of the industrial carbon tax; pre-approve multiple LNG projects; and sue Cleveland-Cliffs for breaking its contract to the Prime Minister. Which of these have you completed?
Mr. Speaker, I love it when the Conservatives quote from our plan. It just validates us even more. Jokes aside—

Mr. Speaker, my colleague just referred to how we can support our steelworkers. Our steelworkers are victims of the American tariffs, and we have been there to support them. That is why we will make sure we protect the jobs in Hamilton. Stelco needs to get back to us in 11 days. The CEO cannot say that he will advocate for American tariffs at a time when he committed to making sure that our steel would go south of the border tariff-free.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister broke his promise of getting a steel deal. The Liberals continue to allow the illegal dumping of foreign steel into the Canadian market. The Liberals refuse to cut the industrial carbon tax so that it is less expensive to work, produce and invest in Canada. The Liberals could take action today by taking Cleveland-Cliffs to court as they said they would. The Liberals' lack of action makes Canada look weak. Will Canada continue to get bullied by Trump and his buddies, or will the Prime Minister file the lawsuit today?

Mr. Speaker, we have started the legal process under the Investment Canada Act. Under the Investment Canada Act, we need to send a demand letter. The demand letter is supported by true evidence. Of course, we can provide it to the Conservatives if they want. It is 15 pages long with all the evidence. The undertakings are clear. We need to make sure that Cleveland-Cliffs protects the jobs at the Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, but it also needs to abide by the commitment of advocating in favour of tariff-free access. It cannot have its cake and eat it too.

title: Oral Questions: Labour
turns: Mr. Speaker, starting November 3, under a new Liberal policy, corporations will not have to prove they tried to hire a Canadian first. Instead, the Liberals are siding with corporations and institutions that do not want to put in the work to hire and train Canadians. They are doing this after 68,000 Canadians lost their jobs last month. Can the immigration minister tell those 68,000 people why their government decided they do not even deserve to get a first look?

Mr. Speaker, we will always favour Canadian labour and Canadian workers. What we are doing is ensuring that candidates with strong Canadian work experience for job offers in high-wage occupations are prioritized. It is a simpler process for key in-demand fields and for ensuring that we can recruit top, skilled talent. We are talking about health care. We are talking about engineering, technology and the skilled trades. This is core to our ability to build a strong economy, for our economic success and for supporting Canadian businesses right across the country.

Mr. Speaker, everything that member just said is wrong based on the immigration minister's announcement. The rule for giving a Canadian job to a temporary foreign worker before November 3 is simple. Before they hire from abroad, they must prove they tried to hire here. That is the whole rule, and it protects Canadians from wage suppression, but the Liberals have announced that they are scrapping it. That is nuts. In the middle of an affordability crisis, which part of trying to hire a Canadian first did the immigration minister think was too tough to manage?

Mr. Speaker, I welcome that question. In fact, I have been waiting to answer that. We have a clear focus building the strongest economy in the G7. Let me tell you what the Canadian Chamber of Commerce just posted: We welcome these changes to Express Entry and applaud the government and Minister Diab’s endeavour to reduce red tape in the immigration system, while also ensuring that international talent remains in Canada to fill labour gaps. In particular, eliminating the LMIA requirement for qualifying job offers—

Mr. Speaker, as we sat here, some sombre news just broke. BioWare, an Edmonton software firm, which produced beloved video games like Mass Effect and created jobs for Edmontonians, is being shuttered. The immigration minister just scrapped the last safeguard that forces IT corporations to try to hire Canadians before offering the job to somebody from outside the country. What does she have to say to those people from BioWare who just lost their jobs and who might not get a look because of her policy decision?

Mr. Speaker, let me set the record straight. The member has been in that seat for 10 or 11 years, and she knows better. She is continually misleading Canadians. This is a measure for permanent residents who are already here. This is cutting red tape and making it simpler. It is better. It is good for businesses. It is good for employers. Skilled individuals will be using it. This is not for temporary foreign workers.

title: Oral Questions: International Trade
turns: Mr. Speaker, steelworkers are losing their jobs. Four in 10 manufacturers have moved production south or plan to. That will mean over 100,000 jobs lost in two months. Those workers cannot wait another two and a half years for a deal. Will the Prime Minister deliver a better deal than he was looking at in August or should we be waiting for the next public opinion poll to find out what a good deal is?

Mr. Speaker, I think our colleague on the other side of the House is confusing our government with the weak-kneed approach of the Conservative Party in dealing with the Americans. We know they would have accepted any deal at any time to just get a deal that would not be in the interest of Canadian workers, the Canadian economy or the sovereignty of our country. We are going to do that difficult work that is necessary to protect our economy, and when that deal is available we will accept it.

Mr. Speaker, what is weak-kneed is concession after concession for over a year and a half, rather than building the strength of this country. Two straight months of zero growth and now the economy is shrinking. Parents are skipping meals so their kids can eat. We have another $733 billion of debt, with $6,000 per family just to pay the interest. Canadians did not elect a performer. They were promised a negotiator. Will the Prime Minister finally get the great deal he promised, or will this just be another month of political theatre while Canadians suffer?

Mr. Speaker, we understand that Canadian businesses and Canadian workers are facing extraordinary pressure because of these unjustified and illegal tariffs, unlike the Conservatives who resisted our government's strong decision to put in place retaliatory measures to protect sectors of our economy facing these unfair tariffs. Our government has said we will do whatever it takes for as long as it takes to protect Canadian workers but we are also talking to the Americans about getting the right deal for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Prime Minister said he was prepared to wait out the President for two years. Then he suddenly called six by-elections and suddenly getting a deal with the Americans is back on the agenda. As a member of the gill caucus, I can tell members that a fish out of water flip-flops less than the Prime Minister. Canadians were promised a master negotiator. When will he put Canadian jobs ahead of his political agenda, or are Canadian workers simply pawns in these by-election campaigns?

Mr. Speaker, I was Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for two years. I understand what a fish out of water looks like. Mr. Speaker, perhaps if you look to your left, you might have seen one. However, what is important is that all Canadians know, even the Conservatives should acknowledge, that our government will do everything it takes for as long as it takes to support Canadian workers and Canadian businesses facing these unfair and illegal tariffs. Yes, we will talk to the Americans and we will do the hard work necessary to get the right deal for Canada and Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, the economy has stalled with two straight months of zero growth and now it is shrinking. Manufacturers are packing up and heading south. Four in 10 have already moved production to the United States or are planning to. Stelco workers are still out of a job. Last week, the Prime Minister said he could wait two and a half more years without a trade deal. This week, he called the by-elections and he announced he is ready to start talks again. Will the Prime Minister finally get the deal he promised or will this just be another month of political theatre?

Mr. Speaker, the deal we will get will be the right deal for Canada, not just any deal. Our first priority has always been the future and well-being of Canadian workers. As for Stelco and all the other steel companies around, we will continue to support and work with companies that believe in Canada and that continue to invest in Canada. As for those that do not, we will not support them. By the way, there are five days left for Stelco.

Mr. Speaker, here are some facts: Homebuilding is down, food bank lineups are up and growth has flatlined. Now the great economist has broken his own fiscal anchors, piling on more national debt. This is the debt that our children will have to pay. The Prime Minister promised Canadians a great deal. He said he was the man to deliver it, and we are still waiting. He calls the by-elections, and then he calls Trump, so I will ask this again: Will the Prime Minister finally get the deal he promised, or is this just some more by-election political theatre?

Mr. Speaker, we will not take lessons from the Conservatives on political theatre, because that is all they do in the House. We are standing up to support Canadians. Conservatives can promote falsehoods all they want and string as many of them together as they want, but they do not constitute a truth. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. We have saved over $60 billion on government operations. We have the strongest fiscal position in the G7 and topped the G7 in the second quarter in terms of GDP growth. We have seen a spike in new business and foreign direct investment, and we have used our fiscal space to help Canadians—

title: Routine Proceedings: Petitions
turns: Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition on behalf of many Yukoners calling on the federal government to work with the Government of Prince Edward Island to develop and implement a guaranteed basic income demonstration project. For Yukoners, there is a particular interest in this project, given the higher cost of living in the north. The petitioners believe a well-designed demonstration project could provide valuable evidence to help inform future policy discussions aimed at reducing poverty and improving economic security across Canada. I am pleased to present this petition on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table a petition on behalf of Canadians who are concerned about the rising rate of crime in Saskatchewan. The petitioners believe these rising crime rates put Canadians at risk and pose a formidable threat to public safety, community well-being and economic prosperity. They also believe local businesses should not have to suffer the financial and economic consequences of the government's lack of action in addressing crime. As such, the petitioners ask all members of Parliament to repeal policies that have failed to effectively discourage criminal activity and protect public safety, and they call upon the federal government to deliver a detailed plan specifically addressing the rising rate of crime in rural Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to present a petition on behalf of my recently retired colleague, Larry Brock, signed by the great residents of Brantford—Brant South and people across western Ontario. The petitioners are raising the alarm over the planned expansion of medical assistance in dying, or MAID, to all Canadians diagnosed with any mental illness, starting on March 17, 2027. This June, the Special Joint Committee on MAID released its report, urgently recommending that the government immediately pause the expansion of MAID and exclude people suffering from a mental illness from accessing MAID. Even the Liberal chair of the committee said only elected parliamentarians should debate and decide this significant moral question, as they are held accountable to their constituents. Mr. Brock's petition calls on the government to immediately suspend the expansion of MAID scheduled for March 17, 2027, as recommended by the joint committee and allow Parliament to do its job by voting in favour of Bill C-218, which would exclude persons suffering from mental illness alone from receiving MAID.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present a petition on behalf of many Guelph residents, highlighting the important role Canada Post plays in communities across our country. The petitioners are calling on the government to continue supporting a strong, reliable and accessible postal service and to ensure that Canada Post can continue serving Canadians well into the future.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people from Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. Today, I rise to present a petition asking for federal funding for the fast-tracking and rebuilding of the Red Bridge, which is a very important monument of significance to the people of Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc and Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. I stand with the good people of Kamloops. This is my third time presenting such a petition.

Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to rise today to present petition e-7386, which over 2,100 Canadians signed. This petition comes out of the tragic death of Finlay van der Werken, a 16-year-old from Burlington who died waiting over eight hours in an Oakville hospital. His death demonstrates systemic failures that are occurring nationwide as a result of not having national standards when it comes to sepsis care. Finlay's family is turning tragedy into action and has moved this petition forward. They are calling on the government and the Minister of Health to strengthen federal oversight of the Canada Health Act, tie health transfer funding to enforceable national standards for pediatric emergency care in sepsis treatment and require transparent reporting and compliance to ensure timely, life-saving care for all Canadians. Over 18,000 Canadians die every year from sepsis. We can do better.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present two petitions. The first one is with regard to the post office in Mission, British Columbia, at 33191 First Avenue. Residents of Mission are concerned about the oversight of Canada Post, its management and the ineffectiveness of that management. Petitioners are calling upon the Government of Canada to work with our community to maintain full operations of the Canada Post location, which they note is the only representation of the federal government, save for the penitentiary, in our community.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition I would like to present today is with regard to the West Coast Corridor Resiliency Partnership. This is an agreement between Abbotsford, Chilliwack, Hope, Merritt and Princeton, calling for stronger, more resilient infrastructure along western Canada's critical trade corridors. The petitioners note that the 2021 floods, which they have still not received any funding for from the federal government, despite many promises, outlined the critical deficiencies in our infrastructure. If Canada is to actually meet its export objectives, some of the issues that need to be addressed in this corridor need to be fixed in order for Canada to meet those objectives.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise and table a petition that recognizes the $5 billion committed over three years by the Government of Canada to build on our health infrastructure. The petitioners are asking for the federal government to make sure that we allocate money toward re-establishing emergency services over at the Seven Oaks General Hospital. It is a very important issue for my local constituents. They are asking the federal government to make sure that they get an allocated portion so that they can get those emergency services restored.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to introduce three petitions. The first is petition e-7227, on pensions for injured workers. I rise to point out to the House that the petitioners note that when federal government employees experience severe or prolonged disability caused by a recognized occupational injury, they face financial disadvantages, including the loss of pension entitlements. While the Government Employees Compensation Act provides some compensation, the Public Service Superannuation Act does not protect these workers' pensions. As such, these petitioners call on the Government of Canada to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act to ensure that a recognized workplace injury causing disability does not result in the loss of a pension.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition is identical to many previous petitions introduced in the House over the years that express concern about the welfare of live horses exported for the purpose of slaughter. These horses often endure long journeys and inhumane conditions, and the federal government has no ability to ensure animal welfare in the importing country. The Government of Canada must take preventative measures to combat the undue suffering of animals. In light of the Minister of Agriculture's official response, in which he does not commit to ban this practice, the petitioners reiterate their calls to amend the health of animals regulations to ban the export of live horses for slaughter.

Mr. Speaker, finally, the third petition notes that when federally regulated workers are terminated without cause, their pay in lieu of notice of termination, as well as their severance pay, is inadequate, particularly for those who have served for many years. The petitioners point out that under common law, workers are entitled to significantly more severance pay, but almost all employers will only provide the minimum amount required by the Canada Labour Code. The petitioners call on this House to increase the statutory maximum pay in lieu of notice of termination and introduce penalties for companies that routinely underpay owed severance.

Mr. Speaker, dozens of my constituents, through my constituent Henry, provided me with this petition and asked me to present it on behalf of residents and citizens calling upon the House of Commons to support Bill C-218. They raise the point that Canadians with mental illness should be provided with treatment and support. Mental illness is complex and can include suicidal thoughts as a symptom. Several constituents have since recognized the AMAD report, but wanted me to present this. With that, I present this petition on behalf of constituents of the riding of Waterloo.

Mr. Speaker, I also received a petition from Robert with regard to the passage of Bill S-211. The petitioners are concerned about the proliferation of gambling advertisements. They recognize that many studies have now come out to show the increase in problem gambling among young men in this country. The petitioners are calling upon the assembled House of Commons to enact a national framework to regulate sports gambling advertisements. With that, I present this petition on behalf of constituents, not from Waterloo, but from the Toronto area. I said I would present it, and I am here to do so.

Mr. Speaker, this petition is very timely, given that Saturday is World Mental Health Day. These petitioners highlight that mental health is health, yet too many people in Canada cannot access appropriate and timely mental health addictions and substance use care. They highlight that mental illness is a leading cause of disability and imposes enormous human, social and economic costs, including lost productivity and lives lost. Canada's first national mental health strategy called for mental health spending to reach at least 9% of total health spending, while mental health advocates now call for a 12% target to address the growing needs. Only 6.3% of health care spending in Canada is directed to mental health. The petitioners are calling on the federal government to ensure that the $5-billion federal commitment for mental health services announced in 2017, which is set to expire in 2027, be renewed. M-31, on spending for mental health services, calls on the federal government to establish a national target of 12% of total health care spending for mental health services, and the petitioners ask the government to work with the provinces and territories to achieve that. Canada's premiers have called on the federal government to renew these expiring health funding agreements. The petitioners want them to be renewed and increased, and they want dedicated, long-term, predictable funding for mental health addictions and substance use services beyond March 2027. The petitioners call on the government to implement the objective of M-31 by establishing that national target of 12% of total health care spending for mental health services and ensuring that transparent public reporting on mental health funding access and outcomes is embedded in it.
Mr. Speaker, may I have unanimous consent to present a petition?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues. I present a petition on behalf of petitioners within my community. They note that during COVID, the use of virtual services became more common, particularly for people in the disabilities community. What has happened since is that the existing criteria for tax exemption for supports for people in the disability community have not been extended to these virtual services. There is a tax unfairness that should be remedied. Petitioners ask that the Government of Canada please establish a new standard for tax exemptions to enable organizations to offer tax-free virtual support services and programs to disabled Canadians and increase their access to these services and supports in their daily lives.

title: Adjournment Proceedings: Correctional Service of Canada
turns: Mr. Speaker, I am returning to a question I raised regarding CORCAN last week. CORCAN is the inmate skills development wing of Corrections Canada. Last week, I asked why CORCAN employs 608 individuals, at a cost of $66 million in salaries alone, to train only 1,056 inmates in rudimentary tasks like farm chores, apple picking and sewing. The public safety minister responded to my question with a heartwarming story about a trip he took with the Governor General to a prison in Saskatchewan. That was a very unsatisfactory answer, so I am back again to point out that the per-prisoner cost of a CORCAN education per year is $62,000, which is half the tuition at Harvard University and is also more than the average Canadian earns in a year. At this price, one would assume that the investment is justified by astoundingly good public safety outcomes and a very low rate of recidivism for people who receive CORCAN training, but as it turns out, that is not the case. The government has defended CORCAN by pointing over and over again, when I raise these questions in this place, to a research report by Corrections Canada published in 2014 that found that former inmates who find post-release employment are less likely to reoffend. Of course that is true, but I am not sure that the government read the rest of the research report, because it concludes, based on measurable data, that “Involvement in CORCAN employment [while incarcerated] was not found to have a significant impact on the length of time that offenders retained their first job post-release” and that “CORCAN participation was not directly linked to reductions in recidivism.” In other words, CORCAN does not make a person any more likely to maintain employment after serving time in prison and therefore makes no difference to that person's employment status and does not reduce their likelihood of reoffending. In fact, the research in the same study found “no significant differences” whether prisoners worked for CORCAN, worked a non-CORCAN job in prison or did nothing at all. Here is an interesting fact. Eight times as many prisoners, 7,944 to be exact, worked while incarcerated in non-CORCAN jobs last year compared to only 1,056 in CORCAN jobs, at a much lower cost. CORCAN is therefore as redundant as it is inefficient and expensive. Why are we spending $66 million to add nothing at all to the skills prisoners receive? The minister asked us to look at what he calls the remarkable success of CORCAN. I see no success whatsoever. Why does this program exist at all?

Mr. Speaker, through CORCAN, the Correctional Service of Canada actively enhances the safety and security of our institutions and our communities. CORCAN programming does that by providing offenders with a sense of purpose, promoting pro-social behaviour and allowing them to participate in meaningful work. This reduces the risk of violence among offenders in CSC institutions, thereby benefiting the safety of other inmates as well as our correctional staff. CORCAN's public safety benefits extend much further than within our correctional institutions, as CORCAN actively enhances public safety by providing offenders with the employment skills and experience necessary to become productive, law-abiding citizens and skilled workers when they return to their communities. We all want safer communities for our friends, our loved ones and our constituents. That is why I am proud to acknowledge that employability-related training is available at all federal institutions. This is in addition to the CORCAN-operated on-the-job training sites at 34 CSC institutions across the country and in six community-based operations. Additionally, Correctional Service Canada provides apprenticeship opportunities to offenders through certain on-the-job training assignments in institutions, as well as through the CORCAN community industries program during transitional employment. Research clearly demonstrates that offenders who are employed in their communities are less likely to reoffend and return to federal custody. This is why vocational training for offenders remains so important. Not only is it our duty to do so, but it is effective and it works. It provides offenders with knowledge and skills that are transferable to the workplace and are aligned with industry and the Canadian labour market. Vocational training also results in industry-recognized certificates that enhance the employability of offenders, thereby promoting greater rehabilitation. In fiscal year 2025-26, there were 20,714 certificates earned by offenders for their work in vocational training programs. Further, staff and contractors, and general employment services available in the community, assisted offenders under community supervision to obtain 2,425 community job placements. In response to the member opposite's question, I would like to advise that offenders participate in training and work programs that are directly transferable and in line with the Canadian labour market. This includes areas of farming, construction, welding, manufacturing and work in the food industry, among others. These are the skills being promoted by CSC facilities, including within CORCAN.

Mr. Speaker, the government asked Corrections Canada to make cuts to save $132 million over the next three years. To that end, Corrections Canada has eliminated 25 community employment coordinators. These are the people who actually help prisoners find jobs after they are in prison. Firing these employment coordinators saved $2.7 million. Now, it seems to me the wrong cuts are being made. Eliminating a totally unnecessary and ineffective program like CORCAN would save at least $198 million, and that is just the salaries, over the next three years and would save the jobs of the employment coordinators, who actually make a difference in finding jobs for ex-convicts and making our communities safer. Does the government have it backwards? Were the researchers at Corrections Canada right when they said, in a report to the minister, “CORCAN is an outdated model”?

Mr. Speaker, I do not share that opinion. I think CORCAN does help the labour market, and it helps inmates to achieve their rehabilitation and be productive in our society. I would just remind the hon. member that as members of Parliament, we all want safer communities for our friends, loved ones and constituents. Having inmates going into permanent jobs, jobs that are giving them skills and a salary, is a good way to prevent reoffending. It is in pursuit of this goal that I am pleased to highlight the positive interventions provided by CORCAN that provide offenders with the skills and competencies necessary and that are aligned with labour needs. As stated, there is a direct correlation between an offender's ability to find employment and rates of recidivism.

title: Oral Questions: International Trade
turns: Mr. Speaker, I ask when. Today is the mid-terms, and that reminds us the Prime Minister promised in the election he was going to negotiate a victory for Canadians, a big win. Since that time, he has done nothing but lose, with American tariffs doubled and vastly broadened. While Canadians are lined up at food banks, businesses are leaving and Canadians are losing their jobs, the Prime Minister said he could wait another two and a half years to get a deal. Then suddenly, on Sunday, he put out a headline-grabbing tweet saying he would get a deal in the next few weeks. When will the theatrics be over? Will the Prime Minister get back to the table, fight the tariffs and negotiate the promised win?

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition would probably be the leading expert in the House of Commons in terms of theatrics. I think what is important for Canadians is to know that their government will always be there to support workers and industries that are facing the effects of these unjustified and illegal tariffs. One point where we perhaps agree with the Leader of the Opposition is that this is causing economic hardship for Canadians. That is why we are supporting Canadians and we are not going to rush into any old bad deal that the Leader of the Opposition would have accepted a year ago because he would not have had the guts to face—

Mr. Speaker, that is an easy one. If the member had the guts to face down the Americans, he would be at the negotiating table right now, but he is not. He is not, because the Prime Minister's tweet on the weekend was not about getting back to the table. He is not at the table; he is doing photo ops. It was, once again, theatrics designed to distract from his disastrous record here at home. Just today, Daily Bread Food Bank in Toronto is saying that demand is up 333% since 2019. When will the Prime Minister stop the theatrics and get a deal?

Mr. Speaker, again, the Leader of the Opposition is the expert in theatrics from trying to cover up a disastrous record. There is no better expert in the House than the Leader of the Opposition. He is right. We are not at the negotiating table right now. Do members know why? It is because we walked away when it was in Canada's interest to show the Americans that we were not going to accept a bad deal. The Leader of the Opposition would never have walked away. He would have accepted a bad deal that would have undercut our sovereignty and hurt Canadian workers. That is not what we are going to do. We are going to continue to pursue those conversations with the Americans to get the right deal.

Mr. Speaker, he has accepted a bad deal. He has accepted 50% tariffs on steel, aluminum, mould makers and others. For the 100,000 people who lost their job in the last month, it is a bad deal. It is a bad deal right now for the one in three Canadians who is skipping meals because they cannot afford to eat, and for the 50% of Canadians who are plunging into their savings just to pay for the basic essentials of life. When will we get the good deal that Canadians demand so Canadians can afford to eat and to pay their bills?

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has been very consistent from the beginning: We are going to do the difficult work Canadians expect of their government to get the deal that is in the best interest of Canadians. Meanwhile, unlike the Leader of the Opposition, we are not going to neglect to support Canadian workers and Canadian businesses, and to work with provincial governments to support those sectors of our economy that are facing these unjustified and illegal tariffs. We are going to do both, and we are going to stick with it for as long as it takes to get the job done.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister blames this economy on the president's tariffs, and then turns around and says that we can wait the president out for another two and a half years. Both cannot be true. These tariffs are either serious enough that he walked away from negotiations and left Canadians to absorb the costs, or mild enough to wait it out until 2029. He should tell that to the steelworker whose shift was cut, tell that to the lumber town for which the mill was the town and tell that to the two million families living with uncertainty. Will he pick a lane today, or will he keep exploiting the pain of our people for by-election politics?
Mr. Speaker, what our Prime Minister has been doing is helping create jobs in this country when they are not doing it, like the 8,000 jobs in—

Mr. Speaker, what our Prime Minister is doing is helping create jobs in this country, like the 8,000 new jobs in Montreal, the 18,000 new jobs in Darlington, the 20,000 new jobs in Pickering and the 8,000 new jobs in Kitimat. All the Conservatives do is talk down this country. They are the pirates of pessimism. Why do they not help build some jobs in this country?

Mr. Speaker, we have lost over 100,000 jobs over the last two months. Canadians elected a negotiator. Instead, they got Beijing's new world order and, at Davos, a world in rupture, with concession after concession. We got a negotiation from weakness on terms he did not define, and then he walked away on terms he still hides. He was rebuffed by Britain over the defence bank and rebuffed by France and Germany at a nothing summit. He called by-elections; then he called President Trump. It is grand theatre, with nothing for taxed and tariffed jobs. Will the Prime Minister return his minister to Washington or make two million workers wait two and a half years because Liberals put politics and party ahead of the country?

Mr. Speaker, what the Prime Minister will do is not talk down Canada. He will build Canada. That is why we are creating jobs. We are creating jobs in Newfoundland, jobs in Nova Scotia, jobs in Quebec, jobs in Manitoba, jobs in Alberta and jobs in British Columbia. Why do the Conservatives not try to create a job or two?

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister got elected on the promise that he could do a deal with Trump. Instead of getting the deal done, the Prime Minister has been playing political theatre. First, he called six by-elections. Then he called Trump. All the while, the ongoing trade war is hurting rural manufacturers and farmers. Costs are going up, revenues are going down, and life is more unaffordable. The Prime Minister continues to use defence as a political pawn, which is making our military less capable and Canada more vulnerable. The Prime Minister has been in office 599 days. When will he finally get the deal he promised?

Mr. Speaker, Canada is proudly rearming, rebuilding and reinvesting in the Canadian Armed Forces. The member is aware of this. We have met the NATO 2% target five years ahead of schedule and accelerated our investments to put Canada on a path to meet our new target. He is aware of that as well. Canada's defence industry is a major contributor to our economy, generating more than $17 billion in annual revenues and supporting over 81,000 jobs across the country. Now more than ever, we need to be united in this House. We need to reaffirm Canadian sovereignty by strengthening our military. This is exactly what we are doing.

title: Oral Questions: National Defence
turns: Mr. Speaker, the cadet program has taught generations of young Canadians self-confidence, teamwork and leadership. As a former 533 Sabre Squadron cadet myself, I know that this program provides tremendous value for Canada. The Liberals have been killing this program for years. They cut summer camps to a fraction of their pre-pandemic size. New cadets do not even receive uniforms anymore. After cadets volunteered for weeks selling poppies outside grocery stores, the Liberals are delivering more disappointment for these kids by cutting fun weekend activities for the rest of the year. Why do the Liberals have $500 million for Brazilian rainforests but none for our cadets?

Mr. Speaker, with all due respect to our colleague, I agree with only one point he made, and that is that the cadets serve a very important purpose in this country. It is a great opportunity for young people to learn vital skills, particularly leadership. In fact, that is why the government increased funding for the cadet program, an increase in funding that led to the number of recruits being at 50,000. Now it is in excess of 70,000. We take note, of course, of the very important points that parents have raised and that organizations have raised on this, and we are committed to the cadet program from start to finish.

Mr. Speaker, it is all good news from the government. It cut the glider weekend, but the cadets still get to march up and down the square every Tuesday night. The review that the Liberals are talking about is not doing anything to make up for the disappointment that the cadets are facing right now. The Prime Minister has cannibalized this program, and these latest cuts are just another nail in the coffin. In fact, cadets in Alberta who fundraised for a weekend activity have now been told that it is cancelled, because these Liberals cut the staffing budget. This program is a critical part of our national identity, but instead of supporting it, the Prime Minister is cutting it. Why will the Liberals not step up and stop these cuts to cadets?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for highlighting how important cadet programs are to all our ridings and provinces. We have heard the concern of the cadets, and the minister issued a statement today that the program will be revised. The last economic statement really provided additional funding: $250 million for the program to train more of the armed forces and $27 million for the cadets. It is a very important program. We support the cadets. This program will ensure the—

Mr. Speaker, this is a lot of talk from the Liberals about sweeping cuts to Canada's cadet programs that are undeniable. It does not matter what they are saying about what they have done and what they have announced. For tens of thousands of Canadians across our country, young Canadians, the cadets offer team-building, mentorship and opportunities to build confidence and leadership skills, yet the Liberal government has cancelled their training and competition, everything but the cadets' weekly parade night. Will the Liberals reverse this incomprehensible cut to Canada's cadets, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, I do have respect for the member. We have worked together for many years. However, he knows, with all his experience, as we all do, that when members of Parliament have an opportunity to really speak, they speak with their vote. In the spring economic statement, there was funding allocated for many things, including cadets. They voted against it. Now they have an opportunity to correct that mistake. In the supplementary estimates (B), they can vote for it and therefore support cadets. Let us get behind cadets. This program is great.

Mr. Speaker, let me get this straight. Liberal MPs claim they are making historic investments in our military. They say the military is investing in people and training. They say billions of dollars have been added in national defence, but the Liberals will not fund Canada's cadets. Why would the Liberals cut this successful leadership program in communities right across Canada? It makes absolutely no sense, and they continue to spin their wheels. Just restore the funding.

Mr. Speaker, in this place, votes always do the talking. We will see how they vote. Will they correct themselves when they have a chance to vote for the supplementary estimates? Again, it is the supplementary estimates (B), for every member of the House. In fact, if Conservatives want to continue down this path of questioning, I am more than happy to respond. Every single one of us is. It opens a pathway to talk about defence. We are absolutely behind the Canadian Armed Forces with historic funding in support of the men and women who defend this country. We will never waver from that. They voted against it every single time.

Mr. Speaker, the cadet program teaches young Canadians discipline, value and honour, yet this week, the government paused military cadet training until April 2027. I think of the cadets in Hearst, Timmins, Cochrane, Kapuskasing, Kirkland Lake and all of Canada, young boys and girls who gather every week at their local armoury to build skills and serve their community. Why is the government cutting funding for programs that turn young Canadians into soldiers?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know the member very well, but I do know something about his background. I know he has served his community as a mayor in the past. He has the respect of his community. Certainly, mayors, premiers, prime ministers and all governments understand the importance of service. Cadets fit within that, of course. This is why we affirm our commitment to the cadets, a program with its origins going back to the 1800s, 1862 in fact. We will not waver from that. We support the cadet program. In fact, the comments yesterday of the deputy minister at the public accounts committee, which are on public record, are an affirmation of this. I point the member to—

Mr. Speaker, in communities throughout Columbia—Kootenay—Southern Rockies, cadet programs give young people valuable opportunities to develop leadership, discipline, confidence and teamwork. For many youth in our rural communities, these programs provide experience, skills and mentorship they might not otherwise have access to, yet the current government is forcing cadet programs to scale back training, cancel activities and restrict opportunities because of funding cuts. Why is the government taking opportunities away from young Canadians in our communities who are working hard to build skills, serve others and become the next generation of leaders?

Our colleague is an outstanding member of Parliament, Mr. Speaker, who has served his community as a police officer. He fundamentally understands the importance of service. I would simply repeat what I said earlier. All Conservatives have an opportunity to get behind supplementary estimates (B), which affirm support for the cadet program. We will see what they do. Votes always do the talking in this place. What will Conservatives do? I point them to the statement of the hon. Minister of National Defence earlier today.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals promised to expand the reserves and rebuild our military, yet reservists have faced limits on paid Remembrance Day participation, while cadet training weekends and competitions are being cancelled in Ontario and British Columbia. How does the minister expect to recruit more Canadian soldiers when his government cannot support those already serving? Will he restore these activities, or does the military expansion happen only in Liberal announcements?

Mr. Speaker, focus on recruitment has been a steadfast commitment of this government and that will continue. Efforts to promote diversity within the forces are within that goal, and we respect everyone and everyone's faith and background. This includes within the Canadian military, of course. As far as the cadet program is concerned, again, I point my colleague to my comments from earlier. He can vote for the supplementary estimates and affirm his support for the cadet program.

title: Oral Questions: Natural Resources
turns: Mr. Speaker, true sovereignty is the ability to live our lives as we choose. In 2026, achieving that goal requires secure access to critical minerals and energy. Last week in Montreal, the Prime Minister and the European Union launched the Canada-EU alliance for the future. Can the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources tell the House how this new alliance will open doors for clean British Columbian LNG and critical—

Mr. Speaker, here is what our relationship with Europe is doing: three million new tonnes of LNG being shipped to Europe, creating thousands of jobs in this country; a new treaty with the European Investment Bank to invest in Canadian mines here in Canada, creating jobs in this country; and a European country investing $30 billion in our energy sector this year. That is what our relationship with Europe is doing.

Mr. Speaker, 10 first nations have now gone to court to challenge the designation of the so-called Pacific link pipeline in the national interest. They point out that it contradicts and violates their treaty rights and constitutional rights, because how can they possibly assess whether a project impacts their treaty rights when the route is not finalized, the engineering has not been done and there is no environmental impact statement? The Tsartlip First Nation is one of the 10 and is completely within the boundaries of my riding. I thank them in their language, SENĆOŦEN: HÍSW̱KE SIÁM. Someone has to stand up for the British Columbia southern coast, for the Salish Sea, for our precious marine protected areas—

Mr. Speaker, the consultation that happened in listing the project the member is referring to was the most intensive consultation ever held. There were more than 100 submissions. There were more than 100 in-person meetings. It was the most comprehensive consultation that has been done on a project, and it was the earliest consultation that has been done. We will continue to work with indigenous peoples to make sure projects are properly reviewed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am persnickety about the Standing Orders, and I particularly like Standing Order 16. I have never heckled in this place in 15 years. I know some members do, and I find it offensive when opposition members heckle members of the government's cabinet, but I find it even more offensive when the hon. member for Simcoe North, who happens to be one of the MPs whom I never hear heckle, is shouted down by the bellowing of the Minister of Energy. I would ask that cabinet members try to set an example.

title: Oral Questions: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have lost total control of immigration to our country. Now they are planning a staggering 662,000 new permanent residents in the coming year. That is an all-time Canadian record at a time when young Canadians are locked out of the housing market, youth unemployment is surging and hospital wait times, listen to this, are nearly 30.7 weeks long. Why is the Prime Minister hiding a record 662,000 permanent residents in the budget instead of fixing the problems he created in housing, in jobs and in health care?

Mr. Speaker, I am proud of our immigration plan, which keeps our levels stable, predictable, sustainable and growing our economy. All the other side wants to do is oppose. The Conservatives want to oppose giving provinces more freedom to retain valuable workers. They want to oppose doing the right thing for Ukrainians and Hong Kongers. They want to oppose welcoming doctors and top researchers. They want to oppose giving rural communities the flexibility to thrive. Immigration policy is economic policy, and the other side does not get it.

Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada data shows that young men aged 18 to 34 now vastly outnumber young women in 40 of Canada's 41 biggest cities. In Windsor, it is 127 men for every 100 women. That ratio is worse than China's gender imbalance after their one-child policy. Meanwhile, youth unemployment is at record high levels. Immigration data confirms how it happened. The Prime Minister has invited far more young men than women to Canada. Can the immigration minister explain why she has allowed this massive gender imbalance to happen?

Mr. Speaker, my department looks at gender balance analysis. Let me tell the House this: Our immigration levels plan is predictable, sustainable, balanced and right for Canada. If the member opposite does not want to believe me, and I know she does not, why does she not believe the business council of her own province, which said it “welcomes the Government of Canada continued focus on strengthening Canada’s economy...including through economic immigration and reforms to better align...programs with local labour market [needs].”

Mr. Speaker, to recap, the Prime Minister has just announced the biggest permanent resident increase in Canadian history. Statistics Canada data shows his immigration selection process has already created a massive gender imbalance among youth. Youth unemployment is at record highs, and today The Globe and Mail warned, “it can be a toxic combination when those thousands of 'extra', unattached men also struggle to find well-paying jobs”. What is the plan to address this gender imbalance and unemployment rate among youth in Canada?
Mr. Speaker, our budget has a number of initiatives for young Canadians. Young Canadians and all Canadians are the first—

Mr. Speaker, our budget 2026 has a number of initiatives for young Canadians. We also have many initiatives for employment and all people who are Canadians in the country. Conservatives want Canadians to see record arrivals. We know that is not true. Let me tell the House what lawyer Rick Lamanna is saying. He says, “These people...have been here for quite a while”. Daniel Bernhard of the Institute for Canadian Citizenship, says, “They're already housed. They're already working.” RBC Economics is saying these will create no housing affordability risk from modest population growth.

Mr. Speaker, for thousands of Hong Kongers across the country, Canada represents hope. In 2021, when we opened the Hong Kong immigration pathways, we made a promise that those who had already given so much to Canada would be able to stay and continue contributing. However, strong demand for these pathways led to long wait times, turning hope to uncertainty. Can the immigration minister please share how our new immigration levels plan will keep our word to Hong Kongers and benefit all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her strong advocacy. I am very proud of our immigration plan that will finalize all Hong Kong pathway applications in 2027. We met members from the community, heard their stories and saw first-hand what this commitment means to them and their families. These are highly skilled individuals, physicians, engineers and entrepreneurs, who are already contributing to our economy and strengthening our communities. Our commitment recognizes their contributions and gives them the certainty to continue building the future. That is the right thing to do.

title: Statements by Members: The Budget
turns: Mr. Speaker, they are the masters of a looming disaster. Job one for the Liberal government should have been saving Canadians money on fuel, food and homes. Instead, they added $765 billion in new debt. The Liberals keep claiming Conservatives are talking down Canada. We are not. We are calling out a government whose out of control spending keeps Canadians down and dependent on the government. After 11 years, the Liberals have one answer for every problem, and it is another program, another bureaucracy, another billion dollars. They drive up the cost of living then hand Canadians another government program. That is not compassion; it is dependency by design. The Liberals measure success by more spending, more programs and more sign-ups. For the Liberals, programs are more important than people, spending money is more important than getting results and growing government is more important than Canadians standing on their own feet. Success should not be measured by how many Canadians are signing up for programs, but by how many Canadians get off them. The Liberal culture of dependency is a dangerous way of thinking. As long as the Liberals keep governing this way, they will keep making life worse for the Canadians they are trying to help.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government had one job, to make life more affordable for Canadians. Instead, the costly credit card budget adds a staggering $765 billion in new debt over five years, the largest borrowing spree in Canadian history. The Prime Minister may divide spending across three credit cards to make it look smaller, but Canadians know the truth. Borrowed money must be paid back. That means higher debt interest costs, higher taxes in the future and more pressure on family budgets today. Conservatives called for relief on fuel, food and housing costs, and for a serious effort to reduce wasteful spending. Instead, the government plans even more spending while breaking its promise to reduce debt. The budget is not a plan for prosperity. It is a plan for being mastered by debt, and Canadians will be left paying the bill.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians expect their government to manage public finances responsibly. That means a credible fiscal anchor to bring debt under control, a path to a balanced budget and a full accounting of government borrowing. This costly credit card budget falls well short. Federal debt continues to rise with no plan to balance the overall budget. Debt interest will cost Canadians more than $60 billion this year, more than health care and more than national defence. CPP contributions are there to support Canadians' retirement. They should never be used as permission for Ottawa to borrow more. The $765 billion more in debt piled on in this budget will ultimately drive up interest rates and taxes. For people in Waterdown, Paris and Binbrook in my area, this costly credit card budget means higher mortgage payments and higher car payments, the very last thing they can afford.

I would really like to thank all of the citizens and organizations in Nipissing—Timiskaming who participated in the budget process. They submitted briefs and participated in round tables. I want to say a very special thank you to the North Bay and District Chamber of Commerce, because it organized a special round table for small business. I really look forward to coming back to my riding and speaking about the productivity mega deduction that applies to small businesses.

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, we have yet another stunning example of public policy decisions benefiting well-connected Liberal insiders. Dominic Barton, the chair of Invest in Canada, and Patrick Pichette, the head of digital transformation Canada, were early investors in Cohere AI through Radical Ventures and Inovia Capital, respectively. Both have long-standing ties to the Prime Minister and were recently appointed to major government roles. The Liberals just gave Cohere $1.6 billion in taxpayer money, which will increase the value of Cohere and, potentially, Barton's and Pichette's ground-floor investments. Why is it that when the Liberals claim to be acting in the public interest, it is well-connected Liberal insiders who do well self-dealing while the people they govern suffer?

Mr. Speaker, the theme of today's question period appears to be talking down Canada and talking down Canadian champions, so let us get after this. Cohere is a Canadian champion, one of the only LLMs in the world that is not owned by the U.S. or China. It is a Canadian champion. It is a Canadian powerhouse. It promotes and preserves Canadian AI sovereignty. It allows us to build a strong AI network here at home. It does that by ensuring that Canadians are part of that success.

Mr. Speaker, this is not about Cohere. Canadians have seen this self-dealing Barton Liberal playbook before with McKinsey. They shape public policy and then benefit from the results. Patrick Pichette and Jordan Jacobs were both appointed to the Prime Minister's AI council, and both sit on the board of Cohere. Jacobs co-founded Radical Ventures, where Barton is a partner. Together, they backed Cohere in its early stages and advised the Prime Minister on Canada's AI strategy. Now the company they invested in has received $1.6 billion in taxpayer funding. When will the Liberals stop using taxpayer dollars to align public policy that enriches well-connected Liberals?

Mr. Speaker, the real scandal here is the fact that the Conservatives are ignoring the facts. The facts are that Cohere is going to create more than 1,000 new high-paying jobs to employ Canadians and that Cohere is going to invest $1.7 billion into creating capacity in Canada. That is how we build Canadian champions. The Conservatives may not like success. That is clearly what we are seeing from their own success and their own record. The reality is that we are going to help build Canadian champions. We are going to make sure Canadian companies create the jobs here at home so they can remain at home and build Canadian companies that are going to make Canadians proud for decades ahead.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is again off signing unenforceable and meaningless declarations overseas while he fails to feed a single Canadian or house a single young couple here at home.
