In fact, since Food Banks Canada released a damning report that revealed that here in Canada there is a 116% increase in the number of people relying on food banks, which is at a crisis level according to the organization, the Prime Minister has not uttered a single, solitary word. Why not stop spending our money abroad, and bring home affordable food at home?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians know better. They know that the Leader of the Opposition speaks a good game, but when it comes to voting in the House, they know that he did not vote in favour of the Canada groceries and essentials benefit. That is the measure that is putting food on the table. That is the measure that is helping 12 million Canadians. On this side of the House, we know what we need to do. We are going to fight for Canadians every single day.

Mr. Speaker, Food Banks Canada is reporting an 8% increase in visitors this year compared to last, double what it was seven years ago. One-fifth of visitors were actually employed and one-third were children. Food inflation is outpacing wage growth again this year according to the report, and things are becoming more difficult for many families despite the many promises from the Prime Minister. Will he at least acknowledge that relying on food banks is the unfortunate reality for far too many Canadian families, or is he totally out of touch with reality?

Mr. Speaker, I would like, on behalf of all members of this House, to thank the people at Food Banks Canada. They do very important work across this country, and I think we should all applaud their work and thank them for their work. We implemented one of the recommendations, which is now called the Canada groceries and essentials benefit. With that, 12 million people in this country will receive a benefit to help them with groceries. On this side of the House, we are always going to do what is right to support Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, for a year and a half those arrogant Liberals have been standing in the House and telling us how great everything is. The Prime Minister says affordability is the best it has been in a decade. If that were true, I would not be getting emails like this every single day, and 2.35 million Canadians would not be using the food bank in a single month. Then we have Julia from St. Thomas, the mother of an 11-year-old. She owns a home and has done everything right. She is selling her belongings on Facebook Marketplace so that she can buy her daughter shoes. Are the numbers wrong or are the Liberals?

Mr. Speaker, any mother who is facing hardship and has to sell things on Facebook Marketplace to feed her child is something I think we could all say would be an abomination in Canada. That is why I think that member of Parliament should go and tell that mother, Julia, that he voted against the school nutrition program, that he voted against the Canada child benefit program and that he voted against the investments in skills training. Let us add the groceries and essentials benefit. Every solution that we have proposed, as the Government of Canada, to help vulnerable people in this country, those guys vote against. In fact, they—

Mr. Speaker, we live in an era where global events are having local impacts. Rising protectionism, energy shocks and supply chain disruptions are all converging to drive up costs. Families and workers in my constituency of Davenport are doing their best to navigate this rapidly changing world and are looking to the Canadian government to provide long-term economic vision and a bridge to the future. Can the Minister of Finance tell workers and families how our government is stepping up to help make their lives more affordable?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for the great work she is doing for all of her constituents in Davenport. She really is an exceptional member of our team. She is right. This team, this government, and this Prime Minister have always been acting to make life more affordable for Canadians. One of the latest measures we announced was the extension of the suspension of the federal excise tax on fuel. This is going to help Canadians. Canadians know, and they are watching today, that we will have their backs. We are always going to be there for them. Every day is a good day to work for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, a policeman told me there is a hot new meat market in Edmonton. It is not a trendy butcher shop. It is literally a “hot” meat market, as in stolen meat. There has been a rash of meat thefts. Brazen beef bandits fill shopping carts with the pricey stuff. They escape and sell the meat on the black market. After 11 years of Liberal soft-on-crime laws and government overspending that feeds inflation, this is Canada today. When will the Liberals stop butchering our economy and do something to get it back on track?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the concern expressed by my friend. That matter is an issue of local jurisdiction for Edmonton police. I invite the member opposite to bring that up with Edmonton police to ensure that those who are responsible for this are held to account.

title: Oral Questions: Justice
turns: Mr. Speaker, in Kelowna, a man violently chokes his wife. He is arrested. He is released on bail. Thirty minutes later, he shows up again. He assaults her again. He chokes her again. He is arrested again. Under the Liberal laws, guess what: He is released on bail again. The Liberals promised they would fix the broken bail system, but nothing has changed. Under their watch, intimate partner violence is up 40%. How many times must a woman be attacked before the Liberals put her safety first?

Mr. Speaker, because we are so concerned about incidents such as this, we put forward the Protecting Victims Act in Bill C-16, and we put forward the bail reform legislation. It all passed in June. Those laws have been implemented starting July 15, but it is the job of the provinces to make sure they are applying these pieces of legislation. The changes have gone into effect in the code. It is time for the provinces to catch up.

Mr. Speaker, the criminals are laughing at the Liberal justice system, and the victims are the ones paying the price. A guy with 274 convictions gets bail. Convicted child killers and rapists are attending cooking classes and law school. McDonald's, booze, drugs and illegal guns are being delivered by drones into our maximum-security prisons. It sounds insane but that is the sad reality under the Liberal government. Will the Liberals put the criminals behind bars and stop putting Canadian lives at risk?

Mr. Speaker, the federal government is responsible for the Criminal Code of Canada. We have made an unprecedented number of changes to stiffen our laws, to make sure criminals will serve longer sentences and so repeat offenders do not get bail, but it is the job of the provinces to apply these new changes. I hope the provinces will catch up.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals constantly boast about how they fixed bail in their eyes. We as Conservatives warned them that they did not go far enough. Recently in Kelowna, a man was accused of assaulting and choking his intimate partner. He was released on bail. Within 30 minutes, he is alleged to have been back at her house, again choking her, and now breaching a no-contact order. He was again released on bail. People expect the government to protect the most vulnerable. Will the Liberals admit that their bail changes did not go far enough, and commit to acting?

Mr. Speaker, if my hon. colleague had actually read the legislation that we put forward, he would know that, on the advice of the provincial government in British Columbia, we added specific provisions to address cases of intimate partner violence that involve strangulation, because we know and accept that it is predictive of future violence. When we adapt these laws, we expect provinces to put them into action by appropriately resourcing the system and those who are appointed to make decisions to put these rules into force. Tragic circumstances such as these can motivate change. We have taken action, and we are looking forward to seeing the changes implemented by the people within positions—

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice asked whether I bothered to read his bill. Did he bother to read my bill on the intimate partner violence that happened to Bailey McCourt? I will let the House know that this offence occurred in Kelowna. Do members know what else occurred in Kelowna? The murder of Bailey McCourt, who was killed three hours after her abuser left the courthouse after conviction. It is our job as parliamentarians to protect the most vulnerable. The Liberals should have passed our jail not bail act, which was exponentially harder on bail. Will the Liberals admit they have a problem on their hands and they need to fix it now?

Mr. Speaker, the member questions whether I read his bill. He should know very well that I have, because we worked together across partisan lines to rewrite that bill. He should know that we worked together with family members in the tragic circumstances of Bailey McCourt's murder to ensure that she did not die in vain, and to change the law in this country to protect future victims of intimate partner violence and murder against harms we know are preventable. I appreciated the member's non-partisan spirit of collaboration. It is a shame that it seems to have come to an end.

title: Oral Questions: Points of Order
turns: Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions, and I believe that if you seek it, you will find unanimous consent to allow the member for South Surrey—White Rock to repeat his S. O. 31.

Mr. Speaker, Standing Order 16(2) specifically indicates that we are not supposed to interrupt people when they are speaking. I know that it certainly does happen in the House. However, when the member for South Surrey—White Rock was giving his S. O. 31, the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan was extremely loud in an otherwise very quiet room, directing some very personal comments toward the member. I understand that something may have happened in committee that upset the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan, but the reality of the situation is that we have established a precedent. I would strongly encourage my colleagues to reconsider, because they know that they have found themselves in that position from time to time, and they would hate to set a precedent of starting to routinely shut statements down if this happens. Perhaps at the very least, the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan could stand up and apologize to the member for South Surrey—White Rock for his actions while the latter was giving his S. O. 31.

Mr. Speaker, the last time the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries rose in the House, he said the following: “It is interesting that the Conservatives have a member from Alberta asking questions about—

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. There are frequently comments and heckles during member statements and question period. The question is, with respect to Standing Order 16(2), where is the line crossed? I think the reasonable expectation would be that if something interrupted the ability of the member to actually get a recording, if the sound was so loud that the intervention could not be properly heard, then I would say that violates Standing Order 16(2). My understanding is that, in this particular case, that did not happen, and in fact, the recording is fine. We cannot hear the commentary of the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan. As a result, I suggest that Standing Order 16(2) was not, in this case, violated and that there therefore is no need to redo the S. O. 31 statement.

Mr. Speaker, I do want to thank my colleague in the riding to the north of mine, the member for Lanark—Frontenac, because he is absolutely correct. I think I would agree with him that there should be an establishment of breaking in one's speech and not being able to talk. If the member reviews the video of the S. O. 31, which he can do, he will see that the member for South Surrey—White Rock actually stopped at one point, waited and then restarted. We can see that; the video is there. I just want to thank my colleague for coming to our defence. We really appreciate that.

Mr. Speaker, I had raised the issue previously of the grossly unparliamentary anti-Alberta remarks of that member. When I had, the Speaker responded, which is a matter of past practice, as you know. The Speaker said at the time, “It would not be proper if somebody did that, but unfortunately, the Chair did not hear that.” He later said, “I do not know [what] it was. I will check the record.” The Speaker acknowledged that remarks of that character were improper. The Speaker has yet to come back to the House to rule on the unparliamentary anti-Alberta comments of the member for South Surrey—White Rock. I think that member needs to address the way he speaks about people from my region. If comments like that were made about members from B.C., where he is from, members from Quebec or members from Ontario, I think the House would have no problem acknowledging that they were unparliamentary and the member would have to retract those comments. The member needs to be accountable for the way he talks about Alberta.

Mr. Speaker, my point of order, unusually at the end of the question period, relates to something that happened yesterday in this place at approximately four o'clock. I think it was the member for Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay who had the floor and was speaking when the House was disrupted, very much contrary to Standing Order 16(2), in a gross violation of decorum. It was probably an accident that the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance thought it was appropriate to enter the House waving the budget and essentially turning this place of parliamentary business into a Liberal rally. I was deeply offended. I have never seen anything like it. I know the Speaker called for order at the time and did his best to remind people to take their seats, but a presentation of a budget, and I have been to many of them, is a moment when members are keen to hear from the Minister of Finance, not to have the budget paraded as a document with lots of cheering and whooping it up. I just wanted to put it on the record. The event has now passed, but people can find lots of photos of it on The Globe and Mail's website.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. On this point of order, related to the same standing order, I know you were in the chair yesterday when this happened. I was in the House. The Prime Minister and the finance minister walked in, waving the budget around like we were in some sort of Roman Colosseum. Maybe sometimes it seems that way, but I will say that I believe, Mr. Speaker, if you look back at the tapes, you will see that the member who was speaking was disrupted at that point as she was talking about government business. I believe her privileges to speak freely and not be disrupted in this place with respect to government business were breached yesterday. I would ask that the Speaker take it back, look at the tapes and look at the way they entered this place and disrupted the proceedings of the House.

title: Routine Proceedings: Request for Emergency Debate
turns: Mr. Speaker, once again, I urge you, I implore you, to consider my request for an emergency debate within the House of Commons. There are new revelations today that warrant this request. The Alberta referendum is quickly devolving into a crisis on multiple fronts. The integrity of the elections process is in question. Foreign interference in our democracy, allegations of illegal collusion by separatists and a potential national unity crisis are looming on the horizon. This is happening right now. This morning The Canadian Press revealed that with less than two weeks to go until Alberta's referendum, more than 3,000 mail-in ballots have been returned with errors that make them invalid. We have been warning for months that Elections Alberta is underfunded and does not have the needed staff to process ballot packages or to count the votes. The new, complicated voting process introduced by Danielle Smith's government has created enormous accessibility barriers to voters. This is a scandal, and this is on top of the reports this weekend detailing the extent of collaboration between Alberta separatists and Republican operatives in the United States. This is not a provincial matter. It is a very serious threat to Canada's democracy and national unity. The Alberta Information and Privacy Commissioner, Diane McLeod, called the leak of Alberta's private data “the worst [data] breach in Canadian history” and said her office was flooded with calls and emails from Albertans concerned for their safety. My constituency office has been inundated with calls from Albertans concerned about the process, including seniors who have learned there are no polling stations inside seniors residences, which means many seniors in Alberta will not be able to vote because they cannot wait hours in line. Alberta's referendum is failing every single democratic test we have. Today's news raises serious questions. Can Albertans trust that their votes will be counted? Can they trust that the process and the outcomes have not been influenced by foreign actors? Parliamentarians need the opportunity to ask the federal government what it is doing to ensure the electoral integrity of this. As a member of an unrecognized party, I do not have the ability to raise these issues in committee. This is my only opportunity to ask questions of the government regarding its responses. The Alberta civilians, the Canadian citizens, I represent deserve those answers. Mr. Speaker, I am asking you today to let us ask the important questions and demand transparency and security from the federal government as Albertans question whether their votes are safe, whether their data is safe and whether we are headed to a national unity crisis.

title: Oral Questions: Business of the House
turns: Mr. Speaker, it is time for everyone's favourite moment of the week in the House of Commons, the Thursday question. I would like to ask the government if it could update the House as to the business for the rest of this week and for the week following. Perhaps the government could tell us why it has chosen to table a budget on a Thursday afternoon right before a break week. Is it because the Liberals are afraid of getting questions on the budget, especially after the Parliamentary Budget Officer's update, which paints such a bleak picture of the Liberal government's fiscal and economic management? Will the government be bringing in any legislation to provide relief at the grocery store? It tried the exact same tactic that the Trudeau government tried of giving out rebates, and food inflation continues to rise, wiping out any benefit that Canadians might have received from that. Will it bring in any legislation that will actually deal with the root cause of inflation, which we know, of course, is massive amounts of borrowing, pushing up the cost of debt as well? Will it bring in any legislation to unblock our resources, for example, potentially repealing the shipping ban on Canadian energy off Canada's west coast? That would open up Asian markets and would improve the economic performance of the country. Will the government be taking any of the measures to undo the terrible policies that it has inflicted on this country for the past 11 years?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to offer my condolences to the Canadian Armed Forces members in Wainwright who are dealing with loss, Canadian military families across Canada and the families of the injured who are still dealing with the aftermath of the fire. My prayers and thoughts are with them, and I know the people of London West are also thinking about the people in Alberta. I also want to recognize that on Monday, Albertans voted to stay in Canada. They voted to believe in building a strong country. They voted for building our nation together with Canadian workers, with Canadian material, and that together we will continue to build a strong country. I want to recognize that. The member opposite mentioned our budget that is going to be tabled on November 5, which is a Thursday. I would like to remind the member that after the many years he has sat here, he is well aware that we also sit on Friday. I welcome him coming in on Friday, November 6, to ask a lot of questions. Many members will be in the House to answer those questions. On Wednesday and Thursday of next week, we will call Bill C-34, the digital safety act, at second reading. Finally, I would like to inform the House that, pursuant to Standing Order 66(2), we will resume debate on Motion No. 10 to concur in the 10th report of the Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities, on Tuesday, October 27.

title: Oral Questions: Employment
turns: Mr. Speaker, Canada has hit an alarming 29-year low in workforce participation. A smaller proportion of Canadians are in the workforce today than at any point in almost 30 years, but the Liberals shut down debate this morning on the unemployment crisis and continue to claim that everything is fine. How bad does workforce participation have to get before they notice: a 60-year low, a 100-year low?

Mr. Speaker, in fact, Canada this year has created 160,000 jobs and has created a huge workforce. I am actually quite pleased to take the opportunity to announce that last week we made a major announcement of $430 million over five years for union-led training, new expanded training centres, new ways to recruit and train apprentices, and new modern equipment. That is how you build the skilled workforce of the future. That is what we need to do in this country. We need to build this country. Let us build this Canada together.

Mr. Speaker, it is unbelievable to me how much the minister has his head in the sand. These are Statistics Canada job numbers that were released the week before Friday. It is clear, in black and white, that we are at a 29-year low in workforce participation. I have a news flash for the minister: That is not good news. That is not “everything is fine” news. That is a five-alarm fire. When will the minister stop patting himself on the back, recognize that Canadians are struggling, and actually do something about it?

Mr. Speaker, the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan has been at committee many times, advocating for substandard education for youth through private career colleges, which was part of the topic that we were discussing with the opposition just moments before. That is not the kind of thing that helps retain young people and get them into good jobs. In fact, what we have is strong evidence about the work that we do to make sure young people have access to quality jobs, through Canada summer jobs and work-integrated learning, and those result in not only stronger labour force attachment but better earnings over their lifetime. Maybe that member should stop—

Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada reported that Canada lost 68,300 jobs in September, amounting to 110,000 jobs lost in just two months. Young Canadians are the ones bearing the brunt of these losses. For a young Canadian trying to land their first job, build experience and save for a home, these are not just statistics. They represent lost opportunities and a delayed future. Will the Liberals reverse course on their policies that are holding young Canadians back?

Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that Canada's economy grew by 0.08% in the second quarter, and one of the leaders in that growth in the economy was the Government of Saskatchewan. We are seeing record investment, not only in potash but in uranium mining. Saskatchewan is an exciting part of our country. We want to continue fostering that development, and one of the things that has led to the excitement in Saskatchewan is that most of the federal Conservatives—

Mr. Speaker, maybe that member does not know, but Canada has the second-highest unemployment rate in the G7, and the labour force participation rate fell below 65% in September, the lowest level in almost 30 years outside of the pandemic. That is the result of over a decade of harmful Liberal policies that have chased jobs and investments out of this country. Canadians who are facing job losses need action now. Will the Liberals take that real action and unleash our economy and commit to reversing Bill C-69 and Bill C-48?

Mr. Speaker, when I listen to my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, they never mention the American tariffs. They never mention what the trade war is doing to our economy and how much, notwithstanding these unjustified American tariffs, we are fighting back. I will give some examples. We were able to announce just today, with Xona Space Systems, 126 jobs; at Hitachi Energy in London, Ontario, last week, 550 jobs and $500 million of investments; and also, at Jubilant Radiopharma, 255 jobs in Montreal. We will continue to create jobs across this country.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Mr. Speaker, I asked this question twice last week but did not get an answer. It is an important question because it speaks to the fiscal credibility of the Prime Minister , so again I will ask it. Last budget, the Prime Minister established a fiscal anchor of a declining deficit to GDP. The PBO projects that the government will not keep to this fiscal anchor. Will the government keep to this fiscal anchor in the upcoming budget?

Mr. Speaker, in the last election, Canadians elected a leader with economic and business credentials that can lead our country and can rebuild, retool and pivot our economy. Let us look at some economic signs, despite the fact that the Conservatives do not want to hear them. We have the best net GDP in the G7, wages are outpacing inflation, and we have one of the fastest- growing economies in the G7 and the best credit rating in the world. On this side, we are laser-focused on building a strong economy. The other side of the House can continue to talk our country down.

Mr. Speaker, the net debt calculation the government used in its last budget is the IMF's net debt calculation, which includes the Canada pension plan. I am sure that Canadians listening would not like to know that the government's calculation involves using the assets of the Canada pension plan to offset its rapidly growing debt. The Prime Minister came to office with a much vaunted fiscal resume, and again I ask the question, will the government keep to the fiscal anchors it established in the last federal budget?

Mr. Speaker, when an economy is faced with challenges, we can do one of two things: We can blame everybody else and throw our hands up, or we can actually get down to building and to focusing on building a strong economy. We just hosted the Canada Investment Summit, where over half a billion dollars was pledged to build Canada strong. We are doubling non-U.S. exports at a pace not seen in decades. Foreign investment is coming into our country at a level not seen in decades also. We are focused on building a strong economy for Canadians—

Mr. Speaker, a former governor of the Bank of Canada, David Dodge, has a simple rule: The government should be wary when it spends more than 10% of its revenue on debt service costs. The Parliamentary Budget Officer says that figure will grow to nearly 14% in just a few years, and in fact, debt service payments are the fastest-growing line item in the budget. Does the government want this to be the fastest-growing line item in the budget? The Liberals' actions suggest they do not even care.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7 and a AAA credit rating, which keeps our debt service costs low relative to our peers. The Bank of Canada governor confirmed in the finance committee today that it is not just how much governments spend but what, specifically, they invest in. Let us look at our track record. What are we investing in? We are investing in increasing the productive capacity in our economy. We are investing in affordability measures for Canadians. We are asserting our sovereignty. We are assuring that we have self-reliance and independence for the future. Our budget 2026 is called “Masters of our Destiny” for good reason.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague very much, but let us spare Canadians the lecture. When Paul Martin was the finance minister, he met every single deficit reduction target and fiscal anchor that was imposed. At the very first opportunity, the Prime Minister is choosing to break it. In fact, there has not been a finance minister in over a decade that has bothered to even care to keep the fiscal promise. What good is a promise if the Prime Minister has no intention of keeping it?

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the opposition is very concerned with Thursday's budget, called “Masters of Our Destiny”. That budget will continue our progress investing in the things that matter to Canadians. What does it matter if Canada has a strong fiscal position if it is not willing to use it in an affordability crisis, where Canadians want their government to stand up and help them? That is exactly what we are focused on. God forbid the Conservatives should write the budget. It would be called “Prisoners of Pessimism”.

title: Statements by Members: Diesel Prices
turns: Mr. Speaker, across Canada, farmers are bringing in the harvest. The work that began months ago is coming down to these critical weeks where the weather, the crop and the clock all come together. There is no postponing the harvest because conditions are not perfect or the economics are unfavourable. When the crop is ready, farmers have to get it off the field. Tractors and trucks, combines and harvesters, a swath of machinery has to run to bring in the crop. For the vast majority of that equipment, that means diesel. My brother, a farmer, is paying 84% more for diesel this September versus last. That is 24¢ per litre more than the American average. The Conservative emergency fuel relief plan proposes eliminating federal taxes on diesel until at least Canada Day 2027 and the removal of the industrial carbon tax and clean fuel standard. Longer term, it proposes emergency permitting for diesel refineries, production and distribution, and a strategic refined petroleum reserve. Will the government support our motion today to address these high diesel prices?

Mr. Speaker, farmers across Canada are now harvesting the crops they worked all year to grow, but as harvest begins, farmers are facing a major challenge: the skyrocketing cost of diesel. Diesel powers the combines and tractors working in our fields. It powers the trains that move our grain and the trucks that deliver it. When the cost of fuel goes up, the farmer's revenue goes down. A single combine can use more than 1,100 dollars' worth of diesel in one day of harvest. Farmers should be focusing on harvesting their crops, not on how they are going to pay their diesel bills. The Liberal government needs to act. Our emergency fuel relief plan would cut diesel taxes and get more fuel produced here at home. Canadians need affordable fuel to get through the harvest and keep our economy moving. It is time for the government to put Canadians first.

Mr. Speaker, diesel is the lifeblood of Canada's agriculture and transportation industries, but today, with prices in Manitoba now reaching $2.40 a litre, Canada faces a diesel price emergency. Farmers cannot farm without diesel. Truckers cannot move goods without diesel. Trains cannot haul commodities without diesel. When diesel costs more, producing food costs more and Canadians pay more. Conservatives are calling on the government to eliminate all tax on diesel until at least Canada Day, remove the GST on fuel, permanently scrap the 19¢ per litre industrial carbon tax and secure our diesel supply. Sadly, Liberal policies add costs to the production of diesel today and discourage investments into refineries tomorrow. Canadians cannot keep paying the price for these Liberal failures. The Liberals must cut all taxes on diesel and give farmers, businesses and families the relief they deserve.

title: Oral Questions: Housing
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised that he would double homebuilding, but once again, it was all talk and no results. In fact, homebuilding is down, and today, Habitat for Humanity International published a report showing that 56% of Canadians who do not own homes believe they never will. That is the highest number out of 22 surveyed countries. Also, two-thirds of Canadians have skipped other payments so that they can pay for their housing. Canadians are paying for this costly Prime Minister. When will he adopt our plan to build homes and not bureaucracy?

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition, this summer, when asked what he would do about building housing, said absolutely nothing. That was his response. Leave it to the market to solve all our housing woes. We have established Build Canada Homes to build affordable non-market housing. We have over 19,000 homes under way right now. We are building Canada strong and we are offering Canadians in Ontario up to $200,000 off the price of a new home. This is leadership. We are delivering that. We are delivering the homes that Canadians need.

Mr. Speaker, I said I would do nothing to bail out Liberal, condo-owning insiders. The Prime Minister wants to force hard-working young people who cannot afford a home to pay taxes to bail out multi-millionaire investors who speculated and lost. Maybe that is why 56% of those who do not own a home revealed in a survey to Habitat for Humanity International that they never will. Again, the question is for the Prime Minister. If he cares enough about those aspiring young people, when will he get government taxes and red tape out of the way so that youth can afford homes?

Mr. Speaker, not only are we cutting red tape, working with local governments to make it faster to build and reducing development charges dramatically, we have also had a first-time homebuyer break on the GST. The Conservatives fought it all last year. They fought against giving first-time homebuyers an opportunity to save on their first home purchase. We went to the next step with a GST break for all Canadians on new homes. Did this have support from the other side? No. Again and again, they say one thing. One might think they care about affordable housing, but they do not give a hoot about it. They never vote for it.

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, the member raises the question of veterans, ultimately. I would remind him of the Conservative record on veterans and the endless cuts we saw under Conservative leadership. We can leave that aside for a moment. The decision, as articulated yesterday, was taken through a transparent and open process. I leave that to the member to consider.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister made big promises that he was going to buy Canadian. Then we learned that in his first year in office, he spent $7.8 billion more than the previous year on American companies, with Canadian tax dollars. This week, we learned that he cast aside the Commissionaires, the single largest employer of veterans in Canada, to favour an American security firm linked to Donald Trump and ICE. Why did the Prime Minister, after making his big promise, cast aside our veterans to favour an American firm at Canadians' expense?

Mr. Speaker, let me be clear. As highlighted yesterday by the Secretary of State for the Canada Revenue Agency, the CRA followed a fair and open procurement process for guard services. It selected a registered Canadian—

Mr. Speaker, let me be clear. As highlighted yesterday by the Secretary of State for the Canada Revenue Agency, the CRA followed a fair and open procurement process for guard services. It selected a registered Canadian business headquartered in Ontario that employs thousands of Canadians. Our government will always stand with Canadian workers and Canadian businesses as we build the strongest economy in the G7.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals promised elbows up, and instead, they elbowed aside our veterans. Now their excuse is that they cannot control any of it, that all these billions of dollars for purchases are going out the door and the elected government has no authority to do anything about it at all, that this is just a bunch of self-determining bureaucrats. That is not what the Prime Minister promised. He said he was going to ensure that our Canadian tax dollars went to Canadian firms. At the front of that list should have been Canadian veterans. The Commissionaires should be protecting us. Why did the Liberals favour an American firm instead of Canadian veterans?

Mr. Speaker, as I just said, the CRA followed a fair and open procurement process. I, of course, share the view that veterans have the right opportunities to find rewarding employment of their choosing when they are ready. It is at the core of the national veterans employment strategy. Again, as has been stated, this was a contract decision made by the CRA. Our government has worked and will continue to work with veteran employers as we build the strongest economy in the G7.

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised to build Canadian and buy Canadian. Now, LNG Canada phase two is a massive private sector investment, but the inputs for the facility portion are not coming from Canada. Canadian steel fabricators say that they have the capacity to supply significant portions of this project, but they were not consulted. Before billions of dollars of fabrication went overseas, did anyone in the Liberal government actually ask Canadian industry stakeholders what they could build here at home?

Mr. Speaker, the modules that he is referring to are not made in Canada because there is no steel that can make those modules in Canada. All of the steel, the 15,000 tonnes that are going to go with the pipeline, is going to be made in Canada, along with the 6,100 jobs and the $50 billion in royalties for Canada. Instead of talking down a project that builds Canada, maybe they should support us in helping to build Canada.

Mr. Speaker, that was not the question. Canadian steel and pipelines do not answer why Canadian companies were not consulted about the fabrication of the LNG facility itself. It is out of touch to point to steel used somewhere else in the project while ignoring Canadian fabricators who say that they can have a substantial portion of this work completed here in Canada. The Prime Minister talks about “buy Canadian”, but Canadian companies apparently were not even consulted. Therefore, who determined Canadian industry could not complete the work? Was it LNG Canada, the Liberal government or nobody because no one even bothered to ask?

Mr. Speaker, those are nice comments, but they are completely inaccurate. We actually talked to people at the steel companies, and they said they cannot service those orders. They asked us to make sure the rest of the steel was bought in Canada, and it will be bought in Canada. The Conservatives are talking down projects that create 6,100 jobs. They are talking down a project that creates $50 billion to pay for health care, to pay for dental care, to pay for schools and roads. Why do you not stop talking down Canada, and start trying to—

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister tells Canadians to buy Canadian, but government contracts to American companies have increased by 50% since he took office. Now, LNG Canada plans to use foreign steel for its expansion, while Canadian steel companies say they can do the work. Canadian steelworkers need jobs. The Liberals give slogans, all talk and no results. Conservatives are fighting for lumber workers. Conservatives are fighting for auto workers. Conservatives will continue to fight for the steelworkers of Canada. When will this Prime Minister?

Mr. Speaker, instead of talking down the country and instead of talking down projects, they have to build it up. This pipeline is going to provide tens of thousands of jobs and Canadian steel. We are talking about supporting jobs in Hamilton in steel. Why do the hon. members not support Hooper Welding in Hamilton, which employs 100 people? They are making steel. In Peterborough, Kawartha Metals employs 60 people. They are supplying metal. In Windsor, there is Central Stampings. We are supporting the companies making steel because we believe in building in Canada, buying in Canada and believing in Canada.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Mr. Speaker, today the Auditor General released a sobering report on Canada's anti-money laundering watchdog, FINTRAC, which reports directly to the Minister of Finance. Here is the bottom line up front. The AG said, “FINTRAC did not effectively carry out its role in overseeing compliance with Canada's anti-money laundering laws” and that “limited FINTRAC's ability to help detect, prevent, and deter money laundering.” Does the Minister of Finance accept the Auditor General's findings that his agency is failing to prevent money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, our government is committed to protecting the integrity of Canada's financial system and supporting the institutions that safeguard it. We are taking concrete steps to develop a national anti-fraud strategy in collaboration with industry partners and agencies. We are also creating the financial crimes agency, which will lead the fight against sophisticated financial crimes with increased RCMP resources. If the Conservatives are concerned about combatting money laundering, we encourage them to support Bill C-29.

Mr. Speaker, if the government was serious about this issue, it would have created the agency, which it promised in 2021, and it would not have missed the legal deadline to review the Proceeds of Crime, Money Laundering, and Terrorist Financing Act. The reality is that police need timely access to this information, and yet the Auditor General found that it took on average 112 days for FINTRAC to give law enforcement information, and said that it was, “too late to be useful.” Why is the Minister of Finance not giving police across Canada the tools and information they need to stop money laundering and terrorist financing?

Mr. Speaker, again, our government is committed to protecting and safeguarding the integrity of Canada's financial system. We have taken concrete steps to develop an anti-fraud strategy in collaboration with many partners. We are in the process of creating the financial crimes agency that will lead the fight against ever more sophisticated financial crimes. We have given the RCMP additional resources to help coordinate these efforts. If the Conservatives are concerned about this issue, they should support our bill, Bill C-29.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada says inflation is rising and economic growth is slowing, while the Parliamentary Budget Officer says interest on the national debt is the fastest-growing government expense. The cost of government is driving up the cost of living and these Liberals have broken every fiscal promise, smashed through every fiscal guardrail and cut loose every fiscal anchor they have ever set. For 11 straight years, they have tabled deficits. When will the government finally stop its inflationary deficit spending?

Mr. Speaker, unlike the Conservatives, we believe in the independence of monetary policy in our central bank, and we know that inflation is being driven by the war in the Middle East. Unlike the Conservatives, we are stepping up every single day in this House to offer more affordability supports for Canadians when they need it most. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. We have enhanced and increased access to federal benefits, like the groceries and essentials benefit, and we are investing to create tens of thousands of new jobs all across Canada. That is how we build Canada strong. That is how we support Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, unemployment is up, grocery costs are up, inflation is up and now interest rates are up. Yesterday, deficit-fuelled inflation caused the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates, with the six big banks following. For those who own a home, their mortgage payment just got more expensive, and for those aspiring to buy one, that dream has just been pushed further out of reach, all because the Prime Minister could not control his spending. With their upcoming budget, will the Liberals stop their inflationary spending?

Mr. Speaker, as the Conservative caucus members from Saskatchewan awaken from their slumber, this is what has been happening in Saskatchewan. Since June alone, I have been part of federal announcements representing a more than $467-million investment in Saskatchewan, and canola sales are increasing. We have spent money in support of child care, and canola sales are improving. We have spent money in community infrastructure, and canola sales are improving. We have spent money in indigenous communities, and canola sales are improving. I think maybe the member and the entire Saskatchewan—

Mr. Speaker, Breakfast Club of Canada told committee this week that the $1-billion school food program has lost 22% of its grocery purchasing power because of inflation, yet the minister keeps insisting that the program feeds an extra 400,000 kids a year. The math does not math. When we divide the money over five years and 180 school days per year, it averages less than three dollars per target child per day, but a five-province study found that the average lunch costs $6.45, double, which feeds a lot fewer kids. Will the minister table the national data and costing behind her claims? Hungry kids want to check her homework.

Mr. Speaker, we absolutely take no lessons from the other side of the House when it comes to the national school food program. I was at that committee meeting, and I heard from the Coalition for Healthy School Food, from the Breakfast Club of Canada and from students who have written to our Prime Minister about how the national school food program is helping them every single day in their schools. The member should listen up.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are being hammered by the rising cost of living, and yesterday brought another blow with the Bank of Canada hiking interest rates for the first time since 2023. This means higher credit card bills, bigger mortgage payments and more expensive loans for working families. It will put added strain on small businesses and things will get worse. The Bank of Canada forecasts inflation to soar through 2027. Why is the Liberal government failing to bring down the cost of living and make life more affordable for Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, we know that the Bank of Canada and its monetary policy are independent. It has to keep inflation within the target range. Obviously, inflation is being driven by conflicts in the Middle East and the oil price shocks. The member opposite knows that well. We have invested in the Canadian economy. We have strengthened affordability supports and measures, and social support programs like the groceries and essentials benefit. That is real support. It amounts to thousands of dollars per month with child care, dental care and the national school food program. There are all kinds of supports that really impact families' lives. That makes life easier. We are doing all that while investing in a more prosperous future.

title: Oral Questions: Housing
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are like the Toronto Maple Leafs. They spend more, deliver nothing and repeat the same thing every single year, and the PBO has confirmed this. She said spending is up, borrowing is up and housing results are down. The Liberals quadrupled the spending on housing over the last 10 years just to have housing starts go down. Home affordability in Vancouver was the second worst in the entire world when the housing minister was the mayor. If Vancouver could not afford this guy as the mayor, why should the rest of Canada have to?

Mr. Speaker, we are totally focused on scaling up housing across the country and on affordability. The Conservatives seem to have missed that, for 25 months in a row, rents have come down across Canada. It is a big achievement for us. That is thanks to an unprecedented boom in rental housing. That is thanks to programs that the government is implementing right now to get more housing built. We will do that in partnership with provinces and cities, unlike Conservative governments of the past that preyed upon local governments and did not support building affordable housing. We are focused on those partnerships. We are focused on building.
Mr. Speaker, it is hard to believe this guy when he promised people in Vancouver he would end homelessness by—

Mr. Speaker, it is hard to believe the minister when he had promised the people of Vancouver that he would end homelessness by 2015. How is that going? The Prime Minister will do the impossible. He will outspend Trudeau in just six years. By 2030, every Canadian will have to pay $2,000 more in debt interest alone. The Prime Minister is taking money out of hard-working Canadians' pockets and giving it to his banker and bondholder buddies. Bay Street gets the interest; Main Street gets the bill. Why are the interests of the Prime Minister's banker buddies more important than those of Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, to go back in time to the years when I was a mayor trying to solve homelessness in my city, that was when there was a Conservative prime minister who never lifted a finger to end homelessness in this country. It made it very difficult for cities, provinces and territories across the country to do anything. Homelessness has scaled up ever since that time. We have a Prime Minister who is taking a stand for the most vulnerable Canadians. The government is focused on ending homelessness. We are working with provinces, territories, cities and indigenous partners. We are going to achieve that goal, and we expect their support.

title: Routine Proceedings: Petitions
turns: Mr. Speaker, since 2012, the First Nations Education Steering Committee, British Columbia and Canada have worked together on the British Columbia Tripartite Education Agreement to promote successful education outcomes for first nations learners. The petitioners note that education is a fundamental human right, and the BCTEA is the primary source of funding for first nations students of schools based on the public education system in British Columbia. It was expected that renewed funding commitments would be confirmed in the spring economic update, as the agreement is set to expire on June 30, 2026. Canada instead confirmed that the funding for the proposed renewed BCTEA was not secured and that the status quo funding was confirmed for only a one-year extension. Therefore, the petitioners in Mission—Matsqui—Abbotsford call upon the government to approve the proposed renewed BCTEA and associated funding commitments for a 10-year term in the fall budget to ensure that the education of first nations students is not needlessly disrupted.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise today to table this petition on behalf of constituents of my riding. The petitioners cite that Canada's national inventory identifies more than 1,300 wrecked, abandoned and hazardous vessels, including more than 900 in British Columbia. These vessels pose serious risks to marine ecosystems, fisheries, indigenous food harvesting, coastal communities, navigation and public safety. The petitioners highlight that coastal communities continue to experience vessels grounding, sinking or breaking apart in sensitive marine habitats, resulting in pollution and fisheries closures. Preventing vessels from becoming environmental hazards is safer and less costly than emergency response, salvage and remediation after they sink or break apart; that existing federal vessel removal and disposal programs are inadequately funded, limited in scope or have expired; that Canada lacks a comprehensive strategy and sufficient infrastructure for the responsible retirement, recycling and disposal of end-of-life vessels; and that Washington state demonstrates a proactive approach using dedicated vessel registration revenues to help address vessels before they become abandoned or hazardous. The petitioners call on the government to establish a permanent national strategy for the prevention, removal, recycling and responsible disposal of wrecked, abandoned and hazardous vessels; create a self-sustaining vessel retirement and turn-in program funded in whole or in part through vessel registration fees; restore and expand federal funding for timely vessel removal; and improve federal procurement and response processes so qualified regional marine contractors can be deployed quickly to prevent environmental damage and invest in Canadian vessel recycling and disposal infrastructure, including capacity in coastal British Columbia.

title: Oral Questions: International Trade
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister announced that he is pursuing his so-called strategic partnership with Beijing. He seeks to trade American dependence for Chinese dominance. This is his Faustian bargain—

Mr. Speaker, this is the Prime Minister's Faustian bargain: temporary relief today and Chinese dominance tomorrow, when it should be Canadian independence always. Conservatives will not stand idly by while the Liberals permit Beijing to undermine Canadian workers through predatory imports of steel, aluminum, electric vehicles and more. The Prime Minister must commit to no more market access that threatens Canadian workers and our sovereignty. Will he do that?

Mr. Speaker, we have good news for Canadian farmers and harvesters. Through the hard work of the Prime Minister, Canada has expanded our trade arrangement with China through 2028, with new tariff relief on about $400 million in Canadian exports, from frozen pork and Greenland halibut to Pacific spot prawn, geoduck and sea cucumber. That builds on the two-year extension for canola meal, peas, lobster and crab announced earlier this month. We will continue to work hard to make sure that our farmers are able to grow good food and share it with the rest of the world.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian values are not for sale, and not long ago the Prime Minister agreed. He said that Beijing was Canada's greatest security threat. At Davos he said Canada must be principled and defend fundamental values: human rights, the rule of law and democracy. Beijing shares none of these values. The question is which Prime Minister Canadians should believe: the one who professes a belief and commitment to these values or the one who turns his back on them through his actions.

Mr. Speaker, due to the work that we are doing to help our farmers and harvesters, this is what the Premier of Saskatchewan, Scott Moe, had to say in a social media post: “More good trade news today for Saskatchewan's strong and steady economy.” Their minister says, “That helps so much in them being able to plan their crop rotations into next year,” because it's good for our farmers. We hear the same thing from the Canadian Pork Council, which said that this is a welcome announcement of tariff relief on most frozen Canadian pork cuts exported to China, because it reflects sustained engagement and strong—
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is in Beijing right now, bragging about his strategic partnership with the CCP, a partnership that allows 50,000—
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is in Beijing right now bragging about his strategic—

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is bragging about his strategic partnership with the CCP, a partnership that allows 50,000 EVs onto our streets, putting Canadian auto jobs and national security at risk. Today, we learned he has weakened our steel and aluminum sector even more by reducing tariffs on these products from China. Canadian auto workers are concerned that foreign-made EVs are going to put them out of work. How can the Liberals continue forward with their plan to flood our market, putting more workers and their families at risk?

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's visit has delivered real results for Canadian farmers, seafood harvesters and exporters. China is the world's second-largest economy, and I really struggle to stand here and talk down our canola farmers, our fishers and our beef farmers. They are calling us out, telling us it is a really good deal that we have continued with our two-year extension. We are going to continue to work on open markets around the world for our harvesters and our seafood and beef.

Mr. Speaker, in January, the Prime Minister spoke of the values and the strength of the middle powers in Davos. Chief among those values are human rights and freedoms. From the regime in Beijing to Qatar, Turkey and the U.A.E., the Prime Minister has made the deliberate choice to deepen relationships with countries that do not share our fundamental values and freedoms. Trade matters, but so do Canadian values and Canadian sovereignty. Will the Prime Minister tell Canadians that he will not compromise on human rights and Canadian sovereignty in exchange for a strategic relationship with Beijing?

Mr. Speaker, we are making trade deals all around the world for the benefit of all Canadians. We are doing everything possible. Our Prime Minister is leading the way. We are acknowledging all different industries and sectors. We are being supported by them. We are not standing behind them; they are standing beside us. They are supporting us every step of the way. I spent a week in Beijing and Shanghai, and I can tell the House that the industries and stakeholders that were there on that trade mission were very grateful for everything we are doing on this side of the House.

title: Oral Questions: Taxation
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's 16¢-a-litre fuel standard tax is bad enough, but what is even worse is where the money goes. To quote energy expert Heather Exner-Pirot, “To meet their carbon intensity targets, many Canadian refiners blend biofuels into their petroleum products. But Canada is not self-sufficient in their production. More than half of Canada's biofuels are imported, predominantly from the United States.” The Government of Canada forces the people of Canada to pay 16¢ a litre more to buy American biofuels. Why?

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada understands and acknowledges the challenges in the global economy. However, it is Wednesday, and I have good news. In fact, Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7, the lowest net debt to GDP in the G7 and one of the lowest deficits to GDP in the G7. The Bank of Canada has seen that we are going to have the second-fastest growth in the G7. On top of that, we are investing to be an energy superpower. We are going to build Canada strong together.

Mr. Speaker, not only did the Prime Minister not answer the question, but the finance minister did not even seem to hear it. The question was about the 16¢-a-litre diesel and gasoline tax charged at the pump. Now, it is bad enough to tax the Canadian people. It is even worse to force them to pay that money to the United States of America to buy U.S. biofuels. While Canadians cannot afford groceries, while they must empty their bank to fill up their tank, why is the Prime Minister forcing them to pay a 16¢-a-litre tax at the pump to Trump?

Mr. Speaker, I have some good news for the member opposite. Canola prices are up 8% this year. The amended clean fuel regulations will create significant new demand for canola. Rather than fight against canola farmers, why does he not help us build Canada strong?

No, Mr. Speaker, the minister wants to build America strong, because the cost of the majority of the biofuels that the government is forcing refiners to purchase with this 16¢-a-litre tax is not going to Canadian farmers. It is going to megacorporations south of the border. On this day when the Bank of Canada governor says that food prices are rising because of higher diesel costs, the Prime Minister is imposing a tax on Canadians at the pump and on truckers who deliver us our food. Why is he putting that money in the pockets of the Americans?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to correct my last statement. Canola prices are up 8% because of clean fuel regs, but they are up 30% this year. Thirty per cent, and the Leader of the Opposition is trying to talk us down. We have been helping the farmers. We have been helping the people in Alberta. He is talking against them. We should work together and build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, at Trump Tower, they will be popping the champagne today, knowing that this government is defending a 16¢-a-litre tax that sends Canadian money south of the border to subsidize large U.S. corporations selling us overpriced biofuel. That single mother who is turning back items at the grocery store, because it costs too much for the trucker to deliver those items, or the family who cannot quite fill up the minivan can take comfort in knowing that the Prime Minister has a “make America great again” tax at the pump.

Mr. Speaker, we all know that the Leader of the Opposition likes to talk, but he should listen. He should listen to the voices in this House, like when we extended the suspension of the excise fuel tax. That is helping Canadians. That is helping families. That is helping truckers. That is helping farmers. That is helping fishers across this nation. I hope Canadians are watching at home today because this gentleman has voted against supporting Canadians.

title: Oral Questions: Taxation
turns: Mr. Speaker, it is all well and good to watch the results south of the border, but we have real problems as well here in Canada, real problems in the real lives of real people who cannot afford eat, heat, or house themselves, real problems that have gotten much worse since the Prime Minister took office. Meanwhile, the Prime Minister distracts with grand theatrical gestures, so my question is, will he actually stand up and do his job in the House, in our country, to save Canadians money by taking all taxes off gas and diesel so Canadians can afford to eat, heat, and house themselves?

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the government have and will continue to, and I note that the budget is tomorrow, support Canadians who are feeling pinched by foreign wars, wars in the Middle East and a number of external factors, including trade wars, that have affected their quality of life and affordability. I have to also note the systematic opposition of the Conservative leader and party to every single possible initiative that we put forward to help Canadians in need.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister actually believed that, he would stand up and say it himself. The question was about the 20¢ a litre he adds to the price of gas, including with a tax that takes money out of the pockets of hard-working Canadians to subsidize American biodiesel and biogas firms. In the middle of a trade dispute that the Prime Minister has been unable to solve here at home, he drives up the costs for single moms, seniors and small business people to subsidize the Americans. Enough is enough. There are real problems here at home. Will the Prime Minister take his taxes off gas so Canadians can afford to eat?

Mr. Speaker, we take affordability very seriously. That is why, in fact, many people in the Leader of the Opposition's community and, frankly, in communities right across the country, are going to be able to, with this heating season, take advantage of the heat pump rebates we have put in place. That is going to be a very tangible way to save Canadians, on average, over $1,000 every single year. These are true savings. If the Leader of the Opposition wants to talk about clean fuel regulations, I am sure he might like to have a conversation with Imperial in Strathcona. It is right outside his riding.

title: Oral Questions: Justice
turns: Mr. Speaker, people going through depression and mental health issues go through the darkest valleys. They need hope. Several years ago, the Liberal government legalized medical assistance in dying for people whose only condition is mental illness. Many people would not be with us today if that policy had been in place before. The Conservative member of Parliament for Cloverdale—Langley City has put forward a bill to stop that from happening and protect the people who are most vulnerable. Will the Prime Minister announce that he will vote for that bill today, for hope, for life and for a better future for the people suffering?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the sponsor of the private member's bill for starting a conversation on a very important issue. I am pleased to share with the Leader of the Opposition that just a few hours ago, I announced that Canada would be moving forward with the exclusion of medical assistance in dying for people who are seeking that on the sole basis of a mental illness. We are going to be moving forward legislation that we will put forward during this fall sitting to ensure that the law maintains that exclusion in an indeterminate way.

Mr. Speaker, Shane Ertmoed took the life of Heather Aspin-Thomas, an innocent 10-year-old girl, for sexual gratification. He should never see the light of day, according to counsel for Heather's mom. Those are not my words. Victims are tired of hearing that the parole board is independent. They want to know whether the Liberals will repeal the laws that the independent parole board enforces that allow someone such as Shane Ertmoed to leave jail to take cooking classes that Heather will never get to take. I will look directly at the Prime Minister, who appears to be talking to somebody else. Will he commit—
Mr. Speaker, I will look directly at the Prime Minister and ask this: Will he commit to repealing Liberal parole so our children can remain safe?

Mr. Speaker, the case that the member refers to is a horrible case, and my sympathies go out to the family. As mentioned previously in the House, we are reviewing the act, and we are open to changes. However, I must remind all people viewing, and especially the Conservatives, that the act that currently exists to oversee these procedures was created by a Conservative government. The Corrections and Conditional Release Act is a Conservative act.

Mr. Speaker, wait until the Liberals find out who has been in charge the last 11 years. Imagine that. Right now, we do not know whether Shane Ertmoed is out figuring out the difference between a béchamel sauce and a Béarnaise sauce, while Heather's family has to serve a psychological life sentence. The government gives empty words. I will ask this for a third time: If the Prime Minister believes in the answer his minister just gave, will he rise in the House and agree to a meeting with Heather's family, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, I can tell the member that we were in power this spring when we passed six pieces of criminal justice legislation on things such as hate, bail and safe spaces. Where was the member? Every time the roll was called, he sat in his place and opposed the law-and-order agenda of the new government in Canada. We are the anti-crime party. We are the people taking the measures. The member should get up and support them.

Mr. Speaker, Darren Scott Ray raped, tortured and murdered a 14-year-old boy, Darren Pepin, in Scarborough. He strangled this child to death and dumped his body in the garbage room of his apartment building. He was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison. Today, many of Darren's young former classmates, who now call Oshawa and Durham region home, are in the very community where this killer was granted a 72-hour unescorted temporary absence. When will the government fix broken Liberal parole and finally put victims and public safety first?

Mr. Speaker, my thoughts are with Darren, his family and his community. I will just assure my colleague opposite that we are working with victims, survivor groups and those representing families in order to strengthen our parole process. This is an issue, as I have indicated in the past, that requires collaboration among all the parties. This is not to be politicized. It is important that we work together toward strengthening victims' rights. That is exactly what we did with Bill C-16 that passed this spring. It is the same thing we did with Bill C-14 on sentencing and bail reform.

Mr. Speaker, that is an out-of-touch response from the minister. This is not an isolated case. This year alone, Canadians have watched multiple pedophile child killers who have received life sentences get unescorted temporary absences from prison, including two in B.C. within 10 days of each other. Darren Scott Ray received a 72-hour unescorted temporary absence in Oshawa and has been promised two more. Will the government finally act and fix broken Liberal parole—and it is broken Liberal parole because they voted against our bill that would have changed it—and ensure that pedophile child killers serving life sentences stay where they belong behind bars?

Mr. Speaker, as mentioned before, we are open to reforms and are currently undergoing a review process. However, I must remind everyone that this is a Conservative act that we are undertaking a process to improve. Our government, for the last 18 months, has been reforming the Criminal Code of Canada to modernize it and to make sure that criminals stay behind bars.

Mr. Speaker, first the minister approves it, then he gets caught and now he says they have paused it. Under the Liberals, convicted child killers are getting released for cooking classes, and now we have these guys handing out paper straws to prisoners to snort coke. The system is a complete joke. Our streets, our parks and our downtown areas are being destroyed by drugs and disorder. There should be zero tolerance for illegal drugs in our streets and in prison. Will the minister stand up today and finally end it completely, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, I believe I have answered this question, but let me just address the second issue that came up. I want to take a moment to remember Heather Thomas, who was 10 years old when she was killed. My thoughts are with the family of the loved one. I understand that the Parole Board has decided to postpone the decision that my friend opposite is referring to. Our government is committed to strengthening our criminal justice system and protecting victims' rights. That is what we will continue to do. We are looking for collaboration from the other side in order to make constructive criminal justice reforms.

Mr. Speaker, today the Liberals are taking a cynical gamble with vulnerable Canadians' lives, asking Parliament to reject Bill C-218 for a phantom bill that has not even been written. They are playing political games at a time when lives are in the balance. The study was done. The broad consensus is there. The bill is tabled. Every minute we waste on an unwritten bill brings us closer to the deadline. Rejecting protection already before Parliament is reckless, and Canadians could pay with their lives. Will the Liberals do the right thing, work with us and support Bill C-218 today?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her work to advance an important conversation when it comes to mental illness as the sole underlying mental condition that would justify medical assistance in dying in this country. This is a serious conversation. However, I would like to point out one inaccuracy in her question that is very important. Today, there is no access to medical assistance in dying because it is excluded in the Criminal Code. Before that exclusion expires in March next year, we will advance and adopt legislation to, in an indeterminate way, continue the exclusion of access to medical assistance in dying when it comes to mental illness as the sole condition that would justify its use.

title: Oral Questions: The Budget
turns: Mr. Speaker, in 2015, the Liberals promised two years of modest deficits that would lead the budget to balancing itself. Instead, they added $750 billion to the national debt through 11 years of credit card budgeting. Interest on national debt is now the fastest-growing government expense, threatening to choke out priorities like health care and national defence. How can we trust the Liberals to get their spending under control when yesterday's budget adds another $765 billion to the national debt?

Mr. Speaker, managing debt is important, and so is intellectual honesty and context. The reality is that our debt servicing is at 1.7% of GDP, comparable to the Harper years that they lionize, and well below the 6.5% in the nineties. We have the lowest net debt. We have the second-lowest deficit. We are using that fiscal capacity to grow our economy, including in our home city of Calgary, where we are seeing significant growth and significant investments, including tens of thousands of jobs and thousands of youth jobs. There is much to be excited about. I hope they get on board.

The Speaker, for 11 years in a row, the government has tabled spending, borrowing and deficit projections that breached their previously promised targets, and the member wants to talk about honesty. The projections in yesterday's budget confirm that they have broken last year's fiscal anchor of a declining deficit to GDP and the government's old fiscal anchor of a declining debt to GDP. After 11 years of broken promises, how can Canadians trust the finance minister?
Mr. Speaker, the deficit is down. Rents are down. Housing prices are down. Economic activity is up. The plan is working. We welcome members to get on board.

Mr. Speaker, families in Richmond Centre—Marpole are cutting back on groceries and other essentials to make ends meet. They expect the government to show the same discipline, yet this costly credit card budget has another $62-billion deficit for this year and over $60 billion in debt interest, which is more than the Canada health transfer. A family of four will pay $6,000 just on Canada's interest payments. This is a budget mastered by deficit. When will the Liberal government cut spending, reduce the deficit and give struggling families breathing room?

Mr. Speaker, I have great news this Friday. Budget 2026, announced yesterday, is leveraging our fiscal strength to support small businesses right across the country. With the productivity mega deduction, Canada is the most tax-competitive jurisdiction for new business investment in the world. From mines to mills to auto manufacturers and from bakers to dry cleaners, we are giving businesses the confidence, through a tax deduction, to invest in themselves today. With the Canada growth incentive, we are, more than ever, supporting successful entrepreneurs to reinvest—

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have fittingly titled their new fiscal approach as though it is the next instalment of the Marvel universe. For over a decade now, Liberals have self-identified as heroes, unbound by the laws of physics or economics, and nothing is real. A former Liberal hero once made the fantastical claim that budgets would balance themselves. Now, in this fourth instalment, “masters of deception”, the Liberals' newest star, surrounded by the same old supporting cast, is using his cloaking superpower to render his gargantuan deficits invisible to the common eye. Can anyone over there distinguish fantasy from reality anymore?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for that tour through the Conservative cinematic universe, but let us get back to the facts here. The reality is we have seen in our home province of Alberta an increase of 40,000 jobs since the start of the year. We are seeing debt servicing at low levels internationally. Our deficit is the second lowest in the G7, 2.5% compared to the U.S.'s 8.5%. We are on track to meet the targets we said we were going to meet a year ahead of schedule, in fact.

Mr. Speaker, back in the real world, in 2015, Canada had a balanced budget and the richest middle class in the world. After a global economic meltdown, Canada's federal debt was $616 billion. Yesterday, we found out that after a decade of mismanagement, the Liberals' costly credit card budget would add more debt in the next five years than our country accumulated in 148 years. The Liberals have a predictable and increasingly tiresome response, an almost trance-like repetition of all the new things they are spending on in, entirely fuelled by massively out-of-control debt. When will this unconstrained explosion of deficit spending end?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague is speaking about heroes, but we are all wearing the poppy, and about the spending for our veterans. Here is what the budget would do. Veterans were always there for Canada, and we will be there for them. Our government is committed to ending veteran homelessness. That is what budget 2026 would do. It proposes $6.5 billion over 10 years to renew Reaching Home and the veteran homelessness program, supporting community-led initiatives to prevent and address homelessness. Those who serve our country deserve a safe place to—

Mr. Speaker, what we are is award-winning. Not only are the Liberals selling airports and our public assets, but Christmas came early for billionaires and corporate executives. Budget 2026 delivers $36 billion in mega deductions for corporations, but there is no mega deduction for everyday people. The temporary groceries benefit will quickly be swallowed up by rising food prices. Instead of gifting corporations $36 billion in mega deductions, will the Prime Minister redirect those resources to build a network of public grocery stores to introduce competition and bring down prices?

Mr. Speaker, the colleague knows very well that we are here for real Canadians with real programs. We are investing in affordable homes. We have committed to ending homelessness in the next 10 years. We are putting $10 billion through Build Canada Homes to build transitional housing, $5 billion to support projects that bring together housing and social projects, $6.5 million to renew the Reaching Home program and $2 billion for a health infrastructure that will help Canadians with mental health and addiction problems. We are here for Canadians, real Canadians.

title: Oral Questions: Public Safety
turns: Mr. Speaker, Canadians are losing faith in the parole system, and it is time for the Liberal government to take responsibility. Zakaria Amara, the ringleader of the Toronto 18 terrorist plot who wanted to bomb Parliament, who wanted to bomb National Defence bases and who wanted to bomb CSIS, was recently granted full parole. No wonder the people of Canada have lost faith in the parole system. When will the Liberal government take responsibility and reform parole?

Mr. Speaker, let us be very clear. The parole system works independently of government. It is people who are tasked with ensuring that parole is administered in a manner that is based on the information before them. Like the previous Conservative government, we continue to ensure the independence of the Parole Board, and the decisions it makes are fully independent of our government.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, those independent decisions are based on the laws that this House passes and this House must act now.
