Another reason Canadians are losing faith: Christopher Roulston, a designated dangerous offender who is doing time, an indeterminate sentence for sexual assault with a weapon and uttering threats, was recently granted day parole. He is a dangerous offender, a terrorist. When will these Liberals take accountability, stop blaming independence and reform parole?

Mr. Speaker, what is clear is that the Conservative Party members come up with allegations. They come up with types of law reform that they are looking for, but when this government brings forward law reform, like we did in Bill C-14 on bail and sentencing, like we did with Bill C-16 on victims' rights and like we did on protecting vulnerable communities, they vote against it or they stall. This is doublespeak. I will invite the member opposite to ensure that when we have legislation in front of the House, like Bill C-22, they pass it and they co-operate on—

Mr. Speaker, recently I spoke with Tina from my community, whose nine-year-old son was murdered by Douglas Lambier. In the 21 years since her son's murder, her life has never been the same. While his parole was recently denied by the government, Mr. Lambier has been allowed to have a 60-day unescorted absence to attend a program. Why is the Liberal government allowing a murderer who the Parole Board deems unfit to rejoin society to have a 60-day unescorted absence?

Mr. Speaker, let me express my condolences to Tina, her family and her community. What the individual has done is unspeakable, but let me be very clear. The decision of the Parole Board is independent. It makes decisions based on the facts in front of it. That is the way that the Conservative Party, when it was in government, implemented the Parole Act, and we continue to do the same.

title: Adjournment Proceedings: Small Business
turns: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to return to measures I raised in question period during Small Business Week. I specifically proposed two measures. The first would be increasing the small business deduction threshold from $500,000 to $700,000, which would have reduced the taxes collected from Canadian businesses to help them keep more money in their pockets. The second proposal I brought forward during Small Business Week was about increasing the GST small supplier threshold from $30,000 to $60,000 and indexing it to inflation moving forward. This would have saved many Canadian small businesses from the hassle of being a GST registrant. We are specifically talking here about the real small businesses, side hustles like maybe a car detailing business or a mom doing baked goods in the evenings to support her kids' dance and hockey activities. These recommendations were both supported by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. Both of these recommendations would have saved real money for Canadian businesses that are struggling right now. I have travelled across the country and spoken to thousands of small business owners. Many of them right now, at a period when we are seeing more and more insolvencies, are struggling to pay their commercial rent. Their input costs have gone through the roof. Their employee taxes, CPP, EI and payroll taxes, have all gone up in the last number of years. There are additional days off: In certain provinces there has been the addition of mandatory sick days. In many respects, small business owners say it has been a death by a thousand cuts, so in good faith, before the budget, I brought these proposals forward to the government, hoping it would support them, because it would simplify the tax code and life for small business owners in Canada. Unfortunately, it rejected these proposals. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business called the federal budget a “mega disappointment”, so I want to ask a straightforward question. My two specific proposals were, number one, increasing the small business deduction threshold from $500,000 to $700,000 and, number two, increasing the GST small supplier threshold from $30,000 to $60,000. Why did the government reject them? We even have Liberals on record supporting these policies at the industry committee. Why would the government reject them? It would not have cost too much money. In fact, if we took even a portion of what we just gave Brazil, which was over $500 million, we could have afforded these measures.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for her remarks, but she did not respond to my two very specific questions on two very specific policies. I am not opposed to the mega deduction in the budget, but the reality is that the taxation burden held by small businesses right now is becoming increasingly hard to shoulder. Businesses have been hit with input cost increases and with payroll tax increases that have limited their ability to grow and limited their ability to invest in things like new equipment, even if they get a really good capital cost writeoff. What we need to do in Canada, and what businesses are asking of the Government of Canada, is to lower their overall tax burden. I would like the member to comment on that. When can they expect lower taxes in Canada?

title: Routine Proceedings: Request for Emergency Debate
turns: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 52(2), I am requesting an emergency debate regarding Canada's failure to prevent and respond to residential school denialism, in response to the Permanent Peoples' Tribunal ruling from September 30, 2026, and the white nationalist demonstration that occurred on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve on September 27, 2026. Days before the sixth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, an all-white nationalist hate group gathered on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve. The Kamloops RCMP stated this in a news release: The posting of a banner bearing the words “got bones,” combined with the use of masks to conceal their identities while making such public statements is a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division. The statement on the banner is in reference to the mass grave hoax conspiracy, an overt form of residential school denialism seeking to dismiss a genocide that was recognized unanimously in the House of Commons in 2022. Just last week, the Permanent Peoples' Tribunal, an international court, ruled that Canada committed the international crimes of genocide and crimes against humanity against indigenous peoples and that these crimes continue to be present. The ruling also stated that Canada continues to fail to comply with its international legal obligations to respond to these crimes and has been reluctant to counter denialist misinformation. Under resolutions of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, states have a duty to restore and guarantee the fundamental rights of indigenous peoples after systemic human rights violations. This includes residential school denialism through the mass spreading of disinformation, which the tribunal called on Canada to criminalize. The tribunal also ruled that Canada is failing to provide remedies to restore the fundamental rights of indigenous peoples and guarantee the non-reoccurrence of these abuses. It says, “Canada is compromising the future.” The failure to address these matters reflects poorly on Canada in the international community. However, the escalation of hate by white nationalist groups in Canada that led to the violent demonstration last week underscores the direct risk that residential school denialism poses to the safety of indigenous peoples. It is classified as an emergency and a matter of urgent consideration for Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I am seeking an emergency debate today because Canada is facing a serious threat to our democracy and our sovereignty, and that is happening right now. In just two weeks from today, Albertans will vote in a referendum on the future of our country. The Globe and Mail revealed this past weekend the extent of co-operation, maybe even collusion, between Alberta's separatist movement and extremist Republican political operatives connected to the Trump administration. There are credible reports that these separatist leaders are using American political technology to target, identify and mobilize voters. There is talk of a $500-million slush fund, and the separatists have reportedly offered access to Alberta's oil and water in exchange for assistance. Let us be absolutely clear about what that means. These are not simply Albertans having a political disagreement with Ottawa. These are extremists seeking foreign assistance to break up Canada. There is a word for people who put foreign interests ahead of their own country: traitors. Under Canadian law, they would be investigated, and if convicted, they should face the full force of the law. However, this goes even further. Nearly 2.9 million Albertans had their personal information exposed after the provincial list of electors was improperly obtained. That information does not simply disappear. We now have legitimate questions about whether Albertans' data could be used as part of political targeting and foreign influence operations. Who is the foreign political figure at the centre of all this? It is Donald Trump, a man who has repeatedly threatened Canada's sovereignty and talked about making Canada the 51st state. American Republican operatives are now showing an interest in an Alberta separatist movement that could fundamentally weaken this country. That should alarm every Canadian from every political party. This is precisely why we need an emergency debate right now, not after October 19, not after foreign actors have had another two weeks to manipulate Canadians, not after Albertans have cast their ballots, but now. Parliament must demand answers about foreign interference, foreign political financing, the use of Alberta's personal information and involvement of American political operatives in Canada's constitutional future. Albertans have every right to debate their future, but that future must be decided by Albertans, not by Donald Trump, Republicans, Russians or malignant foreign interests. This is an emergency. Canadian sovereignty is at stake, and the people trying to trade it away for foreign political support should understand how seriously Canadians take this threat. Canada is worth fighting for. We need to have a debate in this House now.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister made a big show of promising to buy and build Canadian, but it was all talk and no results. Today, an analysis by the Toronto Star demonstrated that he increased the amount destined for American companies to $7.8 billion. The share of the money for government contracts that goes to the U.S. is up 50%. Why did the Prime Minister put on a big show of theatrics with elbows up, break his promise and force Canadian workers to send more of their tax dollars south?

Mr. Speaker, this government has put in place “buy Canada”, and with buy Canada, we have $2 billion invested in General Dynamics in London, and we have over $100 billion coming up in submarines, to be invested in Canada, across this country. The Leader of the Opposition may have been sleeping, but last week the Government of Alberta, the Government of Canada and Pembina announced the largest pipeline in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, after announcements and promises, today we found the results. The Prime Minister promised, just like he is promising today, that he would repatriate production and Canadian purchases to this country. Instead, he has actually increased the dollar value and the share of federal government purchases that go to the United States of America. While Canadians are out of a job because tariffs have prevented them from working, the Prime Minister forces them to send their tax dollars to the same American companies we are competing with. Why is the Prime Minister sending our money south?

Mr. Speaker, while the Leader of the Opposition is sleeping, this government is acting. I am going to give him a little geography lesson. At the Matawinie mine in Quebec, we have shovels in the ground. At the Contrecoeur terminal at the port of Montreal, we have shovels in the ground. At the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, we have shovels in the ground. At the north coast transmission line in British Columbia, we have shovels in the ground. For the Darlington project, which is in Ontario, we have shovels in the ground. We are building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister cared about it, he would stand up and answer the question himself. Instead, he is worried that he might accidentally say affordability is the best it has been in over a decade. He is totally out of touch, while Canadians are out of money. As the MNP report that was released today said, more than two in five Canadians report being $200 or less away from insolvency, more than half say they do not have enough savings to support themselves if they are unemployed for six months and a third believe they would not be able to cope financially for three months if they had an unexpected event. Will the Prime Minister look them in the eye and say affordability is the best it has been in over a decade?

Mr. Speaker, I know the member of Parliament is now an Albertan MP, but in Ontario, I was so excited to announce with Minister Calandra the extension of the Ontario early learning and child care agreement with Canada that will retain child care at an average of $19 a day per child in Ontario for the next four years. That is a savings of $9,000 per child per year for families. That is the kind of affordability that families are looking for. This is a reliable affordability partnership at all levels of government. It is something I think the member of Parliament just does not understand.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are as totally out of touch as Canadians are totally out of money. That is why the Prime Minister cannot answer questions from the Canadian people. For example, diesel prices have hit record highs. Nobody blames the Prime Minister for the war in Iran or the war between Ukraine and Russia. However, what we blame him for is the fact that diesel is 24¢ a litre more expensive in Canada than in the U.S. and 32¢ more expensive than the worldwide average. Will the Prime Minister vote for our plan this Wednesday to save Canadians on fuel and make us self-sufficient at home?

Mr. Speaker, we work with our allies to try to bring diesel prices down. Diesel prices have gone down 6% over the last three days because of coordinated ally action. While the Conservatives talk down things, they are apparently sleeping. We are building 6,000 new jobs in LNG Canada phase one. We are building 140,000 new jobs from the new Pacific link pipeline. Maybe they should wake up and start to build with us.

Mr. Speaker, he says there is coordinated action to bring down global energy prices. It turns out that he has not been able to take any action at all, despite wrongly telling the media he would release 24 million barrels of oil. It turns out he does not have 24 billion barrels of oil. He does not have one barrel of oil, because Canada is the only G7 country without an above-ground strategic oil reserve. We have a plan, though, to take all tax off diesel, to produce more of it here at home and to store up a strategic reserve so that we can actually profit from reducing prices around the world. Will the government adopt our plan?

Mr. Speaker, he asked us to wake him up, so I will give him a bit of good news. Diesel production in Canada is up 16% this year. We are operating at maximum capacity. We export diesel. Why do they not start trying to help build Canada instead of talking Canada down?

Mr. Speaker, the world economy has been disrupted by rising protectionism, global conflicts and a reshaping of the international order. As a result, the cost of living for Canadians has taken a hit. In response, we are focusing on what we can control, by putting money back into their pockets. With Thanksgiving just around the corner, my constituents want to know what steps the government has taken to make their lives more affordable.

Mr. Speaker, that was a great question. From the middle-class tax cut to the pause in the excise fuel tax, we are delivering affordability for Canadians. Today, millions of Canadians are going to receive the groceries and essentials benefit, meaning up to $170 for an individual and up to $340 for a family of four. That will bring 77,000 Canadians out of poverty. On this side of the House, we are going to focus on affordability for Canadians. The other side can continue with the rhetoric.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, Canadians are hungry, literally. They cannot afford to feed themselves. Today, Food Banks Canada released a report revealing that the number of visits is up 9% since the Prime Minister was elected on the promise that he would make food affordable. There were 2.35 million visits in one single month, and food banks are literally running out of food. The Prime Minister said on his first day in office that he would be judged by the price at the grocery store, so what is the verdict according to the 2.35 million people lined up at food banks?

Mr. Speaker, before I answer, I want to thank the hon. member for the work he has done in his riding at CFB Wainwright. We all stand with the families who lost loved ones and the families of the injured. We thank him for the work he has done in the community, and we all stand together on that tragedy. In terms of affordability, the government has taken multiple measures on affordability, and we look forward to the opposition at least once supporting those measures, whether it is our national school food program, the dental program or child care. Just once we would love to see the opposition support affordability measures.

Mr. Speaker, this is more proof that the Liberal government and the Prime Minister are out of touch, as Canadians are out of food and out of money. Food Banks Canada's CEO said this report “is the story of what happens when millions of people are out of options.” She also said, “In the past, most people in Canada could absorb a small financial setback... those days are over. Canada’s bleak new reality is that millions of people are making impossible trade-offs every day as they choose between food or rent”. How could the Liberal government and the Prime Minister vote yesterday against the basic recognition that we are in an affordability crisis?
Mr. Speaker, there is a big difference between talking about something and doing something. The opposition had their opportunity—

Mr. Speaker, there was an opportunity to vote for the groceries and essentials benefit to put $1,900 in the pockets of Canadians. They voted against it. There was an opportunity for Conservatives to support the national school food program. What did they do to help kids? They voted against it. They voted against dental care and child care. At every opportunity, they talk about affordability, and they do nothing to help Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, he is absolutely right. There is a big difference between talk and results. The Liberals talked about how they were going to make food affordable, yet what did they do? They delivered 2.35 million visits to food banks. They talked about how they were going to reduce the cost of living, but what did they do? They are 50% over target on inflation numbers. They talked about doubling homebuilding, yet they delivered a 4% decrease in construction, and now they are not even talking about doubling homebuilding. When will we have an end to all the Liberal talk and actually get some real results?

Mr. Speaker, we are delighted to bring some real results that I wish the opposition supported. For example, we took the GST off new homes, saving $250,000 for new homebuyers. They do not support that. We took the federal excise tax off gasoline, saving people 25¢. They do not support that. This is a critical moment in our country. Whether we are building affordable homes or supporting families, for once, the opposition should use this opportunity to work and build this country strong.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister told Canadians he should be judged by their experience at the grocery store. For Becky, her experience has been a nightmare. She said she works hard, but she still cannot afford to put food on the table for her and her son. She is not alone. There have been more than 2.3 million visits to food banks in Canada in one month. The number of Canadian families forced to use a food bank is up 116% since 2019. Will the Prime Minister admit that relying on a food bank is now a reality for many Canadians, or does he truly believe that affordability is the best it has been in a decade?

Mr. Speaker, there certainly is hardship in Canada. We should not ignore that fact. What we should do is work together and not politicize the hardship of Canadians. The member knows that. All members know that, or should know that. We have six million Canadians receiving the Canada child benefit. We have 6.5 million Canadians receiving dental support. We have 400,000 children receiving the support of the school food program. We have 900,000 children and their families receiving the support of the child care program. We will continue in that vein on the basis that we represent our constituents and always have.

Mr. Speaker, the member said to not politicize a food affordability crisis, a crisis that lies clearly at the feet of the Liberal government. In its 10 years, food prices are up 30%. The number of Canadians being forced to a food bank has doubled. In my riding, in Okotoks, in one quarter, the food bank served 26,000 people. Shockingly, 30% of those people had full-time jobs, but they still were forced to a food bank because Liberal policies have made feeding their families unaffordable. Will the Liberals check their egos at the door and eliminate taxes to make sure Canadians can put food on the table?

Mr. Speaker, if he is going to cite Food Banks Canada and its report, he should look at the recommendations. The recommendations are clear. The groceries and essentials benefit is something the organization called for. This government enacted it, and 12 million Canadians are now receiving it. The organization also called for, among other things, housing. We have a serious focus on housing and the building up of critical infrastructure. In particular, the report called for expanding energy options in this country so Canadians can have access to cheaper energy. I invite the Conservatives to put aside partisanship in the same way that Premier Ford has, in the same way that Premier Smith has, in the same way Stephen—

Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of the Liberal government, Canadians are paying more and getting less every single time they visit the grocery store. According to today's Food Banks Canada report, Canada had over 2.3 million food bank visits in March of 2026. That is an increase of over 200,000 visits since March of last year, yet the Liberal government continues to insist its economic plan is working. Will the Liberals finally acknowledge that relying on food banks has become a reality for too many Canadians, or are the Liberals just too out of touch to admit it?

Mr. Speaker, I want to start by acknowledging and thanking representatives of the Daily Bread Food Bank for being on the Hill and meeting with parliamentarians yesterday. It is one of the biggest partners in this study. Its report asks us, and provincial governments in particular, to build a future where no one goes hungry, and that is what we are committed to doing. That report talks about the importance of income security. It talks about the groceries and essentials benefit. It talks about the Canada disability benefit and the Canada disability tax credit. It talks about the Canada workers benefit. What do these measures have in common? The opposition voted against them.

Mr. Speaker, Conservatives will support measures that keep Canadians' money in their own pockets. Just yesterday, the Liberals were the only party in the House to vote against acknowledging that Canada is in an affordability crisis. Meanwhile, families in Oshawa are living it. Over 3,600 people rely on the food bank in Oshawa every month. It has been forced to limit visits and close its doors to people who need it, because the resources are not there. How can the government claim to have a plan to fix Canada's affordability crisis if it does not even admit there is a problem?

Mr. Speaker, I think the problem Canadians have is that they see through the rhetoric on the other side of the House, which would cut the income security programs that a report such as this calls for and that are supporting Canadians right now. If the member stands up and again votes against the national school food program, a program that is in 80% of public schools in this country, that is what Canadians have learned to expect of the opposition when it comes to the supports we are delivering for Canadians and Canadian children.

Mr. Speaker, there are 2.4 million food bank visits in a single month. That is the highest ever recorded in this country, and one in three is for a child. What greater failure of a government's economic record is there than that a parent who works all day still cannot provide for their children? After more than a year and a half under the Liberal Prime Minister, Canadians are working harder but falling further behind. Will the Prime Minister explain why, in a country such as Canada, honest work is no longer enough to provide for one's family?

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to ask why members opposite can stand in the House on this issue without answering the question as to why they vote against school food. Why do they vote against dental workers?

Mr. Speaker, time and again, we take action on this side of the House. The government has advanced a national child care strategy, dental care and a national school food program, among other efforts to help Canadians make ends meet. Members opposite continue to vote against these things that have direct impacts on the people in their communities who rely on things such as checkups at the dentist and affordable child care. It makes no sense.

Mr. Speaker, the member says that they are working, but the reality is that whatever they are doing is, in fact, not working, not when there are 2.4 million visits to a food bank in a single month and one in three of them is for children. I would encourage the member to stop measuring success by how many Canadians need government assistance, and start measuring by how many no longer do. Therefore I ask again, why, after 11 years of the Liberal government, honest hard work is no longer enough to provide for one's family.

Mr. Speaker, the national school food program is reaching an additional 400,000 children across this country with nutritious meals. That is 80% of public schools across this country that are benefiting from this support. Again, why do the members opposite vote against things such as breakfast for children in elementary schools, dental care and other things that help families make ends meet?

Mr. Speaker, earlier this year, the Prime Minister said that affordability is the best it has been in over a decade, but despite the Prime Minister's promise, Canadian families are in trouble. In Yukon, food bank visits are up 24% from 2025. In the Northwest Territories and Nunavut, food bank visits are up 29% from 2025, and 32.5% of food bank visitors are children. Will the Prime Minister admit that food banks are now the sad reality for too many Canadians, or is he really that out of touch?

Mr. Speaker, apart from the suite of supports that my colleagues have outlined already today, we are also diversifying our trade partners, supercharging major projects, investing in workers, drawing down costs and keeping the needs of Canadians foremost in every decision. The other side of the House is just playing politics today. Why do the Conservatives not come along with the projects that are actually making a difference for this country and in people's lives?

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister made a flashy announcement about promising to buy and build Canadian, yet we have learned this was all talk and no results. It was just a big political stunt. The Toronto Star confirms that since he made that promise, government purchases from American companies have actually increased by 50%, to nearly $8 billion. The Liberals are completely out of touch, and Canadians are rightfully shocked by this. Why is the Prime Minister choosing to send billions of Canadian tax dollars to the United States in the middle of an unjust trade war?

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud of the buy Canadian policy that we announced in December. It now applies to procurements above $5 million. When we look at the numbers the member is referring to, we have made a choice to encourage investment in Canada and to prioritize Canadian content. This means contracts like the one to General Dynamics in London, with 1,700 employees in London, workers in London, and 600 suppliers. That is the kind of contract the member says our government should not do, one that is supporting Canadian industry and Canadian workers here at home and incentivizing Canadian content.

Mr. Speaker, we always have to dig deeper to get the truth when it comes to the Liberals' big announcements and promises. The Liberals claim they are buying Canadian, but that is not the case in two multi-billion-dollar examples. The reannounced LNG phase two project will be using Chinese steel instead of supporting laid-off Canadian steelworkers, and shockingly, the Liberals are handing out billions in federal contracts and work to American companies. So much for buy Canadian. The Prime Minister pretends to stand up to President Trump while giving out $8 billion to the United States in contracts. The question is simple. When will the Liberals stop sending Canadian jobs and money to Beijing and Washington?

Mr. Speaker, again, I will raise with the opposition that foreign direct investment is a very important part of our economy. It employs tens of thousands of people. These companies design, engineer, retain IP and have headquarters. All this matters. It matters as much as Canadian companies. We can do two things at a time. We can support both. Companies like L3Harris, Safran and Airbus are big companies in Canada. We will continue to support them as long as they continue to invest here at home.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has told Canadians time and time again how during a generational trade war, the Liberals plan on strengthening the Canadian economy. However, the data suggests otherwise. According to the Toronto Star, the Prime Minister has increased Canadian contracts to the U.S. by over 50%. Canadian industry needs support from the Prime Minister, not inconsistency and more political grandstanding. Our Conservative plan would save Canadian jobs, not send them down south. When will the government prioritize the Canadian economy and spend Canadian dollars on Canadian goods?

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues have given a number of examples of how we are supporting Canadian jobs, Canadian materials and Canadians throughout our procurement process. If the Conservatives want to support perhaps the most quintessential of Canadian investments, they could get out of the way of Alto high-speed rail going from Quebec City to Toronto and now also studying very closely the possibility of high-speed rail between Edmonton and Calgary. Will the Conservatives stand up for—

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister chose his words very carefully yesterday when asked whether he had discussed the $2.3 billion given to his long-time friend and fundraiser Dan Goldberg, CEO of Telesat. He said that he was not involved in the decision. That was not the question. Section 9 of Canada's Conflict of Interest Act prohibits public office holders from using their position to influence others to advance their own private interests and those of relatives or friends. Let us try this again. Has the Prime Minister ever discussed Telesat with his ministers, any of his staff, or public servants, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, the question was asked yesterday, and the answer was provided many times yesterday. Canada has world-leading rules and regulations when it comes to ethics, disclosure and compliance. All members on this side of the House take that very seriously. The answer yesterday, as the answer is today, was that we follow these rules and we take them very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, that is the exact same response the Liberals gave as the SNC-Lavalin and WE scandals were unfolding. It is what they said on the green slush fund scandal and Trudeau's trip to billionaire island. In every case, after they repeated it, the truth came out. Let us hear it one more time. Who wants to hear it one more time? Did the Prime Minister have any discussion about Telesat with any ministers, any staff or any public servants during or after 2.3 billion in tax dollars was given to a near bankrupt company run by a well-connected Liberal insider and friend of the Prime Minister, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, for those who have just tuned in, on the Conservative side, we have just entered the conspiracy TV segment of the show, where conspiracies come left, right and centre. Some are right-wing focused; some are really right-wing focused. Again, we follow the rules here. The minister spoke to this. The Prime Minister spoke to this. We will always follow the rules on this side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, let us try this again. There is no doubt that the AI minister, the Prime Minister and the Telesat CEO are good friends. They hang out together. They are in running clubs and book clubs. Their kids all go to the same rich private school, so there is a close relationship. Why did the AI minister put Dan Goldberg of Telesat on his ethics screen but the Prime Minister did not?

Mr. Speaker, what I will say is that when we look at Canada in terms of ethics and when we look at all the other rules and regulations as they pertain to ethics, Canada leads the way. As members of Parliament, all of us here follow them every single day, and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, after being here for a few years, I thought Justin Trudeau was going to have the most corrupt government ever in the history of the country, but the Prime Minister said, “Hold my beer. Watch this.” He is giving $2.3 billion to Telesat and to a close personal friend. We all know the Prime Minister thinks he is better than the average Canadian, but why does the Prime Minister think he is above the law?

Mr. Speaker, we are about 15 minutes into question period and they have already jumped the shark three times. It is amazing. Our country, again, has the most focused, stringent ethical rules of any nation in the world. We are focused on them every single day. The Prime Minister spoke about this on several occasions today, and the answer is that we follow the rules every single day. Why? It is the right thing for this country.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that corporate power brokers would simultaneously like to get a paycheque from a company and go work for the regulator that approves that company's applications. It is too bad that kind of arrangement does not work out for single moms, seniors and small business owners who cannot afford to eat. One in three Canadians is skipping meals, according to the Salvation Army today, because they cannot afford groceries. Nearly half of young people fall into that category, and 50% of Canadians are digging into their savings to pay their bills. Will Canadians at least get a budget on Thursday that will save them money so they can afford to eat?

Mr. Speaker, I remember when the Conservative Party actually used to care about jobs. Let us talk about what the Major Projects Office is doing: 8,000 new jobs at the port of Montreal, 1,000 new jobs at Nouveau Monde Graphite, 10,000 new jobs at Darlington and 18,000 jobs at Pickering. Why does the Leader of the Opposition not support the hard work of the MPO, which is creating jobs where men and women can work hard and feed their family in this country?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, I shared a conversation around my family dinner table about how difficult life has become for young families like my daughter's, but some families face something far worse. A new report reveals that one in eight Toronto children relies on a food bank, and more than one in four surveyed families reported a child missing meals because they could not afford food. These are children going hungry while the government piles on debt and spends over $1 billion a week on just paying interest. How many more children must go without supper before the Prime Minister makes affordability a priority?

Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House, we not only thank the Food Banks Canada network for its important advocacy, but also read those reports and heed their advice. That is why in the third paragraph of the report that the member would have read, it says, “In recent years, we have welcomed and see hope in measures such as the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, the National School Food Program”, which the member continues to deride, “Build Canada Homes and the Canada Disability Benefit.” It is worth noting that all of the measures the food banks network is supporting and recommending that we are doing, they voted against.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Prime Minister spent, and today Canadians are paying the price. He doubled the deficit that Trudeau left behind, increased government spending to the highest share of GDP since 1996 and is threatening to add $700 billion more in debt. More deficits cause more inflation, which today caused the Bank of Canada to bring in more interest on Canadians. How much will Canadians have to pay before the Prime Minister finally hits the brakes on his out-of-control Liberal spending?

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada was very clear about the global causes of inflation and why it acted. It was very clear that our growth is going to pick up next year and the year following, the strongest in the G7. Let us be clear about the fiscal record of the government: the lowest net debt in the G7, the second-lowest deficit in the G7, operational spending down from 8% to 2%, a 10% cut in the civil service and a 20% cut in consultants, $60 billion of savings. That is even before the budget next week. We are building Canada strong—

Mr. Speaker, how completely out of touch that is. Canadian families are the most indebted anywhere in the G7, and today they will go home to learn that their mortgage payments, car payments and line of credit payments will go up because the Prime Minister could not control his spending. He doubled Trudeau's deficit and has imposed a new fuel tax that is driving up the cost of diesel to 30¢ higher than in the U.S., which is one of the causes the Bank of Canada cited in raising rates on Canadians today. Will the Prime Minister get his hands out of the pockets of Canadians so they do not have to pay more in their rates?

Mr. Speaker, I repeat: Spending is down from 8% per year to 2%. This is new information. The operational budget will be closed next year, one year ahead of schedule. There is a 10% reduction in civil service, a 20% reduction in consultants, the strongest growth in the G7 in the coming years, and mortgage affordability down every month in the current government's time.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister says affordability is better. Everybody out there knows that is false, and it is worse today. The Bank of Canada governor said that food price inflation will be even higher next year: “Higher diesel prices raise freight and operating costs in fuel-intensive sectors such as food processing [and] agriculture”. The Prime Minister is not to blame for world prices, but he is to blame for the fact that our prices are much higher than the world's, in part because of what the Nova Scotia Energy Board calculates is 16¢ a litre in extra fuel standard taxes that the Prime Minister is imposing at the pump. Will the Prime Minister reverse this tax so that we can reverse the inflation and reverse the rate hikes?

Mr. Speaker, there is a problem with starting to quote the Bank of Canada. It is all on the public record. If we look at the Bank of Canada and affordability metrics, there was 54% of disposable income affordability before this government came into place, and it is now at 41%. For 24 straight months, asking rents have gone down. We are improving affordability in a tough housing market. Next time the Leader of the Opposition goes through Edmonton, he might want to confirm that the price of diesel in Edmonton is the same as in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, could he be more out of touch? That sounded just like his statement back on March 25, that affordability is the best it has been in a decade. The same month he said that, Food Banks Canada registered a record-smashing 2.35 million visits, 9% higher than when he took office, with fewer Canadians believing they will ever be able to afford a home than in the other 21 countries polled by Habitat for Humanity. Will the Prime Minister admit that affordability is not the best it has been in a decade?

Mr. Speaker, let us talk about affordability and steps that governments can take to improve affordability. The Canadian dental care plan benefits over 17,000 people in the riding of Battle River—Crowfoot. The Canada child benefit supports over 14,000 families. There are EDC summer job grants. I could go on. They have two things in common: first, that this government proposed them and passed them; and second, that the Leader of the Opposition voted against them every single time.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised to move at speeds not seen in generations, but Canadians did not realize that what he meant was accumulating debt at speeds not seen in generations. In five years, he plans to add more debt than all prime ministers before Justin Trudeau combined. Today, because of the Liberals' inflationary spending, the Bank of Canada has raised interest rates, making government debt even more expensive. Can the Prime Minister explain who will repay this mountain of debt and how?

Mr. Speaker, all the opposition members do is talk down our economy and our workers, but they do not realize that criticism does not create jobs. Their negativity does not make life affordable. Did the Conservatives vote for the groceries and essentials benefit? No. Do they vote to make life more affordable? No. In the member's own riding, when we support Technical Steel Corp or Exco Engineering, do they support that investment in businesses to create jobs? No. They should get with the program, and we should build this country strong together.

Mr. Speaker, the member did not answer my question. My question was about the vicious cycle that the Prime Minister is building, which is more debt, more interest and more borrowing. In fact, he is borrowing to pay for the interest he already owes on the debt that he already took on. Today, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates. Now, the government pays more to borrow, families pay more on their mortgages and more taxes go toward interest instead of services. When will the Prime Minister break his vicious cycle and finally get this borrowing under control?

Mr. Speaker, Canada has the fastest growing economy in the G7 and the lowest debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7. We are creating jobs. The Conservatives talk about making life more affordable, but they do not do anything about it. Do they vote for affordable child care? No. Do they vote for national school food lunches? No. Do they vote for dental care? No. All they know how to say is no to Canadians. We will continue to say yes to building Canadian, yes to building strong and yes to making life more affordable for everybody.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister assumed in his first budget that interest rates would stabilize and go lower, except they have actually been going up, including at the Bank of Canada. That means that Canadians will pay more when they renew their mortgage, but it also means taxpayers are on the hook for billions more. Why is that? It is because the Prime Minister chose to double the size of the deficits he inherited, and he has pushed borrowing to record numbers, including nearly $600 billion this year alone. Will the Prime Minister tell Canadians how much his mistake has cost Canadians with higher interest rates?

Mr. Speaker, I will share that we have chosen to be there for Canadians. In fact, thanks to our government, we have cut taxes for 22 million Canadians. This means more money stays in their pockets. While things are challenging at the grocery store, we have delivered the national groceries and essentials benefits so that the average family of four in our ridings receive close to $1,900. That is real support, and we are going to continue to be there. The good news, also, is that we have increased the Canada child benefit. That is an additional $160 per child this year.

Mr. Speaker, we live in an era when global events have local impacts. The people of University—Rosedale understand that there are forces affecting our economy that are beyond our control. They do not want to hear parliamentarians talk down our economy, our businesses and our workers. They want us to address affordability by building on our strengths and our shared values. Can the Secretary of State for the CRA and Financial Institutions tell us about the work under way to make life more affordable for people in Toronto and across this great country?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member for University—Rosedale for her strong advocacy on the disability tax credit and automatic federal benefits. We are going to build a strong, resilient economy for all Canadians. We are attracting outside investment. We are going to build Canada strong. We are cutting taxes for 22 million Canadians. The groceries and essentials benefit is offering $1,900 for families. We will continue to focus on and deliver on affordability measures for Canadians. On this side of the House, Canadians know who stands with them. It is our side.

title: Oral Questions: Taxation
turns: Mr. Speaker, potato farmers in P.E.I. have told me that they are bracing themselves for the impact that high diesel prices are going to have on their farms. Nathan told me that fuel prices have already doubled to $14,000 for harvest this year. Skyview Farms told me that their fuel price was $19,000 in one month. Ike said that when diesel prices in P.E.I. go up, the price of everything goes up. High diesel prices are driving up costs on farmers and grocery prices for every single Canadian. Will the out-of-touch Liberals support our Conservative plan to reduce taxes on diesel, or will they turn their backs on farmers at harvest?

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party of Canada is not turning its back on farmers. We are making all kinds of investments alongside farmers. We are working alongside them, and we will continue to work alongside them. We announced more than $370 million in new biofuels production incentive programs to support Canadian producers and biodiesel. With the Imperial Strathcona project, which we heard of yesterday, 2.5 million tonnes of canola are being used to produce about a billion litres of biodiesel fuel. We are going to continue to invest alongside farmers.

Mr. Speaker, here are the consequences of bad Liberal policy. Stephen, a grain farmer, told me that high diesel prices are costing him $5,000 a day. During harvest, they are going 24-7. The bill is going to be more than $100,000 just in additional fuel prices for one farm. Farmers, truckers and manufacturers are all paying soaring diesel prices, and now Canadian families have to brace themselves for even higher grocery prices. Will the Prime Minister support our plan for diesel price relief to give farmers a break today?

Mr. Speaker, this is how the member opposite can help his concerned member: vote for Bill C-38 and extend the exemption on the diesel tax. Why do they not do something that will actually make a difference?

Mr. Speaker, how out of touch was that? Diesel in Deer Lake has reached $2.77 a litre. Michelle, a farmer in Cormack, expects her diesel bill to reach a staggering $135,000 this year, up nearly 56% since 2024. Diesel costs for farmers, fishermen and truckers mean higher grocery bills for Newfoundland and Labrador families. Will the energy minister support our Conservative emergency fuel relief plan, which would eliminate federal taxes on diesel until at least Canada Day 2027 and provide real relief for Canadians and farmers like Michelle?

Mr. Speaker, if the member opposite would like to do something tangible for the residents of her riding, she needs to speak to them about the benefits they received through the food and essentials benefit yesterday, and also—
Mr. Speaker, I will go from the top. If the member opposite would like to support her constituents—

Mr. Speaker, if the member opposite wants to do something tangible for the residents of her riding, the first thing she can do is speak to them about how important it was to receive the food and essentials benefit yesterday. Second to that, she could support Bill C-38, which will see the extension of the excise tax relief on diesel. These are tangible benefits for Canadians, not rhetoric.
Mr. Speaker, if those programs were working, residents from her constituency would not be reaching out to me asking me—

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are paying roughly 24¢ per litre more for diesel than Americans and 31¢ more than the global average. The government cannot control conflicts overseas, but it can certainly control taxes and barriers that it imposes here at home. Will the members opposite support our Conservative plan to cut diesel taxes and remove the barriers preventing Canada from producing, refining and transporting more of its own fuel?

Mr. Speaker, off the top I will say to the member to support Bill C-38. I will remind her that I speak with residents in her riding and across Newfoundland and Labrador on a regular basis, and they support the $1 million for small craft harbours. They support the $81 million for wild Atlantic salmon, which is going to see real benefits in our province. They support Churchill Falls and what it is going to mean for our economy. They support 5 Wing Goose Bay and the millions of dollars that are going to move into that community and the province. These are tangible results. She needs to speak to more of her residents.

Mr. Speaker, last week I met with Kelly, a grain farmer from back home. His diesel bill jumped over $26,000 this year from last year. That is $26,000 that he cannot use to buy groceries for his family or put toward next year's crops. He has no choice but to absorb this cost because grain farmers cannot pass it on, and he has to plant and harvest his crops no matter the price. The Liberals could offer real relief on his fuel bill for next growing season by voting for a motion to remove all federal taxes on diesel. Will the Liberals do the right thing and support our emergency fuel relief plan to save Canadians like Kelly some money?

Mr. Speaker, one of the things we are not going to do is take advice from the Conservatives. We will never take advice from them because, while they talk about this plan, they do not have a plan. They simply do not. I will point out to my colleague from Saskatchewan that not only have they not done anything for 11 years, but today we delivered the groceries and essentials benefit, which helps families right across Saskatchewan and Canada.

Mr. Speaker, for 11 years, Liberal taxes and red tape blocked pipelines and new refineries from moving and producing Canadian fuel. Canada is the world's fourth-largest oil producer, but diesel hit $2.63 a litre last month, up 71% from a year ago. When diesel costs more, farmers, truckers, builders and families all pay more for everything. Canadians need lower taxes, not more excuses. Will the Prime Minister support our emergency fuel relief plan and scrap all federal taxes on diesel to save Canadians money?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians know that war has driven up fuel prices around the world. That is why we suspended the federal carbon price and the federal excise tax on diesel. Since last September, we have taken 25¢ off a litre of diesel. We continue to respond by making Canada more energy-secure and less beholden to global energy price volatility by building the energy infrastructure we need. We would really like the Conservatives to help us do that as well.

Mr. Speaker, he can tell that to the Canadians paying up to $240 more each time they fill up. That is the cost of Liberal failure. The Prime Minister cannot blame wars abroad for taxes at home. Liberals can scrap the industrial carbon tax, the fuel standard tax and the GST on diesel today, but instead of relief, Canadians get Liberal talk and no results. Farmers cannot fuel tractors with Liberal excuses, and families cannot eat announcements. When will the out-of-touch Liberals cut diesel taxes so Canadians can afford to drive and feed themselves?
Mr. Speaker, I would invite the member opposite to join us in voting for Bill C-38 to extend the excise tax reduction.

Mr. Speaker, farmers in Haldimand—Norfolk grow the food that Canadians depend on, but that food must be planted, it must be transported and it must be harvested. Every step of the way depends on fuel. When diesel prices rise, farmers and truckers pay more, and those costs are transferred to consumers at the grocery store checkout line. Our Conservative motion would provide emergency fuel relief and bring those costs down. Will the government support our motion and give farmers—

Mr. Speaker, everybody is familiar with the story of the Strait of Hormuz and what it is doing to the world, including global market prices on diesel. This is not just a Canadian problem. It is a world problem. We suspended the excise tax. We also cut the carbon tax when we were first elected, a promise we made to Canadians across this country and to farmers. We will continue working hard for farmers as we go forward.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are all talk and no results. Our Conservative motion would save families money. After 10 years, Canadians need relief, not another Liberal promise. Families cannot put a press release on the dinner table. In Haldimand—Norfolk, I represent farmers who produce the food and families who can no longer afford to buy it. Will the government support our motion for emergency fuel relief, or will it keep Canadians lining up at food banks just to survive?

Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House, we are going to continue to focus on affordability. We cut taxes for 22 million Canadians. We just paused the federal fuel excise tax, saving Canadians 10¢ a litre when they fill up. If we combine that with the consumer carbon tax, it is 28¢ in savings. Yesterday, Canadians received their groceries and essentials benefit. That benefit will lift 77,000 Canadians out of poverty.

Mr. Speaker, higher fuel prices are official Liberal Party policy. Higher diesel prices mean that everything that moves by truck, train or cargo ship costs more. Canadians are suffering due to Liberal inaction. They cannot feed their kids press releases. Just like with the carbon tax and the gas tax, the Liberals will not do anything for Canadians until the polls shift. Will the Liberals stop wasting time and join us in passing the emergency fuel relief plan?

Mr. Speaker, respectfully, I reject the entire premise of the question. We have been taking action on supporting affordability across this country. We have before the House right now the ability to extend the federal fuel excise tax removal on gasoline and diesel. The hon. member and her party have the opportunity to support the government's initiative in that matter. Yesterday, the groceries and essentials benefit, which is providing recipients somewhere between $200 and $300 per family, found its way to Canadian families. We know there are challenges happening around the world. The government is taking the initiatives it can to be able to support Canadians. We would certainly like the Conservatives to join that effort. The member is from Pembroke. There are lots of farmers in Pembroke. We have a lot to say for farmers. The member ran on a platform in April 2025 with not a single thing to say for Canadian farmers. That is the record of the Conservative Party.

title: Routine Proceedings: Instruction to Legislative Committee on Bill C-39
turns: That it be an instruction to the Legislative Committee on Bill C-39 that, during its consideration of Bill C-39, An Act respecting certain measures to strengthen the economy, the committee be granted the power to travel throughout Canada to hear testimony from interested parties and that the necessary staff do accompany the committee. Mr. Speaker, New Democrats want to build big things in this country and so does the labour movement across this country, but we cannot do that if it means hurting our labour rights in this country. We have to protect labour rights, we have to respect indigenous rights and we have to ensure the benefits of economic development flow to Canadians. It cannot mean giving cabinet sweeping powers to remove or override those rights. I am bringing forward this motion because this is one of the most consequential pieces of legislation this Parliament has ever dealt with and Canadians deserve a voice in the legislation that will fundamentally reshape our economy. Bill C-39 is exceptionally broad, with consequences for workers and communities across Canada. The government has an opportunity to take this legislation and talk to Canadians. They should be interested in hearing what Canadians have to say across this country. As a member of Parliament for Alberta, I can tell this House that there are a lot of frustrated Canadians outside Ottawa who feel like decisions are being made that affect them, that decisions are being made and their voices are not being listened to. I had people come to my office last week to talk to me about Bill C-39and how deeply opposed they are to it. Those individuals do not have the opportunity to come to Ottawa. They do not have the opportunity to attend the committee. The committee has an obligation. The committee has the potential and ability to travel across this country and meet Canadians where they are. With a piece of legislation this broad, with a piece of legislation that is so dangerous for workers' rights, for indigenous rights and for environmental protection in this country, it would be a grave mistake to rush it through and to not hear from the Canadians across the country who will be impacted by this bill. I want to be very clear. New Democrats, alongside our colleagues within the labour movement, want to make sure we are building the infrastructure that Canada and the Canadian government have neglected for decades. We want to build the housing, railways, ports, clean energy infrastructure and projects that will make Canada and Canadians more economically independent. We should be building transit and hospitals and investing in our cultural communities. These are things that all Canadians want to see the government invest in. These are strong projects we should be doing. Canada's unionized building trades have the skills, the expertise and the highly trained workforce to deliver these projects, so of course we should be using Canadian workers, Canadian steel, Canadian aluminum and Canadian materials to build infrastructure in this country. We should be investing in apprenticeships, in training and in the next generation of skilled tradespeople. Major projects should create lasting benefit for Canadian workers and Canadian communities. We have said, time and time again, this bill should be split. The broadness of this bill means that we have been put in a position in which, to protect workers' rights, to protect the rights of indigenous people in this country and to protect our environment, we will be voting against this legislation although we want to see parts of it. There are parts of this legislation that we want to see go forward. I want to be very clear. New Democrats have been very propositional. The committee is sitting today. It sat last night until midnight. Many amendments were brought forward by all parties, including New Democrats. My colleague, the member for Winnipeg Centre, brought forward a number of meaningful amendments to try to improve this piece of legislation. We are not trying to obstruct the building of our infrastructure in this county. We are trying to protect workers' rights, indigenous rights and our climate, and this broad omnibus legislation would not allow us to do that. We will work with the government to fix this, but I want the government to take the time to travel across this country and hear the concerns that Canadians have with this piece of legislation. I am going to tell members a bit as well about the extraordinary opposition we have heard from labour leadership. When we hear the government of the day talk about the fact that this is a good bill for workers and fail to listen to every labour leader who has expressed deep concern and disappointment with this legislation, it is so disrespectful. It is disrespectful to the labour leaders, labour movements and workers who built this country. I think of Bea Bruske, the President of CLC, who spoke about the ministerial intervention that undermines bargaining and encourages employers to hold out. I think of Lana Payne, the national president for Unifor, who commented that this attacks free and fair collective bargaining at a time of economic uncertainty. Marty Warren, the national director for the United Steelworkers, says that it gives corporations even more power over workers. Mark Hancock, the national president of CUPE, says this unnecessary attack on constitutional rights will worsen labour relations. He said it will not make them better, but worsen them. Tom Doran from ILWU said that the economic importance of workers' jobs cannot justify taking away their rights. David Chartrand, the general vice-president of IAM, says that employers have little incentive to bargain if they expect Ottawa to intervene. Sean Strickland, the executive director of Canada's Building Trades Union, says they support repealing sections of clause 107 and stand with the labour movement on getting rid of that attack on workers' ability to strike. On October 15, workers rallied outside MPs' offices in 21 communities across Canada, including outside the office of the Prime Minister and many of the cabinet ministers. The CUPE National Executive Board unanimously committed to defy the proposed strike restrictions if passed without amendment. On October 29, Canada's labour leaders announced the creation of a national labour war room to coordinate legal, political and communication efforts against the restrictions in Bill C-39. International labour organizations, including the International Trade Union Confederation, IndustriALL and the OECD trade union advisory committee have also expressed concerns with this legislation. How many more voices from labour does the Liberal government need to hear to understand that Bill C-39, as it stands, would hurt labour relations in this country? It would hurt workers. It would undermine workers' ability to bargain. It is a bad piece of legislation, and the Liberal government has been told by the labour movement time and time again to fix it. Whether it is through a committee, a press conference, written submissions or letters, labour cannot be more clear. Not only is this legislation dangerous, but it would cause more labour disruption in this country. It would not help us build more things better. It would make it worse. It would make it harder for Canadian workers to build the things this country needs right now. Every one of us wants to see that happen. Every one of us wants to see that economic sovereignty, economic independence and investment in our infrastructure in this country. Every person wants to see that, but we cannot do that if we are undermining the rights of workers. Today is the Canadian Labour Congress' Hill day. Members of Parliament from all parties will in fact be meeting with members of the labour movement, who will be raising concerns about Bill C-39. They will be meeting with members of Parliament to express those concerns. This is an opportunity, this motion is an opportunity, for the Liberal government to listen to those workers. It is an opportunity to slow down, take this legislation to Canadians and talk to Canadians across this country. I am going to go through a list of things that I think the government could be looking at as well. If this committee were to travel—
Mr. Speaker, I am being interrupted, and I am not sure why.

Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps that the Conservatives do not want us to stand up for workers' rights either. I am not 100% sure what that outburst was about. The committee has an opportunity to hear from British Columbians: from port workers, longshore workers, coastal communities that will be impacted and first nations. In Alberta, it is an opportunity to hear from the building trades, energy workers and indigenous communities, and municipalities. It is an opportunity to hear their perspectives on Bill C-39. In Saskatchewan and Manitoba, it is an opportunity to hear from agricultural producers, mining communities and railway workers. In Ontario, it is an opportunity to listen to the steel workers, manufacturing workers and auto workers. In Quebec, it is the CSN, the FTQ and other labour organizations and affected communities. In Atlantic Canada, it is an opportunity to hear from the fishers, port workers, energy workers and coastal communities. This is an opportunity. The government has a chance right now to meet with northern communities and with indigenous communities in northern parts of this country to hear what their concerns are and why they are so against Bill C-39. This is the chance to do that. This is the chance to bring forward changes to this legislation. The government should want the committee to travel, because of a few key things. Government members have argued that they want this legislation to create economic certainty. Canada's labour movement is warning that it instead would create years of labour unrest and constitutional challenges. Indigenous leaders are warning that the legislation would fail to respect their rights, and rushing legislation through Parliament does not create certainty. We have seen this playbook before. It ends in the courts. Good consultation before the legislation is passed prevents delays, litigation and costly mistakes. Listening to Canadians is not an impediment to building Canada. If we cannot take the time to listen to Canadians before passing legislation, how much time will we have to spend dealing with the consequences of getting it wrong? Both the Liberals and the Conservatives voted for Bill C-39 at second reading. Every single New Democrat voted against it. To Liberal members of Parliament, your own government says this legislation is about strengthening Canada's economy, so why on earth would they oppose hearing from the workers who make that economy function? If this legislation is to strengthen our economy, workers have to be at the heart. Workers have to be the ones who are leading this charge. To Conservative MPs, you talk regularly about Ottawa being disconnected from ordinary Canadians. Here is—

Mr. Speaker, I would encourage the Conservatives to talk about connecting with ordinary Canadians to support this legislation. This is an opportunity for the Conservative Party to put action where its words are. Members do not even need to oppose Bill C-39 in order to understand the importance of listening to Canadians with this legislation. We need to be listening to workers, to indigenous communities and to Canadians from coast to coast to coast. This is about giving the committee the tools to do its job properly. I want to build big things in this country. New Democrats want to build big things in this country. Canada's labour movement wants to build big things in this country. There is no reason we cannot do this and do it while protecting workers' rights, while ensuring that we are respecting indigenous rights and while protecting our environment. Let us split the bill. The Conservatives should work with us, look meaningfully, engage with our amendments, work with Canada's labour movement and, for goodness' sake, take the time to get out of Ottawa and listen to Canadians. These are the people who built Canada, and the very least we can do is give them a voice in how we go forward. I urge all members of the House to support my motion.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is really important that we reflect on the last federal election, when the Prime Minister made a commitment to build a stronger and healthier economy and society here in Canada, an economy that works for all Canadians. I reflect on my history as someone who has advocated for workers from the days when I was in the Manitoba legislature in the late eighties, and I disagree wholeheartedly with the assessment that the member has put on the record today. With respect to the debate on Bill C-39, for example, governments take actions to support the economy, and they can also support the rights of workers. The Province of Manitoba, through the Manitoba Labour Board, forced 350 health care workers back to work after not even one day of a strike. I think that there is an opportunity for us to pass Bill C-39 and to continue to build that stronger, healthier economy, and that there is no need to divide the bill or have a committee go around Canada. That principle could be applied to virtually every piece of legislation that passes through the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, obviously this is one of the biggest bills we have ever had. It is such a broad bill that would fundamentally change our economy, so it is not like any other bill. The member knows that. He is very aware of it. We have heard him speak in this place many times. I will say that there are 100 labour leaders here today for the CLC day on the Hill. For every one of those 100 labour leaders who is meeting with their MP today, there are thousands if not tens of thousands of workers who were not able to come to Ottawa, who were not able to take the time to be here or who did not have the means. The government has an obligation to listen to those workers as well. Certainly, I hope the parliamentary secretary has taken the time to meet with the CLC today or has plans to do so, but by all means, let us remember that for all the workers who are here advocating for the right to strike for workers across this country, there are thousands or tens of thousands more workers who are not here whom the government has an obligation to represent.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear that the hon. member supports the motion. I think that is important. The Bloc has been very strong in standing against Bill C-39, and I appreciate its efforts to do that. The hon. member asked about some potential amendments. The amendments we have brought forward in committee include things such as repealing section 107 of the Canada Labour Code, removing the proposed new ministerial powers to terminate legal strikes, protecting free and fair collective bargaining, preventing employers from determining how workers organize themselves through geographic certification, protecting collectively negotiated paid sick leave benefits, strengthening protections against worker misclassification and wage theft, strengthening successor rights to protect workers against contract flipping, improving access to first collective agreement arbitration, strengthening enforcement of the Canada Labour Code, protecting indigenous rights with meaningful consultation, ensuring robust environmental assessment and public participation and ensuring that major projects deliver tangible benefits for Canadian workers and communities. We have brought forward all those amendments. I am interested to see what the Liberal government does with them.

Mr. Speaker, the member opposite has suggested that we need to consult with workers. Our government has consulted extensively with workers. Their right to strike is constitutional. It would not in any way be threatened by Bill C-39, but they are very frustrated at situations in which 95% of the agreements are well negotiated but in 5% are sometimes working for years without a contract. Sometimes they are frustrated because people are not acting in good faith. That is what Bill C-39 would address. Would the member not agree that for workers to be able to negotiate a good deal and for Canadians to not continually be impacted in their businesses by strikes due to not negotiating in good faith, we need to do something to make the situation better?

Mr. Speaker, I think that is such a misguided look at what the legislation would do. Let us be honest. Labour leaders have said very clearly that this would put the power into the hands of the employers. It would take power away from workers. I think what she is describing is a fix to a problem that does not exist, at the risk of undermining the ability of workers to negotiate fair wages and working conditions. A strike is not something anyone wants to do. Workers do not want to go on strike. It is a tool that workers have, and it is supposed to be uncomfortable. That is the point of a strike. It is supposed to be uncomfortable because it is supposed to force the employer to come to the bargaining table and bargain in good faith. If that right is taken away, why would the employer do that? Why would the employer negotiate in any way if a minister can put their finger on the scale? We have watched the Liberals do it time and time again. They have done this over and over again. We cannot trust that the minister is not going to negotiate in bad faith in backroom deals to take away the negotiating and bargaining capacity of workers. We cannot trust the Liberals with that. We cannot trust them with the legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague, the member for Edmonton Strathcona, for bringing the motion forward. The motion is about bringing Bill C-39 to communities across Canada to seek their input. What has happened in the House with Bill C-39, of course, is that the government has rammed the bill through. It is already at committee, with limited witnesses. Why does my colleague think the government is resisting the idea of actually hearing from everyday people across the country with Bill C-39?

Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question. I do not understand why the Liberal government is pushing so fast and so hard to not listen to workers, to Canadians and to indigenous leaders across the country who have raised concerns. This is an opportunity. We are not saying that the government should just stop. We are saying to listen and to take the time to listen to Canadians. Take the time to travel across the country. Spend some time. Rushing and pushing the legislation through will not result in good legislation. It will not result in our being able to build the economy and the infrastructure we need. It will result in court cases, in litigation, in delays, in strikes and in wildcat action. That is what will happen. Let us do it right. Let us listen to Canadians. Let us listen to labour. Let us get this giant piece of legislation right.

Mr. Speaker, the member is absolutely correct. This puts environmental protection in the hands of ministerial power. This is a problem. I think about my own province of Alberta, where the federal government has an obligation to step in on coal mining in the eastern slopes. We have been waiting for years for selenium regulations to come forward. The government refuses to bring them forward. We cannot trust the current government, which continually undermines our environmental obligations, to do the right thing. We just cannot. The member is absolutely correct.

Mr. Speaker, it is really important that we recognize there is a constitutional right to strike. The New Democrats have a hidden motivation on this issue. On the one hand, they say they want to build a healthier and stronger economy, but what did they do on Bill C-5 when it came to one Canadian economy? They voted against it. What did the New Democrats do in regard to Bill C-39 at second reading? They voted against it. Coming out of the last federal election, the Prime Minister made a commitment to Canadians to work collaboratively with the different jurisdictions and the many different stakeholders, including unions, to build a stronger, healthier Canadian economy and society, an economy that works for all Canadians. That is what Bill C-39 is all about. On that point, I move: That the House do now proceed to orders of the day.
Mr. Speaker, we would request a recorded division.

title: Oral Questions: Health
turns: Madam Speaker, Canadians injured by the COVID-19 vaccines do not deserve to be dismissed or left waiting. These are people who followed the government's advice and mandates and are now struggling with lost income and living with serious permanent injuries and ongoing medical costs. Thousands across many communities have come to me over the years expressing concern over how the government has treated them and those they know and love. They say the Liberals are all talk and no results. Will the Liberals finally fulfill the promise they made to Canadians who were injured by the vaccines they told them to take?

Madam Speaker, it is a very important question. We recognize that vaccines save lives, definitely, but we also recognize that there are people impacted negatively by vaccines. This is why we launched the vaccine injury program. We have taken that program internally to make sure it is administered properly. We will continue to work with members across the aisle to make sure people are supported through any vaccine injuries.

Madam Speaker, at September’s Allison Inquiry, COVID vaccine-injured Canadians repeatedly described the vaccine injury support program as an unmitigated disaster. Of the $56 million paid to the contractor, Oxaro—

Madam Speaker, at September's Allison Inquiry, COVID vaccine-injured Canadians repeatedly described the vaccine injury support program as an unmitigated disaster. Of the $56 million paid to contractor Oxaro, $36 million went to administration and only around $20 million went to those who were injured. That is one-third. Following revelations of financial mismanagement, the government took over the program. What is the government doing today to ensure that vaccine-injured Canadians receive the compensation they deserve?

Madam Speaker, our government will always work to ensure that Canadians can make evidence-informed choices about their health. We heard frustrations with the previous administration of the program for vaccine-related injuries, which is why we took the program internally and launched the vaccine impact assistance program. We will continue to work very collaboratively to make sure the program works.
