Madam Speaker, following the tainted blood scandal, Canada established compensation programs worth billions for those affected with HIV and hepatitis C. Today, Health Canada has recorded approximately 12,000 serious adverse events following COVID-19 vaccination, yet compensation remains limited. At the Allison Inquiry, we heard from Canadians facing devastating medical bills and lost incomes. Why are vaccine-injured Canadians still struggling to receive compensation, and when will the government deliver meaningful financial support?

Madam Speaker, our government has taken the vaccine injury program internally from the previous administration, from the third party. We will continue to work hard to make sure the program works for vaccine-injured individuals. We are looking forward to working with members across the parties to make sure it works.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Madam Speaker, yesterday, the Prime Minister pulled the curtain back on how he is using the power of his office, aligning public policy to line his pockets. When the Prime Minister announced that two billion tax dollars would be used to subsidize heat pumps, he stood at a microphone knowing he owned shares in Trane heat pumps, Schneider Electric and Brookfield, which owns Enercare, a seller and installer of heat pumps. The conflict of interest is so obvious, but, worse, it is a breach of trust. The Prime Minister is funnelling billions of dollars to heat pump subsidies while he and Brookfield-connected companies are positioned to benefit. Are Canadians supposed to believe that this is just a coincidence?

Madam Speaker, leave it to Conservatives, as we head into the heating season and Canadians are thinking about affordable energy to heat their homes, to talk about knocking out a program that on average will save Canadians $1,400 a year. That is a lot of money in the pockets of Canadians in all of their communities and all of our communities. This is important for making sure that we are supporting families who need it the most.

Madam Speaker, Canadians are concerned about corruption and cronyism. This is about breaching public trust by using the power and levers of the Prime Minister's Office to announce public policies funnelling billions of tax dollars that will personally benefit the Prime Minister's assets, blind or not, and he knows it. At a minimum, this is cronyism, but some could argue that this crosses the line of not just a conflict of interest but self-dealing happening within the Prime Minister's Office. Will someone on the other side have the guts to call the Prime Minister out on this conflict like so many Canadians have over the past 24 hours?

Madam Speaker, shame on the Conservatives. They are all about character assassination. Let me tell the House what the government and this Prime Minister have accomplished over the last 18 months. That is how we deliver for Canadians. We deliver by major projects. We deliver by tax breaks. We deliver by dealing with issues like affordability and the environment and by building a stronger and healthier economy. They should stop the character assassinations and get onside with team Canada.

Madam Speaker, the only thing higher than the member's voice is the Prime Minister's stock portfolio this week. The Prime Minister is delivering for Liberal insiders, not ordinary Canadians. His $2-billion heat pump announcement yesterday stands to benefit companies like Trane and Enercare. The Prime Minister's ethics filing shows that he owns shares in Trane, and guess who owns Enercare. It is Brookfield. We know that the Prime Minister's ethics disclosure shows he has millions of dollars of shares in Brookfield. What is he pumping, heat into Canadian homes or cash into Brookfield?

Madam Speaker, since we are not going to be able to count on Conservatives to tell their constituents how the program works, let me explain it. What we have done is created a program that will give all homeowners access to $2,000 to $10,000 to buy a heat pump so they can lower their bills. On average, that is going to deliver $1,400 a year in savings. They will be able to apply online and get a response within 24 hours. That means if their heating conks out, they will be able to get funding to support a new heat pump quickly.

title: Oral Questions: Rail Transportation
turns: Mr. Speaker, Alto is being sold as a national transportation project, but the reality is that it will only serve a few major urban centres. The rest of Canada will still pay the billions of dollars in taxes required to build it and subsidize it, and they will not even have a realistic opportunity to use it. There is no business case for high-speed rail or for this to be a viable project. Why should Canadians pay for a Liberal vanity project that only serves Liberal voter hubs and makes no economic sense?

Mr. Speaker, Alto will serve 40% of Canada's population. It will serve Québec City, Trois‑Rivières, Laval and Montreal. It will serve Ottawa. It will serve Peterborough, perhaps Kingston. It will serve Toronto and also Windsor. We will be building this transformational project that will serve as the spine for mobility and change the way we live, work and play in this country. It will create jobs. It will add to our GDP. Alto is the way of the future and it is electric.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals plan to fast-track their multi-billion dollar-boondoggle, Alto high-speed rail, and destroy prime farmland in Ontario and Quebec. I met with dozens of farmers and business owners yesterday who are sick and tired of being railroaded by the Liberals. One of them even said, “I am more angry at my own government than Donald Trump. Donald Trump is not trying to take away my home.” The Liberals will waste $150 billion destroying the very family farms that put food on our tables. Can the minister tell me exactly how many farms will be destroyed by Alto, and what the impact will be on food production and grocery prices?

Mr. Speaker, we intend to deal with all landowners, including the agriculture community, in an equitable way, in a transparent way, and in a way that fully compensates them and more for the potential loss of a 60-metre corridor for a linear project through their property. We will deal extremely fairly and with great sensitivity with the entire farming community. That is the commitment of the government.

Mr. Speaker, this is what the farmers have received so far. They are being completely ignored by their own Liberal MPs, harassed by drones and living in fear that they are going to lose generational farms, businesses and their homes. I asked them yesterday what their biggest fear is from this. Their biggest fear is not having any answers to the questions they have asked. In fact, Alto will not even meet with local officials or farmers unless they sign a non-disclosure agreement. If Alto is such a great idea, why are the Liberals blocking studies at agriculture and transport? Why the secrecy? This is their own project. What are the Liberals trying to hide?

Mr. Speaker, again, we will deal with farmers and the agriculture community with great sensitivity. Any land within a 60-metre-wide linear corridor will be compensated at more than market value. We will deal incredibly fairly. When we are done building this project, the entire country will benefit from transformational, electric, high-speed rail capabilities that will increase our economy, create jobs and make life better for Canadians.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, inflation is going to bring a $20-billion revenue windfall to the government. That is great news for the Prime Minister but terrible news for the people lined up at food banks and the young people who cannot afford a place to live. It is still not enough to offset the irresponsibility of the big-spending Prime Minister, who is going to add $733 billion to our national debt over five years according to the Parliamentary Budget Officer. That is $40,000 for every family in Canada. Will he acknowledge that he is out of touch and that Canadians are out of money?

Mr. Speaker, the leader, as Canadians know, has no credibility when it comes to the economy. He has never worked one day in it. On this side of the House, we have a plan. We have a plan to build Canada strong. At the Canada investment summit, there was $500 billion in investments. Non-U.S. exports are set to double over the next decade. Foreign direct investment is at levels not seen in decades. On this side of the House, we have a plan to invest in our economy and to build our economy strong. The leader continues with the rhetoric.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister had any results at all, he would stand up and answer questions about his record deficit and the fact that the fastest-growing item in the budget is not health care, not the military and not borders, but interest on the national debt, enriching his banker buddies at the expense of hard-working Canadians. The average family of four will spend $6,000 this year on taxes to fund interest on debt. Will he acknowledge that he is out of touch, that Canadians are out of money and that the debt is out of control?

Mr. Speaker, do members know what a good leader does? A good leader does not raise his hands up, blame everybody else and offer nothing constructive as a solution. On this side of the House, let us look at some economic facts: the best net debt-to-GDP in the G7, the fastest-growing economy in the G7 and the best credit rating in the G7. On this side of the House, we have a Prime Minister with economic and business credentials. The leader has never worked one day in the economy and is in his third decade in the House producing nothing.

title: Statements by Members: Alberta Referendum
turns: Mr. Speaker, on October 19, the citizens of Alberta will vote on the question of Alberta pursuing separation from Canada. Unequivocally, I urge Albertans to reject separation as the path forward for our province. Without question, the Liberal government in Ottawa has worked against our province over the last 10 years, and those actions have led some to believe that separation is the only answer. I disagree. I urge Albertans to put their energies and their votes into making our Confederation work in the way that it was designed to work. The federal government must respect the division of powers in our Constitution and ensure that provinces are unfettered in their areas of authority. To my fellow Albertans, yes, Canada is imperfect, but our shared history, our culture, our hopes and our dreams are worth working on and fighting for together. On October 19, I will be voting to ensure a stronger Alberta and a united Canada. Please join me.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is a family. Families share, support and succeed with each other. Families also have conflict and fight. Families often fail because one member of the family does not feel heard. Too many Albertans are frustrated, not with the country of Canada but with the federal government, an important distinction. As a person who lives under too much government control via the Indian Act, I empathize with this. One hundred and fifty years ago, before Alberta became a province, Treaty 6 promised Canadians and first peoples a timeless agreement to respectfully walk alongside each other, to share land and resources, and to thrive together. Canada's own Constitution is based on the principle that power should reside closest to the people. Governments should respect individuals, communities and provinces' autonomy. It is time to remember and lead with first principles, when our ancestors locked arms to sign a treaty to make a Constitution and create a country. On October 19, it is time for all first peoples and Albertans to vote for a stronger Alberta and a united Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on October 19, my fellow Albertans will vote on whether Alberta should remain united with our great country or go down the uncertain path of separation. Our country has challenges, but I would choose our country over any other, any time. Former prime minister Harper once said, “Canada is, and always has been, our country.” We want Canada to be a true north that is as strong and as free as it can be in every way that matters, the best country in the world. My fellow Conservatives and I believe in this vision. That is why we serve. That is why Conservatives are fighting for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada, an Alberta that can reach its full potential without being held back by Ottawa. I urge my fellow Albertans to heed this call. Let us be a true north that is as strong and as free as it can be. May God bless our country. Long live Canada.

title: Oral Questions: Health
turns: Mr. Speaker, the cost of the $300-million PrescribeIT scandal just went up again. Conservatives have obtained the termination letter sent to Michael Green, the disgraced CEO in charge of the Liberals' PrescribeIT failure. According to the letter, Mr. Green was awarded a million-dollar severance package, including another massive performance bonus. The million-dollar package was approved by Canada Health Infoway. The health minister's official is a member of Canada Health Infoway's board. Did the minister's official vote to reward Michael Green with more tax dollars after he already wasted $300 million?

Mr. Speaker, as this matter is before the courts, we have no comment. More broadly, we look forward to seeing the outcome of the Infoway third party audit and organizational review. We will base our next steps on those results.

Mr. Speaker, she has parliamentary privilege, so she can answer questions like that, no matter what court they are in front of. This is Canadians' money. Canada Health Infoway has blown $300 million on its failed PrescribeIT program. Taxpayers got nothing—

Mr. Speaker, they spent $300 million on PrescribeIT. In response to my question on June 8, she announced she would halt the $50 million she planned to give Canada Health Infoway this year. On June 18, her spokesman, Alexandre Bergeron, told The Globe and Mail that they actually are going to give the $50 million away to this totally incompetent organization after all. Which is it and why? Why will she not permanently save Canadians this money?

Mr. Speaker, we remain committed to ensuring value for taxpayer money. Infoway has received no funding this year. Health Canada is currently examining the next steps. As I said, more broadly, we look forward to seeing the outcome of the Infoway third party audit and organizational review before considering the next steps.

Mr. Speaker, the Canada Health Infoway CEO who oversaw this disaster, Michael Green, was paid $1 million a year to do nothing of value. Conservatives have obtained his termination letter. It says that Canada Health Infoway plans to give him another year's worth of salary and $200,000 in performance pay, and continue his car allowance for this year. Michael Green now claims that he was fired in order to prevent him from testifying at the health committee. Is this why she is still thinking of giving Canada Health Infoway another $50 million? Is it to buy silence from this incompetent CEO?
Mr. Speaker, as with the previous answer, Infoway has received no funding this year, and now Health Canada is assessing the next steps.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Madam Speaker, Thanksgiving should be a time for families to gather around a full dinner table, not worry about whether they can afford to put food on it, yet Thanksgiving dinner is projected to cost an extra 10% again this year. At Simcoe Hall Settlement House in Oshawa, food donations are just one-third of normal levels. After 11 years of the Liberals, will the government finally admit that Canada is officially in an affordability crisis, and explain why they voted against our Conservative plan, which would have lowered food costs while families in Oshawa struggle to put food on the table this Thanksgiving?

Madam Speaker, what would lower food costs is if the member actually stood up and supported jobs in the Durham region. She and her party voted against the Canada Growth Fund, which invested $2 billion in the new nuclear project at Darlington, creating 18,000 construction jobs and 3,700 jobs in operations once the SMRs are in operation. That is significant support. That is how we build an affordable lifestyle. It is giving workers and young people chances to earn a good living and have wages outpace inflation. That is exactly—

Madam Speaker, I would have a lot more respect for the member for Whitby if he was standing up for the auto workers in our community. The Simcoe Hall Settlement House food bank in Oshawa is now capped at 70 households a day. Demand has not fallen; it is having to turn people away, but food being donated has. Grocery costs are still rising while meals are getting smaller and smaller for families. After years of reckless Liberal deficits and tax-and-spend policies, families cannot afford a basic Thanksgiving dinner. Will the Liberals please tell us by which Thanksgiving exactly we can expect to have grocery prices stop rising, or will the Liberals admit they have no plan?

Madam Speaker, our government cares deeply about affordability, whether it be prices at the grocery store or rent. Indeed, we have seen across Canada, 24 months in a row, that rents have been coming down. We are also making historic investments in housing, including in Oshawa, in the member's riding, where, with the help of the ACLP, we have invested $188 million to build 502 homes on the former foundry lands. These are homes for Canadians. We are also getting them to build those homes, which is creating jobs, and many of them will be affordable.

Madam Speaker, Thanksgiving is a time to be grateful. There is a lot to be thankful for, including the beautiful country we live in, but since the Liberals took office 11 years ago, costs have been on the rise, including for Thanksgiving dinner, which will be 10% more expensive this year. Conservatives have shared our plan to cut fuel taxes and save Canadians money. Will the Liberals admit that after their 11 years in power, there is an affordability crisis in Canada?

Madam Speaker, earlier this week, over 35,000 constituents of the member across the way received the groceries and essentials benefit. That is an important support that we put in place to try to address the increased cost of living that we know families are experiencing. I would ask the member to go back to his riding and support the national school food program, because that program in Alberta is helping to put food on the table for kids going to school in 63 public school jurisdictions and is supporting close to 60,000 kids. Those are important measures.

Madam Speaker, in the face of over 68,000 jobs being lost last month, this Thanksgiving, families on Vancouver Island are doing the math at the checkout. Statistics Canada reports that grocery prices have risen 30% since August 2021. Neighbours are stepping up and donating, volunteering and picking up the phone to check in on one another. Canadians should not have to carry this alone. The Liberal government talks up its relief plans, which never reach most Canadians at the till. When will the Prime Minister close the gap so that all Vancouver Island families can afford a Thanksgiving?

Madam Speaker, we know that British Columbians are facing affordability challenges right now, and we are working with Canadians to support them. That is why we made things, such as the national school food program, permanent. That is why we have the groceries and essentials benefit, which was paid into bank accounts on Monday. That is why we have the Canada child benefit. My colleague across the way is from Vancouver Island, where we know that over 70,000 families have received that benefit. It is important. These are the steps we are taking to support Canadians.

Madam Speaker, Canadians have much to be thankful for in our beloved country, but many Canadians are struggling with the high cost of food. Dalhousie University reports that turkey is up 10% from last Thanksgiving, which of course was up from the year before, because 11 years of Liberal taxes, spending, deficits and declining economic productivity have created a homegrown Canadian affordability crisis. Will the Liberals admit that their response to this crisis is all talk and has produced no results?

Madam Speaker, we certainly recognize that there are affordability challenges across the country, but I would reject the premise and the way in which the member opposite has framed it, which is that this is a homegrown challenge. There are challenges across the G7. We are dealing with circumstances with a blockade at the Strait of Hormuz and its impacts on energy. The government has been focused on what we can control in this country. That is why we have lowered taxes. That is why we have implemented the groceries and essentials rebate, which is supporting up to $1,800 for a family of four in the country. We are building the Canadian economy strong. That is our focus right now.

Madam Speaker, Thanksgiving is supposed to be about sitting down with one's family and being thankful for what one has. However, for far too many Canadians, that dinner table has become a place where they sit down and worry about how they are going to make ends meet. Under the Liberal government, groceries cost more, housing costs more and the bills keep piling up. Canadians do not need more talking points. They need results. Can the government finally admit that, after 11 years of Liberal rule, Canadians are facing an unprecedented affordability crisis?

Madam Speaker, if the Conservatives really cared about affordability, they would actually vote for affordability measures. We just took the excise tax off gas. The PBO says that is going to save the average family $276 a year. We just launched a heat pump program that will save an average family $1,400 a year. Will the Conservatives support that? No. Do they support child care? No. Do they support the national food program? No. Do they support the measures that we are taking to build affordable homes? The answer is no. In the member's riding, we are supporting businesses and affordability. He should get on board.

title: Oral Questions: Employment
turns: Madam Speaker, the government must answer for today's devastating job numbers. Canada now has the lowest labour force participation in 29 years. A smaller percentage of Canadians are working today than at any point in the last 29 years. On the eve of Thanksgiving, we see that Canadians are not just losing jobs; many are losing hope. Canadians will judge the government by the results, so will the government finally reverse course on policies that are making Canadians poorer and depriving them of opportunity?

Madam Speaker, I should not need to remind any member of the House that we are in a trade war, and a trade war causes economic volatility. The job numbers last month reflect that volatility; that is clear, and we empathize with Canadians who might be struggling to keep their jobs. What we are doing is controlling what we can. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. We have saved $60 billion in government operations, have signed 20 new trade and security agreements and have seen the second-highest growth in the G7 and the highest foreign direct investment. This is how we respond in the face of a trade war.

Madam Speaker, that answer is both callous and fact-free. This is not just a month-over-month escalation. We were shedding jobs as a result of Liberal policies long before this trade war, and job losses are concentrated in sectors that are not trade-exposed. There were 68,000 jobs lost in the last month and 110,000 in the last two months. Unemployment is up to 6.5%, and youth unemployment is up to 13%, with 50,000 jobs lost in Quebec alone. We did not get to a 29-year low in labour force participation overnight. It is not just month over month. It was not always like this in Canada. It will not always be like this in Canada, but we need an implementation of the economic action plan that Conservatives have put forward. When will the Liberals act to get Canadians—

Madam Speaker, while the Conservatives focus on QP skits and clips for their online social media feeds to scare Canadians, we are stepping up to support them every step of the way. We are investing in our economy and have made generational investments. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. In fact, the productivity mega deduction that the Prime Minister announced at the investment summit makes Canada the most tax-competitive advanced economy in the entire world. That is going to bring in new investment, help counteract the trade war and create jobs for Canadians.

Madam Speaker, it is Thanksgiving, and this morning's latest job numbers are devastating. Almost 70,000 jobs were lost in September, bringing that to a staggering 110,000 jobs lost in just two months. Unemployment has skyrocketed to 6.5%, which is the second highest in the G7. Recently I spoke with Jordan, a father in Richmond Hill who is worried about losing his job while struggling to keep up with the Liberal affordability crisis. While hard-working Canadians worry about their next paycheque, the out-of-touch Liberal government keeps delivering more talk but no results. How many more Canadians have to lose their jobs before the Liberal Prime Minister puts down the $500 buttercups and admits that he is failing to do his?

Madam Speaker, Canadians are looking for a serious government with a serious plan, and that is what we are delivering. Global volatility, economic uncertainty and trade tensions are having a direct impact on Canadian families, workers and businesses, but we are focused on what we can control. We are focused on investing, driving growth, attracting investment and investing in people and skills and the retraining we need. Our per capita job creation has nearly doubled that of the United States since September 2024, and our private sector is holding strong, creating 24,000 new jobs in September and adding 163,000 jobs—

Madam Speaker, we Conservatives have a serious plan to save Canadian jobs and save Canadians' money. Let us talk about Emily, who is a young graduate from Richmond Hill who did everything right. She studied hard and earned her degree, but is still left jobless after almost two years and is living in her parents' basement. Young Canadians like Emily are watching their opportunities disappear after 11 years of the Liberal government. She is not alone. Nearly 67,000 youth jobs vanished in just two months. Meanwhile, wages have grown at just 2.3%, below the latest inflation rate of 3%. Worse, 35% of young adults under 35 still live with their parents. Is this how the Liberal Prime Minister wants to bring together families on Thanksgiving?

Madam Speaker, my colleague opposite had the chance to vote in support of team Canada strong, which is making generational investments to hire up to 100,000 new Red Seal trade workers to support building and support the investments we are making right across the country. As part of team Canada strong, we are opening up paid apprenticeship placements in early 2027. We have introduced a new apprenticeship training grant, with a $5,000 completion bonus and $10,000 in wage incentives for employers to hire new apprentices. This is the kind of serious action that Canadians—

Madam Speaker, as we head into Thanksgiving, the latest StatsCan jobs report is in, and the numbers are devastating: nearly 70,000 jobs lost in September. That is on top of the 42,000 jobs lost in August. Unemployment is up, and Canada has the second-highest unemployment rate in the G7. In the face of these dismal jobs numbers, does the Prime Minister take any responsibility?

Madam Speaker, this Thanksgiving, Canadians should know that we are stepping up to support them with the cost of living. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment, while we have moved forward with affordability measures like the Canada groceries and essentials benefit, which will put $1,890 over the course of the next year in families' pockets. We also moved forward with the home retrofit program, which was announced just yesterday, and the national school food program. Do members know what the missing ingredient is at this Thanksgiving dinner? It is the Conservative Party being willing to stand up for Canadians. We have not seen that for some time in this House. It would—

Madam Speaker, 110,000 Canadians have been out of work in just the past 60 days. We have the second-highest unemployment rate in the G7, with the worst labour participation rate in 30 years. Meanwhile, real wages continue to decline. That is the Prime Minister's record. The Prime Minister promised the strongest economy in the G7, so will he acknowledge that once again his rhetoric does not match reality?

Madam Speaker, we all know that we are in a very challenging trade war. That is why the thing to do is build major projects and create jobs. That is exactly what we are doing. At Darlington, we are building North America's first grid-scale small modular reactors, with 18,000 construction jobs and 3,700 energy jobs. In Pickering, we are rebuilding the nuclear plant, with 30,000-plus jobs. East of Saskatoon, crews are building a potash mine, with 5,500 construction jobs. We are building the jobs. If only the Conservatives would come on board and join us.

title: Adjournment Proceedings: Canada Revenue Agency
turns: Mr. Speaker, I am rising to follow up on a question I asked during question period about the performance of the Canada Revenue Agency. As I pointed out in my question, the CRA shows no quarter to average Canadians while it regularly fails at its own metrics or even pays out millions of dollars to fraudsters. Most Canadians have a dim view of the CRA. At least, that is my experience. On the one hand, it is understandable; nobody likes the tax man. On the other hand, it does a pretty bad job sometimes, so some criticism is warranted. I want to share two stories, and hopefully the parliamentary secretary will listen to them and perhaps give some answers. The first is from a resident in my riding, Carolyn. She was recently approved for a CPP disability credit. This required that she refile taxes going back several years. She did that, and she consistently followed up and looked at the status. It consistently told her the adjustment request was received, but there was no more information. She called in, time after time. Eventually, she got to a CRA agent who told her she would just have to wait a bit longer, perhaps a couple more months. It could even be eight months, she was told, and if no one was assigned to her file, then she would have to file a complaint. How long should she have to wait to get a resolution? In the meantime, while she was waiting to get a decision there, the CRA reassessed her on another issue and said that she owed the government money. Like any good taxpayer, she paid when she had to, because the CRA shows no quarter to average Canadians. She had to pay on time or face the consequences. On the other hand, the CRA can wait for months and give taxpayers, residents, no answers on their issues. How long should she wait for a response? The second example is from Justin, an accountant in my riding who was helping businesses during a sale of some assets. Several companies were involved. The CRA, unfortunately, made a mistake. The CRA capitalized some expenses incurred during the sale rather than expensing them. I am not an accountant. I am not an expert here, so I am going to take him at his word on this. Assuming the CRA did make this mistake, Justin estimated it would take 18 months and thousands of dollars to file the necessary objections to get the CRA to correct its very own obvious mistake. My question to the parliamentary secretary, who I hope can provide some clarity here on the CRA's insufficient behaviour, is this. How long should residents have to wait for responses from the CRA, and who should pay when the CRA makes a mistake and costs taxpayers money?

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to hear the questions from my colleague, the member of Parliament for York—Durham. The stories he provided were very compelling stories. In my role as the member of Parliament for Yukon, I have heard stories as well and real cases involving real people and their frustrations with CRA. First and foremost, I want to assure the member that the Government of Canada takes the concerns raised about the integrity of our tax system and the accountability of the Canada Revenue Agency very seriously. Certainly, recognizing the individual case frustrations is something that I am happy to bring back to the ministry to ensure that we continue to improve and work on the services and accountability of the CRA. Upholding the integrity and fairness of Canada's tax system is one of our top priorities, and on the flip side, combatting fraudulent claims remains a part of those efforts. The CRA takes this responsibility seriously and works tirelessly to uphold the trust placed in it by Canadians. The CRA actively pursues those who fail to comply with tax laws and takes action to recover funds owed, ensuring fairness for all taxpayers. Understanding the root causes of taxpayers who are non-compliant is essential to preserving the integrity of the tax system and protecting Canada's revenue base, which supports the public programs and services that Canadians rely on. I also want to emphasize that the Canadian tax system is based on voluntary trust-based compliance and self-assessment, assuring that everyone contributes their fair share. In order to safeguard the integrity of the tax system, the CRA has implemented strong controls that are continually strengthened to address evolving risks. I also want to highlight that the CRA has implemented additional safeguards to ensure greater consistency and accuracy in refund processing. These include strengthened controls, intensified quality assurance oversight and tightened authority levels. Another means of addressing evolving risk includes collaboration with multiple partners, such as law enforcement and financial institutions. The CRA also employs technological tools, such as enhanced business intelligence and advanced data analysis, to improve risk assessments and to detect and deter the most serious instances of non-compliance. In fact, better data and more advanced analytics have allowed the CRA to better target its audits on the files with the greatest impact for Canadians. The CRA also collaborates with international organizations such as the OECD, the forum on tax administration, the FTA, and the joint chiefs of global tax enforcement, the J5. These partnerships enhance the CRA's ability to combat offshore tax evasion and ensure that multinational corporations and digital economy participants pay their fair share of taxes. Furthermore, the CRA maintains a strict approach to non-compliance, which includes publishing all convictions on Canada.ca. Despite these efforts, fraud tactics continue to evolve, which is why the CRA remains vigilant and committed to consistently enhancing its processes. When fraud occurs, the CRA has established processes to recover funds, including reassessing returns, recovering refunds, applying civil penalties and, when warranted, referring cases to the criminal investigations program. This commitment reflects not only the CRA's mandate, but also the trust that Canadians place in our tax system.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's acknowledgement and his sympathies for my residents, but respectfully, I would request better performance from the CRA rather than sympathy. He has tried to paint a picture of actions that the government is taking to try to make things better or get better, but respectfully, the data does not back that up. Just this year, after the 100-day service improvement plan, which ended in December, the Office of the Taxpayers' Ombudsperson's annual report in June showed that the problem remains. It was the most complaints they had received in three years. They are up 27% from last year. The ombudsperson said that the complexity of the tax system is one of the biggest problems, and I see that all the time. They made one recommendation that the CRA itself could not accept. It was to expand automatic tax filing to taxpayers who are in simple tax situations. Will the government do that?

Mr. Speaker, I again want to reiterate that the CRA is committed to accountability, continually improving service delivery, addressing fraud and upholding the integrity of our tax system. The CRA has strong controls in place and continually strengthens these measures to address evolving risks. As fraud tactics evolve, the CRA remains vigilant in enhancing its processes to prevent unwarranted refunds and recover any funds lost to fraud.

title: Oral Questions: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister cooked the books on immigration. He either lost count of, or lost altogether, 300,000 people in this country. Last year, the Liberals announced a cut in levels, only to bring in two backdoor programs to sneak in thousands more. Therefore, the population is again growing and levels are again at historic pre-Trudeau levels, or higher than pre-Trudeau levels. Will the Prime Minister cook the books again today to hide the number of people he is bringing in to profit big corporations with lower wages and higher rents?

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition needs a little work on his maths. The population growth in Canada was the lowest rate in decades. This government has taken back control of immigration. The number of asylum seekers is down by 70%; temporary foreign workers, down by 60%; foreign students, down by 80%; and permanent residents, down by 100,000. In a few hours, they will see the next phase of that immigration platform.

Mr. Speaker, that is cooking the books. When they compare themselves to insanity, it is insanity. He is comparing the numbers to the Trudeau-era levels. Let us compare them to the Conservative government. The asylum claimants backlog is up from 10,000 to 259,000, a 2,500% increase. The number of temporary foreign workers is up to 166,000 from 71,000, a 130% increase. The number of temporary residents is up 300% and he has 700,000 people here on work permits, even though there are thousands of youth who cannot find jobs. Will he stop cooking the books, and put Canadians first?

Mr. Speaker, I am not comparing myself to insanity. I am comparing myself to conspiracy. We have taken back control of immigration. The number of non-permanent residents has slowed from over 7% to just above 5%. We believe in this country. We are building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, last year, the Liberals set the immigration levels and then promptly added a couple of side programs to inflate their numbers nearly 40% higher, a classic Liberal smoke-and-mirrors confusion campaign. Even worse, they blew through their targets. Instead of 385,000 temporary residents, they have issued permits for 950,000. They planned for 60,000 temporary foreign workers, but they have issued permits for 120,000. Today, the government will issue a new immigration levels plan with more smoke and mirrors. Does the immigration minister really think Canadians do not see when she cooks the books?

Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister and I have said a number of times, we will not budge from sustainable levels. We have acted on the mandate that Canadians gave us to restore sustainability and durability to the immigration system, and the results are clear. The temporary resident population has dropped. We have stabilized levels, and as a result Canadians are seeing lower prices. I very much look forward to tabling our government's immigration levels plan later today.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians do not believe that. That is why they are asking for lower immigration levels. The government likes to pretend the numbers are coming down, but they are comparing them to the highest levels in Canadian history, created by the Minister of Justice over here. What really matters? On housing, our housing starts are decreasing. The levels plan will not consider where those people will live. On jobs, unemployment is rising, especially for our youth. The levels plan will not consider where they work. The current plan is adding a city the size of Saskatoon every year. Where will these people live, work and find a doctor?

Mr. Speaker, we have made reforms to the immigration system to restore sustainability, stability and balance. These reforms are working. As the Prime Minister said and as I have said, we will not budge from sustainable levels. While the Conservatives are focused on division, our government is focused on building a strong Canada and a sustainable immigration system. Again, I look forward, very shortly, to tabling our next immigration levels plan.

title: Oral Questions: The Budget
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said he would spend less, but the budget watchdog exposed $331 billion in new spending. He will also borrow $868 billion in six years, which is $65 billion more than Trudeau borrowed in a decade. Canadians cannot afford food, fuel or homes, but the PM gives more than $500 million for forests in Brazil and $8 million for rice in Vietnam. The Liberals are giving hundreds of millions to other countries, but the more they spend, the more Canadians pay. Where is the relief here at home? When will the Liberals finally put Canadians first?

Mr. Speaker, stewarding the nation's resources responsibly is a duty that the government takes extremely seriously. That is why Canadians hired a world-class economist to be their Prime Minister at a pivotal moment in our history. As our country faces threats to our economic security and sovereignty, what we are doing is leveraging our fiscal strength, the strongest balance sheet in the G7, to invest in our people, unite our country and grow a stronger economy. That is exactly what Canadians gave us a mandate to do, and we are never going to apologize—

Mr. Speaker, the truth is that the budget watchdog says the Liberals used an accounting scheme found nowhere else in the world. The Prime Minister counts assets as pensions that cannot repay debt and as Crown corporation loans that drive up interest, with $135 billion in spending as capital, unlike international standards. The PBO warns these costly credit card Liberal tricks make Canada fiscally unsustainable. It is no wonder the Liberals cooked the books to hide it. Why must Canadians pay more for everything, while the out-of-touch Prime Minister breaks his promise to spend less?

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to question the PBO at the finance committee earlier this week. She confirmed that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7 and that we are meeting our fiscal anchors. Those are two points that the Conservatives fail to mention. Budget 2026 leverages Canada's fiscal strength to invest at a time when Canadians need it and expect it. They expect their government to step up with new supports around affordability, like the groceries and essentials benefit, which we are topping up, which is going to put hundreds more dollars into Canadians' pockets.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised fiscal prudence but instead delivered a budget that adds $765 billion in new debt and brings higher costs for Canadians. The fastest-growing line item in the budget is now debt interest, and under the Liberal plan, taxpayers are paying more on that interest than they are on health care transfers. At a time when so many Canadians are struggling to fill their gas tanks, make their mortgage payments or even put food on the table, why will the Liberals not stop their costly credit card budgeting so Canadians can afford to live?

Mr. Speaker, just this week, the Parliamentary Budget Officer confirmed that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7 and that the Government of Canada is sticking to its fiscal anchors in budget 2026. What does budget 2026 focus on? It focuses on income, housing, food and energy security. Those are ways to protect our economy from the shocks that are hitting us externally, which are beyond our control. We are doing everything in our power to utilize the strength that we have to invest in Canadians, protect our sovereignty and grow our economy for future generations. That is what we mean when we say build Canada strong. Conservatives would build—

Mr. Speaker, what the Liberals' budget focuses on is more debt and more inflationary spending. In fact, the Parliamentary Budget Officer reports that spending is up $331 billion under the Prime Minister. Of that, 61% is on government operations, not investments, and over $500 million is even going to forests in Brazil. Job number one in this budget should have been saving Canadians money. Instead, the Liberals delivered a budget that does the exact opposite. Why do the Liberals not stop their inflationary spending spree so Canadians can afford to get ahead?

Mr. Speaker, it is very clear to Canadians that the Conservatives have no economic plan at all. All they have is an Internet disinformation plan to divide and weaken the country. That is all they purport to do for Canada. In fact, most of what they propose is a do-nothing agenda. They say to get out of the way and everything will resolve itself. That is not what we believe on this side. We believe we were elected for a purpose, and we are fulfilling that purpose by leveraging the strength that Canada has to beget more strength in our economy, support Canadians and unite this country.

title: Routine Proceedings: Petitions
turns: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour today to rise to present two petitions on behalf of constituents. The first is with regard to EI parental benefits and the tragedy of stillbirths. The petitioners are asking that, should a parent experience a stillbirth, they be entitled to the EI they had agreed to and that the government honour that commitment it had entered into with the parent.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition is with regard to climate change and environmental protections. Petitioners note that there are increasing extreme weather events in our country and around the world. They are urging the Government of Canada to honour and ensure Canada's 2030 and 2035 emissions targets and strengthen the policies that make them achievable, for the love of our children and grandchildren.

Mr. Speaker, in January, the Minister of Agriculture released his plan to cut 665 positions and shut down seven research stations across Canada. Later in the spring, the minister also confirmed that six scientific positions would be cut as part of this plan at the Brandon Research and Development Centre. This is a frankly backwards and wrong-headed decision at a time when Canada faces food affordability, food sovereignty and food security crises. The petitioners call on the Government of Canada to: recognize the critical role of agricultural research in supporting farmers, food security and economic growth; immediately reverse the decision to close the seven research facilities and eliminate 665 positions, including the reversal of the decision to cut six scientific positions at the Brandon Research and Development Centre; and commit to maintaining and strengthening agricultural research capacity in Brandon and Westman.

Mr. Speaker, petitioners in Mission—Matsqui—Abbotsford are concerned about uncontrolled population growth, which has put too much pressure on our housing, jobs and health care systems. An unsustainable immigration surge has overwhelmed critical infrastructure. The influx has outpaced housing development. Hospitals and clinics are struggling to keep up with demand, with wait times for surgeries and doctor's appointments reaching unprecedented levels in some regions of Canada. The influx has sparked concerns about wage suppression and job competition, particularly in low-skilled sectors. Therefore, the petitioners call upon the government to rebuild an immigration system that works for Canadian citizens, a fair and orderly system that prioritizes economic contributions and sustainable growth, and to keep the rate of population growth below the rate of housing growth, job growth and health care accessibility.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a petition initiated by Crystal Braunwarth of Burnaby and supported by 5,585 signatories. The petition highlights that Canada's motion-picture industry supports more than 181,000 jobs and generates over $10.2 billion in annual production activity. The petition is calling on the Government of Canada to eliminate the federal grind on the production services tax credit so provincial incentives no longer reduce the federal credit. This change would strengthen Canada's competitiveness, attract investment and protect jobs for Canadian workers in the film and television industry.

Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure to speak today on behalf of many veterans across the country, particularly after we just celebrated Remembrance Day ceremonies across the country. These individuals are concerned about the unauthorized wearing of military decorations and insignia, which is commonly referred to as “stolen valour”. This has been a problem in Canada for many years, and veterans have asked me to present this petition on their behalf, asking for changes to the Criminal Code's section 419 on the unlawful use of military uniforms and certificates, to reclassify the offence as a hybrid procedure, which would enable the prosecution to pursue stronger sentences for those who violate stolen valour by using an insignia in a public way. It is my honour to present this petition on behalf of 301 Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of presenting petition e-6982 today. This petition was initiated by Richard Hackett, a constituent whose passion for his son led him to advocacy. His son suffers from ADHD and has not been able to receive access to an occupational therapist for well over four years. Richard and the 12,000-plus signatories are calling for the universal access to education and health care in this country to be negotiated with the provinces. It is a difficult feat to be sure, but I do not discount the passion, determination and love, frankly, that Richard has for his son. It is an honour to present a petition on his behalf today.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to present two petitions from constituents in my riding of Victoria. The first recognizes that in the context of the Iran war that began earlier this year, globally oil and gas companies are projected to make up to $90 billion in excess profits. Canada is in the middle of an affordability crisis and is feeling the impacts of the climate crisis. The petitioners call on the federal government to investigate and implement an excess profits tax of 75% for fossil fuel companies so that the profit they are gaining from these geopolitical events can go to support the important investments Canadians expect, including renewable energy, public transit and an east-west electricity grid. The second petition is in a similar vein. It recognizes the dire impacts of climate change for this country and for Canadians from coast to coast to coast. It calls on the federal government to invest in sustainable industries and to work toward decarbonizing our economy, including by reducing subsidies for fossil fuel companies and investing in clean infrastructure, building retrofits and active transportation.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise in this place after my neighbour from Victoria with his excellent petitions. The constituents of Saanich—Gulf Islands have asked me to deliver this petition, which reminds the government that the poison drug opioid crisis remains a public health emergency, although not recognized as such by the government. They point out that, since 2016, there have been over 34,000 drug-related deaths in Canada. While checking statistics recently, although the number has dropped slightly, the deaths continue to mount in 2026. The petitioners call on the Government of Canada to declare a public health emergency due to the poisoning crisis of fentanyl and opioids, to follow expert recommendations, to decriminalize possession of unregulated drugs for personal use, to reduce stigma and barriers to care, and to regulate and provide a safe supply, such that we can pursue addiction treatment and treat this as a health crisis and not a criminal justice issue.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people from Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. For the seventh time, I rise to present a petition on behalf of constituents who want to see funding for the rebuilding and fast-tracking of the Red Bridge, which is a cultural and important landmark that connects the mainland to the Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc area. It is very important that we see federal money earmarked for this. It is time that Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola is no longer left in the cold when it comes to federal funding.

title: Oral Questions: Agriculture and Agri-Food
turns: Mr. Speaker, farmers in my community are worried about the increasing cost of diesel. Now, many are spending thousands of dollars every single day just to keep their operations running. One farmer put it very plainly. He said that when fuel prices rise, so do grocery prices for every single Canadian. For 11 years, Liberal policies have driven up the cost of fuel and made life more expensive for Canadian families. Tomorrow, Conservatives will put forward a common-sense motion calling on the House to adopt our emergency fuel relief plan. The question is very simple. Will the government vote in favour of Canadians and vote in favour of saving them money?

Mr. Speaker, members of the chamber are well aware today that this is a global issue. It is caused by a geopolitical situation. Farmers are on the front line, and we sympathize with them. That is why we brought in the reduction of the excise tax. That is why we are seeing all the countries around the world working together to reduce the cost of diesel. We will continue to work with our farmers. We will continue to support them through programs, and we appreciate everything they do.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the Liberals are completely out of touch, because the cost of diesel in Canada is far more than the cost of diesel in the United States of America, which has been equally impacted by global markets. That argument just does not work. At the end of the day, farmers have a job to do, and it is to produce food, but that means being able to take the crop off the field, and it means being able to get commodity to market and ultimately to get food on store shelves. That all takes money because of diesel costs. At the end of the day, it is the consumer who pays those costs. It is Canadian families. We as Conservatives have a plan. We are putting it on the table. We are bringing it forward tomorrow. We would love to work with the government on it. Will it vote yes—

Mr. Speaker, seeing as the member opposite is from Alberta, she would be very excited and would want to support projects like Imperial Strathcona, creating renewable diesel right here at home using Canadian canola from Alberta. Fifty per cent of canola from Alberta would go toward the feedstock for the renewable diesel at Imperial Strathcona. I will ask her this question: Will she continue to support the CFRs and continue to take action so that we can make renewable diesel here at home?

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Mr. Speaker, the numbers I cited are from his government, so he must be in on it then. He cooked the books on immigration. He cooked the books on debt. He will stand up now and give fake and phony statistics on debt and deficit, but that is because he is dividing his expenditures onto not one, not two, but three different credit cards, using accounting rules that no one else in the world uses. If a company did it, they would be criminally charged for defrauding their shareholders. The Parliamentary Budget Officer says that the Prime Minister will add $700 billion of new debt over the next five years. How much will Canadians pay?

Mr. Speaker, we will see in a few hours how to manage the government's finances and the country's finances. We will see a government that is taking control of spending, that has slowed it from over 8% to less than 2%. We will see a government that is balancing the operational budget. We will see a government that knows how to invest in the future of this country because that is what Canadians want. I understand the Leader of the Opposition, who has only ever torn things down, does not understand how to build things up at this time.
Mr. Speaker, the government needs a serious fiscal anchor, less debt and a path to balanced budgets. That is what Kevin Lynch, former finance deputy minister and clerk—

Mr. Speaker, the government needs a serious fiscal anchor, less debt and a path to a balanced budget. That is what Kevin Lynch, former deputy minister of finance and clerk, said today. It is what economist Chris Ragan said yesterday. It is what former finance official Don Drummond has been saying for months. The PBO has said that the interest on the national debt has doubled since 2021 to $60 billion a year, more than health care or defence. Will the Prime Minister deliver a credible fiscal anchor in today's budget to reduce the debt and skyrocketing interest payments?

Mr. Speaker, while the leader cannot master his own caucus, in a few hours we are going to table budget 2026, “Masters of our destiny”. We are going to build Canada. We are going to bring down barriers to investment. We are going to double non-U.S. exports. We are going to invest in major projects, in housing and in infrastructure. We will also do what they never do. We are going to make sure we look after the most vulnerable.

Mr. Speaker, borrowing costs are rising, growth is stagnating and risks are tilted to the downside. Canada's fiscal buffers are depleting, leaving us unable to deal with the next major crisis that the Prime Minister's own national security strategy says could be coming. The government's fiscal anchors have done little to rein in government spending and borrowing, so will the Prime Minister ensure a credible fiscal anchor in his budget, and more importantly, will he ensure a full accounting in the budget so we do not have to learn about things at some future investment conference?

Mr. Speaker, despite the fake rage, we have a plan to build our economy. The fundamentals of our economy are extremely strong: the best net debt to GDP in the G7, one of the strongest fiscal positions in the G7, wages outpacing inflation and a AAA credit rating. Despite them wishing it is not so, we have a plan to build Canada strong. We are going to invest in our country and our economy.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are masters of illusion. They say, “Look over here at the operating budget, but do not look over there, where we are taking on unprecedented levels of debt.” They say, “Look at the operating budget, but do not look over here, where we are hiding billions of dollars in Crown corporations.” They say, “Keep looking over here at the operating budget, not at the billions of dollars being relabelled into capital investments.” Who is going to pay for all this debt and how?

Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are so committed to their pessimistic world view that they cannot see past the paper that was handed to them in their lobby to read off these QP questions that are repetitive every single day and punching down the Canadian economy. We are here to promote Canada. We are here to invest in Canada. That is exactly what our government is doing, supporting people with affordability measures, growing the industries of tomorrow and creating jobs for tens of thousands of Canadians. That is what we were elected to do. We will not apologize for being positive about the prospects of this country.

Mr. Speaker, there was a lot of shouting, but if you noticed, there was still no answer. The Liberals are masters of fiscal illusion. They are hiding behind the net debt-to-GDP ratio so they can borrow even more. What they do not tell us is that that calculation subtracts Canadians' pensions, money that Canadians worked decades to save for retirement. That money is not for the finance minister to spend or borrow against. When will they stop using Canadians' pensions to justify the amount of debt they are leaving for our children and our grandchildren?

Mr. Speaker, it is well known everywhere but the Conservative caucus that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. That is not an exaggeration. That is the IMF, a world rating agency. We have a AAA credit rating. We had the strongest second quarter growth in the G7. We have the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio by far. We are not compromising that fiscal position in strength. We are leveraging it to the hilt to get the best results for Canadians, to get returns for Canadians. Those dividends will be jobs for the future and higher-rising incomes.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians cannot afford another inflationary Liberal budget. Under the Liberals, millions of Canadians are lined up at food banks. According to a report from the Daily Bread Food Bank, 38% of food bank users are employed. That means even a paycheque no longer guarantees a full fridge under the government. While Canadians are working harder to get ahead, they keep falling further behind. Will the Prime Minister end this inflationary spending in today's budget, or will Canadians keep paying the price?

Mr. Speaker, Manitoba is a powerhouse for aerospace, the third-largest in Canada, and the member opposite keeps voting against every measure to support it. Magellan and StandardAero are creating good jobs in Manitoba. We just invested $8.8 million in the University of Manitoba to support research and create jobs. These are all measures we are taking to support the work to grow the economy in Manitoba, and the member opposite keeps voting against them.

Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of Liberal government, food affordability continues to get worse. A recent Salvation Army report found that one in three Canadians is skipping meals. In Niagara Falls, visits to Project Share increased by 23.7%, while visits to Newark Neighbours in Niagara-on-the-Lake have doubled since 2022. Will the Liberal government's budget deliver tax cuts to help Canadians who are struggling right now?

Mr. Speaker, the very first day that the government formed, we delivered a tax cut for 22 million Canadians, and affordability has been at the top of our agenda ever since. We are going to continue making progress when that member gets to see the federal budget later this afternoon. We are going to be committed to the programs that we have created and brought forward, things like our national school food program and our groceries and essentials benefit. These are programs that are helping put food on tables and ensure that Canadians have the support they need in their lives.

Mr. Speaker, my team and I recently volunteered at the North York Harvest Food Bank. We witnessed first-hand the growing hardship facing Canadian families. One in four food bank clients is a child, and 53% of clients have skipped meals to afford other necessities. The Salvation Army reports that 31% of Canadians are skipping or reducing meals, because they simply cannot afford groceries. Will the Liberal government finally get its spending under control and cut taxes, instead of forcing struggling families to pay the price for another unaffordable budget as its programs are not working?

Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague knows this, but the number one way to help out Canadians with affordability is to ensure that they have a safe and affordable home to live in. That is why our government has thousands of shovels in the ground. We have a budget today that will build more affordable homes for all Canadians, homes like the Lou Fruitman Reena Residence in that member's riding, in Vaughan, where 138 of her constituents live. Despite her opposition to supportive housing, we are getting the job done. Her Conservative leader has a record on building housing; he built six when he was the minister of housing. Not only that, he stands in front of people's homes, embarrasses them and shames them. The Conservatives have a bad record on housing—

Mr. Speaker, people across Canada are struggling with the high cost of living. Food is expensive, housing is out of reach, and gas prices are out of control. Families are having to choose between paying rent and filling their prescriptions, but instead of providing real relief to Canadians, Liberals are wasting hundreds of billions of dollars on corporate handouts, excessive military spending and oil pipelines the private sector will not touch. Will the government change course and deliver meaningful investments in non-market housing, affordable groceries and better health care in today's budget?

Mr. Speaker, in just over an hour, the finance minister will deliver budget 2026 in the House. I know we are all very excited, including the member opposite, who I know cares about a number of issues that are affecting Canadians. We too, on this side, care about Canadians. We are stepping up to support them with affordability measures. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. We have stepped up with the groceries and essentials benefit. We have made the national food program permanent, saving families hundreds of dollars per month all across the country. I know the member opposite supports that program, and it is great to see him so excited to—

title: Oral Questions: Indigenous Affairs
turns: Mr. Speaker, Conservatives believe in self-determination and first nations deciding their own paths for themselves. At Monday's first ministers' meeting, first nations helped determine the agenda on economic partnership, land, and treaty rights, but the Prime Minister could not focus on that important conversation and instead resorted to speculation about abolishing the Indian Act, which was not the focus of the first nations' agenda. Why is the Prime Minister now inviting the uncertainty and division that comes with resurrecting the Liberal Indian Act white paper of 1969?

Mr. Speaker, the Indian Act has a long and harmful legacy of colonization, racism and discrimination, with lasting impacts on first nation individuals, families and communities. The discussions underscore the importance of continuing to strengthen the relationship between Canada and first nations, one that is grounded in respect for first nations' self-determination, laws and inherent rights. Fundamentally, our focus remains on how our relationship can be strengthened with first nations on a nation-to-nation basis.

Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of Liberal reconciliation rhetoric, how can anybody trust the 1969 white paper-musing Prime Minister, who delays legislation for any interests other than his own and ignores court rulings that require him to uphold the government's commitments? On Bill S-2, he is demanding that elders sign a five-year non-disclosure agreement because he does not trust the supposed partners in reconciliation. On safe drinking water, he still has not passed legislation the Liberals promised in 2022 and is still fighting them in court. How can international partners trust the Prime Minister when he cannot even fulfill Canada's treaties with first peoples here at home?

Mr. Speaker, to be clear, any process about how we move beyond the Indian Act must be first nations-led. It has to be co-developed with rights holders. First nations are diverse. They have distinct histories, they have treaties and they have governance structures that we have to respect. Their voices have to guide this process and decisions about what comes next. We are committed to working in partnership with first nations to chart a path forward together that respects their rights, reflects the priorities they bring forward and supports their self-determination.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are fast-tracking indigenous human rights violations in Bill C-39 while refusing to pass Bill S-2, in an attempt to keep sexism and racism in the Indian Act. Their bait-and-switch is to say, “Hey, look over here; we are pledging to abolish the Indian Act.” First nations have seen this playbook before, used with the white paper and handed down by Harper. Will the government stop the bait-and-switch in the House today, withdraw Bill C-39 and pass Bill S-2 without delay, or do they want to see another Idle No More?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for the many questions on this topic. The reality is that this legislation is not about changing standards; it is about changing processes. That is a key distinction in this legislation. We take on a special duty. Our special duty is to focus on the duty to consult, but deeper than that, the reality is that projects from coast to coast to coast not only need first nations buy-in but need first nations partnerships.

title: Oral Questions: Justice
turns: Mr. Speaker, rural residents in my constituency feel under siege. At yet another crime meeting on Saturday, the message was blunt: People are done with a catch-and-release justice system. This fall, the Prince Albert RCMP recorded over 58 break and enters, a staggering 71% increase. We had a 29-year-old woman who was abducted during a vehicle theft. Residents have had enough, and without action, somebody is going to get hurt. My question is for the Minister of Justice. Will he immediately fast-track Bill C-293, the safe at home act, so violent home invaders are kept behind bars?

Mr. Speaker, of course, everyone in the House is completely against any of those crimes' being committed in his community and all our communities. What I will say, though, is that the government has taken decisive action, especially when it comes to bail and sentencing reform. I have an article here from Radio-Canada where the justice made it very clear: “This is no longer the Canada that gave recidivist offenders the benefit of the doubt". It is “[n]ot anymore”, he said.

Mr. Speaker, it is so effective that crime is up 71%. Statistics Canada confirms what rural Canadians already know: The crime rate outside our cities is 42% higher than in urban areas. Saskatchewan is being hit the hardest, worse than Manitoba and Alberta. While urban Canadians get the resources, rural communities are left to fend for themselves, and rural residents in my constituency are paying the price. I ask the Minister of Justice once more, will he finally sit down with his provincial counterpart in Saskatchewan and deliver a concrete action plan to stop this rural crime invasion?

Mr. Speaker, Canada's government has passed significant pieces of legislation that have enhanced our public safety and our national security: the Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act, the bail and sentencing reform act, the Combatting Hate Act, the Protecting Victims Act and the lawful access act, 2026. Every single piece of legislation has the support of the frontline men and women of our national police forces across the country. The only group of people who do not support our tough-on-crime legislation is the Conservative Party of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in 2022, Arnold and Joanne de Jong were brutally murdered in their Abbotsford home. Three men were found guilty for these horrific murders, yet four years later, the De Jong family is still waiting for justice. A B.C. judge has ruled that, according to the faint hope clause, these murderers can seek earlier parole. The family has suffered unimaginable losses and should not have to keep fighting for justice. Will the Liberals defend the restrictions on earlier parole eligibilities, or will the rights of convicted killers continue to come before the rights of victims and their families?

Mr. Speaker, in less than a year, Canada has implemented three very bold legislations that will be able to attack the issues of crime in this country. These laws provide stricter bail, tougher sentences, hate crime protections, and better protections for victims and children. The government takes crimes seriously, has acted and will continue to act.

Mr. Speaker, the member did not answer my question. This is not just about parole. It is about protecting victims from violent offenders in the first place. In September, a man in Kelowna choked his wife and was released on bail. Just 30 minutes later, he returned. He attacked his wife again, and he was released on bail again. He was released on bail three time. This is ridiculous. Canadians deserve a justice system that protects them. Will the Liberal government explain why violent offenders are being released repeatedly, while victims are left fearing for their safety?

Mr. Speaker, again, we put forward tougher sentencing and bail legislation this June, and it has been enacted. I want to remind the member that not only is it working in the justice system, but a judge from Newfoundland publicly declared yesterday in the news that violent offenders aren't getting let out on bail and are receiving sentences that fit their crime. Just this week, the Newfoundland judge cited our government's bail and sentencing reform act—

title: Statements by Members: Remembrance Day
turns: Mr. Speaker, as Remembrance Day approaches, I rise to recognize the retired master corporal Matthew Logan, who served with the Seaforth Highlanders of Canada. Together with his daughters, Juliette and Alexandra, he helps organize Newton's annual Remembrance Day gathering. They share memorial cards that tell the stories of fallen service members. These cards help us remember the people behind the names. This year, Matthew is sharing the stories of Canadians who died in the Korean War. Their efforts encourage younger generations to learn about these stories and keep their memory alive. On November 11, residents will gather at Newton Seniors Centre to honour those who served and remember those who never returned. We thank Matthew, Juliette and Alexandra for their dedication.

Mr. Speaker, at the 11th hour on the 11th day of the 11th month, we pause to remember those who sacrificed so much for the country we call home. Each year we stand in a moment of silence, and this year, new names are carried within that silence, because on October 17, four Canadian soldiers lost their lives during training at CFB Wainwright. Among them was Private Hayden Lykkemark from Langley, British Columbia. He was only 19 years old, a young man with dreams for his future and an entire life ahead of him. The tragic loss reminds us why we gather every November 11 to honour the great generations of Canadians who served us, those who made the ultimate sacrifice and those who returned forever changed. As we gather in remembrance across Abbotsford—South Langley and across Canada, we stand with every veteran and every Canadian family that carries the weight of loss. We will remember them. Lest we forget.

Mr. Speaker, as Remembrance Day approaches, I rise to honour Pilot Officer Gordon James Strutt from Shawville, Quebec, who made the ultimate sacrifice during the Second World War. Born in Shawville, Gordon enlisted in the Royal Canadian Air Force and served with the 58th Squadron. On August 6, 1942, he and five fellow airmen took off from Wick, Scotland on a patrol over the North Sea. Their aircraft never returned, and the crew members were never found. Gordon's story reminds us all that behind every name on a cenotaph was a person, a family and a community forever changed by their sacrifice. We will remember Gordon James Strutt and all those who served and sacrificed for our country and for freedom. Lest we forget.

title: Statements by Members: Latin American and Hispanic Day on the Hill
turns: Mr. Speaker, For the 10th consecutive year, we are celebrating the contributions of the 1.7 million Spanish-speaking Canadians who enrich and help build our community from coast to coast to coast. In the presence of hundreds of Canadians of Latin American descent who have travelled to Ottawa to join us in Parliament, today is a wonderful opportunity to discover the richness of Latin American and Hispanic cultures and strengthen the bonds that bring us together. Of course, it is also a chance to enjoy incredible music, performances and delicious food.

Mr. Speaker, today I am proud to join my colleagues, ambassadors, community leaders and friends in celebrating the 10th Annual Latin American and Hispanic Day on the Hill. This special occasion recognizes the extraordinary contributions of more than 1.7 million Spanish-speaking Canadians, many of Latin American and Hispanic heritage, who help to strengthen our communities and our country every day. This year's theme is community, and I can think of no better way to describe the spirit of this event. For 10 years, it has brought Canadians together to celebrate culture, foster connections and build understanding. I wish everyone celebrating today a wonderful Latin American Heritage Month.

Mr. Speaker, today, on the 10th annual Latin American and Hispanic Day on the Hill, I rise to recognize the millions of Canadians of Latin American and Hispanic heritage from coast to coast to coast. From music and the arts to public service to professional sports, Latin American Canadians make vital contributions to our communities every single day. As co-chair of the Canada-Dominican Republic parliamentary friendship group, I wish to specifically recognize the long-standing relationship between our two countries. As the second most populous country in the Caribbean, the Dominican Republic has been a key regional partner for Canada for more than 70 years on issues including trade, tourism, investment and a shared commitment to democracy and open markets. That is why later this month, we will have the privilege to welcome to Ottawa His Excellency, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic. This visit promises to further strengthen the partnership between our two countries. This October, I wish the Dominican Canadian community and all Latin American Canadians a meaningful and happy Latin American—

Mr. Speaker, today I rise to pay tribute to Ron Schlegel, whose passing leaves a profound loss for the Waterloo region and for communities across Canada. Driven by a deep Mennonite faith and a commitment to helping others, Ron devoted his life to building stronger, more caring communities. Through Schlegel Villages, the Research Institute for Aging and the elder wisdom program, he transformed the way we care for seniors and improved countless lives, while also making lasting contributions to mental health, research and community development. Ron helped establish the University of Waterloo's School of Public Health Sciences and was awarded the Order of Canada, the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Medal and honorary doctorates from multiple Canadian universities. Those who knew Ron remember not the awards, but his humility, kindness and genuine interest in people. He always focused on improving the lives of others. On behalf of the people of Kitchener—Conestoga, I extend my sincere condolences to the family and loved ones of Ron. His legacy of service, compassion and community building will endure for generations. Ron will be missed.

title: Oral Questions: Natural Resources
