turns: Mr. Speaker, we all want Canada to grow and diversify its export markets. Today, I have good news. Strathcona Resources, a Canadian oil and gas producer, wants to export 250,000 barrels a day of crude oil from Prince Rupert. Strathcona will ship by rail existing in place today. It just needs the Liberal government to get out of the way and remove the west coast tanker ban. My private member's bill, Bill C-264, will do exactly that. Will the Prime Minister get out of the way and repeal the tanker ban so Strathcona can help Canada become an energy superpower?

Mr. Speaker, here is what we will do. We will work with B.C., Alberta and affected first nations to build the Pacific link, which will massively increase oil exports. We will also work with first nations to build interties between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, to build hydro in Quebec, to build nuclear in Ontario and to build the north coast transmission line in B.C. Rather than fight against indigenous peoples, why do the Conservatives not help us build Canada?

Mr. Speaker, it was Bill C-48 that killed the indigenous-owned Eagle Spirit Energy project, so the member opposite had better reconsider his position on those issues. It is time for the Liberal government to ban the tanker ban and not leave it merely open for consideration. How about repealing it completely so that producers like Strathcona can build our energy industry and bring jobs and prosperity to Canada? Will the Liberals get out of the way, remove the tanker ban and let Strathcona Resources export a quarter of a million barrels of oil?

Mr. Speaker, we will up the member by four and get a million barrels a day to the west coast by working in partnership with first nations, not against them. Maybe he could start working with us to build jobs in Canada in partnership with first nations.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister talks about making Canada an energy superpower, yet he continues to stand in the way. Strathcona Resources has a proposal to ship up to 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil a day by rail to Prince Rupert, with exports to overseas markets to begin in as little as two years. The railway already exists. The company is ready to pursue the project. What is missing is to repeal the Liberal tanker ban. Will the Liberals finally get out of the way, remove the tanker ban and allow Strathcona Resources to move forward with this proposal, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting that the member is focused on something in B.C. Maybe she should focus a little closer to home. Her premier, Premier Wakeham, said that the federal government was instrumental in getting Bay du Nord built, a $10-billion energy project in her province that the Conservatives are not helping support. Maybe they should figure out where they should spend their time.

title: Oral Questions: Housing
turns: Mr. Speaker, he is out of touch and people are out of money. Giving back a tiny fraction of what the government takes away will not cover even one mortgage payment, and that is if people can afford a home. Today, we have a report from Habitat for Humanity, which did a survey of 22 nations and found that Canadians were the most likely to have given up on the dream of home ownership. It said 56% of them believe they will never own a home, which is twice the average of the international community. This is after the Prime Minister promised that housing would be affordable. When will we have an end to the promises and of home ownership—
Mr. Speaker, I have to keep reminding the Leader of the Opposition that I just got here. He has been here for 20 years. Every single month this government has been in office—

Mr. Speaker, I would note the Leader of the Opposition's 240 months and counting, and my 18 months. What has happened in those 18 months? Every single month, rental affordability has improved in this country. Every single month, housing affordability has improved in this country. Jobs are up. The economy is up. We are moving forward. We know we have more—

Mr. Speaker, the guy who said he was going to build at unimaginable speeds says he just got here, after 18 months. It is not that he has failed to make things better after the 10 years of Liberal government that he helped advise on. It is that things are getting so much worse. Rent is up 86%, almost double, from $970 to $1,800 today. The Prime Minister is now leading an economy where the largest number of Canadians have given up on home ownership. When will we have an end to the big talk and actually get some home ownership results?

Mr. Speaker, every single month that this government has been in office, rental affordability has improved. Every single month that this government has been in office, housing affordability has improved. It has gone from 54% of disposable income to the low 40s per cent of disposable income, on average, in this country. There is more to do, but we have momentum. We are building Canada strong.

I will turn it over to you, the people out there. Is your rent payment really going down? Is your mortgage payment really going down? Is anything really getting built? Where are the results in your life back home? Mr. Speaker, this is the Prime Minister who set up a new bureaucracy that he said would double home construction to 500,000 a year. It has built only 2,000 homes, not even a drop in the bucket, and homebuilding is down 4% year over year. Will the Prime Minister stop with the big promises and the big spending and actually deliver some real results?

Mr. Speaker, real results are 140,000 more Canadians in work. A real result is the fastest-growing economy in the G7 in the last quarter, at 3.8% annualized. Real results are incomes growing, rents coming down and housing affordability improving. We are building Canada strong.
Mr. Speaker, I know the Prime Minister makes the excuse for being out of touch because he is not ever here—

Mr. Speaker, maybe that is why he misspoke a moment ago. He claimed that home ownership costs have gone down to the low 40s as a percentage of disposable income. I just pulled up the numbers from the RBC affordability index, and it actually takes 53% of disposable income for the average family to make payments on the average home. That is the highest it has been, outside of this Liberal government, since 1990. Will the Prime Minister stand up, correct himself and admit that a year and a half into his mandate, and 11 years into this Liberal government, Canadians cannot afford to own homes?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that major players like RBC are observing improving housing affordability, brightening job prospects and stabilizing prices. Indeed, throughout the summer in Ontario, we saw that housing sales for new homes were up 130%. We have now seen across the country for 24 consecutive months that rents are coming down. Our plan is working. We are investing in Build Canada Homes to build affordable housing from coast to coast to coast, with more than 19,000 units under way. We care about affordability, and we are delivering.

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister vowed to make Canada its own best customer. He promised that when his government spends, it will select Canadian suppliers and Canadian jobs first. When it comes to election time, the Prime Minister is elbows up, but when it comes to contract time, he chooses America first. He awarded a U.S. security firm with ties to Trump's ICE a $12-million contract over the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires, the largest employer of veterans in Canada. Why did the Prime Minister sacrifice Canadian veterans' jobs to put America first?

Mr. Speaker, our priority is to put Canadian content, Canadian companies and Canadian workers first, and to use our purchasing power to grow production here at home. That is companies contributing substantively to our economy, employing people, creating good jobs here in our communities and paying taxes here in our communities. That is what we are doing to build Canada strong and build Canadian innovation.

Mr. Speaker, actions speak louder than words, and the government did exactly the opposite of what the member just said. The Canadian Corps of Commissionaires is a not-for-profit that prioritizes the hiring of Canada's veterans. For generations, the Canadian government has provided it the right of first refusal for security contracts. The Commissionaires put in a competitive bid, but the America-first Prime Minister chose Trump's favourite security contractor, Allied Universal, for the job. Was this yet another concession by the Liberal government? Why is the Prime Minister putting the interests of American corporate profits over job opportunities for our courageous veterans?

Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House, we are working hard to attract more investment into our country, investment that delivers tangible results and lasting benefits to Canadian communities and supply chains. They want to talk about results. I point them to the contracts that have been awarded. I look at General Dynamics as an example—

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, we can point to the results and the impact that this policy has been having already in just a few months. We have seen, most recently, a contract awarded to General Dynamics. Those are tangible results. Those are jobs in communities that matter to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Commissionaires is a not-for-profit organization, Canada's largest private sector employer of veterans. What commissionaires earn goes back to veterans, not shareholders. Justin Trudeau once told veterans that they were asking for more than he was able to give. That was a slap in the face. Now the Liberal government has handed a CRA security contract to Allied Universal, an American company tied to Trump's ICE deportation machine, just to save $80,000. That is a backhand to the face. When will the Prime Minister stop beating down on veterans?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his military service and for raising his concerns. Let me be clear again. Veterans Affairs Canada does not award guard services contracts on behalf of other departments or agencies. I, of course, share the view that we must ensure that veterans have the right opportunities to find rewarding employment of their choosing when they are ready. It is fundamental to the national veterans employment strategy. Our government has worked with and will continue to work with veteran employers as we build the strongest economy in the G7.

title: Oral Questions: Housing
turns: Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister promised what he called the most ambitious housing plan since the Second World War, Canadians can be forgiven for assuming that meant more homes, not fewer, but the Liberals' own housing agency, the CMHC, says that housing starts are down this year and that Canada is on track to build fewer homes this year than last year. It says the key risk is that we will not build enough. Is it still the Liberal government's promise to build 500,000 new homes per year, or has the Prime Minister abandoned that target?

Mr. Speaker, we are very focused on delivering affordable housing for Canadians, as seen by Build Canada Homes start-ups. We have over 19,000 homes now under way with Build Canada Homes, affordable non-market homes that are scaling up. We are going to continue to extend that work, and we are going to give Canadians every opportunity to buy or rent an affordable home. We are going to scale this work as aggressively as possible, and particularly if we have support from the members opposite, we will be able to go faster and farther.

Mr. Speaker, for all the talk and all the announcements, by the minister's own admission there are only 19,000 homes, but only 2,000 are actually under construction. That is all talk and no action. This week, the Liberals announced a new housing project, and I thought maybe we are going to get some progress. The announcement was $7.8 million for affordable housing, but, oops, it is gender-equitable affordable housing in the Dominican Republic. Why are Canadian taxpayers paying for gender-equitable housing in the Dominican Republic when they cannot afford a home at all?

Mr. Speaker, clearly the member opposite is not paying attention. Not only do the member opposite and his colleagues not support investing in affordable housing, but they voted against Build Canada Homes. They voted against—

Mr. Speaker, the noise from the other side illustrates that the members of the opposition do not care about affordable housing. They do not care that Canadians need housing. This side of the House continues to advance, to push hard for affordable housing to be delivered and to work with provinces and territories. Last month, we launched the Canada rental protection fund, $1.5 billion for 7,000 affordable rental homes that are protected. Are we going to see support from the other side? I do not think so.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised Canadians the most ambitious housing plan since the Second World War, yet his own government's numbers tell a different story. According to CMHC, housing starts dropped 11% in the month of September. After a year and a half of more spending, more bureaucracy and more Liberal promises, fewer homes are being built, while home ownership slips further out of reach. How many more young Canadians must give up on the dream of home ownership before the Liberals admit their plan has failed?

Mr. Speaker, there are some basic facts around the housing market that we are challenged with as a country right now and that many other countries are challenged with. The world is struggling with uncertainty, and we have to focus on delivering on affordable housing. If we look at the results across the country, we have successful cities that are increasing their housing starts. We have some markets that are slow. We are intervening. We put GST on the table across the country right now. In Ontario, one can save up to $200,000 on a new home. That is significant action. That is not being supported by Conservatives. On this side, we will continue to take action on housing—

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the veterans minister talked about creating employment opportunities for veterans. This week we learned the Liberal government awarded a $12-million security contract for the CRA to an American firm with ties to ICE instead of a Canadian not-for-profit that employs veterans. The difference between the two bids was less than 1%. The Liberals have been in here this week talking about the procurement process, but we are looking for an answer to a very simple question: What part of this decision included the employment of veterans?

Mr. Speaker, the member knows better. Let us be clear. This government will always stand with veterans. That is why veterans are prioritized when it comes to hiring at the CRA and across the public service. When it comes to operational security matters at the CRA, they are handled independently by the experts at the agency, not politicians. We will always stand with veterans.

Mr. Speaker, for days the Liberals have been leaning on this claim that it is an independent procurement process while ignoring their responsibility to have a framework in place that prioritizes the employment of veterans and buying Canadian. That is what they have been talking about, a buy Canadian strategy. Instead, they picked a U.S.-owned company with ties to Donald Trump's ICE and in the headlines for all the wrong reasons instead of prioritizing employing Canadian veterans. Why did they not hire veterans or buy Canadian?

Mr. Speaker, we have always supported and will always support veterans, including with respect to employment opportunities. The process the CRA undertook was independent, which resulted in the contract going to a Canadian subsidiary with over 10,000 workers. Let us talk facts. This contract was about for 60 employees, of whom 33 have been rehired, including 12 veterans.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised that Canadian companies would receive preferential treatment on contracts worth more than $5 million. After being outbid by less than 1%, a CRA security contract was awarded to U.S.-based Allied security, a company with ties to ICE's mass deportation efforts in the United States, instead of the Commissionaires, a Canadian not-for-profit that employs thousands of veterans and RCMP officers. Why is the Prime Minister ignoring his own procurement policy by giving a major federal contract to an American-owned company instead of supporting a 100-year-old Canadian institution?

Mr. Speaker, that member knows better too. It is simply not true. The contract was awarded after a rigorous process that included technical criteria. As I mentioned, contracting is done free of political interference. Maybe on that side 12 years ago they had political interference. On this side, we do not do that. We are talking 60 employees. Thirty-three were rehired. Twelve of them are veterans.

Mr. Speaker, this was a $12-million security contract with the CRA that was awarded to an American-based company that refers to itself as America's most patriotic company. It is also a company known for paying lower wages and benefits to its employees. For 100 years, the Commissionaires has employed thousands of veterans, RCMP officers and former members with good wages and benefits. Was supporting Canadian veterans and Canadian workers ever a consideration with this contract or was it always intended for the same corporate networks that keep benefiting from the Prime Minister?

Mr. Speaker, as my colleague has already spoken to, and as I spoke to yesterday, this was a contract awarded through the CRA following a fair and open procurement process. It selected a registered Canadian business headquartered in Ontario, which employs thousands of Canadians. Our government will always stand with Canadian workers and Canadian businesses, and we will build the strongest economy in the G7.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have again betrayed veterans, stripping the Commissionaires of a $12-million CRA contract only open to Canadian companies. It went to Allied Universal, an American company with just 1% of its workforce in Canada and tied to Donald Trump's ICE deportations. The Liberals wrap themselves in the flag at election time, and then pay Americans at contract time. Here is the kicker: Allied Universal has been suing the government for $420 million. Will the Prime Minister give the contract back to the Commissionaires?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague across the way for his service to Canada and for his advocacy on behalf of veterans. As we have stated, this was a fair and open procurement process. The decision was made by officials at CRA. We will continue to stand with Canadian workers and Canadian businesses.

title: Oral Questions: Fisheries and Oceans
turns: Mr. Speaker, Canada faces a 29-year low in workforce participation. The job-finding rate has dropped again, now down to 30.6% under the Liberal government. Canadians are losing jobs and they are losing hope. While Canada has a job crisis, the government has chosen to give public subsidies to a company that fired Canadian workers to hire foreign workers. Why did the fisheries minister approve a public subsidy to Ichiboshi L.P.C. after the company had already been caught firing Canadians to hire illegal workers?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Conservatives, while they talk down Canada and talk down our workers, that this country is building. Let me give some examples. Maybe the member has forgotten about LNG Canada phase two, with $33 billion in private investment and 4,000 new construction jobs. The Nouveau Monde Graphite project means 1,000 new jobs. At the Darlington nuclear station, there are thousands of jobs. Canada is building. I hope the Conservatives join us.

Mr. Speaker, that response had absolutely nothing to do with the question that was asked. Canada faces a 29-year low in workforce participation. This question is about fisheries. There was an Order Paper question the government tabled on February 19, question 885, that admitted that the government provided public subsidies through that department to a company that had fired Canadian workers to hire illegal workers. Why can the fisheries minister not stand up and answer that question? Why are you subsidizing a company that fired Canadians to hire illegal workers?

Mr. Speaker, the member talks about workforce participation. What this government is doing is building. We are building projects right across the country, with Canadian steel, Canadian lumber and Canadian unionized workers. Let us remind the Conservatives of some of the projects that are going on in this country. There is BHP's Jansen potash project, six new icebreakers in Quebec City and LNG Canada phase two, with 4,000 construction jobs. There is the Pacific link pipeline. We are building this country. Workers are excited. Unions are excited. Let us go build this country.

Mr. Speaker, the question is about fisheries. The fisheries department gave a subsidy to a company that fired Canadians to hire illegal workers. The government tabled the Order Paper question response in the House, question 885, on February 19. Again, why did the government, through the fisheries department, provide public subsidy to the Ichiboshi L.P.C. company after it fired Canadians to hire illegal workers?

Mr. Speaker, the minister recently announced the renewed Atlantic fisheries fund with her provincial counterparts. This new fund will provide $300 million over five years to our fishing sector to spur innovation, enhance infrastructure, build on science and develop new markets. We are providing harvesters with the tools they need to grow the sector and create market diversity during these uncertain times.

Mr. Speaker, the minister recently announced the renewed Atlantic fisheries fund with her provincial counterparts. This new fund will provide $300 million over five years to our fishing sector to spur innovation, enhance infrastructure, build on science and develop new markets. Our government is here to build, and that includes strong fisheries and coastal communities.

title: Oral Questions: Natural Resources
turns: Mr. Speaker, Canada has the oil the world needs, the workers to produce it and the rail lines to get it to the Pacific. Strathcona Resources is ready to ship up to 250,000 barrels per day through Prince Rupert to global markets. This would mean more jobs, a stronger Canadian economy and more customers for our oil, and the best part is that no government subsidies are necessary. In fact, this is a company that is ready to bring in its own private dollars and make it happen. The only thing standing in the way is the Liberals' tanker ban. Will they do the right thing, advocate for the well-being of Canadians and remove it?

Mr. Speaker, let me share what the new Conservative Premier of British Columbia just said: “Our government’s focus is on the project in front of us.... Pacific Link has been declared in the national interest, it takes a southern route, and it will create...jobs [for] British Columbia.” Other Conservatives seem to be able to get on board and support Pacific link. These guys just look for opportunities to fight. We are interested in building, not fighting. Why do they not join us?

Mr. Speaker, this is not an either-or decision, and at the end of the day it is a federal matter, so it is up to this government to make the choice. Will it take the tanker ban and remove it or, at the bare minimum, at least grant an exemption so that this private investment can go through, so that Canadian jobs can be created, so that oil can get to world markets and so that we as a country can be proud of what we produce here at home? The government is more than happy to give handouts to corporations that come begging. This one is not. It just needs this obstacle out of the way.

Mr. Speaker, here is what this government is doing: expanding the Taylor to Gordondale pipeline; expanding the Sunrise pipeline; building Pacific link, a million-barrel-a-day pipeline to the west coast; building LNG Canada phase one; supporting Woodfibre; supporting Tilbury; and supporting Ksi Lisims. All the Conservatives do is complain and look for things to fight about. Why do they not help build Canada with us?

Mr. Speaker, under the Liberal tanker moratorium, up to 34 tankers can be approved every month on the southern route, yet the northern route is equally safe, has less marine traffic and can have the same protections as the south. Having navigated the navy's tanker on the B.C. coast for years, I know what it takes to operate tankers safely, and the northern route can also meet the same standards as the south. This is a Liberal embargo on Canada and companies like Strathcona Resources that are standing by to ship Canadian oil overseas. Will the Prime Minister immediately grant an exemption for the northern route, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, there is so much going on on the west coast that is driving up economic growth and opportunity for that member's constituents that it is hard to name them. In addition to what my colleague, the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, just laid out, let me just congratulate the port of Vancouver for an all-time record of shipments going out of that port that is building our country strong and diversifying our trade markets. It has us on the path to double non-U.S. exports over the next 10 years. We are building British Columbia and we are building Canada—

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, anyone who is paying attention would know that the Defence Investment Agency, over the last 12 months, has done a lot to deliver for our armed forces. We are in contract award for new aircraft. We are in contract award for armoured vehicles. We are advancing projects such as submarines and AEW&C aircraft. All these things are happening. Bill C-40 would give our Defence Investment Agency a more commercially minded organization that could do things faster and do much more than just buy things for the military.

Mr. Speaker, part of the question was incoherent, but let me address the part of it that I think I could hear. Bill C-40 would still have all the safeguards for oversight and government accountability that we have in the system we have right now. With regard to the member's comment about the GlobalEye, we did the necessary analysis to make the choice to download Saab as the preferred supplier. This is great for Canada. These airplanes are built in Canada. They could be militarized in Canada for our own needs and exported to the world. This is good for Canadian jobs, good for Canada and good for our armed forces.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister announced a global aircraft project that does not meet operational requirements, to the surprise of the air force. L3Harris Canada and other contenders were not consulted. With no open competition, clearly politics was put ahead of defence. This is not the type of procurement Canada needs. Bill C-40 would bring an updated DIA Crown corporation with no defined procedures. However, there would be 13 exceptions for sole-source contracting, with no written reasons required. How would the government bring open competition and enhanced accountability, when Bill C-40's focus is on giving the DIA more power and the government less accountability?

Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to find out, when people are criticizing what we are up to, what they did when they had the keys to the car. The Conservative Party let NATO defence spending fall below 1%. The Conservatives actually got us out of NATO AWACS. That was a specific, conscious decision by the Stephen Harper government. Regarding the NATO airplane we are looking at buying, everybody in the world wants it. It is built in Canada. It will be built for Canadians and built for our allies. We are very proud of that.
Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for mansplaining the past. The government has failed to meet even the 2%. The Prime Minister has made numerous defence announcements that have—

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has made numerous defence announcements that have no signed contracts, including the GlobalEye project, which bypassed open competition. Now, Bill C-40 would turn the Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation that would give the Liberals unprecedented powers to bypass parliamentary oversight and easily approve sole-source contracting without fair competition. Will the Liberals commit to releasing the DIA's full procurement procedures and provide written justification to Parliament for all major sole-source military procurement contracts?

Mr. Speaker, Telesat and MDA is a signed contract. Bombardier is a signed contract. General Dynamics Land Systems—Canada is a signed contract. May I remind the member that he voted against defence spending in 2024 at the defence committee. We will take no lessons from the Conservatives.

Mr. Speaker, nobody trusts the Liberals or the secretary of state. After a decade, the Liberals always play political games. We are now on the third iteration of the Prime Minister's attempt to reinvent the wheel. Nothing changed in the last six months, except that media reported that Doug Guzman wanted to resign after less than a year as CEO of the Defence Investment Agency. Is Bill C-40 nothing more than an attempt to keep the Prime Minister's BFF from rage quitting because he had to be accountable to taxpayers?

Mr. Speaker, it is very obvious that the member opposite does not want to talk about his lack of support for the Canadian Armed Forces. Every single time we have brought forward defence spending at committee, the Conservative Party has voted against it. Mr. Speaker, in budget 2025, we invested more than $81 billion in defence over the next five years. We have met the NATO target of 2% five years ahead of schedule. I do not understand why the member opposite cannot get on board.

Mr. Speaker, let us talk about reality. In May, the Liberal solution was turning the brand new DIA into a stand-alone agency. Six months later, the Liberals changed their minds again and are trying to turn the agency into a Crown corporation. In reality, the Liberals are attempting to circumvent Treasury Board rules and give a new associate minister unprecedented power over a Crown corporation that would have to do everything the associate minister would say, do and spend. Is this a new attempt by the Prime Minister to decrease accountability and increase political interference in defence procurement?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of National Defence was in Alberta to talk about the incredible investments we have been making. At CFB Edmonton, we highlighted nearly $8 billion in defence investment, including nearly $4 billion to support future fighter capabilities at CFB Cold Lake. There is $750 million for a new chemical and biological laboratory at Suffield. There is $550 million to establish the western operating base for the Royal Canadian Air Force's Husky fleet. There is over $580 million over the next three years for maintenance and repair work across bases in Alberta. There are over 12,000 members of the Canadian Armed Forces and DND employees in Alberta, and we support them.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Madam Speaker, Food Banks Canada just reported a record 2.3 million visits in one month, up 117% since 2019, with nearly 800,000 by children, and one in five visitors has a job. Think about that. Working Canadians cannot afford to feed themselves or their families. Meanwhile, Liberal announcements keep piling up, but so do all the bills. Canadians cannot take another Liberal promise to the checkout counter. After 11 years in power, what do the Liberals have to say to working Canadians who have done everything right and still cannot afford to eat?

Madam Speaker, what I have to say to Canadians is that we have their backs. This government has the backs of Canadians. We understand that the cost of living is the most important thing for many Canadians: the price of food, the price of gas and the price of a home. Canadians are calling, and the answer is that 12 million Canadians will receive the Canada groceries and essentials benefit. We will always be there to support Canadians.

Madam Speaker, no one can afford another out-of-touch Liberal lecture about how good they have it, just like that. Alberta food bank visits have soared 156% since 2019. Food prices have jumped 30%. Higher fuel costs hit farmers, truckers, stores and families alike. The Conservatives proposed cutting all federal diesel taxes until Canada Day. The Liberals defeated it. The Prime Minister admits food is too costly, but blocked relief. Why is he all talk and bad results? When will the Liberals finally support our Conservative plan so Canadians can afford fuel and food?

Madam Speaker, I am sure what the people in Alberta and across Canada are wondering is why the Conservatives are missing in action every time we have a vote to support Canadians. Where was the member when we voted for the Canada groceries and essentials benefit? Where was the member when we extended the suspension of the excise fuel tax for people across the country? At a time when Canadians need support, I would say that Conservative members should join with this government and support Canadians every step of the way.

Madam Speaker, in Prince George, the Salvation Army served over 6,000 people in a single month. That is a 20% increase in just three years. One in five food bank clients has a full-time job, and over 32% of those clients are children. After 11 years of Liberal taxes and inflationary spending, Canadians are struggling to put food on the table. Relying on food banks is now the unfortunate reality for 2.5 million Canadians every month. How is that okay?

Madam Speaker, unlike the Conservatives, when we receive a report, such as the hunger report from Food Banks Canada, we do not just read the headlines; we read the recommendations. What do not feature among any of the recommendations are any of the things the Conservatives have put on the table to combat poverty. It is a complex challenge, and we are listening to what Food Banks Canada says. One of the policies it suggests is to expand funding for deeply affordable, supportive, non-market housing, co-operative housing, which is something the Conservatives not only vote against, despite the fact that the Conservative leader actually lives in government housing, but also stigmatize. They call it Soviet-style housing. It is a shame.

Madam Speaker, how unattached is this Liberal Member of Parliament? It is like using a dumpster fire for a wiener roast. Food bank usage in Williams Lake rose over 39% over the last two years. When are the Liberals going to wake up? These are families, seniors and working Canadians who are being forced to turn to the food bank because they can no longer keep up with the cost of living. Are the Liberals that arrogant and out of touch that it has become okay for children, seniors and full-time workers to have to rely on food banks? When will they finally take responsibility for the affordability crisis they have created?

Madam Speaker, what Canadians would like are actual solutions from all sides of the House that would help reduce poverty in this country. Literally everything the Conservatives have put on the table has been rejected by poverty elimination experts. Not even one single policy recommendation from the Conservative Party appears in the list of policy recommendations in Food Banks Canada's hunger report. One of the most important recommendations is affordable housing, which is true non-profit, non-market housing, and it is something the Conservative Party has voted against consistently over the last seven years since I have been here. They should look at their own record when talking about eliminating poverty.

Madam Speaker, of course, the member used the opportunity to attack Conservatives instead of focusing on a solution. One in nine households in the Waterloo region struggles to afford food. Across Canada, food banks saw 2.36 million visits in March alone, and one-third of those were children. There are 800,000 children going hungry in Canada. Canadians cannot afford excuses, and they cannot afford the government. When will the government take responsibility for making life more expensive and finally admit that we are in an affordability crisis?

Madam Speaker, with great respect to my colleague across the way, I would ask, when can Canadians expect the Conservatives to get on board with the income security policies that the very report they have been holding up this week speaks to? We are talking about the Canada disability benefit, the workers benefit, and the groceries benefit, as well as the national school food program, which is serving over nine million meals to kids in that colleague's province. Those are real solutions to many of the challenges that Canadians are facing right now and that this government is squarely focused on.

Madam Speaker, the Parliamentary Budget Officer confirmed what Canadians are feeling every day. The economy is weakening, inflation is on the rise and Liberal spending is driving up the debt. The Liberals' projected deficit is now $38 billion higher than promised. After years of broken promises, why are the Liberals forcing Canadians to pay the price for their reckless spending with an affordability crisis? Just this week, they voted against recognizing the affordability crisis. When will the Liberals finally admit that one exists?

Madam Speaker, I know it is Friday, so let me give my Conservative colleagues a takeaway as they go to their ridings to help their constituents. They should probably talk about the fact that Canada is projected to have the second fastest-growing economy in the G7 in 2027. They probably should talk among themselves as to why they are voting against measures that will support Canadians with respect to affordability. Most of question period today was about affordability. The sad thing for the people watching at home is that they say they are asking questions and they are talking a good game, but when it is time to vote they are missing in action. Why will they not vote to support the government? I am sure that we—

title: Oral Questions: International Trade
turns: Mr. Speaker, the PBO announced the financial impacts of the Canada-U.S. trade measures, yet unfortunately, successive barriers since 2025 will result in a 1.4% GDP net loss. To make matters worse, if those barriers remain, 185,000 Canadians will lose their jobs. The Prime Minister promised to get a deal for Canadians. When will he make good on his promise and get a deal?

Mr. Speaker, let us agree that Canada had a very good day yesterday. It was a very good day for Albertans and a very good day for Canadians. That member will want to join with the government in thanking all Albertans who participated in this debate, but more importantly, those Albertans and other Canadians who are now going to continue putting their shoulder to the wheel to build this great country, to develop our resources, to create a future here at home and to create the kind of growth that gives us the best quality of life and makes Canada the best country in the world.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is trying to convince Canadians that he can replace a trillion dollars' worth of trade between Canada and the U.S., yet up to this point, his hard deals only represent 1% of trade between Canada and the U.S. in 2025. Canadians cannot live on 1% of previous trade revenue, so why does the Prime Minister not just do his job and get a good deal for Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, our colleague should be very reassured that the Prime Minister is doing exactly that: his job. He is building a strong Canadian economy. He is diversifying our trading relationships with reliable partners around the world. He is doing what we campaigned on in the last election. I know the hon. member may prefer to forget the last election. We remember clearly the commitment we made to Canadians to control what we can control, build a strong economy here at home the right way and work with Canadian workers and businesses to grow the economy.

Mr. Speaker, Mariposa Dairy in Lindsay supports 200 Ontario dairy goat farms and exports more than $60 million a year in cheese to the United States. Because of U.S. tariffs, the company is being hit with a $4.5-million bill every month. It has warned that without an immediate solution, the entire Canadian dairy goat industry will be decimated. What specifically is the government doing to secure relief for Mariposa Dairy before it is too late?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague for his important question. I am indeed seized with the issue. The minister in charge of FedDev Ontario is as well. FedDev has provided funding, we will provide more funding, and we will work together on the solution because we need to make sure that Mariposa Dairy is secured.

Mr. Speaker, Mariposa Dairy has been warning the government about this threat since March 2025. It told Ottawa then that tariffs could devastate the Canadian agricultural industry when it comes to dairy goats. On one hand, the Liberals are saying they are here for workers, yet after a year of waiting, time is running out as the company takes on more and more debt. Will the government commit today to securing a solution that will keep these farmers and workers in business?

title: Oral Questions: Fisheries and Oceans
turns: Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago, I got up here and sounded the alarm on the France crab grab, and the Liberals tried to dismiss it as fearmongering. Once they started to realize that this was a $60-million issue, all the minister did was say that she was disappointed in France's intent. Newfoundlanders and Labradorians do not want a government that is simply disappointed. Will the Prime Minister stand up for Canadians, stand up for Canadian sovereignty and say no to the France crab grab?

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I will not play politics with issues as important as this. What I will say is that French officials confirmed that no new snow crab licence was issued. What I will say to the member is that the residents and constituents in his riding reach out to me regularly to talk about the things that matter: small craft harbours, the Churchill Falls agreement, the work on training our young people for Red Seal certifications, and on and on it goes. It is enough of the nonsense. We have work to do. Canadians know we need to work together. The member needs to—

Mr. Speaker, selling out our fishing industry to foreign interests is not nonsense. I would have the member for St. John's East understand that. The Prime Minister and the President of France two weeks ago announced a 1,500-tonne quota of crab to be caught in waters that are controlled by Canada. The Minister of Fisheries expressed her disappointment. The Canadian fishing industry deserves better. Will the Prime Minister stand today with our fishing industry and stop this giveaway, or has he already sold it out to foreign interests?

Mr. Speaker, it is nice to hear the member stand in the House again. It has been a long time since we have heard from him. I want to take this opportunity to see if he still believes that our school nutrition program is garbage. Let me remind him that we are facing a time in our country when we need to come together. Newfoundlanders and Labradorians understand this. The constituents in his riding understand this. It is a shame that he still has to play cheap politics.

Mr. Speaker, crab fishermen and plant workers back home were not amused with that response from the member for St. John's East. The Minister of Fisheries should at least know that next year's crab quotas will be set next year, which is in opposition to what she said, that the quotas have not been announced. Maybe she is catering her response to the French fishermen she met last summer. Will the Liberal Prime Minister stand with our fishing industry, or has he already sold it out like he did with our steel producers?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind my colleague across the aisle that I work in dialogue and actually have very strong relationships with the fishery sector in Newfoundland and Labrador. I certainly do not need lessons on how to speak with people from the member, but I will remind him that we are doing the work that Canadians have asked us to do. We are meeting this moment with strong strategies and programs that work, and we are meeting it in relationship and in dialogue with the people who need us to work alongside them. This rhetoric is not doing anyone any benefit.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the hon. Minister of Fisheries. In 2019, the federal government committed to shutting down what are sometimes called open net-pen salmon farms. In my riding, my constituents asked me to call them toxic fish factories, which is what they are. The government promised to shut them down by 2025, but in 2024, it extended that to 2029. Now the First Nation Wild Salmon Alliance is demanding to know, on behalf of 37 first nations in B.C., the wild salmon fishery organizations, the salmon foundation and the sport fishers, if the government will commit to keeping its promise and shut down these toxic fish factories by 2029.

Mr. Speaker, our government understands the importance of salmon to communities on Canada's west coast. The government's interdepartmental task force has conducted over 120 engagements with first nations and stakeholders. The government is reviewing the different perspectives to consider how best to move forward on sustainable aquaculture in British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, during one of the answers to a question from a colleague of mine, the member for Desnethé—Missinippi—Churchill River said their government was working, and I do not want him to inadvertently mislead the House. I was wondering if he would withdraw that comment.

Mr. Speaker, the member for The Eastern Peninsulas asked a legitimate question of the Minister of Fisheries, who, during her very condescending response, gave the member, or at least somebody on this side, the bird. I would ask that she apologize. The Minister of Natural Resources could confirm that and so would the tapes.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the member that whatever he said I did was just a hand movement, and I find the statement offensive.

title: Oral Questions: Public Services and Procurement
turns: Mr. Speaker, I will confess that I have no idea how to build up $733 billion of new debt, which is what he is planning to do, and it is going to the Liberal club. The Prime Minister has attempted to distract using the Trump card to justify the 2.3 billion tax dollars he has given to Telesat, the company of his friend Dan Goldberg, but the excuse does not work, because Telesat is giving a billion of those dollars to Elon Musk's SpaceX for launch capabilities. Has the Prime Minister ever discussed Telesat with his public servants, his ministers or his staff, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, I have not been involved in any decisions related to contracts with Telesat or the financing of Telesat. Those decisions began with the Conservative government in 2007. They ran through the public procurement process. The final decision was made by the Secretary of State for Defence Procurement. I had no knowledge of those decisions. I did not participate in those decisions. I am proud of Canada, however.

Mr. Speaker, how he chooses his words so very carefully. Earlier on, his government claimed he did not have any discussions about Telesat, and now he has deleted that word, just as he deleted mention of his friend and that company from a later edition of his book. The company got the contract in August of this year, a decade after the Conservatives left office. Here is the question for the Prime Minister: Did he ever discuss Telesat with any public servant, any staff member or any minister, yes or no?
Mr. Speaker, I was not involved in any decisions related to that company—

Mr. Speaker, I was not involved in any decisions related to that company, but if the Leader of the Opposition would like to learn something, he might want to read the national security strategy. He might want to recognize that one of the key determinants of this country's sovereignty, which this budget is going to help deliver, is control of space. We will build Canada strong in space.

Mr. Speaker, I asked the Prime Minister if he had ever talked to a minister, staff member or public servant about Telesat. He got very nervous. He refused to answer the question, and he talked in generalities about his budget—

It looks like they are all getting very nervous over there, Mr. Speaker. Let us look at the reality. It is illegal under the Conflict of Interest Act, section 9, for the Prime Minister to in any way discuss matters that could favour the interests of a friend. Dan Goldberg is his friend of 20 years. The company got a $2.3-billion taxpayer-funded contract in August of this year, and contracts have exploded under the Prime Minister. Again, did the Prime Minister ever discuss Telesat with a public servant, a minister or a staff member? Did he ever discuss Telesat, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, as the leader well knows, because he is subject to the same rules, Canada has world-leading rules in terms of ethics, disclosure and compliance. Of course, we will always at all times comply with the legal provisions of the Conflict of Interest Act and other applicable laws. We have the most stringent rules in the world, and obviously every member on this side of the House spends a great deal of time devoted to complying with those regulations.

Mr. Speaker, Telesat received a $2.3-billion contract from the government. The CEO of Telesat just happens to be a close personal friend of the Prime Minister. Section 9 of the Conflict of Interest Act states that a public office holder shall not influence a decision to further the interests of a friend. Did the Prime Minister discuss, and I emphasize the word discuss, this $2.3-billion contract with his staff or anyone in government, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, as the member well knows, Canada has among the most stringent ethics guidelines and laws in the world. These measures and these rules are followed rigorously by all members on this side of the House and, indeed, I assume, all members of the House and all senior officials. The Conflict of Interest Act and other measures are constantly followed and constantly updated. We will continue to follow them.

Mr. Speaker, that was a yes-or-no question. The Prime Minister has a blatant conflict of interest in relation to his friend, the CEO of Telesat, which received a $2.3-billion contract. Again, did the Prime Minister discuss any aspect of this contract with his staff or anyone in government, and why did he not issue a public declaration of recusal as required by law?
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, like, I assume, all members of the House, rigorously follows all of the various kinds of ethics requirements that are in place.
Mr. Speaker, hello, everyone. It is nice to be here with all of us—

Mr. Speaker, the AI minister, the Prime Minister and the Telesat CEO are all buddies. They sent their kids to the same elite private school. They are in the same book and running club. They even ran a marathon together. The AI minister took the correct steps of adding Dan Goldberg to his ethics screen. Why will the Prime Minister not do the same? If the AI minister can do it, why can the Prime Minister not do it?
Mr. Speaker, no one in the House will ever match that member for describing his friendships to the world.

Mr. Speaker, we see another example of the Liberals deflecting and dodging a very important question about $2.3 billion of taxpayer money. What we are pointing out is that the AI minister took the correct steps of adding Telesat CEO Dan Goldberg to his ethics screen. The question is why the Prime Minister cannot do the same. Their personal friend Dan Goldberg has been personally enriched by a government contract and Canadians deserve to know why the Prime Minister will not acknowledge his friendship in his conflict of interest ethics screen.

Mr. Speaker, as that member knows, Canada has among the most stringent ethics requirements in the world. Those requirements are followed rigorously by the Prime Minister and all members on this side of the House at all times.

Mr. Speaker, Telesat was not legally bankrupt, but it was facing severe financial distress, insolvency warnings and an immediate risk of defaulting on its massive debt obligations. The Prime Minister's buddy Dan Goldberg, the CEO of Telesat, received 2.3 billion Canadian tax dollars just as $1.71 billion U.S., or roughly $2.3 billion Canadian, in debt was coming due on December 6. Is it a coincidence? Perhaps. To the Prime Minister, does “masters of our own destiny” apply only to his club of well-connected Liberal insiders taking care of themselves while those not in the clubs, such as hard-working families, seniors and single-income moms, pay the price?
Canada will always have extremely high, if not the highest, standards of ethical behaviour for public officials. That will continue to be the case, and we will continue to live by those standards.

Mr. Speaker, I have two questions. Can the Prime Minister explain why hard-working, taxpaying Canadian families, seniors and single-income moms gave $2.3 billion to his CEO friend and Liberal Party fundraiser at Telesat with a big government contract just as a nearly identical amount of debt was approaching maturity? I would also love to have the Prime Minister answer this one. Can he also explain what safeguards were put in place to ensure that these tax dollars are not being used to relieve the company of his lifelong buddy, a well-connected Liberal insider and fundraiser for the Prime Minister, of its financial pressures near insolvency?
Mr. Speaker, Canada has among the highest ethics—
Mr. Speaker, Canada has among the highest ethics standards in the world. Those will continue to be maintained and vigorously adhered to.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, the evidence is impossible to ignore. Yesterday, The Salvation Army reported that one-third of Canadians are skipping meals or cutting their portions, up almost 30% from just last year. Food bank visits have hit 2.35 million in a month, and that is double from 2019. This is not just some rough patch caused by something somewhere else far away. It is a slow and consistent leak in every household budget. The Liberal government has offered absolutely nothing to fix it. It has an affordability problem. Will Thursday's budget fix it?

Mr. Speaker, any time a child or family in Canada is hungry, it should stop us all. It is why this government made the national school food program permanent. It is why we tied the Canada child benefit to inflation. It is why we introduced the Canada disability benefit. It is why we are not finished. I would invite the member opposite to stay tuned tomorrow, when we introduce budget 2026. Those guys talk about spending in the budget and they talk about inflation, but they leave to the rest of our imaginations what they would cut. We know that and Canadians know that, because they vote against all of these measures time and again.

Mr. Speaker, if any of those programs worked, then food bank use in Toronto would not be up 333% since 2019. On Monday, I asked if the government would cut taxes on gas. There was no answer. On Tuesday, I asked whether Canadian tax dollars would stay here instead of going to Europe. There was no answer. The government has an affordability problem and it looks like it does not care. Once more, will the budget offer anything, one word, one sentence, to help save Canadians money?

Mr. Speaker, if we look at the report from The Salvation Army, it notes that 83% of respondents say that support services improved their family's well-being, and 53% say that it improved their access to food. That is why our government is funding these services through things like the national food security strategy. When we look at these reports, they talk about services like the groceries and essentials benefit, the Canada child benefit, the school food program and even the work that we are doing through Build Canada Homes to create affordable housing. These are the ways we bring about affordability for Canadians. We are focused on it and they are not.

title: Adjournment Proceedings: Climate Change
turns: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise tonight to follow up on a question that I originally asked on September 23. I did not get an answer to my question. I would like to save time tonight and make sure the parliamentary secretary focuses on the question I wanted an answer to, which was whether we are going to see a cost-benefit analysis for what is now being called, for public relations purposes, the Pacific link, the pipeline to be built by the Government of Alberta and the Government of Canada in the absence of a private sector proponent. It is a project that expands greenhouse gas emissions. There were commitments made by the Government of Canada to meet the Paris Agreement commitments. However, my question was specifically about public expenditure of money. The minister gave an answer about how good their climate plans were, but completely avoided the question of whether there is a cost-benefit analysis to justify the expenditure of public funds on a project that is now, since the time of this question, designated as a project in the national interest. I will also add, because I will not get to it in the rebuttal, that part of the answer from the Minister of the Environment, in not answering my question, was to highlight what she calls clean energy, “to highlight Churchill Falls...14,000 megawatts of power”. That was not at all relevant to my question. Since we have not had an opportunity to debate that in the House, every time I hear a Liberal member talk about how Churchill Falls and Gull Island expansions will create clean energy, I would ask Liberals to be aware of the fact that it cannot be called clean energy if it poisons indigenous people. There is abundant evidence, many studies, on how the expansion of Churchill Falls and the Gull Island plant will increase methylmercury in the waters, and therefore in the fish and the food that indigenous people have a right to harvest and eat. We do not want to expand the poisoning of indigenous people by methylmercury. I will also point out that, as a matter of claiming that this has any relevance at all to climate targets, Gull Island is predicted, if everything goes according to plan, to be on stream by 2034 and the Churchill Falls expansion by 2035. That puts the provision of this so-called clean energy at the point when our commitments under the Paris Agreement will have already fallen due. According to the Canadian Climate Institute, there is no possible way that we are going to achieve the 40% to 45% below 2005 levels by 2030, which was our legally binding commitment under the previous government of Justin Trudeau. It does not even meet the legally binding commitment that was put forward as an intended nationally determined contribution by the previous government of Stephen Harper. It is again, on many levels, an affront, and I hope the parliamentary secretary can take on board at least this. Here we have in budget 2026, page 125, the only commitment under any of the projects they are describing as being potentially of national importance, a commitment “to provide $37 million in [budget year] 2027-28 to support robust cost-benefit analysis of proposed interties”. I favour those proposed interties, absolutely, but I find it puzzling that there is no reference in any other government document or financial projection for any cost-benefit analysis on any other project other than the interties question. I find it baffling that we would think it wise to pour tens of billions of dollars into a project that will lose Canada money and wreck through our targets.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise and respond to my dear friend from Saanich—Gulf Islands. We all know that Canadians are facing a changing world. Climate change is bringing more severe wildfires, floods and extreme heat, but at the same time, families and businesses are dealing with affordability pressures, economic uncertainty and growing demands on our energy systems. These challenges are interconnected, and we need an approach that recognizes that reality. Adapting to today's economic and global circumstances does not mean that we will walk away from our climate action. It means being pragmatic, adjusting our approach and focusing on results that strengthen Canada's economy while continuing to reduce emissions. Our commitment to a net-zero future remains an important part of that work, and budget 2026 sets out how we intend to get there. Our approach is built around four major building blocks: building clean energy supply, switching to cleaner technologies, transforming energy productivity and innovating for the solutions of tomorrow. We are mobilizing investment, supporting clean energy development, expanding our electricity system and creating the conditions for Canadian businesses to compete in a changing global economy, and we recognize that while the world is making the transition to a lower-carbon economy, Canada has an important role to play as a reliable and trusted energy supplier. That is why we established the Major Projects Office to bring federal expertise together, coordinate complex processes and give projects a clear path toward the approvals and investments they need. The Building Canada Act gives us additional tools to advance projects of national importance, but efficiency cannot come at the expense of our responsibilities. We remain committed to respecting indigenous rights, meaningful partnership with indigenous peoples and strong environmental protections. The Major Projects Office also benefits from the advice of an indigenous advisory council, helping it ensure that indigenous perspectives and interests are reflected in this work. Canadians should not have to choose between economic prosperity and a healthy environment, nor should they have to choose between reliable energy, good jobs and a secure future. Our approach recognizes that we need to deliver on all of these priorities together. We will continue to take meaningful action on climate change, strengthen Canadians' economic resilience and create opportunities for workers and communities across this country. That is what responsible nation building looks like, and that is how we will continue to build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my friend, the hon. parliamentary secretary, for raising the concept of net zero, so I can put to bed the false claim that net zero by 2050 has anything to do with the Paris Agreement. Net zero by 2050 is a convenient public relations exercise, invented by the government when it was led by Justin Trudeau, to create a timeline that is so far out there that it can keep pretending that somehow by 2040 the government will start achieving things, or by 2045. Net zero by 2050 is actually antithetical to our legally binding commitment. By 2035, under the Paris Agreement, we have committed to reduce Canada's emissions by 40% to 45% as against our 2005 levels. As the commissioner for the environment and sustainable development has pointed out and as the Canadian Climate Institute has pointed out, on current practices, we are miles from that. To the hon. parliamentary secretary, the government has a moral obligation to future generations, as does every MP in this place, to fight for our future.

Mr. Speaker, I understand. I do have young children, and I want to fight for their future. The Major Projects Office is already helping turn our approach into results. It is advancing 18 projects and nine transformative strategies across sectors such as nuclear energy, liquefied natural gas, hydroelectricity, critical minerals and transportation. Together, these represent more than $192 billion in investment and approximately 337,000 new jobs. In Quebec, two projects have already broken ground less than seven months after referral to the office. This is about creating the conditions for investment, strengthening our economy and delivering the infrastructure Canada needs, and we will do so while respecting indigenous rights and upholding environmental protections.

title: Oral Questions: Labour
turns: Mr. Speaker, workers and unions in my riding have emphasized the importance of protecting workers' rights and ensuring their voices are heard at the bargaining table. Our government shares this commitment and believes meaningful collective bargaining leads to better agreements. This is why we are giving workers and employers more time to negotiate and greater support to resolve disputes. Could the minister explain how Bill C-39 will protect workers' rights, strengthen collective bargaining and ensure government intervention is reserved for exceptional circumstances?

Mr. Speaker, our government believes that the best agreements are reached at the bargaining table. Bill C-39 strengthens the bargaining process by providing employers and unions with more time to negotiate, earlier access to dispute resolution tools and additional support to help the parties reach agreements before disputes escalate. At the same time, the bill preserves the fundamental right to strike while introducing important guardrails around the use of section 107, ensuring that government intervention remains exactly what it should be: rare, exceptional, transparent and a measure of last resort.

Mr. Speaker, I have good news. Today, the Liberals have a chance to vote for our NDP bill to repeal section 107 and protect the right to strike. Unions and workers everywhere have supported it. The government has a clear choice, continue its unconstitutional attacks on workers in Bill C-39 or vote in favour of our NDP bill. Which is it? Will the Liberals finally respect the demands of workers or continue caving to CEOs by violating the right to strike?

Mr. Speaker, obviously, we honour the role of workers, honour the role of organized labour and recognize that, in fact, there are rights to collectively bargain, but sometimes those rights, in order to be exercised, need federal support, especially in Canada Labour Code situations. We will, under Bill C-39, put in place new, expanded measures in order to support parties that find it difficult to achieve a collective agreement. We want to make those strikes all too rare.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order regarding what happened earlier when a colleague in the House—

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order regarding what happened earlier when a colleague, who represents his community here in the House, was trying to ask a question to a minister. There was a lot of noise, purposely to stop him from—

Mr. Speaker, maybe this time they will listen. Members purposely made noise to try to stop the member from speaking. I think we are getting into the territory of privilege. If a member cannot speak and ask a question in the House on behalf of the people he represents, there is a potential question of privilege.

title: Oral Questions: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship
turns: Mr. Speaker, recent data shows that we have an innovation exodus to the United States. It is up 142%. Thirty-four per cent of immigrants with a Ph.D. leave Canada within 25 years, and the innovation sector earns 46% more in the United States. The Liberals have brought in too many people too fast for housing and health care, and now Canada's best and brightest are leaving, including those who bring real innovation and jobs to our economy. Why is the Prime Minister not trying to reverse this brain drain instead of planning for higher immigration levels?

Budget 2025 launched an international talent attraction strategy and action plan. This will support recruitment of world-class researchers and advance Canada's global competitiveness and research excellence. What we have also seen in the last six to nine months is that a large number of U.S.-based, top-notch researchers have come to Canada, including to Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, and this will accelerate—

Mr. Speaker, on the contrary, we are sitting in an immigration system that has over 30,000 people who want to come to Canada under the start-up visa program and are stuck in bureaucratic purgatory. That is not progress. That is a failure of our system. On the flip side, today's national security strategy is a nothingburger and fails to address the serious screening problems for non-citizens seeking entry to Canada. The CBSA had 675 reports seeking deportation on national security grounds, but only 44 people were actually removed. This is a disaster, so will the Liberals reduce immigration levels—

Mr. Speaker, this is a historic day for Canada. We released a national security strategy that encompasses an all-of-government approach toward strategic national security. We will, in the coming weeks and months, release specific strategies toward public safety, as well as intelligence, defence, the economy and foreign policy. This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity for us to ensure that we have a strategic view of national security.

Mr. Speaker, the strategy the minister mentioned could have been an email. It was very slim, and it said nothing about one of Canada's biggest security issues, which is the failure to screen people who are coming into the country. Now the Prime Minister wants to increase immigration levels. CSIS screening requests hit a record 538,000 in 2024, and permanent residency files for full security screening are now projected to take years to clear. Why does this national security strategy say nothing about these things?

Mr. Speaker, the national security strategy is all-encompassing and has many elements of what my friend opposite is seeking. I can assure her that as part of the public safety portfolio, we are working toward finalizing a more comprehensive response that includes security screening. It is an essential part of keeping Canadians safe.

Mr. Speaker, actually, if I hit Ctrl+F on that document, I cannot find anything about improved security screening for non-citizens entering Canada. I would refer him to that document, and I would also refer him to the results. When Ahmed Eldidi entered Canada, he was allowed to do so in spite of the fact that there was a video circulating that showed him essentially committing an ISIS-level crime. He was convicted of a crime afterward, and the Persian community now wants clear public screening criteria that distinguishes forced conscripts from senior officials and terrorist leaders. Why did this strategy not do any of that?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly hope the member opposite went beyond Ctrl+F to read this document. It is an essential part of ensuring the safety and security of Canadians. There are elements in there that will, over the next several weeks and months, make it abundantly clear that this is about ensuring the safety and security of every Canadian while ensuring that strategic security objectives are met.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, Canadians are struggling. They cannot afford groceries, they cannot afford gasoline, and they cannot even afford to heat their homes. They are pinching pennies just to make it to the end of the month, but while Canadians are stretching their budgets, Liberals are doubling down on their out-of-control spending, which includes a $200-billion vanity project and sending $500 million for forests in Brazil. Why are Liberals mortgaging the future of our grandchildren when most Canadians cannot afford to make their monthly minimum credit card payments?

Mr. Speaker, we are absolutely focused on affordability measures, be it on helping Canadians to buy heat pumps or being able to actually increase the groceries and essentials benefit, but if we are going to talk about the tropical forests, they are the lungs for the world. We have invested, through a loan, into a fund, co-managed by Norway, that is going to protect one billion hectares of tropical forests across 70 countries. We are doing that with our allies, and we are making sure that we have a strong future for our children.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are not listening to us. Canadians, the people who sent us here, need their help. They are sending billions of dollars in pursuit of Liberal ideological fantasies, including $1 billion to a trust fund to supposedly accelerate the transition from coal in Indonesia, Philippines and South Africa, while Canadians can barely afford to heat their homes. The good news is that the $1 billion is not spent yet, because they are so incompetent they cannot even spend money. Will they get their $1 billion back, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, the government is focused on delivering on what we were elected to do, which is to build Canada strong and help families and workers all across this country afford the life they want to be able to afford. We know that Conservatives would not invest in ending homelessness in the country. We know they would not help make the affordable housing market work. We know they would not invest in having an electricity grid that underpins productivity and a prosperous future for our country. We know they certainly would not step up to provide a groceries and essentials benefit that supports Canadians with hundreds of dollars.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are making empty promises at speeds not seen in generations, even worse than Trudeau. New homes cost between $500,000 and $600,000 in Edmonton Northwest. We are seeing catastrophic youth unemployment, a cost of living crisis, adults forced to live in their parents' basements and record-high debt servicing costs. That is not youth mastering their own destiny; that is government selling out their future. That is why I voted against this budget. How can the government expect young families or anyone outside the Brookfield class to save even a down payment for their first home?

Mr. Speaker, the youth I talk to want a fair shot at success, and that is exactly why we are investing $8 billion in the team Canada strong program across the country, not to mention the billions of dollars we spent in youth employment workforce strategies that include paid work experiences across this country for young people all across the country to get the kinds of skills, talents and connections to employers that they need. What happens when we put these programs on the table? Those parliamentarians vote against them. We need a Conservative Party that understands that youth need a fair shot at success.

Mr. Speaker, families do not want to rely on government programs to put food on their tables. They want to earn a paycheque that actually covers their bills. Families in Edmonton Northwest are barely getting by with the cost of essentials like rent, groceries and fuel. This budget for the banker class puts the dream of buying a home or starting a family out of reach for too many young Canadians. Conservatives measure success on how many people can get off government programs. Do Liberals really think that families should have to rely on government programs to survive?

Mr. Speaker, creating those opportunities is exactly what budget 2026 does. The fiscal plan and the plan of this government is working. In the province of Alberta, 63,000 full-time jobs have been created since the start of the year, with 4,000 youth jobs within that number. House prices are down and rents are down. Affordability is becoming more in reach to people as these programs come forward. I welcome the member to join us in making sure that we can push this success even further. We know there is more to do. We are going to do it with or without them.

title: Oral Questions: Taxation
turns: Mr. Speaker, job one for the budget is very simple: save Canadians money. It needs to save Canadians money on their groceries, save Canadians money at the pump and save them money on the materials that go into building homes. The fastest way to save Canadians money is to get rid of all taxes on gas, get rid of the so-called fuel standard tax and the GST on gas and diesel, and get rid of the excise tax until Canada Day. Will the Prime Minister accept our idea to save Canadians money by axing taxes on gas?

Mr. Speaker, I will say it once again, because it is so astonishing. The member opposite represents the second-largest canola-producing riding in Alberta, has a canola crusher in his riding and is right adjacent to Imperial Oil's Strathcona refinery, which actually produces biodiesel supported by the clean fuel regulations. This is good for canola farmers across our country. It is good for his own constituents, and I would hope that he would stand up with them.

Mr. Speaker, it is no wonder Canadians are out of money. The Liberal government is out of touch. Yes, the farmers in my riding say the single biggest expense this year is the cost of diesel. Some of them are spending $25,000 or $30,000 on diesel. One farmer spends $5,000 a day during the harvest. All of it gets passed on in higher food costs. The Liberal government continues to add 20¢ a litre in taxes. The best way to save Canadians money is to scrap all those taxes. Will the government accept our idea to save farmers, small businesses, seniors and Canadians money?

Mr. Speaker, I have great news for Canadians and great news for that party across the House. On Thursday, we will table our second generational budget, budget 2026. We will build Canada strong. We will invest in our country from coast to coast to coast. We will make sure nobody is left behind. We will continue with the groceries and essentials benefit and fight for affordability measures for Canadians. On this side of the House, we deliver on affordability. They continue with the rhetoric.

Mr. Speaker, this will be their second generational budget in one year. Canadians cannot afford another generation of Liberal taxes. They are out of money. The member is out of touch to say they have delivered on affordability when food bank demand is up 9% year over year, with 2.35 million record-smashing visits to the food bank and the largest number of people who cannot believe they will never be able to afford a home is in this country, of any of the 22 countries polled by Habitat for Humanity. Why will they not stop wasting time and save Canadians money?

Mr. Speaker, as always, on that side of the House, it is hands up, no plan and no focus. There is nothing on that side of the House. On this side of the House, we are going to table budget 2026. We are masters of our own destiny. We are going to build Canada strong. We are going to build a strong, resilient economy. We are going to invest and build Canada while looking after those who need help the most. We just paused the excise tax on fuel. We are going to continue to deliver affordability measures for Canadians. That side continues with nothing.

Mr. Speaker, the member had trouble following what is a very clear and direct path to make life affordable. The shortest distance between two points is a straight line, and the straight line is this.
