I was just in Sarnia, where a local business owner told me he was surprised to learn that several corporations were registered on his local residential street with no sign of an office or any operations. The Prime Minister cannot pretend he did not see this loophole coming. After years at Brookfield, a company with dozens of subsidiaries registered in offshore tax havens, he knows exactly how corporations exploit loopholes to game the system. He knew that his policy was fool's gold, but he sold it to Canadians anyway. Next week, Canadians will remember the people who served our country in uniform, so it is fair to ask why the government chose to end an 80-year promise to Canada's veterans. Many Canadians walk past a commissionaire without knowing the story behind their uniform. The Canadian Corps of Commissionaires was founded in 1925 to provide employment to soldiers coming home from the First World War. In 1945, as hundreds of thousands more soldiers came home from the Second World War, Ottawa made them a promise: When the federal government needed guards for its buildings, the Commissionaires would get the first right of refusal. That promise was kept by every government and every party for 80 years, but in February of this year, the Liberal Minister of Veterans Affairs wrote to tell them that the promise was over. Her letter said that the government was confident the corps was positioned for “continued success in this new procurement environment”. Less than four months later, the Commissionaires found out what that new environment looks like under the Liberals. The government awarded the security contract the Commissionaires had held to a subsidiary of an American company, Allied Universal. Allied Universal reportedly took more than $290 million U.S. in contracts from the Trump administration's Department of Homeland Security this year alone. That is who the Liberals chose over Canada's veterans, while they told Canadians to put their elbows up. When Cartier got his barrels of treasure back to France, it did not take long for the truth to come out. With a simple test, everyone could see that it was fool's gold. The Liberals' buy Canadian policy has been tested now, too. It has failed the test. What frustrates me the most is that the real gold in the story was right in front of them the whole time. For 100 years, the Commissionaires have been standing guard at the doors of our federal buildings as Canadian veterans. That is the real gold in this, but the government shamefully traded it for fool's gold.

Mr. Speaker, Jacques Cartier, right this way I'll put your coat up on the bed Hey man you've got the real bum's eye for clothes It was interesting hearing the member opposite talk about fool's gold. I guess he is an expert in that, especially in conspiracy theories. We are doing this study right now in the government operations and estimates committee, and the definition of what is Canadian has been explained to the member, I do even know how many times. It is a physical presence in Canada, tax registration and sourcing of Canadian goods and labour. It is pretty straightforward. It also follows well-established practices. Would the member opposite agree that Canada's buy Canadian policy is important in the context of a global trade war?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe the member actually just stated that. He is telling me that the government actually supports dealing the buy Canadian policy to companies such as Huawei. It simply has corporate affairs in here. It has been registered and identified as a national threat to our country, and it is okay for our government to be buying products from Huawei. Is that what the member is telling me?

Mr. Speaker, the global message from the Liberal government is that it values veterans less than it values American companies, which is absolutely shameful and disgusting. I cannot imagine being a veteran here, going to defend our country and then coming back to a slap in the face. It is absolutely deplorable.

Mr. Speaker, there are two issues we are talking about. One is an American company's getting a contract that is normally reserved for the veterans of Canada, those who served in our armed forces. However, more importantly, the non-profit Commissionaires uses the revenue to help veterans from the armed forces who otherwise would not have it. The company in question, Allied Universal, a United States-based company, is not going to provide that same service to our veterans. Can the member please comment on that?

Mr. Speaker, the member asked a very good question. What kind of government that is supposed to be looking after our country and our veterans would consider that to be a good, very sound decision and as standing up for Canada? I can tell the House that a Conservative government would never make that kind of decision.

Mr. Speaker, gross exaggeration is probably one of the ways I would describe many of the comments made by my friend across the way. The company he is shooting down employs Manitobans. The footprint in Canada is significantly large. The Commissionaires defend the commissionaires until the end. At the end of the day, I believe in the support they give. However, the member should not give the false impression that the commissionaires are 100% veterans. They are not. It is probably closer to about 20%, and the company that has taken over the contract has rehired 30, maybe 33, of the 60 who were working there, a dozen of whom are veterans. Let us not grossly exaggerate the situation. Would the member not agree?

Mr. Speaker, the member said “false impression”. My gosh, it is smoke and mirrors. The Liberals are masters at this. They are absolutely outraged. How dare we question one thing about this policy? I went on for 10 minutes explaining to the Canadian public and to all those attending here today how much the government is misleading Canadians. It has to stop. The bigger question is, what kind of government would do this to the Canadian people?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by saying I will be sharing my time with the member for Surrey Newton. I welcome the opportunity to debate the motion from the hon. member for Battle River—Crowfoot. At a time of open challenges to our economic security and sovereignty, I can think of few more pressing public policy issues than the question of where and when key government contracts go to Canadian firms and suppliers. This is at the root of the motion put to us today, and I can assure all members that the government shares this concern. Since last December, the buy Canadian policy has been at the centre of a suite of measures introduced by the Government of Canada to stimulate the growth of Canada's builders and suppliers. Last September, we launched Build Canada Homes, a new federal agency that is building affordable housing at scale, fuelling a new and thriving housing industry. With an initial investment of $13 billion over five years, Build Canada Homes is investing in the development of public lands sites in partnership with Canadian builders, suppliers, other levels of government and indigenous communities. That investment is already making a difference, with multiple direct-build projects across multiple cities delivering up to 4,000 new homes on federal land, with at least 40% at below market rents. There is also the Defence Investment Agency. The need for a more strategic and responsive approach to defence procurement has long been acknowledged in Canada, but only in the last year has real action been taken. Since its inception last October, the Defence Investment Agency has been delivering for the Canadian Armed Forces while driving investment, innovation and industrial growth by targeting procurements that support strategic defence sectors such as aerospace and advanced manufacturing. The agency is driving the creation of high-quality, skilled jobs to communities across Canada and bolstering our country's industrial capacity and technological competitiveness. Finally, the Major Projects Office was introduced last year to put transformative, nation-building ideas on a viable path to fruition through the co-operation of federal departments, provinces and territories, indigenous peoples and industry. The goal is to identify projects with maximum benefit for Canadians. For example, just last month, the government announced that the new west coast pipeline, known as Pacific link, would be listed as a project of national interest. Whether it is the need for affordable housing, state-of-the-art defence capabilities or major infrastructure, these initiatives do not simply recognize the great reservoir of talent and experience within Canadian industry. They bank on it, and so does the buy Canadian policy. In fact, the policy is something of a common thread that runs through all these initiatives. The buy Canadian policy prioritizes Canadian suppliers and materials, strengthens supply chains and incentivizes Canadian content in strategic federal procurements. It applies to the ongoing work of the Major Projects Office, the Defence Investment Agency, Build Canada Homes and Crown corporations and their subsidies, as well as the hundreds of federal grants and contributions programs. In just over eight months, between December and October, Public Services and Procurement Canada awarded over 1,600 new contracts, worth approximately $23.8 billion. Of these, roughly 1,340 contracts totalling $17.7 billion were awarded to suppliers operating in Canada. These efforts are transforming local communities across the country with long-term, well-paying job opportunities for skilled workers. Last February, Kitchener's Colt Canada was awarded a $307-million contract to supply the Canadian Armed Forces with assault rifle systems under the Canadian modular assault rifle project. By investing in local expertise, we are ensuring that the forces are ready for the challenges ahead. In August, the government awarded a $768.6-million construction services contract to PCL Constructors Canada for the full construction of a new federal regulatory science facility at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency's Ottawa laboratory in Nepean, Ontario. On average, the site will employ about 250 workers a day. Also last summer, the government announced an investment of $2 billion over four years to General Dynamics Land Systems-Canada to build 190 armoured combat support vehicles. This strategic partnership is truly a pan-Canadian feat of co-operation, with several companies supporting the effort. Ryan Manufacturing in Richmond, BC, will supply military-grade cable and wire harness assemblies. InterPro in Regina, Saskatchewan, will supply advanced armour. Thales Canada in Saint-Laurent, Quebec, will supply thermal imaging systems. IMP Aerospace and Defence in Enfield, Nova Scotia, will supply other specialized components. The difference under the buy Canadian policy is that Canadian suppliers are now prioritized as a matter of practice. Suppliers must demonstrate that they meet the policy requirements, including through eligibility and Canadian content attestations, and the government has put compliance and monitoring mechanisms in place. The buy Canadian policy goes beyond giving preference to Canadian suppliers. In strategic federal procurements covered by the policy, bids receive additional evaluation points for higher proportions of Canadian content and value added activities, such as manufacturing and research development. This encourages businesses to source more from Canadian partners, extending opportunities to Canadian firms that supply components, materials and expertise. Our goal is to create an incentive for businesses to do more in Canada and to have more Canadian workers, more Canadian suppliers in their supply chains, more Canadian manufacturing, more Canadian research and development, and more investment in Canadian facilities and communities. In conclusion, it was said once that the world needs more Canada. With these policies and programs, the government is taking the position that Canada needs more Canada. International co-operation with trusted partners, both public and private, will always be a part of our efforts as a responsible federal government, but if the last two years have taught us anything, it is that our future is best placed in our own hands. We have made significant progress in less than a year, but this is not the finish line. We will continue expanding opportunities for Canadian businesses, strengthening Canadian supply chains and ensuring that federal government procurement serves as an economic lever for this country, because federal procurement is more than just purchases; it is an opportunity to build Canadian capacity, support Canadian workers and invest in Canada's economic future. This is the essence of the buy Canadian policy, and I look forward to seeing where it takes us in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member from Winnipeg for outlining, in general terms, the buy Canada policy. In reality, many small businesses across our country do not know where to start or where to go to apply for a government contract. In addition to that, the red tape to enter into an agreement is still very challenging for many of the small businesses that are facing the uncertainty referenced in his speech. In good faith, what areas can the government improve in procurement to actually see small businesses take up the government contracts? Since the announcements from the secretary of state for small business have come into force, we have not seen the increase in those contracts going to Canadian firms.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question is a very good question. It is a very timely question. We do know that, when a new program is introduced, there are questions. We need to be expanding what we are doing and the information we make available, but the offices of members of Parliament are already available. My own office, and I am sure the hon. member's office as well, is assisting small businesses in the riding to take advantage of these important government programs.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's valuable work with me on the health committee. Yes, we do have a social contract with our veterans, and there are established practices, but of course we talk about things that have been going on for over 100 years. A hundred years is a long time. There are going to be changes in our processes. Our government procurement decisions have to be made with the best decisions for all stakeholders in Canada at the time.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is absolutely right. The process is being streamlined. I, like I am sure almost every MP in here, have people working in my office who work directly with constituents, including constituent companies. When they call us, they want to know what is available. We make sure that they know the programs that are available and exactly how the process works. If they have problems with the process, we can help them navigate those and call the relevant departments for clarification.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to reaffirm the Government of Canada's commitment to the buy Canadian policy. We are incredibly proud of how this initiative is transforming government procurement, giving Canadian businesses, workers, manufacturers and suppliers greater access to opportunities and delivering real results for Canada. The government will always stand with Canadian workers and Canadian businesses, and that is how we will build the strongest economy in the G7. We remain committed to prioritizing Canadian suppliers and Canadian-made goods and services in federal procurement. This is a pledge we have made to Canadians and it is unwavering. Since the buy Canadian policy came into force in December 2025, it has been reshaping how the federal government spends by prioritizing Canadian content, materials, suppliers and workers at every opportunity. From steel and aluminum to wood products, the government's purchasing of goods and services is being used as a powerful tool to back key industries and strengthen domestic supply chains. The rollout of the buy Canadian policy marked a major step toward building a more resilient Canadian economy. It was designed to ensure clear advantages are available to suppliers who invest, innovate and produce here at home. By prioritizing Canadian suppliers, Canadian materials and Canadian content in federal procurement, we are becoming our own best customer by reducing reliance on any single trading partner and building—

Mr. Speaker, by prioritizing Canadian suppliers, Canadian materials and Canadian content in federal procurement, we are becoming our own best customer. By reducing our reliance on any single trading partner and building resilience through strong domestic demand, we are bolstering Canada's economy. The policy on prioritizing Canadian suppliers and Canadian content in strategic federal procurements initially applied to procurements valued at $25 million or more. In June, we lowered that threshold to $5 million, significantly expanding its reach. We are also putting Canadian materials at the centre of major federal construction and defence projects. For procurement of $25 million or more, the policy requires Canadian-produced steel, aluminum and wood. We are making it easier for Canadian small businesses to compete for federal opportunities through the small business procurement program, which will simplify procurement processes and introduce new digital tools. Ultimately, the test of this policy is whether federal spending creates economic activity here at home. In the spirit of the buy Canadian policy, the government continues to work to identify opportunities for Canadian suppliers to benefit from federal procurement policies and ultimately support Canadian workers, Canadian businesses and Canadian communities. This includes attracting investments that deliver tangible and lasting benefits to Canadian communities and supply chains. This is about driving growth, creating opportunities and enhancing prosperity for all Canadians. In the current situation we are in, this has never been more important, particularly when it comes to protecting Canada's sovereignty. We know that the world has changed and that Canada must change with it. That is why Canada is also making generational investments to rebuild and reinvest in the Canadian Armed Forces. These investments are guided by Canada's first-ever defence industrial strategy, a whole-of-government approach to transform Canada's defence industry. The strategy will prioritize Canadian suppliers and materials, invest in Canadian innovation and streamline defence procurement. It is supported by the new Defence Investment Agency. Between December 2025 and October 1, 2026, Public Services and Procurement Canada awarded a total of 1,644 new contracts worth roughly $23 billion. Of these, 1,342 contracts, representing about $17.7 billion, were awarded to suppliers operating here in Canada. That is the kind of progress we want to build on. With regard to today's motion, the Canada Revenue Agency, following a fair and open procurement process, decided to award the contract to a company that operates extensively in Canada and employs Canadian security guards, supervisors and managers. This brings me to an important point of what we mean when we talk about a Canadian supplier. Being a Canadian supplier is not simply a question of who owns the shares of a company. We also need to look at where the economic activity takes place. Under the buy Canadian policy, the definition of Canadian supplier is based on substantive economic activity in Canada. That includes having a place of business here, being registered here, filing taxes here, conducting ongoing activities and employing people in Canada to deliver goods and services. That distinction matters. A company can be part of a global enterprise and still employ thousands of Canadians. It can pay taxes here. It can operate facilities here. It can conduct research and development here, and it can purchase from Canadian suppliers and invest in Canadian communities. Those jobs are Canadian jobs. Those investments are investments in Canada, and that economic activity matters to Canadians and Canada. Buy Canadian is not simply about where a company's headquarters is located. It is about where the jobs are, where the investment is, where the innovation happens, where the supply chain is built and ultimately, where the economic benefits land. We continue to work closely with businesses, suppliers and stakeholders to develop and refine procurement measures that support Canadian industry, strengthen supply chains and drive our country's economic growth. Our government will always stand with Canadian workers and Canadian businesses, and we will build a stronger economy in the G7. We will always support our veterans with job opportunities. I want to assure this House that we are fully committed to our buy Canadian policy, the substantial opportunities it is providing for Canadians and the powerful benefits for our country. We are transforming our economy through buy Canadian. We are supporting our industries today while keeping a clear focus on this sustainable future. That is our promise to Canadians, which is one that we are delivering on.

Mr. Speaker, the member outlined, in reference to some of the criticisms of the program, namely, the change of threshold from $25 million down to $5 million, but there are still certain policies related to the buy Canada policy at large that need to be addressed, largely related to subcontracting. Some have labelled it a superficial economic illusion that dilutes the intended benefits of this policy we all support. Is the government open to changing some of the subcontracting policies to allow for that work to stay in Canada and not be sent offshore to non-Canadian entities when the policy in and of itself is to support Canadian small businesses and Canadian companies?

Mr. Speaker, the member understands very well that I come from a small business, and 85% of the businesses in my constituency, in fact even in his constituency, are small businesses. That is where our government's focus is: lowering that threshold from $25 million to $5 million, and now we are looking at other ways the government can provide support. He and I have to keep advocating and making sure that our government does what is necessary for small businesses to succeed. That is what I will continue to fight for, and that is what I have been fighting for in the many years I have been in Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier, most of these projects have gone to Canadian companies. If we look at the numbers I talked about, between December 2025 and October 1, 2026, Public Services and Procurement Canada awarded a total of 1,644 contracts worth roughly $23 billion. Of these, 1,342 contracts, representing about $17.7 billion, were awarded to suppliers operating in Canada. That is the kind of progress we want to build on, and we will continue to build on having more contracts going to Canadian suppliers in the coming days, weeks, months and years.

Mr. Speaker, when I first came to the House in 2015, I remember that the defence budget was less than 1% of GDP. Now it is over 2%. Of course, the economy has also grown in that perspective, which means it is actually a tripling of the defence budget. We have similarly seen increases in the Veterans Affairs budget. I think everyone in the House agrees we need to build Canada strong, we need to hire more Canadians and we need to buy more in Canada. Would my friend, like to comment on the significant investments and the improvements we have made both for Canadian defence and for Canadian veterans?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has already answered the question that he asked. There was a promise made by our government and a promise kept when it comes to veterans and making sure that we take good care of veterans. Every member of the House, irrespective of the side of the House they are on, respects the sacrifices they made, and we will continue to work hard for those veterans and—

Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Cowichan—Malahat—Langford. There is an increasingly familiar pattern emerging from the Liberals. The Prime Minister of this 11-year-old government makes grand new announcements about Canadian sovereignty, and Canadians are assured that a bold new era of government is about to arrive. Unfortunately for the government, somebody always pulls back the curtain to see what is behind it, and that is where the troubles start. This truly is a government of loud announcements and empty promises. For example, the Liberals backslapped each other over reaching our nation's 2% NATO commitment. Only later did we discover that it includes an unarmed, unionized civilian Coast Guard. Projects like the F-35 are stalling amid political games. The PBO cannot provide a clear picture of what the future holds, and, increasingly, it looks like the Liberals cannot either. There is a difference between grandstanding and governing. Grandstanding is convincing Canadians that they believe in something. Governing involves showing them when decisions actually have to be made. The Prime Minister seems more interested in Brussels and Middle Eastern controversies than Canadian veterans. We are talking about the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires, an institution that has served veterans for a century. I served as a captain in the Canadian Army Reserve, and that experience gave me an appreciation for the military that goes well beyond government documents. One thing people learn in university is the ethics of duty. They also learn that the military does not disappear from our lives the minute we take off the uniform. My father passed away many years ago, but I want to revive an argument we had when he was alive. I think, looking back, he would be okay with that. My dad was a young air force officer who later scoffed at veterans attending military functions in uniform after retiring. He said that they were living in the past. He called them old soldiers who kept reliving their glory days. I heard my dad then. I disagree with him now. I think veterans carry what they have learned in the military forward in life, regardless of whether they retire after one tour or after most of their working lives. Here is what my father learned, and I do not think he would mind me sharing it. He was a farm boy who joined the air force to become a pilot, because pilots were cool. That is pretty much the only reason. Here is what happened. He failed. He became a bombardier instead. He completed one tour of duty, and then he largely avoided military events afterward. However, he learned something in the military. He learned that he did not like failure. In fact, he apparently made the grandiose promise to my mother that he would never fail again. Now, I do not know what my dad's win-loss column was in life, and I do not think it matters that much, but he learned a lesson, admitted it and moved on. He went on to earn a Ph.D., become an internationally famous biologist and later in life received the university gold medal as the most accomplished graduate of his undergraduate class. I suspect that hard work brought him more success than failure. Other veterans take different paths, and many of them stay in longer and need help making the transition to civilian life. That is why we need organizations like the Commissionaires. The Canadian Corps of Commissionaires was created in 1925 to help returning soldiers with employment. Today it employs about 22,000 Canadians, including thousands of veterans. It is a Canadian not-for-profit organization, and it is our country's largest employer of veterans. It recognizes military experience, and it offers veterans a way to keep contributing. One would think that an organization like that would pretty well fit into the Prime Minister's buy Canadian economic sovereignty plan. Of course there is this enthusiasm for telling the rest of us to buy Canadian. In response to President Trump's trade war, he first promised a deal. When that failed, he promised federal spending would default to Canadian suppliers. When his buy Canada policy took effect in December 2025, he declared that Canada would become its own best customer. Unfortunately, when it came to an actual procurement decision, the Canadian content of his political record turned out to be greater than his appreciation of Canadian ownership. Let us look at the CRA contract. In June, the Canada Revenue Agency awarded a contract worth nearly $12 million, not to the Commissionaires, a Canadian non-profit dedicated to helping veterans. Nope. It was awarded to UPSSC, a Canadian subsidiary of an American multinational, Allied Universal. The difference between the bids was about $80,000, which is less than the cost of the Prime Minister's banquet bill. It is a 1% difference between a Canadian veteran organization and an American multinational. So much for buy Canadian. So much for Liberal promises. Obviously, governments have to get value for taxpayers' money, and I am not arguing that the Commissionaires should automatically win every contract by virtue of just being Canadian, but the government should be able to tell us why it did not value Canadian ownership and veteran employment more than the cost of a prime ministerial banquet. If the assessment was fair, it should release the criteria and explain the decision to Canadians. The $80,000 gets interesting when we examine government spending priorities. According to a government response to an Order Paper question, catering aboard an aircraft carrying the Prime Minister and his entourage during one trip to China, Qatar and Davos cost well over $100,000. I am not suggesting the Prime Minister should go hungry abroad, but apparently there is considerable flexibility when it comes to expenditures at 35,000 feet. Apparently, veterans ask too much of the government. The government explanation is that Allied Universal operates through a Canadian subsidiary. I have no criticism of its Canadian workers, but that is not really the point. If an American-owned multinational with a Canadian address is the same thing as a Canadian not-for-profit dedicated to veterans, what exactly does buy Canadian mean? There is nothing wrong with hiring American companies, but this is a Prime Minister who has made anger at Donald Trump central to his government, and his government awarded a federal contract to an American-owned company with substantial business ties to the Trump administration. Apparently, his elbows are up for the camera but down when the contracts are signed. What is buy Canadian supposed to mean? If we treat Canadian not-for-profits no differently from foreign-owned companies, ministers should say so. They should also explain to Canadians why they say one thing and do another. Maybe the procurement process did follow the rules, but if those rules do not recognize the value of Canadian veteran employment in a period the Prime Minister himself calls Canada first, then it is the rules that need changing. We should demand a remedy, not another excuse. Quite honestly, what is the message that Canadians are supposed to get from this fiasco? The Prime Minister wants to sell Canadians on buy European. His ministers want to sell us on buy Canadian, and the groaning bureaucracy of procurement buys American. I will finish with what my father taught me. He wanted to be a pilot and failed, but he did not spend his life redefining success or explaining away that disappointment. He accepted it, learned from it and went on to accomplish extraordinary things. I still disagreed with him about those “old soldiers”, but he was absolutely right about failure. As Remembrance Day approaches, ministers will again solemnly tell Canadians how much they respect our veterans, but respect is demonstrated through deeds, not speeches. The government should begin by admitting that passing over a centuries-old veterans institution while campaigning on buy Canadian is at least a decision worth revisiting. My father understood that failure was not something to disguise with an excuse. It was something to learn from. What matters is what we do afterward. He learned from failure and went on to an extraordinary life. The Prime Minister still has that opportunity with the government, but first, he will have to do something that seems remarkably difficult for the government: He will have to admit that he made a mistake.

Mr. Speaker, throughout the day, the member has heard different types of arguments that provide the answers to many of the questions he posed, but of course, the Conservatives do not want to listen to the answers. Rather, they have their spin and speaking lines to try to give a gross exaggeration of the reality of this. For example, the company that won the award has thousands of employees, some of them in my own province of Manitoba. It has a very significant footprint. CRA is independent of the government in putting out tenders. The Commissionaires, which is a fantastic organization that I have been saying nothing but positive things about, has evolved. Does the member know what percentage of the Commissionaires is made up of veterans?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Liberal logic that goes into this. Let me talk about the F-35 for a minute. It is from an American-owned company. It would create between 2,500 and 5,000 Canadian jobs and thousands of indirect jobs, and it just happens to be the only airplane that could provide deterrence in the Arctic. By that logic, we should pick the F-35, yet we cannot do that. We will not do that. For some reason, we are just going to wait for a while. If Canadian jobs and American ownership are not an issue, why do we not have the F-35?

Mr. Speaker, my job is not to determine the exact makeup, but I will say that when we have something as glaring as an American-owned company and a Canadian-owned non-profit, we do not need to take it to a large jury to find out which one we should be picking.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to recognize my colleague's service and his father's service. It was very nicely woven into his speech today. He was just speaking about the not-for-profit organization, where money is reinvested into veterans. I would like to hear his thoughts on that as an excuse. Why would the Liberals not want to keep a contract with the Commissionaires, which does such great work and supports veterans?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is fairly obvious that we should be, and it is unfortunate that the Liberals refuse to admit the mistake. It is a simple mistake. They should just change it. Let us buy Canadian again if we are going to buy Canadian. Unfortunately, with the Liberals, the logic seems to shift a lot. It shifts one way for the F-35, but if we are talking about something else, it will shift another way. We have competing logics that run around, and whatever applies at any given time is the logic they are using.
Mr. Speaker, I have good news. We do have the F-35s. We have Canadian pilots being trained on the F-35s. Would the member acknowledge and express his appreciation for the fact that we have them?
Mr. Speaker, 88 have been scheduled, but we do not have 88, nor do we have a go-ahead on those 88.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of our motion on federal procurement. I rise to speak about our flag and the Canadians who fought under it. I rise for the veterans of Cowichan—Malahat—Langford on Vancouver Island. I rise for the commissionaires who stand watch at our federal buildings. I rise for all the families who have been handed a folded flag. I served under that flag for 28 years. I have conducted many burials at sea, and I have handed that flag to grieving families, including a father and his two sons. I know the cost those who serve under that flag pay. The motion before us may be about one contract, but veterans will tell us it is about much more than just one contract. It is about a pattern of betrayal. We can consider that just this year, with respect to Bill C-11, the government waited until the last minute to reverse amendments agreed upon in committee and ignored the survivors of military sexual trauma. They told me it felt like the government had spat in their faces. We can consider new restrictions on military clergy of every faith, even on Remembrance Day; or veterans poisoned by mefloquine in Somalia, fighting their own government in court for over 25 years; or veterans who asked for help and were instead offered euthanasia by Veterans Affairs Canada. Now let us consider the Commissionaires. I will remind the Liberal members opposite, who seem to have forgotten, who the commissionaires are. In 1915, in the middle of the First World War, the governor-general proposed a corps to give returning soldiers meaningful work. In 1925, the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires was founded with one commitment. Those who served Canada would come home and not be forgotten. For more than 100 years, that commitment had been kept. For generations, Ottawa stood behind it with a right of first refusal. Before a federal government department's security contract was opened to bidding, it was first offered to the Commissionaires, yet in February, with a single stroke of a pen, the Minister of Veterans Affairs ended that right. Though veterans affairs officials said the department wanted to reassess the right of first refusal, it simply cancelled it. Then came this contract. The CRA posted it as open only to Canadian suppliers. Here is what most Canadians do not know. Under the current government's new buy Canadian rules, a supplier needs only a place of business in Canada. No one asks who owns the company or where its headquarters are. That is how the Canadian subsidiary of Allied Universal, an American company, qualified. By the company's own numbers, just 1.3% of its 700,000-strong workforce is in Canada. It won the CRA contract by undercutting the Commissionaires by less than 1% of the contract value, or only $80,000. Now let us hold the government to its own words. Again and again, the Prime Minister has promised that Canada would become our own best customer. He said, “we will select Canadian suppliers by default.” In January, he told Canadians yet again, “We'll buy Canadian. We'll build Canadian.” Well, the CRA had a Canadian supplier, a not-for-profit built for veterans, and when the moment came to be our own best customer, the government went shopping in America. The Secretary of State for the Canada Revenue Agency says politicians are never involved in the CRA's decisions, and that is true of the contract scoring but not true of the rules. The CRA runs the competition, but the government writes the rules for the CRA to follow, and the government chose a buy Canadian policy with no test of ownership. Those were not the CRA's choices. They were the government's choices. Last November, the Prime Minister declared that Canadians must honour our veterans' patriotism with our own, and for once, I agree with his words, but his actions ring hollow. Patriotism is not a line in a statement. In this case, it is a choice in that contract. The government also defends this decision by claiming the Commissionaires could no longer meet its veteran hiring target. Here is what the government will not tell us. The Commissionaires knew the target was a problem. The organization raised it itself. It asked veterans affairs to reassess the target and to update it. Instead, the door was closed. The Commissionaires, which is a not-for-profit, reportedly could not get a meeting with the minister. Meanwhile, senior officials found time to quietly meet with for-profit competitors. Lobbying records prove this. Allied Universal has had a registered lobbyist working the Canadian government since at least 2023, pursuing federal security contracts exactly like this one, yet only three years ago, the department's own briefing said that the right of first refusal was still aligned with the Government of Canada's priorities. What changed? It is not the veterans but the government. The government called it a competitive procurement process, but this is not competition. This is a retreat. Here is the kicker. Allied Universal's Canadian subsidiary is suing the Government of Canada for $420 million. It lost a federal airport screening contract and took the government to court. Let us consider what the Liberals have done. In a courtroom, Allied is fighting the government. Meanwhile, in an office, the government is handing an American company a contract taken from our commissionaires, who should be protected by the right of refusal that is not set to expire until next year. Let us look at Allied Universal's work with the Trump administration. According to public reporting, it has received more than $290 million U.S. from the Department of Homeland Security this year alone, and its subsidiary received $83 million U.S. from ICE, the agency running the Trump deportation program. This summer, Newsweek named Allied Universal one of America's most patriotic companies, and I do not doubt that it is. It is an American company, and it should be proud of that honour. However, I would ask the members opposite this: Since when is it the Canadian government's job to reward America's most patriotic companies? Canada already has its own patriotic organization, and has had for more than 100 years, called the Commissionaires. Eighteen months ago, the Prime Minister asked Canadians to trust him to stand up to Washington, and many Canadians gave him their trust and their vote for the first time in their life. They believed he was the only one who could handle the president and get a deal. They did not vote to send the veterans contract to a company tied to an American deportation program. Every Canadian who trusted the Liberal slogans should know this: They did not misplace their patriotism. The government misplaced their trust. At election time, the Liberals wrapped themselves in the flag, but at contract time, they pay Americans. At election time, they stand at the cenotaph, but at contract time, they leave the commissionaires standing at the door. At election time, the government promises to put Canada first, but at contract time, it puts Canada second. I can assure the members opposite that veterans from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland are watching the government closely. It is not enough to expose the illusion, so let me set out plainly how a government that keeps its word to veterans would restore that promise. First, it would give the CRA contract back to the commissionaires. Second, it would have Veterans Affairs restore the right of first refusal and update the promise made generations ago to reflect the veterans of today. According to court filings in 2025, the department's own deputy minister suggested renewing that policy with new measures strengthening our commissionaires, not cutting them down. Third, it would lift the restrictions on clergy, the priests, imams, rabbis and other faith leaders, who serve in uniform, so they may pray in their own faith at public ceremonies, Remembrance Day included. Fourth, it would stop fighting veterans in court, sit down with them, hear them and come to an agreement. Let us end where we began, with the flag I handed to the father and his sons. Veterans define what it means to be Canadian. They come from every province and territory and every faith background and walk of life. From Vimy to Juno Beach to Kandahar, our veterans raised their hand and swore to our flag. They never asked what the flag would give them. They asked what it needed. I am proud to have served. I am proud to be Canadian. I say to the government and to every member opposite plainly, be Canadian. Be Canadian when the cameras are gone and the contract is signed. Be Canadian in the courtroom, at the cenotaph and at the chapel. Be Canadian for veterans who put Canada first. Keep your promises, honour your own words, and if you cannot be Canadian, then for the love of this country, step aside for those who will. Our flag is not a costume for election time. It is a sacred promise. Our soldiers fought and died for it, and our veterans kept that promise. It is time the government did the same.

Mr. Speaker, the fact that the Liberal government has not only taken jobs away from veterans but has decided to give them to a company that is involved with ICE in the United States is absolutely appalling. There are a lot of veterans living in Winnipeg Centre who are houseless and do not have a livable income. I have talked to many veterans organizations in Winnipeg that support my idea of a guaranteed livable basic income. Veterans make a sacrifice for whatever reasons they find in their spirit, but when they come back, we do not look after them. It is not only through employment but also if they are unable to work for whatever reason. I am wondering if the member supports my idea of putting in place a guaranteed livable basic income for veterans.

Mr. Speaker, the homelessness of veterans is a horrible crisis this country faces. In fact, I was just at a home for veterans in Ottawa serving Thanksgiving dinner to them not too long ago. If the government was running the economy the way it pretends it does and was giving and protecting veterans' jobs, that would not be necessary. Our veterans would have jobs, would be working for the Commissionaires and would not be homeless.

Mr. Speaker, indeed, a common trend is not just betraying veterans, as I outlined in my speech, but a lack of accountability. We see that with the Defence Investment Agency. Absolutely, I am outraged at some of the accountability issues, the irresponsible spending and the claims that their programs are helping people. They are not helping. Canadians are drowning under 11 years of the government, and occasionally it lifts Canadians' heads above the water for a breath of fresh air and expects them to be happy because the program it is spending too much money on is working. That is the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's service. I was just sitting in the veterans affairs committee, which is meeting with the Commissionaires. In his speech, the member highlighted that the Commissionaires were never invited to the table, and that can be confirmed from our meeting. I would like to hear his thoughts about what I asked earlier. The Commissionaires is a non-profit organization that invests in veterans and has confirmed that it has never received any complaints. In fact, it has an 86% approval rating from clientele. I would like to hear what the member's thoughts are with regard to that information.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the excellent work he does supporting veterans on the veterans affairs committee. It was confirmed not only at committee but in court papers that the Commissionaires attempted to contact Veterans Affairs to resolve this issue, but clearly that has not happened. The Liberals are contracting out security services for veterans to American companies. What are the Liberals going to present to Canada next, that they are going to contract out to American companies to provide our military services? This is ridiculous.

Mr. Speaker, as we wind up the debate, I want to recognize not only the valuable role but the very existence of our veterans and what they have done in the past. November 11 at 11 o'clock is a very special moment in time when we should all take time to pray and give thanks to our veterans, both past and present. I suggest that all members recognize the true value of that. I would ask them to recognize and appreciate that there are many different things the government does for vets and that all members support veterans in Canada. We continue to look forward to the fine work that the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires does every day in serving in different capacities, many of whom, 20% plus, are veterans.

Mr. Speaker, indeed, I am sure that all members of this House will say they support veterans, but the members opposite show it in a pretty funny way. If we look at this contract and how they are betraying veterans, or at the other examples that I laid out in my speech, they certainly have a very different way of supporting veterans. The member mentioned praying. Right now, there are restrictions on the prayers that clergy from all faiths in the military can say. They are not allowed to give religious speeches while in public, which is another way the Liberals are backstabbing veterans.
Mr. Speaker, I would ask for a recorded division.
Mr. Speaker, I suspect if you were to canvass the House, you would find unanimous consent to call it 6:30 p.m., to begin the late show.

title: Private Members' Business: Ukrainian Heritage Month Act
turns: Mr. Speaker, I want to start by thanking former senator Stanley Kutcher and the MP for Etobicoke Centre for championing this bill. This bill would designate the month of September as Ukrainian heritage month. September was chosen to mark the first recorded arrival of Ukrainians to Canada during the month of September more than 125 years ago. Canada is now home to more than 1.3 million Ukrainian Canadians. Personally, I am honoured to be able to speak in this place to support this bill. I come from Edmonton, Alberta, where many Ukrainian Canadians live. I know first-hand the strong contributions they make in our community. New Democrats are proud to support a month that would recognize the significant contributions that Ukrainian Canadians have made and continue to make to Canada's social, economic, political and cultural fabric, including artistic, linguistic, culinary, religious and folkloric contributions. The establishment of Ukrainian heritage month would not only be to celebrate Ukrainians in Canada. It would also be instrumental in educating future generations about the impactful role that Ukrainian Canadians have played and continue to play across this country. We need this bill now more than ever. It has been four and a half years of horror in Ukraine since the further illegal invasion by Vladimir Putin and the Russian Federation. Putin's brutal genocide has killed and injured thousands of Ukrainians, displacing hundreds of thousands more. As we speak, Ukrainians in Kyiv and other cities and communities across Ukraine continue to face bombing threats and abhorrent violence at the hands of Putin and his forces. Russian oligarchs continue to profit from this war, and Ukrainians stand bravely in defiance, defending their sovereignty and their lives. I think about a time in 2023 when I travelled to the towns of Irpin and Bucha. I remember going into the communities. I remember standing and looking at the buildings that had been bombed. One of the things I saw was a slide in a children's playground, and it was riddled with bullet holes. This was a child's slide. It was not a military target. Russia's attacks were directed at civilians and civilian infrastructure. It was not just playgrounds. It was hospitals, schools, homes and apartment buildings. One year later, I watched as Ukrainians worked to rebuild their communities. That same indestructible spirit led Ukrainians to Canada following the Holodomor, over the decades since those unspeakable horrors were inflicted. Now, as families seek refuge from Putin's genocidal attacks, they have come to Canada to build their lives, and in the process, they have helped to forge our nation. In Edmonton, Ukrainian Canadians and their descendants have helped shape our city and our culture. My friend, former MLA Deron Bilous, announced the province's first official Ukrainian-Canadian Heritage Day. William Hawrelak served three separate terms as mayor, and the most beautiful park in the city, located in my riding of Edmonton Strathcona, is named for him. The first Holodomor monument in the world rests outside Edmonton city hall. Edmonton is home to the world-renowned Ukrainian Shumka dancers and to the Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies at the University of Alberta in my riding. In November, the Ukrainian Canadian Congress Alberta Provincial Council will present the 29th annual Hetman Awards, honouring the many Ukrainian Canadians in Alberta who contribute so much to our communities. As the foreign affairs critic for the new Democratic Party of Canada, I have fought hard to ensure that Canada's response to the genocide happening in Ukraine is strong. I am proud to have sponsored four motions in the House that received unanimous consent. I want to be very clear: Unanimous consent from all parties is a message we can send as parliamentarians to Putin and the Russian Federation that when it comes to Ukraine, we stand united. I called on the government to help document Russian war crimes and crimes against humanity, to declare that the Russian Federation is committing acts of genocide, to designate Russia's Wagner Group as a terrorist entity and to honour those who gave their lives in defence of our shared values. I am proud that New Democrats and all parties in the House stood together to support Ukraine when it mattered. Make no mistake. The threats from Russia expand far beyond Ukraine's borders. We see now how Russia is spreading misinformation online and engaging in foreign interference. These are attacks on democracy itself. While this genocidal war rages on and attacks on civilians continue, and with the growing threat of nuclear engagement, New Democrats will continue to push the government to do what it can to end this war and to work for peace and justice. The people of Ukraine need and deserve our support, and we must recognize that democracy, not just in Ukraine but around the world, is under threat. It is under attack. Canadians and New Democrats stand with Ukraine. We will always stand with Ukraine. We celebrate the close ties Canada has with Ukraine and with Ukrainian Canadians, remembering and celebrating the rich history binding our nations. I look forward to passing this bill so that next September, we can celebrate Ukrainian heritage month together. Slava Ukraini.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to stand today and speak to Bill S-210, which would designate September as Ukrainian heritage month. Canada is home to a rich and vibrant Ukrainian culture, from beloved foods such as borscht and perogies to cherished traditions and events such as Canada's National Ukrainian Festival. Through their culture, traditions and civic engagement, Canadians of Ukrainian descent have made lasting contributions to our country and have helped shape the diverse and multicultural Canada we are all very proud to call home. Ukrainians have deep historical ties to Canada. Ukrainian immigration to Canada began as early as the 19th century, and now Ukrainian Canadians make up 1.3 million people in this nation. For more than a century, Ukrainian Canadians have contributed to the growth and prosperity of our country in countless ways. I am often reminded of those contributions in southern Alberta, the region that I am proud to call home and that I get to represent. In my community of Lethbridge, Ukrainian Canadians played an important role in building Alberta's sugar beet industry. For those who are not familiar with this, it involves beets that get planted in the ground and are used to produce sugar. This is our only domestic source of sugar and something we should be very proud of in this country in terms of food security and being able to do that right here at home in a way that also respects human rights. Following the Second World War, thousands of Ukrainian immigrants came to Canada through programs that brought workers to Alberta's sugar beet farms. They arrived ready to work, often under difficult conditions, and their hard work helped establish an industry that became an important part of southern Alberta and Canada's agricultural economy. These families did not simply come to Canada to work for a season; rather, they built communities, put down roots, raised families and contributed to the growth of southern Alberta. Their journey is a powerful testament to how deeply Ukrainian Canadians have shaped the heart and history of our great country. Ukrainian Canadians have contributed to agriculture, education, business, culture and public life. They have built churches, community organizations, cultural institutions and businesses, all while preserving the traditions and heritage that connect them to their Ukrainian roots but respecting the values we have here in Canada. Perhaps one of the most remarkable parts of the Ukrainian Canadian history is the resilience that has carried through generations. Many Ukrainians came to Canada fleeing war, persecution and political oppression. They came from a homeland where their culture, language and identity had been threatened by totalitarian rule. For decades, Ukraine was under Soviet power, yet the Ukrainian people never abandoned their desire for freedom, democracy and self-determination. That desire for freedom is a defining part of Ukrainian history, and it is a history that Ukrainian Canadians have worked hard to preserve and to share with Canadians. This includes remembering the Holodomor, the horrific famine inflicted by the Soviet regime in 1932 and 1933, which claimed the lives of millions of Ukrainians. Ukrainian Canadians have fought for decades to ensure that this history is remembered and that the victims are never forgotten. In 1991, after decades of Soviet rule, Ukraine declared its independence. On December 1, 1991, the people of Ukraine voted to approve that independence. The Ukrainian people chose freedom and self-determination. The following day, under the leadership of Conservative Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, Canada became the very first western country to recognize Ukraine's independence and to congratulate it on this. Canada and Ukraine have been close allies ever since, and we continue to enjoy that relationship. Sadly, however, Ukraine's fight for independence did not end there. In 2014, Vladimir Putin illegally annexed Crimea and launched war against Ukraine. For the Ukrainian people, the threat of Russian aggression was once again at their doorstep. Canada responded. Under Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper, Canada was among the strongest voices in the international community to condemn Russia's aggression against Ukraine. Prime Minister Stephen Harper took a stand with the Ukrainian people. His government imposed sanctions on Russian officials, provided financial assistance to Ukraine and supported Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Prime Minister Harper also travelled to Kyiv in 2014, just days after the illegal annexation of Crimea, demonstrating Canada's commitment to standing with the Ukrainian people. His message was clear: Ukraine has the right to determine its own future. That principle has remained at the heart of Canada's relationship with Ukraine. I wish things had stopped there, but they did not. In 2022, Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Once again, the Ukrainian people were forced to defend their homes, their families and their right to live as a free and democratic nation. Once again, Ukrainian Canadians stepped forward. Across Canada, Canadians have rallied. We have rallied in our communities, have fundraised, have welcomed Ukrainians who are fleeing the war, and have advocated for stronger support for the nation. Ukrainian Canadians have welcomed their fellow women and men from the country. These are people who have endured tyranny, war and persecution, but they have never surrendered their desire for freedom and their commitment to democratic principles. That history is important. It is important for us as Canadians to remember. It is important for members of the House to remember. It is important because Ukrainian Canadians have contributed so much to the country we know today. They have helped build our agricultural communities, strengthen our cultural fabric and enrich our public life. It is so important, because their history reminds us that freedom and democracy cannot be taken for granted. Many Ukrainian Canadians have preserved their culture while becoming an important part of the Canadian story. They have taught their children their language and traditions, built communities across the country and continued to stand with their homeland in its fight for freedom. Few Canadians embody this more boldly or better than Mr. Wayne Gretzky. He is not only viewed as the greatest hockey player, but he is also a proud Ukrainian Canadian. For Canadians from coast to coast, Gretzky remains a tremendous source of national pride. During his remarkable career in the NHL, he set countless records and led the Edmonton Oilers to win four Stanley Cup championships. Even though he has been retired from hockey for 25 years, Gretzky's legacy continues to inspire generations of young Canadians. His contribution goes beyond what he accomplished on the ice. He uses his platform today to speak out in support of Ukraine. He understands that for Ukrainian Canadians, the war is not a distant conflict. Instead, it is an attack on a country for which millions of Canadians have deep family, cultural and historic ties. Wayne Gretzky is more than a hockey legend; he is an example of how Canadian Ukrainians can proudly embrace their heritage while contributing to the country we call home. Bill S-210 gives us an incredible opportunity to honour the Ukrainian Canadian community, to celebrate its contributions to Canada and to ensure that future generations understand the important role Ukrainian Canadians have played in shaping our country. The Ukrainian Canadian story is a story of resilience. It is a story of hard work, of community and of an unwavering belief in freedom and democracy. I am proud to support Bill S-210 and to recognize the generations of Ukrainian Canadians who have helped make Canada the country we are proud to call home and who so dearly hold true to the values on which we are founded.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to speak to this bill, which comes to us from the other place. I want to give thanks in particular for the hard work of the member for Etobicoke Centre, who has been championing the cause of Ukraine, of Ukrainian Canadians and of Ukrainians in Canada since his election here and since before then, and for his hard work to get the bill to this point in Parliament. It is a special pleasure to speak about Ukrainian heritage, because in my riding of Taiaiko'n—Parkdale—High Park in west Toronto, Ukrainian heritage is something that is lived every day. It is lived in the context of war, which has led to a rediscovery and a reimagining of the Ukrainian heritage brought to us by people who have fled that war to find comfort in Canada. It is building on a legacy of institutions that go back decades in this beautiful corner of west Toronto and on a heritage that continues to live, to thrive and to inform not only Ukrainians and Ukrainian Canadians but, in fact, all our constituents. It is something that has been resurrected in the last few years due to the invasion and to the illegal and unjustified attempt to suppress the Ukrainian spirit and the Ukrainian language. If someone comes to Taiaiko'n—Parkdale—High Park, as well as to other parts of west Toronto, where Ukrainian culture and language are live and living, where we continue to welcome Ukrainians who are fleeing persecution and war, they will see a heritage that cannot be defeated. It is a culture that is living. It is a heritage that we, people such as me who are non-Ukrainian, not of Ukrainian heritage, are so blessed to get to see. It is an example of the continuation of culture that perseveres in the face of a real attempt to wipe it and its language off the face of the earth. To see it resilient in Taiaiko'n—Parkdale—High Park is something for which I have the utmost appreciation. I want to talk a bit about our culture, our Ukrainian heritage, specifically in Taiaiko'n—Parkdale—High Park and in west Toronto. Ukrainians and Ukrainian Canadians started to arrive in our part of Toronto as many immigrant communities do. They came from other parts of Toronto and other parts of Canada. In some cases, they received a bit more wealth. In some cases, they were finding jobs and opportunities in meat-packing and in trades such as roofing, plumbing, painting and bricklaying. Eventually they found each other and found places to settle in Bloor West Village and in Etobicoke. These waves of immigration continued not just after the Second World War but also into the sixties and seventies, and then more recently, tragically, as a result of the war. The institutions of Ukrainian heritage, language and culture are everywhere in west Toronto and Etobicoke. In fact, there is a building in the riding of the member for Etobicoke—Lakeshore that is known as UNF hall. It contains dozens of Ukrainian organizations. Ukrainian civil society is alive. It is well. It is strong. I just want to point out a couple of organizations in our riding that have recently celebrated some important anniversaries. For instance, the Levada and Orion choirs of Toronto celebrated their 40th anniversary at Runnymede United Church in Toronto just this past weekend. Ukrainian youth ensembles show the power of song and the power of voices coming together. Voices coming together is one of the ways of expressing the indomitable spirit of a people and the indomitable spirit of a language that continues to persevere even when people try to take that away. Since 1985, youth ensembles, the Levada Women's Choir, the Orion Men's Choir and the Vanguard Concert and Marching Band have been connecting people through music. They are promoting and preserving their musical culture and traditions. We have a more recent phenomenon, which is celebrating close to its 20th anniversary: the Vyshyvanka Day parade. Vyshyvankas, of course, are the beautifully embroidered Ukrainian textiles, sweaters, dresses and other garments that a college student in Ukraine rediscovered. They decided they needed to celebrate these unique regional parts of their heritage. Ukrainian Canadians and Ukrainians will often wear vyshyvankas that come from distinct regions of Ukraine. One can tell from the distinct knitting and the distinct textiles where those vyshyvankas, such as sweaters and other garments, might come from. In High Park, Bloor West Village, we celebrate the Vyshyvanka Day parade every year. The Bloor West Village Toronto Ukrainian Festival has been around since 1995, so we have just celebrated its 30th anniversary. It was started by Jurij Roman Klufas, who has been there since the beginning. The first festival in our riding had 300 people just in a little parking lot off Bloor and Jane streets in the west part of Taiaiko'n—Parkdale—High Park. It is now the largest annual Ukrainian festival in North America. It takes perseverance over 30 years to take something that one truly believes in and build the institutions up. Now prime ministers, leaders of the opposition, dignitaries from all sides and the entire community are coming to west Toronto, to Bloor West Village, in mid-September to celebrate Ukrainian heritage and to see the dozens of Ukrainian organizations. A particular conversation I had with a number of women from the Ukrainian brigades was deeply striking to me. These are Ukrainians who recently arrived in Canada. They want to go back to Ukraine, but in the meantime, they are doing mutual aid. They are selling goods. They are bringing their charitable, intellectual Ukrainian spirit to the community and raising resources that can then be brought to help with the self-defence of Ukraine. I also want to point out the Shevchenko Museum. It is the only Taras Shevchenko museum in North America and is just down the street from our constituency office on Bloor West. Taras Shevchenko, known as Ukraine's greatest poet and artist, was exiled by the Tsarist Russian regime and sent for punitive military service in the eastern region in the 19th century. He was eventually pardoned, 10 years later. Taras Shevchenko made the bold bet of speaking and writing in the Ukrainian language, which the Russians wanted to suppress. We are fortunate. I am very grateful to my colleague Matthew McCauley, in our office, who got from the parliamentary library the following dedication, which was read by the late prime minister John Diefenbaker at the unveiling of the monument to Taras Shevchenko in Winnipeg in July 1961. He read the following verse at that dedication: Our souls yield not to grievous ills, To freedom march our stubborn wills. Though waves of trouble o'er us roll The waves move not the steadfast soul. Our living spirit is not in chains, The word of God in glory reigns. Prime Minister Diefenbaker then said the following: These sentiments are the epitome of the yearnings of the human soul. If Shevchenko were here today he would see the fruits of his poetry—freedom enjoyed by those of his race and all races...—the manifest manner in which those of Ukrainian descent in Canada have devoted themselves to freedom by service in two world wars, and in the days of peace in so many fields of national endeavour. To those words from Prime Minister Diefenbaker 65 years ago, we now have to, unfortunately, add a remark: “and a war of aggression by the Russians in Ukraine, which has brought more Ukrainians to Canada, and yet they are still devoting themselves to freedom and yet are still devoting themselves in so many fields of national endeavour.” It is that kind of endeavour that we can pay tribute to today. It is a lived heritage that is being experienced today. Another poem from Shevchenko speaks to the yearning for freedom that underlies the spirit of this act and the opportunity to debate this act in Parliament, which is the kind of debate that our Ukrainian friends in Ukraine yearn to have publicly and openly without fear of persecution. Here is the last verse of that poem, as translated by John Weir, My Testament, by Taras Shevchenko: Oh bury me, then rise ye up And break your heavy chains And water with the tyrants' blood The freedom you have gained. And in the great new family, The family of the free, With softly spoken, kindly word Remember also me. There is so much Ukrainian heritage that we take for granted in our communities today because it is the spirit of freedom on whose shoulders we stand. Ukrainians and Ukrainian Canadians in west Toronto, in Taiaiako'n—Parkdale—High Park, speak their language and celebrate their textiles. They bring their works to places like the Shevchenko Museum, share poetry and share innovations, despite years of war and despite being very recently arrived in Canada. They are bringing innovations, charitable endeavours and the culture and language that the Russians are attempting to suppress. They are bringing it as a living example not only of their heritage but of what it means to be Canadian, with Canadian democracy and Canadian freedoms. To have Ukrainians and Ukrainian Canadians of decades ago, and their families and Ukrainians today, provide this to our riding of Taiaiako'n—Parkdale—High Park is something we are very grateful for, and for that reason, I urge everyone in the House to support this piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is such a pleasure to stand and speak to an important piece of legislation, Bill S-210, as well as to thank the member for Etobicoke Centre and the Senate for advancing the legislation to where it is today. I think the member for Etobicoke Centre embodies a lot of the good things about our Ukrainian heritage community, but he does not stand alone. There are many leaders within our Ukrainian heritage community who are second to no other in their understanding of the true value of diversity. The best thing we can do here in Canada is to share our heritage. That has blessed all of us in Canada. When I think about the Ukrainian heritage community in Winnipeg, I think of individuals like Joanne Lewandosky, an outstanding Canadian with such a heart for Ukraine and a passion to share Ukrainian heritage with anyone who has an interest in the community. I represent Winnipeg North. Its strength is there today, in part, because of Ukrainian immigrants from generations ago. People can drive down streets like Main Street, Burrows Avenue and McGregor to see historical churches and cathedrals that are absolutely beautiful to walk into, not to mention inspiring. The faith that takes place every week, going back generations, contributes to building and strengthening our Ukrainian heritage community in Manitoba, which is very much alive and continues to contribute in many different ways. If people want a sense of the festivities, whether that is heritage clothing, dance or heritage buildings, they can participate in Folklorama. They have a choice, as this is one of those communities that has not one but two pavilions. In the first week, people can go to either the Kyiv pavilion or the Spirit of Ukraine pavilion, where there are performances to sold-out audiences for seven days, with four or five shows a day, depending on whether it is a Saturday or a weekday. They are virtually sold out all of the time. There is a sense of excitement because people relate to the types of food. Personally, I found out when I was in Kyiv that pierogi are actually called varenyky. I can tell colleagues about the delighted faces one witnesses when people are biting down on borscht and pierogi. I would argue that the best pierogi in the world come from the north end of Winnipeg, from the many volunteers in the basements of our churches. The performances, whether of dance or other arts, provide education on what is taking place in Europe today, which has already been referenced significantly, or just how our Ukrainian heritage community has made Canada a better society. All of this can be experienced over the two wonderful weeks of Folklorama, as it has every summer in Winnipeg for the last 50-plus years now. In terms of contributions to labour and the economy, I think of the late Leo Ledohowski, founder of Canad Inns, a prominent fixture in Winnipeg and beyond, from a business perspective. I think of the Ukrainian Labour Temple, which was constructed back in 1918 or 1919. It still stands today as a heritage site, and it is used, well used, by not only our Ukrainian heritage community but even the newer communities and our first nations. It is a focal point. It is one of the jewels of Winnipeg's north end. It is not just the north end of Winnipeg that has benefited but some of our rural communities, such as Dauphin, in good part as a result of our Ukrainian heritage community and the many contributions it continues to make. I could talk about those families that have been there for over 100 years, or I could talk about those who have settled over the last few years because of the war taking place in Europe today. I want to let those settlers know that they have advocates here in Ottawa who recognize the valuable contributions they make to Canadian society. There are the many rural northern communities in the Interlake. I see that my colleague from Selkirk—Interlake—Eastman is here. If members go to Gimli, to Winnipeg Beach or to many of these communities, they will see that the settlers from the last few years are bringing more life to our Ukrainian heritage community. It is important that we do what we can to support them. I feel a great sense of pride in the many contributions of this community that many of us feel very passionately about, 1.3 million people of Ukrainian heritage, and many more of non-Ukrainian heritage, who contribute to making Canada what it is today. Recognizing September as a month to celebrate and recognize Ukrainian contributions is, I think, a very strong, positive thing we can do. It would provide many opportunities to recognize the community and would say to schools, to people in the workforce and to our employers that in Ottawa, in the House of Commons, we designate the month of September as an opportunity to show love for and to cherish the many contributions of our Ukrainian heritage community here in Canada. I have found that the more we recognize the rich heritage that makes up Canadian heritage, and the more we celebrate it and promote it, the better we are as a nation. That is why I am pleased to stand today and support what the member for Etobicoke Centre has brought before the House. It would make a difference in recognizing our diversity and honouring the past, today and into the future. It is of great value for every Canadian when we do things of this nature. I thank all those who were involved in making today possible, and having this bill. Slava Ukraini.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise to speak to Bill S-210, which, if passed, would declare September Ukrainian heritage month in Canada. I would like to start by thanking the sponsor of this bill in the Senate, former Senator Kutcher. I would like to thank all colleagues for their thoughtful remarks and their support for this bill, but also their support for Ukraine at this critical time. The first Ukrainian immigrants arrived in Canada on September 7, 1891. Since then, generations upon generations of immigrants from Ukraine have arrived in Canada. Many of them were fleeing oppression and seeking a better life. They found that life here in Canada. Canadians have supported them, and Ukrainian Canadians have made great contributions to Canada. Those contributions span our economic, political, cultural and social life. Watching this debate at home today are leaders and members of the Ukrainian Canadian community. Some of them are immigrants to Canada from Ukraine. Some of them are children and grandchildren of immigrants to Canada from Ukraine. My mother and my grandparents were immigrants to Canada from Ukraine. My grandparents, Ivan and Olena, came to Canada fleeing oppression and seeking a better life, like so many people who have come to Canada from Ukraine over the past 135 years. My grandparents were incredibly proud of their Ukrainian heritage, but they were also incredibly proud to be Canadian. In fact, I have said many times, and some of the members have heard me say, that my grandparents were among the proudest Canadians I have ever known. To ensure that I learned about my Ukrainian heritage, my grandparents and my parents insisted that I attend Saturday school every week, where we would learn the Ukrainian language, heritage, culture, etc. Every Saturday, after Saturday school, my grandfather would pick me up, we would go for lunch and then he would sit down with me and help me with my Saturday school homework for the following week. When I was a teenager and when I was a kid, I was not all that fond of Saturday school, and I was not fond of doing homework on Saturdays either. One day, I was really frustrated. I was struggling with what we were working on. I said to my grandfather, “Dido”, as I called him, “I do not want to do this anymore. I want to stop.” He said I could not stop, and he told me why. He said he was incredibly proud of his heritage, and he thought if I learned more, I would be too. He said he wanted me to learn about the history of the Ukrainian people because so many of them came here to Canada. They came before I did. They came before he did, and they helped make this country great. He wanted me to learn about the people who made Canada great.
