That is one of the three reasons why I think it is so important that we adopt this bill today. The first reason is just that. It would be a national acknowledgement of people whose contributions have shaped Canada for 135 years, as my colleagues have spoken to. Through this bill, Parliament would be recognizing these contributions. The second reason is that it is an opportunity to celebrate Ukrainian heritage, which I know we have all experienced in our communities. Some of the members have spoken to that very experience. It is important to honour that as well. The third reason is that since 1891, Ukrainian Canadians have come to Canada, and for 135 years, Canadians have supported them. Through this bill, Parliament would be recognizing Canadians. It would be recognizing the support Canadians have offered to that community and the support Canadians have offered to Ukraine, which go on to this very day. I would argue that there is no more important time to pass this bill than now. For the past four years, Ukrainians have been defending themselves against Russia's brutal invasion, and Canada has been a global leader in supporting the Ukrainian people in that fight. We do that not just because it is the right thing to do but because it is the right thing for Canada. This is because Ukraine's victory is vital to Canada's security. If Russia wins, it is not going to stop at Ukraine. We know this because Vladimir Putin has told us so. Vladimir Putin, right now, is showing us so. If Russia succeeds, NATO will be next. That means Americans, Europeans and Canadians will be next, defending ourselves against Russian aggression. We can either pay a small price now to help Ukraine win or we can pay a much bigger price later in Canadian dollars and in Canadian lives. Our government understands this, and that is one of the reasons why Canada has been a global leader in supporting Ukraine since 2022, with over $26 billion in support. That is military support, sanctions, financial aid and much more. In June, when meeting with President Zelenskyy, Prime Minister Mark Carney said—

I apologize, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister said, with President Zelenskyy present, “The tide is turning as expected in this war.... Ukraine will win. It's just a question of time.” We must support the Ukrainian people until they win, because Ukraine's victory is not only vital to Ukraine but the only option for Canada as well. Ukraine's most prolific poet, Taras Shevchenko, once famously said, Translated, this means, teach, read and learn from others, but always be proud of that which is your own. Today, I feel the way I think my grandparents would feel, the way the people watching at home would feel, the way their parents and grandparents would feel and the way generations of immigrants would feel if they were here today. I am proud of the contributions Ukrainian Canadians have made to Canada, proud of their Ukrainian heritage and proud to be Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, I request a recorded vote.
Mr. Speaker, rising on a point of order, I suspect that if you were to canvass the House, you would find unanimous consent to call it 6:30 p.m. so we could move on to government business.

title: Oral Questions: Government Priorities
turns: Mr. Speaker, British Columbians are concerned that the government's priorities are backward. The Liberals can find $560 million for a rainforest fund in Brazil, yet five years after the most costly natural disaster in all of Canada, my community and many others are still waiting for flood protection infrastructure they were promised. Why is the government choosing foreign projects over protecting Canadian families, farms and our national supply chains, which are essential to our national interests and the government's own export objectives?
Mr. Speaker, while these people are against working with forests—

Mr. Speaker, while the members opposite are against protecting forests around the world, I am going to give them an opportunity to be for something. This government is putting forward the first-ever national forestry strategy, something that would help that member's province: $6.5 billion for the forestry industry. I sure hope they will vote for the budget.

Mr. Speaker, as bad as that was, it gets so much worse. The same Global Witness report detailed horrifying slave labour abuses, for which Brookfield was charged, was convicted and had to pay huge fines. All of this is true, and this conviction happened while the Prime Minister was the vice-chair of Brookfield. This is a very expensive record of hypocrisy. At a time when Canadians cannot afford to eat, why is the Prime Minister sending the money of good, hard-working Canadians to fix his own horrible legacy in Brazil?

Mr. Speaker, I would have thought conservation was something Conservatives could get behind. Tropical forests are among the world's most vital ecosystems, and protecting them delivers environmental benefits—

Mr. Speaker, tropical forests are among the world's most vital ecosystems, and protecting them delivers environmental benefits that extend around the world, including here in Canada. Our loan for this facility is part of a global partnership that will help protect over one billion hectares of tropical forests across more than 70 countries. Climate change does not stop at our national borders, and—

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister found half a billion dollars for tropical rainforests in Brazil, but budget constraints for cadets here in Canada are costing our kids life skills like maritime knowledge, first aid and orienteering. Switch the kids to baseball instead, one might say? Well, those kids will have to pay a brand new membership fee next season after federal cuts to Baseball Canada. The Prime Minister may say he speaks for the trees, but who is going to speak for our kids? Why can the Liberals find hundreds of millions of dollars for a foreign fund while youth programs in Canada are being scaled back?

Mr. Speaker, I know first-hand the importance of the cadet program. In fact, before I was elected, I was on the civilian committee of my local cadet corps, and I have even been advocating since I was elected to increase funding for the Canadian corps of cadets. Through the 2026 spring economic statement, our government announced $195 million over five years beginning in 2026-27 and $45 million annually thereafter. If the members opposite would listen, they would hear me say we will continue to support the cadets.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Mr. Speaker, the previous Liberal government over the last decade blew through every single fiscal anchor it had established. Last year, we got a new Prime Minister and new Liberal leader, who established new fiscal anchors in the last budget, with deficits double that of its predecessor. Well, here we are, less than a year later, and the PBO projects that the Prime Minister is going to blow through these new fiscal anchors. Will the Prime Minister confirm the PBO's projection that the upcoming budget will blow through the fiscal anchor?

Mr. Speaker, our government has been clear: We are spending less to invest more in the Canadian economy. We found over $60 billion in government savings, reported a lower deficit in the spring economic update, and are on track to balance the operating budget a year ahead of schedule. We have done all that while cutting taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment, and supporting Canadians with groceries and essentials, while seeing the highest level in foreign direct investment in nearly two decades. That is how we demonstrate fiscal discipline and build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what stats the member is cherry-picking, but business capital formation has declined in five of the last six quarters, and GDP growth is under 1%, effectively zero. As to spending, the debt is growing at double the rate of the deficit, and interest payments on the national debt are skyrocketing to 14¢ per dollar of revenue by decade's end. I ask the government to answer the question. Will the government blow through the fiscal guardrail in the upcoming budget, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, Canada starts with the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have seen the net debt-to-GDP ratio is the best in the G7. We have a AAA credit rating, the best in the G7. In Q2 of this year, we had the highest GDP growth in the G7. I do not know how many stats the member opposite needs. We saved $60 billion in government operations. We have attracted over $500 billion of new commitments in investment in the Canadian economy. I am not sure what the member opposite needs in terms of stats to understand that Canada is doing well and only getting stronger under the current government.

Mr. Speaker, the Canada health transfer child benefit, EI, the child benefit and equalization payments do not have much in common, but they do have one thing in common: Canada spends less money on each of those than it does on interest on the debt. After the Liberals doubled the national debt, the Prime Minister doubled the deficit in his first year alone. Eleven cents of every federal dollar is now for interest payments. That is not social programs, it is not health care and it is not police. It is just interest. Will the Prime Minister get out of his seat and tell Canadians which matters more to them: their services or his creditors?

Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are blinded, I think, by their pessimism and negativity. They cannot even see the opportunities that our government is seizing in the Canadian economy: $500 billion in new investment commitments from domestic investors; doubling non-U.S. trade by the year 2030; and projects such as Darlington, Contrecoeur, Grays Bay, Roberts Bank and Churchill Falls. These are generational projects that will secure long-term prosperity for Canadians. Budget 2026 next week, on November 5, will build on that progress. The Prime Minister says, “Fortune favours the bold.”

Mr. Speaker, in just the time that it took the member to answer that question, Canadian taxpayers were forced to pay $112,000. That $112,000 will not pay for one of the government's social programs. In five out of the last six quarters, investment has been down in this country, despite what the member says. That is Liberal hypocrisy in a nutshell. Their fiscal recklessness means less money today and even less tomorrow. The member cannot explain it. Will the government support our motion today and have the Prime Minister come to committee and at least try?

Mr. Speaker, let me put a few facts on the record for the member. We are building a strong economy that benefits all Canadians. We have the second-fastest growth in the G7 and the best balance sheet in the G7, and we are the most competitive country for business investment. We have higher per capita job creation than the United States. This is a government that is focused on what matters to Canadians, like bringing the cost of housing down, ensuring that they have affordable child care and ensuring that there are investments in the skills, training and education that they need to build the brightest future possible. That is our record.

title: Oral Questions: Finance
turns: Madam Speaker, the Liberal government is spending without restraint. It has added $700 billion in national debt over the last 10 years, but it is adding another $733 billion over the next five. The Liberals are costing us an additional $82,000 of debt per Canadian household. What is the outcome? It is a record 2.4 million visits to the food bank in a single month. That is the highest in Canadian history. If spending was the solution, surely Canadians would be better off by now. What good is all this spending when the very Canadians paying for it are getting poorer?

Madam Speaker, I have enormous respect for the colleague who just asked the question, but she knows better. She knows that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. She knows that Canada is the only country, with Germany, to have a AAA credit rating. She knows that Canada has the lowest net debt to GDP in the G7. She knows that the IMF just confirmed in its forecast that Canada will have the second-fastest growth in 2027. She knows that this country has everything to build, and that is what we are going to do, with Canadians.

Madam Speaker, they say that they are building Canada, but the reality is that the PBO just slashed Canada's growth rate to a mere 0.9%, less than half of the U.S.'s, and the reality is that they are building generational debt. What is the fastest-growing expense for the government? It is not health care and it is not defence. It is interest, $83 billion in interest. The Liberals are driving Canadians into dependence on government programs, and they are taking on massive amounts of debt to pay for it. How can this Liberal government possibly claim that its economic policies are working?

Madam Speaker, what Canadians are watching today is the Conservatives always talking down the Canadian economy. We have the most talented workers. We have strong industries. We are one of the few countries that can build a car, can build a plane and can build a ship. We have the critical minerals to power the economy of the 21st century. We have an abundance of energy to make things here at home, and we are the only G7 country with free trade with all the other G7 nations. We have everything to build Canada strong, and that is what we are going to do.

Madam Speaker, the markets are predicting it, the government's own parliamentary watchdogs are predicting it, and even Tiff Macklem is indicating interest rates could go up by a quarter of a point as early as next week. That is going to mean higher mortgage payments for the residents of my community. That is going to mean higher costs for our business owners. The Liberals are literally fuelling the affordability crisis they deny exists. When will the Liberal government finally curb its spending and allow Canadians to live their life?

Madam Speaker, I am sure the member has been reading the international press and has been following what the international agencies are talking about with regard to Canada. The IMF just recently said that Canada would have the second-fastest growth in the G7. We have been acting on the three most important things for Canadians: the cost of food, the cost of gas and the cost of homes. We are going to continue to work for Canadians because every day is a good day to fight for Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I will be honest. I have not been speaking with the IMF, but I have been speaking to people from the food bank in Newcastle, which has seen a 3,000% increase in usage since 2015. When will the Liberals finally get the message to curb their spending so Canadians can afford to live?

Madam Speaker, I hope the people in the member's riding are watching TV this morning, because they will know that the member, and all the Conservative members, voted against every affordability measure we put forward to support Canadians. It is a shame. Every time we said that we would support Canadians with the price of food, with the price of gas and with the price of all, the Conservatives were missing in action. Why do they not come on board and help us to support Canadians? That is what the people in the member's riding are expecting.

Madam Speaker, barely a day goes by without the Liberal government's making an announcement of billions of dollars of new spending. Press releases are issued, media content is bought, consultants are paid and dollars go out the door immediately, yet results for Canadians are years away, if at all. The bulk of this announced spending is part of no budget plan. This is government by blank cheque. Just this week, the Parliamentary Budget Officer released the fall economic outlook, showing just how out of whack the spending has become, and the economic outlook just gets worse. Can the minister stand here and explain how more spending leads to worse results?

Madam Speaker, I know it is Friday, but let me help my Conservative friend. Six million people are going to receive the Canada child benefit, 400,000 kids will be supported with the national school food program, 465,000 people will receive the Canada disability benefit, 12 million Canadians will receive the Canada groceries and essentials benefit, and 900,000 kids will be supported with early learning and child care. I could go down the list, but I will give it to him so he can inform his constituents the next time he engages with them.

Madam Speaker, a sign of a strong economy must be how much the government can give people because they cannot afford to pay their own bills. The economist Prime Minister promised Canadians two things: to balance the budget by 2029 and to maintain a declining debt-to-GDP ratio. He is failing badly at both. To quote the PBO report, “the two fiscal anchors have imposed limited fiscal discipline on government spending and borrowing.” Our escalating debt is consuming way too much of our tax dollars. The bottom line is that if the PBO were a doctor, she would tell Canadians that the government is on life support. When will the Liberals think about Canada's future and stop spending as if—

Madam Speaker, Canadians know better. They are laughing at the question. They understand that Canada will have the second-fastest growth in the G7 in 2027. They understand that we have the lowest net debt-to-GDP in the G7. They understand that we have one of the lowest deficit-to-GDP ratios in the G7. They understand that their country is the only one, with Germany, with a AAA credit rating. Canadians are proud of this country. They know we are going to build Canada strong. I just hope the Conservatives get on board.

Madam Speaker, the PBO's latest report shows that unemployment will soon rise to 6.9%, but in my region it is as high as 8.3%. That includes families in Penticton, Grand Forks and Castlegar who cannot find work and are choosing between buying gas or buying groceries, yet this report shows that Liberal spending will only increase, with more debt. Therefore, higher taxes will follow. Can the Liberal minister explain how their fiscal plan of fewer jobs and higher taxes will help families—

Madam Speaker, I am sure Canadians who are watching are a bit puzzled. On one hand, the Conservatives are voting against measures to support Canadians and build the economy, and on the other hand, they are wondering what is going on. Thank God we are not taking a lot of their advice. We are listening to Canadians. We are investing in this economy. We are supporting Canadians. We are investing in our sovereignty. Canadians are proud. They want this country to go forward. That is exactly what we are going to do.

title: Oral Questions: Steel and Aluminum Industry
turns: Mr. Speaker, for months, our aluminum extrusion industry has been sounding the alarm, yet just weeks ago, the industry minister could not even remember that the industry exists. The government calls aluminum and steel critical to Canada's sovereignty and success, yet leaves downstream aluminum producers facing 100% U.S. tariffs going into the U.S. while allowing record volumes of U.S. imports into Canada. When will the minister publicly acknowledge the industry exists and protect the downstream aluminum industries just like they have steel?

Mr. Speaker, 100% tariffs, that is punitive. That is ridiculous. That is the world we live in. That is the world we live in with the neighbour we have, with the neighbour that the Conservatives seem to like a lot. What are we doing? We are helping the local businesses in that industry, in aluminum, as we do with steel and other derivative products. It is important for us to keep those industries alive because we need them to build our ships, to build our airplanes and to make sure that we are sovereign in our own country.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised a deal with that neighbour to the south that was just referenced. It is all talk and no results. The Leader of the Opposition and my Conservative colleagues recently visited Can Art Aluminum Extrusion in Windsor, Dajcor Aluminum in Chatham and eight other industry representatives. They are not asking for handouts or more debt. They are asking for a fair Canadian market to compete in. They submitted a proposal to the Minister of Finance in June 2026 and have yet to receive a response, despite the rhetoric from across the aisle. When will the Minister of Finance act to save this downstream industry before it is actually lost and our sovereign capabilities are gone forever?

Mr. Speaker, I have also visited a number of companies in those industries in Quebec as well as in Ontario. That is an industry that is crucial to our sovereignty. We will keep that industry alive. That is where our spending goes. The Conservatives keep saying it is inflationary spending. That is where our money goes, to making sure our industries stay alive. We are facing an attack from outside with 100% tariffs. That makes no sense. We have to stay alive throughout this period. That is what we are doing. That is what the regional initiative on tariff relief is all about, and we will continue to maintain it.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's housing crisis will not be solved if builders cannot get the materials they need. A building supplier in my community says jobs are at risk because rising steel costs are hurting roof truss production. No trusses means no roofs. No roofs means fewer homes. The Liberals promised to double homebuilding, yet only 2,000 homes are under construction, and now they are failing to make homebuilding more affordable. When will these Liberals give builders relief on this deal that holds Canadian homes together?

Mr. Speaker, our government is taking action on buy Canadian with all of the housing that we are financing. We are financing a significant amount of housing. Last year, over 8,000 non-market homes were built, which is a record of many decades. We are seeing a big scale-up in rental housing. The builders across Canada are using Canadian materials increasingly. We need to support that. We could use support from the Conservatives for buy Canadian rather than taking pot-shots at our own industries and not supporting affordable housing.

title: Oral Questions: Automotive Industry
turns: Mr. Speaker, these Liberals and the industry minister have done absolutely nothing to stop the sale of the Stellantis plant in Brampton and now we know why. On July 14, four Liberal MPs toured the plant with Roshel, including the member for Brampton Centre. The industry minister has done nothing to stop this since the MOU was signed in September. Is this minister actually going to try and stand up here now and pretend that she is against the sale when Liberal MPs were touring the plant in July and she has not sued to stop the sale?

Mr. Speaker, the number one priority of this government is to protect jobs, jobs that are affected by American tariffs and tariffs that have not yet been denounced by the Leader of the Opposition. Colleagues should know that we will continue to fight for these jobs. We were able to fight and win at Stelco in Hamilton. We will do the same in Brampton.

Mr. Speaker, do colleagues know what was missing from that? It was a denial of what I just said, and that is telling. Here is what we know. We know that she issued a notice of default 10 months ago and did nothing. We know Liberal MPs toured the plant in July with Roshel. They were in on it. They did nothing to stop it. The MOU was entered in September. They did nothing to stop it. How about we have some honesty from this minister? When did you know the plant was going to be sold? Why did she not sue to stop it the second you found out?

Mr. Speaker, the only company we are negotiating with is Stellantis, and that has always been clear. Do members know what is also clear? I would like to remind members what my colleague from Dufferin—Caledon once mentioned. He said that we have solid contracts with job guarantees at Stellantis. Do members know what? That is true. Either they protect the jobs or we will get our money back.

Mr. Speaker, I am looking for some clarification. The Prime Minister said that he called the Stellantis sale a betrayal. We then learned from a CTV report that, in fact, the Liberal government not only knew the terms of the said sale but they also participated in the discussions behind closed doors and did nothing to stop it. I have a question for the industry minister. When did she first learn about the potential sale of Stellantis and what did she do before a deal was signed to protect auto workers in Brampton?

Mr. Speaker, there is no big secret here. We have been negotiating for months, for a year actually, working with Stellantis, working with Unifor and working with the Ontario government. We have always said that any solution needed to protect the workers, period. Do members know what? Stellantis is on the hook. If they go ahead with the sale, there is no problem. Do members know what will happen? They will have to pay back the government and Canadian taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars, period.

Mr. Speaker, we know what Stellantis did but what I was asking is what the industry minister did to protect the workers at Stellantis. The Brampton workers deserve some accountability. One cannot facilitate and participate in negotiations around a sale behind closed doors and then stand up in the House and pretend one is against said sale. I have a simple question for the industry minister. Will she stand up, take some accountability and finally tell us why she has done nothing to protect the jobs of the Stellantis workers?

Mr. Speaker, the position is clear. If they go ahead with the sale, we will go after our money. Meanwhile, if they want to keep the jobs in Canada, we are willing to put an aggressive package to support the workers. Do members know what will happen—
Mr. Speaker, I hear them heckling, calling it corporate welfare. Do members know what? While they call it corporate welfare, we say it is about protecting the jobs and we will do the work.

title: Oral Questions: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship
turns: Mr. Speaker, Canadians are lining up for blocks for scarce entry-level jobs, are waiting 20-plus hours in emergency rooms and are unable to find a home, in part because the Liberals brought in too many immigrants too fast. Last week, a senior Indian government official suggested that Canada bring in 15 million more immigrants, a population the size of Ontario, an idea also pushed by Liberal insiders at the Century Initiative. Conservatives oppose Liberal mass immigration because it has depressed wages and outpaced integration. Why is the Prime Minister saying he is going to increase immigration even more?

Mr. Speaker, here is what Canadians need to know. We have made reforms to our immigration system to restore integrity and balance, and those reforms are working. The temporary resident population is down, the asylum level is down, our system has been stabilized and Canada has met our levels targets for the first time in a decade. Canadians know that immigration helped build this country, and it will continue to contribute to our success. I very much look forward to tabling our levels plan in the next few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, foreign governments are not the only ones pushing Liberal mass migration. So are foreign companies like Tim Hortons, which profit from cheap foreign labourers and depressed wages. Liberal mass immigration has cost Canadian jobs and wages. It has contributed to young Canadians not being able to afford to have kids. Conservatives will remove non-citizens who have no legal right to be here. Conservatives will sharply cut immigration so we can hire, train and house Canadians first. Does the minister agree with Conservatives or with pro-mass migration foreign governments and corporations like Tim Hortons?

Mr. Speaker, the member knows full well that for a company to apply for temporary foreign workers, they have to have had offers to Canadian workers first. They have to ensure that Canadians come first for any work across this country. To allege that—

Mr. Speaker, maybe I will start over. The member knows that Canadians come first for any work in this country and that, in fact, temporary foreign workers are only permissible when a company has done due diligence in areas with low unemployment rates that have a dire need for labour. We monitor those companies—

Mr. Speaker, Canadians who want to become electricians, bricklayers and heavy-duty mechanics used to get up to $4,000 from the apprenticeship incentive and completion grants. The Liberals cancelled these programs. Instead of hiring Canadians for skilled jobs, unbelievably, the Prime Minister's government announced that it is going to let employers recruit foreign labour for highly trained jobs without even trying to hire a Canadian. Talk about a lack of due diligence. Conservatives believe there should always be way less immigration, and the government should be focused on training and hiring Canadians first. Will the Liberals cancel their plans to make it easier for foreign labour to take these jobs away from Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, maybe the member of Parliament wants to speak to his colleagues, the members for Bellechasse—Les Etchemins—Lévis, Côte-du-Sud—Rivière-du-Loup—Kataskomiq—Témiscouata, Mégantic—L'Érable—Lotbinière or Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, who have all written to me for more temporary foreign workers. In fact, we regularly get backdoor requests for more temporary foreign workers from the Conservative members of Parliament. We will continue to do our job to protect Canadians' rights to first available labour.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's government let corruption take over Canada's immigration system. Let us talk about that. Some employers shook down foreign workers for up to $50,000. Immigration consultants under the Liberals pocketed fees for shady job placements. The Liberals allowed corrupt colleges to charge tens of thousands of dollars for classes that did not exist. Now the minister is scrapping one of the few safeguards left in the immigration system: proving that no Canadian is available to take a skilled job. That lets shady employers and corrupt consultants profit off foreign workers. Why is the minister opening the door to even more immigration corruption?

Mr. Speaker, if the member wants to talk about advocating for corrupt private colleges, he should talk to the member who regularly comes to the committee that I represent. Members of Parliament from the opposite side are always advocating for these private career colleges that rip off Canadian students every single year. We changed that. We have made those colleges ineligible for public support. We hope opposition members will get on board and start fighting for Canadian students.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's mass immigration policies hurt immigrants too. Too much immigration has strained housing, health care and jobs, and has hindered successful integration. Refusing to deport non-citizens who have committed serious crimes leads to wrongly blaming law-abiding newcomers. Liberal policies fuel rising anti-immigrant sentiment and a broken immigration consensus. Conservatives would lower immigration and restore order and fairness. Why will the Prime Minister not do the same?

Mr. Speaker, I can confirm that last year, there were over 23,000 removals of people who were ineligible to be in Canada. Over a thousand individuals with criminality were removed from Canada. We continue to ensure the safety and security of our border, and we are managing and ensuring that we have control over immigration.

Mr. Speaker, they are talking from both sides of the Conservative mouth. On one side, we have people saying, “no immigration”. On the other side, they are saying that there are great employers in need of workers that could benefit from the temporary foreign worker program. We believe in being there for Canadian workers first and for Canadian companies that are seeking talent. We have the balance right. Maybe the Conservatives should stop weaponizing immigration for those great hard-working companies they say they support.

Mr. Speaker, I think Canadian companies, especially in the province of Quebec, must be very confused right now because, in fact, as many of its members who have spoken to me know, there are dire shortages of labour in particular parts of the country, including in rural and northern areas. We expect that Canadians always come first for labour. We will protect that, but we will also protect Canadian companies to continue to manufacture, to grow and to create those great jobs for everyone else.

title: Routine Proceedings: Petitions
turns: Mr. Speaker, today I am presenting a petition on behalf of Kitchener Centre residents concerned about the Rogers radio closures and their impact on our community. During the Shaw acquisition campaign, assurances were made that local radio would not be impacted. Petitioners want to know what the response is to these closures, and whether Rogers will be held accountable for breaking those assurances. These closures threaten local jobs, access to local news and voices of our community. Kitchener residents deserve answers, and this petition is an important step towards holding Rogers accountable.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present two petitions. The first is from a group in Prince Edward Island that is working on the basic income pilot. In November 2020, the final report of the Special Committee on Poverty in PEI recommended that the Government of Prince Edward Island begin immediate negotiations with the Government of Canada to develop and implement a basic income guarantee demonstration program for Prince Edward Island. The petitioners are calling on the Government of Canada to begin immediate negotiations with the Government of Prince Edward Island to develop and implement a basic income guarantee demonstration program in the province of P.E.I. that will be implemented, monitored and evaluated for five to seven years.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition I am presenting comes from a group of citizens in my riding of Burlington who are in favour of the Canada-wide early learning and child care initiative. The petitioners are calling on the government to continue investment in this program to ensure that every child across this country has access to high-quality, inclusive child care. They are looking to ensure that there is more infrastructure and that the dollars are tied to inflation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present a petition brought forth by Aaron Hagey-Mackey and signed by 765 Canadians. The petitioners ask our government to establish an open, transparent and legally binding public naming process for major infrastructure projects. The petitioners seek a process that would allow citizens and residents of Canada to submit name proposals for projects. They seek a voting mechanism that would allow publicly approved names to then be adopted as the official project name, subject of course to reasonable standards of decency. The petitioners seek to embrace democratic principles of citizen engagement by allowing public naming of public projects.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present two petitions on behalf of the people of Abbotsford—South Langley. The first petition calls for long-term investment in resilient infrastructure across British Columbia's west coast corridor. Every British Columbian remembers the 2021 floods that devastated our communities and exposed serious vulnerabilities in our critical infrastructure. Therefore, the petitioners are calling on the Government of Canada to recognize the West Coast Corridor Resiliency Partnership as a strategic partnership and to provide predictable long-term investment in flood protection, transportation infrastructure and disaster preparedness.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition calls for immediate relief for the rising diesel costs and stronger Canadian energy security. Diesel is essential to all Canadian farmers, truckers, businesses and workers. When diesel prices rise, the cost of producing food, transporting goods and operating businesses rises with them, and that puts pressure on all Canadians. Therefore, the petitioners are calling on the Government of Canada to provide immediate relief from federal taxes on diesel until Canada Day, support new refinery and fuel transportation infrastructure, and take steps to strengthen Canada's domestic fuel supply so Canadians have a less vulnerable system and fewer shortages in supply and distribution.

Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to rise for the great people in Simcoe—Grey. I am presenting a petition on behalf of a local constituent, a young gentleman who has been quite dismayed with the current state of democracy in our Canada. His petition states that “Under the ‘rights of information act’ (1985)”, every person who is a Canadian citizen, or a permanent resident, “‘has a right to and shall, on request, be given access to any record under the control of a government institution.’” The petition also says, “Canadian democracy relies on government clarity.” The petition goes on to say that on April 29 during a health committee meeting, the new government majority voted to shut off public recordings of the meeting, going in camera and restricting public access to speeches, interviews and comments from MPs. It says that the Prime Minister has “openly attempted and successfully poached opposition MPs against the wishes of their constituents”, that the current Prime Minister is the first Canadian prime minister to gain a majority government through backdoor deals rather than through votes, and that one of the Prime Minister's first acts with his “manufactured majority” was to “stack” parliamentary committees in order to gain control.

Mr. Speaker, I stand in my place to bring awareness of a petition that is circulating in Saskatoon. Petitioners are extremely concerned with the rate of violent crime in our city. Since 2015, it has skyrocketed, and the government has poured gas on that fire with the epidemic of mental health and the addiction crisis from coast to coast. The people of Saskatoon who have signed this petition are very concerned that, since 2015, violent crime has increased by 32%, gang-related homicides have increased by over 90%, violent repeat offenders obtain bail much more easily, and increased daily activity of crime and violence is putting Canadians at risk. These are the stats, but if I ask any Canadian whether crime is getting better or worse in Canada, the vast majority believe we are headed in the wrong direction. It is time to change course with the tired government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to table more petitions for a safer and more reliable Ontario Highway 11 portion of the Trans-Canada Highway. At the intersections of highways 11 and 101 in northern Ontario lies the town of Matheson. Whenever a major storm or accident forces Highway 11 to close, transport trucks and commuters are often left stranded in Matheson due to dangerous driving conditions. These closures place a significant strain on Matheson, delay the delivery of essential goods and prevent people from getting home safely. Matheson is just one of many northern Ontario communities paying the high price for the poor conditions along Highway 11. It is time to designate that part of the Trans-Canada Highway as a project of national interest.

Mr. Speaker, I am presenting a petition signed by over 5,000 Canadians. I am going to read it verbatim. Whereas public confidence in federal leadership is essential to the effective functioning of Canada’s democratic institutions, many Canadians have expressed concerns regarding transparency, accountability, and decision-making at the highest levels of federal leadership, and recent developments in federal leadership, including—
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I apologize to the member opposite, but he just said that he is going to read the petition verbatim. Members cannot read a petition in the chamber.

Mr. Speaker, I will summarize the last paragraph. Recent developments in federal leadership, including the role and influence of the Prime Minister, have raised questions among Canadians about governance and public trust. The petitioners are asking the Government of Canada to take immediate and meaningful action to restore public trust and confidence in federal leadership, as they are concerned about federal leadership, accountability and transparency, including pursuing appropriate democratic processes that allow Canadians to express their confidence in the current government.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to present petition e-7622 on behalf of concerned members of the Pakistani Canadian community. Signers of the petition are disturbed by the Liberal government's decision to have the Minister of Foreign Affairs meet with the Pakistani Minister of Interior while visiting Islamabad last summer. This individual has been known to engage in targeted state-sanctioned harassment against families of Canadian citizens and members of the Pakistani diaspora. Signers of the petition are calling on the government to ensure that future collaborations with the Pakistani Ministry of Interior be conditional on its immediate cessation of harassment against the families of Canadian citizens. I am pleased to have the opportunity to present this petition here today in the House of Commons.

title: Oral Questions: Steel and Aluminum Industry
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister loves to take credit for projects that were approved before he ever became Prime Minister. Soon enough, he is going to be announcing that he is granting a permit for the Canadian Pacific Railway. Speaking of those projects, not only has he failed to buy Canadian; he now cannot build Canadian. Just after the announcement that, after a 10-year delay, LNG phase two is going ahead, we now learn that the steel will not come from the out-of-work Hamilton steelworkers. It will come from China. Why is the Prime Minister sending our steel jobs to Beijing?

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Leader of the Opposition has brought up the second-largest private sector investment in Canadian history, an LNG Canada success story that will make this country more independent and more prosperous. It is a project that will have 15,000 tonnes of Canadian steel in the broader ecosystem. This government is building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, the principal supplier of steel for the project will, again, be China. That is something we found out the very week the legendary company Stelco announced it was going to be laying off 350 people and idling its plant in Hamilton. The Prime Minister puts Canadian steelworkers out of a job and grants a permit for Beijing to dump its artificially subsidized steel on Canadian soil. Why can we not build Canadian with Canadian steel?

Mr. Speaker, there is a chance to build with Canadian steel. It is called the Pacific link pipeline. The Leader of the Opposition might be sleeping and he might be in the ground, but we are putting Canadian steel in the ground with the Pacific link pipeline. The workers of Stelco deserve better from their American-owned parent, which made representations. This government will pursue it to the full force of the law to honour those commitments.

Mr. Speaker, of course they deserve better from their American owner. Canadians deserve better than a Prime Minister who sends their tax dollars down to reward those same companies with purchases up 50% as a share of government purchases. We then have LNG phase two. It took the Liberals 10 years to get it going. Those steelworkers, who thought they might have a hope to supply the bones of that project, learned that the Prime Minister has sold them out and granted a permit for that steel to come from China. Why will he not put Canadians first, with Canadian steel in Canadian projects?

Mr. Speaker, there is 15,000 tonnes of Canadian steel in Coastal GasLink for LNG phase two. LNG phase two was approved less than two years from the start of LNG phase one. The Leader of the Opposition and all of the members of his party have a chance to stand up for Bill C-39 to get Canada building strong right across this country. That is what this government is doing.

Mr. Speaker, there was devastating news last week. Chris, a Stelco employee, called me to say that he and 350 of his fellow union Local 1005 steelworkers are out of a job. This is the human cost of the Prime Minister's failed attempts to get a tariff deal, the same deal he promised Canadians over a year and a half ago. Now the tariffs are still here, bigger than before, and Hamilton steelworkers are paying the price. When will the Prime Minister turn rhetoric into reality to protect Canadian jobs and Hamilton workers?

Mr. Speaker, we know that the news at Stelco was a gut punch to the workers, their families and the entire community of Hamilton, and our government stands with them. I had personal conversations with the owner of Stelco, Lourenco Goncalves, who owns Cleveland-Cliffs. We offered the company support, and notwithstanding the fact that we were at the table until the last minute, it decided to turn it down. Now we know also that the CEO of Cleveland-Cliffs has been in favour of tariffs against steelworkers—

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have talked about holding the company accountable, but I am going to do my job and hold the government accountable. The Prime Minister's duty is to keep Canada in a competitive business climate, but he has failed. I have stood in the House multiple times to warn the Prime Minister this was coming. The out-of-touch Liberals need to understand we cannot build without protecting the people who actually build Canada. With the Prime Minister, it is all talk and no results. Again, how many more families must lose their livelihood before the Prime Minister protects Canadian—

Mr. Speaker, we have been there for steelworkers and will continue to be, and we will work together, along with the member, because we believe in Stelco and its workers. That being said, at the same time, Cleveland-Cliffs and Stelco have obligations under the Investment Canada Act, and we will make sure that we use the full force of the law.

Mr. Speaker, the reannouncement of LNG Canada phase two is old news, but we now know that steel being used for that project is from China. The Prime Minister promised Canadians he would buy Canadian and use Canadian-made steel for major projects. Instead, he is allowing companies to use foreign steel while Canadian steelworkers are facing layoffs. We have seen the government buy American, and now we are seeing it buy Chinese. When is it time to buy Canadian?

Mr. Speaker, maybe it is time for the Conservatives to get behind 6,000 new jobs in Canada for LNG Canada. Maybe it is time for them to get behind 180,000 new jobs for the Pacific link pipeline. Maybe it is time for them to get behind 2,000 new jobs for the Sunrise pipeline. How about getting on team Canada?

Mr. Speaker, 350 Canadian steelworkers are losing their job at Stelco, all while the government knew and allowed LNG Canada phase two to use Chinese steel. The Liberal government granted a remission order on anti-dumping duties in phase one, so it cannot claim ignorance. Why did the Liberals not fight for Canadian-made steel, for Canadian jobs and for Canadian businesses?

Mr. Speaker, when we look at the type of steel that is made at Stelco, we see that it is for the auto sector right now. It is almost always sent to the U.S. The type of steel at Stelco needs to be changed, and we need to build the type of steel for Canada. That is exactly what we are doing elsewhere in the country. There are 200 new jobs at Tenaris in Sault Ste. Marie, building steel for pipelines, and it is exactly because of our plan that it is hiring.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals promised to stand up for Canadian workers. Back in Windsor, we are still waiting. Last week's layoffs at Stelco are just the latest warning. Last October, Windsor workers called out the use of foreign steel on the Banwell-E.C. Row project, even though Canadian producers were ready to compete for the work. Canadian projects should use Canadian steel and Canadian workers. When will the Liberals stop the rhetoric and actually deliver the results they promised Canadian workers?

Mr. Speaker, we are defending Canada's steel industry. We are defending the auto industry. We are investing in businesses, including in the member's riding. We have delivered $7.5 billion in support to businesses and workers across the country, including steel companies. I was at Daybar, which uses Hamilton steel for doors and frames that it can export, and there are many other companies. The Conservatives should get on board and start building this country up, not tearing it down.

title: Routine Proceedings: Petitions
turns: Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people from Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. I have two petitions to present today. The first is on behalf of 70 signatories from Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. The signatories exhort the Canadian government to invest in renewable and clean energy. The petitioners also ask for a broad electrical grid and nation building. They again exhort the Canadian government to provide leadership in this area in commitment to the 2030 and 2035 targets.

Mr. Speaker, with the second petition, I rise for, I believe, now the fifth time, to ask for federal funding for the fast-tracking and rebuilding of the iconic Red Bridge in Canada. The bridge was a landmark that was destroyed by arson. It is something that the people from the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc area and the people of Kamloops have asked for. Federal funds are needed so the bridge could be rebuilt. Hopefully we will see it in the November 5 budget.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to present two petitions today. The first one I do not agree with but present in good faith on behalf of my constituents who are concerned about the proposed west coast oil pipeline project. They do not want it built, and I do, but I said that, in good faith, I would present the petition.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition I would like to present today is about the greener homes loan. I am tabling the petition on behalf of residents who are concerned about the affordability of home energy efficiency upgrades, such as heat pumps, and the role those play in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The petitioners indicate that the Canada greener homes affordability program has helped thousands of households reduce emissions and improve the energy efficiency of their homes. The petitioners call upon the Government of Canada to reinstate the program as soon as possible and to provide interest-free financing to help Canadians undertake home retrofits aimed at reducing carbon emissions and home efficiencies.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise to present e-petition 6929. I mention the number because very close to 28,000 Canadians signed this petition. It is an honour to present it. The petition deals with really painful disabling diseases that Canadians suffer from in large numbers, yet these particular diseases, despite long diagnostic delays, medical complications and barriers, are not publicly funded and have not been recognized by Health Canada as diseases that are disabling. The diseases of which I speak, and the petitioners are particularly concerned with, are endometriosis and adenomyosis, which are chronic, painful and disabling yet are not covered in the same way other disabilities are. The petitioners call on the House of Commons to officially recognize endometriosis and adenomyosis as conditions that qualify as disabilities federally and provincially. The federal government can only really resolve the federal disability program, but it certainly is the case that the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and related agencies play a large role in evidence-based decision making and can help the provinces also recognize this.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to table a petition today on behalf of the petitioners. The petitioners highlight that Canada continues to permit live horses to be exported by air for slaughter for human consumption; that horses are transported from feedlots to Canadian airports and flown overseas in wooden crates, with journeys potentially lasting up to 28 hours without feed, water or rest; that horses are highly sensitive animals with strong fight-or-flight responses, and prolonged transportation and confinement can cause significant stress and expose them to injury, illness and death; that existing federal regulations govern the conditions under which horses may be transported but do not eliminate the inherent welfare concerns associated with long-distance transport for slaughter; and, last, that Canadians have repeatedly called upon Parliament to end this practice through petitions, public advocacy and proposed legislation. Successive attempts have been made in Parliament to prohibit the live export of horses for slaughter, and the Government of Canada previously committed to ending this practice, yet these exports continue. The petitioners are calling on the government to act without further delay to permanently prohibit the export of live horses from Canada for slaughter for human consumption, including horses exported for fattening before slaughter, through all necessary legislative and regulatory measures.

title: Private Members' Business: Privilege
turns: Mr. Speaker, I just want to add some further commentary to the question of privilege that is currently before the Chair and to rebut some of the arguments offered yesterday by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons concerning my question of privilege about the apparent leak of details in Bill C-40. The key thrust of the parliamentary secretary's argument was, basically, “trust me”. I agree with him that, consistent with the traditions of the House, we take members at their word. To that end, I accept that the parliamentary secretary himself did not leak the content of Bill C-40. The “comprehensive investigation” which he spoke about frequently, but not extensively, is another matter. The parliamentary secretary gave no insight into the scope or thoroughness of the so-called investigation, just that it happened and nothing was found, but how hard did they look? In 2001, after details about the Anti-terrorism Act 2001 had been leaked to Bob Fife ahead of its introduction in Parliament, in addition to Mr. Speaker Milliken finding a prima facie case of privilege, as referenced in my original intervention, the Privy Council Office initiated its own investigation. The Standing Committee on Procedure and House Affairs, in its 40th report, outlined what was involved with that investigation: Mr. Fadden explained that the Privy Council Office had initiated an administrative review of the unauthorized disclosure of information regarding the anti-terrorist legislation, and contracted with the firm of Deloitte & Touche. The final report, dated November 20, 2001, was provided to the Committee. It indicated that, during the period October 25, 2001 to November 20, 2001, Deloitte & Touche itself had conducted 53 interviews, including 11 Ministers, and Departmental Security Officers had conducted 419 interviews, for a total of 472. These were people who had been identified as being involved in the drafting process, the review process and the roll-out and communications process of the bill. The Deloitte & Touche report indicates that nine persons interviewed admitted to having spoken with the media with respect to what became Bill C-36, but only four spoke with either Mr. Fife or [Luiza] Chwialkowska. Of these four, three persons admitted having spoken to the two journalists in the few days prior to the appearance of the article in the National Post on October 13, 2001. All nine persons adamantly denied having provided any unauthorized information to the media in general, or to Mr. Fife or Ms. Chwialkowska in particular. Four hundred and seventy-two professional interviews compared to who knows what, but take him on his word. He insists. Next, I want to turn to the argument he offered that the government had never really decided to pick a lane on structuring the Defence Investment Agency. Let us look at the actual sequence of events that he scattered throughout his intervention. On April 27, Doug Guzman, the Defence Investment Agency's Chief Executive Officer, told the Standing Committee on National Defence that there were “a number of ways” in which the Defence Investment Agency could be set up, including a Crown corporation. According to the parliamentary secretary, this was a sign that there was “still a live debate within the government.” Fair enough, but the very next day, April 28, the government answered the question and settled the debate when the Minister of Finance and National Revenue laid upon the table the 2026 Spring Economic Update. On pages 82 and 145, the minister signalled the government's intention to establish the Defence Investment Agency as a “stand-alone entity”. That policy announcement assumed legislative expression through the introduction of Bill C-31 on May 6, which the following day, the minister referred to in a press release as making good on the government's pressures, among others, “establishing the Defence Investment Agency as a stand-alone entity”. The government had never made any statements here in Parliament or, indeed, anywhere else, repudiating its policy or its proposals in Bill C-31, currently before the Standing Committee on Finance, that is, until Bill C-40 was tabled. Let us be honest about what actually happened. Mr. Guzman threatened to rage-quit from the government because of his impatience with public servants, something we also know because of sourced reporting on the pages of The Globe and Mail, and Bill C-40 suddenly became an urgent Liberal measure to keep the Prime Minister's Bay Street pal kicking around Ottawa. I worry that the parliamentary secretary might find himself in trouble if the Prime Minister actually catches wind of his argument yesterday. The most frequent Liberal spokesperson in the House has basically stood up and told the world that we cannot rely on government decisions announced in Parliament, that we cannot rely on the word of the finance minister, given a mere seven sitting weeks earlier, and that we cannot assume that legislation introduced by the finance minister six sitting weeks earlier represents the actual policy of the government. For a government that is making a big show about negotiating foreign deals and seeking foreign investment while talking about other governments signing agreements in pencil, the parliamentary secretary's argument that we should not rely on federal government announcements, economic updates and budget implementing legislation as authoritative representations of government policy is actually quite chilling. In the current era of heightened global uncertainty, it is what is called “political risk”, which has fundamentally driven many business and economic considerations of late. For his part, the parliamentary secretary has single-handedly signalled to investment markets that they need to recalculate Canada's political risk, because the finance minister's word and the government's word apparently cannot be relied upon even in the short term. Alternatively, the parliamentary secretary is saying that in the government's pecking order, Mr. Guzman actually outranks the finance minister and that we should value their respective pronouncements accordingly. Either way, it is not good. Finally, another argument the parliamentary secretary offered is that the media got it all wrong and therefore there could not have been any leak because it was reported that the legislation would provide for an associate minister of national defence, when in fact Bill C-40 would create the position of associate minister of national defence for procurement. This sounds like a distinction without a difference. If anything, the phrase “associate minister” is the dead giveaway, the smoking gun, that there was a leak of details found within the bill. The phrase is a very precise and specific expression. It is very much an inside baseball term in the Ottawa field known as the “machinery of government”. The phrase was nowhere in the defence procurement lexicon until the night before Bill C-40 was introduced. It certainly was not in any of the quotations offered by the parliamentary secretary yesterday. All told, Mr. Speaker, I would urge you to give the parliamentary secretary's intervention the appropriate weight, namely an acknowledgement that he himself did not leak Bill C-40 to The Globe and Mail or the CBC. When we strip away the verbiage of his intervention, we are left with a threadbare argument by a government seemingly desperate to avoid any committee investigation related to the leak of this bill.

title: Oral Questions: Employment
turns: Mr. Speaker, the government keeps talking about its ambitions, but today's jobs report from Statistics Canada tells a very different story. Unemployment is up 6.7%, youth unemployment has jumped to 13.7% and 50,000 private sector jobs have vanished in just one month. Meanwhile, the government is projecting five more years of massive deficits, exceeding $50 billion annually, along with mounting debt servicing costs. When will the government stop making promises and deliver a credible plan to create jobs and put Canadian finances back on a sustainable footing?

Mr. Speaker, Canada has one of the lowest debt service costs in the world. We have a AAA credit rating, and long-term bond yields are rising less than other countries in the G7. Everyone in the world recognizes the strong fundamentals in the Canadian economy except the Conservative Party of Canada. It is the only one doubting Canadians and this country. We will never apologize for investing in Canadians and putting our country on track for a prosperous future. That is what we were elected to do. When will they get on board?

Mr. Speaker, pretending one's grades are better than they are is not a way to improve one's performance. The question was about jobs. The answer did not mention jobs. The budget barely mentioned jobs. We see the results today in the Statistics Canada jobs report. That report is not about aspirations; it is about results. Over 50,000 private sector jobs were lost in one month alone. Youth unemployment spiked. Unemployment overall spiked. Less than 20% of Canadians who were looking for a job found a job in the last month. Canadians are struggling. Jobs are down. When will they actually fix the problem?

Mr. Speaker, the budget that was tabled yesterday shows that we care about Canadians. It also shows that we are investing in the future of Canadian workers. Just yesterday, Canada's Building Trades Unions said: Canada's Building Trades Unions (CBTU) welcomes the federal government's investments in infrastructure, housing, energy, and major projects in Budget 2026. These investments represent an important opportunity to build Canada's economy, strengthen energy security, and create good-paying, unionized jobs with lasting benefits for Canadian workers and their families. Canadians believe in this budget. They should too.

Mr. Speaker, nearly one in five young people in Windsor-Essex who wants to work cannot find a job. That is thousands of youth being denied the opportunity to get ahead, buy a home and build a future for themselves. After 10 years of the Liberal government, youth unemployment in Windsor-Essex is higher than the national average of 13.7%. Young people are paying the price for a decade of failed Liberal budgets. Why does this Liberal budget have nothing for the youth in Windsor-Essex?

Mr. Speaker, the general uncertainty that has been prompted by the tariffs levied against Canada in such an unjustified way has created uncertainty in business. We know that the Conservatives almost always fail to mention this, but it is a key point, and it is a key point relating to the youth unemployment rate. The productivity mega deduction has been mentioned here at length today. It should be. It creates the most competitive tax jurisdiction in the industrialized world. That means investment. That means jobs. That means jobs for young people. Let us work together to continue to make this happen.

title: Oral Questions: Natural Resources
turns: Mr. Speaker, B.C.'s new Conservative premier wants to build out ports and rail to get Canadian energy to global markets. Strathcona Resources proposes to ship 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil a day through Prince Rupert. It is a Canadian company, Canadian oil, Canadian jobs and a direct deepwater route to Asia, but the Liberals' job-killing Canadian oil exports ban blocks it. Will the Liberals finally get out of the way, repeal Bill C-48, cut dependence on the U.S. and let Canadians sell Canadian oil to the world?

Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, we are working with Alberta, we are working with British Columbia and we are working with first nations to sell Canadian oil to the world. We are doing it. We are selling electricity. We are selling oil. We are selling hydro. We are selling nuclear. We are selling copper. This is all in partnership with indigenous people. They want to fight with indigenous people. Why do they not stop fighting and start building with us?

Mr. Speaker, no other major energy producer in the world derails and stops its own exports like the Liberals do to Canada. During the last antidevelopment decade, smaller companies got killed. Multinationals moved investment out but got golden handshakes from the Liberals. Canadian-owned Strathcona invested more in Canada and does not want tax dollars. If the Liberals mean a single word about making Canada an energy superpower, will they support the Conservative plan to repeal their shipping ban to export Canadian oil so Canada can be self-reliant, affordable and united?

Mr. Speaker, here is who is investing in Canada. Shell just put $30 billion into the upstream in Alberta. Equinor is putting $10 billion into Newfoundland. Petronas is putting billions of dollars into this country. There are people from all over the world coming to invest in this country because of Liberal policies. Maybe the Conservatives should get on board.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals like to talk a big game when it comes to dealing with the United States, yet they refuse to lift the ideological and unscientific tanker ban that land-locks Canadian resources and depresses the Canadian dollar, giving our oil away on the cheap to the Trump administration while Canadians struggle with the cost of living crisis here at home. However, there is now a plan, a private sector proposal, to export Canadian oil by rail through Prince Rupert. Will the Liberal government finally get out of the way, repeal the tanker ban and allow this country, Canada, to achieve true energy independence from the United States?

Mr. Speaker, we are all very proud of the work that my colleague is doing with these major projects across the country. We are talking about Coastal GasLink. We are talking about LNG one and two. We are talking about the north coast transmission line. We are talking about some of the biggest port infrastructure investments in Canadian history. Guess what. The member is new. He lives with regret because he is not the premier of British Columbia today. We built not one, but are about to build two major pipelines to the west coast of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives want to scrap B.C.'s north coast oil tanker ban, putting our coastal communities and indigenous livelihoods at risk. The Prime Minister has already promised to uphold the ban, yet Canadians are being asked to shoulder the financial risks of another costly pipeline. As the Prime Minister meets with first nations leaders and premiers, this is a moment to build trust, not break promises. Will the Prime Minister stand up today and unequivocally commit to protecting the north coast tanker ban, respecting indigenous rights and keeping his government's promise?

Mr. Speaker, I want to be very clear. The building Canada strong act would not change the duty to consult. The bill proposes a centralized Crown consultation hub so that indigenous peoples can spend less time navigating government red tape and more time having meaningful conversations. Our government is focused on building Canada strong, and we cannot do that without indigenous peoples.

title: Oral Questions: Steel and Aluminum Industry
turns: Mr. Speaker, last Friday, the industry minister said resolving the Stelco dispute was a “question of days”, yet Cleveland-Cliffs is proceeding with indefinitely idling its Stelco cold-rolled and coated steel operations. It has been 13 days since Stelco first responded to her letter and six days since the minister said it would be resolved, and now we learn she is giving them an extra 15 days. Canadians are having a hard time keeping up, and workers cannot pay their mortgages with another government warning. Will the minister stop issuing warnings, do what she said she was going to do and start enforcing Stelco's employment commitments?

Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what we are doing. We are making sure that Stelco respects its commitments under the Investment Canada Act. We are following the process. In 15 days, if nothing happens, legal action will be taken. Our aim has always been to protect Canadian workers and the Canadian industry. That is what we have been doing, and that is what we will continue to do.

Mr. Speaker, every single day, it seems like the Liberals' timeline keeps changing. There are so many things they could do right now to increase competitiveness in this industry. First, they could enforce the contracts they have. Second, this industry needs more customers, competitive costs and market access, yet the industrial carbon tax remains, American tariffs remain and workers face layoffs. Conservatives would eliminate the industrial carbon tax, pre-approve LNG projects to create demand for Canadian steel, and restore access to our largest export market. Will the Prime Minister adopt our proposal so we can give steel and auto workers a fighting chance?

Mr. Speaker, let us try to make some sense out of all this. First of all, we never asked for this. Second of all, we are responding to an attack from the U.S. administration. Our aim is to protect Canadian workers and to protect Canadian industries. We will always do that. That is also why the Prime Minister goes abroad sometimes and signs trade deals to diversify our economy so we can protect our industrial base.

Mr. Speaker, three weeks ago, Stelco laid off 350 Hamilton steelworkers. Two weeks ago, the Liberal minister sent a letter threatening legal action, and today she is giving them another 15 days. The Liberals wrote a similar letter to Stellantis. Eight months later, those workers are still waiting for results. The minister stated today that “no act of God” can change the commitments made to Canadian workers, so will the Prime Minister finally take Cleveland-Cliffs to court, or is this just another empty Liberal threat?

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the member was missing in action yesterday. We just announced with the Government of Ontario more than $8 billion to support a number of sectors in Ontario: our steel sector, our brave men and women who work in the automotive industry and those boosting our critical minerals. Instead of talking our workers and our industry down, why does he not support the government and work with us to make sure that we keep jobs in Canada and grow our industry and make sure that we build Canada strong together?

Mr. Speaker, the only action missing yesterday was the action not taken for Canadian workers. Last Friday, the minister said the resolution was a “question of days”. Today, she gave them another two weeks. Stelco's third quarter this year was the strongest since 2024, yet Cleveland-Cliffs still broke the job commitments it made when it bought Stelco. Its CEO even praised President Trump on his unjustified tariffs on Canada. We cannot let Canada and its workers be bullied by President Trump and his buddies. Will the Prime Minister file a lawsuit today, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, the question has been asked and answered, but I will ask a question. Why is it that this opposition party cannot stand with Canadians, the Province of Ontario and the premier, as we have, to protect steel workers, to protect the steel industry, to protect the automotive industry and, yes, to invest in the Ring of Fire in northern Ontario? I know the member of Parliament for Kenora has written about the Ring of Fire. Why are they not applauding that investment? Why are they not applauding the kind of critical mineral exploration and development that our country needs? It is appalling.

Mr. Speaker, the damage from Canada's steel crisis is not stopping at the steel mill. Stelco is idling its coating lines and laying off workers, and the downstream industry is taking a hit. A stamping manufacturer in my community of Cambridge bought its steel from Stelco for years. Now that the supply is gone, it is not able to source what it needs. It will lose its contracts and customers because it cannot get its steel in time. That is more jobs that will be gone for good. What is the Prime Minister going to do to keep these businesses open and Canadians working?

Mr. Speaker, I have some good news for workers in Cambridge and all across Ontario. The Premier of Ontario and the Prime Minister stood together yesterday and said that they were going to control the things they can control. One of the things we can control is investing in our companies to make sure they can produce steel for the automotive sector, for the critical industries that are powering our nation and, yes, for the critical mineral sector in northern Ontario. Guess what. We believe in doing things. The opposition is going to stand up and complain time and again, but we are going to stand up for workers.

Mr. Speaker, throwing more money at the problem will not produce the steel this company needs at this time. How does this make industry more competitive? Conservatives have a plan to eliminate the industrial carbon tax, to pre-approve LNG projects that create demand for Canadian steel and to restore access to our largest export market. If this Cambridge manufacturer cannot secure the material it needs, it will be forced to shut down. Families will lose their paycheques, and customers and contracts will leave Canada. We have a serious proposal to save Canadian jobs. Will the Prime Minister adopt our plan and give businesses a fighting chance?
Mr. Speaker, we actually have a serious proposal to save jobs, and we are putting the money behind it. What we are not doing is standing up there and criticizing every single idea—

Mr. Speaker, when industry speaks and tells the Government of Canada and the Province of Ontario what kinds of supports they need, we listen. We listen, because we know we can actually pivot these industries and support Canadian workers. When northern Ontario puts its hand up and says it wants to be part of the solution and wants faster action on the Ring of Fire, we partner with Ontario. We build those roads. That is what we are doing. We are working hard every day for Canadian workers, and that is how we stand together as a country.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Industry was on Bay Street saying, “We used to be able to transform aluminum in Canada, and we don't anymore.” The minister should know there are over 80,000 Canadians employed in the downstream aluminum industry right now whose jobs are at risk. Her comments saying the industry does not exist are a slap in the face to every one of those workers. Why is she already writing the industry's obituary when it is the Liberals' failure to get a deal that is killing these jobs?

Mr. Speaker, the only thing I hear in the House of Commons today is the members of Parliament from the Conservative Party who have clearly given up. We are not chasing after things that we actually cannot bring to fruition. We are working on the things we can control. When the Premier of Ontario, the aluminum industry, the steel industry, the automotive industry and the critical mineral industry say this is what we need, we invest in those industries. We invest in the workforce that we need. We support workers when their jobs are at risk. All I see from these guys is them voting against Canadians, voting against workers, criticizing provinces and—

title: Oral Questions: Employment
turns: Mr. Speaker, skilled workers build this country. In my riding of Carleton and across Canada, young people want a path into the skilled trades, and unions are ready to train them. Can the Secretary of State for Labour tell this House how the union training and innovation program will help more young Canadians get into the skilled trades and build Canada strong?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Carleton for supporting the skilled trades. Canada is embarking on one of the largest nation-building efforts in our history, but we cannot build big without skilled workers. That is why last week we announced $430 million for the union training and innovation program to expand apprenticeship training and modernize the union training centres that will support the next generation of skilled trades. When we invest in workers, we are building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians cannot afford the Liberal government. Candace is a 25-year-old mother from Aylmer who has applied without success to over 500 jobs. Here is what she wrote me: “Every day I wake up wondering how I am supposed to provide for my family. My husband's income alone is no longer enough to cover our mortgage, vehicle expenses, groceries, utilities and the necessities our daughter needs. If I cannot find employment soon, we may lose our home and be forced to move.” She is not alone. Will the Liberals admit that this is now the new normal in their Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know Candace's background, but I can tell members this. We are working hard to make sure every single Canadian has a pathway into good jobs. Not only that, there are great jobs out there. We are making sure that people have the skills that they need to take up those good jobs. I would be happy to correspond with Candace and tell her about some of the work that we are doing and some of the opportunities that exist across this country. If we cannot all stand up for people like Candace, then we are really not doing our job. I would say that the member could guide that constituent to—

Mr. Speaker, when members of Parliament have letters like that from constituents, it is important to share that information. I am very glad that member of Parliament has. I hope that he is telling Candace about the opportunities that exist for her and her family.

title: Private Members' Business: Wartime Service Recognition Act
turns: Mr. Speaker, it is a tremendous honour to be here in this House today as the sponsor of Bill S-246, the wartime service recognition act. What this bill would do is simple.
