It asks National Defence to set a national framework that would have objective and transparent criteria on what is considered wartime service within 12 months, and then to apply that criteria to every conflict since 1943 and to future conflicts. I do not think most Canadians know that Canada has not officially recognized any military operation as wartime service since the end of the Korean War. In fact, Korean War veterans had to fight for 27 years to get it recognized as a war. Persian Gulf War veterans are still fighting after 36 years, for decades, just for their own recognition. Also, veterans of the war in Afghanistan are only now just starting to realize that the government officially, legally, does not consider them to be war veterans. I know this matters, because a few months ago I was door knocking in my riding, and I met a woman at the door who had served in Afghanistan. When I told her about the bill and she realized that she was not a war veteran, she had to hold back tears. That is because words matter and labels matter. That is why this bill is so incredibly important. The bill is very simple. It is about correcting the disconnect between what veterans experienced and what we all know. We all note the war in Afghanistan and the Persian Gulf War. Veterans know what they went through. The bill is about correcting the disconnect between that and the label the Government of Canada applies to their service. It is about telling the truth about their service. It is about respect. It is about recognizing veterans, and it is about validating their service. The bill would not specify which conflicts are or are not wartime service. It asks for a criteria. The bill would also not impact benefits or compensation. Why does the bill matter, then? I asked veterans that question myself. About six years ago, I was at an event at the Canadian War Museum, and we had the Kuwaiti ambassador there. We were celebrating the 30th anniversary of the end of the Persian Gulf War, the first Gulf War, the one that liberated Kuwait. I met several Persian Gulf War veterans. Many of them are here today. I met Harold Davis, Mike McGlennon and others. I heard them say that they felt the Kuwaiti government was recognizing what they went through in ways that the Canadian government was not. That was very disturbing to me. I asked Mike McGlennon why this mattered so much to him. His answer has always stayed with me. His answer that day was that he just wanted his grandchildren to know that their grandfather was a war veteran. That term, war veteran, is an incredibly powerful term. A few months later, the Persian Gulf War veterans had a documentary. They said that very few people had seen this documentary, so I hosted a screening here on Parliament Hill. I was not expecting veterans from across the country to come to that screening with parliamentarians. I will never forget that one Persian Gulf War veteran came with a box full of mementos, things he had brought home 30 years ago. He told us that he had not opened the box in 30 years, but that because he was on Parliament Hill, he felt that he could open it and share what was in it for the first time. I also heard from veterans who said they did not wear their medals because, often, the way we recognize or not recognize veterans is something that gets internalized. Today, I would like to share the words that Mike McGlennon shared earlier. He said, “Please restore our pride that has been stripped from our service.” This bill is about restoring that pride. I would like to quote from retired Colonel Mark Gasparotto, who said, about the war in Afghanistan, “The Afghan mission was a war by every metric, and the current terminology of special duty area rings hollow when judged against the life and death realities we faced on the ground.” This bill is about those realities. It does not matter if there was an actual declared state of war. It does not matter what the war was called. It is about the lived experience, realities and conditions that the veterans faced. My parents were liberated in World War II by Canadian soldiers in the Netherlands. My father got his first candy in 1945, when he was five years old, from a Canadian soldier. Growing up, I remember my parents would be walking down the street and they would point to somebody and say, “Do you see that man over there? That man is a war veteran.” Even as a little girl, I knew from the hushed tone and the reverence that that meant the man or woman had done something very important, very special, because those words, the words “war veteran”, matter. When Canadian military personnel or others return from war, often they do not talk about it. If we acknowledge it by calling them war veterans, by giving them a nod of respect, a handshake or a quiet thank you for their service, that lets them know that we see them, we understand what they went through and we acknowledge them. That is a respect that is so needed, especially by veterans who come home with invisible or visible injuries, and the veterans need to have that validation and recognition from the Canadian government itself. This is also a very important bill because it is not just about how veterans feel, how they see their service or how Canadians see their service. It is about who we are as a country. It is about understanding the history of Canada as a country. Of course, it is true that Canada is a peaceful country. Canada is a country that will always put diplomacy, conflict prevention and peacebuilding first. However, Canada, historically and today, is a country that has been willing to fight when it was necessary. Canadians have stepped up. We will fight when it is just. We will fight against oppressors. We will liberate. We will fight when it is necessary to restore peace, freedom and democracy around the world, including our own freedom. That is a part of history. I sometimes hear young people and others ask, “Why do we have a military? We have not had a war since our grandparents' time.” Can members imagine what that sounds like to the veterans who served in war, the living veterans and modern veterans today? Making sure we understand and say that we have sent our Canadian Armed Forces into war is something that will also help young people understand. This is about the future veterans and the future young people, like a young cadet thinking they may want to serve. The young people who are thinking of serving their country are watching. They are watching how we treat the veterans of today. They are thinking about whether or not they are going to serve as well. This bill would show them that we would provide the right recognition if, God forbid, we ever have to send them into a war. This bill is also extremely important for women veterans. It was not until 1991 that women in Canada were permitted to participate in combat roles, and 1991 was the Persian Gulf War. For women veterans, for their valour and for their sacrifice, this is an incredibly important recognition of their service. It is also very important for families. As we know, anybody who serves does not serve alone. Their families are there alongside them. We lost 158 Canadian military personnel in Afghanistan. I would like to read some words we heard earlier today from an incredible young woman who I just met, Olivia Vernelli. Olivia's father, Master Corporal Scott Francis Vernelli, was killed in action in Afghanistan when she was only six months old. Today, she said, “I grew up without a father. Father's Day meant visiting the National Military Cemetery”. She continued, “For years, Canada's involvement in Afghanistan has been referred to as a mission. However, the word mission does not accurately represent the years of combat, the Canadian soldiers killed in action or the families who lost their loved ones. These are the realities of a war. Calling it a war is about giving that service the recognition it deserves.” I speak of families like Olivia's. I am so pleased that this bill has all-party support in the House. It passed in the other place by Senator Yussuff with a unanimous vote. I am encouraging our colleagues to do no less in the House. There is urgency. We need to pass the bill quickly. It is already 70 years late. We have thousands of living veterans today. With every week that passes, they are getting older. We are losing some of them without them ever knowing their government was going to recognize their service properly. That is why I am asking everyone in the House to please pass Bill S-246 quickly, so we can recognize, see and validate their service.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for sponsoring the Senate bill here, and for her kind words about our veterans, especially now. Here we are leading up to Veterans' Week and Remembrance Day. It is important that we recognize the service and sacrifice made by so many of our veterans, including those who were in the Persian Gulf War and Afghanistan. I think about Canada's contributions to Libya as well. That was a hot war. Canada was in there kinetically. It was the first time a Canadian warship came under fire, back in 2011. Conservatives have always stood with our veterans. We have stood with the Canadian Armed Forces. Recognition is important, as is making sure people are properly given the honour, as well as the supports, for their service. I would ask the member this: Could she tell us, from the government's perspective, how quickly we can expect it to do this analysis to ensure that, with respect to those operations of war and conflict, we are properly recognizing the great service of those Canadian veterans.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Selkirk—Interlake—Eastman also for all of the work he does for veterans and those who are still serving. There are timelines in the bill. This was very important to the veterans. It states that, within 12 months, there needs to be transparent and public criteria, a national framework that includes those criteria, and that it needs to be published. It also sets a timeline. They need to go back and make a list of all of the operations since 1953, and then apply the criteria backward. If there is a future conflict, there is six months, 180 days, in which the government must take that criteria and apply it to that conflict, because we do not want other veterans to do what some of the veterans who are here today had to do and fight for decades for their own recognition. In the future, that will be done within six months of the end of the conflict.

They need to have, almost as a prerequisite, recognized wartime service, not for all medals, but for many of them, such as Victoria Cross and others. I do believe that they need to be able to have wartime service recognized in order to have those medals.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for all her hard work. When she takes on an issue, she puts her whole heart into it. Perhaps she can just tell us one story. I also sat on the veterans affairs committee when we studied this issue, and there were just so many stories from veterans who are here today. Perhaps there was one story that really stuck with my colleague and made her realize that this effort was worth her time. Maybe she can talk about that a bit.
Mr. Speaker, I would say it is when Mike McGlennon looked at me and asked why veterans have to fight for their own recognition. They should not have to. We will do it for them.

Mr. Speaker, first off, I want to thank Senator Yussuff in the other place for sponsoring this bill and bringing it forward in the House. I want to thank the Persian Gulf War veterans, in particular Mike McGlennon and Harold Davis for their incredible leadership, persistence and unrelenting push for Canada's Parliament to recognize the incredible service of so many Canadian Forces members and police officers who have served here in Canada. I want to thank all my colleagues across all the parties as well for the collaboration. There are many joint seconders of this bill from every single party, I believe, represented here in the House of Commons. This is something that is important. As I said, I was talking about the Persian Gulf War veterans. Going back to 2022, even the late Right Honourable Brian Mulroney was pushing the government to recognize the incredible contributions of the Gulf War veterans. He was our prime minister at the time during that war. The angle I am going to go with on this is that I am just going to tell a story. Let us picture it is early May, just after dawn. There is a Canadian combat team made up of a couple of hundred Canadian soldiers, infantry, armoured soldiers in tanks with mine rollers, engineers, sappers in support and an artillery troop ready to provide close, direct fire support. We have intelligence assessments. We have close air and fast air on standby in the air. Everybody is ready to go. There is even embedded national media travelling with this Canadian formation. They cross the line of departure. Within literally minutes, the enemy combatants open fire and there is a full-fledged fire-on-fire contact going on between the Canadians and the enemy combatants. Intelligence reports indicate that this operation is likely going to result in full combat. Mines are blocking the routes. For many of these soldiers, it is their first time in combat. They have never experienced this yet on deployment to an overseas country. Needless to say, there is chaos. There are snipers. There are rocket-propelled grenades. It does not take long for the Canadian formation to have attack helicopters and support coming in. This goes on for the next three to four hours. What war am I talking about? Am I talking about the Second World War? Am I talking about Vietnam? No, I am talking about Afghanistan, which according to our Canadian regulations and government was just a special duty area. I do not think so. That conflict, that battle on May 7, 2007, went on for many hours that day. The next morning, on May 8, we were back at it again. It did not take long to come in with different tactics, approach the objective area, but on the way in, let us guess what happened. Another improvised explosive device disabled a tank. Luckily, there were no friendly casualties. As we were dismounted, moving into position to hit this objective area, again, the enemy, the Taliban, open fired. The Taliban is back in control in Afghanistan. That is something I am not going to talk about at length, but needless to say, they were not the brightest at the time. Our position, our combat team was in what I would call a perfect right flanking position. After about an hour and a half, the Taliban was on the losing end of that conflict. Luckily, no Canadian soldiers were killed that day, but there were incredible examples of heroicism that morning, especially on that second day. I can remember the squadron's second-in-command having to shoot his tank to take out an enemy RPG position right over the heads of Canadian-friendly soldiers in order to save their lives. I believe what we did in Afghanistan was absolute war, and I do not know why we do not recognize it as such. There are bigger aspects to this, too. Afghanistan is just one example. I again thank the member for Ottawa West—Nepean for her leadership in sponsoring this bill in the House. We just had a press conference. We heard from the Persian Gulf War veterans. We heard from the Afghan war veterans. We heard from women veterans, indigenous veterans, families and, in particular, a Silver Cross daughter who lost her father when I believe she was only six months old. The sacrifices that families make in combat are incredible. In Afghanistan, 158 Canadian Forces members lost their lives, but, in reality, that number is not even close. We have lost hundreds and, arguably, 1,000 due to post-traumatic stress, suicide, unfortunately, and other factors that make it so difficult for our veterans who serve in these conflicts to carry on and get up every morning. We owe them. As a Parliament and a country, we need to make sure they are recognized for what they did. One other aspect came to my mind within the last hour at the press conference when the retired assistant commissioner from the RCMP spoke, and that is police. I have served in Bosnia, Afghanistan and Iraq. Who was on every one of those deployments? It was Canadian police. I am not just talking about the RCMP. I am talking about the Toronto Police Service, the OPP, the Sûreté du Québec and many other community police forces. The importance of this bill alone, once this framework is established, is that these individuals would be formally recognized as veterans. Right now, the way Veterans Affairs Canada is set up, it is only members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who have that recognition. We need to fix that. As the member for Ottawa West—Nepean highlighted, this is about setting up that framework into the future as well. Right now, I do not know the exact numbers off the top of my head, but I think approximately 3,000 Canadian Armed Forces members and, I guarantee, police and other aspects of the Canadian government are in Operation Reassurance, on the front lines in Latvia, in an ongoing mission. I will use that word now. It has the potential to be triggered into an all-out war with Russia at the snap of fingers. We need to make sure we have a framework established to recognize our men and women, when they put on a uniform, for the service they do. I believe Bill S-246 is a step in the right direction. In closing, I want to take this opportunity to remember six fallen heroes from my deployment in 2007: Sergeant Donnie Lucas, Corporal Aaron Williams, Corporal Brent Poland, Corporal Christopher Stannix, Private David Greenslade and Private Kevin Kennedy. They made the ultimate sacrifice that day in Kandahar province. I again want to pay tribute to the four fallen Canadian Armed Forces members from the tragedy in Wainwright that just happened a few weeks ago. God bless. Pro patria. Lest we forget.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party in support of Bill S-246, the wartime service recognition act. Before I get started, I want to thank all veterans and currently serving members of our military, RCMP and all police services, as well as their families, for their service. I thank the senator who brought the bill forward. I thank my colleague for Ottawa West—Nepean for her advocacy and the work she has done to bring us all together across party lines on something that should not be partisan. I thank my colleague for Bruce—Grey—Owen Sound for such a powerful speech and for his incredible service to our country. He is a true hero, and the people he served with, including those who never came home, are heroes. I also thank my colleague for Vallée-du-Haut-Saint-Laurent for her very powerful speech. It demonstrates how we can work together on something of such importance, supporting our veterans. At the heart of the bill is a simple principle: When Canadians put their life on the line for our country, then their courage and sacrifices deserve to be properly recognized. This should not be controversial, yet for far too many Canadian veterans, securing that recognition has been a long and frustrating battle. We heard about that tonight, and we heard about it in the press conference. I have met with veterans who served in the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan and the former Yugoslavia, women and men who have spent years, sometimes decades, fighting to have that service properly acknowledged. For some Persian Gulf veterans, that fight has lasted 35 years. Mike McGlennon and Harold Davis from the Persian Gulf Veterans of Canada have been relentless. They stood with us today. We owe it to them. Just think about it for a moment. It has been 35 years of trying to convince their own government, our government, that the dangers they faced and the conditions in which they served deserve recognition. These veterans did not choose the conflicts they were sent into. They answered the call of duty, faced life-threatening situations and did everything their country asked of them, yet after all these years, they are still waiting for their country, our country, to fully acknowledge what they went through. This simply is not good enough, and it is the injustice that Bill S-246 seeks to address. The legislation before us would require the minister of national defence to establish a national framework for recognizing wartime service based on clear, objective criteria and a transparent and accountable process. Whether a veteran's service is recognized should not depend on an outdated definition, an arbitrary distinction or the label that a government happened to attach to a military operation. It should depend on what actually happened. Were our service members exposed to hostile fire or life-threatening conditions? What was the nature, duration and intensity of their operations? Did they face circumstances that could cause lasting physical or psychological harm? These are the questions that should guide the recognition of wartime service. Importantly, the bill acknowledges something that should be obvious: Wars do not become less dangerous simply because governments choose not to formally declare them. A bullet does not distinguish between a declared war and an undeclared conflict, and neither does an explosive device or the trauma that follows a veteran home, often for the rest of their life. Bill S-246 would also require the government to consult veterans and their representatives in developing this framework. This is critical, because if we want to understand what military service was really like, we should start by listening to the people who were actually there, as we heard from our colleague for Bruce—Grey—Owen Sound tonight. It should not just be government officials reviewing files in Ottawa but the women and men who lived through these experiences, the ones who served. Their voices have to be at the centre of this process. The legislation also presents the Liberal government with an opportunity to honour its own commitments. In its 2025 platform, the Liberal Party promised specifically to expand recognition of military service, including reviewing the designation of missions in the Persian Gulf. That promise was made to Canadian veterans, but they are still waiting. Here is an opportunity for the government to deliver, for all of us. The government has already acknowledged there is a problem. Now it needs to do something about it. Let us be clear about why this matters. Recognition is not simply a designation on a service record. It is about dignity and respect. We heard that at the press conference today. We heard, specifically from the indigenous veterans association, that this is about respect. It is about ensuring that veterans and their families know that their country understands what they have been through and has not forgotten them. Although this bill is about recognition, it would not, on its own, establish new financial benefits for veterans, but New Democrats believe that recognition needs to be accompanied by meaningful support. Veterans who return home with physical injuries, psychological trauma or other service-related hardships should never have to fight their government to get the care and benefits they have earned. We cannot thank veterans for their service with one hand and put bureaucratic obstacles in the way with another. That is why we need a veterans system that reflects the realities of modern military service, one that is fair, accessible and grounded in respect for the people who have served. Bill S-246 is an important step in that direction. Every November, as earlier today in the House of Commons, members of this place stand together to honour the courage and sacrifice of Canada's veterans. We wear a poppy, we attend ceremonies and we speak solemnly about the debt of gratitude our country owes to those who served. Those traditions matter, but gratitude cannot end when ceremonies are over. If we truly believe that we owe our veterans a debt of gratitude, then surely the very least we can do is acknowledge what they have done for our country. When someone puts their life on the line in service to our country, the very least we can do is to make sure their service is properly recognized. Veterans who have served in dangerous and demanding circumstances deserve recognition that reflects the risks they took and the sacrifices they have made. Far too many veterans have spent years fighting for this recognition, but they should not have to ask for it. This bill is an important step to correcting that. It is about making sure veterans who face the dangers of wartime service receive the recognition that they deserve, along with the benefits that should come with it. Again, New Democrats fully support this initiative. Canada's veterans should never have to fight for recognition after everything they have already done for our country. We owe them more than words of gratitude. We owe them fairness, dignity and meaningful action. It is time we got this right. Our veterans should not have to spend decades fighting for this recognition. They have already done their duty. Now it is time for us to do ours. The Senate moved the bill through rapidly. It moved it through committee. I hope the House can move things through quickly and that the bill can move through committee quickly. I want to thank my colleague from Manitoba who is leading on the Conservative side. He has been pushing for that. He is pushing for it to move through committee rapidly. We wholly support that. This is an opportunity for us to move the bill fast and for the minister to support it. New Democrats are proud to support the bill, and I urge all members of the House to do the same and to help do everything they can to move the bill fast into law.
Mr. Speaker, I think you will find that it is the will of the House that the bill pass unanimously.
Mr. Speaker, I suspect if you were to canvass the House, you would find unanimous consent at this time to call it 6:30 p.m. so we could begin Government Orders.

title: Routine Proceedings: Petitions
turns: Mr. Speaker, today I am presenting three petitions on behalf of residents in my riding regarding Canada Post. The first petition is about something many people thought Conservatives would do but the Liberals are doing, and that is about door-to-door delivery. Community members are calling on the Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement to reinstate the moratorium on community mailbox conversions and instruct Canada Post to maintain home delivery to all addresses that currently receive it. Who would have thought? The second petition is to save rural post offices. The Canadian postal service charter affirms that the provision of postal services to rural regions is an integral part of Canada Post's universal service. These residents call on the Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement to reinstate the moratorium on the closure of rural post offices and to direct Canada Post to explore opportunities to strengthen the rural postal network instead of making it weaker. In the third petition, petitioners in Mission are especially concerned about the future of our beloved post office in downtown Mission. They are calling on the Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement to instruct Canada Post to maintain the post office located at 33191 1st Avenue in Mission as a fully functioning post office, as well as a sorting and delivering depot. These petitioners note that Canada Post needs a new business plan and that the Government of Canada has not taken the necessary steps to make sure the CEOs are doing due diligence with Canadian taxpayer dollars. They do not want to lose their services because of bad management in Ottawa.

Mr. Speaker, today I am presenting three petitions. The first petition was signed by over 7,500 individuals. They are calling upon the Canadian government to ensure that all eligible residents of Canada can access required health care, including gender-affirming care, as outlined in the Canada Health Act and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We know that gender-affirming care is a form of life-saving care and is evidence-based health care. The Government of Alberta has limited who can have reasonable access to health care through Bill 26. The petitioners also note that the Canada Health Act states that eligible residents of Canada must have “reasonable access to [required] health care services”. I am very proud to table this petition on behalf of petitioners today.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition that I am tabling is in support of my bill, Bill C-247, and to pass it into law without any amendments to repeal section 107 of the Canada Labour Code and stop the violation on the right to strike. The petitioners call on the government to stop abusing section 107 of the Canada Labour Code, which has happened over eight times under the Liberal government. The petitioners talk about how the government has repeatedly invoked section 107 to violate the right to strike and undermine fair collective bargaining, including against striking postal workers, railroad workers, port workers and flight attendants. Petitioners also point to the Supreme Court of Canada, which recognized, in 2016, the right to strike as an essential and indispensable component of the right to collective bargaining. At a time when countless workers across Canada are seeing the cost for essentials like housing, groceries and transportation skyrocketing, petitioners are calling on our leaders to pass my bill with haste.

Mr. Speaker, the last petition I am presenting today calls on the government to suspend the AAFC staff terminations and to continue operating the research centre, research farms and the organic and regenerative research program for at least 24 months to provide cost-benefit transparency and ensure irreplaceable research capacity and long-term studies are not lost due to hasty decisions. The petitioners are urging that we cannot base our good public health decisions on political sound bites. They have to be based on research.

Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to rise on behalf of the people of Simcoe-Grey and cite specifically those in Clearview Township. I present a petition from the residents who are opposing the location of an over-the-horizon radar system. The Department of National Defence has bought one large swath of land of over 700 acres that is prime farm agricultural land and plans to build over-the-horizon. That would be phase one. In phase two, it will be up to approximately another 3,000 acres. Many of the residents are fearful of expropriation and what that will do. All of the petitioners understand that there is a balance between food security and national security. They realize, from looking at a map, there are other locations out there. They may cost money, but for them and future generations, we need to save this land. It is right beside the Minesing Wetlands as well, so there are a lot of issues with this particular area. The petitioners are calling on the government to stop the building of the over-the-horizon site on the already purchased property, prevent future acquisition of prime farmland and the building of the over-the-horizon site on the prime farmland of Clearview Township and register the previously purchased property with the Ontario Farmland Trust to preserve its agricultural status.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to present a petition from Canadians from across the country who are opposed to the expansion of MAID to those who have only the underlying issue of mental illness. They note that mental illness is often recoverable. They are asking for the Government of Canada to recognize this and to adopt Bill C-218. This bill would stop the expansion of medical assistance in dying to those who have mental illness. We need to ensure those with mental illness have hope and not MAID.

title: Oral Questions: Housing
turns: Mr. Speaker, Canadians cannot find homes, jobs or health care, and mass Liberal immigration is making it worse. The Prime Minister's plan to bring in a record 650,000 permanent residents next year, which is 50% more than Trudeau's highest number, happens just as the Parliamentary Budget Officer reveals that the Prime Minister has officially abandoned his promise to double homebuilding. That is not fair to people here or to newcomers. Will the Prime Minister stop adding people faster than homes?

Mr. Speaker, budget 2026 is an unprecedented housing budget. We are focused on affordable housing first and foremost. We are focused on making sure the market provides the housing that Canadians need right now. We have put important pieces on the table, whether that is GST relief or development charge and red tape reductions. We are taking action on housing, in particular for non-market housing and ending homelessness within 10 years.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is simultaneously blowing the budget on his failed housing expenditures while delivering fewer homes built. Just today, we learned that homebuilding is down 3% year over year, not doubled as he promised. Meanwhile, he is increasing immigration to record-smashing levels of 650,000 people. It is clearly not in the interest of Canada to do this, but it is in the interest of the corporate power brokers who will be able to pay lower wages to incoming low-wage workers and charge higher rent. Why is the Prime Minister putting corporate profits ahead of the Canadian people?

Mr. Speaker, the criticism from the opposition member is hardly credible in this case. He only built six units of housing as housing minister. We will take no advice from that member. When we look at the opportunity in front of Canada right now, it is building affordable housing. We have had four decades of not building enough affordable housing. This government is turning that around. This government is focused on non-market housing, solving homelessness and making sure we are supporting the market and the builders to build the housing Canadians need.

Mr. Speaker, according to the Parliamentary Budget Officer's damning report today, housing starts are down, funding is up and the government is falling behind its promise to double homebuilding. It also seems to have stepped away from its earlier commitment to build 500,000 new homes per year, yet the government plans a record-smashing 650,000 new permanent residents. That is 50% higher than the highest level under Justin Trudeau. Who benefits from this? Billionaires and Liberal-linked developers trying to fill overpriced, vacant condo units do. Who pays the price? Canadians do, with higher rent and home ownership. Why will he not stand up for the Canadian people?

Mr. Speaker, I will tell the Leader of the Opposition who benefits. Canadians are the ones who benefit when we invest in infrastructure and when we invest in housing. We have made generational investments in housing. The minister has been building across the nation. Just in the last budget, budget 2026, we put an additional $45 billion to our effort to build more homes, more affordable homes, across the country. We continue to build the country because every day is a good day to fight for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in 2017, the Liberals promised to reduce chronic homelessness by 50%. In 2020, they promised to eliminate it altogether. Now, in 2026, the Liberals say they will end homelessness in 10 years. When the housing minister was the mayor of Vancouver, he made the same promise. Instead, it grew under his watch. The Parliamentary Budget Office report today confirmed that the government is not even on track to meet its commitment to double housing starts. With that kind of track record, why should anyone believe it will deliver on its promise to end homelessness?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for her concern on homelessness. I think every member of this House has a responsibility to help deliver. This budget proposes unprecedented investment in solving homelessness with supportive and transitional housing in particular: $15 billion is focused on that solution. That has never been implemented before at this scale in our country. We have to do this in partnership with our provinces, cities, local communities, indigenous partners and builders all at the table to get this done together. Having unanimous support in this House for a budget that has unprecedented support to solving this problem will take us—

title: Oral Questions: Steel and Aluminum Industry
turns: Mr. Speaker, Hamilton is proud to be Canada's steel city. It is part of who we are. This is—

Mr. Speaker, we are talking about real jobs for real people, and this disruption is extremely disrespectful. Hamilton is proud to be Canada's steel city, and thousands of families depend on steelmaking. It—
Mr. Speaker, this is a critical issue for all Canadians, and it would be nice if the opposition were interested in what is happening. In the face—

Mr. Speaker, Hamilton is proud to be Canada's steel city. Thousands of families depend on steelmaking for their livelihood. In the face of the illegal and unjustified American tariffs, can the Ministry of Industry give the House an update on what our government is doing to protect Canada's steel industry and support steelworkers?

Mr. Speaker, we know that the steel industry helped build this country. We have it as a pivotal industry as we are building Canada strong. Last week, I joined the Prime Minister and the Premier of Ontario to announce an additional $5.2 billion to support the steel industry from the unjustified American tariffs. We will make sure that people in Hamilton get that support, that we create growth in the country and, more importantly, that we create jobs across the steel industry.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday, the industry minister said she would provide the demand letter she sent to Cleveland-Cliffs, because it outlines the way in which the company has breached its contractual commitments. Yesterday, I stood up in the House and asked her for a date on which she would provide us with that letter. She did not answer the question. Meanwhile, we hear from Cleveland-Cliffs repeatedly that it is not in violation of any of its contractual commitments, and workers are still awaiting some transparency. I will ask the minister this again: Will she provide us today with the demand letter that she sent to Cleveland-Cliffs so workers can get some transparency?
Mr. Speaker, the question is not that. The question is whether the Conservatives are in favour of protecting the jobs at Stelco. I have not heard that from them. My question to my colleague is—
Mr. Speaker, the question is not that. The question is, are the Conservatives in favour of protecting the jobs at Stelco and Hamilton, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, Cleveland-Cliffs's CEO admitted that he bought Stelco because Canadian steel was hurting his American business. He admitted to blocking Stelco from selling steel to the United States, and now 350 Hamilton steelworkers are losing their jobs. Conservatives demand that the Liberals take Stelco to court, stop illegal steel dumping and secure a tariff-free steel deal. Instead, the Liberals keep sending love letters and extending deadlines. Stelco's CEO is protecting American profits and his American workers. What are the Liberals doing to protect ours?
Mr. Speaker, let us be serious. There are people hurting because of these layoffs. There are people who are wondering whether they will be able to—

Mr. Speaker, let us be serious here. There are people right now who are asking whether they can pay their mortgage. There are people who are asking themselves whether they will be able to pay their bills. That is why we did not stop. We did not wait. The Conservatives are late. We have been at it and starting the legal process for more than 10 days now. They should, basically, read the news.

Mr. Speaker, the only thing late is the minister filing a lawsuit to protect Hamilton workers. This is the third pay cycle that Hamilton steelworkers are missing. I spoke with Stelco workers this morning and they want action. The CEO admitted yesterday that he bought the company as a defensive measure to protect his American profits. We also know he supports Trump and his unjustified steel tariffs. The Liberals approved this takeover. Now they are watching Canadian steel jobs disappear. Will the Prime Minister stop being bullied by Trump's buddies and file the lawsuit today?

Mr. Speaker, I met with and I have been in contact in the past two weeks with the head of United Steelworkers, Marty Warren. The union is fully supporting the position of the government. Of course, I was in the studio at CBC when Cleveland-Cliff's CEO made the admission regarding the fact that he bought Stelco to get rid of a competitor. We take that admission very seriously and will act.

title: Routine Proceedings: Committees of the House
turns: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the 10th report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Human Rights in relation to Bill C-223, an act to amend the Divorce Act. The committee has studied the bill and has decided to report the bill back to the House with amendments.

Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of tabling a dissenting report on the creative spaces study done at the heritage committee. This study comes at a critical moment as the Liberal government is actively working to strengthen ties with the Chinese Communist Party. In our dissenting report, we discuss the state of creative and performance spaces across Canada. During our study, we heard how the CCP has targeted and intimidated artistic organizations in Canada, including Shen Yun, which has faced bomb threats and performance cancellations because of foreign interference from the Chinese government. When Conservatives brought forward a simple motion at committee to condemn this, the Liberals voted against it. Witness testimony reminds us that safety and security are very basic needs and that without them, sectors like the performing arts do suffer. When the government turns a blind eye, it puts Canadian artists, cultural institutions and our sovereignty at risk. Our report calls on the government to take responsibility and ensure that no foreign regime can intimidate Canadians or silence artistic expression on our soil. I also have the opportunity to table our Conservative dissenting report with regard to a journalism study that was done at the heritage committee. The committee study raised serious concerns about the state of journalism in Canada and the role the Liberal government has played in shaping a media environment that favours government-supported outlets, while showing considerable hostility toward independent and community-minded journalism. From the minister turning a blind eye to serious allegations of toxic workplace culture and political bias at the CBC, to government subsidies that disproportionately benefit established legacy media, to independent journalists being denied access to government press conferences and smaller outlets being left out in the cold by being denied financial support, the evidence paints a deeply troubling picture of Canada's media landscape. Our report puts forward solutions, however, like greater accountability at the CBC, fairer support for independent journalism, repealing Bill C-18 and giving Canadians greater choice in the journalism they support. Canadians deserve a media landscape that is diverse, fair, balanced and independent.

title: Oral Questions: Major Projects Office
turns: Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of Liberals, there are two worlds: one where Canadians follow the rules and count every dollar but cannot get ahead, and another where political and business insiders get a seat at the big table and make up their own rules. Companies pay staff in the Liberal Major Projects Office, which makes decisions worth billions of private and public dollars. I questioned it six months ago and last night, but the minister will not even say which sectors the staff are from. So much for accountability and transparency for taxpayers. How many MPO staff are paid by companies whose projects the office reviews, and will the minister name the companies?

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to have this conversation with our colleague on the other side last evening at the building Canada committee. She just asserted that we did not talk about which sectors these interchange employees come from. Last night I said, and I am happy to repeat it again, the transportation sector, financial services sectors and agriculture sectors. Many of these interchange positions, something that has existed in government for well over 50 years, include other orders of government, and they also allow public servants to work in the private sector and for non-profit organizations as well.

Mr. Speaker, last night the minister actually called disclosure a “gotcha moment“ when accountability is literally his job. Companies help pay staff inside the Major Projects Office, but conflicts are reviewed internally without independent ethics oversight. The Liberals want Canadians to trust the safeguards but hide how and to whom those safeguards apply. The minister should release the rules, name the companies and say how many staff have been recused. If the safeguards are so strong, why is the secrecy even stronger, and what does the minister have to hide?

Mr. Speaker, while the Conservatives want to think about conspiracy, what we do at the MPO is create jobs, like the 5,000 new jobs at Churchill Falls, the 8,000 new jobs at Contrecoeur, the 1,000 new jobs at Nouveau Monde Graphite, the 5,000 new jobs at LNG Canada and the 7,000 new jobs at Ksi Lisims. Instead of talking down the MPO, why do they not help us build jobs?

Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of the Liberals, one thing is clear. There are now two Canadas, one for hard-working Canadians who play by all the rules and one for the Liberal club. While Canadian families struggle to put food on the table, private corporations are paying employees who work inside the Major Projects Office, and the Prime Minister refuses to reveal who they are. Imagine an employer having their own employees working inside the very office responsible for advancing the projects the employer's company wants approved. Can the Prime Minister tell Canadians exactly how many corporate-paid employees are working inside his MPO and which companies are paying for that?
Mr. Speaker, I actually have some very good news for the member opposite. Today we were proud to announce the removal of China's tariffs for two years—

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take it from the top, if I could, because this is such important, good news for the province I share with the member opposite. There is a two-year removal of the Chinese tariffs on lobster and crab, which is so significant for Atlantic Canada. On top of that, there is over $300 million over five years for AFF funding. Instead of reading prepared notes, let us get together and do something that actually makes sense.

Mr. Speaker, I would not want to talk about the Major Projects Office either. Last year, the Prime Minister told Canadians to prepare to make sacrifices. Well, guess what. They are already making them. Food bank visits have reached a record 2.35 million in a single month, with 776,000 of those visits being made by children. Canadians are being made to make sacrifices, yet private corporations are paying employees working inside of the Prime Minister's Major Projects Office, and the government refuses to disclose which companies are involved. Again, Canadians deserve transparency. How many employees working inside the Major Projects Office are being paid by—
Mr. Speaker, rather than come up with conspiracy theories, why does the member not talk about what the MPO did at Churchill Falls? It is the largest renewable energy—

Mr. Speaker, rather than come up with conspiracy theories about the MPO, the member might recognize that the MPO helped make Churchill Falls happen. It is the largest renewable energy project in the history of North America, with 5,000 new jobs in her province, new mines in her province. Instead of coming up with conspiracies, why does she not help the MPO get—

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised lots of things about his new Major Projects Office, but he forgot to mention that it would be done with unprecedented secrecy. It could be up to one-third corporate-sponsored employees working inside the office, and we do not know which private corporations are paying them. Canadians have a right to know who has a seat at the table. These insiders have direct access to government decisions that could benefit their employers. Yesterday at committee, I asked a simple question. Which companies do they work for? The minister refused to answer, so I will ask again. Will the minister be transparent and release the list of corporations, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, just as with the last member, I would invite the member, rather than focusing on conspiracy theories about the MPO, to focus on the 18,000 jobs at the Darlington nuclear reactor. It is one of the most important renewable energy projects in the world, the first SMRs in the world, and the Conservatives are talking down the office that made that happen. Maybe they should get with the program.

Mr. Speaker, there is clearly something to hide. The minister refused to identify the corporations that are paying their employees to work inside the Major Projects Office. This is the same Liberal government that has been found guilty of ethics violations time and time again, and now Canadians are supposed to trust them. Why should they? How can Canadians be expected to believe that large corporations are paying employees to work inside the Major Projects Office simply out of generosity? Canadians do not know who these companies are, how conflicts are being screened or whether those companies stand to benefit from government decisions. If the government has nothing to hide, why is it hiding?

Mr. Speaker, we have talked about Atlantic Canada, we have talked about Quebec, and we have talked about Ontario. Now it is time to talk about British Columbia, where I was last Friday to announce, with the help of the MPO, it must be said, the listing of Roberts Bank Terminal 2. It is a megaproject for all of Canada, with $6 billion and 17,000 jobs for British Columbians and Canadians, to export our goods, our farm goods and the products of our ingeniosity over to Asia and create—

title: Adjournment Proceedings: Indigenous Affairs
turns: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise at this hour in Adjournment Proceedings to pursue a question I asked in question period on May 5. We were nearly at the anniversary of June 3, 2019, the date of the long-fought-for report. It was such a traumatic experience just to get an inquiry into missing and murdered indigenous women and girls. That inquiry wrapped up, and as I asked my question on May 5, I noted that it was almost seven years ago that the report of the inquiry into missing and murdered indigenous women, girls and two-spirit plus people had been given to the government. Back then, we hoped. The government of the day said it would do its very best and certainly was committed to achieving all of the calls for justice within the report. There were 231 calls for justice. In other reports, one might just call them recommendations, but I think it was powerful that they were called calls for justice. The horror of the number of missing and murdered indigenous women and girls in this country remains with us, because many of those women and girls are still missing, and many more have gone missing since we got the report back on June 3, 2019. The response I got from the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations was compassionate, caring and thoughtful, as is she. She did not provide a number of how many of the calls for justice had been achieved. She did, of course, express the concern that justice, as she said, was “not with respect to just one project, but a life we need to continue to live”, and that violence against indigenous people must end. However, it remains the fact that here we are in late October 2026, and we still are dealing with the reality that women are missing and murdered. I have a lot of friends from all kinds of backgrounds, close friends, but it is only among my indigenous women friends that it is rare to find a friend who is indigenous in this country who has not been beaten up and abused. One of my close friends, I thought I knew about her life until she said, “I never told you about the time I was left for dead in a dumpster.” She said it as if it was a sort of normalized experience for indigenous women and girls, and it is, in fact, far too common. I tried to find a number for tonight's debate, from Statistics Canada and other sources, as to how many indigenous women and girls have gone missing since we got the recommendations, which have not been fulfilled. It was hard to find a number because Statistics Canada and sources do not necessarily agree, but it is a large number of women and girls from the indigenous communities of this country who have gone missing since the report came out. I will quote, because it was at least authoritative, the Native Women's Association of Canada, which states, “Despite half a decade passing since the release of the National Action Plan, the implementation of the 231 Calls for Justice has been insufficient.” It states that “many federal commitments remain delayed, fragmented, or difficult to measure in ways that reflect the realities Indigenous communities [face] every day.” What we are looking at is an ongoing crisis. We have recommendations that were really important and sweeping, such as bringing in a guaranteed livable income, such as ensuring that there is safe and efficient transportation in rural and remote Canada, a recommendation that would serve all parts of society in rural and remote Canada, where people cannot get from A to B unless they own a car, other than hitchhiking and putting themselves at risk. It is now, with a few seconds left, time to ask again. What is the level of commitment of this government? Will we hear a commitment to achieve these recommendations?

Mr. Speaker, the crisis of missing and murdered indigenous women and girls and 2SLGBTQIA+ people continues to affect survivors, families and communities across this country. Of the 231 calls for justice in the final report of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, 215 of them call on the federal government in some capacity or other. On June 3, we released the 2025-2026 federal pathway annual progress report, marking the fifth anniversary of “Federal Pathway To Address Missing And Murdered Indigenous Women, Girls And 2SLGBTQQIA+ People”, which is the Government of Canada's contribution to the national action plan. As it stands now, the Government of Canada has made efforts to advance roughly three-quarters of the federal work outlined in the national inquiry's final report. This year, our government reported progress on 163 of the calls for justice. As I have mentioned, advancing the calls for justice is not a one-time effort or a checklist for one party to fulfill. Many calls for justice require sustained action and an ongoing commitment to collaborate with other governments, organizations and civil society, while continuing to follow the lead of survivors and their families. On Red Dress Day this year, the Prime Minister was presented with a sacred bundle by the National Family and Survivors Circle. That sacred bundle carries teachings, responsibilities and spirit, reflecting the lived experiences of victims, survivors and their communities from the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls. Receiving that sacred bundle reaffirmed the Government of Canada's commitment to end the national crisis of missing and murdered indigenous women and girls and 2SLGBTQIA+ people. Also, on Red Dress Day we announced an investment of $2.6 million over three years for the National Family and Survivors Circle Inc. to continue its vital work in centring survivors and families in the implementation of the calls for justice. We also announced an additional $300,000 investment to help support the next steps on a red dress alert pilot in Manitoba. We continue to invest in indigenous-led approaches that advance the calls for justice through Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada's supporting indigenous women's and 2SLGBTQI+ organizations program. Twenty-two projects have recently been approved to support indigenous-led solutions and advance indigenous-led priorities. We also continue to support healing, wellness and community-led responses through the support of the contribution program for the well-being of families and survivors of missing and murdered indigenous women, girls and 2SLGBTQI+ people. At the same time, Indigenous Services Canada has been expanding access to safe, culturally appropriate spaces through the indigenous shelter and transitional housing initiative, which is part of the $724.1-million comprehensive violence prevention strategy. This investment will have supported the creation of 38 new shelters and 42 transitional homes across Canada, including in northern and urban communities. There is no doubt that there is lots more work to do on this important call to action and the calls for justice. We look forward to collaborating and to continuing to treat this national crisis with the urgency it deserves.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the parliamentary secretary nor any minister would claim that this has been accomplished. I think we can agree that the work is, of necessity, going to be partial, but I am not convinced there is a sufficient level of urgency from the government for the fact that people, especially women and girls, continue to go missing all the time. There is police training and the kinds of supports required under the calls for justice, including trauma-informed therapists going right away to help a woman who has been assaulted or attacked get through that process. Those kinds of steps were very specific in the report, and they really must be treated with urgency, because every single attack of a woman hitchhiking on a rural road is something that was avoidable, predictable and preventable.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the member opposite that the issue requires urgency and sustained effort. The crisis of missing and murdered indigenous women, girls and 2SLGBTQIA people demands urgent and sustained action, and we remain firmly committed to ending it. Of the 231 calls for justice, 215 are directly related to the federal government in some capacity, and we are acting on that responsibility. As I have said, almost three-quarters have been started and are in progress. We are making targeted investments that translate into real support, safe places to go, and culturally informed care and services identified by communities themselves. This includes support for indigenous-led organizations, further investments in a red dress alert pilot and expanding shelters and transitional housing across the country. Everything we are doing is built on working together, being accountable and following the leadership of indigenous partners.

title: Routine Proceedings: Privilege
turns: I am now ready to rule on the question of privilege raised on October 6, 2026, by the House leader of the official opposition concerning the alleged premature disclosure of Bill C-40, an act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security. During his intervention, the House leader of the official opposition argued that specific details of Bill C-40 had been shared with journalists before the bill was introduced in the House. He based his assertion on two news articles published before the bill was introduced in the House, which, in his opinion, provided substantive information that could not have been gleaned from the title of the bill, nor deduced from previous government consultations and announcements. The member noted that these articles cited anonymous sources who were not authorized to discuss this information publicly. He posited that such a disclosure constituted a contempt of the House. During a second intervention, the House leader of the official opposition sought to rebut some of the parliamentary secretary's arguments. He questioned the scope and thoroughness of the government's investigation before it concluded that no internal leak had occurred. He also argued that the policy information the government claimed was already in the public domain could not account for everything revealed in the news articles. Members are right to affirm that it is a long-standing expectation that the House must be the first to be informed of the details of specific legislative measures that will come before it. As explained by Speaker Milliken in his ruling of March 19, 2001, on page 1840 of the Debates: The convention of the confidentiality of bills on notice is necessary, not only so that members themselves may be well informed, but also because of the pre-eminent [role] which the House plays and must play in the legislative affairs of the nation. With this in mind, I felt it appropriate to review the news articles in question and the text of Bill C-40 now before the House. Having done so, I find that the similarities between the text of the bill and the details in the news articles remain at a high level and do not provide sufficient grounds to conclude that a leak of the bill itself has occurred. Further to this point, while members may be correct in stating that the details published in the news articles go beyond what is revealed in the bill's long title, this cannot stand as a reliable test for judging whether the precise contents of a bill have been divulged. The Chair also notes that the news articles do not directly address the question of whether the sources cited had access to a copy of the bill itself, or to its specific provisions, and were therefore even in a position to share it, nor has any convincing evidence been brought to the Chair's attention that would demonstrate that the sharing of information between the sources and journalists, or between the government and the sources, took place in the window between when the bill was placed on notice and when the bill was introduced. After reviewing all the evidence provided, the Chair cannot determine with any degree of certainty that the entirety of the bill, or specific sections thereof, were divulged prior to its introduction in the House. The government's assurance that it has no knowledge of a leak, the substance of the details published in the news articles and the lack of clarity around the nature and timing of the anonymous sources' information all contribute to this conclusion. Accordingly, the Chair does not find that this case constitutes a prima facie question of privilege.

title: Statements by Members: The Budget
turns: Mr. Speaker, the national debt continues to climb, and Canadians deserve to know exactly where their money is going. Budget 2026 promises $8.6 billion in savings but provides no breakdown showing where those savings would actually come from. Spending on consultants continues to rise despite repeated government promises to rein it in. Then the Prime Minister commits over half a billion dollars to a Brazilian tropical forest initiative, while here at home Parks Canada is having to cut its search and rescue dog program and the jobs necessary to keep our parks safely maintained. Canadians deserve a government that puts Canadian needs first. Taxpayer dollars should be invested in the services, infrastructure and support programs that directly benefit Canadian families, not be wasted on expensive consultants or foreign projects while Canadians shoulder the burden of our growing national debt during an affordability crisis.

Mr. Speaker, the new budget shows Liberals will always choose higher spending, no matter the cost. Over the next five years, they are planning to add $765 billion in new debt. What Canadians get in return for their tax dollars is, sadly, only more debt. The Parliamentary Budget Officer has confirmed that debt costs are the fastest-growing line item. Taxpayers are expected to pay $2 billion more on debt interest than for the Canada health transfer. By 2030, interest payments will be $17 billion higher than health care. Despite the Liberals' campaign promise to protect the Canada health transfer, the federal budget plans to cut it by 2% in 2028. The premiers have said these health care cuts are leading to a fiscal cliff. Nurses in Saskatchewan have not gotten a raise in over four years. The Liberal member from northern Saskatchewan has delivered nothing but bad news while sitting in cabinet. I guess it is no different from when he was part of a provincial NDP government that cut and cancelled 54 hospitals in Saskatchewan. Again, I have to ask, what do the Liberals deliver for Canadians besides more debt and bad news?

Mr. Speaker, budget 2026 is good news, just as the finance minister has said. Canada is outperforming the G7; the operational budget will be balanced by next year; and the focus is on people, growth and sovereignty. I was pleased to see $22 billion in affordability measures, recognizing the difficulty Canadians are facing and providing help. The continued focus on affordable housing is great, since this is the number one priority in my riding. The plan to end homelessness within 10 years is also welcome news. The growth continues with investments in 27 nation-building projects, diversification of our trade, supports for businesses and workers through this tough time and, last but not least, the protection of our sovereignty, with a focused plan to build our defences, protect our children online and protect our data. Budget 2026 is so good that I will be voting for the budget for the first time in 11 years.

title: Oral Questions: International Trade
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has tried to distract Canadians from crazy housing and food costs for the last two months with his big project of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU. Nobody knows what it means and the Europeans have now rejected it. We already have a free trade agreement with Europe. It is just that nine of its countries refuse to ratify that agreement. Will the Prime Minister actually get anything real done at this big grand summit, get those countries to ratify the deal, let in our beef or is this just another Seinfeld summit, a meeting about nothing?

Mr. Speaker, if anyone would know anything about Seinfeld, it is that leader who wakes up every day and lives the same recurring nightmare, every single day. The Prime Minister and my colleagues are in Montreal for the annual Canada-EU Summit. This year we are exploring many areas of further co-operation beyond the free trade arrangements we have with Europe. We are going to diversify our markets, we going to diversify them away from the United States, and that is good news for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is actually a recurring nightmare for the Canadian people who cannot afford to pay their grocery bills and whose mortgage payments just went up yesterday because of deficit spending by the government. The Prime Minister acts like George Costanza, running around the office trying to look busy while achieving nothing at all in the real world. Let us look at this. Nine countries have not ratified the EU free trade agreement. Will he get them to ratify? They are still blocking our beef. Will he remove those blockages? They are threatening an industrial carbon tariff. Will he have that removed, or will it just be about nothing?

Mr. Speaker, this guy talks like Kramer. He just walks into the room and, every time, says something weird. More seriously, free trade with Europe is a great thing for Canada. More collaboration with Europe on defence and procurement, and making sure that Canadians and Canadian youth can study and research, and we can co-operate on things like AI. Yes, his least favourite topic will be co-operating on democracy. I want to thank the Leader of the Opposition. It is going to be great.

Mr. Speaker, everybody loves Kramer. If he wants to talk about something weird, the Prime Minister told us that if we brought in a big industrial carbon tax on our steel, aluminum, cement and concrete, the Europeans would let our industrial goods in tariff-free. It turns out they are now threatening a carbon tariff on Canada, at the same time the Prime Minister holds his grand summit. He has already failed to get American tariffs lifted, like he promised in the election. Can Prime Minister tell us, is he going to stand up to the Europeans and make sure there is no carbon tariff on our goods?

Mr. Speaker, among the many areas of co-operation with Europe that we will obviously be discussing today and will be discussing going forward, in terms of our much closer arrangement with the European Union, will indeed be energy. I noted with great pleasure that my colleague, the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources saluted the fact that the first gas shipments going to Germany left the West Coast in these past months, and we can expect much more energy co-operation with our friends in the European Union.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has told Canadians for the last two years to ignore their grocery bills, their rising gas prices and the fact that an entire generation cannot afford a place to live because he has got these grand signing ceremonies of meaningless documents. Here we are, with no commitment from the nine European holdouts to sign on and ratify the existing free trade agreement we have or to allow our beef in or to cancel their planned carbon tariff. Why is the Prime Minister not delivering real results? Is it because this is just another public relations stunt?

Mr. Speaker, we have a free trade arrangement with Europe. It is in effect right now. I have even better news. The Prime Minister has set an ambitious objective for Canada to double our non-U.S. exports. I want to tell the leader the news is in: We are on track and beyond to doubling our non-U.S. exports over the next 10 years. We will do it by investing in our ports. We will do it by investing in projects, in energy and especially in our people by building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, we have to admire the hubris of a party whose members stands up over there and brag about promises that they have made that they have not kept. They are going to a summit with a continent that already has a free trade agreement, but nine of its members have not signed on to it. They will not commit to getting a single one of those countries to sign. In fact, not one of their leaders will be there. Then they are blocking our beef and pork, and the Liberals will not commit to getting that removed at this summit. Speaking of beef and pork, is this not just another big nothing burger?

Mr. Speaker, I think Canadians look, with a great deal of pride, at the events in Montreal today, where our Prime Minister is going to break new trails in terms of co-operation with the European Union, and with new arrangements in AI, in democracy, in transportation and in trade. These are all areas where we can more closely collaborate with our European friends, diversify our markets, build Canada strong, and make sure that Canada works with like-minded nations to keep our people prosperous and keep our people working.

Mr. Speaker, the work our government is doing to diversify Canadian trade matters for the workers in my riding of Oakville West, who produce top-quality products that are in demand around the world. The recently concluded Canada-U.A.E. trade agreement marks a historic milestone for our country to expand trade ties with our largest trading partner in the Middle East. Could the Minister of International Trade update the House on how our record-setting U.A.E. trade agreement will help Canadian businesses across the country tap into this fast-growing market and ensure that Canadian workers and exporters compete and win on the world stage?

Mr. Speaker, through you, I would like to thank my colleague from Oakville West for her work in the House and, of course, on the trade committee. This week, we signed a historic trade agreement with the U.A.E. in a record 47 days, the fastest trade agreement ever negotiated by Canada. Once in force, this new trade agreement will lower tariffs on 99% of Canada's exports to the U.A.E. That means new opportunities for Canadian workers and businesses and a market value of over $700 billion. That is more access for Canadian agriculture, aerospace, energy, lumber and more. Plan A is working. We are diversifying and are building Canada strong.

title: Oral Questions: International Trade
turns: Mr. Speaker, we have been in a trade war, and everyone knows this, with America, and there have been real consequences because of that: The Stellantis plant in Brampton closed, Paccar had major layoffs, Stelco now has layoffs, and hundreds of business across this country are laying off workers. The Liberals had a solution: Buy Canadian. What were the results? They bought American. They have increased the buying from American companies by a whopping 50%, in the middle of a trade war, to $7.8 billion. Why is that?

Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives need to get their facts straight. Of the $8 billion the member is talking about, there is $2 billion for General Dynamics to build 190 light armoured vehicles for the Canadian Armed Forces. There are 1,700 jobs that depend on it in London. That is 600 suppliers. The Conservatives' own member for London—Fanshawe was asking for these investments in Canadian content and Canadian workers. It is a little rich to hear them now complain about these investments that are building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals must have a different definition of what buy Canada means than what we think buy Canada means. If we are buying Canadian, we do not actually increase the amount of money we are sending to America. It is a pretty simple economic lesson. Why did the Liberals do this? It is because their buy Canada is all illusions. They are all talk, no results. If we are in the middle of a trade war, as we all know, we should be buying less from America. Will someone explain why we are not buying less from America in the middle of a trade war?

Mr. Speaker, I will happily explain. It is because we made a deliberate decision to favour Canadian content and attract investment in Canada. If the member is suggesting that we should stop investing in General Dynamics, for instance, to build these LAVs for the Canadian Armed Forces, he should tell that to his colleague, the member for London—Fanshawe. He should say that to our colleagues from across the country who depend on these jobs in their ridings. We are talking about 5,000 jobs for IBM and 5,300 jobs for Microsoft Canada. This was a deliberate choice to increase Canadian content, and our policy is working.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government, since the Prime Minister took office, has given $7.8 billion to American corporations. This is the same Prime Minister who made a big, grand show of theatre in promoting a government policy to buy Canadian, yet since then his government has increased government contracts to American companies. They now make up one-third of what the Canadian government is buying. The out-of-touch Prime Minister is ignoring what Canadians want and what he promised to Canadians. I have a very simple question: Was “Buy Canadian” just another empty Liberal slogan?

Mr. Speaker, if we were to follow the Conservatives' flawed logic, we would tell DP World to go away and to take the 8,000 jobs that are at the port of Montreal with it. They would tell Shell and Petronas to go away and to take the 6,000 jobs at LNG Canada away. They would tell—

Mr. Speaker, they would tell BHP to take the thousands of jobs away it is building in Saskatchewan. The Conservatives do not seem to understand the difference between someone who is invested in Canada and someone who is crapping on Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if the minister wants someone invested in Canada, why has the Prime Minister put 91% of his assets in the United States? This is a very real problem. Canadian businesses in my community and across this country are laying people off because the government has turned its back on them through 10 years of high taxes, high regulations and an inability to get a deal and support businesses. When the Prime Minister told them that they should buy Canadian, they expected him to follow the example and not increase government contracts to the U.S. Was it buy Canadian or sell out Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to remind the House that foreign direct investment in Canada is very important. It is at a 23-year high. These companies that do direct work in Canada employ tens of thousands of Canadians. They have IP. They have headquarters. They retain talent. They do many things here. We will support them, as we will support Canadian industries, as long as they continue to build out their presence in Canada.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, today's hike demonstrates the government's economic plan is not working. Inflation is taking hold. According to the Globe, today's hike means that the cost of a typical variable mortgage will rise $82 a month and a typical home equity line of credit $12 a month, or over $1,100 a year. When is the government going to introduce supply-side reforms to the economy to increase productivity and wages and to make life more affordable?

Mr. Speaker, we have had a display in question period today where the Conservatives are trying to catch up with my colleague with respect to steel. I note the member's question over there. Why can the Conservatives not just once stand up and say that there is a war in the Strait of Hormuz or that there is a trade attack that is illegal and unjustified on Canada. Yes, we are facing economic headwinds, and the G7 is going to be led by Canada despite all of that. The Conservatives should stand up and celebrate Canada's success and its—

Mr. Speaker, the government's plan simply is not working. It is focused on the demand side of the economy. It is spending more and more and driving up the cost of interest, which is the fastest-growing line item in the budget that is projected to chew up almost 14¢ of every dollar by decade's end. Now the Bank of Canada is hiking the interest rate, driving up interest costs on mortgages, lines of credit and car loans. For a typical family, this amounts to more than $1,100 a year. Again, I ask the question, when will the government start focusing on supply-side reforms to increase productivity and increase wages to make life more affordable for Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, every time we propose a measure to make life easier and more affordable and to make conditions for Canadians just a little better, whether it is reducing fuel taxes, whether it is a Canada food and essentials benefit or whether it is the Canada child benefit, these Conservatives, led by that finance critic, get up and oppose it. When we grow the economy, they decry that. When we protect jobs in Hamilton, they—
