Mr. Speaker, like a typical Liberal elitist, the Prime Minister is sending more money to his banker, bondholder and Brookfield buddies in debt interest than what goes to provinces in health care transfers. Just this year, a family of four will pay $6,000 in debt interest. Justin Trudeau doubled the debt. The Prime Minister took that as a challenge. He doubled down and doubled his deficit. Will the Prime Minister show up at the finance committee and tell Canadians exactly why he is so out of touch and why Canadians are so out of money?

Mr. Speaker, let us just think about this for Canadians. That member and that party voted against targeting the Canada child benefit to families that need it the most. They think a family that makes $500,000 should get the same as a single mother who makes $20,000 a year. They voted against a school food program; voted against feeding hungry children. They voted against a dental program that gives dental care to seniors who need it the most. That side has no credibility when it comes to affordability. On this side of the House—

Mr. Speaker, the measure of a success in this country should be how many government programs Canadians get off, not get put on to. Debt interest is the fastest-growing expense, more than health care and more than the military. It is the money that gets sent to the Prime Minister's banker, bondholder and Brookfield buddies every single year. This guy said he would spend less, but he is all talk and no results. That is why 2.35 million Canadians visit a food bank every single month. The Prime Minister doubled Justin Trudeau's deficit. Is he looking to double food bank lines too?

Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House, we are going to continue to focus on affordability measures for Canadians. The groceries and essentials benefit will put up to $1,900 in the pockets of families. We cut the taxes, and they voted against it, of course, for 22 million Canadians. We paused the federal excise tax on gas. We will continue to focus on and deliver for Canadians. That side can continue with the empty rhetoric.

title: Oral Questions: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship
turns: Mr. Speaker, there was a recent news story about a 28-year-old man named Reza Mahmoudian, who is out of work and sent out more than 100 job applications. He did not get a single callback. He says he wants to use his skills in the construction industry, but he is still looking for a contractor who is eager to teach him. Canada's economy is shedding jobs, but lobbyists are pushing for higher immigration so they do not have to train people like Reza or pay them market wages. When will the minister set immigration levels for Reza, instead of for corporate lobbyists who do not want to train him or pay him a fair market wage?

Mr. Speaker, the immigration levels plan reflects a consultation that has been carried out not just with employers but with leaders across the country. That is with municipal governments, and we are further engaging provincial governments as well. The numbers the Conservatives have cited here, such as the number cited earlier by the hon. Leader of the Opposition, for example, are projected numbers for 2027. We will see what the actual number is. Regardless, the key point on this, and this is what unravels the Conservative argument, I am afraid, is that 70% of the positions will be made up of individuals already in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, do members know who the Prime Minister did not consult with? He did not consult with the newcomer who comes to Canada, who now knows it means being an indentured worker at a coffee shop, or it means handing their life savings over to a scam college while sleeping 10 deep in a basement suite. Being a newcomer to Canada under the Prime Minister means being used as a tool for corporate lobbyists to drive down wages. We have to get emotional about this. We have to make sure that immigration levels support workers. When will the immigration minister stop treating workers like profit units and reduce levels so that workers can get trained and paid a fair wage?

Mr. Speaker, our obligation always is to Canadians and Canadian workers. That is why the government has put forward a skills training program that will see 100,000 young Canadians trained in the skilled trades in the next five years. We need to build this country up. We need young, talented energy to make that happen. Conservatives talk about immigration. There is a one-time measure in this budget that would see, among others, temporary residents or non-permanent residents, Ukrainians and Hong Kongers, offered a pathway to permanent residence. A number of Conservative MPs are on record calling for exactly that outcome, but they do not want that now all of a sudden.

Mr. Speaker, the government forgets there is a human cost to its decisions. Prashant was 44 and the father of three kids, aged 14, 10 and three. He came to an Edmonton ER with chest pain he described as a 15 out of 10. The ER was so busy that they gave him Tylenol and told him to wait. Eight hours later, he stood up, put his hand on his chest and died. This is not an isolated case. Our hospitals cannot keep up, but the Prime Minister just announced that he plans to add another 650,000 permanent resident admissions next year. This is by far the highest in Canadian history. How many of these newcomers will suffer like Prashant in overcrowded emergency rooms?
Mr. Speaker, we are building Canada strong, and we are doing that with incredible talent, both here in Canada and with newcomers who have come to Canada to offer their talent—

Mr. Speaker, speaking from both sides of their mouth, as we hear today, and demonizing immigration as a result of the way that they are doing politics, is not exactly the way that we build Canada strong. In fact, what we are doing on our side of the House is making sure that people have the skills, the talent and the opportunity to participate in the project of our lifetime, which is to build up our fine country.

title: Oral Questions: The Economy
turns: Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are spending lots of money. They are just not licensing any new doctors. It is an awful lot like the money they are wasting while Canadians have empty stomachs and fridges. The Prime Minister—

Mr. Speaker, they spend lots of money. They do not get any results for Canadians here at home. While folks in this country have empty stomachs, empty fridges and empty bank accounts, the Prime Minister throws away money on foreign countries. The PBO reported spending is up $333 billion under the Prime Minister, with 60% going to day-to-day operations. It is here today, gone tomorrow, like half a billion dollars for Brazil. Why is the Prime Minister sending our money out of this country when our people cannot afford to eat here at home?

Mr. Speaker, I know it is Wednesday and I have good news for the Leader of the Opposition. It is called “Masters of our destiny”, budget 2026. That is what this country is about: building resiliency, investing in our growth and affordability. There is more than $22 billion in affordability measures in this budget to help Canadians. We will see whether the Conservatives stand up and do one thing, which is to vote for the bill we presented that would help 12 million Canadians. On this side of the House, we will always be on the side of Canadians and build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, they are on the side of corrupt foreign governments, giving half a billion dollars to a country that has an even bigger economy than we do here in Canada, claiming that it has something to do with the rainforest, the same rainforest the Prime Minister's company helped destroy. Nine thousand hectares of land was destroyed by Brookfield. Now he takes half a billion dollars of Canadians' money, supposedly for the same thing. This is part of a $13-billion fund that works out to almost $1,000 per Canadian family. How can Canadians pay their own bills?

Mr. Speaker, I have some good news for the Leader of the Opposition. He is going to have a chance to support the forestry industry in Canada. We are introducing the first-ever national forestry program and investing $6.5 billion in this industry. He has an opportunity to vote for that. Let us see what he does.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians cannot afford to pay their bills, and the Prime Minister is throwing away their money all around the world to the benefit of foreign countries and foreign corporations. Whether it is gender-just rice in Vietnam, supposedly the rainforest in Brazil with his friend Lula or countless other foreign ventures that do nothing to pay the bills, why is it the Prime Minister is so content to send our money out of this country? Why will he not put Canadians first for a change?

Mr. Speaker, again, the member has an opportunity to support us. He has an opportunity to support the 18,000 jobs at Darlington, the thousands of jobs that go with Pacific link, the thousands of jobs that go with the expansion of the LNG industry and the thousands of jobs that go with clean energy. What do they do? They vote against it every single time.

Mr. Speaker, a single father is at a grocery checkout, with milk, bread, ground beef, blueberries, potatoes, butter and carrots. The price adds up. When the juice boxes scan, there is dread. He is over budget. Picture him holding up the line, with his kids, telling the cashier he cannot afford it. Meanwhile, the Prime Minister just pledged over half a billion dollars to a communist in Brazil for a save-the-trees fundraiser. Before another Canadian father has to deal with that shame, will the Prime Minister pick up the phone, call Brazil and tell it Canadian families will not bankroll its national landscaping project?

Mr. Speaker, first of all, we care deeply about supporting Canadians. We see it with our one million homes retrofits, our groceries and essentials benefit and the work that we are doing time and time again. However, I do want to correct some of the misinformation about the funding that went to the tropical forest forever facility. First of all, it is a loan to a fund that is co-managed by Norway. It is going to protect one billion hectares of tropical forests in 70 countries. Other donors include Germany, the U.K., France, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. This is actually a good thing.

title: Routine Proceedings: Veterans' Week
turns: Mr. Speaker, as Veterans' Week begins and Canadians prepare to gather on Remembrance Day, we are reminded of a simple truth: Remembrance matters. Across our country, Canadians will gather in communities large and small. They will stand at cenotaphs and memorials, wear a poppy, observe a moment of silence and remember. They will remember generations of Canadians who answered the call to serve in times of peace, war, conflict and uncertainty. They will reflect on those who never returned home and on those whose lives were forever changed by service. Their courage helped protect the freedoms we enjoy today. Their sacrifices helped safeguard the democratic institutions that define our country. The Canada we know today was shaped not only by the service they gave, but by the sacrifices they made. However, remembrance is not only about those who served in the past. It is also about recognizing service that continues today. We see it in those who continue to serve Canada in uniform. We see it in veterans, whose commitment to our country continues long after their service has ended. As we begin Veterans' Week, we do so carrying heavy hearts following the recent loss of four members of the Canadian Armed Forces at CFB Wainwright: Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark. Our hearts are with their families, friends and fellow service members. We see the profound impact of this loss on all who knew and loved them. Canadians share in their sorrow. We will remember those we have lost, those injured and those still recovering, and we recognize the grief being felt across the Canadian Armed Forces among military families, throughout the veteran community and by Canadians from coast to coast to coast. Canada sees every veteran, every serving member and the families who stand beside them. Canada is grateful for their service, and Canada will always honour their contributions to our country. No one serves alone. Behind every veteran and every serving member are families who share the realities of military life, families who endure separation, relocation, uncertainty and sacrifice in service. In a country as diverse as Canada, remembrance remains one of the moments that bring us together. Canadians come from different backgrounds, live in different regions and hold different perspectives, yet during Veterans' Week, we are united in gratitude for those who have worn Canada's uniform. We are also privileged to serve in this House alongside colleagues who have worn Canada's uniform and continue their service to Canada in public life. It is a responsibility shared by all Canadians. Remembrance is not passive; it is an active responsibility to learn the stories of those who served, to remember them and to ensure that their sacrifices are never forgotten. As November 11 approaches, Canadians can fulfill that responsibility through simple but meaningful actions. Wear a poppy, attend a ceremony or thank a veteran or serving member. These actions may seem small, but they are how remembrance endures: through a conversation, a handshake, a young person learning a veteran's story or a community gathering together. Veterans Week is a time of reflection, a time of gratitude and a time to recommit ourselves to remembering, so let us choose remembrance. Let us honour those who served by ensuring that their stories continue to be told. Let us honour their sacrifices, not only in words but through actions. Lest we forget.

We will remember them: the Canadians who have served and continue to serve our country. It is a tradition of service that men and women, and in fact those who we would say are boys and girls, have engaged in selflessly for as long as we have been a country and before we became one. We will remember them: those in the First World War and the Second World War, and those who answered the calls to Korea and Afghanistan. We honour those who served in the Persian Gulf and those who kept the peace in Cyprus and the Balkans. We must recognize the men and women who continue to serve today, including those deployed at this moment in Latvia with our NATO partners and allies in defence of freedom and security. We remember those who serve at home in disasters, emergencies and training. This point hits home especially hard this year as we reflect on the tragedy that recently took place at CFB Wainwright. Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding, Private Hayden Lykkemark and Sergeant Morgan Wong fell in service to our country on our own soil, while training to mitigate risk while abroad but knowing that their service here at home carried risk as well. Thirty-nine of their brothers and sisters were also injured, including more than two dozen who are still in hospital. Their families are preparing for a life of, in the case of the four who perished, grief and loss, and for the families of those injured, a life of finding ways to support them. I would also like to note the veterans and members of the Canadian Armed Forces whom we have lost to suicide. Their deaths do not diminish their service. They do not diminish their sacrifice. We need to look on those members with dignity and compassion and to thank them for their service. As the rolls of the fallen continue to grow, in this very building we have the Books of Remembrance. I encourage anyone who has the privilege to join us here for a tour of this great place, and all my colleagues who serve here, to take a moment to visit the Room of Remembrance to see the names of our fallen, the men and women, some of whom were just boys and girls, who signed up to serve our country selflessly. The act of remembrance is so important. It is wonderful to look across the House and see everyone wearing a poppy, and to see that in our streets. I encourage everyone to buy a poppy and to wear it proudly, to visit a cenotaph service on Remembrance Day, to visit the grave of a veteran, to thank a serving member and to thank a former member of our Canadian Armed Forces. Members who have served know how important a buddy check is, to check in to ask how someone is doing. They do not have to give us any details or a response beyond an acknowledgement, but checking in on them counts, as does thanking them for their service. It is not something anyone joins to receive bouquets of roses thrown to them. They do it selflessly, so please thank them. The number of names continues to grow, of those we lose every year, those who have served, but we are blessed to live in a country where men and women continue to sign up to serve, protect and defend what we are so blessed to enjoy here. Our gratitude cannot be measured simply by our words of remembrance but must also be measured by our deeds. We collectively need to do better every single day in delivering on our obligations to the men and women who have served Canada. They serve us with unlimited liability. We need to repay that by making sure we take care of them when their service concludes. It is something we all need to put our shoulder to the wheel to do for them, just as they did for us.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise to offer Remembrance Day remarks on behalf of the New Democratic Party of Canada and our leader, Avi Lewis. As Veterans Week begins and communities across Canada prepare to gather for Remembrance Day, we come together to honour all those who have served our country in uniform. We remember those who never came home; we remember those who returned carrying wounds, both visible and invisible; and we honour the families whose love, strength and sacrifice sustained those who served and who serve. This year, Remembrance Day is made even more poignant by the recent loss of four Canadian Armed Forces members during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright: Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark. Many more were injured, some gravely. As their loved ones grapple with this unfathomable, heartbreaking loss, we stand with them today in their grief. Behind every uniform is a human being: a son or daughter, a brother or sister, a partner, a parent, a friend. When tragedy strikes, it is not just military families that mourn, but entire communities and a grateful nation. That is why we wear a poppy, not as a symbol of military glory but as a symbol of remembrance and gratitude; a reminder of lives interrupted, of futures never realized and of the profound human cost of war. The history of military service in Canada is not one story but many, each bound by the same willingness to sacrifice for their country. One of the most remarkable chapters in this history is the service of indigenous veterans. Even when they were denied the rights of their fellow citizens, first nations, Inuit and Métis peoples answered our nation's call. They served with courage and distinction, fighting for freedom overseas even while facing injustice at home. As I hail from Vancouver, I must also recount to this House the many moving ceremonies I have experienced at the Chinatown Memorial Monument in historic Chinatown, along with my colleague from Vancouver East. Like their indigenous comrades, Chinese Canadian soldiers also bravely served overseas while facing discrimination and denial of their own civil rights by the society they valiantly defended. Their contributions, sacrifices and resilience must never be forgotten. Canada stands proud of the oversized contributions that we have made in the cause of freedom. In the First World War, over 600,000 people served, out of a population of eight million. From daring exploits in the air to their unbelievable courage at places like Ypres and Vimy Ridge, Canadian soldiers helped birth the independent country we know today. More than one million Canadians took up arms to defeat fascism during the Second World War, one of humanity's darkest chapters. They stormed the beaches of Normandy, fought through Italy, sailed dangerous Atlantic convoys, liberated occupied peoples and helped defeat the Nazi regime and its machinery of genocide. As fewer veterans of those generations remain with us, the responsibility to carry forward their stories now belongs to all of us. That sacred duty extends to Canadians who served in Korea, the Balkans, Afghanistan, on peacekeeping missions and countless operations undertaken in the service of all of us. In honouring this service, we must also recognize the brutal reality of war. Those who have witnessed it first-hand understand, like no others, that beneath the language of strategy, of victory and of national interest lies something far more profound. War's true cost is measured in shattered families, lifelong trauma and lives that can never be restored. It invariably kills and wounds the innocent as well as the enemy. It destroys property, cities and cultural monuments. Its consequences outlive the conflicts themselves. That is why remembrance is not about celebrating war. It is about understanding its tragedy and renewing our commitment to peace. It also calls us to action. The greatest tribute we can pay our veterans lies in how we treat them when they return home. To fully honour veterans, we must ensure timely access to health care; provide robust support for mental health and operational stress injuries; and ensure that no veteran is ever left homeless, isolated or living in poverty. We must keep the promises made when they answered our country's call. Remembrance requires more than gratitude. It demands respect and resources. Most importantly to veterans, it demands that we work for a world in which our children are never again asked to bear the brutal burdens of war. As we all gather in our communities this week, let us reach out and do something simple but meaningful, such as wear a poppy, attend a ceremony, thank a veteran, listen to their stories and share those stories with the next generation. In the end, we remember because democracy, freedom and human rights have never come without sacrifice. We remember because the most fitting way to honour those who served is to build a country worthy of their sacrifice, and a country that cares for its veterans, rejects the forces of hatred and strives always for a more just, compassionate and peaceful world for all. Lest we forget.

title: Government Orders: Connected Care for Canadians Act
turns: Through Bill S-5, we can make technology work for Canadians, improving lives, improving care and building a more efficient health care system ready for the future. Australia and the European Union have already implemented similar legislation or regulations. Their residents have benefited from connected health care for years. If we act now, we can ensure that Canadians have access to the connected care they need and deserve. Access to health information is not a matter of convenience. It is a necessity. Data saves lives, especially when a full medical history is needed in an emergency. Let me share the stories of real patients and their families. They have experienced the devastating consequences of disconnected care in Canada. Theresa lost her son, Dan, who was only 17, after two visits to the emergency department. She believes real-time access to his file would have helped the family flag critical details sooner. Another patient requiring an urgent surgical procedure outside her home province was compromised because the local medical team could not access vital records from her home province. Without this essential medical history, clinicians were unable to safely perform the procedure. There is the story of Greg Price, whose legacy has been an inspiration for many of us working on this legislation. Greg was a healthy engineer from Alberta who faced systemic failures in our health care system. Like many others, he experienced delays due to poor coordination and inaccessible health information. He died of cancer in 2012. He was 31. This is why today's legislation is so important. We need to break down those silos, so we are changing the rules and we are building the health data infrastructure Canadians deserve. Canadians strongly support change and want better access to their own health data.

Madam Speaker, I was really struck by my colleague's comment that 92% of practising physicians have been hampered by lack of access to information about their patients. The Canadian Medical Association and other medical organizations have been calling for this for a decade. The Competition Tribunal, in June 2022, identified the behaviour of electronic medical record providers as being anti-competitive, and of course we had Bill C-72 before the previous Parliament. My question for the minister, given that the Liberals let Bill C-72 die on the Order Paper when they called an election last January, is, what took them so long?

Madam Speaker, Dr. Margot Burnell, the past president of the CMA, stated: When personal health information can travel freely and securely between patients, clinics, hospitals and labs, people will have better health outcomes and doctors will have more time to focus on care. It also makes it easier for patients to manage their own care in partnership with doctors and other health professionals. I know this is echoed by the new, incoming president. The government has been working on a pan-Canadian interoperability road map for years. What is the difference this time, and what concrete timeline would the government commit to so Canadians are not still hearing about the promise of connected care in five years or 10 years from now? This is something the NDP has been calling on for a long time, and I have been working with the minister on it.

Madam Speaker, I was interested in the point the minister made about Ontario and Quebec already having legislation that this legislation would not supersede. This interested me in particular because, as a physician practising in Ontario, I know that the clinical notes from one hospital that I worked at over the last few years in Guelph, Ontario, could be viewed in the region west of Toronto, but I also worked in Kingston, Ontario, over that time, and clinical notes from my other work in Guelph could not be viewed in that region. Even Ontario has not resolved this problem within the province. I wonder if we are talking about whether Ontario has legislation that calls for this, or about whether Ontario has a reality of interoperability between all the regions in Ontario. Would Bill S-5 affect Ontario as it stands today or not?

Madam Speaker, the minister's enthusiasm for the bill is very well appreciated. The issue of health information technology is very near and dear to my heart, and not always in a happy way. Without naming any names of any particular institutions, one of the hospitals that I worked at for a long time foisted on physicians a health information technology solution without asking the physicians, the pharmacists or the nurses if they should do this or whether it was a good idea. They spent millions of dollars on it, and it frankly ruined our professional lives when it did not work at all. It is important to have good intentions. It is important to be enthusiastic about those intentions, but it is really important that the solutions that end up hitting the ground actually work for the people who use them and for the people those professionals serve. We have to be really careful about a bill like this. The possibility of causing more problems than it solves is a real and present danger. It is always a great honour to be in the chamber. It is always a great honour to speak on behalf of the people of Kitchener South—Hespeler. It is a great honour to give the Conservative response to the minister's speech. This is, I believe, the first piece of legislation pertaining to health care in the 45th Parliament. It has been a long time coming. It has been a year and a half. I am a bit sad to say this is a bill that is warmed over from the last Parliament, when it somehow did not make it through. It has been years coming, and for that reason I would hold it to an even higher standard than if it were invented de novo. The bill before us today, Bill S-5, has the admittedly laudable goal of making it illegal for health information technology companies to engage in what the bill defines as data blocking, that is, stopping the exchange, or impeding the exchange, of personal health information between authorized health information technologies. In sharp contradistinction to many of the government bills that we have been debating over this past month, or even this past week, this is a very short bill. I commend it for that reason. It is perhaps only five pages long, in one language. Even though it is easy to read the bill, which I am grateful for, it is very difficult for me to understand how it could, in fact, work. I spent 95% of my clinical career in hospitals. There are three electronic medical record vendors that hospitals in Canada use very commonly: Epic, Cerner and Meditech. All three, I am sorry to say, are American companies. All three are subject to a 2016 law passed by the Obama administration called the Cures Act. My understanding is that the Cures Act is very similar, both in its intent and its operations, to the bill before us today, Bill S-5. Of course, it would be ideal, internationally, that all three of these systems be able to transmit patient health information between each other, obviously with the consent of the patient involved, but it is a really hard problem. This morning, for instance, my office printer was on the fritz. I was unable to send data, this speech, from my computer to the printer in my office. I had to get a friend in the lobby to print it for me, and that is a much simpler problem than all of the health information in all of Canada. Software vendors and Bill S-5 can have the best of intentions, but the problem of data interoperability is just a hard problem. Let us take, for instance, Meditech. Currently, Meditech has multiple products, multiple product families and different versions of each currently operating in the wild. There is Meditech 6.0, Meditech 6.1, Meditech Expanse, Meditech Expanse 2.1, Meditech Expanse 2.2. Different hospitals may choose to invest more or less money, or use one product family over another. They may choose to update whichever product family they are using often or not, depending on their own IT and human resources. I imagine it is a full-time job, nay several full-time jobs, at Meditech headquarters just to make sure that its own systems can communicate with each other in an interoperable fashion. That is not for a lack of trying. How much work, how many people and how much money will it take to make the Meditech system talk to the Epic system, to make both talk to Cerner and to make all three talk to the 10 to 15 major players in the European market? How much of a barrier of entry to one day starting a Canadian competitor would all of this entail? Let us drill down on a small part of the problem to understand the full scale of the problem. In my work as an ICU physician, any individual patient might have literally tens of thousands of data points stored in the EMR from just one day. Just their vital signs, such as heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, body temperature and blood pressure, might be recorded and time-stamped continuously, providing thousands of data points before we even speak of medications, diagnostic imaging, clinical notes, blood work, etc. Each of these data points has to be filed or coded in some agreed upon, legible way in order to be interoperable. Even to zero in on just blood pressure, there are multiple numbers that go into a blood pressure reading and different numbers one might want to store, such as the systolic, the diastolic and the mean arterial pressure. There are different ways of measuring a blood pressure, namely a sphygmomanometer or a blood pressure cuff, or invasive arterial monitoring. Sometimes we are measuring both continuously throughout the day. One system might store, code and display the cuff systolic and the intra-arterial map every 15 minutes. My system might store, code and display only the cuff three times a day, or when an intra-arterial pressure is available, it might store that, superseding the other. It seems almost impossible to have a government regulatory body come in and say which one is correct. The sphygmomanometer, the intra-arterial blood pressure monitor, the EKG and the pulse oximeter all measure a patient's heart rate, and three of the four measure it continuously. How do we impose a system that ensures that each health vendor will store those in mutually comprehensible ways? Let us consider a patient on continuous EKG monitoring. Literally every beat of their heart comes with multiple measurable waveforms depending on which EKG is looked at. Each monitoring system will come with different alarms and different ways of storing who responded to each alarm, how long the alarm went off, who turned it off and why they turned it off. I cannot imagine setting one standard for how all of this ought to be captured. This is not like saying all smart phones have to use a USB-C plug. There are so many more inputs and outputs to a human body that constitute health information. When I speak of monitoring vital signs, I am speaking of a fraction of a fraction of all the forms of data that go into health and health care. I have just now been speaking about electronic medical records, only one of the types of software we would find in a hospital. There are also prescription management systems, diagnostic imaging systems and scheduling systems, all of which contain personal health information. By the way, health care centres like hospitals are just one sort of organization that uses some classes of devices and some sorts of information technology on those devices. Bill S-5 seems to seek to regulate all sorts of other devices. For instance, I am wearing an Apple Watch. It went off, and the Speaker got mad at me. It also stores personal health information of mine on it, such as my heart rate. If someone has a CPAP machine at home or a blood sugar monitor, the bill would seem to make demands on those device manufacturers as well. This is just the present state of things. Health information technology is changing now at a faster and faster rate. A friend of mine runs an AI-powered ultrasound diagnostics start-up company for use by combat medics to see if a soldier in the field has a pneumothorax in real time. It is a pocket-sized device. It is an amazing invention. He worked so hard on it. He employs so many fantastic Canadian scientists who are designing it and making it better every day. I understand that he spends about 0% of his time making sure that whatever data is stored on that device in a battlefield somewhere can talk to Cerner, Epic and Meditech. He is trying to save lives by making something that has never existed before. How can he expect that whatever data his invention ends up outputting 10 years from now will be legible by these legacy systems? I am hoping that this House will take seriously the scale of the problem that Bill S-5 is trying to make go away. As I said earlier in my speech, the bill closely follows the approach that the Obama administration took in 2016, 10 years ago. Did this approach work in that milieu? If it pleases the House, I would love to table at some point a paper from November 2025 published in the Journal of the American Medical Association and written by Everson et al., entitled “EHR Interoperability Experiences Reported by Family Physicians”. The scientists surveyed more than 8,000 family doctors, asking them what their experience with health information interoperability has been like eight years after the Cures Act. I am sorry to say that despite the best of intentions, the results in this paper are dismal. Only 8% of the family doctors surveyed reported ideal interoperability. From my reading of the paper, it seemed that a majority of the doctors went so far as to give up on accessing outside clinical documentation. I hope we can talk more about this study at committee. Perhaps we could invite the authors of it to committee, should the bill succeed at second reading. If it is the case that the U.S. administration, after eight years of trying, largely failed to regulate the big American health information technology vendors I mentioned, Cerner, Meditech and Epic, how can we expect that the Canadian federal government would succeed in regulating those same American health information technology vendors into making their systems interoperable? As I said, most Canadian hospitals use information technology from these American providers. Many of the Canadian hospitals I have personally worked at, however, cannot afford to use the latest systems or subscribe to the most up-to-date features from each of these vendors. Is it really possible that Canadian regulators will be able to bully these gigantic corporations? Cerner is, in fact, by the way, the health information branch of Oracle, one of the largest tech companies in the world. Are we going to be able to demand that Oracle change what it is doing into solving what I fear may be an unsolvable problem when we are currently shopping in its bargain bin? Is it the case that the federal government has a good track record generally in the field of IT systems management? Who among us here could forget the $2.6-billion boondoggle that we now call the Phoenix pay system? Who could forget the $60-million arrive scam scandal? Who could forget the most recent scandal of all, the $300 million blown on the unworkable PrescribeIT program? I, for one, am not going to forget the PrescribeIT scandal. I think anyone who is familiar with my parliamentary work knows about PrescribeIT by now, because it has been the biggest part of what I have been working on over the last year. In brief, not to belabour the point, as I know the health minister is very familiar with it, it was a 10-year-long attempt by an organization called Canada Health Infoway, which receives funding both from provinces and from the federal government, to solve a simple problem. Ten years ago, when she introduced the legislation that gave the money for PrescribeIT, the minister of health at the time, Jane Philpott, called it the axe the fax program. Members are aware, of course, how much Liberals like rhyming three-word slogans such as axe the fax. Right now, in our country, physicians fax prescriptions to pharmacies. That was the case in 2016 when Jane Philpott introduced the legislation. Canada Health Infoway spent $300 million and took 10 years to make just this small class of health information transfer digitally between a doctor's office or hospital and a pharmacy. We have investigated this matter at committee in some detail. To this day, I do not understand how it is that Canada Health Infoway invented something other than a digital fax, which has existed since 1998. Indeed, by its own admission, it invented nothing. It gave Telus $80 million to provide and manage the software platform, which already existed. That was a good deal for Telus. To this day, our study of this matter at committee having been truncated, I still have no idea what became of the other $220 million. It had a $300-million budget. It bought the software and had Telus managing it for $80 million. I do not know where the $220 million went. After all of that money and all of that time, physicians and pharmacists in our country, by and large, refused to use the solution. Canada Health Infoway seems to have spent a decade designing, or not designing but ordering, a software solution from Telus, without bothering to check in with frontline workers whether they liked the product or whether they would agree to use the product. The product was free, and still over 95% of physicians in our country declined to use the product. That is really bad and frankly activates my PTSD from my home hospital, which had foisted an information management system on us all those years ago. Of all the dogs that have never hunted, the PrescribeIT dog really did not hunt. It was a free solution that 95% of physicians and pharmacists declined to take up. With Phoenix, arrive scam and PrescribeIT, there is not a good track record. Maybe the federal government is about to turn over a new leaf and provide IT systems that work and that people want to use. I wish I could believe that, but do members know who it plans to put in charge of Bill S-5? Can anyone in the House guess? It is Canada Health Infoway, the totally corrupt organization that just blew $300 million on a failed solution. I know this is the Liberals' plan by word of mouth, but I also know it from Senate testimony. This bill is called Bill S-5 because it came from the Senate. It has already gone through Senate committee hearings, and that has been the clear message. They had the now interim CEO of Canada Health Infoway give testimony. It is their intention to oversee the regulation of this perhaps unsolvable problem. For those who have not heard, Canada Health Infoway just fired its CEO because he came to the health committee to answer questions about PrescribeIT. He refused to answer the most basic questions about what he accomplished with his nearly $1-million salary. He would not even answer what his salary was. We had to get that information by other means. Its current CEO is the former vice-president, whom he hired. The $300-million PrescribeIT boondoggle is not even Canada Health Infoway's total spend over the last decade. I believe the organization was in receipt of $1 billion of public money over this time, yet when we had the chair of the board at the health committee and I asked him what it accomplished with the other $700 million, he was unable to describe a single tangible achievement. This is a big problem. Even acknowledging that PrescribeIT did not work, acknowledging that the CEO of Canada Health Infoway was a big problem and acknowledging the extent to which the health minister took credit or did not for his dismissal, even after all that occurred, she planned to reward Canada Health Infoway with another $50 million of funding this year. I came to question period week after week and asked why she would give it this money. To her credit, the minister halted that funding, acknowledging that this organization is in a serious state of disrepair. This is a big problem when we talk about Bill S-5. It is, to my understanding, still the Liberals' intention to have Canada Health Infoway lead the charge on regulating into existence a solution that is maybe not even possible when they have not accounted for the last $1 billion they spent. Do I support Bill S-5 in principle? Of course I do. Of course health information technology should be interoperable. Of course no patient should ever have their care suffer because data transfer between institutions is hard. Do I believe that the government, with its track record of IT boondoggles and its track record with Canada Health Infoway, will succeed in getting this job done with this piece of very short legislation? I fear I do not. I want to hear more about it at committee. I certainly want to hear more from Canada Health Infoway on what its plan was, but I cannot say that I have great faith that it will work out. Solving a problem like the one I have described is not a matter of intention. For instance, I do not want anyone in this country to be sad. If we were to make a law that no one is allowed to be sad anymore, it would not work. That was the question I asked the minister. She said it seemed to be the case that Bill S-5 would not even apply to Ontario because Ontario already has legislation with this intention. However, the reality in Ontario, as I described in my question, is not that health information technologies are interoperable. In the discussion and debate we have in this House, I would love for the government to explain why it will succeed where Ontario has failed if it already has similar legislation.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate that the member clearly indicated that how health information technology is handled is absolutely critical and that he supports the principle of the legislation. I am encouraged by that. In terms of the whole mismanagement area, it was the Harper government that brought in Phoenix. There is no escaping that. In other words, there are ways in which, no doubt, we can learn from past experiences in order to advance the principle of a good idea. I appreciate the member's knowledge, I must say. I am quite impressed with his background and his understanding of the urgency of this. I believe that it would be best addressed at the committee stage. I wonder if he could provide his thoughts on whether he thinks this legislation will pass, given that the Senate has already supported it in principle.

Madam Speaker, I think this is becoming a bit of a running gag. After literally every speech I give in this House, the member for Winnipeg North stands and says, “but Stephen Harper”. I suspect that he checks under his bed for Stephen Harper before he goes to sleep at night. In general, I criticized the federal government trying to do things that cannot be done. This is a vast country. If this problem were solvable, it would be solvable close to home at a low level. If a single province cannot get this done within its borders, I do not understand how any federal government, Stephen Harper's or otherwise, would be able to achieve that. Is it still a good idea to do something that is well-intentioned but doomed to failure? Part of the answer to that is how much money the Liberals plan to spend on their well-intentioned, doomed project.

Madam Speaker, I think it is dangerous. There are two major dangers that I see. One is to free enterprise. If we have some giant regulator, unaccountable to the House, making decisions about what constitutes interoperability, how is that going to affect my friend? He is a professor of medicine. He is, frankly, a genius. He is trying to develop this ultrasound AI-powered technology. It would be easy for the regulator to put restrictions on him that would make it almost impossible for him to enter the market unless he lives up to the standard that the fat cats like Cerner and Meditech get the regulator to adopt. There is a real risk of protectionism and the choking out of health care innovation. I have read the Canadian Constitution front to back a few times. It talks about hospitals being under provincial jurisdiction. We have the Public Health Agency, we have Health Canada, and we have the Canada Health Act. It seems that in many ways in this country, health care currently comes under federal jurisdiction, and the words “health care” do not appear in Canada's written constitution, at least.

Madam Speaker, it is important to hear from somebody like my colleague, who has the medical professional background that he does. He has very eloquently expressed a lot of the problems that currently exist. It is very reasonable for Canadians to expect that their data and their information would be available to them wherever they may be, and I think this is a problem that needs to be addressed. It has been a problem in Saskatchewan. It has been a problem in Ontario, as he has highlighted very well. I passed a bill on the copyright side for interoperability, so I appreciate his talking about the need for data interoperability. I am just wondering, on that very specific point, if he has a little more to add to the remarks he made earlier.

Madam Speaker, something the member was driving at that I think is really important is the lens I would want this sort of bill to take. In medicine in general, we have struggled over the last several decades to be more patient-centred and less institutionally centred in our approach. I would love it if this health information technology bill put health information technology more in the hands of patients, if it adopted the patient-centred approach. Instead of a bill telling Epic and Cerner that they have to fulfill Canada Health Infoway's requirements on interoperability, I would love to see a bill that asks Cerner and Epic to put the health information in the hands of the patient to whom the information pertains, and then that patient could choose to hand it over to Epic or to Meditech if and when they see fit.

Madam Speaker, I was also very pleased and very interested by the speech we just heard from someone who obviously knows and cares very much about how health care systems work and should operate. I am curious to hear his point of view on the connection between research, science and health, health data and health clinical work. Does he believe that providing better access to data to researchers, scientists and health experts could lead to better development of technologies and better use of those technologies?

Madam Speaker, I have a fairly straightforward question. I hope we get the same sort of an answer. The member talked originally about the principle of the legislation being something he appreciated. Then, when he answered my question, at the tail end he planted the seed of doubt as to whether the Conservatives would want to see the legislation go to committee. Can the member indicate whether the Conservative Party will be voting in favour of the legislation to go to committee?

Madam Speaker, my understanding is that the Liberal government has a majority in the House. The legislation will pass if the Liberal Party wants to pass it. I am honestly befuddled as to why the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader is so interested in whether we support the legislation. I am not in a position to speak for the Conservative Party today. For myself, I can say I have not made up my mind.

Madam Speaker, I am wondering what additional data the hon. member is looking for, in terms of what the government needs to provide in order to give not just Conservatives but Canadians comfort that the legislation would be implemented well and would provide for good, truly interoperable portable systems.

Madam Speaker, it comes down to trust. It is my understanding, based on the Senate testimony, that the intent is for Canada Health Infoway to lead this effort. I do not trust Canada Health Infoway. It is a really, really difficult technical problem. I understand some things about health care. I understand not a lot of things about information technology. There are very few people, I think, who actually could make regulations that make sense. Unfortunately, I feel that many of them are currently in the employ of Cerner, Meditech and Epic. If more meat could be put on the bones regarding who would actually be doing the regulations, thinking about the regulations, and how much money it would cost to get those people to do it, then perhaps I would have some more trust in this approach overall.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's speech on this important issue today. I was particularly interested in the part about health care transfers. It is not a big ask for the provinces in order to provide the health care that Canadians deserve. It does fall under provincial jurisdiction, but they are asking the federal government for health transfers. I would like to know the member's opinion on the fact that we are spending more taxpayer dollars on servicing our debt than we are on health care transfers in this country.

Madam Speaker, it is great to see you here today. I will be sharing my time with the member for Bourassa. I rise today to support Bill S-5, the connected care for Canadians act, which is crucial to establishing a connected health care system in Canada. In Canada, health information is fragmented and is scattered among hundreds of health information systems across family doctor offices, hospitals, walk-in clinics and pharmacies. Bill S-5 would break down these digital barriers so a patient's health information could move securely and seamlessly wherever they receive care. It means that patients would no longer have to physically carry medical records from one doctor's appointment to another or repeatedly explain their medical history every time they seek care. Bill S-5 is also about making the health care system work better for Canadians. It would unlock the potential of standardized and anonymized health data to accelerate medical breakthroughs and improve health outcomes for all Canadians. Health information in Canada is often stuck in separate digital systems that cannot be easily shared, first, because of data blocking, a practice that prevents authorized users from accessing health data even when privacy legislation allows it, and, second, because of a lack of common standards. For example, one hospital's database could record a patient's blood type using a numeric code, another could use an alphanumeric code, and a third hospital might use a written description. All three could mean exactly the same thing, but without common standards, their computer systems might not recognize each other's blood type entries. To address this, Bill S-5 would require health information vendors in Canada to adopt common standards and would prohibit vendors from data blocking. These standards would be set out and maintained through regulations, with requirements that would ensure secure access for patients within the protection of existing security law. This is the approach used in other jurisdictions as well, such as Australia, the United States and the European Union. Bill S-5 would build on the shared pan-Canadian interoperability road map, already endorsed by provinces and territories, and on the working together to improve health care for Canadians plan, which committed nearly $200 billion over 10 years, with modernizing health data as one of four shared priorities. When somebody sees a new doctor, they are asked for their medical history. Bill S-5 would enable patients and their doctors to access health records electronically, no matter where in Canada patients receive care. This is connected care. Doctors' being able to access electronic health records is critical to the continuity of care. Without a seamless exchange of information between systems and providers, the burden of health information falls to patients and their families. Moreover, the lack of access to a patient's medical records increases the risks of misdiagnoses, medication errors, duplicate testing and treatment delays. Take, for example, patients in rural and remote communities or patients with very complex conditions who are referred to hospitals in major urban centres for advanced diagnostic procedures, complex treatments and highly specialized medical care. Oftentimes these patients arrive in serious condition, usually with photocopies of their health records, and the information is often incomplete. Patients with a language barrier or limited medical familiarity shoulder the burden of coordinating their own care because there is no digital connection between our health information systems. In all these cases, important health information is often missing or inaccessible. Unfortunately, this happens very often. Bill S-5 would help support these patients with a more coordinated and integrated health care system, with accurate and accessible data so doctors can make clinical decisions with complete information and provide the health care Canadians deserve. In today's rapidly evolving world of medical research and innovation, large, high-quality data sets are the foundation of medical breakthroughs such as accelerating drug discoveries and enabling earlier disease detection. For example, the quality, quantity and representativeness of the data sets largely determines how accurately a health AI model performs in real-world settings. Our government's national AI strategy, AI for all, recognizes data as a strategic national asset that must be responsibly stewarded and mobilized to support innovation and productivity across the economy. Our health care system generates a vast amount of health data, spanning diverse populations, medical conditions and care settings. By leveraging our standardized and anonymized health data, Canadian researchers have an opportunity to become global leaders in medical research and health innovation, driving medical breakthroughs and improving health outcomes for all Canadians. Currently, much of this data remains fragmented in disconnected systems. By securely unlocking its potential by applying common standards, our medical researchers can drive breakthroughs in disease detection, treatment and improved hospital efficiency. For example, in my riding of Don Valley North, we are fortunate to have North York General Hospital, Canada's top-ranked community academic hospital. It partnered with a Canadian health AI company, and by leveraging the data it has collected from the emergency department, it has trained an AI model that analyzes real-time patient vitals, waiting times, triage assessments and hospital capacity to identify where patients can receive care sooner. This has cut the average emergency wait time by nearly 28%. Data can save lives. The knowledge that can be unlocked from our health data sets has the power to transform our health care system. Better health data means a more accessible and innovative health care system. That is why Bill S-5 is such a consequential piece of legislation, and I believe it is a practical path forward that would serve the best interests of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, that is an excellent question. As I mentioned in my speech, in a rapidly evolving world with a lot of cybersecurity threats, and with the development of AI, security is definitely top of mind for all of us. The legislation, at the core of it, would block the ability of vendors to block data, while respecting provinces' and territories' ability to also operate within their privacy laws and acts. We are very mindful of that. We will continue to work with the provinces and territories as we write out the regulations, while respecting the provincial and territorial jurisdictions.

Madam Speaker, I am curious as to whether the member for Don Valley North can comment on how a more connected health care system, through Bill S-5, could help Canadians facing barriers to care, especially those living in rural and remote communities across Canada.

Madam Speaker, I mentioned a few examples in my speech of frustration with always having to remember one's medical care record or the history of one's procedures. We have all experienced that. Sometimes we forget, sometimes we may have remembered things wrong, and it proves a hindrance to our care. Sometimes it causes delays, really dangerous delays. We heard the minister mention the example of Theresa and her family. We want to avoid that. As we continue to have discussions with providers, doctors and clinicians are telling us about the importance of having the legislation passed because it would enable data sharing. It would enable more connected care. It would help them facilitate care that is more beneficial to the health outcomes of patients. We are very optimistic about the future of more connected care in Canada that the bill would enable.

Madam Speaker, I believe it is important that we advance the legislation. Back in the nineties, I was the health care critic in the province of Manitoba. Even back then, we were talking about having better access and about patients being able to see their records. I see the legislation as modernizing something that is long overdue. It is in the patient's best interest. Could my colleague provide her thoughts on the patient's best interest and how the bill would support that?

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my friend and colleague for his long-time advocacy for creating this future of connected care in Canada. Absolutely, that is the goal for all of us, to provide the reality of more connected care in our communities. For far too long, and far too often, we have heard frustrations about remembering one's medical records, having misdiagnoses, having mistreatments or delays. We all want that to improve. This bill would not only provide a path to that for clinicians and health authorities. It would also provide patients with the autonomy of having their personal data and more connected care for everybody .

Madam Speaker, what really resonated with me is what my colleague and friend said about breaking down silos and creating the condition for connected care. That is exactly what this bill is aiming to do. My colleague mentioned that in Quebec, there is already a system in place for that, so I want to ask him to describe the benefits he is already seeing in his community and the benefits he wishes to see once we have a connected system across the country.

Madam Speaker, I think there is a reasonable expectation among Canadians that their health data should move with them. I am from Saskatchewan. If I had a health incident here in Ontario, I would want to know that it would be very easy for my health data to be readily available to whoever is providing the service that I needed in that particular moment. I think it is important that it be up to the individual, in a sense, to decide where that data is available, so I wonder if the member has any ideas, with the bill, on how to make the individual, not so much a company and maybe not even a regional authority, the ultimate person to say that, yes, they want their health data to be available, either across the country or in certain provinces.

Madam Speaker, I will be splitting my time. This bill is very easy for the people of Nanaimo—Ladysmith to associate with. To be diagnosed with a chronic illness in Nanaimo—Ladysmith really is to find out how transportation works in British Columbia, because we inevitably need to receive treatment not only in Nanaimo but also in Victoria, in Vancouver or sometimes in other places on the island. We know very well what the consequences are of medical information not being available where we receive our medical care. Those consequences include misdiagnoses, non-diagnoses, wrong medication and lower quality of care as a result. The reason we need to receive health care all over the island and the mainland, and in some cases why we need to go to other places in our community, is that the Nanaimo Regional General Hospital, which is the main hospital in Nanaimo and the area, has about 345 hospital beds. However, I cannot remember a day when the number of patients in the hospital, when I have been there either visiting someone or for another reason, has been below 400. This means that we travel for health care, and we know what happens when our medical records are not available. We understand the problems that come with needing to stop, find information and have it faxed over from one place to another. In B.C., in fact, we have more than 40 different electronic medical record systems, which are used across health authorities, specialists and family practices. We understand the consequences when those systems do not talk to each other. The BC College of Family Physicians reports that more than 78% of doctors use between two and five systems. Believe it or not, that is actually by design, and it puts our lives in danger. What this bill deals with is a phenomenon known in the health care world as “data blocking”. The minister admitted and said in her speech this morning that 92% of doctors in Canada have said that a lack of access to patient medical records hampers their ability to provide care. Health Canada has reported that only 29% of primary care providers share patient information electronically outside of their practice. That is one of the reasons the Canadian Medical Association and other medical health organizations have been calling for a decade or more for electronic medical records to be available where and when health care providers need them. Dr. Margot Burnell, who is a previous Canadian Medical Association president, has described this as doctors facing “an uphill battle trying to provide timely patient care when they are routinely dealing with health systems that cannot communicate with each other”. That makes this bill a very long time coming. In fact, it is not the government's first attempt to bring this forward. Bill C-72 died on the Order Paper in the last Parliament because the Liberals decided that it was more important for them to go to an election. We ask two questions on this side of the House. The first question is, what took the government so long? Why has it taken this long to bring in a bill that Canadians so badly need and that has been called for by patient advocates, by medical professionals and by patients? The other question is, why did it take the government 18 months to introduce this bill in the House when this bill so clearly needs to be implemented to save lives? The next question we need to ask about a bill like this when it is being brought forward by the government is, what do we need to do to make sure it will get this right? We cannot afford another software debacle or failure in this particular case. We cannot afford for Canadians' medical records to become unavailable or get scrambled the way we have seen with so many other programs the government has tried to implement in the software space. Whether it is PrescribeIT, Cúram, or some of the other problems that we have had, we cannot afford to see that happen in this space. In that context, it is distressing to have learned from the Senate's testimony here, and I believe my colleague recounted this earlier, that the government is considering hiring Canada Health InfoWay to administer this particular program. That is a situation where, given the management issues and health care issues with that organization, specifically those related to health care software in the past, Canadians may have some very reasonable concerns. A second issue that I really believe we need to deal with at committee is a number of definitional concerns. The idea of contextual interoperability can mean different things in different circumstances. We must ensure that the data that travels in between systems, when the software interoperability is implemented, is seamless, is not another data dump, is readable on the other end and is usable. Similarly, we need to ensure that there are clear definitions for terms such as “data blocking”, “good enforcement mechanisms”, and “real remedies for failure”. The Competition Bureau pointed out in 2022, which is another reason why we are asking why this is taking so long, that electronic medical record vendors were, in fact, blocking data deliberately. This bill is now targeting those problems, including vendor lock-in, data blocking and the unreadable data dumps I just discussed, so it is very important that the bill expand the information-blocking penalties to include hospital networks and authorities that sit outside of these systems and may further hamper interoperability. The Senate committee on this bill recognized that vendors are only one part of a wider health data system and recommended that the government consider extending responsibility as I have described. I would recommend that the House committee that examines this bill take a look at that gap, because software can only make the record available. Someone still has to complete the referral, the transfer, and get it to the clinician who is taking over care. Privacy is also something that needs a very precise answer with respect to this bill. Section 5 of the bill says that the interoperability duty does not require access, use or exchange where privacy law prohibits it, but clause 6's data-blocking prohibition has no equivalent expressed privacy law exception. I would note here that the Office of the Privacy Commissioner supports interoperability, but recommends that the ban be subject to privacy law. Therefore, the committee should examine and close that gap where appropriate so that a vendor is not treated as blocking information for refusing an exchange the law, in fact, forbids. There is also a need to ensure that compliance costs are not so high as to prevent entry by new providers. What I would say in closing, is that Bill S-5 would not build the tower that Nanaimo needs. It would not add the staff beds or the cath lab we need north of the Malahat. I will continue to advocate for those things both here in Ottawa and with provincial decision-makers in Victoria. However, this is a good start. I hope we will see the committee do good things with this bill and that it will come back to the House in a format we can support.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend our colleague for her speech. She obviously demonstrated her deep experience and knowledge of how a modern health care system should work, including in her community. It is very clear from what she has said that she really believes in the value of health data to provide better services to Canadians in her community in particular. Does she have practical experience with respect to the ways in which access to data can improve quality of care and perhaps even save lives?

Mr. Speaker, as the member knows, one of the things that happens in our offices on a regular basis is that people contact us with the experiences they have had with the health care system. As MPs, it is very frustrating for us, because we want to help, but health care delivery is something that is up to the provinces. Like my colleague, I have heard many stories of parents taking kids to hospitals and finding out that nobody can remember what the medication is and the records are not available. There are also circumstances where seniors who may have dementia or other issues are taken to the hospital by care providers and are not able to provide a full medical health record. Hopefully, this is something this bill would work to address using a federal power in the background.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to recognize that health information technology is all about the patient. For many years, we talked about information from patients and how it contributes to the betterment of health conditions. This legislation would actually save lives. It would improve the conditions. I am wondering if the member can provide her thoughts on the principle of the legislation. I understand there are some concerns with it, but does she support the principle of the legislation to the degree that she would vote in favour of it going to committee?

Mr. Speaker, I think I explained in some detail in my speech why I do support the objectives of this legislation and why it is particularly important in communities like ours, where the federal government has not provided enough health care infrastructure and health care support to be able to have access to those records when we have to travel between cities to receive care. On the principle side of things, I wonder what took the government so long. In terms of the operation, it is really important that, in committee, we make sure to get the provisions right so we do not have another Liberal health software boondoggle on our hands.

Mr. Speaker, again, I am going to recognize that what we are talking about is doctors, hospitals, institutions and pharmacists, all of which have records. Some provinces are much further advanced than other provinces. I think of the province of Ontario or of Quebec compared to my home province. Having legislation of this nature is ultimately in the best interest of all patients in all regions of the country. I would like to get the member's thoughts on that issue.

Mr. Speaker, I think we all know that sound travels more slowly than light, so sometimes it takes Ottawa longer to hear the needs of British Columbians. We are looking forward to seeing a time when those records are portable. I cannot say it more clearly than that. Let us get this right, though. Let us get it right, because it would save lives.

Mr. Speaker, today, I rise on behalf of the great people of Edmonton Southeast to discuss Bill S-5, the connected care for Canadians act. No Canadian needs reminding of the challenges facing our health care system. On this side of the House, we believe Canadians deserve timely, world-class health care when they need it, regardless of their financial circumstances, yet too many Canadians are waiting for a family doctor, a specialist appointment or a procedure that would allow them to return to work and live without pain. Canadians need better care. In many cases, their lives depend on it. While provinces and territories are responsible for delivering health care, the federal government has a responsibility to work constructively with them to improve access and support better outcomes. Bill S-5 presents an opportunity to address one part of this challenge, the difficulty of sharing health information between the professionals responsible for a patient's care. The principle of this legislation is common sense. However, much more work is needed to ensure that this bill would deliver meaningful improvements for patients. In Alberta, we know that a gap in communication can have serious consequences. In 2012, Greg Price died at just 31 years of age. A subsequent inquiry found that poor communication between providers and breaks in the continuity of care contributed to his death. His family has since worked to ensure that others learn from their tragic experience. More recently, tragedy struck closer to home. Last December, Prashant Sreekumar, a 44-year-old father of three, died at Grey Nuns Community Hospital in Edmonton Southeast after he waited nearly eight hours to see a doctor for chest pain. These cases involved different circumstances, and we should be careful not to suggest that one piece of legislation could have prevented everything that went wrong, but these stories demonstrate why this issue is important. When patients are referred to specialists, they should know whether their referral has been received and who is responsible for following up. When important test results become available, those results must reach the right professionals and therefore be acted upon. A patient dealing with a serious illness should not have to chase records and coordinate communication between medical offices. That responsibility should not fall on a family already worried about the health of someone they love. Bill S-5 would require health information technology vendors to ensure their systems can communicate with one another. It would also prohibit data blocking, subject to regulations. Put simply, a patient's information should be able to follow them securely through their care. A commercial interest in keeping customers tied to one software system should not prevent the appropriate sharing of information needed to treat a patient. It is a practical goal that Conservatives support. According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information, in 2024, only 68% of hip replacement and 61% of knee replacements were completed within the recommended six-month benchmark. Median waits for MRI scans were also 15 days longer than they were in 2019. These delays have consequences. For a person waiting for knee replacement, it may mean months of difficulty in walking, working or caring for their family. For someone waiting for a scan, it can mean prolonged uncertainty about a potentially serious condition. Better information sharing can help prevent unnecessary repeat tests and the delay caused by missing records, but connecting computer systems will not on its own add more doctors or create additional surgical capacity. Canadians need a broader effort to improve access. The government must explain how this legislation will contribute to that work and how its results will be measured. We must also consider the people delivering care. Doctors enter medicine to help patients, yet too much of their working time is consumed by unnecessary administrative tasks. A joint survey by the Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business estimated that physicians in Canada spend nearly 20 million hours each year on unnecessary administrative work. Disconnected records are only one part of that burden, but that is a part we should address. When clinic staff repeatedly request the same records or a physician must enter information already held in another system, valuable time is lost. That time could be used to see patients. The question is whether Bill S-5 would make that work easier. Would referrals become simpler to track? Would doctors spend less time searching for results? Would small clinics receive the training and support needed to adopt new systems? We cannot promise less paperwork while creating another complicated process for doctors to manage. Frontline professionals must be involved in developing these requirements. Furthermore, Canadians must have confidence that their personal health information is protected. Health records contains some of the most sensitive details of a person's life, including their mental health history, prescriptions and diagnoses. Patients share that information because they trust their health care providers. That trust must be maintained. Protecting confidential information must not be confused with improperly withholding it for commercial reasons. During the Senate committee review, stakeholders recommended baseline security requirements for vendors, including encryption, strong authentication and records of who accesses information. These recommendations deserve serious consideration. Doctors should not be expected to become cybersecurity experts to determine whether a vendor's product is adequately protected. Vendors must have clear responsibilities for maintaining safeguards, and patients need clear answers about how their information can be used and what happens if it is compromised. Finally, much of this legislation would depend on regulations developed after it were passed. These regulations would address standards, enforcement and the legislation's application within provinces and territories, which may also require careful examination. Provinces, health care professionals and patients deserve clarity about what would be required, what it would cost and who would be accountable. Conservatives believe in health care that delivers for its patients, but ultimately what Canadians need are shorter wait times, reliable follow-ups, seamless information transfers, and doctors who have more time to practise medicine rather than working on endless paperwork.

Mr. Speaker, this important bill would be a big step forward for the medical system throughout Canada. It seems that doctors still send faxes, which is basically the equivalent of stapling a piece of paper to the back of a dinosaur. It is kind of crazy how backward the health system can be in Canada. Among the IT interoperability, prohibiting data blocking, protecting access to health information and supporting virtual care, I wonder if there are any specific provisions in the bill that the member opposite sees as being the most helpful for the constituents in his riding.

Mr. Speaker, one thing I appreciate about the bill is that it is not too lengthy, but that does not mean it answers all the questions.
