We want to send it to committee for review so additional loopholes can be looked at. As recommended by the Senate review committee, more work can be done on it so clarity can be found, the paperwork can be reduced and the process can be streamlined.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of Windsor West. Given boondoggles such as the $300-million PrescribeIT scandal that we have faced, how much confidence does my colleague have that this legislation would be able to deliver anything of value to the Canadian taxpayer?

Mr. Speaker, that is a really serious question. Given the track record of the government over the last 11 years, a lot of boondoggles have happened that failed to deliver any results needed or promised by the government. However, that does not mean we should not look at the positive side of this bill. The death of Greg Price is a reminder for the government that, after 14 years, we are still figuring out how we can streamline the process so miscommunication cannot happen and tragedies like his cannot happen again, or can be controlled. I believe we still need to look at the bill from a positive angle, and all the positive suggestions should also be welcomed by the government.

Mr. Speaker, the member for Edmonton Southeast mentioned in his great speech that the Canadian Medical Association estimates that some 20 million hours are spent on administrative work. I agree with the member that excessive administrative time is often wasted and should probably be spent in other ways. I am curious as to whether the member can comment on how many of those 20 million hours could potentially be reduced through Bill S-5.

Mr. Speaker, that is a more technical question that more statistical data could answer if the bill is adopted and royal assent is provided. However, before it gets to that stage, we still need to review how we could make this bill better so all these delays and the jargon could be avoided and streamlining could be established.

Mr. Speaker, I am really encouraged by a number of the words the member has put on the record. I want to pick up on the point about saving lives. The legislation would do more than just save lives. It would also improve many people's current health conditions. Could the member expand on that point too?

Mr. Speaker, it is part of the bigger challenge. It is one step towards it. All the professionals' having access to a patient's records is the right step towards streamlining the medical process and the delays that are in the process.

I am pleased to speak today to Bill S-5, the connected care for Canadians act, and its role in supporting a more connected health system. Bill S-5 may seem rather technical, and indeed it is. However, I cannot emphasize enough how important this bill is for patients, physicians and indeed all cadres of health care professionals, for caregivers and for the people responsible for the planning and administering of our health care systems. What is the bill about? Well, Bill S-5 would advance connected care by mandating the adoption of common data standards for health information technologies used across Canada. It would also prohibit data blocking, the practice of restricting access to health information for authorized users such as providers and patients, when privacy laws would otherwise permit it. Data that is reliable, accurate and accessible saves lives, and the standards established by this bill would help make that possible. Research shows that patients who have access to their health information are better able to participate in treatment decisions, identify potential errors and manage chronic conditions more effectively. Improved access to health information would also support the more than four million Canadians who serve as informal caregivers in Canada. Today these individuals often devote countless hours to tracking down test results, coordinating records and repeating medical histories on behalf of their loved ones, often while balancing their own work, family and responsibilities. Thirteen per cent of Canadians say their care was negatively affected due to poor information sharing between providers. The consequences can be profound, even tragic. Indeed, according to a recent physician survey conducted by the Canadian Medical Association, 92% of physicians reported that disconnected health systems, such as the inability to share patient records, test results and clinical notes, affected their ability to provide care. Two-thirds of those physicians say this happens often, highlighting the extent to which the lack of interoperability shapes day-to-day clinical practice. When providers do not have access to a patient's complete health history, they are forced to make decisions without the full clinical picture. This increases the risk of delayed care, misdiagnosis, adverse drug interactions and unsafe treatments. Bill S-5 would enable a seamless and secure exchange of patient health information to support better collaboration among health care providers. For example, a family physician could securely share a patient summary with a specialist, helping support more timely assessments and better continuity of care. The bill would also strengthen team-based primary care, where timely information sharing is foundational to the way care is delivered. Similarly, for Canadians living with complex or chronic conditions and seeing multiple providers across multiple points of care, connected systems are a necessity. This is indeed true for Yukoners, who in many cases are in touch with providers across different jurisdictions. Harms resulting from disconnected care are especially high for people travelling in Canada, whether from northern, rural and remote communities, across provincial and territorial borders for treatment, or simply for work or vacation. For example, an elderly individual became ill while visiting family in another province. Although antiviral treatment was recommended, it could not be provided, because the lab result required to confirm eligibility for treatment was trapped in the patient's provincial digital health system. When systems cannot communicate, the result can be duplicated tests, delays in care, unnecessary costs, and frustration for patients and families. Bill S-5 would help bridge these gaps by mandating the standards that enable information sharing across the health care system. Importantly, disconnected data puts health care providers in the position of having to make clinical decisions with incomplete information. Bill S-5 would help to address this by enabling health care providers to access their patients' complete health care information in order to provide safe, high-quality care. Interoperable health systems can help reduce administrative burden associated with charting, forms, sick notes and tracking down test results. Today, valuable time is spent manually entering data and copying information from one system to another, instead of spending time with patients. Artificial intelligence is already supporting providers by reducing repetitive administrative tasks and improving access to information, and its use will only expand. However, these tools depend on reliable and connected data systems. Bill S-5 would help establish the secure data foundation needed to support that progress. For example, studies have found that physicians spend an average of 86 minutes a day searching for patient data due to a lack of interoperability. Now, 20 million physician hours are wasted annually on unnecessary administrative tasks. This unsustainable level of administrative work can lead to burnout, fatigue and low job satisfaction. Results from the CMA's 2025 national physician health survey showed that 46% of physicians and residents report high-level burnout. Dr. Ewan Affleck, a physician who has spent most of his career in the north and is a leading Canadian expert in digital health information, likens running a health system without connected data to flying blind, which, in his own experience, has cost patients their lives. Bill S-5 would also support the broader use of digital tools that help patients connect with their providers, including secure platforms for booking appointments, requesting prescription refills and communicating with their care team. Transformation of any system requires investment. Whatever the cost it takes, the cost of inaction is likely to be far greater than the cost to do this work. As it is, we are already paying a staggering price for disconnected health data, estimated up to $9.4 billion annually. Beyond the financial cost, the consequences I have talked about today can hardly be measured in dollars but in patient safety, quality of care and the well-being of the health care providers who support them. Bill S-5 is a technical bill but its purpose is straightforward: to connect data to prevent patient harm. Canadians turn to the health care system seeking care and relief. I would encourage my fellow members to join me in supporting the bill so that all Canadians can receive safe health care that is informed by accurate data and is accessible wherever and whenever decisions are made.

Mr. Speaker, I completely agree that data sharing is going to prevent harm. I am curious about the data sovereignty aspect of this. What has the government proposed to ensure that Canadians' health care data remains sovereign and protected through the legislation?

Mr. Speaker, this is really all about supporting data sovereignty and interconnectivity at the same time that we support existing privacy protection. Authorized access remains governed by applicable privacy legislation. The bill is really about making information available when it is legally permitted to be shared and not expanding access beyond existing privacy rules. It is really helping to get that balance right, which is really all about data sovereignty.

Mr. Speaker, I have the benefit of being a member of Parliament in an urban riding, where I do hear about concerns around health data. Could the member talk a bit more about the Yukon, which represents a lot of rural and more disconnected communities? What kind of impact would Bill S-5 have for members of his community in the Yukon?

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned throughout my speech, Bill S-5 is particularly relevant for more remote and northern rural settings, because so much of the health care depends on the interconnectivity of communities to referral centres. For example, Whitehorse hospital is the referral centre for the territory. It receives a lot of patients and a lot of calls from around the communities, but we also access care in British Columbia, in Alberta and sometimes in other jurisdictions. I cannot tell the House how many times I hear, either personally through my former career or from colleagues, about how the lack of interchangeability of data has affected patient care. I am really looking forward to the implementation of this bill and the subsequent actual interoperability of health systems.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague mentioned a piece on Canadian innovation. I would like his comments on how we are going to ensure through this legislation that we do not add red tape and barriers to smaller entrepreneurs, inadvertently creating a market where only the big players can play and smaller innovators cannot compete.

Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question. Data blocking is bad for at least two groups of partners we really need to support and invest in in our health care sector. First, it is bad for researchers who complain, including in Quebec, about data inaccessibility that prevents the development of new technology and connections across health care professionals. It is obviously very bad for patients. Second, it is bad for small businesses that would like to develop software and technologies to compete with bigger businesses. If there is no interoperability, the data controlled by bigger businesses cannot be accessed by smaller businesses, which prevents smaller businesses from competing in this area.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member for his intervention today, particularly given that in 2022, when he was minister of health, there was an agreement between John Horgan and Justin Trudeau for health-sharing information. I asked the then minister for some information about privacy, and his office did send a response. I could read it one way, or I could flip it around and read it a different way, so it was good political communication. Why do we still have the problem in this country that health records cannot be shared between provinces securely?

Mr. Speaker, since I have to be very brief, I will thank the member for his continuous advocacy. He knows there has been progress over the years, but he also knows really well that we need more progress in order to support all provinces and territories, regardless of where Canadians live, in their ability to access and benefit from the health data that is so important to them.

Mr. Speaker, I think there is broad agreement in this place about the problem this bill is trying to address. Canadians should be able to access their own health information, and when they seek care, the people treating them should be able to get the information they need securely and with the appropriate privacy protections. I support interoperability. In fact, I have spoken about this in the House before. In the previous Parliament, the former member for Cypress Hills—Grasslands brought forward Bill C-294. It dealt with the Copyright Act and interoperability, and it eventually became law. I congratulate that member, and I spoke in favour of it at the time. The example I used in that debate was pretty straightforward. It was about a farmer who could own a tractor or combine and buy an implement made by a different manufacturer. It could hook up just fine. Mechanically, there would be no reason it should not work, but technological protection measures could prevent the two pieces of equipment from communicating with each other. I said at the time, “real competition pits products and services against one another, rewarding innovation and productivity, not copyright and exclusivity.” I also said that the right to interoperability was critical for consumers. I stand by that. I still believe it today. However, health care is obviously different and considerably more complicated. Bill S-5 is principally about health information technology vendors. It would require the technology covered by the legislation to be interoperable according to established requirements, and it would prohibit data blocking by vendors. Those sound like very reasonable objectives to me. If a vendor is deliberately preventing health information from moving simply to keep a customer locked into its ecosystem, there is a legitimate role for Parliament, but I think we need to be careful about what happens next. Canada does not just have one health system. We have provincial health care systems, and within those systems, there are health authorities, hospitals, laboratories, primary care providers and other organizations that have brought in different technologies at different times under different contracts to do different things. Some of those systems are relatively new; some are not. Some communicate reasonably well, and some require people to find workarounds just to move fairly basic information. If there were one health care system, one purchaser and one set of specifications, establishing common technical requirements might be simpler, but there is not. I do not think the answer is to turn the federal government into the health care technology purchaser for the entire country, although I am sure there are some members on the opposite side who would enjoy that. Health care is principally administered and delivered by the provinces, like it or not. The federal government needs to respect that. I will be fair about the legislation. There are provisions in the bill that recognize that reality. The federal requirements would not simply apply uniformly, regardless of what a province or territory is already doing. The bill would provide a mechanism that takes into account whether a province or territory has a substantially similar or stronger requirement. I think that is completely sensible, but it also points to a larger problem. The federal government does not run the health care system. I hope we can all agree on that. Some Canadians might reasonably respond that they are not entirely convinced the provinces are running it either. We have seen in Nova Scotia and, more recently, in my home province of British Columbia that the Conservatives of those provinces actively ran for and won majority governments despite the old logic that Conservatives cannot speak to health care issues and only run away. In my home province, there are wait times at the ER, that is if it is actually open. I heard from the daughter of 90-year-old woman that her mother had been kept in the hallway of the Kelowna General Hospital ER for days. She was literally unable to sleep with all the incoming patients, and the first responders and health care professionals trying to do their job while her mother was waiting for a bed. Constitutionally and practically, the provinces administer and deliver health care regardless of how badly. They are dealing with hospitals, health authorities, physicians and procurement decisions, and much of the information is already in place. Therefore, I think this House should ask a fairly basic question: Why should we assume that the federal government knows best when it comes to procuring and implementing complex information technology when its own record does not exactly inspire confidence? Let me give an example. We all remember ArriveCAN. The Auditor General of Canada could not even determine exactly what the application cost because the government's financial records and controls were so poor. She estimated the cost at approximately $59.5 million. She found that federal organizers repeatedly failed to follow good management practices in contracting, development and implementation, and concluded that the application did not deliver the best value for the taxpayer dollars spent. That deserves some reflection. The federal government is now entering into another debate involving sophisticated information technology and procurement, yet in the case of ArriveCAN, or arrive scam depending on who we talk to, the Auditor General of Canada could not even establish the precise cost of the government's own application because the records were inadequate. That is not an ideological argument, but the Auditor General's finding. Then we come to PrescribeIT. This example is arguably even more relevant because it was a health information technology project. The objective was straightforward. It is 2026; why are we still sending prescriptions around by fax? The goal of PrescribeIT was to move prescriptions electronically from prescribers to pharmacies. According to public reporting, more than $250 million was spent on PrescribeIT since 2017, yet fewer than 5% of Canadian prescriptions were being transmitted through the system. The centrally operated service ended this year after Canada Health Infoway concluded that national adoption had not been reached to the scale necessary for long-term sustainability. The organization has moved toward an open national e-prescribing standard instead. Let us think about that for a moment. The problem was not that no one could figure out how to make an electronic prescription. They could. The difficult part was getting a complicated health care system to use it. Adoption mattered. Existing information systems mattered. Costs, I would hope, mattered. Provincial participation absolutely mattered. The day-to-day practices of doctors and pharmacists mattered. Implementation mattered. ArriveCAN could teach us something about federal procurement. PrescribeIT should teach us something about health care technology implementation. Both should give the Liberal government a warning to show a little humility. I am not saying the federal government has no role here. It does. Preventing genuine data blocking can be a legitimate federal role. Working with provinces on common technical standards makes sense. Removing legitimate federal barriers makes sense. The federal government can certainly demand results when it is spending taxpayer money. However, the Liberals on the government benches should be very careful about assuming that because they can pass a law about interoperability, they therefore know how to procure, integrate and operate health information systems better than the people delivering the care. Writing requirements in Ottawa is considerably easier than making technology work on the ground, and Canadians have paid enough money over the years to understand the difference. I have been thinking of all of this because of two conversations I had on my Finding Solutions podcast. One was with Dr. Stuart Edmonds of the Canadian Cancer Society. We were talking about clinical trials and why they matter to cancer patients. I think most Canadians understand generally what a clinical trial is, but it looks rather different when we think about it from the perspective of somebody who has cancer and may be running out of treatment options. There may be a clinical trial available for that person, but somebody has to know that patient exists. They have to know what kind of cancer that person has. They have to know what treatments have already been tried. They may need pathology results, diagnostic information or other testing. Then they have to determine whether that patient might qualify for the trial. At that point, interoperability stops being a debate about software and becomes a question of whether the right information can get to the right people when it matters. With cancer, I do not think I have to tell members, time matters. I had another conversation on finding solutions with Louise Binder, a long-time patient advocate working with the Save Your Skin Foundation. We talked about the postal code lottery in cancer care. We talked about clinical trials, access to new medicines, families travelling to receive treatment and what that all means for someone who is already dealing with a serious illness. We discussed this legislation on interoperable health information and the importance of a care team being able to see the full picture of the patient. That, to me, is the most persuasive case for what the government is trying to accomplish. A cancer patient should not have to become the human interface between computer systems that cannot communicate. If someone from my communities in the Okanagan has to go to Vancouver for specialized treatment, that person should not have to reconstruct their medical history every time they encounter another part of the health care system. If someone has to travel to another province for care, that gets even harder. The relevant health information should not simply disappear because people cross the provincial boundary. The technology should work for the patient. The patient should not have to work for the technology to work. The government itself says that only 29% of health care providers share electronic information securely and seamlessly outside their offices. Obviously, that is not good enough, but that statistic also raises an uncomfortable question. We have been talking about digital health in Canada for years. We have spent money, billions of dollars. We have developed strategies. We have established organizations. We have announced initiatives. We have negotiated funding agreements. Where are the results? This is not an argument against doing more. It is an argument for understanding why what we have already done has not produced the results Canadians reasonably expected. It comes down to this old political trap. There is a problem, something must be done and this is something. Therefore, we must do this. That does not mean Bill S-5 is inherently bad legislation. It means Parliament should not confuse legislative activity with health care results. Passing a bill is relatively easy. Writing regulations can be done. Holding a press conference can certainly be done. We know because we see it almost every day with the government. However, the difficult work comes after that. How does this work with the systems provinces already purchased? What happens to older systems? How much will it cost to make them compatible? What happens when standards change? What happens when one institution is capable of exchanging the information, but another is not? What happens when the barrier is not the vendor? What happens when the problem is an existing contract, an institutional practice, a procurement decision made 10 years ago or simply an old system that is too expensive to replace? Those are not reasons to abandon interoperability. They are reasons to be honest about what this legislation can and cannot accomplish. There is another contrast that I think is worth considering. The federal government already knows how to sit down with provinces and reach agreements on specific health outcomes. The federal government has agreements with British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and the Yukon, covering a range of diabetes medications and contraception. Those are agreements with provinces and territories, yet there are only four. It seems to me that the government is pivoting away from the kind of approach that costs money and instead trying to find another problem to solve. Interoperability, as I said, is a problem, but is that the best use of everyone's time? We need to start asking whether or not the Liberal government is seeking results or if it is just seeking to have announcements. I think the same approach should guide interoperability. What do I actually want to know about this bill? First, would it stop vendors from blocking information that would legitimately be available? If it does, good. Second, would these standards actually work with systems that provinces and health care providers already have? Telling everyone that tomorrow's technology must comply does not necessarily fix the equipment and the software that were purchased five or 10 years ago. Third, how would the government work with provinces, not consult them so that someone can put a check mark beside consultation, but actually work with them? Finally, what would the patient notice? Can they access their information? Can their doctor get the information they need? If I live in the Okanagan and go to Vancouver for treatment, can the professionals treating me see the relevant records? If I end up in an emergency room somewhere else in the country, what happens then? If I have cancer and possibly qualify for a clinical trial, will the information needed to identify that opportunity actually be available? Those are the questions I care about. Frankly, I am less interested in whether a technology vendor can tell the federal government that it has complied with the regulation. I just want to know whether the thing actually works. Do not come back to Parliament in two years and tell us how many meetings were held. Do not tell us how many vendors submitted compliance paperwork. Do not tell us how many pages of regulations were published. Tell us what happened to the patient. I would just mention an incident that I had an occasion to ask a former minister of health about. In 2022, the prime minister at the time, the premier of my province, John Horgan, and the health minister, who is still a member today, reached an agreement on health care information sharing. Billions of dollars were announced. Now, that was four years ago and what has changed? Zip. What I am saying to the government here is that it can make announcements and spend money, but that does not necessarily mean the job gets done. It should start to listen to the people who know the systems, start to put them in charge of the job and make sure that it is seen not only as an announceable, but a deliverable, and make sure the government is behind that. After speaking with people such as Dr. Stuart Edmonds and Louise Binder, I see a case for this bill in health care very clearly, but we have learned enough from previous digital health projects and, frankly, from federal IT procurement more generally, to know that passing legislation is the easy part. Making it work is the hard part. Let us make sure that doctors are not relying on faxes. Let us make sure that the government relies on facts. Let us not confuse passing the law with solving the problem. Ultimately, this is not about databases. This is about people. I ask the government to really focus on the people more than the data and not to focus on the announcements, but on the actual results.

Mr. Speaker, I genuinely believe that Bill S-5, and what the Minister of Health talked about when she introduced the legislation, is all about the patients. It is all about delivering for patients. It recognizes that health information technology has to play a critical role. I agree with the member that there has to be a high sense of co-operation. Passing the legislation would not necessarily make it happen on its own. We would need to have the provinces and territories buy in. We have seen that some provinces are further ahead than others. Would the member not agree that no matter what level of government we talk about, if everyone agrees to the principle of putting the patient first, we should be able to have a better system that would serve those patients?

Mr. Speaker, I talked a little about the agreement that John Horgan, Justin Trudeau and the former minister concluded. It was for over $26 billion, over a 10-year period, to solve the very basic problem of not being able to access health records in another province. I asked the former minister what was still blocking that. It is not for a lack of money or a lack of consensus. It is implementation. The member can say, “We're all about interoperability. We're all about data privacy and sharing of information.” That is great. I can say bravo. Good on them. However, if it does not happen, if that minister is pulling a lever that goes nowhere, it is all talk. That is a point that the Liberal government could probably learn from.

Mr. Speaker, before I ask my question, I want to wish my good friend Dr. Sandeep Sharma, one of the top plastic surgeons in India and past president of the Indian Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, a happy birthday in advance. We have seen this movie before. PrescribeIT was supposed to modernize prescription management, but the service ultimately had to shut down. The Minister of Health has consistently and steadfastly avoided questions on PrescribeIT. Would my colleague agree that before the government embarks on another ambitious digital health initiative, Canadians deserve to know what went wrong, what the cost of that boondoggle was and why the legislation would work this time around?

Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate the member and his intervention. I think it comes down to one thing. It is really easy to pass legislation that forces other entities, in this case companies, usually very large organizations, to comply with particular standards. Again, whether they actually do it or not, they can send in the paperwork required and say they meet all of the requirements under the interoperability provisions of Bill S-5. That is there. However, it is different when the rule-maker now has to be the person to deliver. That seems to be where the Liberal government continues to slide. It is like a vacuum that money, good intentions, announcements, meetings, everything gets thrown into, but nothing ever seems to come out. That is what I think Conservatives are opposed to.

I want to thank my colleague for his speech, which I listened to with great interest. I want to talk a little about data blocking and ask the member opposite whether he believes the banning of data blocking is a good thing. We have seen some very serious instances, in his province and in mine, of companies refusing to let the data be used and refusing to let it exit the electronic systems because they are hanging onto it to monetize it. I wonder if the member thinks it is a good thing that the Government of Canada would put an end to that with Bill S-5.

Mr. Speaker, if monetizing Canadians' information was important to the government, it would be doing it right across the board. When I walk, Apple owns my health data. When I spend, my bank owns that particular data. That is the problem here, that the government only tries to pick and choose when it believes there is something politically popular. As I said, in the case of this particular bill, it seems the government wants to do something on health care, so it has landed on something that is germane and, I think, everyone agrees with. Another member of Parliament brought up the issue of interoperability in the agricultural sector. I think what we need to do more than anything is what the Australians considered, which is the equivalent of a royal commission, where they did intense hearings. I have read through some of their books. They are so far ahead when it comes to the issues of data, monetization, personal privacy and the efficiencies that can be given when consumers are empowered with their own information. There is so much that can be done. I hope the member pushes the government to do more on those things.

Mr. Speaker, if this bill is about putting patients first, why does the government not establish clear consequences and penalties when health care technology companies fail to protect or properly share Canadians' medical information?

Mr. Speaker, that is a tough but fair question, and one for which I must show respect to the member. I affectionately call him the sheriff because of his previous career in law enforcement, during which he served his community ably. I would simply say that we can have a rule, but if we do not have consequences, then people are not going to respect the law. The sheriff is absolutely right. There needs to be more. This is why we should get it to committee, and it is why that member, I hope, will be pushing for those penalties to be clarified.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to pick up on one of the member's comments on the whole idea of technology, because I really do agree with it. We have to ensure that technology works for people and not the reverse, in terms of having access. I will get the opportunity to expand upon that shortly, but I wanted to amplify just how important it is, in recognizing Bill S-5, that the primary focus is on patients in using technology. The member seems to imply that he supports the legislation in principle and wants to see it go to committee. Does he believe it is something that could be passed before Christmas?

Mr. Speaker, I would encourage the member to speak to the hon. Minister of Transport, who in addition to being a part-time minister of that portfolio is also the government House leader. He would probably have a better read on where things are going. All joking aside, I did not get to address this in my speech, but if we look at Europe, if we look at the United States, that is where most of these companies come from, and really, that is where the big money is spent. I do not know whether Canada would see significant compliance from those companies. I certainly hope those companies would look to do this. I just hope, though, it would not slow the adoption of new technologies as they come out, because, again, differing standards in different regions create a de facto trade barrier whether the government wants to admit it or not. I am hopeful that this bill would be helpful, but let us just say it is not unconditionally positive in all respects.

Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time today with the member for Winnipeg North. When I was a health system and academic leader, we used to talk about having two jobs in health care. First was taking care of the patient of today. To do that work, obviously, we need access to the health data across a patient's journey, no matter where they are in the health care system. We also talked about having a second patient, the patient of tomorrow, and that is the work of supporting research, quality improvement and health system innovation. Bill S-5 is a critical piece of legislation that would allow us to care for both the patient of today and the patient of tomorrow, and that is why I am proud to rise in the House today to speak in support of it. All over Canada today, people are going to visit their family doctors. They are going to be talking about their mental health. They are going to be talking about their diabetes and their blood pressure control. They are going to be talking about their cancer journeys. They are going to be getting immunizations, prescriptions and requisitions for medical imaging. They might be getting a referral to a specialist. They might be referred for counselling or for physiotherapy. In pretty much every one of those family doctor's offices today, they are going to find their family doctor sitting and typing away on a computer, generating tasks for the physician or the health care worker and for the patient. If a referral is made, the doctor is going to be typing away, generating forms inside that computer, and if that patient then goes to see a specialist, they are going to find the specialist sitting at their desk taking notes on a computer. If they end up in an emergency situation and have to go to the hospital, all the notes, the test results and the imaging results are going to be stored in an electronic record. In my community of downtown Toronto, those places, the family doctor's office, the hospital, the emergency department and the specialist's office, might be just a few subway stops away from each other. Sometimes they are even in the same building, so one could forgive a patient for assuming those computers are talking to each other. However, it turns out that all too often, that is not the case. People could be forgiven for asking why, in a set of single-payer health systems across the country in any given province or territory, the data generated in the hospital, the data generated in the doctor's office and the data generated in the home care interface are sitting in separate silos, not talking to each other. Bill S-5 seeks to remedy that. By requiring the vendors of the electronic systems we use in our health systems every day to meet interoperability standards and putting an end to data blocking, wherein vendors hold onto the data of Canadians under the mistaken view that they own the data about the health of our people, as opposed to the patient and the health system as a public good, we would be putting in place the necessary infrastructure for a modern health care system across the country. It used to be that in order for electronic systems to talk to each other in a health care system, they had to actually be on the same system. I am pleased that this is no longer the case. We do not need all of Canada to be using a single electronic health record for data to flow in the ways that patients need, because technology has leapfrogged that requirement. When vendors meet those interoperability standards referred to in this bill, the data would be able to move in order for us to take better care of people. The hospital and the clinic would be able to securely share information that is relevant to the care of the patient. Why does this bill matter? Why do we need health records to be interoperable, and why do we need health data to be treated as a public good? I want to speak to primary use and secondary use and begin by talking about the delivery of clinical care and access to one's own records. We have covered well in the House today in this debate the necessity of interoperability of health records for patient safety in terms of clinicians being able to access critical information when a person comes in for care, so I want to focus my remarks on the two other critical aspects. First is the ability of Canadians to access their own health records. Second is the ability to use the data for research, quality improvement and system oversight. The pan-Canadian OurCare consultations, led by Dr. Tara Kiran and an incredible national team of researchers and experts in public engagement and primary care, had conversations with hundreds of people living across Canada to understand what Canadians wanted from a better primary care system. In their conversations, a core refrain arose again and again: People in Canada are frustrated that they do not have access to their own medical information. People shared how not having access to their own medical records made it challenging to get the care they need when they had an emergency, when they moved to a different province, when their doctor moved or retired, when they did not have a doctor or when they were just trying to advocate for themselves or for their loved ones. Through the OurCare consultations, people in Canada spoke clearly and consistently. They want access to their own health records online in a format they can share with clinicians and loved ones and where they can have confidence that the information will be kept private and secure, which is not a very radical or unusual idea. Countries around the world have already given people access to their own health records through an app, like the Nordic countries, for example, but also Estonia, Spain, Portugal, France, England and Australia, just to name a few. As we look to build national infrastructure and to become more self-reliant as a country and as we look to create the conditions for our country to thrive in the years to come, we need to invest in the most foundational of assets: the health of our people. Bill S-5 would open the door for people being able to access their own health records by ensuring that their data would be liberated from the vendors who may be holding on to it. That brings me to secondary use and the patient of tomorrow. This is an aspect of data interoperability we should not neglect, because beyond the care of individual people, we need health data to do quality improvement, to do groundbreaking research, to engage in health system oversight and to develop artificial intelligence and apply it to the biggest problems facing the health of Canadians. This is what we call secondary use of data, because health data is the raw material for improving care. Research and quality improvement teams use data to track people's health outcomes over time, to measure the impact of our interventions and to ask important questions that will lead to the next generation of breakthroughs. Health data also contains the stories of important inequities and outcomes across the country. It helps us to understand whether people living in rural communities, people experiencing homelessness, indigenous people, Black Canadians and other groups are getting the care they deserve. This information can then drive our investments and programs as a government, but to understand the story, we need the data. Our superb Canadian researchers and health system leaders cannot do their jobs without it, and if it is being blocked sitting inside a vendor's records, we are going to be in trouble. Finally, I want to say a few words about artificial intelligence. We are obviously at a new frontier. If we want to use AI to reduce wait times in emergency departments or wait times for specialist care, and if we want to use AI to improve the quality of care being provided to seniors in long-term care, to cancer patients in our cancer centres or to children in our family doctors' offices, we are going to need data and the data will need to be linked in order for us to do it. Bill S-5 would regulate vendors. It would require them to play ball in ensuring that data can be shared across our health systems. Once the data is unblocked and interoperable, a lot of work still remains to be done. This bill would not replace the work ahead on sovereignty, commercialization, data export approaches and indigenous data sovereignty, all of which have been flagged by our colleagues in the Senate, but it would lay the foundation for all those things. Bill S-5 would lay the foundation for us to care for the patient of today and tomorrow. I am proud to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I can sense the passion in my colleague's voice. I want to thank her for her over two decades' worth of service as a family physician. She knows first-hand where the system breaks down. If she could fix one particular thing in this bill, what would it be and how would it help regular Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, in my colleague's riding today, as in mine, there are family physicians like my colleagues who are spending an inordinate amount of time chasing results, trying to figure out what happened to their patient when they were admitted to the hospital and what changes were made to their medications, and calling the pharmacy to try to figure out what occurred. This bill would lay a foundation. It would open the door for the kind of information data flow that is truly necessary to fix these problems. A lot of work would have to happen after that. The bill would not magically fix everything, but if we do not pass it, we will not have the infrastructure necessary to address these important issues.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her service for two decades. She knows exactly about one patient, one data. Can my colleague tell us how the bill would reduce barriers to care? Also, we heard that there is workforce pressure. How would it be more helpful for the patient and reduce the burden of administrative work?

Mr. Speaker, I think we all know that the barriers for health care workers in the system today are considerable. There is a lot that artificial intelligence, for example, can do to improve the productivity of our health systems and reduce administrative burdens on our health care providers, whether they are a home care worker in a home, a PSW in long-term care or a nurse practitioner in primary care. AI can help all those people spend their time taking care of patients instead of running around trying to access information. It can reduce the administrative burden, whether it is from filling out forms or getting appointments for patients. However, all of that requires that the data be accessible, that it be linked and interoperable and that it not be blocked by the vendors of electronic medical records and electronic health records. That is why this bill would make a difference for the workers in our health systems across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I agree wholeheartedly that data transfer between departments and interchangeability are extremely important to help reduce harm in Canada. One thing the member mentioned in her speech is that the bill would lay the foundation for data transferability within Canada, but it would not complete the conversation on data sovereignty. How can we lay the foundation for data transfer but not at the same time lay the foundation for data sovereignty? If we are not doing that, are we not be putting health data in Canada at risk?

Mr. Speaker, it will be critical, in order to do this work, for the data to flow. The data needs to be linked so that across different parts of the health care system, we can follow a patient's journey over time. Once that occurs at the technical level, we have to figure out how we will govern the data, how we will make sure that privacy is protected and how we will ensure that the data is available to the people who need to use it and have permission to use it, but not misused by others, whether that would happen through the regulations coming out of this bill or, more likely, at the level of the health systems as people work through this over time. Right now, people across Canada doing health care leadership cannot even begin those conversations because they cannot access the data because it is being blocked. This is a necessary step on the journey to health system transformation across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak to Bill S-5 today. If we take a look at information nowadays, it has never been easier to access. It has become critically important that when we take a look at our health care system, we look at ways in which we can improve upon it. I want to reflect on some of the days, going as far back as when I was the health care critic in the province of Manitoba, when I was meeting with patients and stakeholders. Even back then, they were talking about information gathered on behalf of clients or patients and how that information is retained and ultimately shared. I remember that when I had to change my family doctor, as my first one made the decision to retire, I was given a yellow envelope to bring to my new doctor. A year ago or so, when I was with my family doctor inside the checkup room, he was sitting at a computer, which I could watch. It was truly amazing how he was able to connect my health care needs through the computer. I did not have to get a prescription issued from the doctor or a piece of paper. Rather, he told me that I could go to X place and that my prescription would be ready. When I take a look at what Bill S-5 is all about, it is all about patients, whether directly or indirectly. That is why I would like to think that all members of the House will see the value of supporting the legislation. I have listened to members opposite all morning talk about the concerns they have, and I am not going to marginalize their concerns. I suspect that all members have some concerns as we move into this area. It is a very challenging area; there is no doubt about it. Someone mentioned that while we could bring in legislation, it would not guarantee that the system is going to work and the patient is going to benefit. There are jurisdictional issues. To individuals who are genuinely concerned about the issue of which level of government is responsible for what, I will say that instead of that being the primary concern, the primary concern should be the patient. If we view this through that lens, I believe we will see more co-operation taking place among institutions, private companies, non-profit companies and the different levels of government, if we are prepared to do what the minister has made very clear. In her statement, she talked about working with provincial and territorial jurisdictions and indigenous communities. At the end of the day, information does matter. What takes place in our doctors' offices, our hospitals, our care facilities and our pharmacies really does matter, as does a person's ability to go into a facility, whatever type of facility it might be, and have a sense that a health care provider has access to the information that is so very important for that patient. If that were to be done right, where we get collaboration and get all systems onside moving in one direction, with the priority being the patient, we would see less duplication. People would understand the differences in medications that might be being taken at one end versus at the other end. Some testing may not have to take place, or in some cases testing would take place, such as an x-ray, a lab test or whatever it might be. The different types of medications an individual takes throughout the year would be known. These are all important pieces of information. In working collaboratively with other jurisdictions, I would argue, as I said at the outset, and putting the lens on the patient, it is the patient who would benefit with the passage of Bill S-5. I had the opportunity to ask members opposite some questions regarding the principle of the legislation. I am encouraged by the Minister of Health and the government's agenda to get this legislation through with fantastic support from the Senate of Canada. I am pleased with the general approach of the opposition, as the principle of the legislation appears to have been accepted. That being said, I suspect there might be a number of issues, based on what I have heard, that would come up at the committee stage. I am sure there would be representation at the committee stage about issues related to things such as data blocking, which has been talked about a great deal. Data blocking is done far too often. Because of a vested interest, information is being retained by one vendor for reasons I will not go into today, but much of it would be driven by the dollar. Data blocking would be directly dealt with in this legislation, which is a very good thing. Then there are interoperable issues. For example, in the province of Manitoba, there might be a care facility using a different technology system from what is being used at the Health Sciences Centre. Because of that, it is the patient who loses the most. That is one of the reasons the compatibility of technologies is so important in the legislation. The data would be able to be transferred. We hear a great deal about data, records and so forth, and it is important for us to recognize that with regard to data and technology, the government is very concerned with ensuring that privacy is respected. As we know, Canadians are very concerned about the issue of privacy, and understandably so. Some provinces are further advanced than others, and I recognize that, but as we roll this out, what would end up happening is that the quality of health care services would improve for all Canadians. The health care worker, be it a nurse or a doctor, would have better opportunity to provide bedside care or to provide consultation, as a direct result of moving forward with Bill S-5. That is not to mention, as some have already pointed out, that it would also save lives. Someone asked why it is taking us as long as it is. I think it is important to recognize that we have a very substantial legislative agenda. In the last 18 months, we have been pushing forward on a series of legislative initiatives. This bill is an important piece to it, because our health care matters in Canada. Canadians want us—

Mr. Speaker, one thing in particular the member opposite said that I would like to concentrate on is that we have to look at this through the lens of the patient. I wholeheartedly agree with that, and the lens I am going to look through is data security. If this is implemented across Canada in partnership of course with the provinces, how would we ensure that, first, it would still be the patient who would decide whether the data is going to be transferred, and, second, how would that data be protected?

Mr. Speaker, the member, in posing the questions, highlighted something I had indicated. If everyone would do exactly what she did with respect to her question, which is to put the patient first and look at it through that lens, I suspect that the debate would be well served not only on the floor of the House of Commons but also in committee. I can assure the member that it does not matter what side of the House one looks at. I believe every member wants to ensure the privacy and protection of data. There is no doubt whatsoever in my mind on that.

Mr. Speaker, there is a long story with respect to health care transfers. We could go back many decades to when the provinces and the federal government made the decision that they wanted some change in tax points to the provinces in favour of having direct cash going to them. I was never a big fan of that. I believe that the federal government needs to not only have a strong, healthy Canada Health Act but also to maintain a basic level of health transfers. That is something the government, under the Prime Minister, has committed to do. In addition to that, I would recognize that the Prime Minister came up with a $5-billion fund to build Canada's capital health infrastructure. I look forward to those health care dollars' being spent across the country.

Mr. Speaker, I just learned that the member for Winnipeg North is a former Manitoba health critic. His comments on a stronger collaboration are well noted. However, I wonder if my colleague can elaborate a bit more on data blocking and vested interests. Why is data blocking important?

Mr. Speaker, the simple reason is that often data blocking is not done in the interests of the patient but in the interests of some vendor that has a vested interest, and often that vested interest is driven by money. Whether it is the Prime Minister or any member of the Liberal caucus, what we are saying is that we need to put the patient first. If we put the patient first, we will have a better, stronger and healthier health care system.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise on behalf of Kitchener Centre to speak to this really important issue. I think we can all agree that every Canadian should be able to access quality health care when they need it, without waiting and regardless of where they live and what they earn. Unfortunately, that is not the reality of our current health care system. Canadians are struggling to find a family doctor. They are waiting months if not years to see specialists. They join long wait lists for surgeries and imaging. Emergency rooms are overcrowded, and patients spend hours waiting even to be assessed. For too many Canadians, the challenge is simply accessing health care. While we can all agree that our health care system is worth protecting, it cannot mean defending something that is failing too many Canadians. Canadian taxpayers spend an enormous amount of money on their own health care. Taxpayers will spend $57 billion in 2026-27, and Canadians are still left waiting for proper care for their investment. Do members know that Canada ranks last among 10 similar countries with respect to timely access to health care? Only one in four Canadians gets an appointment with a doctor or nurse the day they need it. Most Canadians wait two months or longer to see a specialist. We have to ask ourselves how we can make our system work better. It is not just about how much money we put into health care. It is about its effectiveness. How do we support health care professionals, and how do we improve the outcomes for all Canadians? Let us imagine that somebody from Kitchener decides to travel across this beautiful country to Alberta. Maybe they are visiting family, enjoying a family vacation or travelling for work. Then, unexpectedly, they have a heart attack. They are taken to the ER, and the doctors treating them need to know their medical history, such as what medications they are taking, if they have any allergies, if they have had any previous surgeries or if there are any underlying issues or conditions that could affect their treatment. The patient is lucky enough to have a family doctor in Ontario, but their medical records are not in the same system as Alberta's, and the hospital cannot access them. What happens now? The patient literally cannot provide their health information if they have had a heart attack. They cannot give their history. They cannot give their allergies or the pertinent information the doctors may need in that exact moment. The doctors now are spending time trying to access the patient's information instead of immediately caring for them. Tests may be needed or repeated, and information is not available. All this is happening while the individual is not getting the care they need. Would it not make more sense if the patient's medical information could just follow them so surgeons would immediately be able to operate on them, potentially saving lives? A colleague just shared a story with me. A man and his wife were travelling across the country, and they got in a car accident. Because of that car accident, the gentleman needed immediate surgery, and his wife was unconscious. Right on the roadside, penicillin was administered to the man during the operation, but unfortunately he was allergic to the penicillin and passed away. Data transfer can literally save lives in this country. We have already invested in medical records across this country. More than 95% of physicians use electronic medical records today, but that is not the same as having a connected system. A doctor might have a patient's entire medical history on their computer, but if the doctor treating them next door does not have that same information, we have a problem. Only 29% of primary care providers make patient information available outside their own practice. Only a quarter of practitioners make that information available outside that practice. This leaves 75% of the population without records that can be immediately accessed so patients can get immediate care in the times they need it. This costs Canadian taxpayers an extra $9.4 billion a year. Let us think about that. Billions of dollars are being lost because the information that already exists on a system somewhere is not being accessed by someone right next door. Patients are undergoing repeat tests. Health care professionals are spending extra time tracking down records. Important information is being missed when patients move between providers. Doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other health care professionals should be spending their time caring for patients, and that is it. They should not be spending their time trying to access information that already exists on another system. It is a complete waste of, first, the physician's time and, second, the immediate access to care for patients who immediately need it. Not having to chase down medical records or repeat work that has already been done would only help the care of patients here in Canada. We should be giving physicians the tools they need to do their jobs, not making their jobs more difficult by repeatedly investigating the care that a particular person may need. There is a tremendous opportunity with the bill, but there are a lot of questions behind the scenes. We do need to make sure that the details are right with this piece of legislation, because Canadians need to be able to access their own data, and we do need actual improvements for Canadians. This cannot just be another measure where we are saying that we are going to be doing something in Parliament but not actually working with the provinces and territories to make sure that it is implemented across Canada. We have questions that we need to ask, and as we move forward, we will ensure that we ask these questions in committee. Provinces and territories are responsible for their own health care systems. As the federal government, we need to respect the role of the provinces. We should be working with them to make sure that health information can be shared across provinces in a way that all provinces agree with. We have to ensure that we are not going to be encroaching on provincial territory when we are trying to implement a system to access care across systems. This is a key important piece of this legislation that we need to look at. We need to understand how the bill would work with the systems that are already in place and make sure provinces still have a say in how these changes are made. We know that different practitioners use different systems, so what does that mean for the current systems that practitioners are already using? Are they going to be able to keep these systems or are they going to need to move to a different system? None of these questions have any answers to them yet, and these are the things we are going to look at.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate that there is tremendous opportunity behind this bill to ensure that we would have data transfer of our health information, but at the same time, we have quite a few questions we need answered to ensure that we would remain sovereign, would be protecting our innovation and that it would still be within the jurisdiction of our provinces. We need to make sure these details are right, because Canadians need actual improvements. They do not need announcements or grand gestures. They need real improvement to a system in which our data is not being transferred between jurisdictions. Provinces and territories are responsible for making their own health care systems. As a federal government, we need to respect the role of the provinces in this discussion. We should be working with them to make sure their health information can be shared across other provinces but that we would not be creating more red tape in doing so and that provinces would actually have their say on how this needs to operate. We need to understand how the bill would work with the systems that are already in place and to make sure provinces would still have a say in how these changes would be implemented. If one province is using one system and another province is using another system, we have to ensure that there would be compatibility between the two and that they have a say, instead of arbitrarily saying that there is another provider to use and everybody has to make the adjustment to a new system This would cost the taxpayer entirely too much money as we try to implement this across Canada. The other thing we need to talk about is making sure we would not make it harder for small businesses and start-ups to compete in this industry. We do not want so many rules and regulations, so much red tape, that the biggest companies would be the only ones able to develop the softwares that would be used for the data collection and transfer as we move forward. Our innovators and entrepreneurs have great ideas and amazing solutions, but they need a fair chance to compete. We should be encouraging more competition and innovation, not creating barriers that protect the biggest players and keep the little guys out. The third thing we need to talk about is privacy and security. Canadians share some of their most personal information with the health care system, and they need to know that this information is protected. Imagine someone with a communicable disease who does not want everyone to know about it. Some hacker gets in, and then all of a sudden everyone knows about something the person has held very private, kept to themselves. We need to ensure that this information would not get out to the general public. We need to make it easier for doctors and hospitals to share important records and information, but at the same time ensure that they would be the only ones that could access them. They have to be protected, sovereign and secure. Better information sharing is important, absolutely, but it would not fix every problem in our health care system. It would not put more family doctors in communities that desperately need them. It would not shorten the wait times for hip replacements or get someone into the emergency room faster. These challenges still need to be addressed, but this does matter. We need to make sure that the changes would lead to actual results for Canadians. This is one of the things on which we would hold the government to account should the legislation go through the steps and pass: that the government implement something and truly make a change for Canadians, not just another grand gesture with Liberals' saying they did something, but then nothing ever came of it. Another important discussion we need to have is about data sovereignty. As we connect more of our health care systems, we need to think about who controls Canadians' data and health information. Where would the information be stored, who would have access to that information and which country's laws would apply to our Canadian health care data? This is extremely important. We cannot be dependent on foreign companies to operate the technology that our health care systems rely on, because then we could need to answer to the U.S. CLOUD Act or other provisions that would allow the U.S. to take control of our Canadian citizens' health care data. We have to ensure that we remain sovereign, take a very sovereign approach to our Canadian data and protect the most vulnerable information of our citizens. There is absolutely nothing wrong with embracing new technology or working with companies that have offered the technology and can share that information, but we cannot put ourselves in a position where we would lose control over these systems or no longer be able to protect that information at the same time. Canada needs to build its own expertise, strengthen our digital infrastructure and make sure we have the ability to protect our information under Canadian laws. This is the key part. Our data has to be protected under Canadian laws, especially when it comes to our health care data. Being sovereign in today's world means more than just where a company is operated or being on Canadian soil. It also matters where the data is being stored and what server is being used. Is it the cloud? Is it on the premises? How is this information being stored to protect Canadian data? We should be embracing innovation and should be looking for ways to make our health care system more efficient and better connected, absolutely, but we must do this by having control over our own data, not by compromising Canadians' health data. Privacy, security and control matter in this conversation, and we have to make sure we discuss it. Bill S-5 is an opportunity to make progress on an issue that is holding our health care system back. That does not mean we open our data to non-protections to move forward with data transfers. It does not mean that we will not have questions to bring forth as this policy moves forward. When it comes down to it, Canadians are not worried, really, about which software their hospital uses or how systems communicate. What they want to know is that when they need medical care, their doctor has the information they need, they can get their services fast and their personal information will be protected. That is what Canadians care about. That is what this bill should be about, not just better information sharing, but better care, better access and better outcomes for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend my colleague from Kitchener on her great speech. I wonder if there is anything specific she hears from her constituents, with some examples perhaps, about frustrations with accessing their health care data. Is there something that she really feels could be added to this bill to improve their daily lives?

Mr. Speaker, we get emails all the time about how people go to one practitioner and then have to go to the hospital and re-explain their entire medical history. Then they go back to their practitioner to get a referral and go to the specialist with the referral, and they end up on the operating table if need be. They have to share their information across all those different avenues. That is happening all the time. I get emails all the time from constituents who ask why they cannot do it once to make sure they mark the right leg and move forward. Yes, I think this is going to help in specific situations like that.

Mr. Speaker, the bill would give the government the power to establish administrative monetary penalties for health IT vendors that do not comply. I wonder what would stop these penalties from simply being another cost of doing business. How can we ensure that the penalties are strong enough to actually deter data blocking?

Mr. Speaker, these are the questions we will have to bring up at committee, absolutely. How are we going to prevent data blocking? What regulations are going to be put in place? How would we ensure that it would not just be the conglomerates that are able to play in this game anymore? We have to make sure the start-ups, the innovation and the free market can still compete in this area at the same time as we hold regulators accountable to make sure they are sharing that information.

Mr. Speaker, as we can see, my hon. colleague is an expert in the field, being an engineer. My concern is this: How do we protect victims of violence to ensure that their perpetrators do not have access to this information? What controls do we have to ensure that this information is kept secret?

Mr. Speaker, this is one of the sensitive topics that we absolutely need to address when this bill moves forward, because there are going to be perpetrators out there who want to access personal health information, as in the trafficking world. We have to make sure that we are able to protect that data, that the data remains sovereign and that it is up to an individual to share that data. How is the government going to make sure that all those things are in place as it moves this bill forward?

Mr. Speaker, it was the member opposite who mentioned that if we look at this through the lens of the client, the patient, we will be able to come to a consensus on how it needs to work. Absolutely, this falls under provincial jurisdiction, and we have to make sure that we are maintaining that jurisdiction as we move forward. However, the conversation would become easier between the provinces if we looked at it through the mindset of the patient. That is where we really need to focus in this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's explanation. She is an expert in this field. What would the member say is the most important thing here? If and when this bill goes to committee, what would be the most important thing that would need to be addressed or changed in this bill?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for the gravitas for my expertise. There are some key elements here that we need to discuss. Number one, would we stifle innovation and free market through it? Number two, would the data be protected? Number three, would it be up to the individual to even share their data in the first place? These are three questions that I have, and as we move forward, I will be continually asking them.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the member could comment on how we can ensure that interoperability will not come at the expense of privacy and that the government commits to involving the Privacy Commissioner in developing the regulations and security standards under this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is extremely important that we protect data as we move forward with this legislation. It is going to be up to the government to answer the question of how data would be protected and what regulations it would put in place. It is the number one thing we need to focus on to make sure that our data is secure so that someone cannot just hack in and get access to our most critical information, our personal critical information, and so that our data remains sovereign and falls under Canadian law, not under a foreign jurisdiction or a foreign country's law.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her in-depth explanations. Has data sovereignty been an issue in other countries? I am sure we are following and are quite a bit behind some other countries on this issue. Does my colleague know of any other countries that had problems with their data being hacked or their health system being hacked when they were proceeding with interoperability?

Mr. Speaker, I am not 100% sure of other countries that have had their data hacked, but we do hear in the news all the time about different companies that have been hacked. Even AI has been, so there is a real risk there and an opportunity for this information to be hacked. As my other colleague brought up earlier, it could even be a perpetrator who wants information from someone, so they hack into the system and specifically target one individual. There are lots of scenarios we can talk about. We have to really make sure that our data is secure as we move forward with this bill. At the same time, we need to move forward with this legislation. We need to have conversations surrounding it, and we have to make sure we get it right for the interests of Canadians and health care across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this needs to remain under provincial jurisdiction. Nothing needs to change there, but I think the provinces need to work together to make sure that data can be interchanged. It is extremely important to reduce harm and save lives. As I mentioned in my speech, I know of someone who was given penicillin by accident and died because their information was not transferred from province to province. They had gotten into a car accident. The provinces need to work together to ensure we have a transfer of data, but I absolutely do not think this should be removed from provincial jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the residents of Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay to speak to Bill S-5. I am always honoured to speak in the House for my communities. Bill S-5 is an act respecting the interoperability of health information technology and to prohibit data blocking by health information technology vendors. I am pleased to speak to this legislation as a member of the Standing Committee on Health. It has been a great honour, in my time in the House, to provide oversight of our health care system. Canadians are proud of our health care system, and for good reason. However, most Canadians and most members in this House agree that it needs improvement. There are many issues, too many for me to even list here, that we are addressing in our committee. To name one, the Canada health transfer has risen substantially, yet access remains poor. In fact, the Canada health transfer increased from $37.2 billion in 2017-18 to $57.4 billion in 2026-27, a 55% increase in nominal terms. Despite this increase, Canadians are still waiting longer for several priority surgeries and diagnostic tests than before the pandemic. Canada continues to rank poorly, internationally, for timely access. Younger Canadians face particularly poor access to primary care. In 2023, more than one in four Canadians aged 18 to 34 did not have a regular health care provider. One in five Canadians aged 35 to 49 lacked a regular health care provider. We have a gateway system in our health care, and it did work for quite a long while. However, it does not work unless Canadians have a health care provider or a family doctor. Canada ranks last among 10 peer countries examined for timely access to care and, of course, the lack of that initial provider is one of the reasons. In 2025, the C.D. Howe Institute analysis ranked Canada 10th out of 10 countries for timeliness. Again, I know everyone in this House who has had to wait in line or bring a loved one to a hospital for any kind of testing would not question that data. Only 86% of Canadians reported having a regular doctor or place of care, and just 25% can see a doctor or nurse the same day. In the communities that I represent in Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay, it is not 86% that have a doctor. I know a lot of these stats are different for rural communities like mine that have a severe lack of family doctors and specialists. Thousands in Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay right now have no family doctor. Forty-seven per cent of Canadians waited two months or longer for a specialist, and 59% waited two months or longer for an elective surgery. In 2024-25 at least 23,000 patients died in Canada while on wait-lists for surgeries or diagnostic scans. We have to wonder if that number is even accurate because there are a lot of people who might not be included who died of other issues they were having while waiting. It is hard to know if it is even much more than that; I am sure it is. Emergency rooms are under significant pressure. In 2024, 1.2 million emergency department visits, or 7.7% of all reported visits, ended with the patient leaving before being seen and assessed by a physician. Canadians are spending longer in emergency departments.
