In 2024, half of emergency patients waited just under two hours for an initial physician assessment, while one in 10 waited more than five hours. Of course, some of this can be attributed to what we are talking about today and the issues that Bill S-5 is trying to solve. One in 10 patients waited more than 14 hours in an emergency department overall. That is a 28% increase from 2018. Hospital capacity is contributing to extreme delays for patients who need to be admitted. In fact, in 2024-25, one in 10 admitted patients waited more than 36 hours for an in-patient bed after the decision to admit them had been made. That is a 45% increase from 2018. Surgical and diagnostic waits remain worse than before the pandemic. In 2024, only 68% of hip replacement patients received surgery within the 26-week benchmark. That is down from 75% in 2019. Only 61% of knee replacement patients met the benchmark, down from 70%. The most important thing is there are people behind the statistics. There are people who are extremely active, who want to stay active, who do not want to go into a home and do not want to be a burden to their families. They cannot get that hip surgery in a timely manner. They cannot get that knee surgery. They want to continue to play tennis, to play pickleball, to go running, to go walking on trails, and they cannot because they are in extreme pain for months. It is really not fair. Let us go to MRI waits, which are 15 days longer right now than they were in 2019, while waits for CT scans are taking three days longer. The Standing Committee on Health is studying these wait times currently. Knowledge is power and the more we know exactly what is going wrong compared to other countries, the more we will be able to resolve this problem. Waits for specialist care and treatment remain lengthy. The Fraser Institute 2025 physician survey reported a median 28-week wait for referral by a family doctor to receipt of treatment. Again, I believe those numbers are even higher in rural areas that have an even greater shortage of specialists. Canada spends heavily on health care and continues to struggle with access and capacity. Among the 31 high-income countries with universal health coverage, Canada ranked third-highest for health spending as a share of GDP, but 27th of 30 for the availability of doctors, 27th of 31 for MRI machines and 28th of 31 for CAT scan machines. These are things that Bill S-5 would address. Being able to communicate is one of the issues, obviously, with Canadian health care, and that is why I do support much of what is in this bill. It attempts to improve our system by making our health care data accessible beyond our own home province. We are travelling more within the country now. We are buying Canadian, we are travelling Canadian, and we are vacationing Canadian. We need to be able to cross provincial boundaries, into any province, and if there is any kind of situation where we need to see a health care provider, which of course happens all the time, we need them to have our information available, to know, as my colleague mentioned, whether we are allergic to any kind of medication or need some operation, and to know what is happening at home with our home doctor. If we cross provincial boundaries at this point, there is no information available most of the time. We are exploring our great country. We are hiking the Rockies north of the border or we are heading for Montreal instead of Palm Beach now. As more Canadians are exploring the country, they will need to interact with other provincial health care systems. Re-injuring an existing injury or refilling a prescription has become more common. People across our country move between family doctors, community clinics, hospitals and diagnostic labs, yet in far too many cases, their medical history fails to follow them. Systems remain trapped behind digital walls and information remains fragmented. We cannot allow provincial silos to limit our medical services in Canada. Obviously, this runs counter to the spirit of the Canada Health Act and to our health accords. Again, there are people behind all these statistics. The number one thing is that we need to keep the Canadian people healthy. I represent one of the country's eldest regions. Our communities are also full of young families, alongside many recent retirees and long-time residents. Generations of wisdom are always on display, and we are fortunate that so many Canadians from every province choose to make Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay their new home in their golden years, but as they bring their cherished mementos, they can also bring complex medical histories, long-term prescriptions, diagnostic scans and test results. Seniors should not be made solely responsible for ensuring that their medical history is properly updated with local health care professionals, not in a country where our health care is supposed to be universal. I can give two examples in my region that illustrate this need. Penticton Regional Hospital recently lost its entire staff of neurologists, even though our region is home to more seniors than anywhere else in the country and it is one of the eldest regions in our country. Neurology is a vital service to ensure seniors' aging brain and nervous system changes are properly screened, cared for and managed. The loss of these neurologists will mean more seniors will have to travel further for screenings and speak with neurologists many hundreds of kilometres away about the care they received in Penticton. If they need to go to another health authority for specialized screening, it is not always guaranteed that they would be able to see the testing history from their former hospital. We all know that this is true, because sometimes we can drive from one pharmacy on one side of town to another pharmacy on the other side of town, and they have no idea what prescription we are on. If these seniors go to another province, and I have spoken with residents who have seen specialists in Alberta, their data is not available. Similarly, the emergency room in the town of Oliver, has seen sudden, random closures repeatedly over the past few years, more than 40 times, or almost once a week in a calendar year. I would like to take this time to thank the former mayor of Oliver for his service over the past eight years and for sitting as a witness before the Standing Committee on Health to talk to members of Parliament about what it is like for a small community to have their emergency room close randomly, sporadically, multiple times a year. It is more than 40 times a year. I thank Martin Johansson for the service he has given to our communities and for putting those first. Let us remember that, when a small community like Oliver's emergency room closes randomly, it has a domino effect throughout the whole region, because not only is it an emergency that needs to be attended to, but the other hospitals these people have to go to will get extremely backed up. I have received so much mail about the health care system, so much mail and so many calls about how broken the system is. I am going to read a short letter from one of my constituents, Marie-Louise, who says the following: “I am writing to express my concern about the lack of timely medical care in the Emergency Hospital in Penticton. “In the Similkameen—South Okanagan this sad situation is not new.... “Unfortunately, long delays in seeing a doctor can leave all patients, and especially parents of babies and young children, frightened, helpless and anxious.” When a person goes to the hospital's ER, prompt attention from a doctor is expected and needed. Marie-Louise continues: “This happened to our family on Monday of a long weekend. We had our three-month-old baby granddaughter go to the emergency room. The doctor came in to see the baby 3 hours later, and she came after the shift switch. Meanwhile the baby had arrived 3 hours earlier and apparently the emergency room was fairly quiet on that early morning. “These delays in seeing the doctor in due time are not new. “These delays are not acceptable....” This is especially true with a three-month-old baby. I want members to think about the stories of Canadians who check in at one ER in one province and are dismissed, only to end up in the care of another hospital in another province with a checkered history at best of what prior tests were done or of any prior observations by doctors. In its current form, Bill S-5 is intended to address the concern that many electronic health records and health IT systems cannot easily communicate with each other because of data blocking. Data blocking is when health IT vendors restrict access or the exchange of health data to protect market shares or extract licensing fees. This is not acceptable. We cannot allow big tech to act as an armed bandit when it comes to accessing health care records. Other jurisdictions have moved to prohibit this practice, and I am glad we have the opportunity to do that right here. Getting health data right is not something for computers. It is for patients. It is for the people. It is for Canadians. This means fewer duplicative tests and fewer bad diagnoses made with incomplete information. It must mean making Canada's 13 different health care data systems able to connect to one another and not be at the mercy of health tech companies setting costly and artificial restrictions on Canadians' most sensitive information. In other words, legislation must be a win-win for those working in health care and those who need health care. I do want to say, as a member of the health care committee who helped lead the investigation into the PrescribeIT scandal, I can say with some expertise that allowing Infoway to handle the regulations for shared health care records would be a costly and futile disaster for taxpayers, patients and doctors. Even our health minister has agreed that this agency needs an audit as soon as possible. We are waiting for that audit. Infoway should not be put in charge of this new program. Basically, I would like to say I believe the minister knows it is not fit for that—

Mr. Speaker, it is very important that health care in this country, in every province, has the appropriate funding, yet we have to make sure that money is well spent. If we do not have our health information going between provinces, or even within provinces, our health care will only get worse. I believe that we can throw as much money as we want at all the provinces to improve their health care, but if the money is not spent appropriately, it is of no use. Right now, the communication is blocked. That is why we need a bill like Bill S-5. I am looking forward to it going to committee so we can scrutinize it even further.

Mr. Speaker, during the member's remarks, she reflected on the challenges that many rural Canadians face in accessing health care services that the average Canadian in a large urban area would take for granted. Could the member comment more on the challenges that rural Canadians face in equity with respect to health care?

Mr. Speaker, I know much of my colleague's riding is rural, so his constituents have many of the same issues that rural communities have across the country. They cannot access a family doctor. They cannot access specialists. A good example is the Penticton hospital, which is a regional hospital. It services thousands of people and, by the way, it services thousands of seniors, many of whom have neurological issues. All three neurologists at the hospital quit or stepped down, so we do not have a neurologist in our regional hospital. I do not think that would happen in an urban centre. We are going to be in a lot of trouble if that is not corrected. That is just an example of a problem faced in rural Canada right now with health care.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank and congratulate my colleague on her excellent speech. I think she highlighted our broad support for the bill, and the goals and objectives of the bill, while still making it very clear that there are a number of clarity points that we will be discussing with the government at committee when the bill moves to that stage. I wonder if my colleague would provide a bit more clarity and detail on her experience with the Health Infoway scandal. I know we are awaiting the results of the audit, but I would like to hear some more thoughts from her on that.

Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate that the Prime Minister is sitting in the House. Oh, I do not think I am allowed to say that. I really appreciate that most of the Liberal Party is here, so we can go over, again, the scandal of PrescribeIT and Infoway, as $300 million has been lost into thin air. We do not know why because the health minister refuses to come speak to the committee about it. Also, the health minister has even said that Infoway needs to have an audit and does not want to secure its regular funding until there is an audit. There is no way that an organization like Infoway can run the program that is described in Bill S-5. I appreciate the fact that most of the Liberal Party is in the House right now and will address, hopefully soon, the problems with Infoway and PrescribeIT.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people of Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola, and I am going to take this last opportunity to hope that the budget includes funding for things in Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola like the rebuilding and fast-tracking of the Red Bridge. The Liberals can groan all they want about the funding of the Red Bridge, but I will fight every single day for that funding, or for a new Barriere fire hall. It is always wonderful to ask for these types of things. The Liberals may groan, but I am here to fight for my constituents and common-sense measures. My colleague talked about the PrescribeIT scandal. The minister has not appeared at committee. What does it say to Canadians when a minister refuses to go to committee?

Mr. Speaker, I think there are a lot of things that Canadians are looking for in their health care system, but what they are really looking for is trust. They want to be able to trust everyone in the House. They want to be able to trust the system. If they cannot depend on a program, for example, PrescribeIT, which wasted $300 million, run by Infoway, how can they trust any new program that comes forward from the Liberals? We need to, as a House, rebuild the trust of the entire Canadian people and put in new programs like those described in Bill S-5. We need to first rebuild the trust that has been lost by the public, which has read and learned about what has happened with the scandal of PrescribeIT and Infoway.

title: Adjournment Proceedings: Taxation
turns: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on behalf of the farm-filled riding of Algonquin—Renfrew—Pembroke to address the absence of an answer from the Liberal government when asked if the Liberals would support our Conservative emergency fuel relief plan. Soaring diesel costs are putting even more pressure on the cost of food. Diesel prices have risen by nearly 80% over the last year. Diesel powers the tractors that grow our food. Diesel powers the trucks and trains that move it. When those costs rise, farmers, businesses and families pay more. That is why the Conservatives put forward the emergency fuel relief plan to cut diesel costs, produce more Canadian fuel and save Canadians money. Sadly, the Liberal MPs voted it down. Lower costs for farmers who grow our food and the businesses that ship it mean lower costs throughout the supply chain. Our plan to save Canadians money stands in stark contrast to the Liberals' official policy of higher prices. The Liberal plan to ban 90% of plastic in grocery stores will increase the price of food. The Liberal plan to increase ethanol and gasoline has increased, and will continue to increase, the prices at the pump. The Prime Minister's promise to impose carbon tariffs will increase the cost of imports from countries without a carbon tax. The Liberal plan to impose costly new electricity regulations will push up the price of Canadians' power bills. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister claims this is all fake news. He waves his hand and tells us, “These are not the Liberal policies you're looking for.” Instead, the Liberals reach for the Trump playbook, specifically the page on meaningless symbolic renamings. Just as the U.S. president renamed Lake Ontario, the Liberals renamed the GST credit, but the Liberal gaslighting starts when they claim their renamed GST credit is somehow proof that they care about affordability. The truth is that this is evidence of their guilt. Gaslighting is the only way to describe a party led by an economist who makes the claim that giving people back their own money lowers prices. Liberal policies such as the plastic packaging ban, as well as electricity and fuel regulations, increase costs. The Prime Minister's out of control spending is fuelling inflation. The latest PBO report highlights just how much more reckless this Liberal government is compared to the previous Trudeau government. The report reveals that, before any new spending has been announced in the upcoming budget, total borrowing over the next five years will reach three quarters of a trillion dollars. Every Canadian should know that the first $1,500 they send the government in taxes is going to pay the interest on the Liberal debt. Interest payments are the fastest-growing expense. By the end of the government's term in office, the federal government will be spending $83 billion on interest payments, and that same year the federal government is budgeted to spend $64 billion on health care. We have an aging population, but prime minister Brookfield wants to spend more on corporate welfare than Canadians' health care. Out of control spending pushes up demand in the economy and stokes inflation. Liberal regulations push up the cost of fuel and electricity. They will deny this reality as long as they can, but Canadians paying higher prices can see the truth. Higher prices are the official policy of the Liberal Party.

Mr. Speaker, our government recognizes that Canadians are facing economic uncertainty as global instability and rising costs put pressure on household budgets. Tariffs imposed by our largest trading partner are having a significant impact on workers and businesses from coast to coast to coast. At the same time, conflict and instability in the Middle East have contributed to higher fuel prices around the world. In the face of these pressures, Canadians need relief, and our government has delivered. Last spring, we acted to ease the impact of the high fuel costs on Canadians. In April, after disruptions to crude oil shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz drove fuel prices even higher, our government temporarily suspended the federal fuel excise tax. This measure saved Canadians and Canadian businesses up to 10¢ per litre on gasoline and unleaded aviation gasoline, up to 11¢ per litre on leaded aviation gasoline and up to four cents per litre on diesel and aviation fuel. The cost savings were immediate. When the temporary suspension of the federal fuel excise tax was first introduced, gasoline prices declined by 11% per litre on the first day of the implementation, delivering immediate results to consumers. With Bill C-38, we are continuing to provide relief at the pump by proposing to extend the temporary suspension of the federal fuel excise tax until and including January 31, 2027, and to apply 50% of the regular excise tax rate from February 1 through March 31, 2027, inclusively. This measure would help lower everyday costs for Canadians, including truckers and businesses in the food, agriculture, housing, construction and delivery sectors. In short, it would continue providing timely and meaningful relief when Canadians need it the most. We also recognize that groceries do not reach the store shelves on their own. In a country as vast as Canada, moving people and goods is essential and it depends heavily on diesel fuel. Higher diesel prices at the pump have also squeezed business margins by increasing the cost of bringing goods to market. The government remains in close contact with refiners as they maximize diesel production capacity to respond to current conditions. As our government has said many times, we remain focused on what we can control, including strengthening Canada's economy, diversifying our international trade partnerships, managing public finances responsibly and supporting Canadians, who are facing rising costs on a daily basis. Across the country, Canadians are concerned about the cost of essentials, including fuel, food, housing and other basic necessities. Our government understands these pressures and is taking concrete, responsible action to provide relief while safeguarding Canada's long-term economic stability. That action includes temporarily suspending the excise tax on gasoline and diesel.

Mr. Speaker, in the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister's response to my question, he randomly accused me of not supporting farmers in Pembroke. While there are nearly 1,000 farms in my riding, none of them are located in the city of Pembroke. This geographic confusion is easily corrected. There is no better time than autumn for a road trip to the Ottawa Valley. I would like to invite all members of Parliament to take a drive along the scenic Opeongo Line, stop for lunch at Calabogie's Redneck Bistro or enjoy a dinner at Whitewater Brewing in Cobden. There is even still a little time for picking apples at McGregor's Orchard near Renfrew. The Prime Minister's hand-picked parliamentary secretary may have hallucinated farms in Pembroke, but he can be rest assured that I support all the non-imaginary employers in the beautiful riding of Algonquin—Renfrew—Pembroke.

Mr. Speaker, to reiterate, temporarily suspending the excise tax on gasoline and diesel reflects our government's balanced approach to delivering immediate cost relief through very targeted supports. Our government will continue to address affordability measures with fairness, discipline and a clear focus on the results for Canadians. We are helping Canadians manage today's uncertainty and affordability challenges while building a stronger, more resilient and more independent economy. That means once again taking practical steps to lower costs while investing in long-term prosperity. Finally, I would like to say that, if the member is offering to travel to some of these places, I would take that invitation and join her. As a Cape Bretoner speaking to someone from Ontario, I would relish that opportunity.

title: Private Members' Business: Youth Criminal Justice Act
turns: Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of Bill C-231, David's law, which recognizes the serious risks young Canadians face as our country continues to confront a devastating opioid and toxic drug crisis. Bill C-231 would strengthen the ability of police and courts to direct youth toward treatment programs early, before situations escalate. It would expand the use of extrajudicial measures so that intervention could happen outside the courtroom, where appropriate and in a way that prioritizes rehabilitation. Four months ago in the city of Abbotsford, the RCMP issued a statement regarding an investigation of a website that sold drugs. Through this investigation, three individuals were arrested, and numerous packages of drugs were seized. While the existence of these sites is not new, what troubled me most was that the site targeted minors specifically. That should concern every parent in our country. In British Colombia, unregulated drug toxicity was the leading cause of unnatural death among youth from 2019 to 2023, and in 67% of these cases, these youth had a mental health diagnosis or evidence of a mental health disorder. We know that these are not just statistics and numbers. These are young people who were struggling with something long before they encountered the criminal justice system: peer pressure, trauma, escapism, mental health challenges, addiction or, in many cases, a combination of circumstances that can be difficult for a young person to navigate on their own. We cannot ignore the offence. Public safety matters, and there must be accountability for criminal behaviour. With this bill, there would be no automatic amnesty. The young person would remain accountable for their actions, and the courts would retain their decision-making authority. However, accountability must also include asking a difficult question: Why did the young person end up where they are in the first place? We must address more than the crime. We must address the pain behind it. While Bill C-231's scope focuses on what would happen after a crime occurs, it is not just a path to recovery. It is a promise to our youth that they will not be abandoned because they use drugs and that they will not be written off because they were arrested due to those drugs. What happened in Abbotsford is not an isolated incident. Across British Columbia and Canada at large, the toxic drug crisis continues to claim lives. While British Columbia has taken steps to reverse the disastrous impacts of the NDP's drug legalization pilot project, the crisis does not appear to be ending any time soon. Just recently, the B.C. Supreme Court ruled that banning the possession of drugs for trafficking purposes is unconstitutional. This ruling comes after the opioid deaths among youth in B.C. tripled between 2017 and 2021. B.C. paramedics responded to nearly 40,000 overdose calls in 2025. In 2026, one in every three drug deaths in B.C. involved someone under the age of 30. One in nine of those involved a child. Dr. Jennifer Charlesworth, British Columbia's representative for children and youth, noted that young people experiencing brain injuries following non-fatal drug poisonings are often being exploited when seeking or using illicit substances. These heartbreaking trends cannot continue. In the words of my hon. colleague who introduced this bill, we must do “everything we can...to improve the lives of our children” and “show young people in this country that the House [,their House,] cares for them.” Bill C-231 had unanimous support at second reading and has since undergone amendments that would improve the bill's effectiveness. The committee process strengthened Bill C-231 by proposing expanded access to treatment at every stage of the youth justice process. It clarified that police and prosecutors should consider referring young people to treatment, it would formally add treatment as an option to extrajudicial sanctions, and it would allow courts to delay sentencing so a young person could complete a treatment program with consent. It would also ensure that treatment could be included as a condition of probation and supervision orders, while aligning the bill with related legislation and adding a clear coming-into-force timeline. These are practical tools that would give our justice system greater flexibility. These changes sharpen Bill C-231 and should only encourage the House to pass the legislation with unanimous consent once again. Public trust in our laws is being tested. Canadians need clarity, accountability and confidence that our laws can both protect public safety and address addiction. Instead, years of Liberal mismanagement have produced confusion about how drug laws should be enforced and what tools the justice system has in order to confront this crisis. If a young person can overcome addiction, re-enter their community and avoid reoffending, that is a win for them and a win for society. Conservatives have always maintained that compassion and accountability must go hand in hand. At the same time, we must never lose sight of the fact that other people profit from suffering. Those who traffic dangerous drugs should face meaningful consequences for the harm they cause in our communities. That is why Bill C-231 is so important. It recognizes that addiction is not solved by incarceration alone and that intervention, treatment and rehabilitation must be available to our youth so they can rebuild their lives and avoid a future marked by substance abuse and crime. It is a way forward. It would give young people an opportunity to confront addiction, receive treatment and change the course of their lives before it is too late. This is why I support Bill C-231, and I encourage all my colleagues of the House to support it as well.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise in the House and represent the people of Cardigan, and I am pleased to rise today at third reading to speak in support of private member's bill, Bill C-231, a bill that has benefited from thoughtful consideration and study at the Standing Committee on Justice and Human Rights. I am proud to speak in support of Bill C-231, which proposes specific amendments to the Youth Criminal Justice Act. For the sake of brevity, I will refer to the act by its acronym, the YCJA. Bill C-231 proposes to amend the YCJA to help youth with substance use disorders who come in contact with the criminal justice system to access treatment programs that would assist them in meaningfully rehabilitating and in reintegrating into their communities. More specifically, the bill proposes to clarify the instances when a young person in contact with the youth criminal justice system can be referred to or ordered to participate in a treatment program and to enable, in certain cases, a youth justice court to defer sentencing to allow that young person to participate in treatment programs. In addition, the bill proposes to amend the YCJA to enable the youth justice court to include in certain orders the condition of attending a treatment program. The objectives of the bill align well with the objectives of the YCJA and the overall youth criminal justice system. The preamble to the bill calls on communities, families, parents and others concerned with the development of young persons to be active participants in the youth criminal justice system. The bill would invite their involvement to prevent youth crime by addressing its underlying causes, to respond to the needs of young persons and to provide guidance and support to those at risk of committing crimes. Bill C-231 would enhance the YCJA's multipronged approach to problematic substance use and seek to improve outcomes for young people with substance use disorders who come in contact with the criminal justice system. At second reading of the bill, some members shared personal stories, as well as stories from their constituents. These stories remind us that problematic substance use and mental health issues affect all of us, whether directly or indirectly. These heartfelt and informative discussions continued during the committee study of Bill C-231. I want to thank the committee members for their interest and their active participation during the study of Bill C-231. Their candid and at times personal interventions help nourish the committee's discussions regarding potential amendments. I also want to thank the witnesses who came forward and shared touching stories, as well as insightful views on topics related to problematic substance use. We had the privilege to hear from the member for Mégantic—L'Érable—Lotbinière, who tragically lost his son David last year. We heard from Caroline Levesque, who is David's mother and an early childhood educator, and Justine, who is David's younger sister and a nurse. During their testimony, they mentioned that, too often, the criminal justice system focuses on the offences and the punishments without looking into the underlying causes of a young person's offending behaviour. They spoke about the importance for the youth criminal justice system of having the right tools and said that enabling decision-makers to use those tools at the right time would improve the YCJA's ability to support meaningful rehabilitation and reintegration. The committee also heard from Angy Riendeau, a criminologist who has highlighted the importance of early interventions when it comes to preventing and addressing the risk factors that can eventually lead to persistent criminality in adulthood. She noted that the amendments in Bill C-231 would add to the intervention mechanisms already available under the YCJA to better help young people access treatment, specialized assessments, care and appropriate resources in a timely manner. The amendments that were made during the clause-by-clause study of Bill C-231 are consistent with the views that were shared during the witnesses’ testimonies. All the amendments proposed were adopted unanimously by committee members. This showcases the close co-operation that the bill has cultivated among members. To further the bill's objective of improving the YCJA's public health approach to problematic substance use, many of the amendments that were made to Bill C-231 at committee relate to the language used in the bill. For example, the term “addiction” was replaced by “problematic substance use” to align with the more modern and less stigmatizing language used in the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act. Certain clauses of the bill were also amended to refer to “problematic substance use treatment program or any other treatment program”. This is to avoid unintended interpretations which may restrict access to other types of treatment programs, including programs focused on mental health or on behaviour modification and skills development. This broader terminology allows the YCJA to remain flexible and relevant should the types of treatment available to young people evolve over time. Furthermore, multiple amendments were made to Bill C-231 at committee seeking to clarify, and at times broaden, the instances where decision-makers under the YCJA can refer to or order youth to participate in the treatment program. For example, a coordinating amendment was added to ensure that prosecutors, in addition to police officers, must consider whether it would be appropriate to refer a young person to a problematic substance use treatment program before starting or continuing judicial proceedings against the young person. Moreover, amendments were made to clarify the situations when attendance at a problematic substance use treatment program, or any other treatment program, may be ordered as a sentence or as a condition to an order. For example, an amendment was made to explicitly mention that attendance to such treatment programs can be ordered as a condition of probation and conditional supervision. These amendments would ensure greater consistency in the YCJA sentencing framework. When it comes to problematic substance abuse, especially in the context of Canada's overdose crisis and the toxic illegal drug supply, the federal government is committed to a comprehensive public health and safety approach that focuses on connecting people to vital services and supporting prevention, treatment and recovery, as well as destigmatization. This bill aligns with many other actions the federal government has taken to address the overdose crisis in Canada. Bill C-231 would improve and clarify the tools available to police, prosecutors and judges so they can make timely referrals and orders to treatment programs that would address the underlying causes of their offending behaviour. This would help youth receive the support they need to properly rehabilitate and reintegrate into their families and communities. In closing, I believe significant improvements were made to this bill during its clause-by-clause study and it is ready for passage in this chamber. I urge all members to support this bill at third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of Bill C-231. I want to thank all the members who have risen so far this morning in support of this very important legislation and the amendments to the Youth Criminal Justice Act. When our colleague, the member for Mégantic—L'Érable—Lotbinière, first rose to introduce this bill and share his family's personal story, his experience and his son's experience, it was one of the most powerful moments in this chamber since I have had the privilege of serving in the House. I commend him for his advocacy work and for all the effort he has put into bringing this change forward. I know that many of my constituents, and many Canadians across the country, believe this is a really important change to the way our system currently works. This bill is called the for the friends of David law. In every community across our country, there are friends of David. There are people who are going through the exact same challenges and are in need of the exact same help and support that David was in need of. I want to share a story about a particular young man from my community of Oshawa, one of our star football players who was picked for team Ontario three times. I will not share his name out of respect for the family, but the family did an interview with Maclean's magazine where some of these details can be found if anyone would like to read more about it. One of the important parts of their story, as they detailed what it was like as a mother and father to watch their son, a very talented young man who played football in our community, deal with his addiction issues and challenges, is how difficult it was for them to get help. There is a quote from his mother in the Maclean's magazine article where she said, “All I kept hearing was: ‘Our hands are tied.’” Every time she would go to the police or social services to seek out help for her son, she kept being told their hands were tied and there was nothing they could do about it. It is a very heartbreaking story knowing all the talent that was lost when that young man passed away from an overdose several years ago. The parents spoke of the ups and downs they experienced as hope was presented to them and then hope was lost, as there was the possibility of their son getting help and then that possibility going away. It is a very emotionally, psychologically and spiritually taxing experience. I wish there was a perfect solution for it so we could cure people of the illness they are experiencing with just the stroke of a pen. However, what we can do is make it easier for people to get help when they interact with governmental systems and processes. What this bill would do, and why I think it is so important, is that, just like with the young man in Oshawa, where people could see he needed help and were struggling to match him with the help that he needed, it would give the system an opportunity, when there are young men and young women in that same situation, to give them the help they need. This is especially true for young people when they first interact with the justice system. Many of those young men and young women are in some of the most difficult circumstances that one could imagine. Many of them are looking for help, but until someone puts it right in front of their faces or until someone really pushes them and encourages them to take that help, it can often be an opportunity lost. This bill would make it easier for police and prosecutors to refer youth to treatment. That is a really important step in the process of changing how our system works and making sure that help is more readily available to more people. In Durham region, the part of Ontario where I am from, we have seen a massive increase in opioid addiction in particular, with the number of people who have suffered an opioid overdose death tripling since 2015. ER visits have also gone up more than 100% since 2015. Suspected overdose paramedic calls have also increased over 100%, which is a real demand for our local services. People are constantly, whether they are paramedics, police officers, prosecutors or youth outreach workers, trying to find every opportunity they can to get people help. In Ontario, we have seen opioid deaths for those aged 15 to 24 triple from 2014 to 2021. A very important detail is that this is all while treatment medications have fallen 50%. We have seen a change in how much legal drugs are being given out by the system, but it has not changed the amount of overdoses we are seeing in our communities, which is an important proof point for the availability of illicit drugs to young people. I also want to point out that it is important to create these imperatives in the system for people to be able to say they are entitled to treatment. That is one of the things this legislation is able to do. Because people would know their children can be referred to youth treatment, it would create an opportunity for parents and young people to ask for it themselves. In Ontario, we see massive wait times for people to get access to treatment. The Ontario auditor general found that an average wait for live-in youth treatment is 105 days. That number is from 2024. I am sure it has only gone up since that research was made available. We have heard from parents who have said on the record publicly, and also in some of the reports we have reviewed, that there are hundreds of kids on wait-lists waiting for treatment who have not gotten it yet. There is no withdrawal management services specifically for youth in Ontario either. That means it is up to adult services to accept youth, which is often limited to those who are 16 and older. There is a bottleneck in the system, even if someone is willing to accept treatment, for the system to actually guarantee it is available. This was an important point made by one of the witnesses before the justice committee. I want to read some of the words from this witness because I think they put into perspective that, once we all support this bill, and I hope it will be unanimous, there is a lot more work to do to make sure the young people who are affected by this bill also receive the treatment they need. Angy Riendeau, a criminologist from Quebec who appeared as a witness before the justice committee in May 2026, stated, “The question, then, may not be solely how to compel a youth to undergo treatment, but rather how to ensure that, upon the first offence, a youth has rapid access to specialized assessment, care and appropriate resources.” As we vote on this bill, and as we think about what the next steps would be after this bill becomes law, it is important to go back to the question of the resources available to young people, families and, in particular, parents. There are two opportunities before the government right now to follow through on the sentiment behind this legislation with actual resources. One of those opportunities is a budget that we have yet to vote on in the House. That budget has a very paltry amount of resources dedicated to those of all age groups who are fighting addictions, and very little new spending is being contributed to help solve that problem. Perhaps if it would like to continue on with the sentiment behind this legislation, it may consider adding more funding for addiction services in the budget, particularly for young men and young women, before it goes to a vote. I think that would be a fantastic change to what has been presented in it thus far. Another important opportunity before the government to follow through on the sentiment behind this legislation is in its forthcoming national strategy for men and boys' health. We have seen a lot of changes in the initial plan for that national strategy. Just over a year ago, the government first announced that it was going to produce that strategy in 2026. We have since learned it has been delayed to 2027, with no specific dates. We were also told the government was going to do detailed and comprehensive consultations as part of its gathering of information about what should be in that national strategy. We saw it release a report that, quite frankly, omits a tremendous amount of feedback that was given by the Canadian people that should have been included. One of the most important points of feedback that I myself submitted, and also hosted town halls on, and I know the government received this feedback from organizations and individuals across the country, was on how to help young men and boys with addiction issues. That was a specific thing that was raised, and it is not adequately addressed in the report the government put forward outlining the feedback it received on its national strategy. One of the most important things missing in there is any acknowledgement of the government's failed safe supply drug policies, which put taxpayer dollars behind drugs, making it easier, as police departments across this country have reported, for taxpayer-supplied drugs to make their way into the illicit drug market. There are opportunities for the government to do more than just support the bill, but I am very glad to see all parties rise in the House today in support of this legislation. I look forward to voting for it.

title: Government Orders: Privilege
turns: Mr. Speaker, I am rising to respond to a question of privilege raised on October 6 by the opposition House leader respecting the alleged premature disclosure of Bill C-40. I would like to begin by stating that the government takes any allegation of potential premature disclosure of information during the notice period extremely seriously. This is why there has been a slight delay in responding to the points raised by the opposition House leader, as the government looked into this matter thoroughly. I can categorically state that our comprehensive investigation revealed that no one provided any information related to the content of the bill during the notice period. For that reason alone, I would assert that there is not a prima facie question of privilege in this instance. However, I want to provide the House with relevant information regarding the Defence Investment Agency that clearly demonstrates that the subject and nature of public deliberations on the form of the organization to lead this work of defence procurement could have led to the conclusion that the government was considering establishing a Crown corporation for this purpose. As it relates to the comments by the opposition House leader, there are two arguments that I would like to address. The first is the assertion that there is no way that any intelligent observer would be able to infer that the government was proposing that the form of the organization to manage defence procurement would be a Crown corporation. Second, when the opposition House leader refers in media reports to “sources” or “federal sources”, he seems to imply that these individuals provided confidential information to journalists during the notice period. While that may be his implication, it does not in any way corroborate that an individual divulged confidential information about the contents of a bill that was on the Notice Paper. As I have indicated, I can confirm to the House that we have looked thoroughly into this matter, and we have found no evidence of an internal leak of the contents of Bill C-40 during the notice period. In contrast to previous Speakers' rulings where the government stated that it could not confirm who leaked the contents of a bill during the notice period, our comprehensive investigation revealed no evidence that anyone provided any information related to the content of the bill during the notice period. What these inquiries and the public record demonstrate is that individuals did speak publicly about the possibility of a Crown corporation that would report to a supporting ministerial position under the Minister of National Defence over many months, but I can assure the House that these conversations did not occur at a time even proximate to the notice of the bill. The government's objective for defence procurement has remained unchanged since the beginning of the mandate in early 2025: to have an organization that would be sufficiently independent from the public service in order to have the flexibility and agility to procure military materiel to support our armed forces to defend our sovereignty and to meet our international commitments. That objective is at the heart of our work. The form that this would take has been a deliberative effort, building on the diverse perspectives from international engagement on different models for procurement, from input from stakeholders, and from procurement specialists. On April 27, 2026, Mr. Doug Guzman, chief executive officer of the Defence Investment Agency, appeared before the Standing Committee on National Defence and was asked about the Defence Investment Agency and what form it could take. He said the following: There are a number of ways it could be set up, and we're working our way through them. I don't know the answer right now. It could be anything from a Crown corporation to a traditional department, or something in between. The reason Mr. Guzman stated that the organization could take the form of a Crown corporation in the spring of 2026 was due to the fact that it was still a live debate within the government. We were still consulting on whether the model proposed in Bill C-31 was the best way to proceed. Since the 2025 general election, the government has been investigating different models of defence procurement and investment and has discussed these possibilities both in Parliament and publicly. I submit that the subject and nature of these deliberations on the form of the organization to lead this work could have led to a conclusion that the government was considering establishing a Crown corporation for this purpose. I would further add that the proposal to create the Defence Investment Agency in Bill C-31 was introduced in the House on May 6, 2026. The fact that the government gave notice of a new bill related to defence investment and procurement in September telegraphed that the government was thinking of an alternative approach to give more independence and flexibility to a body to undertake these activities. The conclusion would be obvious, based on the public deliberations that had taken place, that it would be a Crown corporation. In fact, whether or not the Defence Investment Agency would become a Crown corporation, this possibility has been in the public domain since the spring of 2026. Individuals who would have been involved in the deliberations on the form of the organization to manage defence procurement would have discussed the possibility that the Crown corporation would ultimately be the preferred mode during this period, but our investigation did not reveal any discussions during the notice period. During the 2025 general election, the Liberal platform stated with respect to various forms of procurement, including defence procurement, that it could be modelled on the powers and independence of a Crown corporation. Page 7 of the platform states: Deploy a made-in-Canada procurement strategy that prioritizes, whenever possible, Canadian suppliers and supply chains, and limiting bidders from foreign suppliers to bidding only on what we have agreed to in Canada's Free Trade Agreements. We will prioritize Canadian contractors in our defence procurement, including the Canadian aerospace industry. Crown Corporations with major capital acquisitions, like VIA Rail, will also be encouraged to meet this standard. On February 17, 2026, the Prime Minister launched Canada's first defence industrial strategy to strengthen security, create prosperity and reinforce strategic autonomy. On page 15 of the document, it states, “The Defence Investment Agency (DIA), created in October 2025, will address these challenges. Initially created as part of PSPC, the Government's intention is to establish the DIA as a stand-alone entity.” The government made it clear, over eight months ago, that the Defence Investment Agency would become a stand-alone entity. What is proposed in Bill C-31, the budget 2025 implementation act, no. 2, is not truly an independent entity. It is a government agency. A federal government agency is not considered a completely stand-alone, independent entity in legal and accounting terms, because it remains part of the core public service. Only a Crown corporation is a true stand-alone, independent entity, and the government's intention to potentially proceed this way was made public over eight months ago. Once Bill C-40 appeared on the Notice Paper, it became clear that the government had decided to evolve its course. It was logical to conclude that the government was moving ahead with what it had previously announced, which is to make the Defence Investment Agency a truly independent, stand-alone entity, as it had previously announced. By definition, this can only be a Crown corporation. As I stated earlier, Mr. Guzman, chief executive officer of the Defence Investment Agency, talked about the possibility of a Crown corporation at committee in April of this year. The government has been on the record speaking about the possibility of the Defence Investment Agency becoming a Crown corporation for many months now. The Globe and Mail article that the opposition House leader references also states the following: Philippe Lagassé, a professor at Carleton University who researches defence policy, said that if Ottawa turns the DIA into a Crown corporation, it would operate at arm's length from the government.... Prof. Lagassé said he will still need to see the mechanics of the legislation.... What is important here is that Professor Lagassé refers to “if” the Defence Investment Agency were to become a Crown corporation and says that he cannot offer a precise analysis because he has not seen the bill or the specific details contained within it. This further makes the case that the details of the legislation were not divulged during the notice period. The opposition House leader also points out that the Globe and Mail story makes mention of the creation of a new cabinet position: the minister of defence procurement. I would like to point out to the House that on page 145 of the 2026 spring economic update, which was tabled on April 28, 2026, it states: In the Spring Economic Update 2026, the government proposes to introduce legislation to establish the Defence Investment Agency as a departmental agency presided over by a new minister and to make related amendments to the Defence Production Act that would, among other things, enhance financial and transactional authorities available to the new minister. The government's intention to create a new minister of defence procurement was made public over six months ago. However, the opposition House leader failed to point out that Bill C-40 would not actually create a minister of defence procurement. Rather, it states that the government may appoint an associate minister of national defence for procurement, not an associate minister of defence, as the article states. In the context of alleging premature disclosure of a bill, these details matter. The opposition House leader also alleged that ministerial responsibility related to the Defence Investment Agency was not “telegraphed...in any previous public statements by the government”. I would assert that, if the government were to give notice of a bill entitled “an act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security”, combined with the previous commitment that this agency would be presided over by a new minister, as announced in the 2026 spring economic update, it does not take much to deduce that new legislation would set some parameters around this process. This is just common sense. All legislation contains ministerial powers and responsibilities. That is how our Westminster system of government works. I also want to point out that the CBC story that the opposition House leader referenced says the following: In the spring, the government proposed to allow up to 14 exceptions, including procurements of national interest. It also made economic security a key pillar of the DIA mandate. How those measures will be reflected in the Crown corporation and whether it will have even greater authority is unclear. I would assert that it is unclear because the bill had not been introduced in the House, which further illustrates that there has been no premature disclosure of the contents of the legislation during the notice period. In conclusion, I have clearly shown that the government has been on the record for many months about the creation of a stand-alone entity responsible for defence procurement and the possibility of a Crown corporation. I have shown that only a Crown corporation is truly a stand-alone entity. I have also outlined how the government has been on the record for many months about a new minister responsible for defence procurement, and I have established the discrepancies between what was reported and what was actually contained in Bill C-40. Furthermore, I have demonstrated that all pieces of the legislation contain ministerial powers and responsibilities as part of our Westminster system of government. Finally, I have shown that quotes within the stories referenced by the official opposition House leader substantiate that details were not available about the legislation and thus are speculative. I would assert to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is a high bar to meet to find a prima facie question of privilege, and I believe that I have provided, on the record, public evidence that refutes the allegations that there was premature disclosure of the bill. Having said all that, I also want to reiterate what I said at the beginning of my intervention, namely that the government takes its responsibilities to safeguard information contained in legislation on notice very seriously. While I believe that I have demonstrated that no premature disclosure took place, the government has taken the allegation seriously and made inquiries with ministerial offices as well as with officials in the public service. These inquiries have concluded that there is no evidence to support that the content of Bill C-40 was prematurely disclosed during the notice period, which further reinforces the point that there is not a case of prima facie privilege in this instance. In fact, the evidence suggests the contrary. There have been discussions within government since the formation of this government in 2025. This process has evolved from establishing an agency through an order in council in the fall of 2025. Then there was a proposal in Bill C-31 to create a new agency, and now there is the proposal to create a Crown corporation. These discussions have occurred publicly and in a committee of the House. While the model to execute defence procurement investment has continued to evolve, the objective remained the constant to create an independent, agile organization to procure defence-related equipment as efficiently as possible. It was not a stretch of the imagination that this could result in an establishment of a Crown corporation. It would appear to me that there are two sets of competing facts before the House. In such cases, Speakers have declared that a dispute as to the facts constitutes debate. On June 19, 2025, the Speaker ruled on a matter that constituted dispute as to the facts and which I would like to quote. He said: If every disagreement is to be raised as a question of privilege, the House would spend its time doing little else. There are many opportunities in our debates for members to challenge each other on the facts of a particular case, and that is the correct way of dealing with such disagreements. As for the conclusion of our inquiry into the possible premature disclosure of the contents of Bill C-40, I can assure the House that no evidence has been found to corroborate that anyone divulged the contents of the bill during the notice period. I would remind the House of the importance of taking members at their word. On December 6, 2011, the Speaker ruled on a member's involvement in inviting individuals to the gallery who were the cause of a disturbance. In this case, the Speaker ruled, and I would quote, “Remembering the time-honoured tradition in this place that members are taken at their word and so in keeping with the precedents just cited, the Chair is prepared to consider this particular aspect of the matter to be closed.” In light of the review of the evolution of the policy to determine the best manner in which to procure and invest in defence capabilities to support our Armed Forces, it was logical to assume that this could be through an establishment of a Crown corporation. The policy evolution has taken place in a public sphere, including in a committee of the House. Therefore, the conclusions drawn in the media reports are reasonable assumptions and do not point to a deliberate internal leak of the contents of Bill C-40 during the notice period. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your time and patience.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege concerning a Canadian Press report published on Thanksgiving weekend. It reported that our colleague, the hon. member for Thunder Bay—Rainy River, is potentially facing professional disciplinary proceedings in connection with his parliamentary committee work. According to this report, the hon. member, a physician, is the subject of a complaint to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, of which he is a member, concerning his supplementary opinion attached to the first report of the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying. Specifically, The Canadian Press reports that a member of the public, whom I understand is also a plaintiff in constitutional challenges concerning the current law, which absent parliamentary intervention is due to sunset next year, has complained to the college about the hon. member's “written arguments against expanding access to [medical assistance in dying] for mental illness until fundamental concerns are addressed.” It is further understood that the hon. member was given until October 22, Thursday, to answer a college investigator, following which the complaint will be referred to a college committee for review. The bottom line is that a member of the House is facing serious legal proceedings over his contributions to a parliamentary proceeding. This, I believe, offends the constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech in Parliament. Paragraph 3.52 of House of Commons Procedure and Practice, fourth edition, explains just how central this is to the work of Parliament: “Freedom of speech is the cornerstone of the rights and parliamentary privileges accorded to members. It is both the least questioned and the most fundamental right of the member of Parliament on the floor of the House and in committees.” While we often think of this freedom in terms of not being sued for defamation for what is said here, the reality is that it is much more widely scoped than that. This privilege is anchored in article 9 of the Bill of Rights, adopted by the Parliament of England in 1689: “That the Freedome of Speech and Debates or Proceedings in Parlyament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any Court or Place out of Parlyament” Those last words “Place out of Parlyament” are key here. To be sure, it should not be interpreted as meaning literally any place outside of here. Public debate and accountability of politicians are fundamental features of a parliamentary democracy such as Canada's. As Janse and LeBlanc explain at paragraph 3.57, “The House of Commons could not work effectively unless its members were able to speak and criticize without having to account to any outside body.” While we have clear jurisprudence in Canada concerning the use of parliamentary proceedings before the courts, and to a lesser extent royal commissions and human rights commissions, we do not have a body of precedent concerning where we ought to draw the line concerning “any outside body”, to borrow the phrase of Janse and LeBlanc, or a “Place out of Parlyament”, to use the wording enacted by the convention on Parliament. Authorities elsewhere have, however, contemplated this matter. For its part, the 1999 United Kingdom Parliament Joint Committee on Parliamentary Privilege commented at paragraphs 91 and 92 of its first report: The prohibition in article 9 is not confined to the questioning of parliamentary proceedings in courts. It applies also to any “place out of Parliament”. This is another obscure expression of uncertain meaning. To read the phrase as meaning literally anywhere outside Parliament would be absurd. It would prevent the public and the media from freely discussing and criticising proceedings in Parliament. That cannot be right, and this meaning has never been suggested. Freedom for the public and the media to discuss parliamentary proceedings outside Parliament is as essential to a healthy democracy as the freedom of members to discuss what they choose within Parliament. So the embrace of the phrase is narrower than this, but wider than merely “courts”: the whole phrase is “...any court or place out of Parliament”. The interpretation of this expression has never been the subject of a court decision. Meanwhile, Parliamentary Practice in New Zealand, fifth edition, at page 702, explores the history of the phrase and its evolved interpretation: the reference to any place out of Parliament, if taken literally, would inhibit criticism or examination of parliamentary proceedings on any occasion outside Parliament. Such a result would be an absurdity that would unacceptably infringe citizens' freedom of speech. Occasional judicial statements have rhetorically imputed this extreme meaning, but these suggestions have not been taken seriously by either the House or the courts. The parliamentarians of 1688 probably had in mind the jurisdiction of the councils formerly established by royal prerogative to exercise executive and judicial functions. The latter functions were in conflict with the jurisdiction of the regular common law courts. In promulgating the Bill of Rights 1688, members sought to ensure that councils established by the King, in addition to the regular courts, could not examine parliamentary proceedings. In the modern State, such parallel, non-curial executive and judicial functions are exercised by tribunals and other bodies established by legislation, and the prohibition on questioning proceedings in Parliament is taken to be addressed today to such bodies. For a practical, contemporary approach to the 17th-century phrase, the 1999 U.K. joint committee opined at paragraph 95: The Parliamentary Privileges Act 1987 (Australia) applied the article 9 prohibition to any court or tribunal, and defined tribunal as any person or body having power to examine witnesses on oath. This seems to provide a clear and sensible basis for the future. In general, power to administer oaths is dependent upon statutory authority. The power is conferred on bodies whose proceedings are endowed with a degree of legal solemnity and formality. It means, for instance, that article 9 will apply to coroners' inquests, lands tribunals and industrial tribunals. Beyond such formal tribunals, article 9 will not apply. By this means the boundary can be clearly delineated, with an embargo on examination of parliamentary proceedings in all courts and similar bodies but not elsewhere. In addition to Australia, the Parliament of New Zealand has since similarly legislated on parliamentary privilege, adopting a comparable definition of “tribunal” in its Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014. Turning back to the immediate case at hand, subsection 76(1) of the health professions procedural code, a schedule to Ontario's Regulated Health Professions Act, 1991, vests the college investigator with the authority of section 33 of the Ontario Public Inquiries Act, 2009. What this means is that the investigator has the power to issue summonses to any witnesses, including the hon. member for Thunder Bay—Rainy River, legally compelling the witness to provide a statement and/or documents. Failing to comply with a summons may result in a contempt of court order, among other consequences. What is more is that the hon. member, as a physician, is under a positive obligation imposed by subsection 76(3.1) of the code to co-operate with any investigation into him. Failing to co-operate could amount to a further allegation of professional misconduct under the regulations made pursuant to Ontario's Medicine Act, 1991, and specifically as behaviour considered “disgraceful, dishonourable or unprofessional.” Beyond the procedural concerns about co-operation with the investigation where the member's supplementary opinions would be questioned, the complainant's goal here is to hold the member accountable for his supplementary opinions. In other words, she wants the member's opinions to be impeached, as article 9 of the Bill of Rights puts it. To quote paragraph 36 of the 1999 U.K. joint committee's report, “the meaning of ‘impeach’ is not clear: possible meanings include hinder, challenge and censure.” A censure is exactly what the complainant is seeking here. To sum up this aspect of my intervention, our colleague is facing legal proceedings with very serious personal and professional consequences to him because of his words published in connection with a committee report contrary to the constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech in Parliament. While the procedural authorities are clear that supplementary and dissenting opinions are not part of a committee's report in terms of representing a committee's views, I would submit that they are nonetheless proceedings in Parliament as far as the protections of parliamentary privilege are concerned. Janse and LeBlanc clarify at paragraph 3.54: Proceedings include the work of the House and members’ actions in the context of the parliamentary process. Proceedings are not limited to debates. Members generally take part in proceedings by speaking during debates in the House and its committees, but also by various recognized forms of formal action, such as presenting documents, petitions or committee reports.... Moreover, committee reports, including any supplementary or dissenting opinions, are publications of the House. Subparagraph (i)(ii) of the special order adopted by the House on February 13, 2026, constituting the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance and Dying, gave the committee the power, among other things, “to print such papers and evidence as may be ordered by the committee”. Janse and LeBlanc add context at paragraph 20.55: “it is now, by and large, interpreted as a power to publish the necessary records and documents at its discretion, namely on the committee's website. It is the practice to publish the Minutes of Proceedings, the Evidence and the reports that committees present to the House.” This is important because, in addition to the centuries-old parliamentary privilege of freedom of speech, the House also enjoys a relatively newer privilege concerning the right to publish papers, traced back to the United Kingdom's Parliamentary Papers Act 1840 and explained by Janse and LeBlanc at paragraphs 3.49 and 3.50: The Parliament of Canada Act provides protection for the publication, by order of the House, of parliamentary papers such that no lawsuit may be brought relating to the contents of the papers or their appendices. This includes all documents published by a committee acting under the authority of the House.... Within three weeks of the opening of the First Session of the First Parliament of Canada, the Senate and the House passed An Act to define the privileges, immunities and powers of the Senate and the House of Commons, and to give summary protection to persons employed in the publication of Parliamentary Papers, which claimed for the Parliament of Canada the privileges, immunities and powers of the British House of Commons. This statute also provided that parliamentary papers were protected by privilege and protected publishers of the authorized parliamentary papers and records against civil or criminal suits. These provisions are now in sections 7 to 9 of the Parliament of Canada Act. Regardless of which privilege avenue the Speaker considers, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario is, through this investigation of a member of Parliament's contributions to a parliamentary proceeding, trespassing over the privileges of the House of Commons. The Canadian Press reports that for her part, the complainant “acknowledges in the complaint that a member of Parliament is entitled to freedom of speech”, yet she then proceeded to ask that the hon. member for Thunder Bay—Rainy River be held accountable for his very speech. What good is the freedom of speech if it is only meant to protect the things that we can all agree on or, worse, that only those in positions of authority agree on? This is why I, a Conservative MP, am rising today on this question of privilege about something concerning a political opponent who sits on the Liberal benches. The case that has emerged is one that I believe could set a dangerous precedent if it is allowed to proceed unchallenged by the House. Every single party represented in the House, including the two unrecognized parties, have members who have come from and are still members in good standing of these self-regulated professions. If members of the House now must self-censor during important debates in Parliament because their opponents outside of the House will weaponize professional disciplinary bodies to imperil their professional reputations and their ability to earn livelihoods after their service here, then we have lost the freedom of speech and the important contributions that those members must make. This is not just a loss for those specific MPs or even for all 343 of us. It is actually a loss for Canadians as a whole. As Janse and LeBlanc explain at paragraph 3.7: ...the privilege of freedom of speech is secured to members not for their personal benefit, but to enable them to discharge their function of representing their constituents without fear of civil or criminal prosecution for what might be said in the House and committees. When a constituency has returned a candidate, it is the electors' right that this chosen representative should be protected from any kind of improper pressure. Facing legal proceedings, professional misconduct investigations, potential blemishes on a professional record and possibly the inability to practise a profession are, I submit, forms of improper pressure. If prospective parliamentarians are told that in addition to the usual challenges we all face to varying degrees, some of them will also be putting their professional careers at risk if, once elected, they speak up for their constituents, especially if they have something to say that does not neatly line up with elite, establishment opinion, what hope do Canadians have that these potentially fine representatives will be willing to offer themselves for public service through election to Parliament? That our constituents can and should hold us accountable in the so-called court of public opinion is natural, appropriate and a vital part of political and democratic life. Cancel culture, however, is not. We must together draw a firm and bright line that defends and supports the essential role the House of Commons and its members play as the beating heart of Canada's democracy. Given the unprecedented nature of this issue, coupled with the somewhat vague and older statutory wording involved, which I have quoted, this is something the Standing Committee on Procedure and House Affairs should study thoroughly. It should, in turn, provide recommendations concerning both the specific case of the hon. member for Thunder Bay—Rainy River and more generally for any future repetition of a challenge such as this. Please join me in standing up for freedom of speech here in Parliament and in protecting our colleagues from the Kafkaesque threat of professional misconduct hearings being weaponized against them because of their parliamentary work. This is not just about special exemptions for MPs from rules that apply to everyone else. This is about protecting MPs from cancel culture and protecting them from having their professional designations threatened for speaking out on behalf of their constituents. Even if a tribunal ultimately rules in favour of the member, in too many cases the process itself is the punishment. The fear of professional repercussions will have a chilling effect on the ability of MPs to speak their minds fully. The words spoken in Parliament or written in a committee report should be judged at the ballot box and the ballot box alone. Canadians themselves hold the ultimate authority in judging the words we use in this place. Should you agree, Mr. Speaker, that this situation amounts to a prima facie case of privilege, and I strongly urge you to do so, I am prepared to move an appropriate motion to refer this matter to the committee.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the manner in which that was presented, and I reserve the opportunity for a member of our caucus to respond.

title: Oral Questions: Housing
turns: Mr. Speaker, a good leader stands up and answers questions in the House of Commons, and a good leader gets results. Now we learn that the government is admitting it will not get the Prime Minister's promised results on housing. In a response to an Order Paper question, the Liberals have now admitted that the Prime Minister has broken his promise to double homebuilding and that construction will actually fall to near-record lows over the next three years, blaming immigration, as the Liberals do, for the housing shortage. How could the Prime Minister be so out of touch with Canadians who need homes?
Mr. Speaker, first and foremost, I would reprimand the member opposite for constantly attacking immigrants.
Mr. Speaker, I think almost every member of the House comes from immigrant stock. Canada is a country of immigrants, and to blame immigrants for a housing crisis is absolutely unfair and unjust.

Mr. Speaker, the member says he wants to reprimand anybody who blames excessive immigration numbers for the housing shortage. Well, let me read directly from a document he tabled in the House of Commons. It is a document on the housing shortage. It says, “One of the drivers of the housing shortage has been the strong growth in housing demand driven by immigration.” Will the minister stand up now and reprimand himself?
Mr. Speaker, there is a difference between immigrants and immigration, first and foremost. When the member opposite—

Mr. Speaker, there is a big difference. The member opposite demonizes immigrants, which is specifically what he said. The member opposite said, “immigrants”. Many countries in the world, including Canada, have challenges around immigration. Lots of people want to come to Canada. We need to keep up with the housing we build, and as the Prime Minister has said, we need to make sure the housing we build fits the immigration levels. We want immigrants in Canada. This is a country of immigrants. We believe in immigration. It has to be controlled, and our housing builds have to match accordingly. That is what we are focused on.

Mr. Speaker, in response to a question about why the Prime Minister is suggesting he will increase immigration levels, even though government officials are warning that housing supply has been impacted, the housing minister gave a completely inane answer that is unbefitting of the gravity of the situation.
