My right hon. Friend speaks very powerfully on this issue from personal experience. I can also share mine as I saw people from around the world caring for my dad. She is absolutely right that we must celebrate their contribution, as I did in my speech at the party conference. We must take on a politics that seeks to say to those people that they have no place here, because they do.

title: Electronic Monitoring of Offenders
turns: (Urgent Question): To ask the Secretary of State for Justice if he will make a statement on the electronic monitoring of offenders.
The Minister for Prisons, Probation and Reducing Reoffending

The Government inherited a justice system pushed to breaking point by the previous Government. When Labour came to power, we had fewer than 100 places left in our prisons, with incredibly serious problems with electronic monitoring. We have taken swift action to improve performance, and are now delivering the biggest expansion of tagging in British history, backed by £100 million of investment. As part of our reforms, there is a presumption—[Interruption.]
Order. At least let the Minister get to the end of what she has to say without interruption.

Thank you, Mr Speaker. As part of our reforms, there is a presumption that eligible offenders released under the progression model will be tagged, giving the Probation Service an additional tool to monitor offenders and protect the public. We are now tagging a record number of offenders, helping to cut crime and make our streets safer. Electronic monitoring is not used in isolation. Those released from prison remain subject to licence conditions and probation supervision, which can include curfews and restrictions on their movements. We have also introduced tougher powers for probation officers, including world-first restriction zones for the most serious sexual and violent offenders where appropriate, as well as the ability to prohibit offenders from driving, attending public events or entering pubs, clubs and bars. Where an offender breaches their conditions or can no longer be safely managed in the community, they can immediately be recalled to prison. We have also ensured that the electronic monitoring service is ready to support the expansion. The service was ready for first-tranche releases on 1 October, with the equipment and staff in place to deliver the presumption to tag offenders on release. Serco has consistently met its contractual requirements since March 2026. The Ministry of Justice routinely publishes extensive data on probation and tagging. It is published quarterly, and the last set of data was published just last week. It is vital that the Government and the public have confidence that the information published by the Department is accurate. Our quarterly economic monitoring statistics, including figures for the number of prison leavers fitted with tags and the figures covering the October period, will be publicly available in January. This Government inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse, with just 500 places being built in the last 14 years. It is this Government who are now building the prison places we need and putting in the strictest measures possible to protect the public.
I call the shadow Justice Secretary.

You would not believe, Mr Speaker, listening to the Minister that the numbers of prison places and prison officers are actually down. It all sounds like it is going very well according to her version of events. Labour told us that to keep the public safe from the dangerous criminals it is releasing early, the Justice Secretary would implement the toughest tagging regime in British history, and that there would be a new presumption that offenders will be electronically tagged and monitored when they leave prison. But the Metropolitan police told Sky this weekend that it will not act on all breaches of tag conditions by bailed offenders, blaming the pressure created by Labour’s early release scheme. Just in London, there have been 100 tag breaches a day by released prisoners since the first early release scheme started, with two to three released prisoners now being rearrested every week. The Met commissioner said that “95%-plus of the tagging breaches that we arrest are simply being bailed back into the community on the same condition”. He says, “there is zero sanction”. One sergeant said: “There are not enough cops” to handle Labour’s early release of thousands of prisoners. The Justice Secretary, when he stops hiding in his Department and sending junior Ministers to answer for him, needs to be straight with the House and the public. Four days after his early release scheme started, he told the BBC that he did not know—that it was impossible to know—how many prisoners had been tagged. He wrote to me yesterday admitting that he still does not know, and that is 26 days later. The Times reports that most prisoners will not be tagged as they are released from prison, and we know that more than 5,000 offenders went unmonitored in the first half of this year because they were not fitted with tags. This is a mess. So chaotic is Labour’s early release scheme that prisoners are being given tents instead of housing upon release. As a matter of policy, these prisoners will be in probable breach of their licence and tagging conditions, which require them to have an approved address, all because the Probation Service is overwhelmed. We know that two thirds of prisoners who are sleeping rough go on to reoffend within the first year. Ministers keep telling us that the full data on tagging and reoffending cannot be published until the regulation publication dates. I ask again: will Ministers publish full data on how many released prisoners have been tagged? Will they publish comprehensive data on reoffending by prisoners let out through Labour’s early release scheme, and will the Justice Secretary apologise to the House for telling the public that they would be kept safe?

While the hon. Member raises some important points, I stress again that we are working night and day to fix the broken system that we inherited. We are working across agencies. We are working incredibly hard with the police, the Probation Service and all those who work in the criminal justice system who want to keep the public safe and ensure that victims get the service they need, too. I caution the hon. Gentleman, because he appears to be conflating a number of issues. He will be aware that it is usual practice, which has been in place under successive Governments, including his own, that prisoners are tagged at their place of accommodation on release, and that was always the plan for 1 October. That said, we know that this creates a gap between leaving prison and having the tag fitted, which is why to address it we have conducted a successful pilot to fit tags at prison receptions. That is currently live in six prisons, and we are working at pace to roll this out to further prisoners who will have a tag upon leaving. [Interruption.] The hon. Member for Bexhill and Battle (Dr Mullan) chunters from a sedentary position to ask about the police. He is talking about local Metropolitan police policy in relation to breaches of court bail where it is the responsible agency. It is important not to conflate the release of prisoners and the tagging policy, which we are working at pace to improve from the situation we inherited, with the other demands on the police, which we are working closely with them to resolve. We inherited a failing tagging system with record backlogs. We are investing £100 million in electronic monitoring, tagging offenders before release and, importantly, strengthening victim protections with a new alert system. To the MPs who share this Government’s and the Prime Minister’s ambition that no one should be street homeless, I urge them to support us in these endeavours and to ensure that their local authorities are working with us to support prisoners on release, to ensure they are tagged and to ensure that victims and the public are protected. That is our key priority, and we can work together across this House to achieve that. I visit prisons and meet prison officers and governors every week who are working incredibly hard to keep the public safe and to transform the lives of individuals in our prison system to ensure that when they leave prison, they leave in a better state than when they arrived. We are working to reduce reoffending and to support the Probation Service in reintegrating people into society, and to ensure in the meantime that people are tagged and victims and the public are kept safe. We are working incredibly hard getting on with the job of fixing the mess we inherited and rebuilding our justice system that was left so broken, and I urge hon. Members across the House to support us in their local area in that work.
I call the Chair of the Justice Committee.

Victims should not have to make their lives smaller, looking over their shoulder because offenders are free to roam; it is the offender whose freedoms should be limited. Will the Minister be more ambitious in using restriction zones, which keep an offender within a defined area, rather than simply banning them from particular areas, as with exclusion zones? If victims are to feel safe, tags must be fitted as they walk out of the prison gate, not weeks later. Will that be in place in January, as intended?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right, and I thank her for her assiduous work on all these subjects. As she says, we are rightly rolling out world-leading restriction zones, ensuring that it is offenders who are restricted, where that is appropriate. Indeed, we have the exclusion zones as well, where they are appropriate, and obviously these decisions are made by probation practitioners. She rightly highlights the work we are doing to accelerate the roll-out of tagging at prisons to ensure the safety and security of the system and so that tags are installed at the prison gate as soon as possible.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

Over 5,000 offenders went unmonitored in the first half of this year due to serious delays in the tagging system, and in the year to March, an average of 300 people per week were released from prison with no fixed address, making it incredibly difficult to ensure that offenders are tagged and then managed in the community. That adds to the strain on both the Probation Service and the police, who are using scarce resources to manage an increasingly large caseload and keep victims safe. The Government have repeatedly promised that they will not jeopardise public safety, but many victims following the stories over the weekend, especially after Mark Rowley’s comments, will struggle to believe them. Will the Government listen to the calls of the Victims’ Commissioner to tag individuals at the gate and roll that out to every prison by January? We also welcomed the Government’s announcement to introduce restriction zones for offenders, which limits the movement for perpetrators rather than victims, but the effectiveness of those zones will require offenders to be properly monitored and any breaches to be addressed without delay. Is the Minister confident that there are enough resources to operate restriction zones effectively, and when will we see a national roll-out of this important measure?

The hon. Lady makes a number of thoughtful and helpful contributions. It is very important that housing and homelessness are tackled among the prison leaver population, to ensure that they have the opportunity to build a life and not reoffend, and we will work with local authorities as effectively as possible to ensure that prisoners are not at risk of becoming homeless. It is a priority of this Prime Minister and this Government to tackle homelessness across the board, which was reinforced by the announcement yesterday of £874 million of priority funding to tackle homelessness. We are already extending the period by which collaboration must happen between the prison and probation unit and local authorities, so that they have the maximum period possible to put in place arrangements that ensure victims’ safety and the public’s safety. The hon. Member rightly raised tagging at source, which we have had a very successful pilot of. This has not been done previously by any Government. We recognise it as an opportunity to really improve the work that is happening, and we are working at pace to ramp up tagging at source. She also raised the restriction zones. I can only reiterate that these are world-leading measures we are putting in place. We are not just fixing the mess that we inherited but working at pace to make this system work in the interests of victims and the public, and creating a society that everyone can contribute to.

I thank the Minister for her responses. Does she agree that more needs to be done to prevent reoffending while offenders are actually in prison, so that they do not commit further crimes when they are released and on tags? What is she doing to ensure that there is appropriate education and training across the prison estate?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right that ensuring that there is purposeful activity in prisons, and that prisoners can gain life skills and work skills while they are in prison, will help to reduce reoffending and help to tackle the prison capacity challenge that we have. She will recognise that the capacity challenge we inherited makes all of this harder—it makes everything we are doing in the prison system harder. That is why we are both building more prison spaces and ensuring that we invest in and support rehabilitation while people are in prison, to reduce the need to recall people when they reoffend. We are tackling this on all fronts, and I appreciate my hon. Friend’s support for our efforts.

The Minister says that the Government are building new prison places, yet she will be aware that there are fewer prison places today than on the day Labour took office. She will also be aware that this vast flood of prisoners being released early has overwhelmed the ability of the Probation Service to find them accommodation and that some prisoners are now being issued with tents, setting them up to fail. Can the Minister tell us how many prisoners have been issued with tents on their release? Has the rate been higher or lower than she expected?

It is not Government policy to provide tents to people being released from prison who are at risk of being homeless. We are clear that tents should never be an acceptable housing solution. The hon. Member will know that overall housing responsibility rests with local authorities in England and Wales. I assure him that we are working very closely with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government to tackle the scourge of homelessness across the board, including among the prison leaver cohort that he is concerned about. He can support this work by encouraging his local authority to engage in pre-release panels, so that this work can be done collaboratively right across the UK to ensure that nobody leaves prison homeless.

Between May and August this year, Kevin Brown committed eight burglaries in Hartlepool, targeting businesses and charities like Alice House hospice and Cornerstone homelessness charity. The court handed him a suspended sentence. That is not good enough for me, and it is not good enough for my constituents. Does the Minister agree that we must build more prison places so that individuals like this are locked up?

I absolutely agree with my hon. Friend that we must build more prison places, and we are working at pace to do that. Obviously, I will not comment on independent judicial decisions that are made in particular cases, but he should be reassured to know that when it comes to tackling acquisitive crime, tagging is appropriate and individualised to the offender, to ensure that it tackles their particular challenges in terms of reoffending. An acquisitive crime GPS tag pilot found that offenders were 20% less likely to reoffend within 12 months. We are working across the board to tackle all these issues in the round.

It is bad enough that dangerous criminals are being released early, but my constituents are frankly terrified that these prisoners are being released without tags—the world has gone mad, Minister. Will this Government commit not to release prisoners without tags?

The hon. Gentleman will have heard the answers I have given on the business as usual that we inherited: it was always the plan that from 1 October, offenders would normally be tagged at their accommodation. We are presuming that more offenders and individuals released from prison will be eligible for tags than at any point in history, and we are investing significantly in that. We have undertaken a pilot of tagging prisoners at the prison, which has been shown to be successful, and we will work at pace to roll that out further as quickly as possible.

Serco continues to be awarded lucrative Government contracts despite repeated failures, while probation officers have been pushed to breaking point. Will the Minister commit to bringing back in-house electronic tagging and probation services, as I proposed in my amendment to the Bill that became the Sentencing Act 2026, so that we are not rewarding private profit over public safety?

The contract with Serco was signed by the Conservative party, and its performance did not originally meet expectations, but we have focused on driving rapid improvement and ensuring that we turn that failing performance around, so that it is meeting contractual expectations and working with us at pace to make the improvements that we want to see in our system. We will continue to keep all these matters under review, as we would with any contract that the Government have entered into.

I welcome the fact that the Government are experimenting with a scheme of tagging prisoners at the point of release, but a question then arises. Those of them who do not have an address to go to and who choose to remove the tag are going to be very difficult to find. Is there a solution to that?

The right hon. Gentleman asks a typically thoughtful question. Obviously, all these matters are kept under review. We work very closely with the Probation Service, which uses a range of measures to manage offenders once they are released into the community, to both support them to reintegrate and to ensure that the public are safe, and we also work very closely with the police on that. When an offender does find settled accommodation, a tag can then be put on as part of their licence conditions, but where there are concerns, the recall option remains available.

When Pentonville Prison was built in 1842, I do not imagine anybody expected that today it would have twice the number of prisoners the Victorians thought ought to be kept there. Furthermore, Pentonville Prison is a London remand prison—people used to be there for six to eight months on remand in pretty terrible conditions, but now they are there for years because of the crisis in the criminal justice system. The question is this: when they are released, what should be done with them? I was speaking to the governor of the prison on Friday, and he said that if the Government wished them to, prison officers would be quite happy to be trained to put the tags on people themselves before releasing them.

I thank my right hon. Friend for her thoughtful question. Like me, she has the greatest regard for our prison governors. They work on the frontline, keeping the public safe and keeping their prisons running, and they do come up with a lot of good ideas, many of which I have heard myself. I meet governors regularly about what we can do to improve matters; I am very much “ear to the ground.” Indeed, many of the proposals that we are taking forward to improve significantly on the situation we inherited come from the very practical reality that prison governors encounter, so I thank her for the suggestion.

The issue of electronic monitoring does not concern only those on early release. Michele, a victim of domestic abuse, has a restraining order against her ex-partner until 2036 that the police say he is regularly breaching. Ten days after his release, she contacted me for the fourth time to say that he still did not have a tag. As we went into half term, she said: “I’ve not left my house all week. The children can’t go out in half term. We don’t feel safe.” The liaison officers know that a breach is going to happen again, and family members are now staying with her, one at a time, to make sure she is not alone. I totally understand the January deadline—there are a lot of people to deal with—but will the Minister make a commitment that serial victims of domestic abuse will be prioritised so that children do not have to look over their shoulder?

The hon. Lady raises an important case. I am very sorry to hear about the situation that her constituent is dealing with this half term. Obviously, that needs to be escalated to the appropriate people. A whole variety of measures are used to ensure victim engagement, including the victim contact helpline, and specific orders can be put on domestic abuse offenders. I appreciate the ongoing concerns, and I would be happy to engage with the hon. Lady about this case.

I thank the Minister for the groundbreaking work of her Department in tagging prisoners before release, but will she update the House on the work that this Government are doing to start fixing the failure of the Conservatives to build more prison places or invest in our crumbling prison estate?

My hon. Friend brings us back to the crux of the issue that this Government inherited. We are dealing with the consequences of a failure to invest in our prison capacity over many years—there was a net gain of just 500 prison places when the Conservatives left Government. We are working at pace to deliver 14,000 prison places, and we aim to do so by 2031. We have already delivered 3,300 places, and I look forward to being at the groundbreaking and opening of many more.

The Lord Chancellor recently addressed Napo’s conference—I was listening in, as I was speaking afterwards—and he told probation officers, “Without you, our criminal justice system does not work.” However, Napo is presently balloting its members on strike action following failed negotiations with the Government for a pay rise after decades of pay stagnation. Does the Minister agree that technology cannot replace dedicated probation officers and that they need the proper pay, proper conditions and proper workloads to be able to do their jobs properly?

The right hon. Lady is absolutely right. Justice Transcribe, which she refers to, has supported probation officers to reduce their workload when it comes to the transcribing of notes; obviously, they must keep careful records, and this system is inevitably helping to manage workloads. She is right that probation officers do a vital job, and I thank them for the work that they are doing today and every day to keep the public safe and manage offenders in the community. In April, we secured the biggest probation pay increase in over a decade, and the current offer increases that by a minimum of 5%. We want to increase our recruitment of probation officers, so hon. Members should encourage people to join the service. We also want to retain our brilliant probation officers, and we are continuing in discussions with them to that end.

Can the Minister confirm that criminals will not get tagged if they are classed as homeless? At the weekend, it was revealed that prisoners released early by this Government were given tents because there was no accommodation for them. So yes or no—will prisoners who are released and given a tent be tagged? Or will they be roaming the streets without any way of locating them, free to commit more crime?

I agree with the right hon. Lady that it is completely unacceptable for a prisoner to be released with a tent. That is not Government policy, and it is not something that we want to see. That is why we are working at pace to improve the current homelessness situation that we inherited from the previous Government, to make sure that nobody, including prison leavers, leaves prison homeless or has to live homeless.

A Lords Committee criticised the Ministry of Justice under the previous Government for reappointing the contractors after repeated failures. Serco had an issue with finding a tag small enough for the elderly mother of my constituent, which delayed her release over Christmas. What steps are the Government taking to ensure that contractors manage to tag all prisoners before they leave prison?

I am sorry to hear about that particular case. There are circumstances where there are physical challenges to fitting a tag—for example, because of a medical reason such as limb loss or swelling. It is important that the vast majority of people who should have tags do have tags, and we need to make sure that happens. The business-as-usual position is to tag an individual who is due to be tagged once they are in their accommodation, but we are trialling, have piloted and will be looking to roll out tagging at the prison as quickly as possible.

I have heard from far too many worried victims and parents of young victims in Yeovil about how much anxiety the potential early release of their offenders, including members of child grooming gangs, has caused. Probation services in rural areas are on their knees, so will the Minister tell victims in Yeovil what work has been done with probation services in the south-west to ensure they have all the personnel, resources and systems in place to safely manage the release of offenders to our communities?

I am sorry to hear about the experience of those young people in Yeovil. We need to be careful about some of the rhetoric around the subject and to always have victims in mind when we have these conversations. Yes, there must be robust challenge to ensure that we get this right and that we push the measures we are taking to the furthest point possible to make sure we keep people safe, but we must also respect the work of our probation teams who are monitoring offenders in the community and working to keep people safe. There are a range of offences that are excluded from the progression model, so those offenders are not eligible for progression. We have increased the tagging of offenders, even where they are excluded from progression but whose crimes are of a nature that we would want them to be tagged and monitored post-release in any event. I want to provide reassurance to young people: we are working at pace and our very hardest to ensure that we keep the public safe, and we manage offenders as they reintegrate back into the community.

One former Conservative Minister wrote a book that discussed the prison system’s failure to reform. Will the Minister confirm that she has looked at Rory Stewart’s book and his concerns that the Department lacked project management capabilities and support from the Treasury, and required a longer tenure for Prison Ministers? Would she recommend the book to the shadow Minister?

Indeed, Conservative Members have made a plethora of public commentary on such issues. As well as the book my hon. Friend mentioned, the former Prime Minister herself and her policy chief admitted that not enough prison places were built. I would be interested not only in whether Conservative Members might want to read the aforementioned book, but in whether they will apologise for the failures of the previous Government—this would be a good opportunity to do that.

The Government have not yet set out the number of domestic abusers who have been released under the early release scheme. Will the Minister set out to the House what that number is, and the total number of domestic abusers who will be released under the scheme?

The right hon. Gentleman knows as well as I do that that figure is not available, but we could not take this issue more seriously. That is why we have tagging under the domestic abuse perpetrators on licence approach, and probation services have a wider set of powers, many of which I have mentioned, including restrictions on licence conditions to prohibit offenders from driving or attending public events. It is right that we bring in our world-leading restriction zones to ensure that it is the perpetrators, not the victims of domestic violence, who have to alter their lives. We will continue to prioritise and work on this issue, and he is right to raise it.

I speak regularly to victims of crime and their families in Harlow, and I find some of their stories absolutely heartbreaking. I feel really angry that there are men in our society who think it is okay to treat women in the way they do, and I am sure that people across the House feel the same way. One thing that victims and their families raise with me is their concern about how easy it is for perpetrators—these vile individuals—to take their tags off. What can the Minister say about the punishment that will be handed down to those individuals who tamper with their tags or try to take them off?

I share my hon. Friend’s anger. Since taking on this role, I have felt very angry not just with some of the perpetrators and the cases that we see come across our desks, but with the 14 years of failure that left us in the situation we are in. We are working at pace to improve the technology and the application of the tagging system. [Interruption.] The Conservatives chunter from the Opposition Benches, but they wasted £100 million on tags that did not work. We are working to ensure that this scheme is effective, and we are working at pace to pick up the pieces that were left behind.

Will the Minister please tell the House how many people who should be wearing an electronic tag are wandering around our communities with no electronic device fitted at all? That should be a simple question.

That question has a simple answer: the hon. Gentleman will be able to see the data when it is published in January. We have just had data published for the previous three months. The data obviously needs to be verified and accurate. We are not in the business of publishing data that is not robust, and we will publish it in due course in the normal way.

I thank the Minister for her very comprehensive answers. Electronic monitoring of offenders can be a useful tool to manage prison capacity for individuals who have carried out non-violent crimes, but there are some serious concerns about regional co-ordination. Can she assure the House that robust safeguards are in place to ensure that private monitoring contractors are sharing real-time flawless data with police forces in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland? What specific metric is her Department using to confirm that tagging systems are genuinely reducing offending, rather than being a sticking plaster for a broken system?

The hon. Gentleman asks a very thoughtful question, and one that probably requires a lengthier answer than I have time to give, but I absolutely acknowledge the point he makes. I am determined that we have the data, the monitoring and the reporting to ensure that this scheme does work and is not a sticking plaster, so that victims can have faith in it, and probation officers and the police can be supported to do what they need to do to keep our communities safe. We are investing significantly in this technology, and we need to ensure that it works. He raises a genuine and good point.

title: Cyber-attacks
turns: What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to improve resilience to cyber-attacks.
What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to help prevent cyber-attacks affecting food supply chains.

The Government are taking vital steps to strengthen the UK’s cyber-security. At the Budget, £154 million was provided for cyber-defences, including our new national cyber-shield. We have introduced the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill to raise resilience and protect essential services, and shortly we will publish the national cyber action plan with clear actions for Government and businesses upgrading the UK’s responses to cyber-threats.

This country is already under regular cyber-attack by Russia, costing businesses billions and billions of pounds, with a knock-on effect to the British economy and British taxpayers. The response has to be to co-ordinate an effort across the country and across Government with businesses and civil society. In July, the Government said that the civil resilience forum would be meeting this autumn. Has that forum met? If not, when it will take place?

My hon. Friend is right to raise the nature of the threat in that way. We are updating local resilience leaders regularly, and I will convene them shortly. National resilience cannot be built in isolation; it requires shared leadership and action across every sector. That is why our Be Ready campaign has been built with more than 500 partners from charities, businesses, emergency services, local resilience forums and local councils, and it is why we will continue to work closely with all of them to deliver the campaign. I am determined to make us the most resilient country we can be.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his answer. A “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it” is how the EU Food and Agriculture Commissioner described the recent fridge and freezer cyber-attacks in Europe. This attack caused millions of euros-worth of food to need to be thrown away. I sit on the Public Accounts Committee, and last month we looked at the resilience of the food supply chain to disruption here in the UK. Does my right hon. Friend agree with me and the National Audit Office that, while UK food supply chains are generally resilient, the risks affecting them are both complex and more likely?

I do agree with my hon. Friend. I recently visited Paris, where we discussed our strong and enduring co-operation on matters relating to cyber-security threats. He is right: food security is crucial to our national security. We work very closely with retailers to protect our supply chain, and we will shortly publish the national cyber action plan, with clear actions that businesses can take to make supply chains even more secure.

Earlier this month, Major General Mike Fayers, the commander of the Defence Cyber and Electromagnetic Force, expressed public concerns that malware hidden in the military network could go bang in the event of a future conflict. We know that the Ministry of Defence has the largest IT infrastructure of any Department and obviously has that capability too. Given that the commander thinks there might be malware in the system, what confidence do Ministers have that the military network and, indeed, wider Government infrastructure are free of any malware from our adversaries?

As the hon. and gallant Gentleman will know, we work very closely across Government, including with partners in the Ministry of Defence and other Departments, to ensure that we are as resilient as we can be, given the nature of the threats, including those he describes. This is a matter that I personally take very seriously. That is why we are progressing work on the legislative front through the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, and we will publish the national cyber action plan very soon.

If the Security Minister is speaking to his colleagues in the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, could he perhaps suggest to them that cyber-security be part of the long overdue food strategy, which we are still waiting to get from that Department?
I always listen very carefully to what the right hon. Gentleman says, and I have done so on this occasion. Let me take that away, reflect on it further and discuss it with colleagues in DEFRA.

title: Violence against Women and Girls
turns: What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to help tackle violence against women and girls.
What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to help tackle violence against women and girls.

Violence against women and girls is one of the biggest challenges of our time, which is why this Government have committed to halving it in a decade. Progress towards achieving that includes rolling out dedicated specialist teams in every police force, providing specialist rape and serious sex offence courtrooms, and introducing domestic abuse protection orders. We have launched a new taskforce to tackle misogyny, we are teaching children about healthy relationships in school and we are preparing legislation to make it impossible for children to take, share and view nude images.

Members will have heard me speak many times about the injustice of victims of sexual assault and rape on the Isle of Wight having to travel by ferry for evidence gathering and treatment, because of the lack of a sexual assault referral centre, yet these traumatic journeys continue and many victims tell me how they feel badly let down. Will the Minister meet me to discuss a way forward so that no one has to leave the island to access that essential service?

I thank my hon. Friend for the work he does in supporting victims and survivors in his constituency. Victims and survivors of sexual violence should be able to access timely, sensitive and appropriate specialist support wherever they live. He is right to raise the gaps on the Isle of Wight, and I would of course be happy to meet him to see how together we can address that.

Chart Way is a major pedestrian route into central Horsham, but its street lighting is operated by the owner of an adjacent office block that was recently purchased by a venture capital company. Unfortunately, the company in question has refused to turn on the lights or respond to any inquiry from councillors or my office, despite the fear felt by women and girls—and, indeed, the danger it creates—as the nights draw in. What avenues do we have to address this problem; can the Minister offer any assistance? We just do not seem to have any powers.

The hon. Member is absolutely right that women and girls need to feel safe in public spaces. We are going further on this, with a cross-Government ministerial board—both the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and the Department for Transport are part of it—and I would be happy to work with him and other Departments to ensure that we get this right.
I call the Chair of the Women and Equalities Committee.

Time and again, powerful men are abusing women and then trying to silence them. Every woman must be protected, so will Ministers ban the misuse of non-disclosure agreements for harassment and misconduct—for everyone, not just employees?

We are clear that NDAs must never be used to cover up workplace harassment or discrimination. Reports this week have shown how important that is and the horrific consequences of imbalances of power. The Employment Rights Act 2025 will stop employers using NDAs to silence workers about harassment or discrimination in the workplace, and there is a consultation on going further and analysis of which groups will be included. We are also looking at what we can do about injunctions. I am sure that my hon. Friend the Minister for the Future of Work will be happy to write to her on this issue.

Thousands of prisoners are being released early on condition that they wear a security tag. Is the Minister aware of media reports that hundreds of prisoners are currently simply refusing, once released, to wear a tag? That must be deeply disturbing to the victims of their crime. Would she work with the Ministry of Justice to sort this out?

We work incredibly closely with the Ministry of Justice. The truth is that we inherited a broken system, which we are fixing. What is important is that serious sexual offences are excluded, and we are supporting victims by introducing the toughest ever range of tools, including world first restriction zones.

Female genital mutilation is one of the most serious forms of violence against women and girls, yet the Government’s understanding of its prevalence is still based on figures from 2011, estimating that 137,000 women were living with FGM in this country. We cannot tackle what we do not measure, so if Ministers genuinely regard violence against women and girls as a national priority, will they stop relying on 15-year-old estimates and commission an urgent, comprehensive study to establish the true prevalence of FGM in Britain?

We are going further than ever before to deal with honour-based abuse. On data, FGM is an under-reported crime and there is definitely work that we can all be doing to ensure that we are raising awareness. A campaign to raise awareness is about to be launched, so that we can get victims to come forward and support them.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

Yesterday, ITV News and The Guardian reported disturbing allegations, only possible thanks to the courage of the women who came forward, of grooming and sexual misconduct made against the celebrity David Walliams. Among the disgusting allegations of sexual advances to girls as young as 15, the years-long investigation also describes how one of the women received a threatening letter from Walliams’s lawyers demanding a written promise that she never speak about her experiences. Will the Minister meet me and my hon. Friend the Member for Chichester (Jess Brown-Fuller) to discuss, cross-party, how we work to end the manipulation of the justice system by rich and powerful men who try to silence their victims?

If this week has shown us anything, it is that no one is above the law. We have heard a lot about rich, powerful men using their positions to use and hurt women and girls, but these are also stories of strong women, both the victims and those in the media who expose perpetrators in positions of power. I pay tribute to their bravery and courage in coming forward to speak about deeply personal experiences so that justice can be served. We all have a responsibility to root out abuse wherever it is found. The Government are working tirelessly to ensure that offenders are held to account and victims are supported. I will, of course, be happy to meet and to work cross-party.

title: Houses in Multiple Occupation
turns: What steps her Department is taking to further regulate the use of houses in multiple occupation.
The Minister for Housing and Planning

The new national planning policy framework, published on 17 August, includes a more flexible and proportionate policy design to provide greater clarity on the circumstances in which article 4 directions may be appropriate, including where there is an overconcentration of small HMOs. We want to ensure that councils can act properly to regulate HMOs where it is necessary to protect the amenity or wellbeing of an area, and we will continue to keep the powers to regulate HMOs under review.

I thank the Minister for his answer. Residents in Wednesbury and Tipton are absolutely sick of family homes being turned into HMOs and—now that that is getting more difficult—into supported exempt accommodation, too. I have campaigned for more controls on HMOs since the day I was elected, but supported exempt accommodation is essentially unregulated. When will this Government bring in further controls on supported exempt accommodation?

I thank my hon. Friend for her question, and for all her campaigning to ensure that an article 4 direction is finally being introduced in Sandwell. On supported exempt accommodation, we published guidance for local authorities earlier this year on developing supported housing strategies. On 15 October, we launched a consultation on draft regulations for a supported housing licensing regime. That consultation closes on 10 December. I am sure that my hon. Friend the Minister for Homelessness, who is responsible for this policy area, will have heard the calls to expedite the laying of those regulations.

Earlier this year, Liberal Democrat-run Three Rivers district council put in a notice for an article 4 direction. However, it will not come into effect until June 2027, with the council citing financial concerns, despite repeated calls from me and local Conservative councillors to do it sooner and protect my residents from overcrowded and unwanted HMOs. What advice can the Minister offer my residents, such as those who live in Muirfield Road in South Oxhey, who have already been affected by this issue?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his question. All HMOs are obviously subject to management regulations, and local authorities must license HMOs in certain cases. An article 4 direction is often the way for local planning authorities to get control, but by the sound of it, that should have come a lot earlier in his local area.
I welcome the Chair of the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee.

Many communities, including those in my constituency, are concerned about the concentration of HMOs. There is a perception that local authorities do not have the powers to be able to tackle this. I want to be very clear that I am not against HMOs in principle; this is about how they are abused. I know the Government have carried out a consultation, but do they feel that local authorities are able to strike the right balance between meeting housing needs and maintaining community cohesion?

I thank my hon. Friend and constituency neighbour for that question. We do keep the powers to regulate HMOs under review, and I do want to know from any Member of the House where local authorities do not think those powers are adequate. The key to ensuring that HMOs are properly regulated, particularly where that is necessary to protect the amenity or wellbeing of an area, is having strong policies in an up-to-date local plan. I know that our local authority is putting in place strong policies in our area.

HMOs are the only way many young people can afford to rent, but their unregulated growth leads to the loss of family homes. However, Bath and North East Somerset council has taken action, and has included in its draft local plan a ban on the conversion of homes that would otherwise mean the loss of three-bedroom homes in Southdown, Twerton and Odd Down. Will the Minister congratulate Bath council?

I will congratulate the hon. Member’s local authority. As I say, it is through up-to-date local plans and strong policies on HMOs that local authorities can ensure that they are properly regulated. After all, development plans are the basis on which decision makers, irrespective of whether they are officers or committees, will make their decisions. There is good practice out there in the country—including in my own local authority area, as I have said—and I encourage any local planning authority with concerns to familiarise itself with that good practice.

To residents across the country, a standard family home being converted into an HMO for a large number of adults is a material change. It changes the character of an area, and it places pressure on parking and local services. Too many HMOs are being used to house people who come to this country illegally, and we know for a fact that many of these men are dangerous. However, the current rules do not reflect the negative impact an HMO can have, with landlords not needing to apply for planning permission if it is for less than five occupants, and the article 4 direction does not go far enough. What work is the Minister doing to investigate changing the rules so that all HMOs, regardless of size, require planning permission so that local people’s voices can be heard?

I feel for the shadow Minister in the sense that that question was clearly drafted before the set of answers I have just given. We have acted to strengthen national planning policy in this area. I have made it clear how important it is to have up-to-date local plans in place and to get strong policies. If he has any particular instances of where the existing powers do not go far enough, I am more than happy to hear from him.

title: Rosebank Oilfield
turns: I inform the House that Mr Speaker has selected the amendment in the name of the Prime Minister. I call the shadow Secretary of State.

I beg to move, That this House, for reasons of energy security, economic growth and jobs, calls on the Government to commit to developing the Rosebank oil field as soon as is practicable and to support domestic energy production. Talk about timely—this debate, an important debate in its own right, has been put in stark relief by news breaking this morning; news that, regardless of how frequently we hear of yet another company exiting the UK oil and gas sector, is no less shocking, no less worrying for workers and no less illustrative of the utter destruction being wrought on our world-leading sector and our energy security by this Government. EnQuest, a British-based, London-listed energy company, is to become the latest in a long and expanding list of companies pulling out entirely from the North sea, explicitly blaming the hostile investment environment and high-tax regime cultivated by this Government. There is no hiding from it: the Government’s policies on oil and gas are hanging a “closed for business” sign over our North sea. I know the Minister will claim that their North sea policies are pragmatic, that they want to “manage the future of that basin” and that, by maintaining a windfall tax of 78% and legislating to ban all new licences, they are showing global climate leadership. Let me be clear: EnQuest is not pulling out of oil and gas. It is moving its operations and focusing its investment on south-east Asia, where it sees “greater potential to deploy capital, build scale and deliver sustainable long-term growth.” This Labour Government did say they wanted growth in every postcode—I did not know that meant postcodes in Kuala Lumpur. This Government are not showing climate leadership. It might not have dawned on them yet, but they should turn around because no one is following. No one in the world that has an oil and gas basin is pursuing the same course as this Government. The USA is not. Canada, Mexico and countries in the middle east are not. Nor are Australia or Norway, or across Asia and South America. Even our own overseas territories, the Falkland Islands, are not. We now have the utterly farcical sight of the former Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero and now Foreign Secretary, the right hon. Member for Doncaster North (Ed Miliband), signing off on the development of a new oil field in the British South Atlantic, and the Attorney General at an international tribunal defending the exploitation of that field by the Falklands, at the exact same moment that the Government they serve are bringing in a total ban on new exploration in the North sea. It is utterly unbelievable. You could not make it up, Madam Deputy Speaker, except it is actually happening. This Government have clearly been captured, in part, by an extremist green lobby whose sole purpose is to kill what remains of our oil and gas sector. That lobby cares little about the jobs and livelihoods of the men and women being made unemployed or who are choosing to move overseas. They do not give a damn about the communities—communities that I represent and that they are destroying in the process. A few weeks ago, we saw a rare demonstration of common sense from this Government when, after months of unnecessary dither and delay, they finally approved Jackdaw. That was indeed a welcome decision, and for the men and women who work in Britain’s oil and gas industry, it was a glimmer of hope in the darkness that their jobs might have a future. Approving Jackdaw unlocked 40 million barrels of oil and gas, bolstering Britain’s energy security, and gas from that field is flowing into the British gas grid as we speak. The British people are hoping that somewhere in this Government we can eke out just a little bit more common sense, because beneath the waves, 130 km off the Shetland Islands, lies yet more opportunity to deliver for the British people, a shot in the arm for our economy and the means to protect thousands of British jobs.

Did my hon. Friend notice, as I did, that Gary Smith of GMB described the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero as the “Department for P45s”? It is putting people out of work and not reducing the amount of oil and gas we consume by as much as one drop.

As ever, my right hon. Friend hits the nail on the head. We are still using gas to heat over 80% of homes in this country. British industry relies on gas to ensure that it can function. It is not that we are using less gas; it is just that we are using more imported gas from overseas, either through pipelines from Norway, or in the form of liquefied natural gas from the United States and elsewhere. It is no surprise that Gary Smith of GMB has described this Government’s energy policy as “batshit”. The opportunity that is open to us is Rosebank. That field, if allowed to proceed, could help Britain turn the corner, reindustrialise, grow and become more energy secure, utilising what is on our doorstep, just as other countries are doing and just like our North sea neighbour, Norway. It is in our best interests—it is in the interests of our economy, our jobs, our security and our climate.

The shadow Secretary of State knows that the energy security argument for Rosebank is extremely weak, because the vast majority of our oil is exported. He talks about Norway: it is on an energy transition, but the great tragedy for Scotland, and for Aberdeen specifically, is that Governments in this place and in Holyrood have failed to invest in that energy transition. Is that not the case? Does he not regret that his Government did nothing about that transition?

I am glad I took the hon. Gentleman’s intervention, because it underlines the complete ignorance in parts of the Labour party when it comes to debate about our energy policy. Some 65% of the oil that is generated from the North sea comes back into Britain as refined product, so we are talking about thousands of jobs in Aberdeen and across Scotland. Given that he is a Scottish MP, I am surprised that he is using that argument. When it comes to debates about the economy and our security, there is no better or quicker way to produce revenue, to secure jobs and to ensure our security moving forward that approving the field, getting rid of the ban on licences, getting rid of the energy profits levy and getting Britain drilling again. That does not have to come at the expense of a transition. If we talk to all the companies based in Aberdeen and just outside Aberdeen, we hear that the very workers this Government will be relying on to deliver new clean technologies are relying on jobs in oil and gas right now.
On that point, will the shadow Secretary of State give way?

I will not. The very technologies that are being used right now in the North sea to export oil and gas are the same technologies that we will need to deploy offshore floating wind at scale, of which I believe the hon. Gentleman is very much in favour.
Will the shadow Secretary of State explain, in the constrained financial times in which people find themselves, by how much Rosebank will reduce bills for consumers?

The hon. Lady knows that Rosebank will generate around £500 million a year in tax receipts, which is money that this country desperately needs. That money could be used to cut taxes on the hard-pressed British people, if this Government were so minded. The opportunity we have is Rosebank. That field, if allowed to proceed, could help Britain turn the corner, reindustrialise, grow and be secure once again, utilising what is on our doorstep, just as other countries are doing. Anyone who has a grasp on reality and the challenges we face as a country understands that simple fact. It is common sense to use our own resources. Rosebank is projected to produce around 69,000 barrels of oil every day at peak, which is roughly 10% of anticipated oil output from the UK continental shelf.

In Northern Ireland, 68% of households use heating oil to warm their houses, and 39% of people in Northern Ireland are in fuel poverty. Here is a golden opportunity to address some of the issues for constituents not just in Strangford, but across Northern Ireland and across this great United Kingdom. Today, in this debate, we have a chance to put things right and ensure that my constituents, and all constituents, can get some benefit from the Rosebank field.

The hon. Gentleman is absolutely right. I know that Members across parties see the benefits in exploiting what we have in our own basin. I also know that Members of all parties who want to see a sensible, pragmatic approach to managing the North sea moving forward do not understand why, in the midst of an energy crisis, this Government are choosing to ban licences and maintain a punitive 78% tax on companies operating in the North sea. We have seen just today companies pulling out yet again from their operations here. Under this Government, we have seen a dramatic slide in refining capacity, demonstrated by the closures at Grangemouth and Lindsey. Sadly, our demand for diesel can no longer be met by domestic processing, but Britain is among the most significant contributors of crude oil to the European market, with 65% of it coming back into the UK. That is barrel upon barrel of British oil keeping this country moving. We can choose to get what we need while we need it from our own seas, or we can buy from jurisdictions further afield, such as America or the middle east, with all the additional costs and emissions brought by shipping it to Britain. There is no escaping the reality that we will be using oil for some time, so let us back Britain. What happens to the oil that does not come back to Britain? Those barrels of oil are used in Europe and displace oil that could have been brought from places elsewhere, such as Russia. Every single barrel of oil that comes from Rosebank is a barrel of oil that does not fuel Putin’s war machine. Last month alone, Russian oil producers earned almost $21 billion. That money will buy the bombs and bullets that are being used in Europe, in Ukraine, right now. I hope—in fact, I know—that most of this House would much rather as much oil bought in this world as possible should be bought from nations that are not actively trying to do harm to Britain and its allies. Although Rosebank is about security, it is also about jobs—the thousands of jobs either directly or indirectly reliant on an industry that is on the brink. Those jobs are held by the talented, dedicated and highly skilled individuals that we need for the future, and whom this Government desperately need if they want to deliver anything close to their own energy goals. Despite that, at a time when we need to protect jobs and prioritise our energy security, this Labour Government have introduced legislation to ban Britain from benefiting from our own resources. The ban on new drilling is putting job security and investment on the line. You do not need me to tell you that, Madam Deputy Speaker, because Ministers in the Department already know it. In fact, the official impact assessment of the Government’s ban on new oil and gas licences estimates that it will cost the British economy £73 million a year and decimate more jobs. That was signed off by the hon. Member for Rutherglen (Michael Shanks)—the Minister sitting opposite me. He is fully aware of the damage that this Government’s policies will inflict, yet his Department and his Government are ploughing on regardless. The Secretary of State was all too keen to come to Aberdeen when the Government wanted to make the announcement about Jackdaw. I presume that, when their ban on new licences passes, she will be just as keen to look those same people—my constituents—in the eye and explain why they are worth less than a steel worker, who is in an industry that this Government are expending vast sums of money and huge effort on to protect. We know that almost one in five Labour Members have signed a letter telling the Government to block Rosebank—maybe the Foreign Secretary is considering adding his name to it. They are not helping us to tackle climate change, but they are threatening to destroy thousands of jobs, weaken our energy security and turn away billions of pounds of investment—specifically, £24.3 billion of much-needed investment into Britain over the Minister’s lifetime. The unions agree, including GMB and Sharon Graham of Unite. I have to admit that it is not often we are in agreement with the unions—quite a few Labour Members probably did not expect to see this day either—but we are, because most of the country can see that the policies of this Government are doing great damage and make absolutely no sense. I know that not all Labour Members want to see the deindustrialisation of this country, the weakening of our energy security and the pain that comes with more job losses. I also know that there are Labour Members who are deeply worried about what the future holds if this path is followed. I appreciate that that may be an uncomfortable position for them to be in, but I implore them: do what is right for your constituents and our United Kingdom. They should make it clear to the Government that they are taking this country down the wrong path and join us in voting for the motion before us this evening. We have a clear choice: we can vote today to protect thousands of jobs, reduce our reliance on foreign imports, inject billions of pounds of investment into Britain and generate significant revenue for the Treasury; or we can shirk responsibility and lead Britain down a path of reliance and insecurity. The Conservative party knows exactly where we stand when it comes to Britain’s energy. We support the men and women who work in our oil and gas industry, and we will do so at every step. We will prioritise Britain’s energy security by drilling for our own resources and letting this country benefit from them. We will allow the British people to enjoy the economic reward that a successful and profitable North sea energy industry will provide. Conservative Members are not divided on this. We would scrap the energy profits levy and the ban on drilling, and we would restore the Oil and Gas Authority and enshrine its single guiding mission: to maximise economic recovery from our North sea. Let us approve Rosebank now and get Britain drilling.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero

I beg to move an amendment, to leave out from “House” to the end of the Question and insert: “notes that the previous Government was subject to judicial reviews in relation to oil and gas consenting decisions; further notes that the Rosebank oil and gas development is currently subject to a consenting decision and is a quasi-judicial matter; recognises that it is essential that the Government ensures that any decision is taken in full accordance with the relevant legal requirements and is legally robust, and that any predication of the decision will only compromise this; and welcomes the Government’s commitment to update Parliament in the first instance on the outcome of any decision.” For years, workers in the North sea have powered Britain. They have provided the gas that has flowed into our homes and the oil that has been the foundation of our economy, at considerable personal risk and in conditions that few others have to face at work. At the outset of this debate, in which I know strong feelings will be expressed by Members on all sides of the House, it is important that we can unite around this point: we owe a debt of gratitude to those workers, past and present, and to those who will continue to provide us with oil and gas for decades to come. Let me begin with the Government’s position and the regulatory status of Rosebank, because clarity matters in this debate. Rosebank is subject to a live regulatory process—a process that the Conservatives know about all too well, having experienced it themselves four years ago. The Energy Secretary must decide whether to agree to the grant of consent or reject it. Once her decision is made, the North Sea Transition Authority must then take the final decision. That process is rigorous for a reason: the project’s environmental effects must be considered and weighed alongside all other relevant factors, including any wider benefits to the country. The decision made must take account of the facts and be in line with the applicable law. Parliament is, of course, entitled to debate the future of the North sea and the choices facing our energy system, but I cannot offer commentary on the merits of an individual application. Any decision must be taken in full accordance with the relevant legal requirements, and if I were to prejudge that decision, it would only further compromise the process.

The Minister says that he cannot comment on the decision that the Government are going to take, but can he at least set out a timetable for when the decision will be made? The industry and my constituents are waiting for that decision, and so far it has just been kicked down the road.

As the hon. Gentleman knows, there is a significant amount of evidence to be considered. The Secretary of State is considering it, and the decision will be made in due course, taking account of the amount of time it takes to consider the evidence; that is the right thing to do in a process like this one. I am sure that in this debate, some Members will point to the recent decision on Jackdaw—as the hon. Member for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine (Andrew Bowie) has done—and ask what it means for Rosebank. The answer is that each case must, and will, be decided on its own facts. In making her decision, the Energy Secretary considered various factors, including the project’s environmental effects; its expected contribution to security of supply, employment, infrastructure and the economy; and the UK’s legally binding carbon budgets. She assessed that Jackdaw would not prevent the UK from meeting those budgets or achieving net zero by 2050.

Could the Minister confirm to the House that Rosebank is expected to average 12 kg of carbon dioxide per barrel of oil produced, which could be reduced to as little as 3 kg if it was fully electrified, compared with a global average of over 30 kg for oil production? The production that is planned there is actually remarkably green. Could he confirm that, on a technical level, those numbers are correct?

The right hon. Gentleman knows that I cannot be drawn on those details while, as I have just set out, there is a live regulatory decision. Jackdaw is expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6% at its peak, safeguard hundreds of jobs, and add billions to the UK economy. However, we should not exaggerate what one field can do; Jackdaw will not remove our dependence on imports, and it will not set the price of gas, which is determined on international markets. That distinction matters. Serious energy policy means acknowledging the contribution that existing oil and gas production can make during the transition, while being equally honest that no single field can insulate families from global fossil fuel shocks. That brings me to the Government’s wider approach. Our objective is a managed, orderly and prosperous transition for the North sea—one that supports workers and communities, strengthens energy security and, importantly, meets our climate commitments. The heatwaves, floods and extreme weather of recent years are affecting homes, businesses, food systems and public services now. At the same time, repeated fossil fuel shocks have shown how quickly events overseas can reach household bills here.

The Minister may not be able to comment on the determination by the Secretary of State, but can he confirm whether the views of elected representatives and of the British people are able to be taken into account by the Secretary of State? It is interesting that 65% of Labour voters across the country want this decision approved.

The hon. Gentleman will know that there were two consultations, and I wonder whether he submitted anything to either of them. I will gladly give way if he wants to tell me what he submitted. No? I will just assume that he did not bother.

I need to make progress. Climate security and energy security are not competing objectives, but point in the same direction: less exposure to fuels whose price we do not control and more clean power produced at home. To achieve that, we need an orderly transition that protects energy security today, while investing in the cleaner, more secure energy system of tomorrow. Oil and gas will remain part of our energy mix for decades as we build the cleaner system that will replace them. We are not turning off the taps. Millions of barrels of oil will continue to flow from the North sea, and existing fields will continue to be managed for their lifetime. At the same time, we must face the reality that North sea production has fallen by around three quarters since 1999. Britain has been a net importer of energy since 2004. [Interruption.] As the shadow Secretary of State chunters from a sedentary position, he will remember that when his party was in government, 75,000 jobs were lost in the North sea in a decade. We cannot and will not make the same mistake. More licences to explore new fields would not change that long-term decline and would not determine prices in a global market.

I thank the Minister for giving way, because he has brought up what we did in government. I will tell him what we did when we were in power, in the face of a global oil price collapse in 2014-15. We introduced a policy of maximum economic recovery from the North sea. We cut taxes on North sea production. We made the North sea the most investable basin in the world for oil and gas production. His Government are deliberately, through policy, driving down an industry. This is not a global price collapse or a global issue for the oil and gas industry. This is a made in Britain crisis—a made by the current Foreign Secretary crisis—that only this country is enduring, because the Government’s policy to ban licences and to stick with the EPL is creating issues. Does the Minister not agree?

The shadow Secretary of State will not be surprised that I do not agree with what he said. We can look at the evidence of what happened when his party was in government: 75,000 jobs lost. I heard no response from him about the loss of jobs during his time as an Energy Minister. The Energy Independence Bill, which was introduced to the House recently, delivers on both climate security and energy security. It ends new licences to explore new fields and introduces transitional energy certificates, so that production can take place in already explored areas on or next to existing fields, linked back to existing infrastructure. That is a practical policy, giving certainty to industry where activity supports existing fields, and a clear limit where new exploration would take us in the wrong direction. We should be candid about that choice. New exploration cannot restore the North sea to its peak. It cannot end imports or guarantee lower bills. Building clean, home-grown power gives us greater control, because the wind, solar and nuclear power we produce here is not priced by events beyond our shores.

Are we not at risk of swapping one set of vulnerabilities in relation to oil and gas and a country like Russia with another set of vulnerabilities in relation to a country like China, given its dominance of critical mineral supplies and solar panel manufacturing? We will be just as insecure, just in a different way.

We are already investing in supply chains in this country for critical minerals, and the hon. Gentleman knows that is what we are doing. The transition will succeed only if it works for the people who have powered this country for generations. That means that North sea workers need a genuine stake in what comes next, with investment, training and good jobs in the places where they live. The clean energy jobs plan sets out how employment, supported by clean energy industries, is estimated to grow hundreds of thousands of jobs by the end of the decade. The number supported by clean energy industries could almost triple in Scotland and at least double in Wales, Northern Ireland and almost every region of England. Those opportunities are already becoming real. [Interruption.] The hon. Member for Broadland and Fakenham (Jerome Mayhew) says that is fantasy; it is happening right now, right across the country.
No, allow me to make progress. I have already given way a number of times.

The transition is happening. Just this week, I visited RWE in my constituency. A young man who undertook an apprenticeship with RWE is now a technician, and, with various shift allowances, is earning £85,000 a year. These are good jobs, they are long-term jobs, and they are happening in places like Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes.

I am always happy to give way to my hon. Friend, and she has made an important point. The effect of these industrial jobs is being felt throughout the country, not least in the north-east of Scotland, where floating offshore wind and other opportunities are being made real.

No, thank you; I need to make progress. Sumitomo has opened the UK’s first high-voltage direct current subsea cable factory at Port of Nigg, creating more than 200 direct jobs. Two major offshore wind projects off Norfolk have reached final investment commitment, unlocking £12 billion of investment, supporting nearly 2,500 jobs, and generating enough power for the equivalent of about 3 million homes. A fair transition cannot mean managing the decline of one industry and simply hoping that another will turn up. It means building the next industries deliberately, with workers and trade unions at the table, and fairness must be measured locally, not just nationally. It means a fabrication contract won in Britain, a training place available before a worker has to transition, and a port community seeing the benefit of the infrastructure that it hosts. It means listening to workers when they say what will make a move realistic: pay, travel certification and job security, rather than assuming that a headline number is enough.

No, thank you. Since July 2024, more than £110 billion of private investment has been announced for the UK’s clean energy industries. The new energy wealth fund will begin with a £2 billion injection, and will link future North sea revenues to investment in renewable and low-carbon energy. That is how we turn today’s national asset into tomorrow’s energy security.

That is a really important point, is it not? The Conservative party would have us believe that the only way in which to drive economic growth in this country is to drill every last drop from the North sea. The reality is that we have burgeoning green energy in this country, and we need to support that, because it will ultimately deliver the jobs for young people, in Bracknell Forest and across the country, that we so badly need.

I agree, and I know that my hon. Friend is committed to making sure that those opportunities extend to his constituents in Bracknell and to those right across the country. This debate is sometimes presented as a choice between climate action and energy security, or between existing workers and new industries. It is not. The serious course is to manage the North sea responsibly, maintain the oil and gas that we need during the transition, and build the clean power that will reduce our exposure to volatile international markets. It is to uphold a lawful process on Rosebank, explain the Jackdaw decision honestly, and invest in the people and places that will deliver the next chapter in this country’s energy story. This is a practical, credible and fair plan. It means lower exposure to fossil fuel shocks, greater control over our energy, good jobs across the country, and a clear path to our climate goals.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

The Conservative motion states that, for three reasons, “energy security, economic growth and jobs”, the House should commit itself to Rosebank “as soon as is practicable”. I listen to Conservative Members, and I ask myself why the party that spent the last decade failing to deliver on the real trilemma of energy affordability, energy security and sustainability finds it so hard to look at the evidence and change course. Why would its Trumpian “drill, baby, drill” approach succeed with this one oilfield when hundreds of new licences did not? I will focus on those three claims, and I will also focus on the elephant in the room in the Conservatives’ motion: the climate impacts of the burning of the oil from the field, the very reason their own original consent for Rosebank was found to be unlawful.

Does the hon. Member not understand that if we produce more oil and gas in this country, it does not mean that we will burn more? It just means that we will import less oil and gas from other nations that have a higher carbon footprint than us.

I will definitely come on to that point. The head of the International Energy Agency has said that new fields, such as Rosebank, will not change that much for UK energy security, and that Britain will remain a price taker. We will still be exposed to the rollercoaster of volatile fossil fuel prices. The oil from Rosebank will be sold to the highest bidder—I do not think that any Members question that. We participate in a global market, in which prices are set internationally, regardless of where the oil is extracted or how much is imported. We know that, because we are part of the global market. We Liberal Democrats recognise that the UK will continue to require North sea oil and gas to be part of our energy mix for years to come, and so does the Climate Change Committee. Much of the reason why is that, as the shadow Secretary of State said, we should have been following dual paths: we should have continued with the extraction of oil and gas over the past decades, but also accelerated reducing our reliance on them. Instead, we have had years of maximising oil and gas extraction. Unlike the examples that the Conservatives brought forward—countries such as Norway—the Conservatives failed to turn those resources into a long-term plan for energy security and transition.

The hon. Lady refers to the Climate Change Committee. Its estimate, as we work towards net zero by 2050, is that the UK will still need 13 billion to 15 billion barrels of oil before then. As we are going to use oil, even if we follow the Climate Change Committee’s advice, does she not agree that it would be better if it was produced in UK waters, using UK men and women, who pay tax to the UK Exchequer?

The Climate Change Committee looks at that. As I have said, we agree with the committee on the abatement curve. We need an energy mix, and we will need oil and gas, but the committee says that that does not necessarily mean that we have to open up new fields, and that we have to consider the climate impacts. It says that the best way to stop importing is to drive up electrification in our country. I will come back to that, because that is where the Conservatives doubled down on policies that left Britain exposed.
