If I can say so in the right tone, Labour Members are flying kites for our paying money to the EU and going back into the EU without having full discussions, and without a mandate to do so. It is important for all Members of this House to recognise that what Labour Members are now proposing, and what was being proposed under their previous Prime Minister, is neither simple nor straightforward. Not only do these agreements take a great deal of negotiation, but they involve trade-offs, some of which we have heard about in interventions from Opposition Members. However, it is also important to recognise that we have to be pragmatic, and through the better use of technology and innovation there are ways in which we can overcome some of the burdens that exist.

The right hon. Lady was trying to make the argument that the current EU-UK summit proposals do not have a mandate, but I want her to reflect on how this Labour Government were elected on a clear mandate for a pragmatic and closer working relationship with the European Union. Will she reflect on, and perhaps correct, her remarks about a mandate? It is the democratic responsibility of this Government to do everything we can to achieve economic growth. I think she might want to refresh her remarks.

Democracy is fundamental. It is part of our values in this country and it is what we all strive for, day in, day out. No one would question that, but Labour does not have the mandate to renegotiate the trade and co-operation agreement and major elements of what came out of Brexit. It is important to reflect upon that, particularly when it comes to issues such as alignment and costs. To be fair to Labour Members, they will have to go back to their constituents and explain all these key areas. They will be trying to wrap it up in Christmas bunting and say that all will be well off the back of a summit, when there are no details on the costs and the implications for British taxpayers more widely and in the long run. Erasmus has been mentioned, but when it comes to migration deals and other aspects, every Member in this House—[Interruption.] There is no point shaking heads: we all will be accountable for the implications of the summit, and that is the point about democracy. We should all be proud of that democratic point.

This is not a sophisticated point, but does the right hon. Lady not accept that if we do a deal that makes it easier for us to export food and drink to the European Union, our businesses will do better, they will pay more tax and we will have more income for the national health service, the defence of the country, education and all the things that everybody in this House believes in? Will she therefore tell those businesses in her constituency that are looking to save money, because they export to the EU and it is difficult, that they are wrong?

I speak to those businesses every single week and engage with them every single day. They are under the cosh because of Labour’s regulation and higher taxes. When it comes to being pragmatic and sensible, we should absolutely use technology and innovation, but the fundamental question has to be: at what cost? It is important for all colleagues to recognise that this will be a moment where we will surrender power, sovereignty and decision making back to Brussels. It is important for every single one of us to understand the long-term consequences of that. The Minister for EU relations, the right hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr Falconer) is not in the Chamber right now, and I am sorry about that, because I spent a lot of time debating across the Dispatch Box with him in previous portfolios. He admitted at the weekend that we will be in the room but we will not have a vote. Laws and decisions on our food products going to the EU and those coming into our domestic market will once again be determined by EU regulations and bureaucracy—by EU politicians with no mandate from the British people and, importantly, no accountability to them. The Prime Minister has admitted, in contrast to what he said in the Makerfield by-election, that he wants to go further. I will air a few points to the House about why I disagree with what is being proposed, but I will first give way to the hon. Lady.

The right hon. Lady talks about EU regulations and bureaucracy. Perhaps she would like to have a conversation with John and Nicki Holmyard in my constituency, who now have to have 17 different documents signed by a vet before they can export one load of their top-class British shellfish to the European Union. Often that shellfish gets sent back from the French port, because one of the bits of paper has been signed in the wrong place or something has slipped. I suggest that there is far more bureaucracy and regulation for their business now than ever before. They are hanging on by a thread, and they are desperate for this SPS deal to go through so that their business does not go under, as so many other fish and shellfish-exporting businesses have since the Conservative Brexit deal destroyed them.
First, I would be happy to speak to the hon. Lady’s constituents about this, because my understanding is that shellfish sales have not gone down at all. [Interruption.] The information is out there.

As my hon. Friend says, the information is in the Library. The hon. Member for South Devon (Caroline Voaden) should check some of the information out there. I represent a part of the east of England where oysters and other fish products go over to the EU. I want to make a number of points. First, when the Prime Minister sought election in the leave constituency of Makerfield, he said that he did not want to rerun the Brexit argument. One of the debates being rerun is about whether Britain should be in or out of the EU, the customs union, the single market or some variation of them. Those are divisive debates. None of this is straightforward or simple, but such debates will absorb the political capacity and bandwidth of the Government when they could be dealing with so many of the other important issues that this country faces and engaging with businesses. That engagement is not just in terms of the EU, but understanding the challenges that businesses are facing. Those of us who served in previous Parliaments after the referendum—there are probably many more of us on the Opposition Benches than on the Government Benches, although the right hon. Member for Leeds South has spoken—will remember that we were in near paralysis over some of those decisions in the debates that raged. It was undignified. Madam Deputy Speaker, you may recall some of those times, too. They did not put this House in a good light. It led to a breakdown of political trust. Out in the country post-referendum, the public just wanted us to get on with respecting the referendum result and with the job of governing. Taking the country back to that period will not be helpful when we all face so many other big challenges. Secondly, the Prime Minister has no mandate to make this change. He has no personal mandate through his by-election and no mandate—I disagree here with the hon. Member for Cities of London and Westminster (Rachel Blake)—through the Labour manifesto. Those so-called red lines are being blurred and faded every time the Prime Minister and Labour Ministers talk about rejoining. They are speaking about more integration, and there is a distinction. I come back to that mandate from the referendum. We have to reflect on and recognise the lessons from the past. The EU is consistently interested in two key elements: one is cost, which means access to British taxpayer funds; and the other is exerting control over us. It is about rules, regulation and decision making. We heard that with the reset argument under Prime Minister Keir Starmer. My other point is that when the Prime Minister is advancing his case to align with the EU and rejoin, he is making the argument around the British economy, and that is misguided and wrong. Growth in the UK has been higher and stronger than much of the EU since the referendum. Outside of the EU, we were free to rebound strongly through the difficult period of the covid pandemic. We have been free to remove burdensome regulations and costs on British people. Government Front Benchers have an opportunity to provide some assurances about what this move will mean for our domestic economy and trade arrangements. Outside of the EU, we have been free to negotiate new trade deals globally, with new deals and new benefits. Labour Ministers and Members have frequently welcomed those deals. They boast about free trade arrangements around the world, whether those are with India or even the comprehensive and progressive agreement for trans-Pacific partnership. Will the Minister give some assurance to this House about what this new EU deal will mean for these existing trade co-operation arrangements around the world, including with countries in the Asia Pacific, whether that is India or even Japan? We have new signatories to some of these arrangements. What will the alignment that the Government are trying to achieve with the EU mean for some of our positions at the World Trade Organisation?

What my right hon. Friend is discussing is essentially the most important issue, in a way. We have now negotiated many of these agreements—very successfully, by the way—including the trans-Pacific partnership and others, meaning we are open for new foodstuffs, including meats, for export. However, if anything changes and we have to adopt a deal, it leaves us unable to negotiate and re-design deals with those partners. How long does my right hon. Friend think it will be before they then say that we do not have a deal anymore?

My right hon. Friend is spot on. Let me say to the House gently that none of this is a walk in the park. It is complicated. When I was in government I had a different portfolio, but I know about trade and have seen what has happened to my local farmers. Wicks Manor produces great pork products that it sends not just to EU countries but across the world, as far away as the United Arab Emirates and Indo-Pacific countries. It will be asking what this agreement means for those relationships. I want to press the Minister on that. Will the Minister, in her closing remarks, commit herself to providing the full funding model and the assumptions of the costs and benefits that underpin the figure the Government have given, namely an economic uplift of 0.4% of GDP over the long term, including the definition of “the long term”? Will she say what primary and secondary legislation the Government will be introducing as part of their renegotiation and this deal? As for the economic factors, inflation has been a fundamental challenge for this country in recent years. That is obviously due to the Ukraine conflict, energy prices and life post-covid, but we should also reflect that it has been exactly the same for the rest of Europe. Our levels of inflation are not higher than those in the rest of Europe. Claims that rejoining the EU or giving more powers to Brussels would lead to lower prices are therefore not accurate, which is why the modelling is fundamental. I appreciate that the Minister is from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, but in this context we need to see the dynamic modelling from the Treasury, because the claims are not backed up by facts. The economic analyses, predictions and models that are often quoted are subject to huge variability, big caveats and questionable assumptions. For example, the 4% figure from the Office for Budget Responsibility, which is often quoted, is not an OBR forecast; it is an OBR prediction that results from looking at other studies. I think that the Government should examine these details and consider the economic implications and consequences before trying to make assumptions on behalf of British businesses. The Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations is not in the Chamber now, so I call on the Minister who will sum up the debate to tell us how many of the goods to which her colleague has referred—including the basket of goods that he was holding up on social media—would have their prices changed by the deal that he will be signing this week, and to also tell us whether there will be a risk of higher prices as a result of increased EU red tape. Let me also caution the Government about using the Cabinet Office to promote pro-EU views. Having been in the last Parliament—we have seen how divisive these campaigns can be—I know that that is deeply unhelpful. Ten years ago, just before the referendum, the Cabinet Office produced a booklet that was sent to every household explaining what it felt was the case for remaining in the EU. It suggested, among many other things, that 3 million jobs would be at risk, that a trade deal with the EU could not be delivered, and that our services sector, which is the best in the world, would struggle. It made so many vacuous and false promises and claims that did not materialise, and it actually did a lot to undermine trust in democracy and politics. We do have a free trade deal with the EU, and we have not seen a huge reduction in the number of jobs. The current problems in our employment market have been well debated in the House this week and in previous weeks, including the week following the Budget, but we have to look at the Employment Rights Act 2025 and the costs imposed on businesses through higher taxes and national insurance contribution increases. We have to carry out a sobering check on all this. We should also bear in mind that the value of goods exports to the EU is up by 30%, from £146 billion to nearly £191 billion. There are some very important economic facts that we need to discuss. We should recognise that the UK and other major economies all face significant structural changes and challenges caused by a range of factors, including demand on public services, high levels of taxation and the impact, as has been noted, of global factors. Taking Britain closer to the EU will not address some of these challenges. It is not a silver bullet. There is no single solution, which is why I think it is wrong to go backwards in debates such as this. I should like to mention one other aspect—
Come on! It has been 20 minutes.

I will speak briefly about one other aspect, namely migration and jobs. I was the Home Secretary who negotiated with the EU on security co-operation at a time when Labour Members were saying that we would never secure a deal on intelligence sharing and co-operation, which we went on to do. I think it very naive of Labour Members to say automatically that all will be well as a result of closer relations with the EU. The Dublin system has been mentioned already; that did not work, as was pretty clear at the time. There is a great deal at stake here, and I think that the Government should go in with their eyes wide open. This is not straightforward, and we should be very cautious about what costs it will mean for the British taxpayer and the British public.
Order. There will now be a five-minute time limit on speeches.

I am pleased to follow the right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel). Given that this is an Opposition day debate and the topic is UK-EU relations, it will inevitably become party political, but I want to follow the spirit of her speech and try not to be party political. In that spirit, I think it worth saying that we have learned from Labour Members who were not in Parliament during the Brexit wars. We sought election to this place in order to do politics differently and better, because we observed the chaos and paralysis, but we have also learned, I think, the right lesson from the way in which Brexit was concluded—that this was a bad deal, which was bad for the people we represent. If we, as democratically elected Members, can make life better for our constituents, we ought to do so. I think that that is what we as a Government, and we on the Labour Benches, are trying to achieve. Let me also say that we need to get some perspective. The proposals are small steps, not leaps. We are not proposing to rejoin through the agreement that will be settled on Friday. The EU that the Government are sizing up is very different from the EU of 10 years ago. The Britain that the EU is sizing up is very different from the Britain of 20 years ago. I want to look forward rather than backward, because, as we heard from my right hon. Friend the Member for Leeds South (Hilary Benn), this is about lifting our eyes, settling on a vision and relating the means to the ends, and I fear that the motion is trying to get bogged down in specifics. Specifics matter, but if a country does not lift its sights and then relate what it is trying to achieve to that, it will just bumble along, and I fear that that is what has happened over the last 10 years. Let me look briefly at what is directly ahead of us. We are, of course, making projections and predictions—no one is sure—but every choice in foreign policy is a hard choice at the moment. Red lights are flashing everywhere. We need to accept that discomfort, do the best that we can, and make the trade-offs that we need to make. When President Trump departs the stage—if, indeed, he does in the next two years—Trump may be gone, but Trumpism will remain. Even if the Democrats go into the White House, elements of the Trump agenda will linger, whether they involve isolationism or protectionism. AI will continue to be a danger; Russia and China will continue to be threats. Things will not get better just because we assume that in two years’ time there may be a new President. We also need to face what, for me, is a real concern. Over the next two years, we may see Ukraine sold down the river by the United States. Russia may be given the space and time to rearm and grow stronger economically, and it may use the final months of Trump’s presidency to test NATO—to do something against Germany or Estonia, or against European allies. If that comes to pass, the UK will need to be as strong as it possibly can be, and that means growing closer in our relations with our European allies—like-minded countries and democracies like us. With two minutes remaining, I will truncate what I was going to say, but I will just say this. We need to stare ahead at a real risk that is coming from Europe. France and Germany are likely to change considerably in the years ahead. The polling currently shows that the far-right Rassemblement National could win the presidency in 2027. The polling shows that the far-right Alternative für Deutschland could become the largest party in the Bundestag in 2029. Britain will need strong European allies like never before so that we can work constructively with those countries under a different style of leadership, but we will also need to work like never before with those European allies in the EU so that they can continue to see their values met and their goals pursued. Those countries will be looking to Britain in that landscape. They will need international leadership of the kind that the UK showed when Russia invaded Ukraine. Given that we have a couple of years before that moment potentially arises, why would we disable ourselves? Why would we not seize every opportunity to lead in Europe and internationally? I have been reflecting on what the midterm elections have meant for our country, but also for our world. One of my reflections is that we in this House are so lucky to have held to a consensus on Ukraine. On both sides of this Chamber, with exceptions, we are steadfast in our support for Ukraine. Let us be equally steadfast in our support for a stronger Britain working more closely with our European allies, and for the strengthening of democracy.

Madam Deputy Speaker, “Each time we must choose between Europe and the open sea, we shall always choose the open sea.” That was Churchill’s view of the continent, or at least de Gaulle’s account of Churchill’s view. Regardless of the veracity of that account, Brexit was very much about the open sea—Britain not turning in on itself but striding back out into the world and striking deals with friends old and new, in a way that is simply not possible under the yoke of EU regulation. I do not want to dwell on the past today because, like it or lump it, Brexit is in the rear-view mirror, and so too is the Europe that we left in 2020. As a member of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, I have sat in a committee room in the Bundestag in Berlin and looked the fascist AfD in the eye. I have watched flinty-eyed EU negotiators in Brussels size up Labour’s starry-eyed pitch for a reset. “How much would you be willing to pay?”, they whispered between steepled fingers. I have seen seafood exporters in my Dumfries and Galloway constituency struggle to get valuable products to the market in Boulogne-sur-Mer, not because of Brexit but because of sheer bloody-mindedness from a protectionist EU. On the positive side, I have seen the Japanese welcome our co-operation on the next generation of fighter jet, Canadians relishing doing business with us on critical minerals and fertiliser, and businesses in Mumbai and New Delhi licking their lips at the prospect of more gorgeous Scotch whisky heading their way. Why would we not turn our face to the new dawn in places such as the Pacific rim, rather than back to the sunset over Europe, where growth is sclerotic and divisions are widening? The Czech Prime Minister, Andrej Babiš, said the quiet part out loud when asked if he supported a UK return to the skirts of nanny Europe. “Yes, of course,” he said, “We need more money.”

Does the hon. Gentleman find it ironic that while large chunks of the Labour party now want to rejoin the European Union, we have great opportunities from trade deals with the United States, India, Switzerland and South Korea? On the one hand, the Labour party trumpets those opportunities; on the other, it now wants to deny us those opportunities. It seems a strange paradox.

There is a certain cognitive dissonance here. The SPS deal, which is much touted, could damage our opportunities around the world, as we have already heard. That is a serious issue. The EU is not the avuncular old pal that some Members pretend it is, any more than dynamic alignment is a good thing. Let us call it what it is: it is rule-taking, not rule-making. Labour has disastrous form here. Let us not forget that it traded away access to our fishing waters for 12 years in the hope of joining SAFE—Security Action for Europe—and the European defence fund. Europe got the mackerel; we did not get the missiles. Europe is desperate to get the sons and daughters of its elite into our vastly superior universities. Erasmus+, which we are rejoining, gives them just that, at a gulping cost to us.

If we are going to talk about Erasmus+, it is important to recognise that it is not just Erasmus; it is “plus”. That means that people from underprivileged backgrounds, people doing vocational training, people in the field of sport, and all sorts of other people now have an opportunity to benefit from Erasmus. That was one of the most important factors for us in deciding to rejoin. If we are going to talk about Erasmus+, we need to talk to our constituents about the opportunities. I am doing that at the moment, so that the World’s End estate and the poorer parts of my constituency can benefit. Let us talk about the world as it is, not the world as it used to be.

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his intervention, but the “plus” is the cost, and the cost is rising. Turing was an excellent scheme, and it came at considerably less cost. Let us strike out across the open sea and deal with people who want to deal with us. Spare me the claim that geographical distance dictates trade. No one tell China that it is far away; otherwise, Temu will go off a cliff. The only thing we have to fear is our own lack of ambition. Our measure of deals with the Mercosur countries of South America and with those in the Pacific rim, represented by the CPTPP, is based on what previous trade deals have done, but there have never been trade deals of such scale and scope. Let us not slip back under the dead hand of the EU and the faceless politicians and bureaucrats of a distant Strasbourg. Yes, let us do deals with them. Brexit was never a goodbye to Europe; it was more of an “au revoir” and “auf Wiedersehen”—until we meet again. We should meet again as friends and equals, not vassals. Adam Smith has been invoked today by the Liberal Democrat spokesman, the hon. Member for Surrey Heath (Dr Pinkerton), and it is worth reflecting that it is the 250th anniversary of “The Wealth of Nations”, which wrote the book on free trade. Smith would not agree with shrinking our markets and aligning ourselves only with Europe, because there is a great big world out there. Britain can navigate the open sea. We can be pragmatic with Europe, but there is a wider, more successful world out there.

I completely agree that there is a wider, braver world out there. I have the privilege of being the trade envoy for Morocco and Francophone west Africa, and since last year we have done another £330 million-worth of business. Who we are up against in Francophone west Africa? The French. Being in the EU has not precluded the French from doing deals and business across that part of the world, and neither does it preclude us from doing so. If we sign a deal, it will not affect the fact that we are out there battling for Britain across the world. I would like that to be recognised. A lot has already been said in this debate, so the House will forgive me for not repeating the determination of the Labour party to get closer to the EU, as we promised our constituents. That is very much welcome in my part of the world. I think the right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) likes to call my residents who live on the World’s End estate, which is among the poorest parts of the country, “liberal bourgeoisie”. No doubt we can look forward to more of that later. In practical terms, we are looking forward to quite an interesting deal that will save British businesses money. If we remove export health certificates, which we hope to do at the weekend, businesses will save £200 per consignment. Would the Conservatives like to keep those? If we remove phytosanitary certificates, businesses will save £25 per consignment, and that adds up. I presume the Conservatives would like those to stay. If we get rid of certificates for inspection of organic products, we will save over £130 per consignment. I presume the Conservatives would like that to stay. If we get rid of routine SPS border checks, fresh produce will come to the market much more quickly and costs will go down. Surely the Conservatives do not want that to be the case.

I think we want to agree on what we disagree about, if we are having a civilised debate. The hon. Gentleman is selecting some particular costs associated with leaving the EU, which, incidentally, the EU has imposed on us; we have not imposed them on ourselves. The problem is that there will be other costs associated with these agreements. It is about whether those other costs, the direct costs of contributing to the EU budget, and the indirect costs of the burden of regulation on British business outweigh the costs to which he refers. That is what we need to have a debate about, because at the moment he is being very selective with his statistics.

I was talking about the deal that we have coming up at the weekend; I was not talking about the other things that the hon. Gentleman is extrapolating. May I just correct one point? Forgive me, but it is absolutely infantile to keep saying the EU did this to us. The sovereign choice of the British people—
Order. This is an Opposition day debate. Let us use moderate and temperate language.

Forgive me, Madam Deputy Speaker. It is not on to claim that the European Union did this to us. We took the decision to leave the European Union. We decided to become a third country. Third countries follow different rules from members of the EU. The EU did not punish us or do this to us; we chose to follow the rules followed by any third country. We now think that it has damaged the country, which is why we want to get rid of border checks on some imports from the EU, including for products such as milk and dairy, red meat, plants and potatoes. All those border checks will go, reducing the cost to import. That has to be good for British people. On shellfish, I have just checked the figures, and forgive me, but I gather that the trade body Seafish says that shellfish exports have gone down 27% since we left the European Union. It is very easy for Members to shake their heads when I make this claim, but they can just google it—it is simple. All sorts of things under the agreement that we hope to sign this weekend will bring down costs for people hoping to export and keep a lid on costs in both energy and food and drink in this country, which surely has to be a good thing. I am particularly keen on giving British business a chance to have a say in shaping European standards, because we cut ourselves off from that when we left the European Union. As I understand it, unlike now, in future and for the first time in many years, Britain and our experts—from the National Farmers’ Union or other technicians—will have a decision-shaping role. Unlike since we took ourselves out of the European Union, we will finally have a role in shaping the standards that so many of our businesses have to follow, which is surely positive for this country. It is another reason why I am so excited about the possibility of an agreement.
Will the hon. Member explain what decision shaping actually means in practice, or what he understands it to mean?

I understand it to mean that we will have the opportunity to sit again on standards committees. The hon. Lady may disagree with my understanding; I can only give her my understanding. We will have an opportunity again, in the way that Norway and other countries have, to sit down and bring our technical expertise to bear. Having discussed this with Members of the European Parliament and others, I know—I do not want to pretend otherwise—that we will not have the ultimate say, because we are not a member of the European Union but a third country, but we will have a chance to influence standards outcomes in a way that we have been deprived of for many years. [Interruption.] I am sorry, but I cannot hear the hon. Lady. If she wants to yell more loudly, I will have a go at responding. I do think we should welcome the cutting of costs and the opportunity to improve the situation for our young people. I do not think we are talking today about any more than welcoming the first attempt to put things right, because leaving has not worked, has it? Let us look at the actual facts, instead of trying to recreate an argument that the British people are tired of. We have to look forward, and we can have a confident, useful, positive relationship with the European Union that does us good. Why not welcome that? Why refight the battles of the past?

Madam Deputy Speaker, I am grateful to be called. We have a time limit, and I will try to stick to it. The main thing I want to say is that we seem to be debating something that is not really the subject for today. We seem to have reignited this whole idea about whether the UK should go back in to the EU, and most of the arguments are proposed along those lines. The problem we have is that the Government are was in favour of leaving the EU for reasons to do with our control in setting our own regulations and our ability to make meaningful trade deals with everybody else outside the EU, while retaining a good relationship with the EU. This has never been anti-EU; it is simply the nature of what is good for the UK. The reality is that a negotiation is going on with the Government. Again, I do not have a problem with the Government asking for negotiations on our trade arrangements with the EU. The question in all of this is: what is the purpose of the negotiations? This is where we have a problem, because the Prime Minister at the moment seems to flit between different statements about his own purpose with regards to the EU. If this is just another narrow attempt to try to make the passage of goods across to the EU happen in the way it did before, I do not have any problem with that. The key issue is: what is the price of making such an arrangement? It boils down to this very simple question: what is the price of our contribution to the EU? What is the price in what we have to take as rules from the EU thereafter in those specific product areas? What price will follow when we deal with others with which we have done trade deals or will do trade deals when the EU wants to make changes in those areas, as I am sure will be negotiated, if we are unable to change those arrangements because we are bound by this agreement in perpetuity? That is really what we should be looking at in this debate. We can have these wonderful debates about whether we should rejoin, but we have left the EU, so we are talking only about such arrangements. We can have these wonderful sweeping remarks about how Brexit has been a disaster and that we have done worse than we ever would have done, but we have outgrown the EU ever since we left. That is because British business and British abilities made sure that we upped our game. Germany has real problems right now: 15,000 manufacturing workers a week are being laid off. France has real economic problems, and it is teetering on the edge of recession. Given all that, why would we want to get bound more deeply to Europe, and why now?
Will the right hon. Member give way?

I will give way in a moment. I have very little time, and I want to make a couple of points, if the hon. Member does not mind. The point I am really making is that the cost is the one thing we should be debating today, and the Government should have put the cost on the table. The part I disagree with is keeping that under wraps and not telling us what is going on until after they have done the deal and then not have a debate.

Given the way a lot of this debate is going, it may help to suggest that we should talk not just about how Germany and France have done in the last couple of years, but about the extraordinary growth in Poland and Spain. Indeed, since we left the European Union, our growth has been 6.2%, while France’s has been 6.2%, Germany’s only 1.8%, that of the euro area as a whole 7.8%, Italy’s 8.7% and Spain’s about 12.1%. Let us put—

I really reject all of that. It is nonsense to make that argument. The reality is that we have outperformed the European Union. Yes, I have nothing but regard for Poland for being able to focus on what it wants to do. Mostly, it wants to increase its defence capability, and I wish we were doing the same here. I wish the Government would step up and say, “We’re going to invest in British industry here to get our defence right,” but that is not the case. Before the hon. Member tries to level that charge at me, I simply say that he needs to check the broad nature of his own argument and whether he is restricting himself, because he is so anti the whole idea of Brexit, that he only looks at figures that match his own points. I simply say that the reality—[Laughter.] Members can giggle as much as they like, but the reality is that this Government are planning to make changes and give commitments to the European Union. They will not tell us at this stage what those commitments are, and they will not put all the costs on the table, yet Labour Back Benchers say that it does not matter and that they will go along with anything in this EU vision. That is where the problem arises. For goodness’ sake, they should hold this Government to account. When I sat on those Benches, I did nothing else but attack my Government whenever I thought they did wrong, and I think it is high time that Labour MPs started behaving like elected representatives, not toy soldiers that get marched into battle. I simply say that our real problem in all of this is that we are not debating the right thing. I want to settle on this: we are witnessing a renegotiation. The question in all of this is: what is the cost of that renegotiation? From its standpoint, the European Affairs Committee in the House of Lords made it quite clear the other day that “costs would be an inevitable consequence”, and the Government should set out the source and scale of the funding, which should be secured by a parliamentary vote, but there will be none. In the same report, it said of adopting EU laws with no say: “Witnesses were in agreement that the volumes”— of our commitments and obligations— “were likely to be significant.” We will therefore become rule takers, not rule makers, so this is significant. It may not be rejoining the EU, but it certainly looks as though it is paving the way towards doing so.

I just want to elucidate for the House the Library’s figures on shellfish. In 2021, we exported £322 million of shellfish to the EU. By 2022, this was £368 million, and by 2023, it was £382 million. The volume has remained roughly the same, except that some shellfish is now exported to South Korea for processing and then directly imported into the EU, so that is no longer included in the total that we export to the EU.

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for making that clear. Correcting the corrected record is always something. I want to draw on the House of Lords report again. It makes it clear what is in line with this agreement. Experts from previous trade deals told the House of Lords that 69 EU Acts were now in-scope for this set of negotiations. That is 69 obligations to change our rules and our laws, and be obligated thereafter under every single negotiation that we will make. We will not be able to change those, short of breaking the agreement. We will not be allowed to debate what comes back on Friday. We will not be allowed to vote on it, because the Government want to hide that. I simply say to hon. Members on the Labour Back Benches that they should be pressing for a full debate and the full detail on the table. Otherwise, they are not carrying out their responsibilities as elected representatives.

I am very pleased to speak in this debate. I thank the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) for his contribution. This is a very timely debate, as we have just finished two days of the UK-EU Parliamentary Partnership Assembly meeting here in London and, as we are discussing, Ministers are heading off to the summit on Friday. I hope it will be highly successful for this country and for my residents in Exeter. Far from the entreaties of the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green, in many ways Labour Members have been pushing the Government to go further and faster on our agreements with the European Union. It has become such a truism that Brexit has been a disaster for this country that I feel that sometimes the Opposition can barely make a good and coherent argument for it. In fact, the shadow Minister made many arguments that I felt were fine arguments for rejoining the European Union. The Conservative party pushed Brexit, convinced enough of the British public—just—that it would be in their interests and then subsequently fought over what Brexit actually meant. In the end, it did not mean staying in the single market and the customs union, as their campaigns promised, but a complete and total withdrawal on the hardest of terms. Only the year after was the TCA negotiated and activated. What a dereliction of duty to the UK public that Tory Brexit deal was. It has fallen to us, the Labour Government and Labour Back Benchers, to fix the mess the Tories left. We did that by starting to rebuild trust with our partners. Our relationship with the EU is fundamental to delivering our domestic economic agenda, reindustrialising our economy and supporting good growth in every postcode, because Britain is part of the continent of Europe and what happens there—be it Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, or work in the single market in the European Union—has everything to do with us. The more we have a say over that, the better for this country and the better for my residents. The EU remains our closest partner and our biggest market. In 2025, almost half of the UK’s total trade was with the EU, yet we are outside, cut off and unable to shape what happens in that massive market. Once politicians accept that fact, then everything flows from there. Let us look at the impact on our country. First, on the economic impact, the OBR confirmed in March this year its existing forecast that Brexit will reduce GDP in the long run by 4%. It says that is due to the impact of non-tariff barriers to trade, causing a reduction of 15% in both imports and exports. That is despite the former Prime Minister, Boris Johnson, promising that there would be no non-tariff barriers to the EU. The evidence is not debunked, I am afraid, because the UK’s gross GDP is higher than that of France, or because it is unrealistic to think the UK would have grown more like the US without Brexit. The UK’s per capita GDP has grown lower than that of France, Italy and the eurozone since Brexit. Pre-Brexit, UK GDP did indeed grow more like the US’s and it has since declined. Next, and more importantly in many ways, there is the social impact. First of all, imagine what a larger economy—larger by £120 billion, by many estimates—could deliver in terms of jobs, investment and the public funding of public services. Secondly, we cut ourselves off from the ability to live in, work in or visit freely 27 countries. The opportunity cost of that is unimaginable. I fear the reduced international influence of us removing ourselves from one of the biggest institutions in the world.

Does my hon. Friend also recognise that many young people in his constituency and mine have been denied the very opportunities that their parents enjoyed to live, work and study freely across Europe? Would he welcome progress on restoring those opportunities?

I absolutely agree with my hon. Friend. When we talk to European colleagues, a lot of their focus is on opportunities for young people. Working together, I think we can share that real opportunity and bring more opportunities to our young people, including in Exeter and Wirral West. The Government are fixing for our people the disaster that Brexit has been. As we look to the summit that is coming up, the SPS deal will help the south-west, with our massive farming, fisheries and seafood sectors. I will not add to the bivalve debate, but I think there is some debate in the House of Commons Library papers about the massive impact on seafood exports as we left Brexit. The emissions trading deal, if passed, will help us to protect our industry, while co-ordinating action on climate change. The youth experience scheme will reopen opportunities for young people to train, study and work in Europe. We will negotiate, hopefully, deeper co-operation on immigration, which is a joint challenge for the entire continent. The economics of the deal, should it go through—I hope it does—is that it will add about £9 billion a year to the UK economy, which will be of massive benefit to this country and to my constituents. As I head to the end of my last minute, I will skip to the fact that the European Parliamentary Partnership Assembly friends who came to the Houses of Parliament this week had one message for us: they miss us and the door is open on all those things if we tell them what we want. The summit on Friday is a really good opportunity to get past the initial summit last year, which was very successful. We need to get those things over the line and move on to what we want to come next. There was vigorous debate, as those who were in the Chamber with us will know. That is healthy and what we should want: discussion, debate and decision, working together as a continent in the face of the global challenges we face. I, for one, am pleased that the Prime Minister is throwing off the omerta of Brexit, 10 years on, to have an honest conversation about what we actually want as a country in the national interest and where we want to be. I look forward to the outcome of the summit on Friday, and I look forward to discussing it next week in this Chamber.

I want to start with something positive that I have found in today’s debate—you know me, Madam Deputy Speaker: I always like to try to find the positive in every situation—which is the tone and tenor of the debate we have been having concerning the European Union. Since the defenestration of Keir Starmer, a new mood has developed on the Labour Benches, which is rather warm and positive. They now know and seem to understand and appreciate just how big a disaster Brexit was. It took us years to tell them that, but they have finally come to that assessment and now understand what it is about. I like what they are trying to do with the European Union: improve the relationship, get a new deal and make sure that positive things are happening. That is all good. What I have a little bit of trouble and difficulty with is what they want to do with that new positivity. Where do they want to take it? I have heard lots of good things about rejoining the European Union. If that is Labour’s ambition and intention, it will get support from me and probably from most Members on the Opposition Benches, other than our friends in the Conservative party, but it will need to spell that out a bit more clearly. The Prime Minister says that he will do that in time and that we have to be patient—we have to wait—but the Government owe us some sort of explanation and set of directions on where they are going. So there is the positive.

Does the hon. Gentleman think he could give us an explanation as to why, when we left the EU, he accused the Westminster Government of a power grab, because we were repatriating powers from the European Union to the United Kingdom, and why he now wants the EU to grab those powers back?

I always appreciate, value and enjoy the hon. Gentleman’s contributions—there is that consistency. I was going to come to the more negative part of my contribution. After welcoming where we are going, I had to listen to and endure the Opposition Front Bench. I can only describe it as drivel. It was an appalling contribution from the Conservatives. The attempt by the hon. Member for Kingswinford and South Staffordshire (Mike Wood), who is no longer in his place, to somehow excuse and defend what must rank as one of the worst negotiated deals in the history of bad negotiations ever was quite commendable. It was very brave and determined of him to try to do that. The extraordinary view of the Conservatives is that the deal is some sort of success. That is as deluded as it is bonkers. Every household in the United Kingdom has suffered as a consequence. Every business that trades with the EU has seen their red tape suck the very life out of it. Whether it is immigration or our ability to live, work and love across a continent, Brexit has corroded practically every institution and part of our society that it has touched. We have heard many of the statistics and figures, so I will not rehearse them. The idea that we should look to France and Germany and be delighted that somehow our economic growth is better and faster than theirs ignores so many different features and facets about why that is the case. And even if it was the case, would it not be great if we were able to add to that all the economic activity that we have lost through Brexit—the years of economic growth, and what we would have done if we had better exports? The Conservative Brexit deal was simply one of the worst deals negotiated in the history of bad deals. It reminds me of somebody continually punching their face but assessing that somehow that is all right because they are in control. That is the Conservative view of what Brexit is doing to us. We were told that Brexit would free us from Brussels bureaucracy, but we have actually spent the past 10 years creating a new British bureaucracy to deal with the consequences of leaving European bureaucracy. We are told—although this has not been said today, which is quite intriguing, but I am sure we will get to it—that all these things are going wrong with Brexit because it is the wrong deal. Apparently it is all because we have got it wrong—the wrong Government, the wrong negotiators, the wrong everything to do with Brexit. But the hard Brexiteers got absolutely everything they wanted; they could not have concocted a better hard Brexit deal than the one that we are having to live with just now—no customs union, no freedom of movement, no single market, no European Court jurisdiction, no EU institutions. This was not some sort of accidental version of Brexit that just happened to be created out of the ashes of us leaving the European Union; it was designed by them—this is what they wanted. And now they turn around and say, “Oh, but it’s the wrong type of Brexit.” What type of Brexit do they want? Do they want to take Britain off its anchor and leave it marooned and stranded in the middle of the Atlantic? Sometimes I think that is what the Conservatives really want. I was here in Parliament during the tortuous Brexit years, and I say to them that there is no having our cake and eating it. Brexit has been an absolute and utter disaster for businesses. The public are way ahead of even this Government on this. The vast majority of the people of Britain want to rejoin the European Union, and they should make a firm commitment to ensure that is going to happen. It is now all over to them. In Scotland there is a desire to rejoin the EU, and we overwhelmingly back that. We wanted nothing whatsoever to do with their bonkers Brexit, but we were still subject to it. That is one of the main reasons why support for Scottish independence remains so high. We have had this betrayal from these Governments about Brexit. We were told that Boris Johnson would never be Prime Minister—what happened to that? We were told that we would stay in the EU—we are out. And that is why we will ensure that we will be departing from the United Kingdom too.
Order. Several Members who intended to speak have left the Chamber, so I am putting the time limit up to six minutes. I call Dame Anneliese Dodds.

It is always a pleasure to follow the hon. Member for Perth and Kinross-shire (Pete Wishart). He talked about the tone of the debate, and I have to say that I am feeling a little bit festive at the moment. I know it is a little early, but we had the right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel) referring to festive bunting—tinsel might be more appropriate, but anyway. We also arguably had pantomime-style scenes at the beginning of this debate, and many ghosts of Christmas past speaking from the Opposition Benches. But I was thinking back to Christmas eve of 2020, and those of us who were MPs at that point remember that Christmas eve very well, as do exporting businesses in particular—they remember that day very well. It was a very stressful day because that was the day we had the deal that had been negotiated by the Conservatives. On that day I said the deal was a bad one for Britain. I said it was as thin as gruel. I was not, then, on message—we might say, “No change there, then”—but I could see back then how trade and investment in our country would suffer because of the additional red tape and blockages to trade created by that deal. Indeed, because of the mismanagement of that process over the three and a half torturous years following its creation, the damage has been even deeper than many anticipated. The right hon. Member for Witham spoke about the need for evidence based on raw data, but of course we have it now. We have it from those Stanford economists. They have gone to Bank of England company data and have looked at trend data—not using inappropriate averages, but looking at what the trend of growth was before, and looking at individual businesses—and their findings suggest a hit from Brexit and its mismanagement of between 6% and 8% of GDP per capita over the past 10 years. That is robust evidence that I believe is extremely persuasive. Sadly, some of those costs are sunk—investment opportunities that have not been and now cannot be taken up; entrepreneurs who have not been able to realise their dreams and now cannot realise them—but there is the possibility now to make up some of that gap, and we have to do so given current global trade turbulence, geopolitical competition and, of course, the need for growth given the cost of living crisis. As many of my hon. Friends have said, this Labour Government were elected on a promise to build a closer relationship with the EU and reduce barriers to trade. That is exactly what the deal that is on the table on Friday would deliver. I want to make three quick comments on it before making some brief remarks on where I want to see the Government going further. First, I find it astonishing that people who would describe themselves as patriots ended up okaying a deal that led to certain British products effectively being banned from being exported into the EU, or being tied up in red tape that effectively made those exports impossible. Excellent British fresh food should be on the continent’s plates, it should be on them more quickly, and it should be on them in greater volume than at the moment.

The right hon. Lady will understand that the reason those products were banned was that the United Kingdom was not part of the single market. She was elected two years ago on a promise not to enter the single market, and yet those products will now be given admittance precisely because the Labour Government are entering part of the single market. How does she reconcile this with that promise in the Labour manifesto two years ago?

I will be very brief to enable others to speak. I regret that the hon. Gentleman was not, I think, in the Chamber for the rest of this discussion; if he had been, he would have heard from many other Members that this is not about rerunning those previous arguments or going back to those previous institutions. This is about having a deal that will remove impediments to trade that have had direct impacts on UK producers. If he was here previously, he would have heard, for example, about Montrose lobsters and so many other examples, including fresh sausages and burgers that cannot be exported. We have to get rid of this situation that is harming our economy. We also need to recognise—
Will the right hon. Lady give way?

No, I will not. We also need to recognise that industries like steel and aluminium are absolutely critical for our economy. I have heard no solutions from the Opposition regarding how those exporters would be dealing with the carbon border adjustment mechanism unless we had the kind of deal that is on the table on Friday—they could be paying enormous costs. Where is the Conservatives’ solution? We have not heard it. Finally, I find the position relating to our young people often very peculiar. I believe they should be able to spread their wings and gain the experience afforded by youth mobility. It is especially important that we politicians do not pull up the ladder that many of us benefited from. When what the Government are talking about will afford opportunities to apprentice sparkies in Sunderland just as much as to a student of Spanish in St Albans—and, beyond that, when there are Members of Parliament here who have benefited from the ability to travel to the EU to have that experience—it is the worst form of elitism to deny them to young people today. I was very pleased to see the Minister placing these issues in their geopolitical context, because, ultimately, our relationship with the EU is about our security, including our economic security. The right hon. Member for Witham talked about our relationship with the rest of the world, and I say respectfully to her that I am sure she will have had the same experience that I had repeatedly: leaders in other countries and other parts of the world saying that they could not understand why the UK, in our more insecure world, had cut itself off from its geographical neighbours. I heard that over and again, so I am sure that she must have heard it. We need to listen to that call when it comes to our own security. I hope the Government will recognise that call even more when it comes to industrial policy. Sovereign AI for the UK alone is proving difficult, if not impossible, to achieve, not least in frontier model AI, despite the strenuous efforts of the Government, especially in supporting novel chip design and AI applications. We do not have the market power on our own to constitute a chokepoint and thus to have the leverage we need to develop sovereign AI. We could have that by working with the EU, so I encourage the Government to take the lessons of the recent withdrawal agreement joint communiqué on this and to go further, so that we can increase our sovereign power in this area. Also, given increasing competition from Chinese manufacturers, let us sort out “Made in Europe” and rules of origin. I commend the Government’s work to this House. Let us not be stuck in Christmas past—let us look to the future.

Order. I will now announce the result of today’s deferred Division on the Employment Rights Act 2025 (Unfair Dismissal) (Removal of Limit on Compensation) (Consequential Amendments) Regulations 2026. The Ayes were 299 and the Noes were 159, so the Ayes have it. [The Division list is published at the end of today’s debates.]

It is a great pleasure to follow the right hon. Member for Oxford East (Anneliese Dodds). It is ironic that she should pick out AI as the sector that she wants to bring under EU control, because that will not be sovereign control of AI; it will be EU control. But the really significant point is: why did the International Monetary Fund just upgrade the United Kingdom’s economic growth prospects? It is because AI is not regulated by the EU, and there is now very significant divergence between the regulation applied to AI in the EU and the regulation that is not applied in the United Kingdom. The result is that we attract the lion’s share of inward investment—more than the whole of the EU put together—and our AI is at the moment contributing perhaps 0.4% or 0.5% of growth in the British economy. There are very significant advantages to being outside the EU. The reason why the economy is growing a bit faster than the economies of some of our EU competitors, despite the burden of taxation and regulation that the Labour party has applied to it, is because we are outside the EU. It is the same in financial services. We were told that the City was going to fall off a cliff if we voted to leave the EU; today, the number of people employed in the City of London is nearly double what it was in 2016-17. The whole foundation of the Government’s case rests on the myth that leaving the EU has somehow damaged the United Kingdom’s economy. Government Ministers rest on one particular forecast, which was incorporated by the OBR into its projections, from 2020. Can I just point out that that is over six years ago? It is six years out of date. The forecast did not assume that there would be any regulatory divergence to give the United Kingdom economy an advantage over the EU, which is what has happened; it did not assume that we would have the best free trade agreement that the EU has ever given another sovereign state—a trade agreement completely without quotas and tariffs; and it did not assume that we would make so many successful trade deals with other countries. The fundamental point about the economy is that what a Government do with their domestic taxation and regulatory policy is by far the most influential factor that affects economic performance. If we do not control that, and it is controlled by our competitors, we are giving ourselves a grave disadvantage. That is particularly true if it is to do with the EU, because the EU has adopted a regulatory system that is inimical to growth and inimical to innovation. That is why we hardly see any large data or internet companies in the EU—they are all American. America has a very different regulatory system that is based on English common law, rather than the preventive, risk-averse Code Napoléon that has been adopted by the EU and is still massively incorporated into the United Kingdom’s present law—it is retained EU law.

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for giving way and I congratulate him on having more time to speak. He talked about AI, but there is also genetic engineering; those are two areas that the EU is deeply reluctant and utterly cautious about, and that has now left it behind. The UK is one of the leaders in those areas.

Oh, but we are told that we are going to be at the table to do the “shaping” of these decisions! Well, decision shaping is not decision making; decision shaping is not sovereignty. We are going to put ourselves at an even greater disadvantage than we were when we were in the European Union. I mean, take financial services, where we were outvoted again and again and again about regulation of the City of London—to our disadvantage. We have started to unpick that now, which is why the City is doing better. At that time, we did not have any say over what was being imposed on us, because the majority of other countries, most of which hardly had a financial services sector compared to ours, were imposing their rules on us. We do not want to be in that situation again, so I do congratulate the Government on two things: on excluding AI and on excluding financial services from this reset. They really would be shooting themselves in the foot if they had not done that. The real question is: what is the effect of the SPS agreement and the CBAM? The right hon. Member for Oxford East mentioned CBAM, which will require British industry to apply very high tariffs to imported aluminium and steel. That will put up the costs of building houses, offices blocks or anything else; it will drive manufacturers out of business through further extra costs. Why does the EU want that system? Because it wants us to buy its aluminium and its steel. It is a protectionist system—that is how the system works. We are far better outside it. We are also far better outside that system for one other particular reason. The EU is now demonstrated to have been, since the joining of the single market, a declining trade bloc. The 27 countries that are now members have lost their share of global GDP—from about 30% down to about 17%. The United States of America has retained about 25% of global GDP, so clearly its system is better than the European one. Why would we want to go back into the European system? During our membership of the single market, the proportion of our goods exports—the single market was only about goods—went down and down and down. From memory, between 2005 and 2021, we only increased our goods exports to the EU by about 23%; we increased our exports of goods to the rest of the world by 85%, and we had no trade deals and no rule taking of other people’s economic systems. We are now at an advantage, because the rest of the world is growing. Why would we want to shackle ourselves to the declining, over-regulated, over-taxed EU as an economic solution? The enthusiasts for European integration on the Government, Liberal Democrat and SNP Benches—we always feel a bit outnumbered in these debates—might at least give us the benefit of the doubt on whether there is a matter to be discussed here. Citing the 4% productivity figure used by the OBR really is an abuse. It is deceitful to pretend that a forecast made in 2020 has been borne out by events, when the facts quite obviously demonstrate something completely different, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Witham (Priti Patel) explained.

My hon. Friend refers to what has happened since 2020. It always surprises me in these debates that no mention is made of the covid pandemic. Who would have anticipated that we would recover as well as we have, given that it cost us more than £400 billion of unplanned expenditure?

We did recover, although it left us with a bit of a headache on the debt front. That should be the priority of the Government. We should be getting the debt down, not handing new contributions to the European Union—for example, for cohesion funds, or an expensive student exchange system that will advantage EU students more than ours. Under the Erasmus scheme, far more students came to the UK than went to the European Union. It is also bizarre that the party that believes in foreign aid should want to subsidise EU students from relatively rich countries, instead of students from much poorer and disadvantaged countries, which is what we did under the Turing scheme, giving them the opportunity to come and have a British education. It is a shame that the Government have scrapped that scheme. I want to come back to the fundamental point—[Interruption.] I will be brief. Our domestic regulation and taxation determine this. Look at the Growth Commission report produced earlier this week—
Thank you, Sir Bernard. Perhaps some interventions later? With no time limit, I call Tony Vaughan.

When we talk about this issue, it is really important to look forwards—not back at the rights and wrongs of the 2016 referendum, but at how we get the best deal for Britain now, given that businesses are suffering all over the country. A good place to see the problems that have arisen from the Conservative Brexit deal is my constituency. We are the gateway to Europe; we have the channel tunnel and the M20 to the port of Dover. The access to Europe that my constituency provides determines whether a local business can get its order to a customer in Lille or Lyon on time. I want to talk about the impact on local businesses of the failed Brexit rules created by the Opposition. Alcaline is a major local employer and an international haulier serving customers right across Europe. It should be expanding; instead, nearly a quarter of its fleet is parked up, but not for a lack of orders. Under the Conservatives’ post-Brexit rules, British drivers can spend only 90 days in every 180 in the Schengen area. Meanwhile, European drivers, who could fill the gap, need work visas and experience friction at the border. The work is here, but the lorries are parked up. It is not making business good for Alcaline. A sole trader called George has been making handcrafted stringed instruments for export to Europe and the world for many years. In years gone by, before Brexit, most of his sales went to the EU. Now, if he sells a €3,200 instrument to a customer in Italy, they have to pay more than €1,000 in import costs. He described the situation to me as “nail after nail being hammered” into the coffin of his business. A Folkestone-based family business called NIC Instruments has made bomb disposal and robotics equipment since 1946. The EU’s €150 billion Safety Action for Europe defence fund keeps most of the European Union’s spending on defence procurement issues within the EU. That can shut out British-made equipment; every bid means a fee, and a less competitive position for that business. With a war on the continent, Europe should be buying from Folkestone; it should be buying its defence equipment from the UK, but we are being shut out by these rules. We simply cannot accept that as an okay state of affairs. These businesses’ stories are the country’s story. More than 16,000 British firms have stopped exporting to the EU because of the failed Tory Brexit deal. This Government quite rightly want to fix that. On Friday, the food and drink deal will get rid of some of the Brexit red tape, including £200 health certificates, £25 plant certificates and inspection fees. For Kent growers, including those in Romney Marsh, it will reopen their natural market. For families taking their pets through the channel tunnel—I have done it, as have many others—the process is currently completely inconvenient and costly, with huge veterinary costs that people really should not have to face. Together with the emissions deal, this deal is worth up to £9 billion a year. The Tories talk about Brexit freedoms, but I would like them to consider what my stringed instrument maker in Romney Marsh has gained from Brexit. He already builds to European standards, because those are the standards that he must meet in order to export to Europe. What Brexit gave him was the freedom to fill in forms and watch his customers pay €1,000 in fees for the privilege—that is, customers who can still afford to pay the prices. He could pay an agency to fill in those forms, but as the hon. Member for Surrey Heath (Dr Pinkerton) said, that is a Michael Gove-inspired “opportunity”. It is a negative—a cost, not the benefit that he considered it to be. Aligning the rules for our exporters who already meet the necessary standards is not surrender but common sense. The Tories talk about handing Brussels a cheque, but there are no payments going into the EU budget for these deals. The real cheque is being paid right now in my constituency by hauliers whose lorries sit idle in a yard. Across the country, it is paid by the economy being 6% to 8% smaller than it could have been, had we not left the European Union. I am happy to take interventions on that statistic, because it is absolutely devastating to any case that the Tories might make on this issue.

The hon. Gentleman said that there would be no payment by the British taxpayer for access to the EU single market. Ministers have been very careful to obfuscate on that point. I wonder whether he has had some special knowledge, or has had a briefing from them, confirming absolutely that no taxpayers’ money will go to the EU for access to the single market.

I am talking about the deals that we will see on Friday. That is a question for the Minister, not for me, but my understanding is that this will not involve what the hon. Gentleman suggests—certainly from what we can see. He had nothing to say about the fatal statistic that the UK’s economy is 6% to 8% smaller than it would have been, had we not left the EU. Nothing that I have heard from the Tories can gainsay that. They tell us to focus on growth, cut red tape and back British business. This deal will do that, so they should back it. The Government are fighting for British businesses. I hope that will mean that Alcaline transport will get its lorries back on the roads and can recruit drivers. For the sole trader instrument maker, I hope that greater co-operation with Europe will ultimately make his business more competitive, and result in lower import charges for him and less red tape. For the defence company making robotics equipment, I hope that this engagement will ultimately result in it being able to access EU defence procurement markets. That will do far more for my constituency than the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership deal, worth a paltry 0.08% of GDP. I urge the Minister and the Government to keep working on cutting Brexit red tape—our businesses really need that, in order to move forward—and to keep going on closer co-operation with Europe. Folkestone and Hythe has always been a gateway to Europe. Our ambition should be to make this country the best place in Europe to invent, make, finance and export. This Government are opening that gateway again. The Conservatives are only offering the closed door that has cost us so much.

This is a really important debate. My main concerns are the lack of transparency and ability to question the Government about what is coming forward. On numerous occasions, the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee, of which I am a member, has asked the Minister responsible for EU relations to come before the Committee to answer important questions about the terms of the SPS agreement, knowing the impact that it will have on our farming community, but our requests have been consistently rejected. It seems, however, that this lack of questioning is not limited to the Commons; it extends to our lordships, too. The House of Lords’ European Affairs Committee has produced a report called “Dynamic alignment: a fundamental change”. It says that the Committee “exhausted all avenues” in seeking to secure a ministerial appearance; it was not given one. That is appalling, and quite unprecedented; in the report, their lordships say that they always have some form of Minister appear before the Committee. I question why we are not being given an opportunity to understand the details, given that we are talking about such a fundamental change in the relationship. It is really important to understand the terms of the SPS agreement. We understand that it will be based on a form of dynamic alignment, of which the Lords give a very interesting and important definition: “Dynamic alignment is a process in which one jurisdiction changes its law as necessary on an ongoing basis so that its law is, in some way, always the same as the law of another jurisdiction.” We are entering into the SPS agreement on the basis of dynamic alignment, which means that we have to take laws from the EU. Dynamic alignment is an EU construct that is quite novel; it is not exercised across the world. Mutual enforcement is another model that we could have adopted, as has happened with Australia and New Zealand.

The House of Lords European Affairs Committee, which is hardly made up of a bunch of leave voters, said that the move to dynamic alignment would “fundamentally alter the post-Brexit relationship between the UK and the EU”. I have looked in the Labour manifesto, and it has no reference to dynamic alignment or anything like it. This is not closer co-operation; it is subjugation.

I thank my hon. Friend for making that crucial point. This is a fundamental change, and it was not put before the electorate in the general election—as he said, it was not in the manifesto—so it is even more vital that it should come before the House. We should have opportunities to understand it. [Interruption.] If the hon. Member for Edinburgh East and Musselburgh (Chris Murray) would like to intervene, he may. The reality is that we are not being given that opportunity. When the deal is signed on Friday, it will be a done deal. It is essential to understand the scope. Are we aligning just on pieces of EU law, or on policy objectives, too? Will alignment be automatic or piecemeal? That is important to our understanding of how the agreement will be implemented. Many of the farming community’s concerns are about wanting more certainty about their business operations going forward. The industry has been saying that it needs to know how long the implementation periods will be—we may need up to three years to implement some of the changes in the SPS agreement—and we have no guarantee. In a world of uncertainty for our farming community, the least we could do is get them a bit more clarity on all this.

The hon. Member is making an argument about putting the outcome of the summit to the House. Does she know of other negotiations—perhaps some of the Brexit negotiations that the Conservative party led—that came into the public domain? Were they debated in detail in public? I very much hope that she will be in the Chamber next week, when we will have a chance to discuss some of the detail. Any reflections she has on how the Brexit negotiations were conducted, and whether they met the standards that she spoken about, would be really interesting.

I thank the hon. Lady for that point, but the reality is that we had years in which we could debate negotiation terms in this Chamber. In this case, the Prime Minister committed us to a pathway before we had the ability to discuss this in the Chamber. This all boils down to what influence we can have. The hon. Member for Chelsea and Fulham (Ben Coleman) is convinced that we will have the fundamental right to shape decisions—to sit at the table from day dot. This does not mean that at all. Decision shaping—

The hon. Member will forgive me for not addressing that directly. I do not fully understand; is she suggesting that when the Government enter into negotiations overseas, they should come back and report—check in and check out—at every point in the negotiation? [Interruption.] She is? Okay. As far as I am aware, that is not what happened with Australia—[Interruption.]
If your intervention is done, that is fine, but you cannot use an intervention to continue your argument when another Member has the Floor. I believe that intervention is done.
It is not, because I was interrupted.
Well, too late. You are out of luck.

He is too late, as we are too late to be able to influence how this is going. The reality is that decision shaping means that the very first instance—at the hint that a decision may be made—is the only point at which we have the ability to comment on it. It does not mean that we get a continuing seat at the table; it does not mean that we get to influence. The House of Lords said in the report that the Government need to be entirely realistic that we will have limited influence.

The hon. Member is giving a detailed speech about a particular issue around SPS. On dynamic alignment, is it not the truth that that is just the thin edge of wedge and that before we know it, everything will be about rule taking, no rule shaping, and dynamic alignment on everything? Is that not a real concern?

It is a concern that I have on the point about dynamic alignment. We are talking about a say-so, particularly regarding three areas—SPS, electricity trading and youth mobility—but in the wider discussion, this also potentially allows, as we understand from the summit agreement, other agreements to follow on the path of dynamic alignment. In that case, if the Prime Minister is going to be honest and we are talking about rejoining the EU—some of the conversations indicate that that is where he may be going—that completely changes our entire relationship once more. It is important that when we come to dynamic alignment, we understand that it is not just on those issues alone; it could go much further and much wider.

I share my hon. Friend’s concerns about the potential implications of dynamic alignment. Whatever view Members on either side of the House take about that issue, does she share this concern of mine? The House of Lords European Affairs Committee report states in its summary: “Our ability to assess the full prospect of dynamic alignment for the UK was hampered because the Government declined to provide a Minister to appear before us until after the next UK-EU summit”. Is that not deeply concerning to my hon. Friend, and hopefully to everyone in this House—that a Minister was not even willing to appear before a Select Committee of one of the two Chambers of this Parliament to discuss it?

My right hon. Friend is entirely right. That is one of the points that I made at the very beginning: the lack of scrutiny is one of the weakest points. The Government are not allowing us to understand the details exactly and they will not come before the House of Lords Committee.
