I stand here as a Conservative and make my points, and those on the Government Benches will disagree with me, but not even a balanced, cross-party group from the House of Lords is afforded the opportunity to understand the decisions being made.

Some of us have been campaigning to draw the Foreign Office to account on endless treaties at the Dispatch Box. I am surprised that great soldiers of the left on the Government Benches are quite happy for those things to happen in their ignorance. Is my hon. Friend not surprised with me? Does that not sound strange to her?

Indeed, it sounds very strange. It is a lack of accountability and a dereliction of duty on behalf of all Members of this House that they do not have the opportunity to scrutinise the agreement correctly. I know that my right hon. Friend was a fierce and vociferous campaigner on various issues. It is our duty to understand exactly what the agreement is, because we in this Chamber are not the only ones experiencing it; so are our constituents and our businesses. This is about the future of our trading relationships across the globe. I get frustrated that technical details are often completely overlooked by this Chamber. Things are often based on vibes, principles and feelings, but that is not the reality. It is not us who have to put this into force; it is our constituents on the very front line.

The hon. Lady makes a good point about the need for Parliament to scrutinise what the Government are looking at. Will she remind the House of her party’s response when people in the Liberal Democrats made that argument in the last Parliament, calling for greater scrutiny of trade deals?
I thank the hon. Lady, but I also remind her that the Conservatives always appeared in front of Select Committees, so we are not even within the same bounds or on the same grounds as her point.
Will the hon. Lady give way?

I will just make a tiny bit of progress. The payments for the agreement have often been mentioned and it is important that we reckon the cost of all that. There will be costs involved with the EU running the activities and costs that we will have to pay into the EU cohesion policy, but we have no idea how much that will be. It is again a dereliction of duty on our behalf that we do not realise what we are committing the British taxpayer to put forward as part of those wider deals. We have to have an understanding of that. Again, the House of Lords Committee, which has had experts on the matter in front of them, has said that it is vital. We should have that detail. If Labour Members disagree, I must really question where their judgment falls on this. The other element we have to debate is how Parliament will function with this. It is estimated in this report that the SPS agreement alone could generate 780 pieces of in-scope EU law a year. We will have to understand the effects of those 780 pieces and how we will bring them in. This goes back to the point about decision shaping. We will have to have early intelligence about all of this. Those 780 measures are just for the SPS, not for any other agreements we might have coming forward. We need to understand exactly what the EU is thinking of doing on all those points, in order to be able to have even a hint of a conversation about them or influence over them. What are we going to do about the prioritisation of the issues between domestic policy and EU policy? Which is going to take priority, and how are we going to organise that? We also have to look at resourcing for this. We do not have committees doing any analysis. We are going to have to rebuild all those committees once more. There will be greater amounts of work for the civil service. This is a realistic decision that we have to think about and take forward seriously. The Prime Minister said in his Mansion House speech on Monday that there were three tests that he wanted to be solved, and the second one was to “improve the Brexit deal to bring it closer to what people thought they were getting in 2016”. I do not understand how dynamic alignment will achieve any of that. What many voters signed up to in 2016 was about not giving away control. We do not want to be a rule taker; we want to be a rule maker. It is worse now because, with these SPS agreements, we are not even going to have a seat at the table. The Prime Minister also said that, at every stage, “the British people will be the boss”. How? How will that happen when the SPS involves dynamic alignment and the decisions are already being made without us even being at the table? There are a lot of decisions, and we have to do much more analysis of what is happening and what the deal in front of us is. I think that is lacking. Even if the deal comes before us on Friday and there is a statement on Monday, the horse has already bolted.

I was really surprised to find out that we were having an Opposition day debate on the European Union, because I did not think that the Opposition wanted to talk about the European Union, and to be honest, now that I have listened to what the Opposition’s argument—
Will the hon. Lady give way?

No, I will not give way yet. Now that I have heard what the Opposition had to say, I am even more surprised, because all that we have heard today is rehearsed old arguments. The only new argument that I would like to reflect on is about the mandate. There has been quite a discussion about the mandate, and it is a legitimate question to put forward. I was extremely proud to stand on a Labour manifesto that was clear that we needed to have a closer working relationship with the European Union. It also contained the clear red lines, which respected the outcome of a democratic referendum. I very much disagreed with the outcome of that referendum, but I respect it.
Will the hon. Lady give way?

No, I will not give way. I was really pleased to see that closer working relationship with the European Union in our manifesto, and that is the mandate that the Prime Minister and our negotiators are going to be taking forward at the summit on Friday. I have not heard any argument at all today against that clear position that we took in our manifesto.

I am most grateful to the hon. Lady for giving way. She talks about honouring the manifesto. Does she therefore disagree with the former Chancellor from her own party, and indeed the former Foreign Secretary, who now say that, far from agreeing with the Labour manifesto, they want to rejoin the European Union? That is the reason we are having a debate. That is why we are as surprised as anybody.

I have always known how much I disagreed with the hon. Member, and now I have an even further reason to disagree with him, because he does not even understand what a manifesto is. He does not seem to understand that we put forward a clear position in our manifesto, which was to have a closer working relationship with the European Union and to have our three clear red lines. Those are the grounds on which we are negotiating in the summit on Friday, and those are the grounds that we will be sticking to. I have made my own views clear about how I think there is a great potential for us to rejoin the European Union in the future. That is my view, and I think that we will be having a conversation about all the options in a future Parliament. There is nothing unclear about those positions. In addition to the argument about a mandate, there have been the old stories and arguments about sovereignty. I do not think those arguments have landed today. Once again, I am surprised that the Conservatives even wanted to come forward with this topic for Opposition day because they have not managed to make it clear that the position we are putting forward in our trade deal would in any way challenge our sovereignty. They have not managed to make the case either that the arrangements we are looking to negotiate with the European Union are taking place under a different form of governance from any other negotiation that we would have on trade. In fact, the arguments have been particularly absent in that area.

Would the hon. Lady not accept that dynamic alignment is by definition a surrender of sovereignty, because rules and regulations decided in Brussels will apply automatically in the United Kingdom without anyone in the United Kingdom having a vote on the subject?

I would not accept that argument. I would make the case that the process of going to the summit is based on our clear mandate to have a closer working relationship, and also on our profound responsibility to seek out opportunities for economic growth, which was another key part of our manifesto. In fact, it should have been a key part of everybody’s manifesto. There is consensus that we need to seek economic growth in this country.

As ever, my hon. Friend talks passionately on this subject. On our mandate and sovereignty, does she acknowledge that when the Prime Minister goes to speak to Europe on Friday, he will be doing so with the support of the majority of the British public who want that closer relationship? It is our duty here to scrutinise whatever he brings back, not to stop him from having those conversations.

My hon. Friend makes a good point about the role of this Chamber in scrutinising the deal once it is completed on Friday. He also makes an important point about the Prime Minister and, in fact, the European Union, knowing that the Prime Minister and the Government go into the summit with the full backing of the people, who are represented here whether by Liberal Democrats, the SNP or the Labour party, to develop a close working relationship with the European Union. We have talked about the mandate and the question of sovereignty—

If the Government seriously wanted the backing of the people, they should start from the principle that a referendum result cannot be reversed except by another referendum and by doing what Iceland did, which is have a referendum before any of the negotiations—of course, it voted against it.

The hon. Member tempts me to give my extremely long—possibly two-hour long—speech on referendums. Maybe I should do my three-hour version on what I think referendums have done to this country. I will not be tempted into designing the next steps, but I think he makes a deeply flawed point, which I will come on to, where he does not recognise how the world has changed since 2016. For me, the questions in the debate are: do we accept that the world has changed; do we accept that every Government have a responsibility to seek out economic growth; and are we prepared to be honest and make the difficult decisions to achieve that? I hope the House looks forward to hearing me talk about the many wonderful places and institutions in the Cities of London and Westminster that have benefited so much from their relationship and heritage with the European Union. Whether that is Tate Britain, the Barbican, Soho or the Square Mile, central London and our economy depends on strong working relationships with the European Union. Anyone who enjoys the creative sector, and I believe most people sitting here probably do, will know how harmful Brexit has been to the performing arts when it comes to touring. We need to ensure touring is part of the conversation on Friday. I accept that it is not one of the big three topics that we have been talking about, but the impact of the changes to touring arrangements has been really harmful to the creative industries, and the issue deserves further recognition. City Hall in London estimates that Brexit has cost our economy £30 billion and that Londoners are on average £3,400 worse off as a result of Brexit. That is simply not good enough. I note that there are not many Conservative Members for London constituencies in the Chamber, and that no Opposition Member has been prepared to come forward to recognise the harm that Brexit has done to the capital’s economy. Relationships based on trade and investment, research collaboration, cultural exchange, economic growth, jobs and opportunity, and our place in the world—[Interruption.] I thought you wanted the three hour version of my speech, Madam Deputy Speaker.
Order. The hon. Lady knows how to lose friends very quickly. No one wants a three-hour speech.

The Prime Minister has acknowledged the uncomfortable truth about the harm that has been done to our economy. He has talked about using “the Makerfield test” at the summit to decide whether or not everybody across the nation will benefit, and on Monday evening he talked about “the London Test”, drawing a clear and powerful example of how the summit needs to meet the needs of all our citizens, regardless of the part of the economy in which they participate. That is really crucial part of the debate. The consequences have been felt across the country: farmers are facing higher costs, exporters are burdened by new barriers to trade, and communities who were promised prosperity are actually experiencing weaker growth. The public increasingly recognise this, as was acknowledged earlier. Recent polling suggests that closer ties with the European Union win out in virtually every constituency in the country. We deserve a better deal, with closer co-operation with our neighbours, a youth mobility scheme to expand opportunities for our young people—please let us move on from the divisive debate that does not recognise our young people’s great potential—much deeper security, defence and co-operation, and definitely a more practical relationship on food and trade. Democracy cannot be a frozen moment in time. It is a living, social contract between the public and those elected to serve them. It is sad that the Conservative party has become the party of Brexit. No Opposition Members have attempted to confront the woeful position that has been taken by the Conservatives, while the Prime Minister is absolutely committed to our manifesto red lines and to having closer ties. The question for us today is not whether we can afford a closer relationship with Europe, but whether or not we can survive a decade with no continued growth without one.

I want to start with a revelation and an admission. The revelation is, in a sense, more of a declaration. If you were to come to my home in Lincolnshire, Madam Deputy Speaker—I hope that one day you might—and we were to enjoy a pot of tea in my study, as you gazed at the walls, alongside the portraits of Benjamin Disraeli and the prints of Chesterton, T.S. Eliot and so on, you would see a small, framed poster from the University of Nottingham in the late 1970s. That poster records the fact that even then I called for us to leave what was then the European Economic Community—the Common Market. From the very beginning of my consideration of these matters, I recognised that the Common Market, which metamorphosised from the European Economic Community into the European Community and ultimately the EU, was incompatible with both our national interest and the common good.

May I apologise in advance that I will not be able to be present for the entirety of what I imagine is going to be a year-by-year account of my right hon. Friend’s journey towards Brexit? However, did he notice in my intervention on the Minister, there was a conspicuous lack of an answer to my question about whether or not the European Union still has as its fundamental objective the dissolution of the sovereignty of its member states and the creation of a unified European political superstate? Does he have any reason to believe that that matter has changed as far as those who direct the European Union are concerned?

I have no such understanding that it has changed. It is typical of my right hon. Friend, with both perspicacity and foresight, to anticipate the very reason that my hostility to the European Union has its roots back in the 1970s. Those roots were of two forms. The first was because I believe that in nationhood, we nurture the sense of belonging that nourishes a true sense of worth—so I believe in the magic of nationhood. The second was because I believe that political power is best exercised closest to its effect. When it becomes remote from its effect, it risks at first becoming unaccountable and ultimately becoming corrupt. For those two reasons, I resist the idea of surrendering nationhood to something supranational. I know that that was the ambition of the architects of the European Community. If we look at what Monnet and others said back in the 1950s, before the treaty of Rome, we see that they were under no illusions that this was a common market and a means of perpetuating good trading relationships. They saw it as a political project, and “project” is the word often used to describe it by them and about them.
Will the right hon. Gentleman give way?
I will. I am always happy to teach liberals a lesson, as the hon. Lady knows. [Laughter.]

We did 10 rounds on this subject last week. The right hon. Gentleman says that he is against supranational institutions. Obviously the subject of this debate is UK-EU relations, but, if we extend his argument, is he also against the United Nations, the World Trade Organisation, the World Health Organisation, NATO and all other supranational organisations in which co-operation happens on a whole range of different issues?

The difference there is in the emblems and totems, the reality of governance and the character of polity. The problem is that the European Union has taken on the function of a polity itself. It is a law-making body. In other words, it exercises governance. Organisations of the kind that the hon. Lady describes—I think particularly of NATO, which I do not think she mentioned—are intergovernmental organisations, in which Governments come together, co-operate and collaborate. Of course, collaboration between nations matters—she and I would agree on a lot of that, actually—but the creation of something that has an anthem, a President, a flag and, more substantially, the ability to make laws that affect this place, irrespective of the will of this Parliament, is of an entirely different nature. I knew that back in the 1970s, and I know it now. That is why, as my right hon. Friend the Member for New Forest East (Sir Julian Lewis) predicted, year by year both my understanding and hostility grew and had their culmination in the magical moment when we voted to leave the European Union in 2016—perhaps the greatest moment of my time in politics.

We have had this idea that somehow the EU is just the same as NATO or any other international organisation all the way through these debates for decades, and I am afraid that it is based on a very fundamental ignorance. The EU is completely different to any other international organisation. It makes laws that are binding on the member states, whether they like it or not, and its courts overrule the courts of the member states. We are putting ourselves in that position through dynamic alignment, which is why it is a breach of the mandate given to the Government. There is nothing about that in their manifesto, and it is a breach of their manifesto commitments.

My hon. Friend, like my right hon. Friend the Member for New Forest East, shows remarkable insight, because I was about to say exactly that. Dynamic alignment is the acceptance of a series of regulations without further consideration here—it is an automatic process. You can believe in that, as many Labour Members clearly do, but if you accept that, you by nature accept the declining influence of this place in altering our destiny.
That is not something I believe in, any more than my neighbour does.

This issue of dynamic alignment is part of the thin end of the wedge that the British people are so concerned about. Nobody asked for a great debate about rejoining the European Union. Does the right hon. Member share my concern that the Prime Minister is using this week’s EU summit as a stepping stone towards trying to rejoin the European Union—as the thin end of the wedge? Turning to immigration, the youth mobility scheme sounds all very fluffy and cuddly, but the previous Prime Minister talked about a youth mobility scheme of 50,000 for a year. Now, we hear it is 100,000 for three years. Where is this going to end? Does the right hon. Member share my concern that it will lead to freedom of movement and mass immigration?

I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for his intervention. He is my neighbour, and we have worked together on a number of matters. I said at the beginning of my speech that as well as a revelation, I was going to offer an admission to the House. My admission is that I have always rather liked the Prime Minister—I worked with him on matters of national security when I was a Home Office Minister and he was the shadow Home Secretary. One of the things I know about him is that he has a degree of political wherewithal, and the move that the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice) has identified is a political move. It is more about the Prime Minister’s political strategy than it is about the strategic interests of the British people. He believes that he can unite the middle-class left around a pro-European position. It may indeed end in an even more arch-pro-European position—which, to give some credit to the Liberal Democrats, they are unabashed about. They are prepared to be naked in their advocacy of the European Union, whereas the Prime Minister is not.

I do not want to move my right hon. Friend on to the next bit of his life, but given his comments in support of the Prime Minister, I think he may be going to Downing Street shortly to receive—how can I put it?—a post.

Another honour, maybe. However, I do want to ask my right hon. Friend a question. Towards the latter stages of covid, I was asked by the then Prime Minister to look at how we could change some of the regulations that were imposed on us. I spoke to the scientists from Oxford who developed the first vaccine. When they sat in front of us, they confessed that although they had all voted to remain, when covid happened and they were hunting for a vaccine, they realised just how constrained they had been in developing new medicines when they were in the EU, because of the nature of the controls. We had lifted all of those controls, and they got the first vaccine, and millions of lives were saved as a result.

It is certainly true that a nation alone can be nimbler and more responsive than a nation that is obliged to agree what it does in concert with many others, where there will be differing opinions about both scale and speed. My right hon. Friend is right—that is a good example of how, freed from those obligations, we were able to deal with a pressing problem. That is part of a bigger point, which I referenced earlier when I intervened on the Minister, the right hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr Falconer). Much is made of how the world is changing and how, in this dramatically altered world, we need the security blanket of our connection with the European Union. However, the counter-argument is just as powerful. In a more confusing world, a Government’s ability to act quickly and cut across some of the bureaucracy that is associated with supranational bodies—the nimbleness that my right hon. Friend the Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) referred to—is all the more important. In a changed world, a free and dynamic country can be a more effective country.

I invite the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) to consider correcting the record, because that claim was fact-checked at the time and found to be untrue. Under European law, the UK was permitted to act independently to approve a vaccine in an emergency, and it was made clear—I was a Member of the House at the time and I remember fact-checking Boris Johnson and Matt Hancock when they made that claim—that it was not the case that we were able to accelerate the vaccine because we were outside the EU. We would have been able to do so anyway, because of the exemption for trialling novel vaccines under a specific medical exemption. I refer the right hon. Gentleman to the Full Fact article on that point.

Madam Deputy Speaker, you will have noted that that was more of an intervention on the previous intervention from my right hon. Friend the Member for Chingford and Woodford Green than it was an intervention on me, so I will leave my right hon. Friend and the hon. Lady to sort the matter out between themselves. The bigger point is the one I made about how we perceive our future. I perceive our future as a nation that is outward-looking but sure about the sovereignty of this Parliament, for though the sovereignty of this Parliament may be spoken of blithely, essentially we are talking about the will of the people exercised through this place. The second point that inspired me to oppose the European Union back in those teenage years was the one about power. Here we are directly accountable to the people who elect us. We are answerable in the most palpable way, are we not, to our voters? Every single Member of this House has regular engagement with all kinds of people in their constituencies, with all kinds of opinions, and that is their constituents’ chance to access and influence power. I studied politics at university, and I have studied the EU ever since. One requires virtually a PhD to understand how it works. Many of the people elected to the European Parliament have only a sketchy idea of how it works. We know how laws are made there. It begins with discussion among relatively junior bureaucrats, who then listen to a series of interest groups and lobbying organisations. It is then elevated to a diplomat, who discusses it, plans it and sets it out in rather more detail. By the way, that is long before it gets to anybody who has been elected. Finally, it gets to the MEPs, and they discuss it, usually in some smoke-filled room—well, I guess these days the room would not be full of smoke, so that metaphor is perhaps becoming rather dated. National Governments are reached very late in the process, and their chances to influence EU laws are very limited. The hon. Member for Chelsea and Fulham (Ben Coleman) said he is a fully fledged—he is not shy to admit it—member of the liberal bourgeoisie. In the case of the current arrangements, he also said we will have a chance to shape some of those decisions. The experts— I shudder when that word is used; I never claim expertise in anything, really, and neither should he—will have some influence on this process, but there is a real difference between shaping and deciding.

This is perhaps not a deeply intellectual point, but what is important about this place is the traditions we have, and those are not just the traditions that have pertained for a long time, but those that develop. May I say how grateful I am to the right hon. Gentleman for inventing a new tradition, which is that every time he speaks, he has a go at me? I look forward to it, and I have not been let down.

I detect just a touch of paranoia in the hon. Gentleman. He knows that I am a soft-hearted soul, and I think he was pricking at my soft heart in the hope that I will be kinder to him in future. The key thing is to understand how dynamic alignment works. It is true, as Labour Members have said, that this agreement that the Prime Minister will reach may slash some of the post-Brexit checks imposed thereafter by the European Union, which may make things easier for some of our exporters, of which food producers are a good example. In return, however, the Prime Minister will agree to align permanently—“in perpetuity” was the phrase used earlier—with EU regulations on food and farming. This process means that the UK will have to adopt new EU regulations in areas as soon as they are passed by Brussels, with no vote on them. I will come in a second to the House of Lords Committee that has already been mentioned, but in essence that will mean scores, perhaps hundreds, of new regulations affecting British businesses, about which we will have no say in this place. That House of Lords Committee said that the deal would mean “significant volumes of EU legislation”, and heard evidence that complying with farming laws alone “might generate at least 780 pieces of in-scope EU law a year”. I am not going to second-guess a distinguished Committee of the House of Lords, but even if that were an overestimate, the principle remains that many additional regulations will be imposed on this country, with Parliament having no say. Much has been said about mandates and Makerfield. Let us be clear about the polling. A recent survey in Makerfield about who should decide UK economic policy on 10 different issues, ranging from medicine approval to state aid, showed that in every single case a clear majority of people there said that the policy should be determined by the UK Government alone. The British people may have bought some of the liberal elite’s propaganda about Brexit per se, but when it comes to deciding where laws should be made and how those making them should be held to account, they are pretty clear that that should happen in this country, in this sovereign Parliament. Let me now draw my remarks to a close, as I know you will want me to, Madam Deputy Speaker. The truth—and I think we can speak it in this private place, can we not?—is that a large proportion of the British establishment resented the EU referendum result from the very beginning, and did all in their power, funded by greedy plutocrats, to try and stop it. The greedy plutocrats, of course, benefited from the cheap labour that came across from Europe, and thank God that ended. Now they hope—exactly as the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness described—that this is the beginning of a process that will reverse that. In contrast, I say this: the referendum result was an expression of the will of the people. I will end with George Orwell, if I may. He said of that very left-wing intelligentsia at the time of the last war that they took their tastes from Paris and their instructions from Moscow. We might substitute that with “instructions from Brussels and Strasbourg.” I take the polar opposite view. I believe that this nation should be governed by Britons chosen by other Britons to do so. I believe in the national interest and the common good—first, foremost, forever.
Back Benchers are now on a five-minute speaking time limit. I call Matthew Patrick.

This debate is giving me déjà vu. The Tories have brushed off their Brexit playbook and are replaying their best hits, but sadly—I think sadly—they have a very limited number of new things to say. Let us be clear: Brexit has caused real damage to this country. It has hurt livelihoods. It has created a status quo that is not good enough and simply must change. I am grateful to the Prime Minister for opening up the debate on how it can change, but I believe that if we are to have a debate worthy of this topic, we need to show a bit of humility. We need to make some concessions, perhaps even change our minds, because few topics entrench views and divide our country into camps—leave and remain—quite like this one, and I think it is dangerous when an issue generates maximum emotion and minimum reflection. Cards on the table: I campaigned for remain in 2016, but my learning did not stop on 23 June. My instinct was that being in the EU was a good thing, but we would survive outside it. We are a strong country and I believed we could get by. For what it is worth, I still have faith in our country. I still think that we are a great country and that we can weather storms, but the question that debates like this bring me back to is this: do we not have higher ambition for ourselves than to be able to roll with the punches? Do we not see the problems facing our country, many of which are global in nature, as needing a joined-up response? They include climate change; conflicts that spark humanitarian crises and block trade, causing prices to skyrocket, economies to suffer, and the flow of irregular and illegal immigration; the race towards artificial intelligence and all that it brings; a culture change that is being ushered in by atomised and addictive algorithms; and the issues that flow from that culture change, such as a falling birth rate, buoyant populism, and dangerous levels of Islamist and extreme right-wing terrorism. The issues go on, and they run deep. I am left asking myself, why add to our problems by failing to address the wrongs before us? It is not just about trade, but about our power to confront the global problems threatening us. At the same time, let us not kid ourselves that a panacea awaits us at the end of a road marked “rejoin”. That binary thinking—that one side is good and virtuous and the other stupid and ruinous, which is an accusation thrown at one another by both camps—has stopped us listening to the reasonable dissenting voices of those who also want the best for our country. Some Brexit commentators have pointed out that the world has changed since 2016. Well, this is not a moment for those who campaigned for remain simply to say, “We were right all along; let’s repent, let’s rejoin and let the good times roll.” First, the public will have a thing or two to say about that, and secondly, I believe those commentators are right. In 2016 we argued about trade. Today our challenges are greater and the stakes higher. We have full-scale war in Europe, an increasingly brazen and hostile Kremlin, and an unpredictable America. Commentators are right to say that the world has changed and that it is a harsher place than it was 10 years ago, as the right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel) said, but they do not recognise that a harsher world ups the price of standing alone. The motion before us is no better, because it ignores the realities and leans back on arguments that serve the Tory party, rather than the country. We might ask, should we rejoin? For me, it is not that simple. I felt uneasy when those advocating for Brexit argued that the status quo was so bad that we should simply jump to something else. That argument ended with a debate about whether the status quo was good, not what change looked like. Those of us who saw then, and see now, the value of the European Union and our role within it would do well to remember that half-argument. In fact, we should ask ourselves, what does this club offer us and what does it want from us? Any decision about our membership of it should be made, clearly and ruthlessly, in our interest. I believe that if we can get to a reformed and strengthened Europe that is ready to partner with us, and that makes us stronger and better equipped to tackle the great challenges ahead, it is a decision worth taking and an argument worth having. I welcome what the Government are pushing forward—a deal that will cut the cost of a weekly shop—but the motion before us ignores all of this. For me, it shows how far the Tories have fallen. Absent new ideas for the future, they go back to an old foe and roll out their greatest hits. They are fooling no one. They know what damage their Brexit has done to this country, but they are just too afraid of Reform to say it.

I represented the south-west of England and Gibraltar in the European Parliament for 10 years, and I have seen my fair share of rules and regulations written in Brussels and imposed on the United Kingdom. While we were members of the EU, we did at least have a say in how those were drafted, even if, rather too often, we ended up with compromises that we would not have chosen for ourselves. What the Government are now proposing in relation to food standards is worse than what we had during our membership of the EU, because we shall be a rule-taker, with no ability to amend the rules. I want Britain to have the closest possible trading relationship with the European Union, consistent with the result of the referendum. That means trading with the EU but not being subject to EU laws, paying into the EU budget or coming under the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice, and that is precisely where the Prime Minister’s approach is going horribly wrong. A reduction in trade barriers is a good thing. We want our farmers and growers to sell their goods more easily on the European market, and we want to enjoy the good products that Europe has to offer us. That could be achieved by the UK and the EU recognising one another’s standards while remaining sovereign jurisdictions. Mutual recognition is a simple solution, yet regrettably something to which we know the EU would never agree. The EU has always demanded more. Its aim is that Britain accepts its regulatory framework and follows its laws, however unsuitable they may be. Its aim since 2016 has always been to drag us back within its regulatory orbit. This deal also means that, whenever there is a dispute about the contents of those laws, it is the European Court of Justice that will decide the outcome. The British people voted in 2016 to ensure that laws affecting this country would be made in this Parliament by representatives elected by the British people. They voted to restore accountability and democratic control, based in the UK. Subjecting ourselves once again to external laws and courts undermines that principle and moves us away from what was promised. The consequences are particularly concerning when it comes to the innovation and technology we have developed since leaving the EU. Britain is a world leader in gene-editing technology. Gene-edited crops can be made more resistant to disease, they require fewer pesticides, and they can withstand drought and changing climate conditions. They are a vital tool in helping farmers to produce more food while reducing costs and environmental pressures. This is exactly the kind of innovation Britain should champion. It is regrettable that the EU sees the hazard in everything. It always takes a more restrictive approach, focusing on potential hazard, rather than a more intelligent, risk-based approach to technological advance. If regulatory alignment means limiting our freedom to develop and deploy these technologies, we risk sacrificing one of the most significant opportunities created by Brexit. Labour Members should ask themselves: why would we voluntarily constrain our ability to innovate when the benefits to our farmers, consumers and food security could be so substantial? The Food and Drink Federation has said that some 400 regulations would need to be amended to facilitate an SPS agreement. These regulations will, of course, apply to the 92% of businesses that do not export to the EU in any event. CropLife UK says that any SPS deal would cost our farmers £800 million in the first year alone. The Government are happy for British businesses to foot the bill, while having no influence over how those rules are made. Of course, each time the UK joins a part of the single market, the EU will demand a payment from British taxpayers to pay for the privilege. Do we believe that laws affecting British farmers, businesses and consumers should be made here in Westminster or in Brussels? I believe that Britain can be a successful outward looking nation without surrendering control over its laws, its courts and its future.

I am all for improving relations with our international partners. I am all for ensuring we have the very best relationships abroad, be it in trade, security, or cultural and social ties. Those relationships are important with European allies, and they are important with the US and so many other countries all around the world. Indeed, Britain is a global leader in international relations, in soft power and in understanding its key strategic place in the world of international politics. But what the Prime Minister is seeking to do this week is not that; it is far more significant, and it relates to the institution of the European Union. By his own admission, he is seeking to fundamentally reset and open up an ongoing debate about the relationship between the United Kingdom and the EU—a debate that was fundamentally settled when previous Governments delivered the will of the people as expressed in a referendum. It is slightly unclear to me, and I think to those of us on the Conservative Benches, quite what the endgame is and what the Prime Minister’s intentions are. I suspect it is probably unclear to many of those on the Labour Benches. Indeed, the Prime Minister’s intentions are probably fairly unclear to the Prime Minister himself, given the amount of different messages he has sent out in the course of the last few months. But he has been very open to the possibility of rejoining the EU one day. He has ruled out rejoining the single market, the customs union and free movement in this Parliament—only in this Parliament. This Parliament may have less than a year to run if he presses the button on a general election next year. Even if the Parliament is a full five-year term, there are little over two and a half years left. So the Prime Minister is absolutely paving the way for a wider debate on re-entering key institutions of the EU and possible future membership. I suspect he may well be seeking to frame the next general election on in/out EU membership negotiations, and I think that is a fundamentally damaging prospect not only because I think our future is best outside the EU, but because that debate has been settled. Even among remainers, both in this place and in the country at large, I sense a serious reluctance to go back to the divisive politics of Brexit negotiations. Even for those who voted to remain back in 2016, I suspect the majority do not want this place and our politics to be distracted for years to come by the same old arguments that divided parties, divided communities and divided families. My worry is that the Government will become so distracted by this that they will fail to do what they were elected to do: to improve the lives of people up and down the country. I do worry that the Prime Minister is seeking to put up a deliberate smokescreen for his failure, and his predecessor’s failure, to deliver the change the people wanted. Having failed to run a successful narrative that it was all the previous Government’s fault—indeed, the former Prime Minister lost his job because of a failed narrative—the current Prime Minister is struggling for a new narrative that it is all Brexit’s fault that the current Government are failing to tackle all those things that are within their power to tackle: the ballooning welfare bill, the stalling economy, the cost of living, and energy prices. They can tackle those things today, regardless of the relationship with Europe. I suspect that it is their failure to do so that they are trying to mask with this bogus argument about whether we should rejoin the EU or its institutions.

I thank Members on both sides of the House for a very lively debate this afternoon. On Monday at the Lord Mayor’s banquet, the Prime Minister said: “The people voted for change and it has not happened. It has come down to that crucial word: control.” So how exactly does this reset offer control to the British people? Does agreeing to subsidise the tuition fees of students from the EU offer young British people greater opportunities for their education? Does paying Brussels to deal with illegal migration policy without any returns deal offer greater control of our borders? Does linking the EU emissions trading scheme, potentially pushing up UK carbon prices by over 40% in some cases, allow businesses and households greater control over their costs? This does not grant the British people more control over their future. We do know from all the leaks surrounding these negotiations that this is a deal that will hurt British farmers. It is a deal that will hurt British students by subsidising tuition fees for those from the European Union. The first-year cost of the Erasmus membership will be a massive £570 million in 2027-28. Staggeringly, this is a one-year membership and it factors in a 30% discount, at a cost still 50% higher than when we left the European Union. It is also a deal that increases the cost of emissions, which invariably will lead to higher inflation. The inability of Energy Ministers to answer questions about these consequences at yesterday’s Question Time suggests that there is a substantial bill coming. This Government simply do not want to tell us how much it will be.

My hon. Friend will know that in the last year that we were members of the EU, it cost us about £17 billion. That was the price of membership then, so it is inconceivable that, now that we are not a member, the EU would not want to charge us something for the arrangement that the Prime Minister is hoping to make.

My right hon. Friend has pre-empted my next point exactly. Analysis of this draft deal from our party has suggested that the country could face a £23 billion bill over the next decade as a result of this botched negotiation. That is completely unacceptable.

In this detailed analysis that the hon. Gentleman has undertaken, has he attempted to quantify the benefit to British business, which will then do far more trade and pay more tax, which we can then use for the NHS, policing, education and combating crime, or has he somehow left that out of his equation?

I thank my old sparring partner from Hammersmith town hall for his contribution. We used to disagree then and we disagree now. As was alluded to by my hon. Friends, many businesses will face increased costs, particularly farming businesses, which will really struggle with the impact of the deal. Every negotiating stance we have heard represents a loss of control for British people. And in exchange for what? For more money going from the British people to the European Union. Should we be surprised? Well, no—because, as the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic said when asked by a journalist if they would welcome the UK back: “Yes, of course. We need more money.” This is what the EU does: it works in its own interest and it rightly sees this Labour Government as an incredible opportunity. Nobody should be surprised. It is like welcoming Dick Turpin into your carriage; you cannot be shocked when he asks you to hand over of all your money. We have heard some really excellent contributions from the Opposition Benches this afternoon. My right hon. Friend the Member for Witham (Priti Patel) started off proceedings and got into an interesting discussion about shellfish. As the Member of Parliament for the lobster capital of Europe, I am delighted that we still land 300 tonnes of lobster every year, most of which is exported to the European Union. My hon. Friend the Member for Dumfries and Galloway (John Cooper) and my right hon. Friend the Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) highlighted the trade deals that have been done since we left the European Union. The comprehensive and progressive agreement for trans-Pacific partnership is a fantastic opportunity for this country, opening markets in countries from Mexico to Malaysia. The trade deal with India is another wonderful opportunity for the United Kingdom, and deals that we are currently negotiating, such as the Gulf Co-operation Council deal—about which middle eastern countries are incredibly excited—could be ripped up before they are even signed as a result of this negotiation. My hon. Friend the Member for Harwich and North Essex (Sir Bernard Jenkin) highlighted Britain’s world-leading AI industry and how it could be impacted by European regulation as part of this negotiation.

I raised this issue not because it is part of the Government negotiating position: I was pushing them to go further. Let me ask the hon. Gentleman how he would deliver digital sovereignty. This is really important. The EU has chokepoints with ASML in the Netherlands. The EU has purchasing power in relation to AI. This Government are working really hard to deliver more of that, but we do not have it at the moment. How would the hon. Gentleman deliver that sovereignty over AI? He does not have any answer.

I certainly would not be adopting the EU’s position, because industry here is far more advanced in our development of AI. We should be proud of that and should do nothing to put it under threat. My hon. Friend the Member for South Northamptonshire (Sarah Bool) highlighted farming, dynamic alignment and the real threat that we face; ninety per cent of farming businesses in this country do not export to the EU, and a future Conservative Government will not be bound by a bad deal. She also highlighted the fact that Ministers have failed repeatedly to give evidence to the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee—

The hon. Gentleman raises the point made by the hon. Member for South Northamptonshire (Sarah Bool) about Ministers not attending the Select Committee in the Lords, but perhaps he could tell her about the letter sent by Sir William Cash in May 2023, which was critical of the actions of one former Trade Minister, which he described as “unacceptable”, adding that they “suggested a deeply concerning approach to scrutiny” from the then Government. Could he perhaps let the hon. Lady know that that Trade Minister is now the leader of the Conservative party?

The former Member for Stone has expressed many strong views over the years, and I always respect what he has to say. The point is that we are engaged in an important negotiation that will impact British farming; the Committee offered a private hearing to the Minister responsible for the negotiations, and that was repeatedly turned down. That is not the way to do scrutiny in this place. My right hon. Friend the Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) took us on something of a journey through recent European political history. I hope that the kind invitation that he gave to Madam Deputy Speaker to join him in Lincolnshire will be extended to other colleagues who want to talk at length about, perhaps, the treaty of Rome, or other such matters relating to the European Union. My hon. Friend the Member for Bridgwater (Sir Ashley Fox) gave us a fantastic insight as a former Member of the European Parliament. It is important that we hear from those on the Conservative Benches with that sort of experience when we discuss these matters. My hon. Friend the Member for Isle of Wight East (Joe Robertson) talked about Britain’s place in the world, and how important it is for our sovereignty that we can project soft and hard power when necessary.

What does the hon. Member make of the Thames Valley chamber of commerce’s statement that the paperwork caused by the Brexit deal is holding back our local exporters? Does he agree that the Conservative party cannot claim to be the party of business when it refuses to listen to businesses on the subject of the EU?

Unfortunately, a lot of problems relating to exports are due to EU intransigence. I worked closely on this matter before I was elected to this place, and I can assure the hon. Lady that when there are Dutch authorities insisting on the use of red biros and French authorities using blue biros, it is farcical. All of this could have been resolved, without any sort of reset, with a simple negotiation on easing trade frictions and digitising systems, so that our brilliant British produce is not held up at the border. I will give another example. The vet who works at the port of Rotterdam finishes at lunch-time on a Friday, so when the port authority decides to check a lorry load that comes in after that time, it is left until Monday morning. That seems absolutely farcical, and it is the fault of not this Government, but the European Union for the rules that it insisted on putting in place.

Does my hon. Friend agree that the EU is in breach of its obligations under the World Trade Organisation agreement to facilitate trade? The EU has those obligations, but it does not seem like they apply to it.

My hon. Friend speaks with great knowledge on these matters. The WTO plays a very important role in facilitating trade right across the world, and the EU regularly finds itself in conflict with it, which says something about the way that the EU operates.

I thank my hon. Friend for raising the point about how the EU behaves. I have such a strong sense of déjà vu. During the original negotiation period, every time that the EU was obstinate, stubborn and difficult, Labour Members sought to blame the Conservatives for that, instead of getting behind this country and standing up to that sort of behaviour.

My hon. Friend is quite right. The spirit in which those negotiations were entered into was, I fear, unnecessarily adversarial, and unfortunately that has meant that issues that it should have been easy to resolve have not been resolved in recent years. Since the Labour Government were elected, there has been a sinking feeling across this country that Labour is a party with no solutions to the big problems facing our society. For instance, in response to the recent Budget, the OBR said that it expects no growth in real earnings in 2027 or 2028, alongside a slight fall in real household disposable income in the near term. Meanwhile, Labour’s plans to bring down welfare spending are set to take over 10 years. Labour could probably produce another five 10-year plans in that time, and we would still be nowhere near funding the defence requirements of this country. Why does that matter? Because this reset does not address the problems that require structural change in the United Kingdom. It is at best a diversion; more likely, it will result in giving away the powers that are needed to deliver changes, and that the UK requires. It does not provide the money that we need to fund defence, or reduce the costs that this Government have imposed on businesses. This is not the difficult debate that the Prime Minister claims it is. It is a distraction started by a former Prime Minister with no new ideas and continued by a Prime Minister with no new solutions. The Prime Minister has reached for the “Now That’s What I Call Brexit” playbook, preferring to play the old hits than to provide the solutions that we need to make the UK a dynamic country, capable of meeting the challenges of this fast-moving and dangerous age. The reset is the embodiment of that mindset; we are giving away control over student finance, migration, border security, and product and food standards, all for the privilege of paying the EU more money. To those who say that the Conservatives are merely prolonging this debate, I say this: if the Government supported this motion, they could bring this debate to a close and make it clear that any future negotiations will be conducted on a generally neutral basis, in the interests of both the EU and the UK. In rejecting the motion, it will be clear that the Government would rather look to the past than the future. The reset is an acknowledgment that we are not going to forge a new relationship based on British confidence and success, but will instead enter a new era in which the EU calls the shots, and we simply ask, “How much?”.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs

I am grateful to the Opposition, to the hon. Member for Kingswinford and South Staffordshire (Mike Wood) for moving the motion, and to all right hon. and hon. Members from across the House who have contributed their views. I am also grateful for the opportunity to respond on behalf of the Government. This has been a long debate, in which we have heard views from across the House. The hon. Member for Kingswinford and South Staffordshire took us on a journey, mentioning a plethora of British sausages, and reminding us that my right hon. Friend the Minister could double up as Bond. The Opposition have rehashed many of the arguments of 2016, reminding me of a saying: they were the future once. It struck me how many Members have, in their own words, reiterated what the Prime Minister said earlier this week: “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.” The British people voted for change and control, and they simply did not get what was sold to them by the Tories. Our economy has suffered, our businesses still face red tape, and our young people have had, and are having, their futures stifled. This Government are convinced that only a strong UK-EU relationship will deliver the opportunity, growth, security and change that the British public have asked for. Nobody voted for a change that hurts British trade and undermines our national security. What we are doing this week—this is what the Prime Minister aims to do when he travels to Brussels on Friday for the second UK-EU summit—is delivering on the key ambitions set out last year by striking important deals that will strengthen our economy for the British people. We are striking important deals on food and drink; emissions trading; linking our energy systems; opportunities for young people and youth experience; and, crucially, furthering our co-operation on defence, security and migration. The SPS and emissions trading agreements will add up to £9 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040. These deals will boost the UK’s economy, cut costs, cut red tape and provide opportunities to young people—the next generation—who have been denied these vital opportunities since Brexit, when the Opposition failed to negotiate them. The UK and EU will also discuss a shared approach to protecting our economic security to ensure that we do not unintentionally harm each other, and instead tackle shared economic challenges together. Policies that disadvantage UK and EU businesses will not make our economy stronger and our countries more secure. The safety and security of the British people is at the heart of everything that the Government do. As my right hon. Friend the Minister said, when the referendum took place a decade ago, Russia had not launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine; we had not witnessed hostile attacks on European soil; and global trade and energy supplies were not being used as geopolitical weapons.

The Minister mentions Ukraine, which we have talked about today. Not having the arrangements with the EU that the Prime Minister is seeking in absolutely no way dampened our ability to work with Europe on Ukraine. We have been able to work together, and stand up strongly for Ukraine, under existing arrangements. What is so bad about them?

The hon. Gentleman makes my point. True European security and competitiveness are best achieved when like-minded and trusted partners work together to bolster everything that we are talking about, from supply chains to defence, competitiveness and economic security. My right hon. Friend the Minister is continuing to work around the clock with his EU counterparts, so that we can conclude important agreements at the summit. Members in the Chamber will have heard my right hon. Friend set out robustly the Prime Minister’s and Britain’s ambition for this upcoming summit and negotiations. This Government respect the conventions of this House, but I will remind Members that this Labour Government were elected on a Labour manifesto to deliver for the British people. We were elected with a clear mandate to make Brexit work, deepen ties with Europe and tear down barriers to trade, and that is exactly what we are doing. The UK Government will bring forward primary legislation next week to implement the agreements. They will be ratified by Parliament, and Parliament will scrutinise the legislation in full, in the usual way.
I have a very simple request. We have heard this figure of £9 billion bandied around endlessly. Could the Minister tell us how that breaks down?

The right hon. Gentleman will know that I am a Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office Minister, and that those are breakdowns that the Treasury can provide. I can certainly get him a written answer on that. Members will understand that I cannot provide a running commentary on these negotiations, and the House would not expect me to, but once the summit has concluded, the Government will, at the earliest opportunity, update the House on what has been delivered and the impact that the measures will have. As the Prime Minister has set out, any deal must pass three tests. First, it has to be consistent with our manifesto and our red lines. Secondly, it has to improve the Brexit deal to bring it closer to what people thought they were getting in 2016. Thirdly, it has to pass the Makerfield test—produce real improvements in the everyday lives of people who live in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long. As the Prime Minister said on Monday in his Mansion House speech, along with the Makerfield test, there is a London test to ensure that this deal supports an even more successful capital city. That means reducing red tape and the cost of doing business, and helping with the cost of living and the price of the weekly shop, as seen in my right hon. Friend the Minister’s video. Rumour has it that he was looking for the cornflake cookies in M&S, but actually he was there on behalf of us all, to make this case. If the deal delivers all this, as the Government believe it can, it will easily pass the Makerfield test and the London test, and we will agree it.

I will make some progress. The agreements that will be announced at the summit should not be the ceiling of our ambition. It is very clear that the status quo is not working. Our Prime Minister has been bold. He has said the quiet part out loud—that Brexit has done more harm than good. As a country we are ambitious to go further. We must restore higher growth and greater prosperity. Our ambition extends beyond Friday’s UK-EU summit. We will begin by evaluating all options for the future and opening a national discussion on these options. This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them. That will inform decisions in the next Parliament. At every stage, the British people will be in charge. A number of issues were raised by opposition Members. Time is short, but I will try to run through them in turn. The hon. Member for Surrey Heath (Dr Pinkerton)—the good doctor—took us through a list of Surrey bangers. It turns out he was talking about his predecessor. He also referred to rejoining the single market and the customs union. I gently remind him that this Labour Government were elected on a manifesto commitment not to join the single market customs union. At Friday’s summit, the Government will pursue those gains that we believe are in the UK’s national interest, while respecting the red lines laid out in our manifesto. The Prime Minister is clear that Brexit has damaged our economy, that we are facing a more dangerous world, and that we need a closer relationship with Europe. The right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel) asked a number of questions in her 20-minute speech. I do not have time to run through all of them, but let me say this on trade with other countries: the UK continues to respect our international obligations and will continue to pursue our trade deals globally. This evening, I am hosting a UK-India reception in Lancaster House to celebrate those trade deals, and I have offered her an invitation. The SPS agreement is fully consistent with our international obligations. On recent free trade agreements, our membership of the CPTPP will not need to be renegotiated. We will bring forward the European partnership Bill to implement the deals agreed with the EU, starting with the SPS and the emissions trading agreement. I remind everybody that Parliament remains sovereign, and this Bill will not change that. Both Houses will have the ability to scrutinise it in full. I made diligent notes on the colleagues who took part in the debate. I wish that I could go through them, but, alas, I am running out of time, so let me conclude. At Friday’s summit, the Government will cement the progress made so far and inject renewed pace and ambition into our future relationship with the EU. At the heart of that is the young people who did not get a say but whose futures are being determined by what is happening now—I think of my own young constituents in Stratford and Bow. The important deals that we strike will pay off for businesses and families and support growth. They will cut back on paperwork and ease pressure on prices. Our position is clear: it is through our partnership with the EU that we will deliver real results for the British people. Question put (Standing Order No. 31(2)), That the original words stand part of the Question.

title: Violence against Women and Girls: Prosecution Rates
turns: What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to help improve prosecution rates for crimes of violence against women and girls.
What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to help improve prosecution rates for crimes of violence against women and girls.

This Government are committed to halving violence against women and girls. Since becoming a Law Officer, I have delivered the early victims’ right to review, giving rape victims a second chance of justice, as well as dedicated victim liaison officers for domestic abuse victims, supporting them from charge to trial, and pre-trial meetings with the prosecution for rape victims, which is now being piloted for domestic abuse victims. This Government are getting on with the job.

I thank the Minister for her answer. While improving prosecution rates and bringing perpetrators to justice as soon as possible must remain a priority, what more can this Government do to support community-led initiatives, such as the Orange Wolves campaign for tackling violence against women and girls in my constituency that I will be taking part in shortly, to ensure that prevention, early intervention and challenging misogynistic and harmful attitudes are given equal priority so that we can stop these crimes happening in the first place?

I thank my hon. Friend for his work through the Orange Wolves campaign. This Government are investing £15 million in the misogyny prevention taskforce to challenge misogynistic attitudes across society, including in schools. I will continue to work with colleagues across Government to ensure that prevention goes hand in hand with a robust criminal justice response. I welcome the vital role that communities like his are playing.

As we approach this year’s 16 days of activism against gender-based violence, what discussions is the Attorney General having with the Crown Prosecution Service to ensure that victims of tech-related violence against women and girls get justice?

The Government are proud to be supporting the 16 days of activism against gender-based violence. We have banned nudification apps and criminalised non-consensual intimate images. The CPS will shortly publish its tech-facilitated VAWG strategy to make sure that it is fully equipped to prosecute these evolving crimes.

Crimes of violence and sexual harassment against women and girls also happen in the workplace, but as it stands the law does not consider this to be a workplace hazard, with legislation such as the Worker Protection (Amendment of Equality Act 2010) Act 2023 yet to drive real cultural change in work practices. Does the Attorney General agree that this should be a health and safety issue for workers and that the law should treat it as such?

I thank the right hon. Lady for that question. It is an issue close to my heart, because I was an employment rights lawyer for over a decade before entering this place, particularly representing women facing discrimination in the workplace. The Employment Rights Act 2025 adds new protections, and we have outlawed non-disclosure agreements in the workplace, but we will always look to see where we can go further to protect women and girls.

Abuse rarely ends with the separation of a couple, with non-molestation orders ignored all the time. One of my constituents secured a restraining order against her ex-partner, but it took her 12-and-a-half years to fully extract herself. One of the biggest issues she faced was being economically attached to him and unable to leave their mortgage. Surviving Economic Abuse, which I have been working with on this, has made it clear that without a legal definition, prosecution of these behaviours is only achievable as a sub-category of coercive behaviour, so judges lack precedent and know-how to deal with it. Will the Attorney General take steps with Cabinet colleagues to produce a legal definition and training on how to prosecute this type of crime?

The hon. Lady makes a really important point about economic abuse being used as a form of violence against women and girls. I will be happy to speak to my colleagues in the Ministry of Justice about what more we might be able to do. We have introduced domestic abuse protection orders and stalking protection orders to make sure that we have the right tools to go after perpetrators, but I will discuss the points she raises with colleagues.
Last week, the Justice Secretary wrote to the Bar Standards Board to demand changes to defence advocacy in rape trials. Was the Attorney General consulted before he did so?

I agree with the Lord Chancellor that rape myths have no place in our courts or our society, and advocacy must not perpetrate myths that have been repeatedly shown to distort understanding of sexual violence. Judges can already give directions to counter rape myths. We are going further in the Courts and Tribunals Bill to stop irrelevant sexual history and previous allegations from being weaponised against victims.

I am not sure whether that was a yes, a no or a maybe. If the Justice Secretary did so as a result of advice from the Attorney General, the Lady Chief Justice has something to say to both of them as she felt compelled to respond publicly to this intervention from the Justice Secretary and others. Last weekend, she told the Bar Council’s annual conference that the debate on the conduct of rape trials is “not fully informed” and risks undermining public confidence in the justice system —ouch. Does the Attorney General agree with the Lady Chief Justice? If not, where is she in error?

The hon. Gentleman will be well aware of the Law Officers’ convention in relation to disclosing what advice may or may not have been given. But I will say this: the Government are determined to tackle violence against women and girls. When it comes to rape, we have announced specialist rape courtrooms in every court in the country, making sure that victims who bravely come forward get the support they need from the criminal justice system.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

With your permission, Mr Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to John Pardoe, my predecessor as North Cornwall’s MP between 1966 and 1979. John, who was a Liberal hero and a true servant to the Cornish people, sadly passed away on Sunday. I hope the whole House will join me in offering our sincere condolences to his wife Joy and his whole family. [Hon. Members: “Hear, hear.”] One of the many victims of Russell Brand’s evil and calculated sexual abuse, a woman named Szilvia Berki, was barred by the High Court from speaking to family, friends and even the police about her assault. On top of that, she was ordered to pay £50,000 in legal costs to Brand and his then girlfriend for the injunction, seemingly with the intention of bankrupting her. Will the Attorney General consider the merits of a comprehensive law on strategic lawsuits against public participation that includes sexual abuse, and commission a review into the weaponisation of such injunctions by the rich and powerful that includes enhanced powers for the Solicitors Regulation Authority to regulate the lawyers and law firms who bring them?

I join the hon. Gentleman in paying tribute to his predecessor, John Pardoe. Turning to the question, I commend the bravery and courage of all victims who have come forward. Powerful men should not be able to use the law to silence their victims. Non-disclosure agreements should not be used to obstruct justice. The Government also recognise the profound financial and psychological impact that SLAPPs have on individuals. With the Victims and Courts Act 2026, we will ensure that victims in crime can tell anyone what happened, despite signing an NDA, and we remain committed to introducing further legislation in relation to SLAPPs.

title: Budget Resolutions
turns: The Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade

It is a pleasure to open the final day of the Budget debate. As we begin, let us pause and remember what is really essential to the debate today. Where are we as a country and what do we really need to talk about in this debate? I would put it like this. In the last year, gas prices have tripled, oil prices are up by over 60% and our borrowing costs—alongside those of all the major economies—have risen; and yet, business investment is rising, our economic growth has accelerated and the IMF has singled out the UK for praise for our deficit reduction plan. That is testament to the extraordinary resilience of the British people, British businesses and the British economy. We know from reading the official documentation that there is no doubt but that ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have driven up costs here and around the world. However, despite these significant economic headwinds, when the Chancellor came here last week, he delivered a substantial cost of living package to help the British people and long-term reforms to strengthen growth, and he commanded market confidence while he did so in a way that eluded the previous Conservative Government. There is not a shred of complacency on this side of the House, but the package he announced built on the success we have already achieved, with year-on-year growth—again, above 2%; an economy growing per head—not just through higher immigration, but because living standards are increasing; and wages rising faster than prices. It is clear, as we stand here today, that we can say the economy is stronger today than when this Government came to power. But we know things are still tough. That is why the Budget unveiled much-needed breathing space for families, businesses and working people. Beyond that breathing space, we are beginning and proceeding with the big changes needed to put our country on a better course: reindustrialising Britain, driving good growth in every postcode, and strengthening our national security. The Budget shows entrepreneurs, inventors and investors that the UK is the best place to start and grow a business, with this Government using our industrial strategy and wider policy platform to back them every step of the way. We cannot insulate people from every pressure or meet every ask in one go, but we can provide the targeted support that is necessary where it can make the biggest practical difference. That is why, to help our high streets and small and medium-sized enterprises, the Budget contains a £1 billion business rates package. In England, shops, restaurants and cafés of all sizes will get a two-year real-terms freeze. Around 70,000 more small retail, hospitality and leisure properties will be taken out of business rates altogether. To ensure that our high streets are vibrant into the future, the Budget also commits us to upgrading 600 post office branches in this financial year. That will help them to provide more accessible, welcoming spaces, simpler transactions and a speedier service for customers. That also includes the essential banking services upon which so many of our high street businesses and SMEs depend. The House will know that all these reforms form part of a much broader package being implemented by the Government to support the 5.7 million SMEs in this country that are the beating heart of our economy and the backbone of our communities. With our small business plan, we are bringing down costs and using the levers of Government to back British business. In particular, we are cracking down on the scourge of late payments that shuts down the equivalent of 38 firms a day and costs the economy almost £11 billion a year. Our Commercial Payments Bill will give us the strongest laws to tackle late payments in the whole of the G7, with the Bill’s Second Reading set to take place this month; I hope it will command cross-party support. We are also reducing the regulatory burden on our small and medium-sized businesses. Indeed, when the Prime Minister, Lord Leong and I met business owners at No. 10 North last month, we proudly accepted 14 recommendations from the small business taskforce, which has been working in partnership with the Government to reduce the bureaucracy holding British firms back. We are now making it simpler for smaller firms to bid for public contracts. We are streamlining Office for National Statistics business surveys to reduce form-filling. At the same time, we are making it easier for businesses to find support on gov.uk and helping them to report disproportionate regulations. We are delivering, too, on our “tell us once” ambition, as part of which we are pausing the Companies House profit and loss filing requirement for April 2028. I thank the Federation of Small Businesses for all its work on this agenda and in particular for its support on that decision. Where there is an opportunity to save businesses time and money, we will seek to do that. As proof positive of that agenda, the Budget included savings of over £600 million per year on regulatory administration, with streamlined company reporting requirements and reduced reporting burdens for asset managers. A simpler home buying and selling process will also save businesses over £100 million a year.

I have to ask, was the right hon. Member listening to a different Budget from the one that I heard? I do not recognise anything he has said there. On burdens and costs imposed by regulations on business, the OBR said that the employment Bill—the unemployment Bill—will actually add to the cost of business, completely contrary to what he has just said.

I do not want to say that the hon. Gentleman should listen a bit harder to the Chancellor when is giving a Budget, but he went into detail on that. I will expand on what the better regulation taskforce will mean. Specifically on the employment rights agenda, we know that the Conservatives do not like it—that is not a secret—but I would simply say to the hon. Member that we have a manifesto commitment to address in particular insecurity in the workplace, including the 1 million people on zero-hours contracts. Let Conservative colleagues not forget that the premise of that particular measure is that where a person works a regular number of hours, they will receive, if they wish to, a contract for those hours—not additional costs. Additional costs are not present when someone get a contract that reflects what they are already working. The rest of the agenda may not be popular with the Conservative party, but it is certainly popular with the country. And because of that agenda—[Interruption.] I know the Conservatives did not stick to their own manifesto commitments, but we will stick to ours. Because of that agenda, of course want to reduce burdens in other places; it is an entirely noble agenda and one that reflects the interests of British business. The hon. Member may be aware—the Chancellor did speak about this in the statement—that there is an aspiration to reduce business burdens by 25% over the course of this Parliament.
