He faces the same problem as many of my constituents: they simply cannot get the transport to employment, so may I beg the Secretary of State to include the Secretary of State for Transport in the work that he does, so that young people in my constituency can get themselves to the jobs that he hopes to create for them?

I thank the hon. Member for raising her own experience and I warmly agree with her that work will offer more than a wage. It will offer pride, purpose and dignity, and when we discuss these issues, we should think about what our ambition is for young people. I really thank her for the approach that she has taken today and the way that she has set out her question, and I assure her that I will work with the Secretary of State for Transport on the issue that she has raised. I can tell the House that, in the many conversations I have had with MPs about these issues over the past year, transport has come up a lot. We have to make sure that young people can get to a job.

I thank my right hon. Friend for this statement that gives hope to young people right across the country. Despite what we have heard, 20 years of the Scottish National party has not fixed youth unemployment in Scotland. A mum came to my surgery recently at the end of her tether because her 23-year-old son with autism had lost his local authority internship and had no hope of meaningful work after some years. Does my right hon. Friend agree that Scotland’s local authorities need to play their part to ensure that young people, regardless of where they live, get a good job?

My hon. Friend raises an important question. The last thing we should do is make an equation between a diagnosis of a condition such as that and a life outside work because, with the right support and help, many people with those conditions can work. Not everyone can, but many can. That is what we should be ambitious enough to do, and I hope that throughout the public sector, every local authority in the land and every Government Department will want to play its part.

The Secretary of State has spoken about fully funding apprenticeships for under-25-year-olds, but it is worth pointing out that this fully funded apprenticeship does not include the salary that the employers will have to pay to those young people. Businesses right across my constituency, particularly in the construction sector, are just not able to afford those salaries, given the increases in employment costs under the current Government. I would be interested to hear what he would say to those businessmen and women who want to do the right thing and employ an apprentice but, under Labour’s high job tax and costs of employment, simply cannot afford to do so.

We have had a few exchanges about pay. There are specific pay rates for apprenticeships, and we believe that people should be paid for the work that they do. When it comes to the minimum wage, the Low Pay Commission takes these factors into account when it sets the rate.

I thank the Government for the statement and the many opportunities it will create for young people from all backgrounds to get into training and employment. My right hon. Friend rightly talks about the inequalities that many young people face in getting into training and employment. May I turn his mind to care leavers, four in 10 of whom between the ages of 19 and 21 are not in training and employment? What targeted support will be available to them through the work that has come out of the Milburn review?

My hon. Friend raises the important point that care leavers often find themselves in a difficult position. Alan Milburn’s report specifically addresses this and calls for extra help for care leavers, who, by definition, are not living in the family home. They need extra help, and that is part of the proposals he has published today.

I welcome Alan Milburn’s call to double the number of young people completing apprenticeships. In Walton, Rianna Farbey of Omni Academy has trained hair and beauty apprentices since 2010, but she tells me that apprenticeship starts have fallen because young people cannot find a salon to take them on—for instance, Rock N Rolla hairdresser in Walton says that it has zero margin to do so. The cost of hiring a young person has risen by about £4,000 under this Government. What conversations are being had across Government about easing the strain faced by small businesses and supporting them in creating the entry-level jobs and apprenticeships that our young people are crying out for?

Hairdressing salons are facing particular difficulties. I have had representations from businesses in my constituency that are facing competition from people with rented chairs, businesses operating from back gardens and so on, so I understand the difficulty facing the sector. We are trying to tilt apprenticeship funding more towards young people, including through a hiring incentive of £2,000 for a small business that takes on a young apprentice; if the young person has been unemployed for six months or more, the hiring incentive goes up to £5,000.

I thank the Secretary of State for making a statement on a report that has really listened to young people and directly referenced their experiences over the past decade. He has rightly made the moral case to support young people into work, because of all the benefits that being in work can bring. However, one thing young people raise with me is that gaps in their CVs or a lack of work experience, sometimes because of covid or being unable to find employment, mean that they struggle when applying for jobs. What more can the Government do to work with employers to ensure that young people are not overlooked?

My hon. Friend raises the important role of work experience. We are providing an extra 300,000 work experience placements through the youth guarantee. I am a passionate believer that those can be a critical bridge between unemployment and employment. Once somebody has a few weeks of the routine, the experience and all the rest, they are much more employable candidates. Of course, the work experience has to be of the right quality, but it can play a really important role.

With almost 1 million young people not in education or employment, getting them into work is, of course, a very laudable ambition, but the Government have another ambition, and I want the Minister to explain the cross-over. The Government want an EU mobility scheme, which would bring tens of thousands of EU young people into the United Kingdom—the EU has said that it would like 150,000 visas in that regard. Will those people not be competing for the very entry jobs that we are hoping to provide to our own 1 million unemployed?

The problem with that theory is that countries around Europe that are already members of the EU, with everything that that entails, have far lower rates of youth inactivity than we have. Our rate is the second highest in Europe after Romania, so it cannot just be down to a youth mobility scheme, which involves a far lower level of mobility than EU members have. For example, the Netherlands has a NEET rate that is one third of ours.

I thank my right hon. Friend for the report. Young people in Paisley and Renfrewshire South want to work, but many are stuck on NHS waiting lists or are unable to get the apprenticeships or technical skills that they need to get a job. I wish I shared my right hon. Friend’s optimism that the Scottish Government would invest in these things because it is the morally right thing to do, but in case they need any further persuasion, will he outline how many people he expects to be lifted out of relative poverty as a result of these proposals being implemented in full?

Alan Milburn says that if we get enough people into employment, relative poverty can fall under these proposals. With regard to the Scottish Government, I remind my hon. Friend, and them, that they have received the biggest financial settlement since the inception of devolution, so I would hope to see youth opportunity make some call on it.

As an ex-secondary school teacher, I always take a strong interest in young people, their future and their wellbeing. Too many young people in Bath do not go to school because it does not work for them, and neurodiverse children struggle especially. What steps is the Secretary of State taking to work with the Department for Education so that the national curriculum reflects the focus on good jobs and a good future for all young people?

There is a big chapter on education in the Milburn report, which I encourage the hon. Lady to read. Persistent school absence can have a damaging effect on a young person’s prospects; it is very difficult for them to learn if they are not there. The Government are therefore treating this issue with urgency. Ministers see a million graphs, but one of the most striking to me showed the huge jump in long-term absence from school post covid. We are now dealing in part with the consequences of that.

I thank my right hon. Friend, Alan Milburn and his team for restoring hope for young people across North Warwickshire and Bedworth. Last week, I visited Flannery Plant Hire in my constituency. It delivers skills boot camps across the country, giving young people access to real jobs in heavy goods vehicle driving, plant operations and construction. How will the Government ensure that skills funding reaches such businesses, so that all young people can access support, regardless of their postcode? Young people in this country want a chance to work.

I heartily agree with my hon. Friend that young people want a chance to work, and training in a skill such as HGV driving can be a really good option for young people. We will work with employers in all sectors to try to create opportunities for young people. As I say, we have recently had good results with agreements with some major hiring sectors. The transport sector could be another.

In my constituency, one in six young people find themselves not in education, employment or training. I have been working with Birmingham City University and Birmingham Metropolitan college, which have identified future jobs and are looking at the skills gap so as to train young people who are out of work. Will the Minister support higher education institutions with the resources they need, and will he join me for a visit to see the great work they are achieving?

As a Wolverhampton MP, I regularly find myself in Birmingham. I am sure that the higher education institutions are doing the best job they can. The hon. Gentleman’s question illustrates another point: a number of constituencies have had persistently high unemployment for many years. I hope that he welcomes today’s figures showing that unemployment has fallen and employment has risen. We need to do more to go in the right direction.
I make another plea to Back Benchers: please keep your questions short.

Many young people live in households without access to a private car, let alone their own car, and many live in areas without a decent, or even any, bus service, thanks to the coalition Government’s cuts to local government, which decimated local bus services. Our Transport Committee inquiry “Buses connecting communities” recommended specific action to support under-25s, and our next inquiry, “Getting to work”, will build on that theme by covering all transport. What work is the Secretary of State doing with not only the Transport Secretary but the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government and the Chancellor, all of whom are vital in this area?
I will take your cue, Madam Deputy Speaker. Transport is really important, and the Government have announced a cap on bus fares to try to make it easier for people to get to work.

Every year, the Treasury collects hundreds of millions of pounds more from the apprenticeship levy than gets spent on training. That money is collected for training, and one of Milburn’s recommendations is for all that money to be spent on training—something that the Lib Dems have long been calling for. Will the Minister commit to doing that with the apprenticeship levy?
I have certainly noted that recommendation in the Milburn review. The hon. Gentleman can be assured that I will always fight for as much funding for apprenticeships as possible.

I know personally the despair that comes from being young, unemployed and desperate to work. The north-east has the highest rate in England not only of NEETs but of disability. Unemployment figures released today show that in South Shields the youth claimant count continues to rise because demand outstrips vacancies. Does my right hon. Friend understand how anxious young disabled people are right now, because although the tone has changed, and that is welcome, we do not have all the details? Can he please confirm that the Government’s plans will not leave these young people financially worse off?

I will say two things. First, I point again to the question: where will the jobs come from? We have to co-operate with employers on this, and that is why I have been pleased to announce agreements with retail, hospitality and tourism to hire 250,000 young people over the coming years. Secondly, we are offering a new settlement here, and it will not always be about money. Ambition can be about support and help and helping young people to change their future. That is part of the new settlement that I am arguing for today.

Alan Milburn is clear about the growing chasm in investment for younger and older generations, yet we know from the Budget that school funding is due to fall in the coming years, and yesterday the Education Secretary refused to commit to protecting schools from those cuts. If the right hon. Member accepts Milburn’s recommendation to hold schools accountable for work readiness, added to delivering far more enrichment activities, far-reaching SEND reforms and underfunded teacher pay rises and no extra cash, what is going to give?

I thank the hon. Lady for her question, and for calling for more funding at the same time that she has called for tax cuts. I am afraid that this is a pattern of her party: it supports every spending demand around, but never any of the revenue raisers that mean we can meet at least some of the spending demands. We have to net everything off and do the best job we can, and that is what we will do for young people.

Bristol is a city where there are areas of entrenched deprivation but also massive opportunities, such as in the Bristol Temple Quarter in my constituency and in the Brabazon new town in the constituency of my hon. Friend the Member for Filton and Bradley Stoke (Claire Hazelgrove). What is the balance to be struck between those companies that can be incentivised to take part in this programme and those companies that need to be required to take part if they do not show willingness to step up and provide opportunities for young people?

I do want to work with businesses. I am grateful to the businesses that have taken this seriously and made offers so far, and we will keep discussing it with other sectors. But there is also more that the public sector could do—major Departments, local authorities and so on, as has been mentioned—if this is to be a cause that employers in both the public and the private sectors can help move the dial on.

Will the Secretary of State join me in debunking this myth? In this place, we have demonised and politicised young people. We need to debunk the myth, as was done in the Fonagy review, that there is a widespread overdiagnosis of ADHD, autism, anxiety and depression. That record needs to be corrected. I welcome the announcement to get young people into work and education. Will he confirm that the investment the Government will be making with employers will not be funding vacancies that they already would have employed people for and will not go to their profit bottom lines?

I do not know whether the hon. Member was in the Chamber for my opening statement, but I very explicitly rejected the demonisation of young people and the negative narrative out there about them—that is a narrative I completely reject. Fonagy, in his review, does talk about the diagnosis debate but, as I have said a couple of times, he also said that work can play a critical role in someone’s recovery—not just after they have recovered, but in the recovery, so he is in line with the recommendations of the Milburn report. The equation that I want to break is between a diagnosis and a conclusion that that person then has to spend their life on benefits. Frankly, I have a much higher ambition for young people than that.

Last week I met AJ Taylor, a local business in Brighton with a long record of providing apprenticeships and opportunities to young people. It told me that one of the biggest barriers it faces to doing more to help young people is the absence of any dedicated skills and vocational training centre, and not just in Brighton but across Sussex. The Milburn report recommends an Open University for skills with regional hubs across the country. Does the Secretary of State agree that it would be a big step forward, and does he think a good place to start would be in Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven?

The report is full of very interesting recommendations. It is over 200 pages long, so we will consider it more fully in the coming weeks. I set out in my statement the main things that I wanted to respond to today, but I have heard the representation my hon. Friend makes for Brighton.

Building on the question of my hon. Friend the Member for Bath (Wera Hobhouse) on school attendance, I have been campaigning to end the current ineffective, punitive approach to tackling school absences. Will the Government commit to replacing it with a supportive approach with alternatives to traditional classroom attendance, to maintain engagement in education when presence in school is not possible?

I am sure the Secretary of State will consider what the hon. Lady has said, but let us be clear that attendance is critical for children. We should all be concerned about the post-covid spike in non-attendance at school. It will have damaging consequences for children, and we should take it seriously.

The Prime Minister rightly recognises that the youth unemployment crisis is not young people’s fault, but the result of decisions made here. I welcome many of Milburn’s recommendations, but if they are funded by cutting disability benefits, the Government will push young people into poverty, undermine their own aims and repeat the very mistakes that they identify as having caused the crisis in the first place. Surely it is not the Government’s view that disabled and sick people between the ages of 16 and 24 are less in need of PIP and the universal credit health element than anyone else.

Let me make clear something that is in the Milburn report. He says that those with severe and lasting disabilities, for whom work is not a realistic possibility, should actually receive more support than they do right now. That is line one of the contract that the welfare state should make with people, and it is something that this Labour Government will always stand by.

Yesterday I met Citizens Advice Thame, which warned me of rising homelessness in Thame, including among young people. What consideration has the Secretary of State given to the removal of UC and PIP in high-cost areas where rents are high and the housing allowance does not cover the full cost of housing?

There are of course issues with rents, but these are disability benefits, and there is something wrong with our system if that is the solution to problems with rent. I tell the hon. Member what would make homelessness a lot worse: the plans of the Opposition party to take £4 billion out of support, because all that would do is end up increasing homelessness, give us less social housing to build and funnel money to people providing the most expensive temporary accommodation.

I welcome the Secretary of State’s statement and report, not least the recognition that this is not about a lack of ambition among young people; it is about the failure of the system to allow them to fulfil it. That is something I heard consistently last week, in Basingstoke Business Week, from both young people and businesses, as it was focused on skills for the future. Will the Secretary of State say more about the support for the nearly 60,000 16 and 17-year-olds who legally already should be in education and training?

That is a good point. I know it is one that the Secretary of State is taking seriously, and the hon. Member is right to say that there should be provision for them in the system we have already. There is more we can do on that before all these extra support mechanisms come into force.

I share the Secretary of State’s ambition that our young people should have better than a life on benefits, but for those reasons I have to reflect my concerns about national insurance. It is one thing to have it for a particular age group, but those NEETs will not stay within that age bracket forever. My constituents who work in hospitality and retail are calling out for a change in the policy on the national insurance increase. Will he confirm to me that he will raise this matter with the Chancellor?

I thank the hon. Lady for her question. It shows that these are problems throughout the UK. On national insurance, I remind her that there is already a tax break in the system for employees under 21 where employers do not pay any national insurance in future. We saw what Alan Milburn has said in his report. The Chancellor hears many representations and, ultimately, tax is a matter for him.

There are over 1,000 people not in education, employment or training in my constituency. From speaking to young people across Erewash, I know that many are frustrated and want help, and it is our job to offer them the hope of good work. Does the Secretary of State agree that the Milburn review represents a major opportunity to transform the support available to young people who are not in education, employment or training?

I think it does represent a major opportunity. As I said, this is a fundamental report. It poses the question: what is the contract between Government and society? That is why it can have a lasting impact, but it will have that impact only if the whole of Government work together to put forward the new settlement that I have advocated today.

We lost my sister Dawn just recently to pancreatic cancer. Her daughter, the amazing Ella, is 22 years old and was born with half a heart, but she and her mum were absolutely desperate that she would live more than half a life. Although Ella is very sad at the loss of her mum, this week she has done herself proud by extending to four days a week her work placement at Matthew’s Enterprise Trust to develop her living and employment skills. Will the Secretary of State congratulate her and say how organisations such as this and the Darwin Nurseries in my constituency can get sustainable long-term funding, to bridge the gap and enable people like Ella to make a valuable contribution to society?

First, let me extend my condolences to the hon. Lady and her family on the loss of Dawn, and let me warmly congratulate Ella. Let me also say that one of the reasons we want more local delivery is so that it can be done flexibly through the great organisations that the hon. Lady has mentioned. Maybe that cannot always be done through big national contracts from my Department, which is why we want to see more local delivery and more flexibility around this.

The social contract with too many young people has broken down, and I welcome the Government’s determination to put that right. In Bedford and Kempston, 8.2% of 18 to 24-year-olds claim unemployment benefit. The young people I meet want opportunities towards a life of purpose and fulfilment—they do not want a life on benefits. Will the Secretary of State ensure that the new youth hub opening in my constituency delivers meaningful pathways into work and timely mental health support, while protecting the welfare safety net for those who are unable to work?

I warmly agree that young people do not want a life on benefits. Alan Milburn found that in his interim report, and he has found that in his final report. Perhaps our ambition has lagged behind theirs. Youth hubs can play a really important role, because they can get the jobcentre out of the jobcentre and get some of the help and services that young people need together in one building, which should be a pretty simple thing, but it has not been happening enough until now.

Work experience should be in the toolbox of every young person to help them move straight from learning to earning, as well as those who are unemployed. However, schools, young people and parents across Mid Dorset and North Poole tell me that they are finding it tougher to find placements, partly due to business and trading reasons but also due to the paperwork. Will the Minister look at an idea suggested by Tammy, who manages the Wimborne business improvement district, to provide liability insurance for employers to remove this barrier for work experience placements?

I have said a few times that I am a great fan of work experience, which I think plays a really important role. I will look at the idea that the hon. Lady mentioned, but sometimes there is a misunderstanding about what is required, some of which applies to children when they do work experience but not to older adults, for whom the paperwork requirements are a bit lighter. Of course, we should make it easy for businesses to do this, because it is such a valuable opportunity for young people.

For far too long our young people have been thrown on the scrapheap. Giving them the skills, confidence and opportunities to succeed and get off welfare is the credible reform that Labour stands for. My constituents in Cannock Chase want to know that this support will be a requirement and that those who refuse to engage for no good reason will face consequences. Could the Secretary of State set out how this will be built into the new system that the report calls for?

Opportunity and responsibility go together. There are responsibilities on the Government to try to help young people and provide opportunities, and equally, there are responsibilities on young people to engage with that and take up reasonable offers.

Alan Milburn talks about the importance of attendance at school and of belonging to school. University of Cumbria research, funded by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, shows that outdoor residentials can improve the self-confidence, teamwork, independence, communication, life skills, leadership, confidence, resilience and aspiration of young people, all of which are vital skills if they are to go on to be successful in finding a job. Will the Secretary of State support my Outdoor Education Bill and persuade his Government that sending young people on outdoor residentials and connecting them with nature can do wonders for their mental health and improve their job prospects?
I have not read the Bill, so I cannot commit to that, but I agree with the hon. Lady: outdoors is good.

I very much welcome Alan Milburn’s report and the Government’s response, as far as it goes. It seems to be a very complex interconnecting set of recommendations. The Secretary of State has not been able to answer on all of them today, but can he confirm that the Government accept all the recommendations? If not, will he undertake to provide a written response, so that we can understand where the Government differ? I accept that we will have to set up a cross-departmental scheme, but there are rumours that some Departments are not fully on board.

The report received a warm welcome in the Cabinet meeting this morning. My hon. Friend is right that it is wide-ranging and contains many, many recommendations. For that reason, we will have to consider it fully and produce a fuller response to it and to the Timms review in the new year. I was able to set out in my statement that we accept the key recommendations of an opportunity and support guarantee, of it being delivered locally, and of a unit being set up in Government to follow through on the delivery.

Around 24,000 young people in Northern Ireland are outside of education, employment or training. If the Secretary of State is to introduce the Milburn proposals, will he confirm that the new tax relief for employers will apply across the whole of the United Kingdom? What funding will Northern Ireland receive for apprenticeships and the additional mental health support that the report recommends? I want young people in Upper Bann to have exactly the same opportunities as those in England.

For the avoidance of doubt, I have not announced any tax changes today. I agree with the hon. Lady that young people in Upper Bann deserve the same opportunities as everyone else. As I said, we recently met the First Ministers in Scotland and Wales. I am very keen to work with the First and Deputy First Minister in Northern Ireland to deliver more opportunities for young people.

My right hon. Friend’s statement today is both visionary for the country and potentially life-changing for so many young people. I want to raise two things. First, I welcome the call for more devolution. Will he ensure that there is accountability as well as responsibility when powers are devolved to mayors and councils? Secondly, small firms often have real difficulties taking on apprentices. Could he look at the Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre in Rotherham and Sheffield, where there are 600 places that are also open to small businesses in the area, so that they can place an apprentice without having all the burdens that often come with an individual scheme?

My hon. Friend mentioned accountability. I think I said in my statement that there have to be agreed standards, accountability and outcome frameworks if we are going to get this right. With regard to the second part of his question, I would be very happy to look at that; I am a huge fan of that institution.

I very much welcome the Milburn report. In my constituency, we are facing a 70% rise in young people with work-limiting health conditions. Although health and skills are devolved, the changes made in Great Britain to universal credit, PIP and national insurance will directly affect our families and small businesses. What discussions has the Secretary of State had with the Northern Ireland Executive to secure fair Barnett consequentials for apprenticeships and mental health support, to ensure that vulnerable young people are not penalised by welfare changes before local jobs are created?

The hon. Gentleman is right to say that support needs to be in place before other changes come in—that is true. He is also right to point out that social security is devolved in Northern Ireland, although the arrangements usually mirror what happens elsewhere in the UK. I am very happy to work with the Northern Ireland Executive and the First and Deputy First Minister to advance an agenda of opportunity for young people in Northern Ireland.
If we look around the Chamber, I can see that a long question will just deny another colleague the opportunity to speak.

The Secretary of State made clear in his response to my hon. Friend the Member for East Kilbride and Strathaven (Joani Reid) that he has been in discussions with the Scottish Government about the implementation of the report. He will share my disappointment that the comments within minutes of the report’s publication were a critique of it. Will he reassure the House, and my young constituents in Motherwell, Wishaw and Carluke, that he will work hand in hand with Scottish MPs, local authorities and colleagues in Holyrood, to ensure that young people in Scotland get every opportunity that young people in England get?

That is the least that young people in Motherwell, Wishaw, Carluke and other parts of Scotland deserve. This is a problem throughout the UK. Our Prime Minister is a great believer in devolution, and he has made an open offer to work with the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government and the Northern Ireland Executive to advance this agenda. I hope that is taken seriously and at face value, and that it results in delivery beneath the level of national Governments. Local, personalised delivery can be valuable in building the right support around a person.

As the Secretary of State will know from his engagement with me since he has been in this role—I thank him for that—my concern has always been about changes that make more young people vulnerable and poorer before mental health and job support is accessed. Young people want to work, as my right hon. Friend saw for himself in February when thousands came through the door at my jobs fair. How will we ensure that the recommendations and policies that the Government are bringing forward will reflect local needs, reach people before any financial support is withdrawn, and be delivered alongside trusted local organisations, including charities, to help young people in education to get mental health support, training and work?

My hon. Friend is a tremendous champion for his area, and specifically the young people in it, and I had an enormously rewarding visit to the fantastic jobs fair that he organised at the beginning of the year. Local delivery can do a lot for the things he mentioned. We must also remember that people with severe enduring conditions that make work an unrealistic possibility will receive continued support—indeed, Alan Milburn recommends that that support increases. For others who could work with support, it is our duty to help them to do that.

I welcome the statement from the Secretary of State. During the Get Britain Working inquiry with the Work and Pensions Committee, we visited a number of jobcentres and hosted groups of young people. One point in Alan Milburn’s report is about trust in jobcentres. How will he ensure that our jobcentres and youth hubs—I thank him for the one that is on its way for North West Leicestershire—become enablers for our young people, rather than the barriers that they have often become?

I must thank staff in our jobcentres who I believe do care about helping people into work. When I meet them, they speak with great passion about that. I also believe that we must get more of the help that can be given out of the jobcentre and into the local community. That is why I am rolling out more youth hubs around the country. Those are also an important feature of the Dutch system, which I visited, and through them we can get help and ally that to other things such as mental health support, housing and so on, and treat the person as a human being and not a departmental client.

Providing all young people with the chance to fulfil their potential is the moral mission of our time. The report recognises that and rightly demands action. In addition to the necessary support for young people who are currently not in education, employment or training, will the Secretary of State set out how the new measures will help those most at risk of being in that position in future?

My hon. Friend is right to say that these problems often start earlier in life. We have talked about the school readiness target and the SEND agenda, and it is important that I and the Secretaries of State for Education and for Health and Social Care, and others, work closely together on this. People do not just become NEET when they turn 16. Very often it starts earlier in life, and we must do what we can to stop that becoming more likely for more young people.

I welcome the Secretary of State’s statement, and particularly the focus on getting the welfare bill down by giving more support to young people and providing them with opportunities. Will he outline how he will work closely with the voluntary sector, and trusted organisations in our communities, to deliver the vision that Alan Milburn has outlined, so that another generation is not written off, as they were under the Conservatives?

Local delivery will help us to work more closely with the voluntary sector, and enable more flexibility. Some local voluntary sector organisations are doing a fantastic job. It is not always easy for a big Department such as mine to find them and know exactly what they are doing, but more local delivery can help us to do that.

I warmly welcome the report. As someone who spent decades working with children and young people, watching too many of them being unable to fulfil their potential, I know this has been a long time coming. How will the Government build on the review to ensure that no young person falls through the gaps between health, education, welfare and employment support?

That is a challenge. It has not always been easy, but we believe that more local delivery can help to narrow those gaps and ensure that, as my hon. Friend says, young people do not fall through them, as that is the last thing we want.

As chair of the inclusion and nurture in education all-party group, I was particularly pleased that the report recognised the value of a stronger nurture offer in schools as part of early intervention, and that it highlighted of the work of NurtureUK and the use of tools such as the Boxall profile to help schools identify needs and target support. Will the Secretary of State confirm that such recognition will help lead to greater investment in early intervention, and to the skills and resources that schools need to put nurture into practice?

I am sure the Secretary of State for Education will have heard my hon. Friend’s plea. I have had fantastic dialogue with the Secretary of State about this, and she shares my passion for ensuring that more young people do not end up in that position. As I said a moment ago, these issues often start much earlier, before people turn up on the benefit books later in life.

I know how much work has gone into the report over the last year or so, and I congratulate the Secretary of State and Alan Milburn on its publication. I agree wholeheartedly with the recommendation that we need a total system reset, so as we rebuild the system for young people looking for work, may I ask that from first principles we build it around the needs of young people, rather than leaving them to negotiate the bureaucracy?
I thank my hon. Friend for his support and encouragement over the past year. This is a landmark report. We need a reset, not just a policy tweak, and that is what we intend to do.

I got involved in politics because our brilliant young people across Stoke-on-Trent North and Kidsgrove had been ripped off for too long. The Sure Start centres that got our kids school ready were hollowed out, and when our young people got older they found that youth clubs and support centres were simply not there any more. Young people need the right scaffolding around them to help them get into work and thrive. Does the Secretary of State agree that Labour Members understand the need to invest now in our young people to save in the longer term?

My hon. Friend is right to point out that we did not get to the number of 1 million NEETs overnight. It was a long time coming, and in my earlier remarks I listed some of the decisions that I think have contributed to it. That is why this will take time to turn round. The new settlement will not be delivered overnight. This is a long-term reset of the system, which is the right and sustainable way to expand opportunity and change lives for the better.

Young people not in education or employment in Ealing Southall should not been seen just as numbers on a spreadsheet. They are all different, with different needs and often very different hopes and dreams. From those who want to work in our local creative industries or set up their own tech businesses, to those who will need mental health support or help to stick to a routine before finding work, how will the new youth opportunity service ensure that young people in Ealing Southall receive tailored support that reflects their individual circumstances and diverse ambitions?

The idea of people wanting to set up their own business and do their own thing is important. I recently launched an initiative with NatWest bank, which is supporting young people to do that, and we need more of that in our youth guarantee work. I have been in discussions with the Chancellor about that, and we should be encouraging and supportive of young people who want to set up their own business.

Given the scale of the NEET crisis, Alan Milburn is right that we need both a Government-wide approach, with a welfare system that encourages young people into work, while protecting those with the most severe disabilities, and education, health and transport systems that pull down barriers. The Secretary of State knows that I have been really supportive of the role of the cadets in tackling the NEET crisis and in giving young people skills, so will he say more about what we can do to drive youth opportunities, including in the cadets, in places where they are most needed?

That is a really good point. I have not mentioned the Ministry of Defence so far, but I am pleased to say that the Secretary of State for Defence is hugely supportive of the agenda and of the point my hon. Friend just made.

As a Cornish MP, I have to reiterate the inequity that transport availability and cost can cause to young people in rural and coastal areas. It can often take four hours a day and £1,100 a year to go 12 miles in Cornwall, whereas such journeys are often free in urban areas. How can the Government ensure that the review’s recommendations correct that inequity?

That issue comes up every time this subject is discussed. Transport is important because if we are going to create opportunities for young people, they have to be able to get to them. I am happy to keep talking to my hon. Friend and other Cornish MPs about this, and to work with her and the Secretary of State for Transport.

The youth who are unemployed today will be the adults of tomorrow. Unless we fix this problem, this country literally will not work. The prospect of a good future feels out of reach for many people in my constituency, so will the Secretary of State reassure them that this Government’s cross-departmental approach will be central to creating better work programmes, so that we ensure better and closer alignment with sectors and industries that will create more, better-paid jobs for our young people?

We have concluded a few agreements with important big hiring sectors, but there is more that I want to do. Employers in the public and private sectors are an important part of the solution, so dialogue with business is key as we go forward.

I strongly welcome the report’s recommendation of local delivery by further education colleges, schools, employers, local authorities and others working together. Does the Secretary of State share my concern that on the day the report is published, the Welsh Government are reporting massive cuts to further education in their draft Budget report, which will have an impact on the delivery that we need so desperately?
The Welsh Government, like the Scottish Government, have received substantial financial settlements. I hope that that money, or at least a share of it, is used to expand opportunity, not contract it.

The measures outlined in the report have the potential to give hope to the community I represent, which has never really recovered since the closure of the wagon works, pits and foundries, so I thank the Minister for that. Investment is really important. The comments made by Conservative Members show that they think that low-paid, insecure work is the answer, but the Conservatives tried that and it did not work. We know that the countries who do best on NEETs are those who invest in them. Nowhere is that truer than with investment in further education, so what will the Government do to ensure our further education colleges can provide the services that our young people need?

Further education colleges have a critical role to play. I work closely with the City of Wolverhampton college, including at its campus in Bilston, in my constituency. Such colleges provide fantastic opportunities for young people, and providing more such opportunities will be a critical part of the answer.

The holistic approach set out in the report will be a gamechanger for thousands of young people in Hyndburn and hundreds of thousands across the country. As somebody who used to work in the voluntary sector helping young people at risk of being NEET, will the Secretary of State say a little more about the role that he hopes charities will play in this new reformed system?

I have had a really good dialogue with charities—they have taught me a lot in the past year since I was appointed to my role. The local delivery model that I am setting out can involve charities in a deeper and richer way than has previously been the case.

The review recommends paring back benefits for most young people, with only those with the most severe or complex conditions receiving additional support. Work capability assessments have been riddled with administrative errors and failures in safeguarding, leading to hundreds of suicides, so how will the Government ensure that any new eligibility criteria do not reproduce those harms for young disabled people in my constituency and elsewhere?

The benefit proposals outlined in the report talk about extra cost benefits for people who could participate more if they had more support, in addition to a local fund for short-term needs, when somebody might require short-term support. There are several levels of support for people with sickness and disability issues recommended in the report, which is right and proper. The emphasis should be on participation and work, where possible, because we want to close the disability employment gap, which has been so stubborn for so many years.

The welfare state must always support those facing extraordinary adversity. It is not, however, a compensation scheme for living through 14 years of the Conservative Government, although I understand why people might feel that they deserve that. I welcome the recommendation from the former Member for Darlington for an opportunity and a right to succeed—the right for people to stand on their own two feet, the right to dignity for young people, the right to earn a living and the right to have that supported. I urge the Secretary of State to get to work with the same determination that the young people of Darlington put into trying to get a job.
I will get to work, and I will use young people in Darlington and elsewhere as my inspiration.

When the Secretary of State visited Bellshill Jobcentre last year, he heard from a number of young people about the challenges that they face. He was right when he said to me that day that we have a moral obligation to deal with the issue. He might have seen the comments over the weekend from Scotland’s First Minister, who seemed to suggest that Scotland does not have a particular challenge in this area. Does he agree that the crisis does not end when we get to the Scottish border? Will he outline his ambitions for making this a four-nation approach that will benefit people in my constituency?

As hon. Members might know, that visit to Bellshill Jobcentre has stayed with me, and I mean that in a really serious way. It has spurred me on to try to do more about the issue. It is complacent for anyone to suggest that there is not a problem in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland—this is a problem throughout the UK. Our passion to help people should not stop at any border within the UK.

For far too long, young people, including in Norwich, have been left behind, so I welcome this landmark report. It could not, of course, have been written without Alan Milburn, but it also could not have been written without the experiences of young people up and down the country. I am sure we will all be going back and speaking to young people and organisations in our areas, so as we decide which measures to implement, will the Secretary of State set out how we will ensure that young people’s voices remain at the heart of that work?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. The voices and experiences of young people have helped to frame the argument in this report. Most obviously, given the chance, young people want to work and to reject the narrative about being snowflakes and shirkers. I rejected that narrative earlier and I reject it again now. We have got to give people a chance, and then expect some responsibility in taking up that chance.

Businesses across Cumbria regularly complain to me that they cannot find the staff they desperately need, but most admit that they do not even consider working with our fantastic jobcentre staff to fill those vacancies. Sadly, the history of local jobcentre closures across the county’s towns has not helped, so will the Secretary of State set out how we can work with businesses in Cumbria to deliver these ambitious and the warmly welcomed youth employment plans?

Of course we have to work with businesses. I talked about getting the help that a jobcentre can provide out of the jobcentre. I believe that the transfer of the skills portfolio into the Department for Work and Pensions a year ago puts an onus on us to have a better, more fruitful and deeper relationship with business than has perhaps been the case in the past.

The Milburn review rightly identifies that poverty and inequality are at the core of the NEET crisis. Will the Secretary of State offer assurances that these proposals will not lower living standards before support is put in place?

I agree. Support has to be put in place up front, and that is exactly our intention. If that happens and we get more people into work or productive education, that is a huge bulwark against future poverty.
I absolutely welcome the work of Alan Milburn and the Secretary of State. These proposals will make a massive difference to young people in Harlow, won’t they?
They will. My message to the young people of Harlow is: we believe in you, and we want you to have a better future.

I welcome the commitment of the Secretary of State to devolving decision making, delivery and support through these reforms. Will he set out how the benefits of these reforms could be delivered in the Glasgow city region?

The Glasgow city region is an interesting example, because it is exactly the kind of place where more local delivery could benefit people. I grew up in Glasgow, and it is very close to my heart. I have been there twice in the last five or six weeks, and I hope that these reforms make a difference to the wonderful young people of Glasgow.

Last year, my right hon. Friend the Member for East Ham (Sir Stephen Timms) visited Bexleyheath in my constituency and heard from charities, disabled people and those giving financial advice. He heard that the DWP’s work in those charities had identified that teenagers with neurological conditions are often the children of adults with neurological conditions. My Bexley Voice parents’ group, which is working with the DWP, has identified not only how to get those young people into work, but how to get their parents back into work. As part of these measures, will the Secretary of State commit to looking at how we work with our voluntary sector on innovative schemes such as that to ensure that disabled people are back in work as they should be?

I thank my hon. Friend for the many conversations that we have had and for how much he has taught me over the past year about parents coping with these issues. He is right to show belief in young people with neurodiverse conditions—I think we owe them belief—and to point out that worklessness can sometimes be intergenerational and difficult to crack. That is why getting one person into work can make a difference for the whole family.

This report recognises something that a generation of young people—my generation—has felt for a long time: that too often, this place has forgotten them. I agree with the Secretary of State that this issue requires a new settlement, but it is so important that we bring young people with us, because, for too long, previous Governments have not. What will he do to engage young people, particularly those who are neurodivergent or living with a mental health condition, to shape the next steps following this review?

The best thing that we can do is show belief in young people. I have spoken a few times today about how I think the Government’s ambitions have probably lagged behind young people’s ambitions. Given the chance, they will want to work, learn or participate in a broader way, and that will help us to close the stubborn disability employment gap that there has been for so many years.

I thoroughly welcome this statement and congratulate the Secretary of State on the sensitive and collegiate way in which he has carried himself to achieve such a groundbreaking proposal. In his report, Alan Milburn proposes that strategic authorities should lead local youth opportunity services and area participation plans, with an extension of their responsibilities to cover 18 to 24-year-olds. Can the Secretary of State confirm that foundation strategic authorities such as Cornwall will have all those powers and funding arrangements? Will he also talk to us about buses?

I will talk to the hon. Member about buses. We want strategic authorities to play a critical role in this matter. In closing, let me repeat something that I said earlier. We want to change the question that the system asks to, “How do we help you to live the fullest life?” That is a good question for the state to ask, so let us get on and implement something about it.

title: Iran: Threats to British Interests
turns: (Urgent Question): To ask the Foreign Secretary if he will make a statement on the threats posed by Iran to British interests. I am grateful to you, Mr Speaker, for granting me an urgent question in this role for the first time. I fear that it will not be the last, but I am grateful to you for doing so.
The Minister of State, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office

I am grateful to the right hon. Member for his urgent question, and I welcome him to his new role. He has always been a good colleague and friend, and I thank him for his service to this country, not only as a former Minister but in his past career. The Government take the threats posed by Iran to British interests extremely seriously. We have acted robustly in response to them, and we will continue to do so. Iran’s hostile activity, both directly and through its proxies and networks, continues to pose a significant threat to the United Kingdom, to our partners and allies, and to the rules-based international system. We know the threats posed by Iran, whether that is directly or through partners such as the Houthis, militias in Iraq, Lebanese Hezbollah and many other groups that the right hon. Gentleman is more than aware of. We will act, because protecting the British public and defending our national security is the Government’s first duty. Yesterday the Government sanctioned two Iranian IRGC—Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps—officers for their role in state threats activity. In relation to Iran, we have sanctioned nearly 240 individuals and entities whose actions threaten our people and security. We will continue to keep all those tools under review, and will not hesitate to take further action where appropriate. Yesterday I summoned the Iranian ambassador to the Foreign Office in response to Iran’s activity, and informed him candidly and forcibly that this Government condemn, in the strongest possible terms, the Islamic Republic of Iran’s continued attempts to undermine the safety and security of the United Kingdom and our allies. Yesterday the Foreign Secretary signed a statement with 35 other Foreign Ministers across the Five Eyes and Europe, making it clear that we will not tolerate state threats activity on our soil and that we are committed to facing those threats together, and earlier this year we strengthened our legislative toolkit through the national security framework. These measures provide enhanced powers to investigate, expose and counter hostile activity that threatens our security, and the right hon. Gentleman will know that we immediately designated the IRGC and the Islamic Movement of Companions of the Right under that framework. We will continue to work closely with the police, intelligence agencies and international partners to identify, disrupt and deter hostile activity directed against the United Kingdom and our allies. As recent events have demonstrated, the threat from Iran is not theoretical. The Prime Minister made it clear yesterday that the incident at RAF Fairford was highly likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran and was almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, although investigations remain ongoing. More recently, in September, law enforcement agencies disrupted an alleged plot targeting Jewish communities in Manchester that involved individuals suspected of links to actors in Iran. We will continue to take the action necessary to protect the public, safeguard our democratic institutions, defend communities at risk and ensure that those responsible for threatening British interests are held to account.

I am grateful to the Minister, whom I call a friend, for his response today. However, after almost a decade of consistent Foreign Office advice to reject photographs with Iranian officials, and particularly handshake photographs, because of the propaganda tool that it gives the regime, it seems that our Foreign Secretary has just been ambushed in New York. Either he was ambushed by a snapper, or there has been a change of policy. It is important that we understand which, because although it is certainly clear that the Foreign Secretary did not look happy, Araghchi was absolutely beaming. If that was not deliberate, has the Foreign Office changed its advice, and if so, why? Frankly, following the Iranians’ threats against UK airbases that both the Minister and the Prime Minister have mentioned, the state threats that the head of MI5 has listed, which have been reported today, the murder of 40,000 of their own people, their expansion of violence in Yemen by using the Houthis to target civilians in Riyadh, and their attacks on Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, I would be very grateful to know what made the Foreign Secretary believe that it was worth giving them a propaganda win. Perhaps the Minister will tell me that this does not matter, but he knows better than that. He knows that images project a message, and in this case they project the message that the Iranian regime is equal to the moment. Well, it is not. The reality is that the Iranian regime—and, in fact, Mr Araghchi himself—is merely a front for the IRGC, which is of course the terror group responsible for the murder of thousands in Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Iraq and elsewhere. I will finish by asking the Minister a few questions. Was the Foreign Secretary aware of his Iranian friend’s threats to the United Kingdom before he decided to shake hands with him and have it photographed? Was he aware that the US and Israel had given warning to the British Government that the Iranian regime’s threats to US airbases in the UK were credible? Lastly, has the policy of the UK now reverted to not giving propaganda wins to such a vile regime?

The Foreign Secretary followed the standard practice of previous Foreign Secretaries of both parties, and of those of many countries, in meeting with the Iranian Foreign Minister. In fact, Foreign Ministers including William Hague, Philip Hammond, Boris Johnson, the right hon. Member for Godalming and Ash (Sir Jeremy Hunt), Liz Truss, David Cameron and others all engaged with Iran. It is important to understand what the Foreign Secretary raised with Foreign Minister Araghchi. He met with him to strongly raise the UK Government’s objections to Iran’s behaviours, to protect our interests. He told the Foreign Minister that Iran should choose de-escalation and diplomacy, instead of prolonging war and conflict. He underlined the importance of restoring freedom of navigation, and of the reopening of the strait of Hormuz. He reiterated the UK’s unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-backed groups on UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community. He made it clear that we will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil, and set out the measures that we would take in response. He also raised a matter that I know will be of great interest to the House: the ongoing detention of Craig and Lindsay Foreman. He repeated our call for their immediate release, and stressed that their welfare remains a priority for the Government. The right hon. Gentleman knows full well that Iran’s threats to the UK are public. Indeed, the evidence that the Prime Minister, the Foreign Secretary and others have set out is public, so we are fully aware of the threat that Iran poses to the UK, our interests, and our allies and partners. I am not going to comment on intelligence matters at the Dispatch Box—he knows why I will not do that. I strongly encourage him to avail himself of opportunities for Privy Council briefings, which we would be very happy to arrange. I know that the Leader of the Opposition and others have taken up those opportunities, and he is very welcome to come in and have a briefing on these matters. The right hon. Gentleman rightly raised issues relating to Iran’s threats—not just directly to the UK and our interests, but more broadly, including to partners in the Gulf. What Iran has done in relation to Kuwait, Bahrain and other partners is utterly unacceptable. I met with all our Gulf partners in New York over recent days to reiterate our support for them, and we are engaged in heavy diplomatic and other efforts to find a resolution. Just this morning I spoke to my Saudi counterpart and the Foreign Minister of Yemen about the appalling Houthi attacks in recent days, not only on the people of Yemen but on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including the attacks at the airport in Riyadh and other threats. The right hon. Gentleman can be absolutely assured that, whether it is direct threats from Iran or indirect threats through its proxies, partners and others, we take these matters incredibly seriously. A substantial amount of our diplomatic and other effort is involved in countering them, and I welcome his engagement and co-operation in the national interest on these issues.
I call the Chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee.

I welcome the calling out of what seem to be the IRGC’s actions in Fairford, not just by the UK but by more than 30 of our friends and partners, from Albania to the USA. I thank them for standing in solidarity with us. Much of the IRGC’s divisive work, whether it is feeding antisemitism or through bots wearing kilts, is done quietly in the shadows and often online. This time, it looks like the Iranians have been caught out through the diligence of a local resident. Does the Minister agree that our approach needs to change and that we need to be clear about what Iranian attempts to hurt our country look like—both offline and online, with more examples—so that the public are confident enough to identify such attacks, just as they did at Fairford?

My right hon. Friend raises very important issues. It is a fact that Iran poses threats across a range of domains, and she rightly raises the issue of misinformation and disinformation. I know that her Committee has been doing very important work on that, and the Government have taken that on board. We have announced a new centre for information defence, which the Prime Minister referred to yesterday, but she is absolutely right to say that we need to be open-eyed about the threats that are posed. We certainly attempt to keep the public informed about the nature of those threats, not just in this country but abroad, and we will continue to implement a range of measures to deter and disrupt them.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

The Iranian regime is a threat to global security, to the UK’s interests and to its own citizens. The question is how best to respond to that threat, while protecting people at home. The unilateral US and Israeli attack on Iran and the conflict that has followed have driven up prices for British families, while emboldening the Iranian regime. I visited Oman last week, and I refer Members to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. At the maritime security centre, we were told that shipping rates are less than half what they were prior to the conflict, with a mere 35 to 50 vessels passing through Omani waters in the strait of Hormuz each night—every one of them at risk of attack from Iranian drones or missiles. What steps are the Government taking, with other maritime nations, to protect shipping and secure safe passage through the straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, to keep food on our shelves and fuel in our tanks at prices that British consumers can afford?

The hon. Member raises the reason why all this matters, which is that the threats are not just to our security, but to our economy; they affect the prices that British people, and indeed people around the world, pay for energy—and for consumer goods on the shelves, because this disruption to energy has a wider implication, in that fertiliser and other things that come out of the Gulf also have an impact on prices. I am delighted that he visited Oman. I was in Oman just a few weeks ago. It is a key partner and friend, and its long-standing historical relationship with the UK is crucial to us. We and His Majesty the King look forward to welcoming His Majesty the Sultan of Oman to the UK soon. It is a crucial partnership for us. The hon. Member is absolutely right to talk about maritime security and the work we do in that domain. I am glad that he saw that work during his visit. Just last week, I visited our Joint Maritime Security Centre at Portsmouth, in which incredible work is done jointly by the Royal Navy, Border Force, UK Maritime Trade Operations and a range of civilian and other agencies. It is crucial that we understand the threats to shipping, and that we are able to provide information to mariners and avoid threats and risk. We continue to work internationally with partners on this issue, just as at the UN General Assembly in New York, the Foreign Secretary, working with Bahrain and others, brought together nearly 80 countries to stand up for the principles of international navigation. It is crucial that we recognise that this is not just about what happens in the strait of Hormuz or the Red sea; this is a threat to the very principles of freedom of navigation and global trade. We need to stand up and defend those principles.

In July, the Government took the very welcome step of designating the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, thus criminalising support for its hostile activities. Given Iran’s support for the Houthis, their recent attacks on Saudi Arabia and their threats to international shipping in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Red sea, are the Government considering taking this step against the Houthis, or are they looking at proscribing the organisation as a terrorist group?

My hon. Friend knows that I do not comment on future designations, but he can be assured that we take the threat posed by the Houthis, both in the region and more broadly, incredibly seriously. As I have said, I spoke with the Foreign Minister of Yemen this morning. I am also utterly appalled to hear that the Houthis are using child soldiers, and are carrying out forced re-education of citizens in areas that they have taken. Attacks are currently taking place around Taiz, where there is a humanitarian crisis, and hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced. This is not just about the appalling kinetic attacks we have seen on Saudi Arabia and in Yemen, but the humanitarian suffering caused by the Houthis’ actions. We stand with the recognised Government of Yemen, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and others. My hon. Friend rightly points to the work that we have done on the IRGC, the IMCR and individuals, and that relates to the sanctions we issued just yesterday.

When the Iranians risked the lives of armed forces personnel by attacking RAF Akrotiri earlier this year, Labour Members took great pleasure in mocking the Leader of Opposition for suggesting that a direct attack required a direct response. Does this latest episode not prove that when we do not respond with force, our enemies are encouraged to come at us yet again?
I am absolutely assured that we will respond to defend our bases, our allies and our partners—and, indeed, UK interests in this country—with absolute resolution and vigour.

I welcome the Minister’s response. As a member of the International Development Committee, I regularly hear about conflicts such as the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Yemen, in which Iranian proxies are actively fighting, destabilising those countries, and causing death and despair. What is the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office doing to support victims of Iran in these countries, and to ensure that Yemen, Lebanon and Palestine have functioning states, free of Iranian influence?

I completely share my hon. Friend’s objective of eliminating Iranian influence and that destabilising factor in all those contexts. She rightly mentioned a number of them, and I have already mentioned what we are doing in Yemen. We have also announced an additional £10 million for the United Nations humanitarian appeal to respond to that terrible situation. She also points to Lebanon; we are working closely with the Government of Lebanon to respond in a range of ways to the crisis there.

Does the Minister agree with me that it sends a strange signal when people suspected of mounting a terrorist attack backed by Iran are let out on bail? Does he also share my concern at recent media reports of several—fortunately foiled—terrorist attacks that were being planned by people who came into this country illegally, on boats crossing the channel?

As the right hon. Member will understand, I will not comment on the ongoing investigations into the events at RAF Fairford, or on police operational decisions, which are very much for them. However, on his broader point about threats and challenges, he will know that MI5 identified at least 15 credible Iranian-backed plots to kill or kidnap people in the UK in 2022 and 2023 alone. This is obviously activity over a sustained period of time. We have made it clear to the Iranian regime at the highest levels that this must end immediately.

As we know, Iran’s use of criminal networks and online disinformation is a threat to national security, and to safety on British soil. I welcome the recent designations, but does the Minister agree with me that further sanctions are required on Iran and the IRGC to restrict their capacity?

My hon. Friend will know that I do not comment on future designations, but I can assure her that we will continue to keep open all possibilities for deterring and disrupting Iranian state threat activity on our soil, or indeed elsewhere. We keep those measures under regular review; I think the action we have taken in recent weeks is testament to that.

The incident at RAF Fairford proved yet again a point that we have long known, which is that Iran is an exporter of terrorism and violence around the world—not just in the UK, but, crucially, in the region. We have seen the support for Hezbollah undermining security in Lebanon, and we have seen the attacks on our ally Saudi Arabia. What are the Government planning to do to increase the support that we provide to our allies in the region to counter the Iranian threat?

The hon. Member is right about the scale of the threat, which is exactly why we announced measures and made a statement yesterday with many countries, who are joining our efforts to respond to those threats. Whether it is the air defence support we are supplying in Saudi Arabia at the moment and the air-to-air refuelling, or the work we did to support air defence for many Gulf partners when they were undergoing attacks, we will not cease in our efforts to support our partners and allies in responding to and defending themselves from unprovoked Iranian aggression.

Just this morning, the chief of MI5 warned about the implications of artificial intelligence reducing the barrier to advance terror and cyber-attacks on the United Kingdom, so what work have the Minister and his colleagues done to assess how Iran is using this technology and how we can defend ourselves?

The implications of AI for our defence and security are obviously significant. My hon. Friend knows that important work is being done by my right hon. Friend the Minister for Artificial Intelligence on this issue. It is crucial that we look at this not just in any one context—he rightly mentions the risk of Iran or others using this technology—because it of course applies more broadly. I can assure him that we are leading international conversations on these issues.

I have a lot of time for the Minister, as he knows. I hope he will confirm to the House that he has read the Intelligence and Security Committee report on Iran, published in July 2025, because many of the issues that it covered have been raised on the Floor of the House today. It was in 1862 that the first Iranian became a British national—a dual national in this country. We now have about 120,000 British Iranians living in this country. Not all of them are dual nationals, but many of them are. Given that Iran does not recognise dual nationality, and given that many British Iranians travel to see family in Iran, what further consideration has the Minister given to the Foreign Office’s travel advice, as the Iranian regime is, unfortunately, detaining people illegally?

The right hon. Gentleman rightly illustrates the risk to people. I strongly encourage anyone, whether dual national or otherwise, to read and heed the FCDO travel advice for Iran. These are very serious threats. We know of the risks involved; people have been detained, and I referred to one very high-profile case. We encourage people to follow the advice very closely. I will certainly look at the report that he mentions.

I thank the Minister for his responses to questions so far, and I reiterate the concerns raised by colleagues about online disinformation, which is clearly designed to undermine our democracy in this country. What are the Government doing to tackle hostile activity by Iran and its network of proxy groups?

We are acting against the threats posed by Iran and proxy groups in a number of ways. I mentioned the statement that we signed in the past few days; also, in June, we issued a joint statement with 23 other countries relating to the lethal plotting and other malign actions by the IRGC, an intelligence organisation, the Quds Force and the Ministry of Intelligence and Security, including threats against dissidents, journalists, and Jewish and Israeli communities. They are undertaking a wide range of activities, and we need to work with key partners to deter and disrupt that activity.

What assessment have the Government made of the threats we face from the IRGC or its proxies, and of the impact of February’s US-Israeli attack? Did that attack strengthen or weaken the regime in Tehran, internally and externally? Do those assessments show whether the UK has become more or less exposed, since February, to events such as those we witnessed recently?

The hon. Gentleman knows that I will not comment on intelligence assessments. What I will say is that we continue to seek diplomatic resolution of the crisis in the strait of Hormuz. There is a huge amount of common ground between all partners on Iran. First, it cannot be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon. It must cease its attacks on partners and allies. In our interests, it needs to stop malign activity in our country, as well as others, and of course, it needs to stop the repression of its own people. I think there is a lot of common ground, but I will not comment on specific assessments.

The threat of Iranian surveillance is very real in my constituency; faith and residential communities have shared with me the real fear that they face. What processes do the FCDO and the Home Office have in place to make sure that communities are as safe as they possibly can be, and that intelligence is appropriately shared?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right to highlight those threats. I co-operate very closely with the Security Minister and others on these matters. I referenced the number of plots that MI5 had identified. Of course, those threats continue, and we have seen some very high-profile examples, which the Prime Minister and others have referred to. My hon. Friend can absolutely be assured that we are putting in place the necessary protective security arrangements, including with faith communities, and particularly the Jewish community, and that we are very aware of where threats are originating from. That is the nature of the response that we have conveyed directly to the Iranian regime.

The regime is using every opportunity to reach deep into our communities and society. Even charities in this country are at risk. The Charity Commission has embarked on an investigation into the extent to which the regime, particularly the IRGC, is percolating into the sector. What assessment has the Minister made of whether Iran has got itself involved in British charities? If he believes that it has, how will he expunge that particular malignancy?

The right hon. Gentleman raises the important wider issue of Iran and other hostile states attempting to undermine or use mechanisms in the UK to conduct their activities. I welcome the work that the Charity Commission is doing. We will look very seriously at any findings that come out of that investigation. Crucially, this is a matter for the Security Minister and our agencies to look at. We take any threats or activity of that nature incredibly seriously, and we will not hesitate to act.

There is wide acknowledgement of Iranian efforts to weaponise social media in order to promote Iran’s propaganda, spread disinformation and shake UK politics. What work is being done to hold to account social media companies whose algorithms boost dangerous content?

It is an important question. My hon. Friend will know of the work that has been done through the Online Safety Act 2023 and other measures, but the wider challenge and threat of disinformation is growing. We spend a lot of time in this place focusing on Russian disinformation and the billions that Russia is spending on it, but of course it is not just Russia; it is also Iran and others. That is exactly why the Prime Minister is bringing together our capabilities, and responding to the Foreign Affairs Committee recommendations with a new centre for information resilience.

There is a real fear that Iran has achieved the aim of its attack on RAF Fairford. We have seen the US respond by removing very important military capability away from Europe and away from the United Kingdom. Does the Minister agree—he is very thoughtful on this point and sympathetic to it—that there is a need for increased military spending?
