Would the Minister be so kind as to confirm that the use of asylum hotels has fallen by 50% under this Government, and that the move to using disused MOD property is to make sure that the accommodation for asylum seekers is dispersed across the country and does not fall disproportionately on poor areas like my own area of the west midlands or her area in the north-east?

My hon. Friend makes the important point that no consent was sought from our communities when hotels that were insecure were put in the middle of them with no notice. MOD Bicester is controlled accommodation that is self-contained—everything onsite and the impact on local communities minimised. On top of all that, we are already saving £1 billion, with more to come as I look forward to closing the rest of the hotels before the end of the Parliament.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

As the Prime Minister conceded, the crisis in asylum accommodation is a direct result of Brexit, when we lost the returns agreement with the EU, which was compounded by the previous Conservative Government’s decision to stop processing asylum claims. Does the Minister share my contempt for the scenes in Piddington last Friday, when the authors of this mess—the Tory shadow Home Secretary and the Reform home affairs spokesperson—entered into an unedifying scrap seeking to blame each other for the problem that both their parties caused? The Liberal Democrats have a plan to clear the asylum backlog within six months, by doubling the number of asylum caseworkers and joining the EU migration and asylum pact. Does the Minister agree, first, that wasting billions on using hotels and military sites, such as MOD Bicester, is no solution to the asylum crisis; secondly, that rather than overriding local planning concerns, money would be better spent employing more asylum caseworkers; and thirdly, that the UK should join the EU migration and asylum pact?

The hon. Gentleman is right that those scenes were unedifying—those who contributed to the mess that we inherited seek to throw stones at one another while we are getting on with solving yet another mess. I am proud of this Government’s record. I enjoyed working with the hon. Gentleman on the Immigration and Asylum Bill Committee, where we went through a number of issues. While we may disagree on the EU pact, we both agree that greater co-operation internationally is key to solving the problem, because patterns of migration move across borders and boundaries. We will continue to bring down the abuses in our system, and I look forward to the hon. Gentleman joining us in voting for the Bill on Report and Third Reading tomorrow.

I welcome the work the Government are doing on closing asylum hotels. Does the Minister agree that former military sites with permanent security and CCTV are much more appropriate and controlled settings for holding those awaiting asylum decisions than the asylum hotels that the Tories not only opened but celebrated opening in working-class communities such as mine?

My hon. Friend makes an important point. These large sites are designed to be self-contained, with basic services provided on site to reduce demand and pressure on local services and minimise the need for anyone to leave. We work with voluntary organisations to ensure that activities are available on site, helping to create an environment that encourages people to remain on site all day and meets their day-to-day needs. As I said, we know that existing sites have operated very successfully with basic on-site services and 24/7 security designed to minimise the impact on local communities.

MOD Bicester site A is just a mile from the Buckinghamshire border, and many of my communities in Mid Buckinghamshire are threatened by its use for 1,256 illegal migrants. I cannot believe that the Minister said earlier that MHCLG had considered all the representations, when 3,177 of those local voices said no and only one said yes—the Government appear to have gone with that one. Equally, I cannot believe that the Minister is trying to say that those 1,256 men will be incentivised not to leave this small camp, built entirely out of portacabins and modular buildings, and sit around playing ping pong, rather than the things we all know they are actually going to do. Given the clear safety risk, and given that it works out at two and a half times the cost of the equivalent asylum hotels, will the Minister at least come and visit, listen to local voices and turn around on this plan?

I am very happy to meet the hon. Gentleman to discuss his representations. As I said, we have listened to the concerns of communities, which are essential to our immigration reforms. That is why we are closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including military sites. We are working to house asylum seekers fairly across the country, engaging with local authorities to reduce the impact on communities. We have already saved taxpayers more than a billion pounds on asylum support costs since the election.

I thought that my hon. Friend the Member for Tipton and Wednesbury (Antonia Bance) made a very good point about hypocrisy from the Opposition earlier. I was relieved to hear the Minister talk about the number of asylum hotels being reduced from 400 to 160, I think, which is dramatic. I read earlier that asylum application processing is at its highest rate for 25 years. Will the Minister reassure me that the Government are getting a grip of the asylum system and the mess that they inherited?

I can absolutely assure my hon. Friend of that. I look forward to the debate we will have in this Chamber tomorrow on Report and Third Reading of the Immigration and Asylum Bill, which is further evidence of us ensuring that we remove those who have no right to be in this country, tighten the appeals system against abuse and have a fair system that has public consent while we continue to bring down the illegal misuse of our systems.

If I may say so, it is a bit rich for Government Members to point at Opposition Members when they voted against every single piece of our legislation to reform the illegal migration system and tackle abuse of the asylum system. Specifically, does the Minister recognise that Bicester, Wethersfield and now Tillingham, in the Maldon district, would not be necessary had her Government not scrapped the Rwanda plan, which has now been adopted by five EU countries—

For deportation purposes, it is the same, because these people are illegal and should not be in our country. Rwanda is a safe country. I ask the Minister: if the policy is okay for five EU countries, what will it take for the Government to relook at those plans, which her Department negotiated in the first place?

The right hon. Lady’s Government had a majority, so I am not quite sure how she can blame us for their legislation not passing. I am afraid there were so many flaws in the Rwanda policy that it was torn to pieces by lawyers, and the reality was that for millions of pounds in taxpayers’ money, only four people went over there.

This Government are committed to listening to local people, which is really important when we think about the sites in not only Bicester but Linton-on-Ouse. Local communities and agencies including in York have set out an evidence base showing why Linton-on-Ouse would be the incorrect site to use: not only will the costs be exorbitant compared with using asylum hotels, putting pressure on the taxpayer, but the infrastructure is completely absent. Will the Minister review the model and ensure that the Government come up with a better model by working with communities to find a solution?

I appreciate the points that my hon. Friend makes. She is always a doughty champion for her constituents, and I look forward to continuing to discuss this issue with her. I am afraid, however, that we are confident that the move towards this kind of accommodation not only protects against the impact on local communities that many people have seen across the country, but provides a fairer deal for the taxpayer and ensures that there is less of a burden on local communities than we have seen over the last few years.

Constituents will be appalled that the Government might spend up to a billion pounds of taxpayers’ cash on opening Piddington—and appalled that the Government accept that it will put women and girls in the locality at risk. There is a simple question here, Minister: why not make it a proper detention centre and detain the illegals behind the wire?

The hon. Gentleman knows perfectly well that we have obligations under the 1951 refugee convention and other legislation that was forged to ensure that when we said “Never again” after the second world war, we meant it. Those people have a right to come here to seek asylum, but we have to ensure that we have 24-hour security on the site. Many of those people are incentivised to behave well because they want their claims to be processed. If the hon. Gentleman took the time to look at existing military sites, he would see that there is zero impact on crime.

I commend the great work our Government are doing to reduce small boat arrivals, but the Minister is aware of my view, because I have told her, that large military sites are unlikely to ever be the best solution for the need to accommodate people who are seeking asylum. What consideration have the Government given to the repurposing of the plentiful vacant office accommodation in our larger cities, where there are existing communities and medical, legal and cultural resources?

I appreciate my hon. Friend’s representations. He knows very well that we have moved to a wide range of accommodation. While emptying hotels that were costly and damaging to local communities, we are looking at a dispersal model of small and medium sites as well as military sites around the country. I encourage my hon. Friend and any local authority that has thoughts and ideas about appropriate accommodation to come forward, because we would always be keen to listen to them.

Some of the language that the Minister has used in the last few answers is quite disturbing. When looking back through Hansard tomorrow, it will seem as though some of the decisions have already been made on Linton-on-Ouse, because the Minister just said in response to the hon. Member for York Central (Rachael Maskell) that these are the most appropriate places to house people. The difference with Linton-on-Ouse is that the village is inside the site. The Minister said that sites would be self-contained. That would suggest that they are secure, but they are not. The children’s playground is but yards from where potential accommodation would be, and the school and the nursery are a five-minute walk away. The Home Secretary said that she would not open hotels or asylum centres near primary schools. Is that still the policy, which would rule out Linton-on-Ouse? The children’s playground is, basically, within the site. Is that a factor? Please will the Minister come to Linton-on-Ouse to see it for herself?

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for his representations. I am very happy to meet him; I hope he has received correspondence from me to say so. To clarify, I am talking about the model. There has been no decision on Linton-on-Ouse; that is under consideration. I want to be absolutely clear on that. As we have made clear, we will take everything into consideration, whether it is local schools, local amenities or local play areas. All of that is taken into account when we make any application. I look forward to meeting him to hear his representations further.

For five years before I was elected, I worked on finding asylum accommodation in Scotland. Time and again, councils and the police would say to us that hotels had been opened by the previous Government without their being informed—they had no clue at all. They would tell us all the time, “If only we knew this was happening, we could put the resources in place and deal with asylum seekers in our communities.” I welcome the Government’s taking a planned approach to asylum accommodation that works with local communities, especially the local police, so that proper resources are in place. Has the Minister been looking at the Home Affairs Committee and National Audit Office inquiries into large sites? Large sites can go well, as they have in Wethersfield, or in Scotland with the Scottish Government’s Ukrainian refugees ships, or they can go badly. Lessons must be learned. Is the Home Office taking steps to look at that?

I thank my hon. Friend for all the work that he and the Home Affairs Committee have done on this issue. We take all the Committee’s recommendations seriously. He is right: the move to military sites and dispersal accommodation is all about having a sustainable and managed approach to the estate, not the chaos that saw the explosion of hotels around the country—often in areas of deprivation because of low cost—that put a huge strain on local communities, with no consent, as he identified, and at great expense to the taxpayer purse.

I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller) on securing the UQ. The issue came up when we were serving on the Immigration and Asylum Bill Committee, and the Minister will remember amendments tabled by my hon. Friend that would have seen the Government needing to bring forward impact assessments about site suitability, cost estimates and a financial breakdown. This is a really emotive issue that is becoming a partisan political football. We could cut through that by taking up those amendments on Report tomorrow. Will the Minister take that opportunity?

I appreciate the amendments; it is important that they are debated fully during the Bill’s proceedings tomorrow. The hon. Member will of course understand that while we will undertake all surveys and mitigations, there are commercial sensitivities, so we may not be able to publish everything at every stage. However, we will always do our utmost so that people have before them all the evidence on these issues that we are able to publish.

The debate has become really unfortunate, and some of the language used to describe the people who will be accommodated in places like Bicester has been truly appalling. It is no wonder that people feel anxious about these facilities when the far-right Reform and the Tories characterise whole groups of people as deviant, a threat and a danger to women and girls in their campaign to divide and to scapegoat whole communities. These are people fleeing unimaginable situations—they deserve and require a right to rebuild their lives. I have asked several times: when will the Government get on top of this? When will they present their challenge to the misinformation and disinformation that spreads from the likes of those sat behind me?

The hon. Gentleman makes a really important point. There are people fleeing war and persecution whom we have historic and moral obligations to support and provide sanctuary. But we also know that our asylum system has been abused. That is why we are taking steps through the Immigration and Asylum Bill, which will be back before Parliament tomorrow, to ensure that we not only protect the rights of people fleeing war and persecution to have protection in this country, but maintain that public consent, which is being eroded by so many, as he said, and driving grievance.

The Minister has been wheeled out to defend the indefensible. She talks about the Government’s consultation, but the Government are clearly not listening, as we see time and again, to the views of the 3,177 people who were against her Government’s project. Why will the Government not listen to local people?

The right hon. Lady expresses shock. I express shock at hearing the Conservative party turning 180° on a policy they were quite happy to champion while they were in power. We are not ignoring concerns raised by residents; we are taking them seriously. They are central to our reforms. As I said, we are closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, because that is what the British public said to us, and that is what they voted on at the last election.

The Government rightly promised to end the use of asylum hotels in their manifesto, but moving illegal migrants out of hotels and in next door was not what voters had in mind. Now, because of the Government’s failure to stop the boats, residents in Piddington are terrified of what will happen to their community. If the Minister is so adamant that there is nothing to see here, why have the Government once again failed to publish the data showing the scale of illegal migrant crime?

The hon. Lady will know of the huge progress made under the Government to end the abuse of our asylum process and to stop the boats. The numbers of people crossing the Channel are down by over 40% this year. Eighty thousand people who had no right to be here have been returned, which is up over 50%. Immigration enforcement has been increased, with an over 80% rise in illegal working arrests. The last Government allowed net migration of 2.5 million in just four years—around one in 30 people in this country came here under the last few years of her Government—so a bit of contrition from the Conservative party would be good.

This is an appalling and frightening decision, not just because of the effect it will have on the people of this small village but because of what it says about the power of the state to impose life-changing impacts on people because the Government have failed in their policy of stopping the invasion of our country by illegal immigrants. Can the Minister confirm whether those who will be housed in this centre will be issued with the Home Office guidance asking them not to rape, sexually abuse or harass the women and children they come across? What assurance does she think that gives to the women of this village, who will be outnumbered by these people by eight to one? Is it not better to send them back to where they came from when they land on our shores, rather than try to rehouse them?

Anyone who has committed a crime on these shores would now be eligible for removal from point zero of their sentence. As I have said, we are removing more people—80,000 people, up more than 50% on the previous Government—so that action will be taken in relation to anyone committing a crime. We take this extremely seriously and we expect anyone coming to these shores to abide by our laws. The right hon. Gentleman seems to be completely unaware that two of these sites are already in operation and the impact on crime has been completely negligible, as expressed by the local chief constable, so his scaremongering does him no service.

My constituents in Woodhouse, Woodhouse Eaves and the surrounding villages in a similar setting to that of Piddington are really concerned that MOD Garats Hay could be next. Will the Minister rule out the use of MOD Garats Hay today and give my constituents some peace of mind?

The hon. Gentleman would be the first to know if we were considering that option. As I have said, we always ensure that we engage with Members of Parliament on any issues pertaining to their constituency. Those whose constituencies are under consideration are fully aware, and that is why we continue to engage with the Members of Parliament affected.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker; I hope your finger is feeling better. Piddington deserves to be heard, but then so did every working-class town and village that Westminster ignored before placing these overwhelmingly fighting-age Muslim men on their streets. Why is it a national outrage when one Oxfordshire village faces a migrant invasion but an acceptable sacrifice for MPs in this Chamber when hundreds of working-class communities across the country suffer the very same fate?

The hon. Gentleman knows that we are proud to undertake our international obligations to support those genuinely fleeing war and persecution. We do everything we can to ensure that those coming here have the right to be here and will be housed in appropriate accommodation. He is right to say that previously there was no consent sought from the communities who had to manage the impact of asylum accommodation on their local communities, with all the costs and impacts on local services. That is why we are making sure, through the use of these former military sites, that people are contained and have a limited impact on local communities.

The illegal migrants this Government intend to house at great expense in Piddington should be deported. The Minister will know that five EU countries have announced their intention to create a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda using facilities paid for by British taxpayers and abandoned by Labour. Does the Minister accept that the only way to stop small boats is to detain those illegal migrants on arrival and to deport them?

I am not going to take any lessons from the Conservatives on stopping small boats, because we saw the situation explode from 2018 onwards on their watch and we are still dealing with the consequences. We have taken action across continents to bring down the numbers of small boats by over 40%.

Does the Minister accept that going down the road of Crown development opens up a totally unregulated vista of permitted development within this site thereafter, and that there are additional permitted development rights for Crown development, including emergency development, under which no one would have to apply for planning permission at all, including development for national security purposes? By adopting the Crown development approach, is not the Minister abandoning all planning control over this site?

The application has been made via this route because the proposed development is considered urgent and of national importance. We are responding to sustained pressures on the asylum accommodation estate, which many colleagues have raised here in the Chamber today, and the need to reduce reliance on hotels. It will enable relevant planning issues to be considered but it does not predetermine the outcome, so no final decision has been taken on the site’s future use.

Like elsewhere in the United Kingdom, communities and constituents in Strangford tell me that they are already feeling the immense strain of the Government’s asylum dispersal policies on local housing, policing and health services, while former military bases are crying out to be used as homes for our veterans. Some 3,177 local residents objected to housing for 1,200 working-age adult men beside a village of 350. The Government have to take note of that, so why are the Minister and the Government riding roughshod over local democracy by using urgent Crown powers? Will the Minister assure the House that similar fast-track powers will not be used to impose large-scale asylum sites on communities in Northern Ireland without full local consultation?

I want to be clear with the hon. Gentleman: we recognise the strength of feeling in local communities. We listen hard to them, as we listen to the representations of Members of Parliament. The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy, but protest must not cross the line into some of the violent behaviour we have seen, including in areas in his part of the world. It is important that we continue to listen to people, and that is why we are closing every single asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into safe, contained accommodation, including these military sites. We want to work with all colleagues in the House to ensure that we house asylum seekers fairly across the country.
I thank the Minister for her responses.

title: Sustainable Farming Incentive: Application Process
turns: What assessment she has made of the adequacy of the application process for the sustainable farming incentive 2026.
The Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs

The sustainable farming incentive scheme that we inherited from the Conservatives was complicated and skewed towards the biggest farms. We have made it fairer and more focused, and this year we ran two application windows, received nearly 19,000 applications and allocated £310 million per year for the next three years. We will open SFI27 as early as we can, and we will work with farmers to see what we can do to change it, including considering alternatives to the first come, first served basis.

Yesterday, we heard in this Chamber many of the shortcomings of this year’s SFI window 2. Just one week after it closed, I visited Ross and Ginny Thomson at Smallacombe farm in my Newton Abbot constituency and their successful herd of milking goats. They described the SFI process as a fiasco. With 40 days and 40 nights of rain, the driest summer on record, multiple heatwaves, plagues of midges spreading bluetongue and now severe drought and yellow warnings of our first named storm, what will the Government do to help Devon’s farmers adapt to the changing climate?

Farmers are bearing the costs of extreme weather, which is why we are supporting them with an extra £65 million to tackle drought, protect crops and build resilience, alongside grants for new technology to boost productivity. For as many farms as possible to benefit from the SFI, we gave small farms a priority in window 1 this year and we have allocated £310 million per year—nearly £1 billion for the next three years—for the scheme. The Government will also invest up to £15 million to help farmers and growers build on-farm reservoirs.

Tomorrow, more than 50 farmers will join me in my constituency for the first ever farming conference, which I have been pleased to organise. We will no doubt discuss concerns related to this year’s SFI, which not only highlights that farmers want to do more to support the environment, but underlines concerns about financial resilience and profitability. Will my right hon. Friend talk more about what the Government are doing to help improve profitability for farmers in South West Norfolk and across the country?

My hon. Friend does a great deal of outreach to the farming community and I commend him for it. We have launched the farming road map, which is the first 25-year plan for farming to give certainty and direction in a very long time. We have set up the Farming and Food Partnership Board, which is looking at how we can improve productivity and profitability, and working on horticulture and poultry growth plans. There will be more to come.

After 18 months of dither and delay, and cuts to the farming budget, Labour’s shambolic SFI scheme closed within hours, leaving farmers unable to access funding to protect and restore nature. We now know, through freedom of information requests, that the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs knew the scheme could collapse within hours, yet the Government pressed ahead regardless. Now, environmental charities, including the Rivers Trust, are warning that that will undermine nature recovery. Does the Secretary of State recognise that by failing the custodians of our countryside, she is failing nature too?

I argue with the hon. Lady’s characterisation of the “collapse” of the scheme. We should not forget that SFI26 made nearly £1 billion of support available for the next three years for environmentally sustainable farming. We have 70,000 multi-year environment land management agreements in place, which are making sure that we support environmentally friendly farming. I would not characterise that as a collapse. I note that the Tories did not spend the whole farming budget when they were in government, they botched Brexit, which led to a 22% fall in trade, and they concluded an Australian trade deal that Tory Secretaries of State now admit has sold out British farmers.

title: Electricity Bills: Levies
turns: What assessment she has made of the impact of environmental and social levies on domestic electricity bills.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero

We are focused on driving down every element of energy bills. We have a strong record of removing levies. We have already moved 75% of the cost of the renewables obligation to the Exchequer and are funding hydrogen projects through public spending rather than consumer bills. No new policy costs will be put on bills until a comprehensive cost control framework is put in place at the spending review in 2027.

That is all well and good, but some 1.5 million households across the UK, including many homes in my constituency, rely on heating oil. They have had no price cap on their heating fuel, yet still face environmental levies on their electricity bills. Why will the Minister not adopt the Conservatives’ cheap power plan to help bring down energy costs for these rural households?

I mean, honestly! The cheap power plan would add over £1,000 in a homes tax by abandoning the future homes standard. The cheap power plan assumes that the price of gas will be stable and low rather than volatile and high, which would be the reality. The Tories are quite literally gaslighting the British people into thinking that higher bills are the result of clean power policies, when what the Tories would do would end up putting up people’s bills.
I call the shadow Secretary of State.

I was going to say, “Finally a dose of reality from the Department for P45s”, with the Secretary of State admitting in an interview on Friday that clean power 2030 was unachievable—a “stretch target” as she put it. That is some stretch. Given that Government now agree with the Conservatives on this and given that the wholesale cost of electricity only contributes 29% of the average electricity bill, why not go the whole hog and, as my hon. Friend the Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) said, adopt the Conservatives’ cheap power plan, and scrap the unfair and damaging net zero taxes and levies that make up so much of people’s energy bills?

The hon. Gentleman needs to be clear about the fact that we are exposed to global fossil fuel prices and are dependent on gas. Greater dependency on gas would make things worse. That is why we are shifting to home-grown, clean, reliable—and therefore cheaper—energy made in this country. That will create jobs and stability, and increase resilience—all the things that the British public are looking for.

title: Late Payments
turns: What steps his Department is taking to help tackle late payments to small businesses.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade

The Government are determined to tackle the scourge of late payments, which causes the closure of 14,000 businesses and costs the UK economy almost £11 billion a year. The Commercial Payments Bill currently progressing through Parliament will give the UK the strongest laws in the G7 and represents the most significant reform of payment practices in over 25 years. The Bill will ensure that small businesses spend more time on growing, investing and creating jobs and less time on chasing late payments.

Late payment destroys thousands of viable small firms each year, and poor practices have seen large firms using small suppliers as a free overdraft. In my constituency, the impact is felt by manufacturers and fabricators, with local metalwork and transport supply sectors facing the longest payment delays in the UK. How is the Minister ensuring that there is a change in payment culture and lifting that burden from small businesses?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right; I know from personal experience how frustrating it is to have large firms use small firms as a source of free finance. The Commercial Payments Bill will clamp down on late payments by introducing maximum payment terms, providing stronger rights to interest and strengthening the powers of the Small Business Commissioner. She is right about the need for a culture change. The message from Government is that this legislation and this change is coming, and large companies should get their payment practices in order right now.

Rising business rates, wages going up, energy prices rising, national insurance contributions—all those things have an impact on small businesses. My small businesses talk to me about the very issue that the hon. Lady referred to: those who do not pay on time. What can be done to help firms who are not getting the money from the suppliers? Is there somewhere that they can refer to for help?

The hon. Gentleman is right to raise the issue. I know it is a huge problem in Northern Ireland, as it is in the rest of the UK. One of the great problems with the current system is that a small business has to be aggressive towards its own customers to chase those late payments. The Commercial Payments Bill will turn that power relationship on its head, and people will expect to be paid on time. If they are not, there will be mandatory interest on that.

title: Illegal Use of Electric Bikes and Scooters: Policing
turns: What plans she has to bring forward legislative proposals to support police to tackle the illegal use of e-bikes and e-scooters.
The Minister for Policing and Crime

We all recognise the concern about the illegal use of e-bikes and e-scooters. We have taken action through the Crime and Policing Act 2026. Police no longer need to issue a warning before seizing vehicles that are being used antisocially. We have also reduced vehicle disposal timeframes to seven days, so we are taking action, but we are very much in the market for seeing what else we can do.

I welcome the new police powers to seize illegal e-scooters and e-bikes that, quite frankly, are out of control. In Epsom and Ewell, Operation Scramble seized 15 vehicles and made six arrests in two days, but some police are hesitant to engage in pursuits because of concerns for wider public safety. It is clear that the police cannot address this issue alone. With Christmas approaching, will the Minister commit to a national awareness campaign to ensure that the general public understand the law around e-scooters, and appreciate that they are legal only if they are part of a rental scheme or are being used on private land?

I thank the hon. Member for her thoughtful question. We hear what she says about e-bikes. We are having conversations with the College of Policing and others about how we can ensure that the police can respond in the way that they want to. In a big operation last month, the Met arrested 187 people and seized 157 vehicles in a crackdown on e-bikes, and Met police are using Sur-Ron bikes in that operation, so we are very much having conversations with colleagues to see what more we can do.

Cumbria police do really good work tackling the use of illegal e-bikes, but with ever-growing numbers of them hitting our streets every single week, Cumbria’s police, fire and crime commissioner and I believe that the single biggest help that we could give the police would be to ban the sale of illegal e-bikes, as my ten-minute rule Bill proposes. What discussions has the Minister had with colleagues in the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade about regulation to achieve that?

I thank my hon. Friend for her work on this issue. We are talking to the Department for Transport about exactly what we need to do to tackle the scourge of e-bikes and e-scooters. Every MP in this place will be facing the same challenge, and I hope that everybody would agree that we cannot allow this kind of behaviour to continue. We are looking at what else can be done. We have changed the powers in the Bill to move us in the right direction. I am talking to the police about what more support they need, and we will continue to have those conversations across Government.

title: Lancashire Fire and Rescue Service
turns: I am really grateful to have secured this debate to raise the financial position of the Lancashire fire and rescue service, and I thank the Minister for being here to respond. I want to begin by paying tribute to all the staff, the firemen and women, and the people who keep Lancashire safe, be it in house fires, wildfires and accidents on the road, or educating and helping our communities. Every one of them makes a contribution, and when the worst happens, they are the ones who turn up and walk into danger to protect us. I know that Lancashire is very grateful, and I certainly am. Obviously, Burnley and Padiham’s fire stations and fire crews are the best. I pay particular tribute to Chief Officer Jon Charters, who is in the Gallery today; the Lancashire fire and rescue authority; and Councillor Azhar Ali, of Brierfield in my constituency, and Councillors Mark Clifford, Ged Mirfin and Luke Parker, who are also in the Gallery. The purpose of this debate is to seek a sustainable funding solution that protects Lancashire’s fire engines, fire stations and firefighter numbers, renews essential facilities and sustains the service’s contribution to national resilience, which we know was tested over the summer in tackling wildfires and more. I will set out the local financial position, the action already taken, and four issues on which I would like a response from the Minister. I have known him for many years, and he is a great friend of our emergency service workers, including firefighters, so I know that he will do all he can to aid our endeavours. The Lancashire fire and rescue authority has set a balanced budget for 2026-27, which is to its credit, but its latest medium-term financial strategy shows that a further £4 million of recurring annual savings will be required by 2030-31. I do welcome this Government’s three-year settlement and the strengthened funding floor for 2026-27. A multi-year settlement is certainly what fire services and public authorities more generally have asked for over many years, and this Government have delivered it. However, that on its own has not removed the £4 million black hole. That figure is not a sign that nothing has been done locally—quite the opposite. In 2026-27 alone, the service has made £1.8 million of recurring savings through changes to crewing, including reduced whole-time crewing levels and dynamic resourcing, on top of more than £1.6 million of efficiencies beyond firefighter staffing. Those savings are already in the budget, and the £4 million is what is left after them, in 2030-31. Support services were cut hard through the long years of austerity, and the authority has concluded that, although further efficiencies may remain possible, certain functions need investment, too. I am here today because, alarmingly, the authority’s own blunt financial assessment is that savings to fill the hole on the scale required would have to come mainly from fire engines, fire stations and firefighter numbers. It is worth being more exact about what that does and does not mean. No specific firefighter posts have been identified by the authority for reduction, but the authority’s judgment is that savings of this size would mean fewer fire engines, and potentially the closure of some on-call fire stations, significantly reducing resilience.

I recently met local firefighters in Blackburn, and I was alarmed and surprised to find that there was just one pump, despite three pumps being available, including the command centre. That means these cuts are putting Blackburn and the surrounding areas at risk. One pump in Blackburn falls short of what the risk assessment for the town has identified. Does the hon. Member agree that we seriously need to look at this?

I think all Lancashire MPs—some are here, and some obviously cannot be here—are as concerned as am I about the funding situation. That is why I have secured this debate, and the hon. Member is right to raise his voice, as he does, for Blackburn. The Lancashire fire and rescue service runs 39 fire stations and 58 fire engines, with an establishment of 600 whole-time firefighters and 423 on-call firefighters, covering busy urban areas alongside a large rural geography, one of the largest in England. It serves some of the most deprived communities in Europe. Five Lancashire districts, including my own town of Burnley, are among those in the most deprived 10th in the country. I say that not to talk down our towns, because I am proud of each one of them, but because deprivation and fire risk unfortunately go hand in hand. The service’s own analysis finds that accidental fires in people’s homes and casualties are concentrated in deprived neighbourhoods. At Prime Minister’s questions in April, I raised the many derelict ex-industrial sites across Burnley, Padiham and Brierfield, many of which are a fire risk or, frankly, have been alight in recent years. I am very happy that the Government awarded £1 million in the derelict building fund at the Budget and I will continue to push for more. At the same time, the service must maintain cover across dispersed rural communities, including through the on-call system. A future funding assessment based on population may miss both sides of that picture, as I am sure the Minister has heard from rural areas as well as from me. But despite pressures, risks and a complicated county to protect, this is also a fire service at the very top of its game. The fire service inspectorate’s 2025 report awarded Lancashire six outstanding and five good grades, with no area graded below good. We are proud of that. Lancashire also holds the national wildfire lead, hosts the specialist national resilience wildfire team in Bacup and this summer supported services in Manchester—it could have been Oldham, Hampshire or Wales—while keeping its own emergency services running at home. It leads nationally on on-call firefighting, firefighter fitness, and on drones and robotics, where a Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government-funded heavy-lift drone programme is now at the testing stage. Its wider capabilities include urban search and rescue, high-volume pumping and international search and rescue deployment capability. Specialist search dog work and the adoption of Lancashire’s assurance monitoring system by other services provide further examples of its contribution beyond the county. Lancashire is about national preparedness, as well as a good local service. That brings me to the four issues I want to raise for the Minister’s attention.
I give way to my hon. Friend.
On the subject of Lancashire fire and rescue service, I call John Slinger.

My hon. Friend is making a very good speech. On exactly that point about his local fire and rescue service, he is speaking about how fire and rescue services help one another at times of great need, and this summer was one such example. Warwickshire fire and rescue service saw an enormous rise in the number of incidents—the highest on record, up by 39% from July 2025. Does he agree that this shows that the concern he is raising today is critically important for all our communities, in Lancashire, Warwickshire and across the country? I know that the Minister cares deeply about this issue and will ensure that our fire officers, who are brave and resilient, will get the resources they need.

I agree with my hon. Friend’s intervention, and he has done well to get his foot in the door—you were particularly understanding, Madam Deputy Speaker. I quite agree and I pay tribute to the fire services in Warwickshire, Yorkshire, Scotland, Hampshire and elsewhere. The first issue is council tax. Lancashire’s band D fire precept for 2026-27 is £94.73, against a national average for combined fire authorities of £100.21. That leaves Lancashire £5.48—for those mathematicians in the Chamber—a year below the average, or roughly 10p a week. The fire authority has asked for flexibility to close that gap in a single year from 2027-28, on top of the £5 increase already assumed in its budget, with the final amount depending on the national average at that point. It estimates that this could raise around £2.5 million a year, which is substantial. I know household budgets in Burnley, Padiham and Brierfield are tight—everybody’s are—and I do not take raising bills lightly, so let me be clear about what is being asked. This is not a rise; it is the freedom for the fire authority to decide locally whether around 10p a week extra is worth paying to protect the fire engines, stations and the services that residents need. So first, I ask the Minister whether that flexibility can be provided and whether a decision can be made in sufficient time to inform the authority’s budget in 2027-28. The second issue is firefighters’ pensions. I know a review is ongoing and the Minister will be limited in what he can say today, but if the pension revaluation—there are some hypotheticals here, I understand—brings down the employer contribution rate, the authority wants to keep that benefit rather than see its Government funding cut by the same amount, because otherwise any subsequent saving from the review will give the service no extra spending power and feels like a lose-lose for all involved. No cash figure is attached, so this is about the principle: if there is a saving at a later date, can Lancashire keep it to support its services? Together, council tax flexibility and retained pension savings are sought to close the £4 million recurring gap and protect fire engines, fire stations and firefighter numbers. Neither benefit is included in the current forecast, and the retention of pension savings is dependent on the review outcome and, I understand, is speculative at this stage. My third issue is probably my biggest concern: capital. This issue is completely separate from the £4 million revenue black hole that I mentioned. A 2025 condition survey found that 38% of stations and corporate buildings run by Lancashire fire and rescue service were in a poor condition, with some buildings dating back to the 1800s. I do not speak for Mr Speaker—I would not dare—but he is aware that I intended to make this reference. I will use the authority’s own assessment of the Chorley estate to back up my points about my concerns. The Chorley training facilities were best in class 40 years ago, and they are now at the end of their useful life, as the authority has said. The facilities include buildings that have reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete. On the estate, priorities include replacement stations at Preston and Fulwood, new training facilities at Chorley, and an estate upgrade across the piece. After capital receipts, plans for backlog maintenance and essential works leave a borrowing requirement of around £50 million to get the Lancashire fire and rescue estate up to scratch, with repayments of around £4 million a year. The authority is asking the Government to reinstate capital grants, last received in 2014, for backlog maintenance and essential works across the wider estate. Closing the revenue gap would not pay for these works, and a predictable programme would reduce the need to borrow, or to fund the works using service budgets. My fourth and final issue is the funding formula. The comprehensive review that we are undertaking is intended to inform funding from April 2029, and funding really does need reform; it is overdue. I am keen to ensure that deprivation, resident vulnerability, incident risk, rurality, on-call sustainability and the cost of resilience are properly recognised in the review; I hope that the Minister can reassure me on that. I suggest that the outcome of the review be tested on Lancashire, and that the results be published before the review’s implementation, so that any loss does not widen our potential revenue gap, and so that we can act as a national example. These are three separate questions. There is the £4 million revenue black hole from 2030 that I am concerned about; the estate needs investment; and there is the question of how funding is shared from 2029. After consulting the authority, I am concerned that local action alone cannot resolve these issues without affecting the frontline. I would be grateful if the Minister could respond to the four points I have raised. First, will the Minister consider the authority’s request for council tax flexibility from 2027-28? Secondly, will he confirm that Lancashire may be able to benefit from any reduction in firefighter employer pension contributions? Thirdly, will he consider capital grants for the backlog? I am not sure if he has brought his chequebook today. Lastly, will the Government test the effect of the revised formula on Lancashire before it is implemented more widely, and ensure that local services are protected from adverse or dramatic funding changes resulting from the review? I understand that not all those commitments can be given at the Dispatch Box today, so I hope that the Minister will meet me and Lancashire combined fire authority to talk about our great county, and our wider fire and rescue needs. Our firefighters are there for Burnley, Padiham and Brierfield—the most important bits of Lancashire—and for the whole of Lancashire, every single day and night. Getting this right will allow them to keep us all safe, and it will mean that they are there when we need them. I said it at the start, and I say it again: I want to give a huge shout out to all the firefighters across Lancashire, particularly at the Burnley and Padiham stations, and specifically those at the Padiham station who are on call, for all the work that they do, and have done over this summer.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government

Before I respond, can I just say that our thoughts are with Ibrar Ali, the councillor from Bradford, following the horrific attack that took place today? Our thoughts are with him, his family, councillors in Bradford, and local Members of Parliament at this time. I am grateful to my hon. Friend the Member for Burnley (Oliver Ryan) for securing this important debate and giving the House an opportunity to consider the funding of the Lancashire fire and rescue service. I congratulate him on his success in securing funding for the Manchester Road train station access improvements —evidence, if it was needed, that he is an effective and committed champion of the people of Burnley. As my hon. Friend knows, our fire and rescue services do so much more than respond to fires. They work tirelessly to keep our communities safe, including by responding to evolving risks, such as wildfire, and undertaking critical prevention and protection work. I echo the thanks to Jon Charters, the chief fire officer, members of the Lancashire combined fire authority, some of whom are in the Gallery, and all Lancashire’s firefighters and control staff, and the wider workforce, for the work that they do every day to protect communities across Lancashire, Blackburn with Darwen and Blackpool. That commitment is reflected in the service’s strong performance. In its most recent inspection, published in August 2025, His Majesty’s inspectorate of constabulary and fire and rescue services rated Lancashire outstanding in six areas and good in the remaining five. That is a significant achievement, and it reflects the commitment of the service’s leadership and workforce. The Government recognise the importance of providing fire and rescue services with the resources and certainty that they need to protect their communities. The ’26-27 local government finance settlement marked an important step in that direction; it was the first multi-year settlement for local government in 10 years. Nationally, almost £1.95 billion in core funding power will be available to stand-alone fire and rescue authorities in England. At the final settlement, the Government announced a further £15 million for fire and rescue services, ensuring that every stand-alone fire authority receives an increase of at least 3.8% in 2026-27. For Lancashire fire and rescue authority, core spending power increases from £78.1 million to over £81 million in ’26-27—an increase of almost £3 million. I recognise the financial and operational pressures that Lancashire continues to face. The multi-year settlement provides an increase in resources, alongside greater certainty to support effective workforce, financial and investment planning. However, we all know that funding is only part of the picture. The risks facing fire and rescue services are changing, with services increasingly needing to respond to a broader and more complex range of incidents, while continuing their fundamental work of preventing fires and protecting the public. That is why this Government are looking beyond individual funding settlements towards longer-term reform and resilience in the sector. I want to reflect on the work of Baroness Blake in the other place, who gives important leadership on this matter. We are investing approximately £97 million through the new dimensions 2 programme, the largest-scale upgrade to fire national resilience in nearly 20 years. This investment will help to ensure that fire and rescue services have the specialist capability and equipment that they need to respond effectively to major and critical incidents. We also continue to work with the sector on the changing role of fire and rescue services, ensuring that they are equipped to respond to current and future threats. Wildfires are an important example. The Government continue to work with the National Fire Chiefs Council, fire and rescue services and other partners to strengthen national wildfire prevention, preparedness and response. The Government have also established a wildfire fund to support additional costs incurred by English fire and rescue services during this summer’s unprecedented wildfires. Following the recent wildfire summit chaired by the Prime Minister, the Government have committed to an additional £45 million to provide lightweight personal protective equipment and ground capabilities to fire services. Lancashire is playing an important part in that work—again, my thanks to Jon Charters, the National Fire Chiefs Council’s strategic lead for wildfire, who works closely with Government on national wildfire policy and capability. Lancashire fire and rescue service is also supporting national capability development through the national resilience wildfire pilot. In 2025-26, the Government provided Lancashire with £440,000 in capital funding to develop and test heavy-lift drone technology for wildfire suppression. That innovative project has the potential to not only strengthen Lancashire’s capability, but inform our national response to wildfires. Lancashire therefore has an important contribution to make as we consider how fire and rescue services can adapt to changing risks and continue to protect our communities. Lancashire fire and rescue service has much to be proud of. It is a high-performing service. It plays an important role in national work on wildfires and on-call firefighters, and its workforce continues to protect communities across Lancashire every single day. The Government recognise the pressures facing fire and rescue services, and will continue to work constructively with Lancashire combined fire authority, Jon Charters, the board and local MPs to make sure that we take full account of the situation. We have done the work on the multi-year finance settlement and fair funding—we have also done a lot to rebuild sustainability in the sector—but we do not take that for granted at all. These are still challenging times for authorities. I am happy to commit to a follow-up meeting, at which we can talk in more detail about my hon. Friend’s fire authority. If he wants to bring the chief fire officer and members of the authority along to that meeting, I will make sure that Baroness Blake and I can be there. [Interruption.] I can see that my hon. Friend might want to moderate who attends that meeting, which is fine. My final word is this: I know that my hon. Friend cares passionately about his community. Not a debate goes by where he does not champion the good folk of Burnley and Lancashire, and long may that continue. I can assure him that he has a Government willing to work in partnership on that endeavour. Question put and agreed to.

title: Continuity of Care in the NHS
turns: What plans she has to improve continuity of care in the NHS.
The Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety

One of the reasons the Government committed to bring back the family doctor was the importance of maintaining continuity of care for patients. I am pleased to say that the proportion of patients who say they are able to see their preferred clinician when they make a GP appointment has risen from 61% to 68% since the election, but we recognise that there is more to do, and this remains an important priority for the Government.

Has the Minister read the Norwegian population study published in the British Journal of General Practice, which says that people who see the same doctor over many years are 30% less likely to need out-of-hours care, 28% less likely to need emergency care and 25% less likely to die? It has been two years since the Government made the pledge to bring back the family doctor, but the basic structure of general practice has not changed. Can we see some changes in the next GP contract negotiations to bring back the system we used to have, in which everyone has their own doctor?

I recognise the enormous experience and knowledge of the former Secretary of State for Health and his work on this issue and patient safety more generally. The Department has started to look at expert advice, with a clinical working group, on how best to support continuity of care in modern general practice. I have not read the report that he referred to, but I am happy to go and have a look it. I am also happy to have a discussion with him, because it would be helpful to understand his thinking on what I know he considers to be a very important issue.

Continuity of care in maternity services is based on women building relationships with maternity practitioners who meet them where they are. I would like to echo the comments of the hon. Member for North Shropshire (Helen Morgan): many obstetricians and midwives have been truly disappointed at comments from an NHS leader yesterday, who argued that more maternity units should be shut and that only consolidation of services can make births safer. Women in this country will not accept the industrialisation of our bodies. This Labour Government have promised neighbourhood and preventive healthcare, which has to include allowing new mums to feel rooted in the communities where they will go through their biggest physical and psychological change. Can the Minister assure me that our bodies will not be treated like a manufacturing supply chain to be optimised as she develops the asks for maternity services in this country?

Gosh, my hon. Friend made a very passionate statement there, and I absolutely agree with what she said. This work will be undertaken with the national maternity and neonatal taskforce, and we will look at all these issues. I hope my hon. Friend will feel able to contribute to that work if she wishes to.

Continuity of care is desirable but not always possible, and in circumstances where it is not, a single patient record offers an opportunity to improve care, but it also brings the risk of unauthorised access to notes. We have seen recent high-profile cases where notes have been accessed that should not have been. That has led to people across the country worrying that this issue could affect them personally in less high-profile cases and about what will happen when the single patient record will be available nationally. How are the Government going to protect patient confidentiality?
Order. It is a struggle to get from the original question to where we are, but the Minister is happy to answer.

I will be mindful of your comment, Mr Speaker. What happened recently is totally unacceptable, and the Secretary of State has made that clear. My understanding is that those individuals who have accessed information about patients, and had no businesses to access it, have been suspended. Disciplinary action will follow, possibly with dismissals. Such actions are totally unacceptable.

Another issue that affects continuity of care is when patients remain in the emergency department for prolonged periods after a decision is made to admit them to a ward. That has gone up by over a third since the general election. Can the Government say why?

Times in A&E are being speeded up. The hon. Lady speaks with experience because she is a clinician, and I am happy to go away and look at that issue and write to her if there is information we need to let her have. My understanding is that we are speeding things up in A&E, and getting people through and on to the ward as quickly as possible.[Official Report, 28 October 2026; Vol. 792, c. 2WC.] (Correction)

title: Level of Threat: Russia
turns: What assessment he has made of the level of threat from Russia.
The Secretary of State for Defence

Terms such as “hybrid threats” and “grey zone” fail to convey adequately the seriousness of Russia’s widespread campaign of what I prefer to call state-sponsored terrorism, which it is inflicting across our continent. We expect it to continue probing and testing Britain and her allies, including through military posturing and reckless military activity. We are not at war with Russia, nor do we seek confrontation, but Russia should be in no doubt that we are ready to defend every inch of NATO territory and that we will not be deterred in our unwavering support for Ukraine.

To deter Russia, we need vigilance at home and the support of our allies abroad. I am sure the whole House will agree that Vladimir Putin’s decision to continue to bomb and target civilian and energy infrastructure in Ukraine is proof that he is not interested in a ceasefire, so does my right hon. Friend agree that, at this moment, our allied response should be to give even greater support to Ukraine and President Zelensky and to look at what further sanctions we could place on Russia?

I wholeheartedly agree with my hon Friend. At the next meeting of the Ukraine defence contact group, I will be continuing to mobilise practical support from our allies. When I was in Washington last week, I made our view very clear that Ukraine’s frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy everywhere, and that we need to stand together to increase the cost of this war to Putin, because only Putin has the means to end this war. If Ukraine were to cease fire tomorrow while Russia continued, it would pay a heavy price in casualties and in the very freedom that the United Kingdom and all our allies seek to defend.

I am grateful for the Secretary of State’s last answer, because it is important that the American President and the US Defence Secretary understand that Russia started this war. Did the right hon. Gentleman also point out that the President’s decision to buy diesel from Russia is actually funding Iran, because the Russians are buying it in from Iran, and that it is therefore counterintuitive to what the Americans are trying to achieve with their blockade?

There is no doubt that Russia presents a threat and is an adversary of the United States as well as of the United Kingdom. We see that with the company that Russia chooses to keep and with the risk that Russia poses to US interests and US personnel as well as our own in the way that it conducts itself. The United States has not been alone in buying fuel from Russia. We have had similar challenges here on the European continent in relation to Russian gas. The more that Putin’s war machine is funded, the longer this war goes on and the higher the price for everyone. That price is being paid most of all by the Ukrainians, who did not start this war and who lack the means to end it. Only Putin can do that. He could stop the war tomorrow; he chooses not to do so.

Part of the growing threat from Russia—and it is growing —includes increased maritime activity, both in the English channel and in the surveillance of critically important undersea cables, including by specialist Russian submarines. Part of our response should surely be to increase our own submarine patrols around our shores. However, for many months, not a single one of our Astute class attack submarines has been on patrol. I know that it is not the Government’s policy to comment on submarine movements, but I am asking about the absence of submarine movements. Why, on Labour’s watch, have our attack submarines been embarrassingly tied up alongside for months at a time, while the Russians are roving in the North sea and the Atlantic?

However the shadow Minister phrases his question, he is not going to tempt me to comment on operational deployments. He understands perfectly well why we choose not to do that. Secondly, I point him to recent exercises we have conducted in the North sea and to our leadership of the joint expeditionary force. To go to the heart of his question about our armed forces and their readiness, perhaps the next time he or his party want to get to their feet to lecture us about the state of our armed forces, they might begin with an apology for underfunding them for more than a decade.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

Last week, Ukrainian forces were reportedly left exposed to Russian attacks after the US President acted to restrict access to Starshield, showing that the White House is prepared to pressure American companies to interfere in allied military operations, and the importance of sovereign control over military satellite communications in facing the Russian threat. Now the Government are reportedly considering a low-ball American bid to operate Skynet—a system conceived during the cold war to guarantee British sovereignty over military satellite capability—threatening hundreds of jobs in Portsmouth, a great military city still reeling from losing shipbuilding. The Government talk about buying British and strengthening sovereign capability, and here we have a proven world-leading system operated by a European company, so can the Defence Secretary explain to me and the people of Portsmouth why he is considering handing operation of this critical sovereign capability to the US?

The hon. Gentleman will understand why I will not comment on that during a live procurement. The matter is still under consideration. To be clear, we take sovereign capability and control very seriously. It is also worth pointing out, after what was unquestionably a challenging week for relations between the United States and Ukraine, that the United States has provided and will continue to provide vital support to Ukraine, whether that is through intelligence sharing, the work we do on procurement with and through the United States, or the diplomatic track. It is worth reporting to the House that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, my US counterpart, was keen to thank the United Kingdom for our leadership on Ukraine. That suggests to me that the United States does know which side it is on.

title: Commonhold and Leasehold Reform
turns: What her planned timetable is for introducing the commonhold and leasehold reform Bill.
What steps she is taking to reform the leasehold sector.
The Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government

The Government will introduce the commonhold and leasehold reform Bill this year, marking the beginning of the end of the feudal leasehold system. We will continue implementing the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 as quickly as possible, and we will bring forward further legislation for the independent statutory regulation of property agents.

I recently met constituents in Grayshott and Haslemere who face poor communication from managing agents, with little transparency on where the service charges and costs that they are forced to pay go. Meanwhile, Surrey and Hampshire are set to lose out under the Government’s funding review, leaving many of those same residents facing higher council tax bills. Will the Secretary of State finally tell us when the leasehold reform Bill will be published, and give a guarantee that any savings delivered through that reform will not simply be wiped out by the higher council tax bills caused by her Government’s funding decisions?

We promised that we would bring that legislation forward soon, possibly in time for it to be a Christmas present—you never know, Mr Speaker. Council tax went up every year under the Conservatives. They left local governments without the funds they needed; we have funded councils on the basis of need. We support the councils; the Opposition did not.

Leaseholders living on Barrington Road and St James’s Crescent in my constituency, in buildings owned by Metropolitan Thames Valley housing association and built by the contractor Guildmore, have been trapped in limbo for more than four years. They are unable to sell and worried about fire safety, while MTVH and Guildmore continue to argue between themselves about who is responsible for fire safety defects in the building, who will complete the remediation, and who will pay for it. There is still no plan or timescale, and communication has stalled. The last substantive update that I received was back in May of this year. Can I ask the Secretary of State for her personal support and intervention in unlocking this completely unacceptable dispute, so that my constituents can at last sleep soundly in their homes and make plans for their futures?

The building safety crisis must be resolved. Homes must be made safe and residents must be allowed to move on with their lives. We brought forward the remediation acceleration plan, which I discussed on the Floor of the House last week, and I am happy to meet with my hon. Friend. I have met with many organisations as part of that plan: some are doing well, but most are not good enough.

title: Airport Drop-off Charges
turns: What assessment she has made of the potential impact of increases in airport drop-off fees on airport users.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Transport

The Government recognise that airport drop-off charges can be a source of frustration for passengers, particularly where payment arrangements are unclear, signage is difficult to follow or motorists face additional charges for late payment. Recognising those concerns about the impact of airport drop-off charges on passengers, the Government have committed to undertake a review to ensure that travel remains accessible and passengers are treated fairly.

I thank the Minister for that answer, but I am sure he recognises that drop-off charges at UK airports have risen sharply in recent years, with Newcastle now charging £6, while London Stansted and Gatwick both charge £10, even though drop-offs are totally free at most major European airports, including eight of Europe’s 10 busiest. The airports justify it as a much-needed income stream, but for many travellers it feels more like pinching the pockets of hard-working families. The Minister mentioned the review; is he able to elaborate on the promise to review those charges? Will the review address the issues of affordability and accessibility for my constituents?

Let me be clear: we expect airports to treat passengers fairly and to ensure that travel remains accessible. The review is going to look at the impacts of airport drop-off charges on users of airport services. The detailed scope will be developed as part of the review process, but it could include affordability, accessibility, travel behaviour and the experiences of different groups of passengers. More broadly, the Civil Aviation (Consumer Protection and Regulatory Reform) Bill, which has just been through Committee, seeks to modernise the United Kingdom’s aviation legislative framework. One of its key objectives is to strengthen consumer rights and protections, particularly for those who travel with disabilities.
I call the shadow Secretary of State.

I really welcome the Government’s U-turn on adopting Conservative policy and deciding to review airport drop-off charges, but in response to my written question, the Minister did not confirm that the Government’s anti-car surface access targets, the more than 100% increase in business rates that many airports have faced, or the crippling increases in employment taxes will form part of that review. Will the Minister ensure that all these important factors form part of the inquiry into what is leading to airport drop-off charges soaring under his Government?

The shadow Secretary of State does not seem to want to face up to the fact that this Government are taking decisive action to help our airports and airlines, whether it is signing off airport expansion across the country or modernising our airspace to provide community benefit alongside efficiencies. I have already been clear that the review will look at questions of affordability and access to airports. That is the right way to ensure that we have a system that is proportionate for consumers and airport users while addressing the fact that, as he mentioned, planning considerations are often built in with mode share targets that are linked to airport drop-off charges. This Government will take a proportionate approach to that review and to the aviation sector as a whole.

title: Poundland
turns: (Urgent Question): To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade if he will make a statement on the situation at Poundland and potential actions to protect jobs.
The Minister for the Future of Work

I declare my interest as a member of the Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers. I am deeply concerned about the uncertainty surrounding Poundland’s future, and the impact that could have on its thousands of staff and their families, who are at the forefront of my mind, especially in the run-up to Christmas. Poundland is not currently in administration and the business continues to trade, but this is a worrying time for employees, suppliers and communities. We are establishing the facts, keeping in close contact with those involved and monitoring developments closely. The Secretary of State and I continue to engage closely on this issue. We have met and are in ongoing contact with the trade union USDAW, which I know is extremely concerned about the jobs and livelihoods of its members, and I thank it for its work and engagement. We will be meeting Barry Williams, the managing director of Poundland, this week. Earlier this week, officials met Gordon Brothers, and the Secretary of State is due to meet it to continue to press our concerns and establish the facts. However, there are ongoing commercial negotiations concerning this private business, and it would not be appropriate for the Government to seek to influence the outcome or comment on the merits of individual bids. The owners should act in the best interests of their loyal UK staff and stores. We want the best possible outcome for Poundland’s workforce and the future of the business. The 12,000 staff and many thousands of suppliers are at the forefront of our minds, and we want to see an outcome that protects as many jobs as possible and keeps as much of the business trading as possible. The Government stand ready to ensure that affected employees can access the appropriate support, should it be needed. The Prime Minister has set out his aspiration to bring good growth to every postcode, including by making high streets a new symbol of Britain’s renaissance. Last week, the Government published our high streets strategy, which goes further and sets out the principles for high street success, practical support for businesses with the business rates system and more policies to support vibrancy and footfall. That includes establishing a “high streets first” principle to ensure that public estate locations drive footfall and opportunities to co-locate public services. The fundamentals for doing business in the UK are strong. Our economic strategy to deliver growth is investment across the public and private sectors and in every postcode. Our industrial strategy, trade strategy, small business strategy and plan to make work pay address long-standing barriers to growth. Retail is vital to employment and the economy, and we recognise that the sector has been through a significant period of change. We want all types of retail to thrive, now and in the future, so we are working closely with businesses to understand what they need to succeed and grow. The Minister for Employment and I are providing a briefing for Members of Parliament in this House this afternoon on the support available to employees who may be impacted. I want to emphasise that in the event that a retail company enters administration, my officials will work, where appropriate, with the administrators, the Department for Work and Pensions, the Insolvency Service and local partners to ensure that appropriate support is available to affected employees. We stand ready to support them if they need to move into new employment. However, our priority is always protecting jobs, and the Secretary of State and I will continue to engage with the company to secure the best possible outcome.

Thank you, Mr Speaker, for granting this urgent question. I thank the Minister for the tone and content of her answer. At the heart of this matter are the 11,000 people whose jobs, through no fault of their own, hang in the balance, and who do not know whether they will have a job at all this side of Christmas. Those jobs are not concentrated in a big factory, but dispersed across this country in towns such as Hanley in Stoke-on-Trent and in your constituency of Chorley, Mr Speaker, as well as in the supply chains and distributors in Makerfield and Harlow, which my hon. Friend the Member for Harlow (Chris Vince) talked about. This company has survived because the workers turned it around. We are in the situation that we are in today because choices have been made by Gordon Brothers. It has rejected solvent bids and is seeking to push a company into administration for its own personal profit. Fundamentally, its interest does not appear to be the 11,000 constituents we all represent, who take home money to look after their kids, put food on the table and live the life that they deserve. I am very glad that the Minister continues with meetings, but the management of Poundland is not the problem; it is Gordon Brothers. If we get to a point where administration takes place and 11,000 jobs and supply chain jobs are put at risk, what levers can the Minister use to save as many jobs as she can? What pressure can this House, through her, put on the owners to accept one of the solvent bids in order to protect jobs? What can this House do to send a message to Gordon Brothers that its predatory capitalism when it comes to this company will not be tolerated? We in this country will always stand with people before profit.

I thank my hon. Friend for his reflections and comments on behalf of his constituents and the many employees across the country. It is deeply concerning to see the uncertainty about Poundland’s future. That is why the Secretary of State, the Prime Minister and I have been keeping a close eye on this extremely worrying situation for staff, their families and communities up and down the country. We have been demanding to know what is happening, and demanding that Gordon Brothers explain why it has not accepted any offer to keep the company going. We continue to establish the facts.
