Until we get to the end of that process, we will not really know where we are in providing competition to the big suppliers, but everyone is aware that it is a problem that we have little choice in this marketplace other than to use some of these global providers, and the Government are actively working to resolve that.

Many of my constituents rely on terrestrial TV and radio, and Friday’s outage showed us what happens when digital goes down. In the light of this morning’s recommendation by the Lords National Resilience Committee, will the Minister rule out switching off terrestrial television—the back-up that keeps working when digital goes down? I am very concerned that not ruling that out would present a very real threat to our national security.

I am very grateful to my hon. Friend for raising the issue of the future of TV distribution, which was raised in our media Green Paper; the consultation on that has finished, and the White Paper will be produced shortly. We took the decision in the Green Paper to turn off digital terrestrial television, but the issue is what date we use. That is examined in the Green Paper; it will be either 2034 or 2044. We have not made a decision as a Government on that date. We have made a decision on what we will do, but not on when we will do it.
I call the Chair of the Culture, Media and Sport Committee.

We are the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee. The Minister has set out very clearly, as have others, the entrenched position of Microsoft in the UK’s digital ecosystem. Considering the great over-reliance of domestic businesses, consumers, Government and local authorities on its software, can the Minister set out how urgent the diversification and resilience building that he mentioned is? Has that urgency changed in the light of what happened on Friday? In addition, the Competition and Markets Authority is currently looking at whether it should designate Microsoft as having strategic market status, and is due to conclude that work in February. Has the Minister’s readiness to respond to that report also changed in the light of Friday’s events?

I am grateful to the Chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee for her questions. It is still DCMS—we need to get that into our minds. The hon. Lady raises two important points. The first, which is about over-reliance on certain suppliers, is well made; that is why the Government have been putting a lot of money into sovereign AI and tech sovereignty in terms of the tech stack. We have the Government cyber action plan that examines the readiness and resilience of individual Government Departments, looking at legacy technology and co-ordination across the piece. We also have the national cloud infrastructure programme, which is about making sure that big, Government-wide procurement can seed UK businesses, looking at cloud sovereignty and making sure that we have a choice of suppliers. We are such a big customer; we need to make sure that we have those suppliers on our shores. We introduced the Government cyber charter to ensure that any strategic suppliers, including Microsoft, are early adopters of Government cyber policy and best practice. That charter sets clear expectations for suppliers, strengthening resilience across Government supply chains and encouraging them to drive the same standards throughout their wider supplier networks. The hon. Lady’s point about Microsoft is well made. The Government contract with Microsoft in a way that is very deep and broad. That gives us an economy of scale with one of the world’s best suppliers in this area and access to new technology, but it also probably gives us vendor lock-in and a lack of choice in what other vendors we might be able to use. However, this was not a cyber-security incident; it was just a technology failure in one of Microsoft’s operations. This problem was caused by a backlog of data going through a very narrow lane, as opposed to the service that Microsoft is normally able to provide.

I thank the Minister for his statement. I am not 100% convinced that we know exactly what happened, but I am pleased that he feels that Microsoft is telling the truth. The Minister said that the first job of Government is to protect their citizens. I completely agree, and my Bill—the Artificial Intelligence (Consent and Misuse) Bill—would go a long way towards ensuring that we protect our citizens as AI advances. As has been mentioned, EU countries are migrating away from Microsoft systems; that was mainly driven by the President of the US claiming that he was going to activate the kill switch for Microsoft, which worried a lot of countries. Can the Minister be clear about how we are planning to migrate away from US-based systems and invest a lot more in British-based systems, so that we can have more data sovereignty?

There are a number of answers to that question, and I am grateful to my hon. Friend for raising it. First, let me go through again what this incident involved. We are working very closely with Microsoft, and it has confirmed that this was not an attack on its systems. One of its servers went down due to a defect that had been found; there was a surge in load that brought that bug—that defect—to the fore. There was another completely unrelated issue, which was that a server that accounts for 14% of capacity was also down for maintenance at the time.[Official Report, 17 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 7WC.] (Correction) This outage was caused by the volume of traffic choking the servers that were left, which produced a backlog and brought the servers down. Microsoft resolved the problem relatively quickly. By 2 pm on Friday, services were coming back online. My hon. Friend asked what we are doing to diversify away from US suppliers and the big international suppliers. I have already mentioned the £500 million sovereign AI fund, which is there to back British businesses and promote that sovereignty; the £1.1 billion AI hardware plan; and the £500 million to try to resolve some of these issues that was in this year’s Budget. We have a tech stack that is dominated by US tech companies. We want more AI sovereignty in the United Kingdom; we are willing to fund that, and we are funding it. That is how we will make sure we have the most resilient services, but also the most technologically advanced services, in the UK.

I am grateful to the Minister for making this important statement. Those of us with rural constituencies represent many people who are very worried about the copper switch-off that is coming as we move to fibre. Fibre is an energy-intensive system, unlike the copper system, and it seems to be coming without a delay being considered. Donald Rumsfeld once talked about the known unknowns. We know that an attack will happen somewhere. The Minister has outlined that this outage was a specific issue, but it shows how reliant we are on these systems. The hon. Member for Rotherham (Sarah Champion) talked about the switching off of terrestrial television. These things are of great concern. I urge the Minister to take away what happened on Friday and look at the broader picture. When the known unknown happens and everything gets closed down, the proven and tried systems of copper connections and terrestrial radio and television should be there as a back-up system on which people can rely.

This is an issue for all of us in this Chamber, because we rely on that technology. Similar discussions about whether we are over-reliant on technology probably happened, if we check Hansard, with the invention of the personal computer and the internet. Technology makes us a better economy and makes it easier for businesses to operate. It makes it easier for us all to stay connected and informed. Resilience is a key part of what we are trying to do in government, whether through our cyber action plan or all the other initiatives that I have mentioned from this Dispatch Box. That cyber action plan has £210 million in funding to better utilise cyber-skills and to deliver once and for all, at scale, a co-ordinated approach across Government to tackle all those critical risks that the right hon. Gentleman mentions. The right hon. Gentleman talks about power and national power outages. We know that telecoms networks have substantial power back-ups at core network sites. We have a resilient electricity system, but we cannot plan for every eventuality. It would be wrong for a Minister of any colour to stand at this Dispatch Box and say that we will not have any other cyber-attacks or any other outages such as this. What we need to do is minimise them, minimise the risk and make sure that the Government are in the best place, including in terms of the wider economy.

I declare an interest, as I have a close relative who is working on the regulation of Microsoft. I thank the Minister for his statement. Will he update the House more broadly on how the UK is planning to be more resilient in this field, particularly given that a relatively small number of suppliers have such a critical role in the economy?

As I have said, we recognise that relying on a small number of suppliers can create risks for resilience, competition and value for money. Those suppliers provide us with the very best technology, and we are not trying to swap one dependency for another, but alongside the large global providers, which bring skills, security and capability, we must ensure that we have our own sovereignty in this country in the areas of the tech stack that we are good at. We have put taxpayers’ money where our mouth is to develop that tech stack and that sovereignty, so that we have resilience.

The statement raises the issues of resilience and preparedness in the public and private sectors. Can the Minister and his team do more to support businesses, both small and large—including through the known communication channels, such as the Federation of Small Businesses, Prosper and others—by more widely distributing advice and messages about digital preparedness tools? This has been a significant enough incident to warrant a ministerial statement, but there are rural and remote businesses and public services that tackle digital challenges every single day of the week due to lack of fibre broadband and other issues. Can more be done to roll out fibre broadband even faster?

There was a lot in that question, and I will try to run through it in order. Building Digital UK has Project Gigabit, which is trying to get to 99% of all premises by 2032. Many of those who are most affected and are the hardest to reach will be in the hon. Gentleman’s constituency in the highlands of Scotland. For that 1%, there will be additional technologies—they are evolving all the time—to make sure that everyone is connected. As I have said at the Dispatch Box many times, we cannot have growth in every postcode without connectivity, and the more rural somewhere is, the more difficult it is to have that connection. From the point view of the wider economy and business, the only thing that I can continue to emphasise from this Dispatch Box is that people should use the National Cyber Security Centre’s free tools on cyber-security. That should be on the lips of every board member sitting around the boardroom table. We will have a much more resilient economy with much more resilient businesses only if everybody plays their part.

West London is part of a cluster of data centres where, if there is a problem with one centre, data can be backed up in another. In my constituency, two data centres have recently been agreed by Ealing council, which has taken the position that only data centres with the highest environmental standards will be allowed. Does the Minister agree that clustering data centres in this way is the right approach to digital resilience, along with the Government’s new data centre covenant, which will ensure that we meet our climate commitments?

I could not have put it better myself. We do need data centres for this. If we are talking about AI sovereignty and tech sovereignty, it is best for them to be onshore here in the United Kingdom. That is a big challenge, but we must ensure that it is done correctly, and I pay tribute to Ealing council for the way in which it has done it in its area.

The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill is in its final stages of parliamentary scrutiny, and in this context I particularly note the role of resilience in ensuring our national economic security. What assessment have the Government made of the potential impact in future outages on critical national infrastructure—including communications and supply chains—on which essential services depend, and what further amendments to the Bill might be needed?

The Bill will return to this House relatively soon. It updates the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 to bring some of these companies into scope, including data centres, and contains a provision to extend the scope, if necessary, to include more organisations and more sectors of the economy. It will be back in this House before the end of the year, and we will be able to debate these matters in more detail then, but its purpose is to ensure that we have greater resilience and to update the regulations.

I thank the Minister for coming to the House in such a timely fashion. I know he will have been disappointed to learn today that the new James Bond is not a Scotsman. The Microsoft outage had a huge impact on residents and businesses in my constituency of Harlow, and I was reassured to hear when I contacted my local hospital that it had not been hugely impacted, but will the Minister reassure the House that he will do everything he can to hold Microsoft to account and ensure that there is no spectre of future outages?

I am glad that my hon. Friend managed to talk to his NHS trust and resolve that issue over the weekend. Only two NHS trusts stood up an incident response unit, but it was no longer required so they stood it back down relatively quickly.[Official Report, 17 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 8WC.] (Correction) That shows that the system does work. The co-ordination of the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and the National Cyber Security Centre to bring together the Government Cyber Co-ordination Centre meant that the information was filtered from Microsoft through the Government to trusts and local government so that they could stand up incident responses if they needed to do so, but they did not need to do so in this particular case.

I thank the Minister for his statement, and for his welcome comments about backing more British suppliers that are small and medium-sized enterprises. May I ask him to extend that review and look into not only alternative suppliers of the solutions, but the decision to have software as a service as the default choice every time, so that we can improve the resilience of the services here and possibly even copy the French by developing our own open-source solution?

I can only re-emphasise what I have said already. The Government are backing our work on the tech stack with taxpayers’ money to see how we can seed good businesses in this country that wish to grow and enter these marketplaces. It is difficult for the Government to do that, because the big suppliers are there for us to secure value for money for the taxpayer. However, the current procurement process through the national cloud infrastructure programme is about ensuring that we not only secure the best value for money but have some tech sovereignty on British soil by seeding those companies to make them grow.

Given the Microsoft 365 outage, the Vodafone outage last year and Storm Éowyn, which prevented my constituents from receiving communications, does the Minister agree that sometimes the older ways are the best? In my constituency, we have a 90-year-old transmitter that still transmits analogue. I worry that if the Government go ahead with their plan to switch off analogue, it will cut off people in a way that we know will happen again. What can the Minister tell my constituents to assure them that old technologies will still be considered critical national infrastructure?

The media Green Paper lays out that the Government have already made the choice that we will switch off digital terrestrial television and move to internet protocol television at some point in the future, but the date has not yet been determined—it could be 2034 or 2044. We are examining the consultation to work out the best way forward. The hon. Lady’s constituents can be assured that no decision has been made, and we will take into account the issues that she raises when making that decision.

The Microsoft outage was, of course, a shock—indeed, it was a wake-up call to us all—but it may be that we got away lightly. Imagine if it lasted for a week or a fortnight, enhanced by bad actors. The Minister and other Members have referred to the need for open-source alternatives. Will he commit to coming back within three to six months on plans and progress for such alternatives?

The rhetoric from the hon. Gentleman is not necessarily helpful, because it was an isolated incident at Microsoft. There have been incidents in the past, which he referred to, and there will be incidents in the future. Our job is to make the Government as resilient as possible, and to put in place the tools and legislation to make sure that the economy is as resilient as possible, so that the UK can stand when these kinds of incidents happen.

I am pleased that the Minister has spoken about the steps that this Government will take in relation to digital resilience, because for weeks I have been pointing out a fault in the General Register Office’s new electronic register for births, deaths and stillbirths in England and Wales, which went live earlier this month. Over 70 senior council officials from around 50 local authorities wrote to the Home Office and told it that when the system fails, it is impossible to issue the death certificates needed for the deceased to be repatriated and buried overseas—something that is very important for many religious communities. In response, the Home Office has simply ignored warnings and continued regardless. Does the Minister agree that the lessons of the Microsoft outage should be learned by the Government as well as corporations, and will he agree to raise this matter with his counterparts in the Home Office so that we can prevent a disaster from happening?

I am not aware of that incident, but I will raise it with Ministers in the Home Office to find out what has happened. The hon. Gentleman asks us to learn the lessons from the Microsoft outage, which we and Microsoft will learn, but we were learning lessons before the Microsoft incident, because this Government want to be much more resilient. The Government’s cyber action plan, which was published at the start of this year, is part of that project, and is backed by £210 million of taxpayers’ money. That is about central direction, co-ordination, pace, consistency and clarity when it comes to the resilience of Government, and it is also about making sure that the wider economy has resilience.

I thank the Minister for his very comprehensive answers and for his interest in this matter. When Microsoft goes down, the country grinds to a halt—“IP meltdown” is how we refer to it. In my constituency last week, problems were not only financial. We saw NHS staff forced to use pen and paper, courts forced to adjourn, and councils and schools left scrambling to function. The IT system in my office, and in Government offices, was down until 1.40 pm on Friday, and my constituents and others were disadvantaged as a result. It raises serious questions about our over-reliance on a single system. What steps are being taken to ensure that every Government Department has proper contingency plans and offline back-ups, so that a technical failure never again paralyses our public services?

The hon. Gentleman talks about people reverting to pen and paper and other systems kicking in. The whole point of having a resilience plan is that when things happen across the tech stack or any of the systems, other systems kick in. That is why we did not see widespread disruption across the whole public sector. Yes, it was an inconvenience. My own emails went down until about 2 o’clock on Friday. I know that because the test email I sent myself on Thursday night arrived at about 2 pm on Friday, and the acknowledgment that it had arrived bounced back. The backlog has been cleared, and Microsoft resolved the problem as quickly as it could, but the whole point of the Government’s cyber action plan is to make sure that all Government Departments, local government and our public sector have resilience, and that the private sector also has resilience.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. There are about 300,000 jobs in tech and telecoms in Berkshire—Reading lies in that county and is the county town—and there are many more thousands of those jobs across the country, yet we only occasionally discuss issues related to this very important area of employment. Could there be a debate in the House on the contribution of tech and telecoms to the British economy?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his point of order. As he will know, that is not a matter for the Chair, but he has put on record the great extent of businesses in his constituency that are reliant on tech.
No, there is none in Harlow.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. We have lots of tech companies in Harlow, but my point of order refers to a mistake I made, and as a former maths teacher, I apologise for getting my numbers wrong. Last Thursday, when I spoke in the Backbench Business debate about the battle of the Somme, I referred to Private Thomas Lewis—he lived in my constituency and, sadly, died in the Somme—but I stated his age incorrectly. I said he was 19 when, sadly, he was killed at the battle of the Somme, but he was actually 21. I am taking this opportunity to set the record straight. —[Official Report, 12 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 403.]
I thank the hon. Gentleman for his point of order. He has sought to correct the record at the earliest possible opportunity, although I am far from convinced that that was actually a point of order.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I would like to correct the record of the debate on Friday on the private Member’s Bill promoted by the hon. Member for St Ives (Andrew George). I incorrectly said: “We also build the infrastructure first. We are extending the grid roads, our famous roundabouts and our redways, which means that bicycles and pedestrians do not have to interact with the roads. Those provisions are set out in our council planning.”—[Official Report, 13 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 468.] What I meant to say was “in the local plan”, because as you will know, the council plan has everything in it that the council does, whereas the local plan has statutory standing in planning guidance. Thank you for allowing me to correct the record at the earliest opportunity.
I thank the hon. Member for her point of order. She has indeed done well to correct the record about the difference between a local plan and a council plan, and I am sure we thank her for that.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. Thank you for allowing me to raise this point of order. In fact, it is the first point of order I have raised, so please bear with me. On 4 November, I spoke in the Adjournment debate on the strategic licensing regulations for London, and I am afraid that, as I am still a newbie to this place, I neglected to state an interest in that my partner is the manager of the trading standards and licensing department at Brent council. I believe I should have raised that at the time. A little time has gone by since then, but I am afraid I did not realise that I should have raised the issue until my partner mentioned it to me over the weekend, having noticed that I had spoken in the debate. I apologise for raising this so late. I hope you can assist me in correcting the record, and I will make sure not to make the same mistake again. —[Official Report, 4 November 2026; Vol. 792, c. 969.]
I thank the hon. Member for what I think may actually have been a point of order. She has indeed corrected the record, and I thank her for that.

title: Cross-border Connection
turns: What discussions she has had with the Scottish Borders council on the cross-border connection.

National Grid Electricity Transmission has concluded its first consultation on the English section of the cross-border connection, with further consultation expected next year. The Scottish section is being developed by SP Energy Networks; consenting decisions on that portion are the responsibility of Scottish Ministers. It is for the developers to progress their proposals and to seek the necessary consents.

The mega-pylons comprising the cross-border connection will have a major impact on residents in the Scottish Borders. Data centres, wind farms, solar farms, substations and battery storage plants will follow in the wake of the pylons, but local councillors and residents feel powerless to influence these developments. Will the Minister meet me and local Scottish Borders councillors to discuss their concerns? Will the Government support my Energy and Digital Infrastructure (Planning) Bill, which will provide certainty to local communities and the council on how such developments should be considered?

I have met the hon. Gentleman in the past, and I am very happy to meet again to discuss these issues, but I reiterate that it is not for me to make decisions on those applications; they are made by the Scottish Government, as are decisions on all planning matters in Scotland. He can shake his head, but it is true. It is important that we bring communities with us on this; that is critical in the planning process. It is why we announced that the communities across the UK who host such infrastructure UK should benefit from bill discounts directly, but there should also be community benefits in communities like his.

The proposed route of the cross-border connection cuts a swathe across the north Cumbria section of my constituency and passes through, or close to, four sites of special scientific interest. I recognise the importance of the project, but will the Minister please urge National Grid to maximise undergrounding on this section of the project?

As I said, individual projects have to go through the planning process and develop their proposals, but the Government have a preference for pylons, rather than undergrounding—the previous Government had exactly the same position—not least because undergrounding is four or five times more expensive, and it is consumers across the country who pay that additional cost. We are very clear that building the grid is absolutely critical to getting clean, cheaper power to people’s homes and businesses. It is a job that the previous Government never did, and that upgrade is now absolutely critical.

title: International Update
turns: With permission, I wish to make a statement on the United Nations General Assembly and related international events that have occurred since the House last met. Before I do so, let me first welcome my hon. Friend the new Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Sagal Abdi-Wali) to her place. What a journey, from child refugee to Parliament, and what a country—that this story of hope could happen here. I know my hon. Friend will enhance this House in so many ways, and I look forward to working with her. I took a clear message to the United Nations: after a decade of turbulence, Britain is back and can be relied upon as a consistent and stable partner in an uncertain world, always upholding the shared values set out in the UN charter, rejecting aggression wherever we see it, and always steadfast in our support for Ukraine, as I assured President Zelensky at our meeting in New York. In the three weeks since that meeting, Russian strikes have intensified even further, with more attacks on civilians: on apartment blocks housing innocent families; on buses carrying innocent children. When I spoke to President Zelensky on Saturday, he described the step change from Russia, including daylight attacks intended to break the will of Ukraine and ours. I can tell you, Mr Speaker, that that will never happen. In recent days, we have announced new funding to help Ukraine get through its fifth winter under Russian bombardment and a new sanctions package so that over 90% of Russia’s oil-producing capacity is now covered by UK sanctions. The quickest way to get diesel back on to world markets without rewarding the aggressor is an energy ceasefire, with both sides stopping their attacks. I raised this with President Trump in New York. It is what Ukraine wants to see, so I welcome President Trump’s announcement yesterday of a reciprocal energy ceasefire. President Zelensky has assured me that Ukraine would immediately implement it when a start date is confirmed, and I will be discussing this further with him in the coming days. NATO is a defensive alliance. We do not seek confrontation, but our resolve to defend our allies and ourselves is absolute, and I was clear in all of my meetings, including with the NATO Secretary-General in Oxfordshire, that we will meet our NATO commitments in full. We know that Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe. In Berlin last week, Chancellor Merz and I agreed a new partnership to tackle these hybrid threats. We must be clear-eyed about attempts to destabilise our democracies. It is why, in my speech to the UN General Assembly, I confirmed our commitment to establish a new centre for information defence, as recommended by the Foreign Affairs Select Committee. More broadly, this is a moment to deepen collaboration with our partners, which is why in Berlin I indicated Britain’s openness to Germany joining the global combat air programme alongside Italy and Japan. In my meeting with President Trump, we discussed the situation in the middle east. I confirmed Britain’s decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling support. I can confirm today that it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis. Since UNGA, we have been in close contact with the US about protective security at our shared bases. I thank our police and military personnel for their swift response to the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth. My right hon. Friend the Home Secretary will update the House on the incident at RAF Fairford, but I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm. In my meeting with the President, I also raised the Falkland Islands and the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British. I emphasised that point in my speech to the General Assembly and that we will also always do whatever it takes to uphold their will. In New York, I also had a positive meeting with the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, about the forthcoming UK-EU summit. I can confirm to the House today that it will take place in Brussels on 20 November. This summit presents an opportunity to make progress on two crucial issues: boosting UK growth and controlling illegal immigration. On the table is a trade deal on food and drink products, a deal on emissions trading, progress towards linking our energy systems, a new youth experience scheme, and deeper co-operation on immigration. This summit presents an opportunity to make progress on two crucial issues: boosting UK growth and controlling illegal immigration. On the table is a trade deal on food and drink products, a deal on emissions trading, progress towards linking our energy systems, a new youth experience scheme and deeper co-operation on immigration. The summit will also be an opportunity to raise our concerns about “Made in Europe”, and it is clear to me that there is an opportunity to make progress in all of these areas. Together, these deals will add the equivalent of over £10 billion per year to the UK economy by 2040, with the potential to add significantly more. We should not turn our backs on this opportunity, and I hope Members from all sides of this House will get behind the Government’s efforts to land a positive outcome. It is a chance to cut costs and bureaucracy for sectors like farming. At present, entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay. Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100 million in lost exports. British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU. Seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned. This is having a real impact on businesses, and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage. For farmers and food producers, it would lift a burden that can reach £1,400 on a single shipment. For our small businesses, it would mean no more export health certificates, which can cost up to £200 each time. For households, it would ease the pressure on prices in the supermarket. It could help lower energy costs for households and businesses alike. In Northern Ireland, the proposed energy deal could cut wholesale energy costs by 20%. On immigration, we could link up our law enforcement efforts once again, sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals, as well as ensuring faster electronic evidence from the phones of those behind the gangs. It is in Britain’s interests to secure a deal along these lines, and I will work hard over the next five weeks to achieve that. I believe that our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term. If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation that we must have. Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today, to consider what is best for our country. Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term. At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach, like the one I am suggesting, but if we go into this further phase, we will proceed with care and complete transparency. This is the leadership we need to draw a line under a decade of drift and division, and to take the country forward. Beyond Europe, a confident Britain is ready to play our part on the global stage as we take up the presidency of the G20 in 2027. I confirmed in New York that we will place artificial intelligence centre stage in our presidency, to capture the incredible opportunities it presents while guarding against the risks. Leading voices like the president of Microsoft are saying Britain is the world leader on AI safety, so we are well placed to take on this role, and to work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards on AI, in our G20 presidency year. The message to the world is clear: Britain is back. On so many fronts, we are playing our part and looking confidently to the future. We are leading again, so our country can hope again. I commend this statement to the House.
I call the Leader of the Opposition.

I thank the Prime Minister for advance sight of his statement. Since we last met, Iran has sponsored an attempted terror attack on a British military base; President Trump has withdrawn support from President Zelensky; and Saudi Arabia has been bombarded with Houthi missiles and asked Britain to come to her aid. UK household energy bills are set to rise by nearly £300 in January, and diesel prices have hit £2 a litre for the first time ever. Against that backdrop, the Chancellor will deliver a Budget in two weeks. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said that there is a £35 billion black hole in the public finances. More borrowing or more taxes are on the way, because we know that the Prime Minister will not cut spending. This is at a time when families and businesses are already suffering under the weight of £70 billion in Labour’s tax rises. So what has the Prime Minister chosen to focus on today? Brexit. His exact words earlier this year were that “the last thing we should do right now is rerun those arguments”, yet here he is, unpicking the deal that this country signed with the EU, a decade after the referendum. He is not going to get a better deal. Not only are the EU tough negotiators, but he has already revealed his entire negotiating hand. He has just blurted out everything he wants in this statement. I will tell him now, as a former Trade Secretary, that that is not how you conduct negotiations. He has told them everything, and negotiations have not even started—unbelievable! Over the weekend, on “The Rest is Politics” podcast, the Prime Minister implied that the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference. Where has that come from? We all remember that in 2018, the head of MI5 said that there was no evidence that Russia had influenced the EU referendum result. Even this morning, the Prime Minister’s own Foreign Minister could not say if the evidence existed. Will the Prime Minister confirm, here and now, whether he believes that the referendum result was legitimate? If he does not, will he publish the evidence that Russia swung the result of the 2016 referendum? From my perspective, this is just another example of him trying to distract the country, rather than solving the immediate challenges we face. Just as some people thought that all Britain’s problems would be solved by leaving the EU, some now think that all our problems will be solved by rejoining it. Neither of those are serious positions; they are lazy thinking from people who do not have solutions to the real problems that we face, such as on defence. The Prime Minister told us that he would set out a target date for spending 3% of GDP on defence at the spending review in the spring. That spending review has now been delayed until next autumn. Labour delayed procurement by a year to hold the strategic defence review, then the defence investment plan took another 18 months. The armed forces now have to wait at least another 12 months to find out what they are getting. The defence of the realm is the first duty of any Government, and kicking it into the long grass is a dereliction of duty. I welcome the support that the Prime Minister has set out for our allies in Saudi Arabia and Ukraine, but they will require money, and serious questions on defence still need to be answered. The United States has withdrawn its bombers from RAF Fairford. Can the Prime Minister tell us why? What does that mean for the safety of our British aircraft and, more importantly, British personnel at that base? The Prime Minister said in his statement that we will not tolerate threats from Iran on our soil, so were he and his Foreign Secretary aware of those threats before the Foreign Secretary met and shook hands with the Iranian Foreign Minister at the UN? Does the Prime Minister now think that the Foreign Secretary was wrong to do that? On 18 July, we were told that the Prime Minister would grant licences for the Jackdaw gas field and Rosebank oilfield. We are still waiting for a decision nearly three months later, as a global energy crisis is looming. Can the Prime Minister now confirm exactly when he will approve those licences? Britain cannot afford to wait until the end of the decade for him to act—he is the Prime Minister for today. Rather than promising things on the never-never, here are some things that he could do right now: cut welfare, fund our defence, drill in the North sea, bring down people’s taxes, get young people into work, build new prison places and put more police on our streets. He could do all those things today if he cut spending. That is what I would do. Instead, he is trying to reopen yesterday’s arguments to avoid today’s decisions. What this statement shows is the difference between Labour and the Conservatives. We have answers to today’s problems; they are living in the past.

I thank the right hon. Lady. She started on the right point, which is the situation in the middle east, and the extent to which it is affecting cost of living pressures here at home—the cost of filling up at the pump, and the costs that people are feeling more broadly. She is absolutely right to say that that is where our focus should be. It is where my focus was when I had all my meetings in New York, and it is why I have taken action to remove VAT from electricity bills this month. We are acting quickly on the cost of living, and we will continue to do that. I was listening carefully to what the right hon. Lady said about the European Union. One could only conclude from what she said about unpicking the deal—the deal that is supposedly so good for Britain—that she will be defending the status quo. I am sure that I heard her say at her conference that increasing growth would be the operating principle of any Government that she leads, so how can she justify turning her back on a deal, which is potentially on the table now, to add billions to the UK economy? How can the Conservatives justify turning their backs on farmers and the food industry, who are finding it hard to export to Europe? I think they need to reflect on that. She says that I have revealed what I want to do, and that this is no way to negotiate—because the Tories were so good at negotiating deals with our partners, weren’t they? To address the right hon. Lady’s point, I implied no such thing in my comments on “The Rest Is Politics” podcast. I think she should go back and look again. It is a matter of record that Russian actors sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time. I have a question for her. I listened carefully to what she said at her conference last week. Twice, she was asked directly whether she thought Brexit had been good for London. Twice, she could not answer—she could not even address the question. That is not going to be good enough for a party that wishes to lead this country once again. It is not leadership to turn your back on growth and on building the British economy. On defence, this Government are already spending £14 billion more every year than the Conservatives did in their last year in government. We will continue to work with our US counterparts on RAF Fairford. Can I say to the right hon. Lady that every single Foreign Secretary, including David Cameron as the last Conservative Foreign Secretary, met representatives of the Iranian Government? She should look back at that, as well as at her own record in government. The Leader of the Opposition stands there today and says that she will build new prison places. Why is there a crisis in our prisons? It is because the Conservatives did not build those places when they were in office. We are dealing with the issues that she left behind. We are the ones providing leadership in difficult times. It is about time that she faced up to some of those realities about the mess they left behind.

I am grateful to the Prime Minister for treating concerted attempts to undermine our democracy with the seriousness they deserve. While it is always difficult to measure the success of such campaigns, it is also difficult to believe that Russia would bother if there was not at least a chance it might succeed. One thing is for sure: over the past 10 years, Russia has certainly got better at it, while at the same time, elements of the British state have been far too complacent about it. To hear the Prime Minister announce a new centre for information defence was encouraging. Can he assure the House that this centre will be publicly accountable and scrutinised by Parliament, and in particular by the Foreign Affairs Committee?

I can indeed give those assurances to my right hon. Friend, the Chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee. I thank her for the work that she has done in making that recommendation. She is right to say that the wrong approach was taken in the past. The Intelligence and Security Committee report in 2020 said that the last Government failed to seek evidence of any potential interference in our democratic processes. We will not make the same mistakes in the next decade as were made in the last. The new national centre for information defence is about putting Britain in a strong place to face the challenges in a difficult world, and that is what we will do.
I call the Father of the House.

Will the Prime Minister forgive me if I put some words in his mouth? Does he think this is a reasonable statement: “Look, I have been elected by my MPs to serve a full term of government. I am going to get on with bread-and-butter issues, such as the care system, pensions and asylum. Of course, we like a good, close relationship with our partners on security in Europe, but”—this is the Prime Minister speaking—“I say this to the people: I am very wary about reopening the whole Brexit wars. There were years of harrowing negotiations and an even worse deal. I give an absolute commitment that I will not seek to join the EU unless there is a general election first and I offer the British people a full referendum”?

May I say to the Father of the House that I stand by every single one of those words? I am not reopening the referendum; I respect the referendum result, as I just said a moment ago. What I will do is take a pragmatic approach when I can boost growth in the British economy and when I can increase co-operation to get a grip on boat crossings across the channel. I will do those things where I believe they can be in the country’s best interests. The deal that I have inherited coming into office represents an opportunity to secure progress on both those things. The case I am putting to the House this afternoon is that it is a dereliction of duty for any Member to turn away from that possibility, when we can support the food industry, we can support farmers, and we can get Britain growing more strongly again. Our responsibility in this House is to serve this country’s best interests, and that is what I will do.
I call the Chair of the Defence Committee.

I welcome the Prime Minister’s statement and in particular his efforts to assist our allies, to forge closer ties and to help de-escalate the situation in the middle east. It is clear that President Trump’s efforts to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and then buy it are a real kick in the teeth for our Ukrainian friends and will allow Vladimir Putin to further fuel his deadly war machine. Nations such as India, which was slapped with tariffs for buying Russian fuel, will no doubt decry that move and be left bemused by these haphazard, hypocritical policies that prevent our long-term strategic aims from being achieved. However, there have also been reports that United States officials have been contacting European counterparts to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, and are also limiting the supply of weapons and intelligence. Has the Prime Minister had any such discussions with our US or European allies about why we need to continue to support our Ukrainian friends?

I will always support our Ukrainian friends, and I can say to my hon. Friend that I called President Zelensky on Saturday afternoon precisely because I recognised that he was in the middle of a very difficult 24 hours. I can also say to the House that the Chancellor of the Exchequer spoke to the United States Treasury Secretary at around the same time, and talked about the importance of an energy ceasefire. It was good to see that proposal emerge from the President yesterday. It is the best possible outcome in the circumstances that we are in: it will get fuel flowing into the market as well as protecting Ukraine throughout the winter ahead of us, and we will continue to make the case for it.
I call the leader of the Liberal Democrats.

Following the loss of his father, Roy, may I start by offering the Prime Minister’s family my deepest sympathies? I am sure that we were all moved by his words about his dad, and his determination to fix social care and tackle the devastating impact of dementia on sufferers and their families. I hope that we can work across this House to make that happen. Let me now turn to the Prime Minister’s words about Europe. His predecessors turned a blind eye to the disastrous consequences of the Conservatives’ Brexit deal, so it was welcome to hear him recognise that damage today. We on these Liberal Democrat Benches have consistently argued that their Brexit deal has made us all poorer, weaker and less safe, so I am glad that the Prime Minister has arrived at the same conclusion, but now it is time to do something about it. The test of the Prime Minister’s ambition is straightforward, if he wants growth and if he wants to cut the cost of living. Will he drop Labour’s red lines now, and open negotiations on joining the single market and a customs union? It would be a real dereliction of duty to refuse now to fix a deal that we know is not working. Every day, every week, every month of delay means more unnecessary costs for British businesses, more pointless red tape, more pain for British families. Being outside negotiations on AI safety, “Made in Europe” regulations and migration agreements does this country real harm. Fixing our relationship with Europe is more important now than ever, especially at a time when President Trump is waging a trade war with Canada while signing a new trade deal with Putin. Never before have we seen a US President so hostile to the UK and our allies, and so friendly to our adversaries. We cannot afford to fudge or dodge on this issue, and especially on Ukraine, so will the Minister bring together a coalition of the willing behind a joint statement condemning Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and calling on him to cancel it? Let me finally refer to the Prime Minister’s comments about Russian interference in the Brexit referendum. That took courage, after the Conservatives had spent so long suppressing the evidence. Will the Prime Minister now present it to the House in full, alongside any evidence of interference in other UK votes, so that we can understand the threat and make it a national security priority to protect our democracy from attacks such as that?

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for his kind words about my dad. They are much appreciated. I agree with the right hon. Gentleman about the harm done to food and farming, and to other industries, by the Brexit deal. It would seem that the Conservative party is in denial about this, and not open to seeing how we can move forward to a better position for the country. Indeed, it is clear that British public opinion has moved, and I believe that the public would now favour that. We are not ideological but pragmatic in taking steps to support growth and improve our approach to tackling irregular migration. If we can secure a good deal, I hope that I can count on the right hon. Gentleman’s support and that of his colleagues when it comes before the House. But as much as I want to improve growth in the UK, I also want to maintain trust in politics, and I am afraid I am not prepared to revisit the red lines in our manifesto. On Ukraine, I have had discussions with Chancellor Merz about bringing forward a meeting of the coalition of the willing. I can update the House further as that proceeds. Finally, on the Brexit referendum, I think it is really important to be open with people about everything that we have lived through in the last decade. I have been open, but I am also making sure that Britain is in a position where we do not face the same again. I hope that the right hon. Gentleman and his colleagues will support the new national centre for information defence, so that Britain never again faces the risk of interference in our democratic process.

I commend the Prime Minister on what has been a flying start on the world stage, and I welcome news of a better, stronger deal with Europe that will cut costs and cut bills this winter. It is very clear to us, on the evidence that we have received, that the deal we inherited has left red tape strangling our businesses in general, and strangling small businesses in particular. The EU’s “Made in Europe” proposals risk destroying any ambitions to reindustrialise our country. To avoid that peril, we will have to get serious with the EU in tackling unfair competition from China. Will the Prime Minister reserve the right to introduce new tariffs on unfairly subsidised imports from China, so that British and European businesses have a fair and level playing field on which to compete?

I thank my hon. Friend—[Interruption.] My apologies—my right hon. Friend. I am still getting used to being back, Mr Speaker. I agree with him about the red tape that our businesses are facing. I have read out examples in the House this afternoon. The Conservatives used to be the first party to stand up and say, “Oh yes, let’s remove red tape from our businesses.” It sounded mightily like they were defending that red tape this afternoon. What has happened to them? They were meant to be the champions of free enterprise, but it falls to us to remove the red tape, and I will work hard to get that deal. I agree with my right hon. Friend that “Made in Europe” presents risks to British manufacturing, and I know that he will have concerns about the automotive industry in the west midlands. I am raising those concerns with European partners. It is important that we get to an arrangement that works for both the UK and the EU. After all, we are both trying to deal with the same issue: the damaging effect that Chinese exports are having on our industries. The way to approach this is to do it together, and that is the case that we are making to the EU.

On the Prime Minister’s international agenda, should he not also focus on the appalling humanitarian situation in Darfur, Sudan, and avoid making policy on Israel, the timing of which enhances Netanyahu’s prospects of re-election? On Yemen, as well as defending Saudi Arabia from the outrageous Houthi attacks, should the Prime Minister not use Britain’s deep historical links and connections to Yemen to support constitutional negotiations and prevent the situation from getting any worse?

I assure the right hon. Gentleman that ending the suffering in Sudan is very high on the Foreign Secretary’s list of priorities, and that tackling the aggression from the Houthis is something that we are taking extremely seriously. Of course, we are providing support to Saudi Arabia, as I have mentioned this afternoon, and we will be prepared to consider further requests as and when they come in, but I cannot accept what the right hon. Gentleman said about Israel and Palestine. In this House, we have long supported a two-state solution. If we do nothing when a tender process to build on the west bank is moving forward, we will allow that two-state solution to die in front of our eyes. The Foreign Secretary is not prepared to allow that, I am not prepared to allow that, and we strongly defend the stance we have taken.

In my negotiations with Commissioner Šefčovič, I agreed not only the re-accession of the United Kingdom to Erasmus+, but that at this year’s summit we would deliver the food and drink agreement to bear down on costs in supermarkets and an emissions trading scheme linkage meaning that hundreds of millions of pounds in carbon taxes do not need to be paid by UK businesses, as well as opportunities for young people to work, travel and study in the UK. So can I say to Prime Minister that anyone who sets their face against the deal that I hope he pushes over the line on 20 November is in favour of adding costs to businesses and households?

My right hon. Friend is exactly right, and I commend him for the excellent work he did to lay the groundwork for this deal. He is right: in these circumstances and at this moment in time, it is incumbent on every Member of the House to do whatever we can to relieve pressure on British business, and that is what we will do. It is interesting that this afternoon the country will be able to see that we are prepared to do it, but the Opposition are not.

The Prime Minister opened today’s statement with the words that he “took a clear message to the United Nations: that…Britain is back and can be relied upon as a consistent and stable partner”. Is the same true of the Prime Minister? If so, can he tell me whether he plans to honour the Brexit referendum outcome, as he said in May when courting the Brexit voters of Makerfield, or is he planning to overturn it either partially or fully?

I say to the right hon. Lady that I am always a stable and consistent partner. Indeed, I will honour the result of the referendum, as I always have for the last 10 years—that is a clear commitment, as is the commitment to our manifesto, as I explained just a moment ago—but I am also going to lead and will be prepared to set out options that I think Britain should consider. If she is saying that she is happy with the status quo, she is in a minority in this country. People know that Britain can do better than this. I am determined to secure better for Britain. I am just surprised that the Opposition are setting their ambitions for our country so low.

I for one am really relieved that the Prime Minister is not going to take any lessons from any member of the previous Conservative Government on negotiating with Europe, given what a mess they made of it. Their irrational hatred of anything to do with Europe meant they took us out of the biofood security alert, meaning British farmers do not get told when there is foot and mouth, and took us out of the Eurodac system—[Interruption.] You took us out. I am watching the right hon. Member for Louth and Horncastle (Victoria Atkins) say, “What?” She might want to look at some of the details that she helped negotiate. They took us out of the Eurodac system, meaning we do not get the asylum data, which makes protecting our borders harder. So will the Prime Minister assure me and my constituents that he will not let Tory mistakes make border control and British farming harder to do, but will put the national interest first, seek that data and ensure that we have a future of working with Europe, not hating it?
Order. I just remind Members to please address the Chair, so we do not get into attacks on each other.

My hon. Friend is right to raise the loss of immigration control that has come with the inability to access data across the European Union. It is something that the people who promoted this idea need to take on board and be held to account for, because the reality is that we are in a weaker position when it comes to controlling immigration than we were just over 10 years ago. It is really important, as we go into this next phase, that those on all sides of the House support the British position in this negotiation. Is any Member of this House truly saying to me this afternoon that they do not want to have access again to that European immigration information? If they are saying that, they need to be honest about it.

I welcomed the Foreign Secretary’s speech on Sudan at the UN General Assembly. The Prime Minister recently said that he would be “really concerned” to lose Sheikh Mansour, vice-president of the United Arab Emirates and owner of Manchester City FC, from Manchester, but does he recognise that the same individual is reported by outlets including The New York Times to have a “central role” not only in Man City’s contested success but in the genocide, famine and forced displacements happening across Sudan because of the Rapid Support Forces? When will the Prime Minister stand up to Sheikh Mansour and the UAE, and call out their dishonest roles in Manchester and in fanning the flames of conflict, leading to the world’s biggest humanitarian disaster in Sudan?

My right hon. Friend the Foreign Secretary is clear that we want a humanitarian solution in Sudan without fear or favour, and we will make that case very clearly to the UAE. On the wider issue, I can confirm, Mr Speaker, that all my dealings will be published this afternoon in relation to any meetings with the owners of Manchester City.

I welcome my right hon. Friend’s statement. He may be aware that the Ukraine Solidarity Campaign is today protesting outside the US embassy in London against President Trump’s diesel deal, which will directly fund Putin’s war machine: a war machine that broke its promise to stop targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure less than 24 hours after it was committed to; a war machine that continues to bombard Oleshky, a city in the grip of a humanitarian crisis where people are being starved to death; and a war machine that is complicit in the forcible deportation and abduction of at least 20,651 Ukrainian children. Will the Prime Minister impress upon the President of the United States that his diesel deal will cost his own voters, my constituents and the people of Ukraine their safety?

I thank my hon. Friend for the powerful way in which she puts her question. I assure her that Britain will always take the strongest possible approach towards sanctions on Russia. The Foreign Secretary recently announced new sanctions on the shadow fleet, crypto and oil companies in Russia. We will continue to take that action and, we hope, set a lead that others will follow.

As the Chairman of the Intelligence and Security Committee who oversaw the publication of the Russia report as soon as the Committee was reconstituted, may I ask the Prime Minister to explain to the House exactly how he thinks Russia was able to alter the result of the referendum?

I have great respect for the right hon. Gentleman, but I did not say that. I did not at any point say that it altered the result. I simply come back to what I said earlier: it is a matter of record that Russia has sought to interfere in elections—the 2019 general election—and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time.

The Prime Minister quite rightly mentioned in his statement the fact that 90% of Russian oil production is covered by UK sanctions. I very much welcome what he had to say about joining international calls for a ceasefire on attacks on energy installations. When he is discussing this matter with President Trump, will he remind him that the biggest reason for high diesel prices here and in the United States is not the war between Russia and Ukraine, but what is going on in the strait of Hormuz and in Iran? Will he remind the President that the action he is taking will not cut the diesel price and that all it will do is fuel the Russian war machine?

I assure my hon. Friend that we are using our good offices on every front to ensure that we get a solution on the cost of energy. As I said before, in Ukraine an energy ceasefire is the best way to get fuel flowing into the market, and that has to be a reciprocal ceasefire. We are also doing whatever we can to support the bringing forward of a solution in the middle east. I discussed both those matters with President Trump in New York, and Britain stands ready to play its part on both fronts.

Iran clearly views this country as its enemy, and I fear that it smells weakness. It has attempted to attack Diego Garcia, Akrotiri and now Fairford. Does the Prime Minister agree that this demands a robust response, and will he confirm that if Iran is successful in attacking one of our bases, we will use direct action against it in legitimate self-defence? Will he provide enhanced support and assistance to our friends and allies who are under constant attack from Iran and its proxies—not just Saudi Arabia, but the United Arab Emirates and Israel?

I assure the right hon. Gentleman that we are providing the most robust response to the situation. We have introduced a tough sanctions regime. We are taking every step that needs to be taken in close consultation with our counterparts in the United States. There is no suggestion at all that Britain is not playing its part.

Derby has the manufacturing talent and capabilities to help Britain succeed on the international stage, and with a brilliant £1 billion order for 29 new battery-electric trains at Alstom in Litchurch Lane, we are on a roll in our city. Does the Prime Minister agree that by championing British manufacturing on the international stage we can secure more of that work, and the jobs our communities desperately need?

I pay tribute to my hon. Friend for the work he has done with colleagues in Derby to secure that investment and those new jobs. The great city of Derby will be a big beneficiary of this Government’s drive to reindustrialise the country. I was at Alstom with my hon. Friend and saw what is being done and the apprenticeships there. We are proud of what is going on in the city. I will ask the Chancellor and the First Secretary of State to do everything they can to drive the maximum value for British jobs from every pound of public procurement in this country.

As Liberal Democrats, we have long been calling for global leadership on AI from the UK, so I am pleased to hear the Prime Minister talk of that. We cannot get the best out of AI if we cannot protect people from the worst, and the UK should be leading on that. We also need to learn from online safety, and it needs to be Governments that lead the charge, not big tech. Will the Prime Minister listen to the Lib Dem call for an international AI safety institute, based on the International Atomic Energy Agency, based here in the UK?

We already have the AI Security Institute, and to be fair, I pay tribute to the previous Conservative Prime Minister, the right hon. Member for Richmond and Northallerton (Rishi Sunak), who was instrumental in the establishment of that institute. It is because of that that the president of Microsoft was on the radio this morning saying that Britain is now regarded as the world leader in AI safety. What we must not be, however, is complacent, which is why I am putting AI at the top of the agenda for Britain’s presidency of the G20. I look forward to working with the hon. Lady and Members from across the House to ensure that Britain brings together a global code of standards and principles that can capture the benefits of AI while guarding against the risks it poses.

First, I thank my right hon. Friend for his speech at UNGA, in which he committed, or recommitted, the United Kingdom to be a consistent and stable partner in upholding the shared values of the UN charter. That will be increasingly important as we enter the G20 presidency. I spent last week with the chairs of the Ukrainian Parliament’s British friendship group, Deputy Speaker Korniyenko and Lesia Vasylenko, and they talked to me about how this El Niño winter is going to be the hardest ever winter in Ukraine. Just this week, Kyiv’s sewerage system broke due to electricity outages because of Russian attacks. What additional support can we give, particularly to Kyiv, in terms of generators, solar panels, thermal batteries and other humanitarian support to ensure that they can get through the exceedingly hard and difficult winter that is coming to Ukraine?

I do not think any Member of this House has done more than my hon. Friend to support Ukraine through its darkest hour. On the issue of protecting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, as well as helping it with renewable and sustainable energy systems, my right hon. Friend the Foreign Secretary was in Ukraine last week and talked about these very issues. He also visited the site of one of the bomb attacks that killed children—people may have seen the photos. We are as engaged as my hon. Friend, and we will not waver in any way, shape or form. We will be there till the end, as I know will he.

I am quite sure that the whole House will applaud the Prime Minister’s reaffirmation of this country’s support for Ukraine and will support the additional sanctions that we are seeking to impose. President Trump has effectively driven a coach and horses through those sanctions, has torn up the bill that he himself signed in the White House and, for the sake of his domestic audience, is seeking to blame President Zelensky and Ukraine for the oil shortages that the United States is now facing, rather than placing that blame where it truly lies, which is with his disastrous expedition in Iran. The Prime Minister did not answer the question from the leader of the Liberal Democrats. Will he answer it now? Will he join my right hon. Friend the Leader of the Opposition in unequivocally condemning this act of treachery by the President of the United States?

I made it clear in my statement that, when I heard the news, I was immediately on the phone to President Zelensky to offer any help that I could provide. I think that where Britain can best provide help is in trying to bring people back together to get a solution that works for Ukraine. More than anything in these circumstances, we have to think about what will be most helpful. Of course, it is critical to get the US, as we discussed in New York with President Trump, back to the concept of an energy ceasefire, and that is what he announced yesterday.

My constituents in Pendle and Clitheroe want immigration to be controlled and managed in the best interests of the country, and I know that the Prime Minister’s constituents in Wigan feel the same. Can he confirm that, as long as he is Prime Minister, there will be no return to freedom of movement?

I take my responsibilities to my constituents very seriously, which is why I have said consistently that the manifesto upon which Labour Members were elected will be fully respected. What we have to look at are the options that are available for the long-term relationship. In the next decade, this country needs to know where it is going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said in my opening comments, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided.

The Prime Minister says that, when it comes to the relationship with the EU, the British public will be the boss. Given that Scotland last had a vote on whether or not to stay in broken Brexit Britain before Brexit was even on the cards, does he not think it is a wee bit cheeky to give the UK public the choice, the driving seat and the reins on whether or not to have a different future with the EU while refusing that same choice to Scotland on its future with the UK?
I am sure that, like me, the hon. Lady looks at opinion polls from all parts of the country, including Scotland. No one in this House today is proposing a referendum.

I also was pleased to hear what the Prime Minister had to say about AI, both in New York and this afternoon in the Chamber. Can he confirm that it remains his view that decisions about global principles and standards for AI should be taken by democratically elected Governments representing working people and not by industry alone?

I agree with my right hon. Friend very forcefully. I am setting up a process under the banner of the G20 presidency that mirrors what this country did in 2008, when international agreement was needed about how to handle the financial crisis. The Canadian Prime Minister, who was very much involved at that time, has been in discussions with me about how we could create a process to mirror that for AI so that individual countries could go back and embed those principles in their own laws and statutes. That is what we are trying to achieve. I would be really pleased if the whole House would get behind this endeavour, as the UK is in the global spotlight.

The so-called energy ceasefire is a farce. All but one of Ukraine’s oil refineries has already been destroyed. It is about protecting Russia’s oil refineries while Russia bombs Ukraine’s power grid into obliteration and it results in a health disaster. Will the Prime Minister commit to sending large-scale generators to Ukraine now, and will he stand by our Saudi allies at the UN Security Council and under chapter VII designate the Houthis as a terrorist organisation—yes or no?

On the first part of the hon. Lady’s question, I heard her strong view on the energy ceasefire, but I heard from the President on Saturday afternoon and he was asking the UK Government to press for such a ceasefire. I think it is right that we hear him and do everything within our power. As I said, there has been some progress on that front in the last 24 hours. On the second matter, I will reflect on what the hon. Lady said and come back to her.

Traders at Grimsby Seafood Village will welcome any action to reduce the Brexit red tape and bring down their energy bills. I think that they would also want to hear the Prime Minister say explicitly—he danced around in his response to my hon. Friend the Member for Pendle and Clitheroe (Jonathan Hinder) earlier—that there will not be a return to freedom of movement and that in these negotiations we will not have to capitulate and join the euro?

As I have said many times this afternoon, we will honour the manifesto in full. The red lines are in place and they will remain in place. The seafood purveyors of Grimsby will probably have noticed, when I was talking about their plight and the difficulties they face, the lack of support for them from the Conservative Benches. I think the Conservatives need to have a period of reflection on their approach on this whole matter and do something to help British businesses that are struggling right now.

The Prime Minister confirmed that the incident at RAF Fairford was likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran. Can he comment on the serious suggestions that some of those who have been arrested and then bailed had Iranian diplomatic immunity?
I hope the hon. Gentleman will understand that I am not going to get into those matters on the Floor of the House. The Home Secretary will make a statement later today and provide more detail.

From catching “Pride” at the National Theatre to jamming the Smiths with Ukrainian troops, we know that this Prime Minister gets culture. Can he revisit pragmatically the Tory mess that has left the Really Useful Group, a theatre group, touring a production of “Phantom of the Opera” in Europe with a Chinese cast because of all the red tape and musicians crippled by costs with no cabotage agreements, because it is killing gigs and venues?

I say to my hon. Friend that those are precisely the issues that we believe need a second look. We need to take a more pragmatic approach, and my right hon. Friend the Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations is having those discussions with Europe. We do want to see better arrangements for our British creative industries, because they deserve it. They are the best in the world and Europe wants to see and hear more from them.

Irrespective of how we voted in the referendum, I hope the Prime Minister will agree that if one wants to be called a democrat, one has to abide by that decision and make it work, but the Windsor framework illustrates that no deal is ever cast into tablets of stone and that things are capable of sensible evolution. Will the Prime Minister accept that at this time, as always, businesses large and small, urban and rural, need certainty? They need to know the regulatory regime in which they are trading, the opportunities that exist and the barriers that they may need to overcome. Will he commit that, whatever evolution he is envisaging, it will be delivered speedily to be able to give confidence, certainty and clarity to North Dorset businesses and those across the country?

I commend the hon. Gentleman on his pragmatic tone. He is absolutely right to approach it in that way. When I visit Northern Ireland, as I do, I hear a call for things to be changed and improved—evolved, as he said—and that is exactly right. I said in my statement that the energy cost-benefit for Northern Ireland could be significant: there could be up to a 20% reduction in wholesale energy costs. Why would I not do everything I could to deliver that for the people of Northern Ireland? He mentioned speed. If the whole House gets behind the drive to improve the deal, we will get it through more quickly.

I thank the Prime Minister for his statement and for highlighting the effect of Brexit on the salmon farming industry. Salmon farming is worth £189 million to the Western Isles, with £34 million of that direct, and over 200 jobs. Similarly, fishing is worth £16 million, with most of that prawn exports to Spain and France. We are physically furthest from that EU market, but we need that deal—we need to get our fish and our produce in. While we are at it, let us get a deal for our young people to get them studying and working again in Europe.

My hon. Friend puts it so well, because he knows these issues so well—because of the travel times to market. If only Opposition Members had the level of understanding he has just demonstrated, we would be in a better place.

I note the Prime Minister’s remarks concerning Russian interference in some recent and not so recent elections, which raise serious questions for all of us who worry about the integrity of our democracy. Will the Prime Minister commit to reviewing whether campaign finance rules—both those in place at the moment and the welcome but limited steps being introduced in the Representation of the People Bill—sufficiently guard against foreign interference through political donations? In particular, may I encourage him to look at a cap on political donations to limit the influence of ultra-wealthy individuals and potential foreign interests?

My right hon. Friend the First Secretary of State is leading a task and finish group on cleaning up politics, and I am sure that she would be very pleased to hear from the hon. Member on her proposals.

On 26 October 2021, when the Conservative Government’s Elections Bill was going through its Public Bill Committee, I was the shadow Minister, and I tabled a new clause relating to foreign interference in politics. The Minister then responsible for keeping our democracy safe replied in Committee that she had not read the Russia report and asked me to explain it to her. Does the Prime Minister share my concern that the Minister, now Leader of the Opposition, may not be fully across the details?
