I came to Camden with my family as a child refugee. It is where I grew up and where I went to school, made friends and discovered the opportunities that would shape my life. This Budget speaks to the issues that matter deeply to the people I represent, from the security of a home to the opportunities available to the next generation. Like so many young people growing up in Camden, I spent my time making friends through the universal language of football. On the football pitch, you quickly learn that it does not matter where someone comes from, what language they speak or what their family does for a living. What matters is whether they turn up for their team mates. Those friendships taught me something important about community, long before I entered politics: that we are stronger when we look beyond our differences and recognise what we have in common. As I came of age, Camden continued to give me opportunities and a sense of belonging, and it gave me the responsibility to give something back. For more than 20 years, I have tried to honour that responsibility through community work and public service, campaigning for change and serving in local government, ultimately as leader of Camden council. That experience has taught me that beyond every policy, every budget line and every statistic is a person whose life can be changed by the decisions made in this House. Holborn and St Pancras is a place of extraordinary character. What makes our constituency so special is not just the landmarks, but the extraordinary variety of places and people. From the leafy streets and village feel of Primrose Hill, the independent spirit and community life of Kentish Town and the neighbourhoods and estates of Haverstock to the historic streets, theatres and cultural institutions of Covent Garden, every part has its own story to tell. We are home to thriving local businesses, historic markets, places of faith and community centres. We have students and academics, artists and entrepreneurs, families who have lived here for generations, and people who have made this place their home from every corner of the world. That diversity is our strength. It is one of our greatest strengths. It is reflected in our languages, our food, our festivals and our music, and in the everyday way that we all come together to look out for one another. It is what makes Holborn and St Pancras not simply a collection of neighbourhoods but a community. The Roundhouse in Chalk Farm began life as a railway engine shed before becoming one of the country’s most well-known cultural venues that also provides creative access to young people. Legends from Led Zeppelin to David Bowie have played there. It is a reminder that places, just like people, can be given new opportunities and go on to achieve remarkable things. In King’s Cross stands the historic German gymnasium, where sporting events were held at the national Olympian games in 1866, long before the modern Olympic games came into being. My constituency has a sporting legacy stretching back over a century, and I am pleased to make a little history of my own, as Holborn and St Pancras’s first Tottenham Hotspur supporter MP, bringing an end to a rather lengthy period of Arsenal and West Ham dominance in our representation in this House. If supporting Spurs had a dictionary definition, it would read something like this: “To remain eternally hopeful despite overwhelming evidence, and to return, every season, convinced that this will finally be your year.” I hope that combination of optimism and sheer refusal to give up will serve me well in this House. Of course, the West Ham and Arsenal dominance that I mentioned came from the distinguished Labour MPs who represented the constituency before me. I am immensely proud to follow in the footsteps of two men who have given so much to Holborn and St Pancras, and whose contributions to our community and my party deserve to be celebrated. The late, great Frank Dobson represented Holborn and St Pancras for more than 33 years. He was a tireless champion for local people, a proud defender of our NHS and public services, and a politician who never lost sight of the people who were behind the policies. I have a childhood memory of meeting Frank at a community event. I had no idea at the time how much of an important political figure he was; to me, he was simply a nice bearded man who took the time to speak to a child. Looking back, that small encounter captured something important about his connection with the community. He was a familiar face to generations of residents—someone who understood the challenges facing working people and was never afraid to stand up for them. Sir Keir Starmer continued that tradition, representing our constituency for more than a decade, leading the Labour party from opposition back into government, introducing generational reforms to renters’ and workers’ rights, and lifting half a million children out of poverty. I have had the privilege of working alongside Keir through our local Labour movement, and have seen another side of his public service: watching him quietly console bereaved families who have lost young loved ones, and hearing his determination to end youth violence. I pay tribute to both men, with enormous gratitude and respect. I will do my utmost to honour the trust that generations have placed in them, and that the residents have now placed in me. It is also an extraordinary honour to become the first woman, black person and Muslim to represent Holborn and St Pancras in Parliament, and the first British Somali woman to sit in this House. I take great pride in those milestones, and in being elected during Black History Month in a constituency whose town hall proudly commemorates Claudia Jones, the pioneering black woman who founded and hosted Britain’s first Caribbean carnival there. I take pride in those milestones because of what they might mean to a young woman or a young girl growing up in our constituency today. I want her to see that her background does not define the limits of her ambition, that there is no ceiling to what she can achieve, and that public life belongs to her, too. One of the issues that first drove me into politics 10 years ago was the rise in homelessness. Alongside people sleeping rough on our streets, families and young people are facing a housing crisis that leaves too many struggling to find a secure, affordable place to call home. That is why I strongly welcome my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister’s determination to end rough sleeping. This Budget turns that determination into action, with nearly £900 million to tackle rough sleeping and an additional £1.5 billion to support the delivery of social and affordable homes. For constituencies such as mine, this investment is essential. There is another issue that matters deeply to me: the strength of our communities and the bonds that hold us together. Growing up in Camden, I saw different people from different backgrounds, cultures and faiths build support networks and look out for one another. I saw how diversity enriches our lives and how cohesion is built through everyday acts of kindness, friendship and solidarity. But that cohesion is hard won, and we cannot take it for granted. During the election campaign, I experienced attempts to question people’s belonging, sow division, and turn differences into reasons for suspicion and hostility. We must stand firmly against the hateful and divisive forces that seek to pull our communities apart. Hope is not naive; it is what gives us the courage to change lives for the better. My parents taught me to work hard and always give something back to the community that has given me so much. I want every young person in our constituency to have the opportunities that I had. I want families to have secure homes, young people to have access to good jobs and apprenticeships, and our public services to always be there for people when they need them most. To represent this community in Parliament is an extraordinary privilege. Camden gave me hope and opportunity. Now, as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras, I will pass that hope and opportunity to others, and give them the same chance.

May I say that it is a genuine pleasure to follow the excellent maiden speech of the hon. Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Sagal Abdi-Wali)? As a West Ham fan, I understand that it is the optimism that kills you; she is a Spurs fan, so after last season, I think I will leave that there. I congratulate her: it is not easy to follow in the footsteps of a Prime Minister and to fight against the leader of another national party. As she pointed out, the racial attacks on her in the lead-up to that election were absolutely disgraceful. I am sure that the vast majority of people in this House stand in solidarity with her. I wish her a successful career in this House; I am sure that she will be a great asset to it. Today’s debate is about growth in every postcode, but I will focus on the genuine threat of war to this country. The Budget does not deal with the defence issues that must be addressed. We could carry on saying that we have a plan to have a plan, and kicking things down the road, but that would be to hide from the reality of what is going on in the world. Just today we saw a cyber-attack that destroyed hundreds of millions of pounds-worth of frozen and refrigerated stock across at least six European countries. We know that such cyber-attacks are taking place every day, yet we are still delaying the real investment that needs to take place. I was recently in Australia with the NATO Parliamentary Assembly. In Australia, inflation is 4%, cost of living is the No. 1 priority and 55% say immigration is too high, yet the Australians have decided to invest in defence. In the 1980s, they felt that their geography gave them the security, and now they have recognised that it does not. They are in the process of doubling their navy, with three air defence destroyers, six frigate submarine hunters, 11 general purpose frigates, six large missile barges and eight launching vessels to protect army capability. Of course, with AUKUS, they also have a built-in 50% contingency. Germany is going to have 15 extra frigates by 2035, Finland is going to have four new corvettes by 2035, and Norway is going to have five new frigates, six new submarines and 28 standard vessels by 2035, yet we say that we are aiming to get to 3.5% by 2035. I have said this before, and I will say it again: targeting a percentage of GDP is false and wrong. The target was only brought in to satisfy the Americans in 2014. Plenty of us have a lot of complaints about President Trump, but at least he got European countries spending. As far back as Eisenhower, the Americans were saying that Europe needed to spend more on defence. George Bush made such a speech in 2007, and Barack Obama made one in 2014 when the target came in. What really matters is article 3. Everybody talks about article 5 and defence. If article 5 is triggered, nations have a choice as to what they contribute to collective defence. Everybody thinks that America will pile in with its troops, tanks, planes and warships, but it could simply say, “We will provide the intelligence,” and that would satisfy article 5. Article 3 states that a country must be able to defend its borders for three weeks. NATO is a reinforcement. We simply cannot carry on saying, “We are going to do a defence investment review in a year’s time”—not actually investing in a year’s time, but doing a review! I welcome today’s news that double shifts might be done at the dockyards to produce more frigates, but that should be happening now. In the time I have remaining, let me say this. I said before in this House that when we cut spending from 5% of GDP—that level was just a consequence of what we needed to spend—the 3% went into health and welfare, and that it would be a brave politician who stood up and said that we should cut those things, especially welfare, to invest in defence. Well, that is exactly what the Leader of the Opposition is now saying. The time has more than passed. The threat of war in this country is on the horizon. We do not want it to happen, so we bury our heads in the sand and say that we can delay the spending. That cannot carry on. The threat is imminent.

When I ask people in my constituency how they feel about the economy, they tell me that their bills are too high and their rent or mortgage take too much of their pay. I am glad that the Budget takes some first steps to address those issues. Four years ago, the Conservatives, led by Liz, crashed the economy and sent mortgages and bills soaring. Before that, they spent more than a decade cutting our armed forces and public services—they left us poorly defended in every sense. The Chancellor’s Budget makes a good start in addressing those problems. The immediate help for 20 million households towards their energy bills this winter is a welcome relief. The changes to business rates will have a huge impact on businesses in my constituency. On devolution, I can only hope that Lancashire will have a mayor by 2028 to share in the proposals that were announced. I urge Reform-led Lancashire county council to grab this amazing opportunity for Lancashire. We have been left behind for too long. The council needs to stop infighting and start fighting for Lancashire instead. I want to come back to how much further we need to go to rebuild Britain. The Prime Minister rightly identified the deindustrialisation of Britain as one of the reasons places such as Blackpool North and Fleetwood have not shared in the proceeds of growth as much as they should have done. He is right that a change of policy is required, but right now Britain is deindustrialising faster than any of our neighbours. Domestic manufacturing capacity is an essential source of our national security. British manufacturers face the highest electricity prices in Europe. I know many Labour colleagues have asked the Chancellor to look at the merits of extending the British industrial competitiveness scheme to all manufacturing firms. I hope the Front-Bench team look carefully again at the proposals and sit down with the TUC and others to discuss how that could be implemented. This Budget offers practical help with people’s bills this winter. The 10-year plan and the spending review must do the same for their jobs.

As we head into winter with bills rising again in January, households and businesses across the country are worried. This Budget needed to match the scale of the energy and climate challenges, but we as Liberal Democrats are concerned that it does not. While the standing charge removal and the proposed energy bill cost control framework are welcome, struggling households cannot wait until the next spending review in 2027 for policy costs to be taken off bills—one of the quickest ways to reduce bills while supporting electrification. The Government could have introduced the Liberal Democrat essential energy guarantee to protect basic household energy needs. If we are truly to break free from the volatile fossil fuel prices driven by despots and Trump’s stupid wars, we must accelerate renewables, grid connections and electrification. That is why I am disturbed by the seeming inconsistencies in the approach taken in the Budget. First, the Treasury says that it is setting an entirely new path on energy, while Ministers tell us that their clean energy ambitions remain unchanged. With the allocation round 8 auction budget due within weeks, Ministers must urgently clarify what that means for investment certainty in floating offshore wind and port regeneration, which is critical for supply costs and supply chains. Secondly, cheaper energy does not automatically lead to electrification on its own. As winter approaches, why is the Treasury cutting the flagship warm homes plan—the surest way to electrify heating in our homes and reduce wasted wind energy? The Budget slashes £1 billion of capital funding from the programme and reintroduces VAT on clean technologies from 2027, effectively creating a solar panel and heat pump tax. I ask the Minister to confirm or deny reports that a further £1.5 billion could be removed from the warm homes plan’s financial transactions funding. That is the very zero-interest loan schemes that have just been launched and lauded. With 90% of domestic bill increases since 2020 linked to wholesale gas price spikes, despite and contrary to all the protestations from the Conservatives and Reform, the answer is clear: a national electrification strategy, making it easier, not harder, for households to move away from fossil fuels. This Budget should have advanced that mission; instead, it risks setting Britain back.

It is a pleasure to speak in this debate, and let me add my congratulations to my hon. Friend the Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Sagal Abdi-Wali) on her excellent maiden speech. This is a Budget to create growth in every postcode, and nowhere is better placed than Newcastle to manufacture, innovate and grow if given the tools and opportunities to do so. My right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer has clearly recognised this, allocating funding for investment and giving welcome attention to our region’s economic potential with the announcement of the international investment summit in Gateshead next spring. We have always been a city that builds, that innovates, that delivers, whether it is in advanced manufacturing, engineering, digital technology, energy or professional services. It was growing up in Newcastle surrounded by the legacy of great Geordie engineers and inventors, in a culture that championed making and building things, that inspired me to become an engineer. The north-east hosts world-leading companies and research institutions, but after 14 years of Conservative austerity, my constituents still find significant barriers to social mobility and opportunity. Newcastle Central and West ranked bottom of 543 constituencies for attainment and outcomes in the “Crossing Paths” 2026 report. Having grown up on a council estate myself, I am heartbroken that the life chances of disadvantaged young people are so curtailed. One fifth of those aged 16 to 24 are characterised as NEET in the north-east, and I echo the Chancellor in saying that I refuse to write them off, unlike the last Conservative Government. I look forward to the upcoming publication of Alan Milburn’s report. He was recently in Newcastle, and I know that he seeks to make a real difference for the intelligent and ambitious young people I meet regularly across Newcastle Central and West. It is a difficult time for so many families across my constituency, squeezed by increasing bills in energy, housing and so on, so it is great to see the Budget directly address that. Some 60,000 properties in the constituency will receive £100 towards their energy bills this winter, and I welcome the £1.5 billion in additional funding to deliver social and affordable housing and, of course, the £20 million in Pride in Place funding for Elswick in my constituency. After years of fighting for the investment we deserve, our region will no longer have to pick up the crumbs from the Whitehall table, with the new north-east good growth fund helping our fantastic mayor, Kim McGuinness, to improve our public transport and deliver major regional projects directly. I hope that giving £20 billion to the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank will support start-ups, spin-outs and research facilities in the north-east, not simply in the golden triangle. I wish the Chancellor had provided more support in two further areas. The attainment gap in education between the north-east and London is the highest since records began. To challenge that, I would like to see further investment in the incredible young people of Newcastle Central and West, on the scale of the London Challenge from 2003. Secondly, there was significant support for businesses, particularly small businesses, in the Budget, but I would like to have seen even more. Growing businesses will provide jobs for our young people, and small businesses have been heavily hit by higher taxes and less disposable income from many constituents. Finally, I hope that the Chancellor’s £15 billion defence investment plan will be used to support regional growth and investment, as he has promised, and in particular to address the unacceptable truth that the north-east sends the highest proportion of young people into the armed forces, yet receives the lowest proportion of defence investment spending. That is something I will be thinking about this Remembrance week. Young people and, indeed, everyone in the north-east deserves growth in every postcode, and I am grateful to the Chancellor of the Exchequer for providing the first steps to achieving that.

The Budget was a missed opportunity for our rural economy, which yet again this Government have failed to back. My message to the Prime Minister and the Chancellor is simple: stop saying that every postcode matters, and start showing it. In Chester South and Eddisbury, around our farms sit the contractors, vets, farm shops, pubs and family businesses that keep our villages alive.

I commend the hon. Lady for bringing agriculture and the farming life to this debate. That is important, and I congratulate her on being the first person today to mention it. The family farm inheritance tax will have a destructive impact on farming in Northern Ireland. The Ulster Farmers’ Union—I declare an interest as a member—says that people will be forced into a tax bracket not because a family is wealthy, but because the value of the land and buildings has risen on paper. Hard-working families are asset rich but cash poor, and the family farms that I live among and represent in Northern Ireland will be those that feel the pain caused by this Government.

The hon. Gentleman is a champion for farmers in his community, and he is right—the Chancellor had the chance to repeal the vindictive family farms tax and family business tax, but he chose not to. Nearly nine in 10 rural businesses have paused investment, and when investment stops, the consequences ripple through the whole rural economy. Conservatives would scrap those damaging taxes. The Government also had the chance to give small businesses some much-needed breathing space. They did not. Our rural businesses, particularly in hospitality and tourism, are being squeezed by rising costs, higher taxes and more regulation. When businesses are struggling they stop investing, they stop expanding and, crucially, they stop taking on staff. These are the businesses that give so many young people their first step into work, and we should be making that easier, not harder. That is the difference between this Government and the Conservatives: we would halve the jobs tax for under-25s and create 100,000 new apprenticeships, because the best way to get young people into work is to back the businesses willing to employ them. This Budget did neither. Then there is the cost of fuel. The fuel duty freeze is welcome, but the Conservatives kept it frozen for 14 years because we understand how much rural communities rely on their cars. This is not just about fuel for transport. On Saturday, I was out chatting to residents in Audlem, and so many of the people I spoke to are living off-grid. The price of heating oil has nearly doubled this year, and families are wondering whether they can afford to fill their tanks before winter. Rural communities are being left out in the cold, quite literally, and the Budget offered them nothing. That is the real cost of this Budget in the countryside: investment on pause, young people not taken on, homes going cold, and family farms wondering whether they will survive. The contrast could not be clearer. The Conservatives would back our family farms, cut taxes on jobs, bring down energy bills through our cheap power plan, and get our rural economy growing again. The president of the National Farmers’ Union described this Budget as “tinkering while Rome is burning”, and he was right. Our farmers, rural businesses and families do not need more promises, more consultations or more plans for the future. Rural Britain needs action now, and this Budget has failed to deliver it.

If I may, I will speak on behalf of the Scottish Affairs Committee, but I wish to make one point from the perspective of my constituency. Glasgow West, which I am proud to represent, has a relatively high level of youth unemployment, a lower than average level of educational qualifications, and a fairly high number of unemployment-related benefit claimants. We also do not have access to a youth hub. There are three in the city of Glasgow, but none anywhere near my constituency. My plea to the Government is this: can we please have a youth hub? Today’s debate is about good growth in every postcode, and I want to consider an issue that the Scottish Affairs Committee spent some time on, namely Scotland’s space launch sector. Last year we visited the SaxaVord spaceport on the island of Unst in Shetland, and saw for ourselves the potential of the UK’s first fully licensed vertical spaceport. What we heard reinforced our view that Scotland is uniquely placed to further the UK’s space ambitions, while delivering economic growth. Unst’s northerly location allows for launch routes over the north Atlantic ocean, making it particularly well suited to putting satellites into polar orbits. That is combined with our expertise in satellite manufacturing—hon. Members might be surprised to hear that the city of Glasgow produces more satellites than anywhere else in Europe, and Edinburgh’s expertise in data in space makes us uniquely placed to benefit from that. SaxaVord also provides a strong foundation for end-to-end space services. For Shetland, the economic opportunity is hugely significant. The Budget talks about the importance of creating jobs across every nation and region of the UK. SaxaVord could help to sustain an island community by creating skilled jobs and giving young people more opportunities to establish careers locally. In a remote community where unreliable connectivity makes economic development, and life in general, more difficult, that new industry could deliver growth in Shetland’s postcodes. However, the economic growth potential of a space launch capability in Shetland would extend beyond Scotland. A successful spaceport could attract international investment and create opportunities for suppliers across the whole UK. There is also a national security interest here. Developing a sovereign launch capability would reduce our reliance on overseas providers. However, we cannot afford to be complacent, and SaxaVord has yet to achieve a successful orbital launch. In September this year, Norway’s spaceport at Andøya successfully launched satellites into orbit. We should welcome that because it is progress for the European sector, but it raises important questions about whether Scotland has lost its first-mover advantage, and what more the Government can do to support innovative businesses such as SaxaVord to realise their economic potential. During our inquiry, we heard that there is sufficient demand to sustain more than one European spaceport. A successful launch from Scotland will be important, but the real test will be whether it can be scaled up into a commercial launch service. That is why I welcome the Government’s space strategy and their £30 million investment in SaxaVord. It is a significant public investment, but it must be spent wisely. The Committee also looked at fixed links. Despite the island having such great ambitions, there are two ferry journeys before anyone gets to SaxaVord. Given that those ferries are not always reliable and the weather is often against us, the islands in Shetland have been looking at whether fixed links would work for them. Working in conjunction with the Scottish Government and the Shetland Islands council, we think that that is absolutely the kind of thing the Government should be looking at to meet their ambition.
With an immediate three-minute time limit, I call James MacCleary.

The Chancellor has promised growth in every postcode, but those of us in the south-east could be forgiven for thinking that the Government have forgotten us altogether. Take London out of the equation, and the south-east, and Sussex in particular, does not seem to be part of the Government’s infrastructure strategy at all. While London has the highest per capita public transport investment in the country, by contrast the south-east has the lowest of any English region, at 11% below the national average. Where I live in Newhaven, nothing stands out more than the A259—the main coastal road that runs the length of East Sussex, passing through Seaford and Newhaven, as well as serving the hugely popular Seven Sisters country park, which attracts visitors from around the world. The road is vital to the local economy. Department for Transport figures show that more than 19,000 vehicles squeeze along South Way in Newhaven every day, which has a massive impact on neighbourhoods and businesses. The traffic system, designed in the 1970s, is now fundamentally failing our coastal communities. Newhaven is a strategic port and Seaford is a town of over 25,000 residents that attracts tens of thousands of visitors to its beautiful beach and serves as a major access point to the famous Seven Sisters cliffs. The road is a critical artery for our area and, like all coast roads, it is hard to expand it in its current location. In 2023, a multi-year major road network study recommended a package of upgrades, including safety improvements to junctions like Bishopstone Road. The county council submitted its business case to the Government to fund the upgrade package, but that is where it stopped. Will the Minister say whether the Government will commit the money necessary to get the A259 finally moving, and press the Reform-Conservative administration at East Sussex county council to get on with funding immediate improvements, like the Bishopstone Road junction, to boost roads in our area? The Chancellor has said that he wants more houses to be built as a result of this Budget, but building more houses without the necessary infrastructure is a road to nowhere. I am very clear about this: it is not reasonable or fair to ask residents in my community to just accept more and more housing, while they watch their roads clog up and their public services deteriorate and while they cannot get access to a GP. Take Ringmer, a beautiful village in my constituency, where over 1,600 new homes have been proposed as part of the district council’s local plan process. It is worth noting that the village currently has only 2,000 households. I have heard Ministers refer to people in villages like Ringmer, who are concerned about how their communities can possibly cope with so much new housing, as nimbys. That is grossly unfair and frankly insulting. If we want house building and growth, the Government need to offer communities a fair deal, not call them names. Housing plans must be led by need. Too much house building is just waved through and sometimes it is not even built at all. If the Chancellor wants to build Britain, he needs to invest in roads, schools, health facilities and public transport to make the new houses and the communities in which they are built truly sustainable, otherwise we are just building problems for the future. This Budget contains many warm words. However, the residents of Lewes, Seaford, Newhaven, Polegate and our local villages will judge it based on what actually changes for them.

I am pleased that this Budget sets a clear priority to address the cost of living. More than 44,000 households in my Smethwick constituency will receive the £100 payment to help with their energy bills, and the business rates freeze will benefit 52% of retail, hospitality and leisure properties in the west midlands, including 1,198 properties in my constituency. It is clear that decisions taken by this Labour Government, the current Chancellor and the previous Chancellor have been instrumental in keeping UK growth at the top end of growth in all G7 countries. Furthermore, in the past two years the Government have set out an ambitious programme of investment in key industries, including in nuclear energy, green energy and defence industries to name a few. Alongside that public investment, those industries will need crucial private investment to grow to their full potential. For that reason, I would have liked to see the restoration of the 30% up-front income tax relief for venture capital trusts, which was reduced to 20% at the last Budget, as that relief is vital in supporting British small and medium-sized enterprises in their early stages of development. Venture capital trusts already support over 1,100 British companies, predominantly in tech sectors, employing over 100,000 people and generating £21.8 billion in revenue in the last year alone. Those businesses often have high up-front costs, long development cycles and uncertain terms that can make conventional finance difficult to secure. In 2006, when the relief was reduced from 40% to 30%, fundraising reduced by around 65%, and it took 16 years for it to recover. At last year’s Budget, the relief was reduced further from 30% to 20%, and as a result, industry estimates suggest a decline in fundraising of anywhere between 30% and 60%, which is equivalent to between £1.25 billion and £2.5 billion less growth equity for UK scale-ups over the next five years. Restoring the 30% relief would incentivise investment in SMEs across the country to support Government investment. It would allow investment into firms that are crucial to the supply chains that will help to secure our place as a global leader, build our national resilience and deliver growth in every postcode. Every pound invested by VCTs unlocks an additional £2.33 in funding from additional sources. The Treasury has already shown a willingness to support small businesses. Indeed, last year the then Chancellor listened to the industry and implemented changes that it had been requesting for many years. I hope that the Treasury will consider restoring the relief to 30% as part of a wider industry strategy that supports our ambition for growth in every postcode.

Scottish voters were promised change, but instead this Budget delivers a real-terms cut of £650 million to Scotland’s block budget. It treats Scotland as an afterthought, syphons off our energy wealth and fails to protect hard-working families facing a bitter cost of living crisis this winter. Rather than delivering economic growth or protecting the vulnerable, this is a Budget of broken promises. Turning first to the cost of living crisis, during the election campaign Labour explicitly promised to cut household energy bills by £300, yet under its watch, energy bills are forecast to surge by 27% this coming January, taking average annual bills to £2,192, before climbing further to £2,389 by April. Scottish families will face energy bills a whopping £1,275 higher than Labour promised. Even worse, the Chancellor’s decision to replace standing charges with higher gas unit prices creates a deeply unfair geographical penalty. Recent YouGov polling shows that 84% of people in Scotland already had to turn their heating on this year, compared to 59% in London, and independent analysis from the Scottish Parliament confirms that over 800,000 Scottish households face higher gas bills under these changes. Scots are effectively being forced to pay higher bills to subsidise warmer homes in the south of England. This Budget ignores the 142,000 Scottish households who rely on heating oil, leaving them exposed to soaring fuel costs with negligible support. At the pumps, drivers face a similar squeeze. Since July, diesel has rocketed by 34p per litre to over £2 a litre in many locations, leaving diesel drivers £130 worse off each year. Regrettably, the Prime Minister and Chancellor are frankly asleep at the wheel. Nowhere is Westminster’s contempt for Scotland’s economic future clearer than in the decision to axe grant funding for the Acorn carbon capture project in Peterhead. Despite explicit promises that capital was secured, the Government have removed Acorn grant funding. Out of the £200 million promised by Ministers, a mere £12 million in grant funding was delivered, with the rest now being converted to a loan or—possibly, maybe—equity proposals. This continues a 20-year history of Westminster betrayals, from Gordon Brown to the Tories, and Acorn being snubbed, with carbon capture projects being left on the scrap heap all over the place. The decision deals a direct blow to a just transition. In its Budget documents, the Treasury has banked £5.1 billion in revenue from Scottish oil and gasfields. Over decades, more than £400 billion in oil and gas revenue flowed from Scotland’s waters into Westminster’s hands, with the Chancellor admitting that a Scottish sovereign wealth fund would today be worth £1 trillion, had that wealth been properly invested, as Norway chose to do. Every single penny generated from Scotland’s natural resources should be reinvested in Scotland to secure a genuinely just transition to a renewables future.

It is fair to say that my constituents in Ealing Southall will not all have been glued to the telly last Wednesday to watch the Chancellor’s speech. Instead, due to wars abroad, many of them will have been trying their best to feed hungry kids, who were off for half term, or stressing about whether to turn the heating on or not. After years of austerity, my constituents have spent more than a decade too worried about their daily lives to be able to pay much attention to Budget day, and all the talk of GDP, OBR and CPI does not seem to have any impact on their lives. This Budget changes that. By cutting energy bills and giving 34,300 households in my constituency a £100 council tax rebate, this Budget recognises the families in Ealing Southall worried about getting through this winter and the next. By reducing tariffs on everyday items, this Budget recognises the hard choices that mums in Ealing Southall have to make every day. By permanently raising the tax-free mileage rate to 55p, this Budget recognises the many nurses, plumbers and care workers in Ealing Southall who use their car for work. By allowing carers to work more hours without losing their entire benefits, this Budget recognises the situation of many carers in Ealing Southall. The Leader of the Opposition dismisses those changes, but in doing so she simply shows how out of touch she is with the reality of working people’s lives. Small changes such as those matter. As well as giving people breathing space, this Budget takes the big decisions needed to finally undo the damage of 14 years of the Conservatives. Investing in skills and apprenticeships so that my constituents can get better-paid jobs is the best way to protect them from the uncertainties of foreign wars and global crises. This Budget’s £15 million investment to restore the union learning fund is one example of that. The Leader of the Opposition dismissed the union learning fund as a “random new scheme employers don’t want”, but in fact it is a brilliant old scheme that 78% of employers said they were hugely supportive of until the Tories got rid of it. Yet again, the Leader of the Opposition shows how out of touch she is. The new union learning fund will address the challenges of today and help to reskill the workforce to take on jobs in AI and advanced manufacturing. It will help the Somali Uber drivers in my constituency to get help from their union, the GMB, when they fear losing their jobs to driverless cars. This Budget also invests in apprentices such as Jack and Aidan, who I met when I visited West London College earlier this year. They can see buildings being built outside their window, and the new apprenticeship brokering scheme will help them to work on those sites. Although they might not have been glued to the telly last week, when the kids had all been fed, the elderly parents had been looked after and the working day was done, people in Ealing Southall switched on their telly and their heating, and they saw a Government who are giving them not just the breathing space they need to make their lives a little easier right now, but the tools they need to face the future with confidence.

“What incentive is there for hard-working families and young entrepreneurs to remain in Britain after this Budget?” That is the question that a constituent put to me at a community meeting I held in Wixams in Mid Bedfordshire last week. Let me start with what I think is the main test that really matters for any Budget: will it make my constituents richer in five years’ time than they are today? Having listened to the Chancellor and the reaction over the weekend, I am afraid that the answer is no. There is simply no confidence whatsoever that this Budget will deliver growth in their postcodes, and it certainly does not give hope in their hearts. Given that the Prime Minister is extremely comfortable looking to the past, whether it is to the 1970s or 2016, but not to the future, I did a little reflecting myself over the weekend. It is fitting that we debate this Budget 40 years on from the big bang in 1986, when regulations that were strangling our economy were swept away, making London into the powerhouse of global finance that it remains today, opening the City of London to the world and delivering prosperity here at home. The courage of that decision in 1986 benefited every corner of Britain, delivering more jobs, investment and tax revenues that paid for schools, hospitals and public services. During my 15 years in the City before coming to this place, I saw at first hand how EU regulations after the credit crunch steadily ratcheted up costs and de-risked our entire economy. The courage and ambition of 1986 have slowly given way to the caution and complexity of 2026. That is why my right hon. Friend the Leader of the Opposition is right to say that Britain needs a new economic revolution even bigger than the big bang. Where are we today? The OBR says that the tax burden will reach a record 38.6% of GDP. The Budget raises tax on savings and rental income—again. It doubles the bank surcharge and leaves Labour’s damaging jobs tax untouched. After Labour’s first Budget, I told the House that it was “a job-cutting Budget”. Some 1.7 million people older than 16 are now unemployed—up by 276,000 under this Government—and vacancies are at their lowest level since 2014. Last year, about 136,000 more British nationals left the country than came home, with two thirds of them under the age of 35. The Prime Minister and the Chancellor may have changed, but this Budget makes it clear that Labour has not. It is still picking the pockets of working people to pay for welfare. That was plain to hear this weekend, as the Chief Secretary to the Treasury redefined working people to exclude employees. It may be a new team at the Dispatch Box, but their contempt for British business and British business owners in this Budget is as strong as ever.

The motto of my constituency —the old Bootle county borough—was “Respice, Aspice, Prospice”. In English, that means reflecting on the past, considering the present and looking to the future. I want to look a little to the past. In 2010 David Cameron said, “I’ll cut the deficit, not the NHS.” Well, that did not age well, did it? In 2010 the national debt was 64.7% of GDP; by 2024 it was 96.5% of GDP. What about the NHS? Waiting lists in 2010 stood at 2.4 million; in 2024 they stood at 7.6 million. Satisfaction ratings were down. Rough sleeping was up. Wage growth was down and did not recover for many years under the Tories. On food bank use, there were 100,000 food parcels in 2010, and more than 3 million by 2024. Some 3.6 million children were in poverty in 2010, and 4.3 million by 2024. There were 168,000 zero-hours contracts in 2010; by 2024 there were more than 1 million of them. Let us look to the present. We have more than 4,500 more secondary, further education and special school teachers. More than 1,300 schools have joined the free breakfast club programme. That impacts on my constituency in a very practical and positive way. Waiting lists are down. The Renters’ Rights Act 2025 protects 11 million renters. We have created Great British Energy—cutting bills for schools and hospitals, and planning clean power for 10 million homes. We have raised the national minimum wage to £13.21, which is a 3.9% increase. We have a £100 discount on energy bills for homes in council tax bands A to D, which impacts 20 million households, and 99.8% of homes in my constituency will be affected by that. Standing charges on household gas have been scrapped. The list goes on. What about the future? We are decreasing annual borrowing, with borrowing forecast to drop from £134 billion to £67 billion by 2031. On the share of GDP, annual net borrowing is expected to decline from 4.2%. We are on track with the fiscal rules. We have real wage growth—and so on, and so on. Child poverty is down. That is what we get from a Labour Budget. That is in addition to the impact of devolution in all our communities, which will be of great benefit to my constituency.

I cannot begin without congratulating the hon. Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Sagal Abdi-Wali) on her speech. I know her constituency well, and she is a distinguished former colleague of mine on Camden council. I am here today to speak about council housing. The Government’s priorities are still not right on this issue, despite the Chancellor explicitly naming in his Budget speech the loss of more than 2 million council homes since the 1980s and the Prime Minister’s focus on rough sleeping. We have millions of people waiting in overcrowded homes, rented homes that they cannot afford and temporary accommodation that councils cannot afford. That goes well beyond a crisis. What have the Government given us in this Budget? We have new money, with £1.5 billion added to the pot for councils to bid on for affordable home building. In paragraph 5.4 of the Budget, the Chancellor says that that will help to build potentially 10,000 more real council homes over the next four years. That is not terrible, but in paragraph 5.5 in the same document we get £4.7 billion for the Government’s new version of the Help to Buy scheme. The Chancellor explains that that will support private, profit-making developers to sell an extra 20,000 new builds. I presume that is without expecting developers to cut their prices or profits—it is possible that they will increase them. I note that the Government plan to collect some small fees from the house builders, but I assume that they have been agreed with them. I also note that one impact of the previous Government’s Help to Buy scheme was to keep house prices rising out of many people’s reach and to boost profits and profit margins for developers, as the recent Government evaluation of the scheme concludes. Can Ministers tell us whether £4.7 billion for loans that they do not expect to be paid back for many years to support 20,000 extra private sales by developers really represents better short-term or long-term value for the public purse than £1.5 billion to enable 10,000 new build council homes? That is three times more funding out of the door for just twice as many new homes. Even under the Government’s broad house building target, is that really the best use of public money? It may not be that simple, so I ask the Government to give us their workings on these choices, especially if I am wrong in my assumptions. Can they commit to publishing, for comparison, the Green Book assumptions and appraisals for each of these investment decisions, and the time it takes for money to move out of their loan scheme and back into it? We need much more investment in real council housing. We need “buy the supply”—the funding of acquisitions. I cannot see why the Government are not putting together an equity loan scheme for councils to help them buy the supply, instead of going with another help to buy scheme, just as the last Conservative Government did.

I start by thanking the Chancellor for presenting us with the Budget, and the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government for introducing today’s debate on growth in every postcode. When the Prime Minister began his tour of the country in August, he started in Ilkeston. There, he, the Secretary of State and I listened to people talk about the loss that they feel, having watched our town centre decline over decades. Whether I am in Ilkeston or Long Eaton, people in my constituency share that sense of loss. They remember how our town centres used to be. They had vibrant high streets and markets and great pubs. They were bustling centres of commerce and the beating heart of our community, all at the same time. The Chancellor is absolutely right to help level the playing field by recognising the fundamental shifts in our economy, and helping out struggling small local businesses while asking thriving online giants to finally pay their fair share. Following the Chancellor’s announcement, almost 400 Erewash businesses will no longer need to pay a penny in business rates. That is money that they can now spend on creating jobs, pass back to their customers, reinvest, or keep hold of to reacquire some breathing space. More than 80 additional shops in my constituency no longer pay any business rates at all, and I know that the Chancellor will be very glad to hear that 10 great pubs have been given full business rates relief, including the fantastic Dewdrop in Ilkeston, and the Mill and Brook in Long Eaton.
Will my hon. Friend give way?

I will not, because so many people want to speak tonight. If the Chancellor is looking for somewhere to celebrate his first Budget, I invite him to Erewash to try out the newly done-up function room at the Mill and Brook, or perhaps enjoy one of the Dewdrop’s famous cheese and onion cobs. I turn to the measures that my right hon. Friend the Chancellor has introduced for families. I was heartened to hear him present such an extensive raft of measures to help pull back the cost of living for so many people across Erewash and the country. Alongside the removal of VAT from electricity costs and scrapping standing charges on gas, there is the direct £100 payment this winter. It is an enormous step that pulls down energy bills for more than 40,000 families, from Sawley to Sandiacre and Shipley View. I also thank the Chancellor for his continued investment in Rolls-Royce. Royce’s is a huge employer in my constituency, and it is a great point of pride for us in Derbyshire that the most groundbreaking innovation in the world happens on our doorstep. The Chancellor has recognised how much Rolls-Royce and my constituents have to offer our country. That is what a Labour Budget is all about—rooting our economy in society and making them both fairer, and supporting working families, pensioners, carers and small businesses. It is great to have a Chancellor and a Government who listen to people, who will allow our communities to hope again, and who will put our communities back at the heart of our economy.

It is worth reflecting on three things. As we have very little time, I make just one comment about welfare. It is necessary for the Government to reduce welfare spending, because we can see what the Government’s own forecast says will happen if they do not do so: debt and borrowing will be higher in every single year. That is hugely down to the fact that the growth in welfare spending is running out of control. I was astonished that the point was avoided during the Budget, and then we had confusion when the Chancellor went on the radio the following morning and said that welfare would be reduced during the course of this Government. He was overridden by the Treasury, which said, “No, it won’t, and he didn’t say that,” but he did. That is the confusion. I do not doubt that the Chancellor wants to reduce welfare spending, but it appears that he will not be able to. The main thing I want to say is that this Budget has not been good for working families, middle-income earners, and those who bother to save. It is really hard on them. Tax is at the highest level on record; the tax burden will hit a historic high next year of 37% of GDP, nearly 38%, and will surge to over 38.6% by 2031. Growth next year has been cut from 1.6% to 1%, and as a result of this Budget, real household disposable income per person is forecast to fall by 0.8% this year. Those are stark figures, figures that economists have produced in their forecasts. The effect of that is to give Government fewer choices. I want to talk about defence, which is important because the threat we face now—from China and North Korea, from Iran and Russia, all linked together along an axis of totalitarian states—is astonishing. That means that our defence spending needs to rise. Every other Government in Europe is raising defence spending. We used to be the leader on this; they would all look to us, but not any more, because we have avoided raising our defence spending. Even the defence review will not take place until well into next year, and who knows what will happen next. This is a failure of the Government—an opportunity that has been missed. To quote Helen Miller, the economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, the Budget “feels like lots of fiddling, short-term things, new complications—a ‘new entrepreneurs allowance’, ‘starter ISA’…etc. I don’t hear a clear, coherent vision or a simplification of tax system”, which is necessary. The reality is that this Budget was an opportunity missed, and future generations will look back at this moment and say, “Where were you? Why didn’t you take the decisions that were necessary?”.

I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, specifically as it relates to Rolls-Royce. This is a Budget that backs grafters, not just in Derby but in towns and cities across the whole country. It backs hard-working families who are struggling to make ends meet with £100 of breathing space on their energy bills. It backs the landlords behind the pubs we know and love through changes to business rates that will help them balance their books, and it backs good growth—not just in DE1 and DE2, not just in our great city of Derby, but in postcodes all over the country. At the heart of that is good growth and reindustrialisation, driving the jobs, investment and opportunities our communities need. In Derby, we know a thing or two about making things. For generations, we have built, engineered and supplied the technologies that keep our country powered. We are proud of that heritage, but we know that our industrial future cannot be built on nostalgia; we need investments that match the scale of our ambition for British workers and British industry, such as the whopping £2.5 billion joint investment delivered in the Budget to keep the next generation of narrow-body aircraft engines right here on our home soil. Last week, I was proud to welcome the Prime Minister, the Chancellor, and our brilliant Business Secretary to Derby to meet the people making that possible—people such as Rolls-Royce apprentices Will, Elliot and Lucy, young people putting in the hard yards, learning their trade and building the skills that will secure not just their own futures, but the future of British manufacturing. That investment will create thousands more opportunities like theirs, be it in the design office, on the factory floor, or in our brilliant small and medium-sized businesses right across the supply chain. Reindustrialisation is not just a headline; it is about creating good, stable jobs close to home. It is about opportunities for our suppliers, services and skilled craftspeople who support our growing factories, and it is about giving local communities a share in the manufacturing success that they help to create. As we in Derby know better than most, that has not always been the case. The manufacturing success that Derby residents have helped to create has not been shared with them, but things are changing, because with £10 million of Government investment behind Team Derby, we are putting that right. We are making sure that every pound of investment works as hard as it can, and makes things better for our city and our residents. Reindustrialisation is about making sure that the people and the place benefit from that work, which is why this Budget backs our communities.

When my grandfather Lieutenant Austin Coghlan, a naval officer, served in the battle of the Atlantic, he did not expect to survive. That he did was in no small part due to the codebreakers at Bletchley Park, who diverted convoys away from U-boats. In the process, the codebreakers invented the world’s first computer, Colossus, which powered the economic development of the post-war world. The spill-over effect from military technology to civilian use is one of the most powerful forces for economic growth, and we can use it now. Many have said that there is not much that is transformative in this Budget, but that overlooks the Chancellor’s decision to invest up to £5 billion in dual-use military technology through the British Business Bank and the National Wealth Fund, and to borrow jointly with our allies through the multilateral defence mechanism. I have called for that for the past two years on the Treasury Committee, so I am grateful that the Government and the Liberal Democrats have embraced that policy. Academics now recognise that the economic dominance of the United States has been powered by public research and development, especially in defence. In my Budget speech last year, I called for £5 billion more on public research and development, so that we spend the same share of GDP on that as the US does. The £5 billion in this Budget, while over four years, is a start. Public investment in research in universities and laboratories is powerful because it de-risks the cost of developing new technologies, and enables private investment to take that research forward in start-ups. The London Business School’s Paolo Surico has found that innovation that is funded by the Government, but taken forward by the private sector, generates productivity and growth that is eight times larger than innovation taken forward by the private sector alone. More borrowing is of course a concern in the current fiscal environment, but as the Government have correctly identified, borrowing jointly with allies can remove most of the credit risk. The latest academic research enables us to forecast the returns with confidence. If this programme was scaled in increments of £2 billion a year annually over the next 10 years, it could lead to: growth finally returning to pre-2008 levels, transforming living standards; a debt-to-GDP ratio that is 2 percentage points or £60 billion lower; and meeting our NATO defence spending commitments. British politicians in the 1930s were labelled the guilty men, because they failed to prioritise defence over the deficit. My grandfather’s generation paid the price. As a reservist, an infantry officer and an MP, I want to ensure that our generation does not.

I welcome the measures taken by the Chancellor in this Budget, which is clear-eyed about the pressures that people and businesses continue to face, but equally clear about our plan of action to support households so that they keep more of their money; to reduce costs for businesses; and to create the conditions for economic growth. People across West Lancashire are working hard to make ends meet. There is no dearth of ambition and talent in our local communities, but when conflict in the middle east drives up global energy prices, my constituents feel the effects in their household budget. The extension of the 0% VAT rate on electricity until July 2027, the removal of standing charges from household gas bills and the £2.6 billion on the energy bills breathing space scheme are all welcome steps. In West Lancashire, 37,000-plus households will benefit from the £100 payment this winter. The costs of global volatility are not only felt in the home, however. The conflict in the middle east has once again demonstrated how vulnerable motorists are to fluctuations in global fuel prices. I therefore welcome the extension of fuel duty tax cuts until July next year. I have spoken repeatedly about the need to improve public transport and rail connectivity in Skelmersdale in my constituency. We need to ensure that our communities are better connected to neighbouring towns, cities and economic opportunities. While I continue to encourage Reform-led Lancashire county council to work constructively with me to improve local transport for my constituents, I also recognise that in many parts of a rural constituency like mine, owning a car is currently a necessity. Measures to ease the pressure on motorists are particularly welcome in such rural constituencies, where the price at the pump is piling additional pressure on already overstretched families. This Budget is not only for families. Our high streets are at the heart of our communities. They bring employment opportunities, economic growth and a sense of community, character and identity. As co-chair of the all-party parliamentary group on theatre, I am particularly conscious of the important role that our cultural venues, and particularly touring productions, play in supporting our local economy. The economic contribution of touring theatre extends well beyond the theatre itself; every pound spent on the theatre ticket generates a further £1.40 in local spending. I look forward to seeing how the Government can further support the touring sector and creative industries, and can ensure that theatres reach audiences across the country. I welcome this Budget, which recognises the importance of our high streets and the contribution of small businesses. This is how we create jobs, strengthen our communities and deliver growth that people feel in every postcode, every day of their life.

The most critical issue facing my constituents is affordability and the cost of living. The Budget should not be an annual announcement to appease markets and to protect and enrich corporations, executive shareholders, the rich and the super-rich, or even those in this place. It should not look after the wealthy at the expense of the poor; it should be about making the lives of the vast majority of people in our country better and more affordable and, for some, just bearable. I met one such person. She lives in Batley, works full time, pays her taxes and does everything that we tell people they should do. She showed me her budget and asked a question that no one in modern Britain should have to ask: “Should I pay my rent, should I pay my bills, or should I buy food?” She asked that not because she is unemployed, not because she has mismanaged her finances and not because she lacks ambition, but because the weekly shop costs more, the gas bill costs more, the rent costs more and the journey to work costs more. Everything that a human being needs to live a simple, dignified life costs much more, and her wages simply do not keep up. That is the reality of the cost of living crisis. This Budget, although there are some welcome measures, does not do anywhere near enough to make life bearable, let alone affordable, for the many by making the few contribute a bit more. We in this place earn more than £98,000. We will not feel the impact of energy prices that are 70% higher than 2020, and that will rise by 4% this month and by a quarter in January. The 60% to 70% increase in petrol and diesel prices will be a blip that will have little impact on our driving or lifestyle. Grocery prices have increased by 38.6% since 2020, according to the Commons Library, meaning that what was a weekly £100 shop now costs roughly £138.60. Car insurance rose by 82% between 2021 and 2024, and insurance premium indexes have increased by 126% since 2020. Nationally, average rents have climbed from roughly £975 a month to £1,375 a month. Too often, Ministers speak about future economic improvements, while households wonder how they will get through the next week. Parliament must take some responsibility, because our duty is not simply to debate suffering, and not merely to acknowledge hardship. It is not enough to express concern. Our duty is to act, and this Government have let the people down.

I welcome the positives in the Chancellor’s Budget, some of which include the freeze on fuel duty, increases in the minimum and national living wage and the small business rate relief threshold for retail, hospitality and leisure properties. There is also the fact that almost 56,000 households in my constituency will benefit from the £100 payment for properties in council tax bands A to D. However, I must advise the Chancellor that there will not be good growth in NE6 and NE28 postcodes unless Ministers pull every lever at their disposal to support industry on the Tyne. The overhead electric cables are a constraint on investment, as they prevent the movement of large structures used in the offshore energy sector. News that the project to underground the cables is now effectively paused will push the 2034 completion date even further into the future. International yards are already capitalising on our offshore wind leasing rounds. Fixed-bottom assets are increasing in size and investment in floating offshore wind, which will see integrated units towed to sea, is set to overtake fixed-bottom by the early 2030s. My constituency has the skills and infrastructure to sit at the forefront of the UK’s green future. It is home to a cluster of offshore supply chain firms and an expanding energy skills academy, and it is less than 100 nautical miles from the world’s largest offshore wind farm. Ofgem, National Grid and Ministers must act decisively, so that Tyneside can seize the opportunities that the green transition offers.

For all the positives in this Budget, the real disappointment is that it does not match the radicalism and the claims of the now endless Government social media and TikTok barrage. It is extraordinary, given everything that he said when he was Secretary of State for Defence, that the Chancellor has kicked the big defence spending decisions down the road. There are warm words, but there is no plan for helping people back into work—and, of course, nothing concrete on Europe, something that even the previous Chancellor acknowledged over the weekend needs to be addressed. A big theme for my constituents is the need for infrastructure to support housing. I believe that there would be less despair and opposition to new houses if central Government listened to calls for transparency and ambition when it comes to infrastructure and public services to support housing growth. Setting and publishing targets for the amount of primary healthcare, transport, large-scale leisure or policing per head of population, based on an analysis of local demographic needs, and showing progress or otherwise against those metrics, would help to restore trust and would highlight where investment is needed. That is all the more important as local councils do not have direct control of most of these areas. The lack of acknowledgment of such challenges, let alone action on them, in the Budget is disappointing. It is also regrettable that there are no rolling funds or investment programmes for major transport improvements. Without them, no hope has been created for a new railway station serving Grove and Wantage, accessibility improvements to Cholsey station, or electrification from Didcot to Oxford. We have to hope that the Government’s slow embrace of devolution, amid the utter shambles of local government reorganisation, will fill this void, but that very much remains to be seen given the number of unanswered questions. There are some welcome measures to support hospitality, but small producer relief for small-scale producers of alcohol still excludes vineyards such as Hendred vineyard, which produces a few thousand bottles a year. That makes little sense: the alcohol intensity of a drink does not inherently correlate with how much it is abused, and English wine has a promising future. Let me end by referring to what the Budget says about science and high tech. Despite some positive measures on AI safety and capital gains tax founders’ relief, the Government’s previous decisions on science mean that this is the biggest area of disappointment. My constituency contains a wide range of science and technology organisations, and the Government’s decision to cut Science and Technology Facilities Council funding significantly is incomprehensible and unforgivable. No wonder that after three months the Government have still not had the basis courtesy to reply to my letters about that. The 15% funding cuts in Harwell’s three national and globally significant research facilities—Diamond Light Source, the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source and the Central Laser Facility—will lead to significant decreases in operating time, of up to 25%. I am used to the Government ignoring me, but perhaps they will listen to the deputy general secretary of Prospect, Sue Ferns, the Liverpool city region mayor, Steve Rotherham, and the physicist Brian Cox, all of whom have warned that the cuts would “cause lasting and possibly irreparable damage to the UK’s scientific capabilities”.

The real tests of this Budget are the families who notice every extra penny at the petrol station, every increase in the energy bill, and the pounds adding to the price of the weekly shop. The war in Iran carries a price tag for the globe, and that is clear at the petrol pump and in our energy bills. For motorists, and for more than 3,500 workers in transport and logistics in my constituency, the price at the pump matters. I therefore welcome the continued freeze in the fuel duty cut until July 2027, a measure that I have called for throughout the year. I also welcome the end to standing charges for gas, and the £100 payment to those in council tax bands A to D. That will make the thought of bills during the upcoming winter that bit less stressful. If the Scottish Government do the same, more than 119,000 households in the West Lothian and Falkirk council areas will benefit. That money must be passed on. Our constituents cannot afford for it to disappear into the black hole created by the Scottish National party’s mismanagement of Scotland’s finances. These measures mean real reductions in bills, shifting the brunt of levies and standing charges away from the consumer just as the worst hits.
Will my hon. Friend give way?

I will continue my speech, so that others can get in. I am mindful that many people have high energy usage owing to health conditions and disabilities, so I would be grateful if the Minister outlined the support that those with health vulnerabilities will receive. I am also aware that many businesses continue to struggle with the high level of energy costs, especially manufacturers in energy-intensive sectors, so I would have liked to have seen an expansion of eligibility for the British industrial competitiveness scheme, and I hope the Chancellor will consider that. I also hope that the Scottish Government will take a leaf out of the Chancellor’s book, and replicate the cuts in business rates to give our high street businesses a boost. The Budget delivers a further £600 million for Scotland, amounting to over £18 billion more since Labour was elected in July 2024. I am calling on the Scottish Government to use that £600 million extra and invest in the services on which my constituents rely and which they use day in, day out. While we cannot predict every shock that comes from overseas, we can choose how we respond to them. We choose to protect families at the petrol pump and in their energy bills, and we choose to back British workers, British businesses and British manufacturing. That is what this Budget is about: giving my constituents greater security today, while building a stronger and more resilient economy for tomorrow.

The Chancellor said in his speech last week that people were looking to Government “not to solve all their problems but to give them a bit of breathing space”.—[Official Report, 28 October 2026; Vol. 792, c. 304.] That may be partly true, but I think it demonstrates the lack of ambition that sits behind this Budget. The Government should be solving the systemic problems in our economy, or at least making a much more serious attempt to do so than we saw last week. Those problems are at the root of why so many families are struggling to make ends meet and so many businesses are failing. When the economy is as damaged as it is, when public sector debt sits at 104% of debt to GDP—according to the International Monetary Fund—when productivity is decreasing, when consumer confidence is down and when housing costs continue to rise, I think it is the Government’s job to do something substantial towards solving the country’s problems. Make no mistake: the various incremental measures that the Chancellor announced, such as those on household energy bills, will be welcome, but they are not sufficient to “move the dial on growth”, in the words of the Institute for Fiscal Studies. As bigger, more difficult decisions are kicked down the road for another time, what my constituents want to know is how they are to absorb another year of no real earnings growth, while mortgage increases are coming down the pipe on the back of a likely Bank of England rate rise this week. My constituents want to know that the public services on which we all rely are safe, and they are not. My constituents want to see genuine hope for a future with better jobs and more opportunities, and they want to know that our food supply is secure and our rural economy will be supported. Across the board, however, this Budget was too unambitious, and ducked the big decisions that our country is crying out for. Let me give two examples that could “move the dial”. First, the Chancellor’s speech was silent on Britain’s relationship with our biggest trading partner, the European Union. Our country prospers when fair, dynamic markets for goods, services, capital and labour operate effectively. If the Government are serious about our economy and want growth, they should get on with opening negotiations for our country to rejoin the EU now. Secondly, if we are serious about getting our national debt under control, we must look at reforming our fiscal rules. Why? Because they do not work. That is demonstrated by the fact that for the last 25 years there has not been a single year in which tax receipts exceeded spending. Our fiscal rules front-load spending in the early years, and difficult decisions—as epitomised by last week’s Budget—are put off, frequently to the other side of an election. There are good international examples from which we can learn. Other countries, such as Switzerland and Sweden, do this better. I therefore urge the Chancellor to take steps to rejoin the EU, and to establish a cross-party commission exploring more prudent fiscal rules.

We live in an ever-changing world where global issues impact on our everyday lives, so I am pleased that this Budget is about making a difference to working people and families in Portsmouth North, with little changes that make a big difference. People in my city are worried about the cost of energy. This Budget responds by extending the removal of VAT on electricity until 27 July, removing gas standing charges and putting £100 directly into the bank accounts of 40,000 households across Portsmouth North. That sits alongside the new British industrial competitive scheme for businesses. However, energy is not the only cost putting pressure on families. For many people in Portsmouth North, getting to work or school means getting in the car, and the cost of filling up hits hard. Extending the 5p fuel duty cut and keeping fuel duty frozen helps motorists and businesses to manage these costs every day. Cost of living measures are also about allowing people to keep enjoying life and coming together, so I am pleased to see that changes in this Budget will mean that half of the retail, leisure and hospitality businesses in our region will no longer pay business rates at all. We must invest in our future. The Your First Home scheme means lower deposits and more opportunities for young people, and I look forward to seeing more details. We must also keep our country safe. In Portsmouth—our naval city—defence means more than national security; it means jobs, skills and opportunities for local people. The Government are spending £14 billion more on defence than the previous Government did, and the £3.9 billion for the naval dockyard is brilliant. That, alongside the investment from previous Governments, is great. One announcement is especially close to my heart: paternity pay for the self-employed. For too long, self-employed men have faced an impossible choice between spending those precious first few days with their newborns and returning to work because their bills will not wait. Labour introduced paternity leave, but self-employed dads and non-birthing partners were left behind. This Budget takes an important step: for the first time, they will be able to receive paternity pay—that is a point of principle. For a builder, a plumber, a taxi driver, a shopkeeper or a farmer, this means real support at the most important moment of their life. Up to £194 a week for two weeks might not be enough, and the Minister will not be surprised to hear that I want to see longer leave and more generous pay, but for someone who currently gets nothing, this change means real help with their bills, less financial pressure and, more importantly, more time with their new-born child. Being there for your child should not be a luxury that is reserved to those who can afford it. I want to quickly thank the incredible campaigners who have helped deliver this change, including all at the Dad Shift, On The Tools and Movember. Most importantly, I thank the hard-working tradespeople across the country who have made their voice heard and trusted me to bring their voice to this place. This victory is theirs, and they should be so very proud, just as I am so very proud of them. How can we ask young men to take up apprenticeships in our trades if we do not protect their future and their families? This is personal for me: my dad was a tradie, my brother is a tradie, and so was my grandad. I am incredibly proud of all of them, and I want something different for my own sons.

I was disappointed that the Chancellor did nothing to change the gift aid rules, which would have helped the Bridgwater carnival and many other community organisations and charities. The Bridgwater Guy Fawkes carnival is the most magnificent spectacle. It is Britain’s oldest carnival and the largest illuminated carnival in Europe, and it is taking place on Saturday. Like so many good causes, the carnival raises much of its funds in small cash donations, often loose change collected in a bucket on the night, yet it can only claim gift aid for a maximum of £2,000 on those small donations—a figure that has not been increased for 10 years.
