Will the Chancellor please consider increasing the limit? That would make a huge difference to organisations that collect so much of their funds in small cash donations. Despite making so many changes in his Budget, the Chancellor has not reinstated the listed places of worship grant scheme, which his predecessor abolished. This means that communities who worship in a listed building, such as the parish of St Andrews in Burnham-on-Sea, will have to bear the full cost of VAT on the repairs that their historic church requires. The scheme that replaced the old one is less generous and has a capped budget. We should cherish our beautiful listed churches and take care of them for future generations. I will continue to press the Chancellor to renew the scheme in full, to make sure that our congregations are not charged an extra 20% for vital repairs. There are 98 separate measures in the Red Book, and many of them will further complicate Britain’s already byzantine tax code. Do we really need a new founders’ relief from capital gains tax? We are told that it will be for “qualifying founders of high-growth, innovative companies”. That perhaps sounds good for a Labour tax relief, but would it not be better to lower the rate of CGT for everyone, rather than add another carve-out for accountants and lawyers to argue about? Britain needs lower tax rates with fewer exemptions, not additional complications that drive up the cost of compliance. The fundamental problem that Britain faces today is simple: we are running out of money. Unless we change course soon, every other problem will become harder to solve. Our national debt is now £3 trillion, and every year Labour is adding tens of billions more. At a time of international uncertainty, we must spend more on defence, but this Government cannot do so because they refuse to cut welfare. We need a plan to cut debt, fund defence and get Britain growing again.

I will speak about the devolution measures announced in the Budget and the fiscal devolution pathway that has been set out. We normally hear two arguments for devolution: first, that decisions should be made closer to the people they affect rather than in Whitehall, and secondly, that investment should be spread more fairly beyond London and certain pockets of the south-east. I agree with both those arguments, but I think there is a more important argument: devolution can help us grow the economy and make the British state work better. After nearly two decades of stagnation, we desperately need to raise productivity, build infrastructure more quickly and unlock growth across the country. I believe that devolution can be one of the best ways of doing that, but it needs to come with fiscal devolution. Some 95% of tax revenue in Britain is raised by central Government, rather than at a regional or local level. Meanwhile, France raises three times as much at a sub-national level, and in Germany it is much higher still. The Centre for Cities has found that there is a strong relationship between fiscal devolution and wages across devolved economies. Correlation is not always causation, but there are obvious economic reasons why that relationship exists. Today, when councils approve new housing, attract employers or build infrastructure, they take the political risk and bear many of the up-front costs, but much of the additional tax revenue goes straight to the Treasury and eventually gets redistributed elsewhere. Even when councils retain that money, it can disappear at the next funding reset, as we saw earlier this year. Local leaders bear the cost of growth, while the Treasury collects the proceeds. That is why I welcome the Chancellor’s commitment to increase business rates retention, giving mayors a share of business rates growth from next year, and to give mayors a share of income tax receipts from 2028. If we want local leaders to take difficult decisions in favour of growth, their communities need to share in the rewards. Stable future revenues can also allow local areas to borrow against future growth to pay for the infrastructure needed today, and it is good to see the Government looking at how that can happen through bodies such as the Greater Cambridge Development Corporation. I hope that is something we can look at in Milton Keynes in the future. I want to finish by saying that although many areas across the country will benefit from the proceeds of the Government’s announcements on devolution, I am disappointed that it was announced this week that my local area will not be one of them. That is despite the hard work and determination of many MPs across this Chamber to get devolution across Bedfordshire and Milton Keynes. Indeed, the Government came forward with a package of nearly £1 billion to get this over the line. It was unfortunately vetoed by one local government leader in Central Bedfordshire, who decided to put politics ahead of the people he was elected to represent. He has let the local area down, and I hope the Government will continue to work with all local leaders in the area to see if they can find a solution.

Taken as a whole, this Budget is really rather insipid, because it deliberately avoids many of the big-ticket areas, such as our runaway benefits budget, which it does nothing at all about, and the need to put together a properly funded programme to adequately build the defence of this nation—again, an issue that this Budget leaves untouched. But at least we have a Budget. I say that because in my part of the United Kingdom, we are entering the eighth month when, because of a catastrophic failure of devolution in Northern Ireland, we do not even have a budget for this year, never mind next year. I say to the Treasury and the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland that this cannot go on. They need to bring that budget through this House so that there is the money to pay for the public service pay rises and everything else, which is now at risk because of the dysfunctional failure of the Stormont Executive. One of the other things this Budget is silent about—yet it is something that, if the Government have their way, will be very important—is the cost of the Government’s intended reset with the EU. I will take but one example, which is the proposition that the United Kingdom should participate in the EU’s electricity market. When we look at the European Council decision that created the mandate for the EU to negotiate with the United Kingdom about the UK entering the EU’s electricity market, we find that the mandate includes the words “an agreement on the financial contribution of the United Kingdom towards reducing economic, social and territorial disparities between the regions of the Union”. In other words, the United Kingdom, as a cost of joining the EU’s electricity market, will be required to make a contribution—no doubt a sizeable contribution—to the EU’s cohesion fund. It is the same with the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement and with all the other targets of the reset, yet this Budget fails to tell us what the cost of any of that will be. The Government need to front up and tell the public not the glossy impression they like to create of advantage from the reset, which is phoney, but the actual monetary cost. What is it, Minister?

Milton Keynes MPs are like buses: you wait a long time, and two come at once. It costs us £133 billion every year because women are excluded from paid work on equal terms with men. I have worked closely with Members from across these Benches, as well as the Women’s Budget Group and the Good Growth Foundation, to put together an unashamedly female agenda for how we can realise the £113 billion of gross value added that we would see every year if women could fully participate in the economy. I want to thank my right hon. and hon. Friends the Treasury Ministers for their engagement on this really important document. I want to talk about what this Budget delivers for women. It bolsters us, it promotes us and it protects us. It bolsters us with paternity leave and adoption leave for self-employed people, with breakfast clubs and with VAT cuts in energy bills. We know that, more often than not, it is women who are trying to make the household bills add up at the end of the month and women who are the first people in the family to go without when there is not enough. The commitment to the gender pay gap and pay transparency is so important, but women are business owners too, particularly on our high streets, where our hairdressers and nail technicians are seeing business rate cuts. High-tech, high-investment, science-based industries will also have fair investment practices, with tech-forward standards to improve workplace culture, £200 million—double the previous commitment—for women-led businesses through the British Business Bank and a scale-up programme to help them flourish. Finally, this Budget protects women and girls. It establishes for the first time a misogyny taskforce to tackle the core issues that are holding women back, keeping them scared and destroying equality in our society, with £55 million of funding over two years to meet the commitment to halve violence against women and girls in a decade. It will strengthen our law enforcement activity, improve protection for victims, and identify and disrupt harmful behaviours. This is a Budget for women, because if women succeed, our country succeeds.
Order. Members have been very disciplined with interventions, but they may wish to note that several Members have absented themselves from the Chamber without any notice.

On growth in every postcode, the Chancellor seems to have forgotten the people in Ely and East Cambridgeshire. There was nothing in the Budget and no funding for the Ely junction improvements, which would increase capacity on that rail line for freight and for passengers and make it more reliable. There was nothing to reduce rail fares, which are getting out of many people’s reach. There was nothing to help the county council with the phenomenal cost of mending our soil-affected roads. It estimates the cost to be £500 million, an amount that no county council can find. It is roughly 10 times its annual budget for road repairs. We have roads that, over this summer, actually had no earth underneath them any more, and when people go out to repair them, they instead have to close the road, because there is no earth on top of which to repair it. On buses, it is great that we have capped bus fares, but many of my villages do not have buses at all. There was nothing in the Budget about improving bus routes and getting more buses. There was nothing on the A10. The money for that has been removed, and nothing has been put back in the Budget. So is growth really for every postcode? Not for mine. As for the farmers, who had that catastrophic sustainable farming incentive process that closed within hours, there is nothing for them. There is nothing to recognise the problems they had over this long, hot, dry summer. We need to back our farmers. They are in my postcodes, and they feed all of us. On the breathing space, there are some good things in the Budget to help people with the cost of living, but not for people on heating oil. I have had a letter from a young mum who tells me that she has to find £650 just to buy the minimum amount of oil that can be delivered, and that would not last her the winter. She cannot ask for money from the crisis and resilience fund, because she had that back in the spring, and she has been told she cannot ask again. Yes, she will probably get £100 in January, but she needs £650 now. To add insult to injury, the Chancellor has cut the budgets for helping people get away from their dependence on oil heating, so I cannot even be sure that all my constituents can take advantage of moving on to heat pumps or other technology. At the very least, will the Chancellor please look again at how he can help people on oil central heating, because they desperately need it this winter, and please can we not just tell them to eat gherkins?

There were many welcome announcements in this Budget to help give people a little breathing space—from the £100 for households in council tax bands A to D to paternity leave payments for self-employed fathers. I personally really welcome the investment in getting more women into tech, as recommended by the Government’s women in tech taskforce. At a time when trust in the tech industry is low, we need women in tech more than ever. I refer Members to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, because I have quite a focus on that. However, following a meeting yesterday at Gresley Old Hall with members of the mineworkers’ pension scheme in South Derbyshire, I want to focus on them. I speak today on behalf of 1,141 scheme members and their families in my constituency. These men spent their working lives doing some of the hardest and most dangerous jobs in our country. They kept our lights on, our homes warm and our industries running. Their pensions are deferred wages earned through years of dangerous work, not taxpayer handouts. I welcome the transfer of the £1.5 billion investment reserve in 2024, and the Chancellor’s announcement to end surplus sharing so that 100% of future surpluses go to members, but the job is not finished. There is still approximately £1.2 billion in the guarantor’s fund, and members need certainty that it will be transferred in full without further delay. Yesterday, what I had hoped would be a meeting to celebrate progress became one where I found myself apologising, because people who have waited decades for justice are once again being asked to wait again, and time is running out. About 100 former miners die every week, and some will never live to see the justice they have spent years campaigning for. This is also about our former coalfield communities. That money will be spent in our towns and villages in supporting local shops, businesses and families, and in helping growth in postcodes in South Derbyshire. I have raised this directly with Treasury Ministers and the Prime Minister’s office. I have also pledged to donate my next annual parliamentary salary increase to charity until miners and their families receive what they are owed. I stand in solidarity with them, not just in words but in deeds too. I want to finish with words from Gary Chamberlain, who I met yesterday: “If you think this is a storm in a teacup, think again. This is just the start of it.” Gary is right. For Gary, for my 1,141 MPS member constituents and their families, and for mining communities across the country, I say this to the Government: please release the remaining £1.2 billion, give members the certainty they deserve and ensure that their bonus payment arrives on 23 December, as originally planned, in time for Christmas. We are the Labour party. It is only a Labour Government who will deliver justice for our miners. We must not be a Labour Government who ask them to wait yet again. Our miners have given enough to this country. It is time this country gave them what they are owed.

It is a pleasure to follow the hon. Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett). She refers to the fact that this is a Labour Budget, but I want to highlight how it does not contribute as I would hope it would—of course, good growth in every postcode is a good thing—to combating widening inequality. I am not sure it lives up to what I believe the Labour party argues for. I submitted early-day motions 939, 940 and 963, which provide constructive proposals to the Chancellor on addressing widening inequality. They were constructive proposals, as one would expect me to provide. The Conservatives want to focus on the benefits bill, and of course we should, but they do not seem to want to focus quite so much on the benefits bill of tax benefits for the wealthy. It is that area that I wish to concentrate on most. Some 23% of the Government tax take—£217.5 billion —is available in tax reliefs, as Treasury Ministers know full well. The Treasury Committee has identified that 80% of those tax reliefs have never been publicly costed or evaluated. I hope the Government will look at these matters. I will come on to one on housing in a moment. The Secretary of State referred to my private Member’s Bill, which is up for debate on Friday 13 November. It addresses both the need for first homes before second homes, and need before greed in the planning system. I hope that Labour Members will come along to support the Bill. What concerns me in particular is the business rates relief system. The Red Book, on page 130, refers to the availability to small businesses of rates relief for the retail, hospitality and leisure sector. That includes, of course, holiday lets. The problem is that, because holiday lets have invariably been second homes, people have flipped their property from council tax to business rates, applied for small business rates relief and then paid nothing at all. The Government have extended the valuation from £12,000 to £18,000, which has then made a larger group of people, who are wealthy enough with their second properties, now able to take advantage of this particular loophole. In areas like mine, with large numbers of second homes, we would like the half a billion pounds that has gone from the taxpayer into the pockets of second home owners, to be put into social and affordable housing. It is driving inflation in the system and creating further inequality. I do hope the Government will look at this issue again, think again and address it.

This Budget contains a series of practical measures that will make a real difference to families across Amber Valley. While some may dismiss individual announcements as small measures, it is their combined effect that matters. Taken together, they provide genuine breathing space for thousands of people across Amber Valley. They include: expanded childcare and free breakfast clubs for families; support for households worried about energy bills; and measures to help people with transport costs for work and leisure.

What my hon. Friend has just said, about the cumulative effect of lots of announcements making a difference, is really important. In my constituency of Clwyd East in north Wales, we pay some of the highest standing charges anywhere in the country, with people in north Wales paying a standing charge of 68p a day, in comparison to the 43p paid each day by people in London. Does she agree with me that not only is that measure welcome but, as well creating that breathing space, it is a huge step to fairness in our energy system?

I do agree with my hon. Friend. It is very important that there is breathing space right across the country, just like growth in every postcode. The Budget is only one part of a much wider programme of reform. The high streets strategy, the modern service framework for dementia and frailty, reforming social care, bringing decision making closer to our communities through devolution, and of course our 10-year plan, will all be transformative for my constituents. I want to turn to another matter addressed by the Budget, which echoes the point made by my hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett). It is a big issue in our local community. It is extremely personal to me and to hundreds of people in my constituency. I am proud to be a former coalminer’s daughter, and I am proud to be a Labour MP with a Government committed to finally delivering justice for mineworkers, because—let us face it—only a Labour Government will do so. Since Labour came into office in 2024, we have seen real progress on this topic. The MPS investment reserve has been transferred to scheme members, increasing annual pensions by around £29 per week. Last week the Chancellor announced that every penny of the surplus from the MPS will remain with the members rather than being split with the Government and the standstill rule has been abolished. Those are important improvements, but as the Chancellor himself said last week, the job is not done. My dad suffers from emphysema, white fingers and damaged knees from years of working at the coalface, and now also late-stage dementia. When I learned that a final settlement for MPS members would not be reached in this Budget, I made it clear to Ministers what that means. It means there is a very real possibility that my dad will not live to see the justice he deserves. That is not unique to our family. Around 19 former miners die every single day. That means that since the Budget, 85 miners will already have passed away without seeing this issue resolved. Let us be clear: this is not Government money, and this is not taxpayers’ money; this is the miners’ money. The Chancellor committed to ensuring the full transfer of the guarantor’s fund and I welcome that completely, but we cannot wait any longer. We cannot wait until a new fiscal event. We must finish the job and we must do it now.
I am sure that hon. Members will be delighted to know that I am putting the time limit back up to four minutes.

I welcome aspects of this breathing space Budget. Additional investment in council housing, support for rough sleeping programmes and some positive news on business rates with action to revive our high streets are all steps in the right direction. But for many families, businesses and communities, such as those in my constituency, the Budget does not go far enough to address the pressure they face every day, including the brutal cost of living. People in Stratford-on-Avon worry about the future of their local high streets, about heating their homes this winter, and about whether their favourite shop, pub, café or restaurant—businesses that give our towns their character—will still be there next year. That is why I believe that the Budget misses opportunities in a number of important areas. Our small businesses on high streets—the independent businesses that make our towns unique and create jobs for local people—face pressure from every direction. Under this Government, rising employment costs, energy costs, business rates and regulatory burdens are all taking their toll, and empty units are blighting our streets up and down the country. We need stronger powers for councils to bring long-term vacant properties back into use, and more support for the independent businesses that give our towns their character. The business rates discount will help some, but many will be left in the cold. Hospitality is of particular importance to Stratford-on-Avon; one in nine constituents are employed in the sector. That is why I am disappointed that the Government did not go further on VAT for hospitality. A temporary reduction in VAT would have provided immediate help to businesses, while helping consumers who are also feeling the squeeze. Businesses in my constituency tell me that a VAT reduction for hospitality would have allowed them to keep the lights on after the busy Christmas period. On fuel poverty, while the payment of £100 is welcome, we know from the Resolution Foundation that 1.4 million low-income households are in higher council tax bands, and they will miss out on that untargeted payment. Will the Minister look at that cohort urgently, so that they do not fall through the cracks? While I am on the subject, council tax is a deeply unfair tax—we know it, and the Minister knows it, and it needs to change. Many households remain vulnerable to high energy costs, which is why I am concerned about the reduction in funding for the warm homes plan. Investing in warmer homes cuts bills and reduces carbon emissions; it is one of the smartest investments that any Government can make, particularly for families and older residents already struggling with the cost of living. The Budget and the Government’s wider plan place considerable emphasis on devolution. Warwickshire is a long way away from a mayor. People in my constituency want local services that are responsibly rooted in the places that they serve. Any organisational devolution must strengthen local democracy and voices, because whether we are talking about high streets, fuel poverty, housing or hospitality, the people closest to those challenges are often those best placed to solve them. For my constituents, the Budget does not go far enough to support small businesses, tackle fuel poverty and help communities thrive.

This Budget puts families and businesses at its heart. It provides a breathing space on the cost of living today, while giving people fresh hope for the future. I am proud to be the granddaughter of a coalminer, and this Government have done so much already to right historical injustices in the mineworkers’ pension scheme. I welcome the commitment to ending the surplus sharing arrangement and standstill mechanism, but that only rights part of the injustice. Since 1994, successive Governments have taken more than £4.4 billion from the scheme, in return for a guarantee that has cost the public purse nothing. It cannot be right that the remaining £1.2 billion in the guarantor fund has still not been released to benefit former miners and their widows. For many, time is running out. I ask again, as I have asked before, that the Chancellor looks at this and delivers justice for mineworkers across the country. I particularly welcome the measures in the Budget to tackle rising energy bills. With conflicts overseas pushing up prices at home, families are understandably worried about how much it costs to heat their home. That is why the £100 household energy payment is so important. In North Warwickshire and Bedworth, around 37,920 properties will benefit. In a constituency like mine, driving is not a luxury. For so many people, it is the only reliable option for getting to work, taking the children to school and going about daily life. It is why my parents made me learn to drive as soon as I turned 17. I ensured that residents’ concerns about fuel costs were heard, and I am delighted that the Chancellor listened, extending the 5p fuel duty cut until July 2027. For a family already struggling to make ends meet, every extra pound at the pump matters. The impact of fuel duty goes beyond families filling up their cars; it affects the lorry drivers delivering food to our supermarkets, the businesses transporting goods across the country and, ultimately, the prices that we all pay at the check-out. Before coming to Parliament, I spent 20 years working as a property solicitor in a high street firm in my constituency. One of the things that I loved most about that job was helping first-time buyers. I remember the happiness of seeing young people come through my door, proud of the amount that they had saved for their deposit. They would tell me about their plans for the future. These were people putting down roots in our communities, and there was nothing quite like the moment when they finally collected their keys. However, the longer I did that job, the fewer first-time buyers came through my door. I watched as owning a home became increasingly out of reach for young people, particularly those who did not have the bank of mum and dad to fall back on. That is not the future I want for the next generation in North Warwickshire and Bedworth. That is why I am delighted that the Chancellor has announced the new £4.7 billion Your First Home scheme, which is expected to help around 70,000 first-time buyers on to the property ladder. This Budget is taking action on the very issues that my constituents have raised with me: the cost of heating their home and filling up their car; supporting the industries they work in; and helping their children and grandchildren on to the housing ladder. It is a Budget that gives families breathing space today, supports the businesses and workers who keep our country moving, and offers young people fresh hope for the future.

I want to thank Nick Coombes from my office for his help on this speech. Unsurprisingly, I am disappointed by the Chancellor’s first Budget. From a new Administration who spent a by-election and leadership campaign claiming that they had all sorts of plans and ambitions to fix the economy after the previous Labour Administration constantly talked us down, we have a “do no harm” Budget that does decidedly little to help pensioners, fund our armed forces, support young people or back the businesses that are essential to creating jobs. The tax burden has continued to rise above record levels; inflation has not been at the 2% target since before the first Budget of this Labour Government; and the welfare bill is set to go up by another £60 billion—and neither the Prime Minister nor the Chancellor is willing to commit to reducing it in this Parliament. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, we are now spending more on debt interest than on the Army and schools combined, which is clearly wrong, especially when we face some of the biggest and most rapidly evolving threats since the cold war. Yet the Chancellor, who resigned as Defence Secretary over the previous Administration’s refusal to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, has delivered a Budget that has deferred the difficult choices necessary to keep our country safe until next year, in favour of the Prime Minister’s plan to prioritise social security over national security. Young people are already struggling for support to get into education, employment or training. The increase in employer national insurance contributions, and now the further increase in the minimum wage, will make young people even more expensive for small businesses to hire, while pushing more and more workers into higher tax brackets. This was the Chancellor’s first opportunity to take bold steps to correct the errors of the previous Labour Budgets, and to provide support for businesses and entrepreneurs, which would have been a notable break from the massive tax hikes and regulatory burdens that have so far fallen on businesses under this Government. The Prime Minister and the Chancellor needed to use this opportunity to take drastic action to slash the size of the state, and to get Britain working again—to support those who are working, and to encourage into work those who are not working, but who are able to. My constituents are happy to support those in genuine need, but this Labour Government have come back every year for more money from the same hard-working people they promised not to raise taxes on to fund an ever-increasing welfare state. This “do no harm” Budget has led to the worsening of the OBR forecasts on inflation, economic growth, unemployment and living standards, and has left my constituents disappointed. I hope that the Prime Minister’s 10-year plan and the upcoming spending review have some much-needed good news and serious economic support for businesses and young people in South West Hertfordshire.

First, I want to rebut some of the nonsense that we heard from the SNP earlier. Scotland’s budget is going up by £600 million because of the choices made in this Budget for Scotland’s public services—that is up by £18 billion since Labour came into office—and talking of a £650 million cut is inadvertently misleading this House. I may say something a wee bit ruder outside the House. This Budget will abolish gas standing charges, abolish VAT on electricity bills and give £100 to 1.8 million Scottish households between council tax bands A and D —if it is confirmed that the SNP will choose to hand it over in that way. The prices at the pumps that our constituents complain about have been brought about directly by the US and Israel’s war in Iran, but we have made a choice to freeze fuel duty, which I welcome, and maintain the 5p fuel duty cut till June. That is alongside the red diesel duty cut, which will be welcome in the many eligible sectors, especially agriculture. As for working people in Falkirk, the permanent increase to the tax-free mileage should help traders who use their own vans for work. I also welcome the tripling of the trading allowance to £3,000. This Budget also rightly supports pensioners. Many pensioners in my constituency live on the state pension alone; as it has risen, too many have ended up with the administrative irritation of paying small amounts of income tax, with all the paperwork and worry that that brings. I welcome the new pension tax allowance from April 2027, which addresses that directly. It means that pensioners whose income is no more than the full state pension will not pay income tax. To deliver good growth in my postcode, it is vital that we invest in the Grangemouth industrial complex, as I said last week. I welcome the British industrial competitiveness scheme, and the back-payment to 2026, but while I acknowledge the heightened cost of extending it to every manufacturing business—I believe that would be about £3.5 billion—I think, as do other colleagues, that we should look at extending it, especially for manufacturing businesses that are reliant on gas, and that have decarbonisation timescales that are not as quick as we might like. I welcome the restatement of the Government’s intent to include refined products in the carbon border adjustment mechanism. It will be a vital tool in levelling the playing field, after the undermining of domestic refining. The same un-level playing field led to the closure of Grangemouth, because it was not dealt with over multiple years. A cross-party group wrote to the Treasury regarding this. I think it is important that we put a deadline on when we will introduce this, because this positive signal needs to be translated into real protection for our existing refining sector, as well as for the bio-refining sector that the Prime Minister rightly believes has huge potential to deliver for Grangemouth. Turning to the Acorn project, I agree with the principle of getting better value for taxpayers’ money across Government capital plans, so that we can free up money for defence. I agree that that should include energy projects in our constituencies. Some of the rhetoric that we have heard from the SNP and their Ministers on supporting the project has been downright reckless and self-defeating. However, I hope that the Minister can acknowledge that much of the reasonable scrutiny on this has not been met with the clearest of answers. I would like to hear confirmation that the new route for previously committed funding has the support of all existing and committed commercial partners, and confirmation about the amount of funding committed already that is not being changed. I would also like to know why funding has been changed for Acorn but not for other carbon capture, usage and storage projects, such as Viking in Humberside, and, more broadly, what the changes will mean for reindustrialisation in communities like Grangemouth that are supposed to benefit from this infrastructure, especially considering that they have not had a fantastic experience with the debt equity model of the National Wealth Fund. This Budget creates breathing space for families in Falkirk who are worried about the end of the month, and for the poorest pensioners who dread getting a tax letter. It lifts some of the pressure. This Government have shown in the Budget that they will act for working people, pensioners and industry. I ask Ministers to turn that breathing space into future certainty, particularly for an industry that can define the next 50 years positively, through new jobs, as it has defined the last 50.

This Budget has around 100 separate measures, but most would never have featured in the previous Chancellor’s Budgets—not because of any particular policy difference, but because they are just too small. It is less “Steady as she goes”, and more “Let this grind to a complete halt.” As far as taxation goes, by far the biggest impact comes from a policy that was not even mentioned: the continued freeze on personal tax thresholds. This year alone, it means another half a million people will start paying tax for the first time, and a further half a million will be pushed into a higher tax bracket—all a function of that handy Chancellor’s trick: fiscal drag. Understandably, the Conservatives give the Government an easy ride on this, as it was their idea in the first place. When it comes to welfare, the critical Milburn and Timms reviews have both been conveniently kicked to the other side of the Budget, but the issues that we face are not what people think they are. It has been said so many times that everyone assumes it must be true that millions of people are getting personal independence payment or universal credit health awards for mild anxiety. The appeal of this story is that it makes people think that we can slash social support for vulnerable people and feel morally good about it. Unfortunately, it is just not true. In reality, absolutely no one gets PIP for mild or severe anxiety, or for any form of mental health condition. That is because PIP is not awarded according to condition. Rather, applicants are assessed according to their daily abilities or lack of them—whether they can wash themselves, cook for themselves or manage short distances walking. There is not even a category for mild anxiety. I find it incredible that politicians, including Members who are the welfare spokespeople for their parties, can continue to ask for something that they must know by now is not possible. What chance have we got of making smart reforms to the economy if politicians cannot even get the basic facts straight? While we continue to wait for all the missing parts of the Budget over the coming weeks and months, I urge caution. Welfare cuts are just a right-wing version of the magic money tree. As a proportion of GDP, today’s spend on non-pension welfare is roughly the same as it was in the mid-80s, when a certain Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister. At that time, the Defence budget was twice what it is today, so clearly the current level of welfare spend is perfectly compatible with meeting our defence targets, and welfare is not the reason why our defence budget is in such trouble. The peace dividend did not go to UC and PIP; it went to the NHS and pensions. Above all, this is a challenge caused by a general decline in the economy, not welfare. Yes, it is always important to control welfare spend, and I support that, but slashing welfare on the basis of an arbitrary financial target invented simply to raise enough to pay for some dramatic manifesto pledge is not a credible path to anything. What we have is a Budget that does not seek to do anything very much about anything; the real battles have yet to come.

For my constituents and those across the country, life is hard, and it has not shown signs of getting easier. The previous Government were the first in decades to preside over a fall in the standard of living and, with Trump’s war in the middle east, things are unlikely to get better as quickly as we would like. That is why I welcome the support being provided to households facing higher energy costs. For many families, an extra £100 will not transform their circumstances overnight—no one is pretending otherwise—but every pound matters, and that support matters, too. In Calderdale, almost nine out of 10 houses are expected to be eligible for the £100 household energy payment. That means that the overwhelming majority of my constituents will receive direct support this winter. For many people, the support will ease some of the pressures on their household budgets at exactly the moment they need that the most. I welcome the expansion of the warm home discount, too. By widening eligibility, the Government have almost doubled the number of households in the scheme to 6 million. That means millions more families receiving £150 off their energy bills this winter. Too often, those on the lowest incomes have faced what is known as the poverty premium, made famous by Terry Pratchett with his “Captain Vimes’s Boots” theory of economics: the less money you have, the more things cost. We see that in our insurance costs, in the costs of credit and, importantly, in the cost of fuel. That is why ending standing charges will make a difference, as those who use less energy will pay less. Helping those households is not simply about fairness; it is also good economics as the money from these measures will not sit unused, stored thousands of miles away in the Cayman Islands, but be spent in local communities on local high streets, helping local people. People will use it to pay bills, buy essentials and support local businesses, which will contribute to their high streets. The same principle applies to our businesses across Calder Valley. Business owners are ambitious to innovate, are determined to succeed and want it to be easier to invest, grow and create jobs. Whether because of energy costs, red tape or being locked out of Government contracts, for many of them the main concern has been staying afloat, not growing or taking on new people. That is why I welcome some of the changes to business rates announced in the Budget. Raising the threshold for small business rate relief for retail, hospitality and leisure from £12,000 to £18,000 means that 70,000 additional businesses will pay no business rates at all. In Calder Valley, that will make a huge difference to our collection of independent shops, cafés and pubs. Speaking of pubs, I am proud to see support for Britain’s small independent breweries. Calder Valley is home to fantastic independent breweries including Eagles Crag and Vocation. I am proud to have made a significant contribution to them over the years, but finding room to grow has not been easy. The support announced in the Budget will be welcomed across the brewing sector. While some Budgets look worse as time goes on—the famous omnishambles Budget and the Liz Truss Budget among them—this is one that will look better, with its help for small businesses and support for households. This Budget backs working people. This Budget backs British industry. It backs communities in Calder Valley, and I am proud to back it.

The Chancellor’s big phrase in this Budget has been “breathing space”. It has been said time and again, but it is utterly false, because the Chancellor has not given businesses any breathing space at all. There is no breathing space on employer national insurance. Labour’s job tax stays exactly where it is, punishing employers for yet another year. There is no breathing space on wages. The national living wage has actually gone up by 3.9% from April, on top of the Employment Rights Act 2025, with nothing announced to help employers meet the costs. Even the Office for Budget Responsibility warns that these policies will seriously damage job creation in this country. There has been no real breathing space on business rates. The Chancellor says that he is freezing business rates for retail, hospitality and leisure in real terms, but the British Retail Consortium has rightly pointed out that this is just “smoke and mirrors”. This is not breathing space at all. This is our businesses being stifled yet again by this Labour Government. I ask the Minister: what are their ambitions for British businesses? It seems evident from this Budget that they do not have any. They are taxing our British businesses again and again. All this matters because it is impacting my constituency, which is full of hard-working people. I think of the independent shops on Cavendish Street and Low Street fighting to keep Keighley a thriving place, as well as the cafés, boutiques and family businesses on the Grove and Brook Street in Ilkley, and those businesses right across Silsden, Steeton and Riddlesden and our wider area who are working incredibly hard. The pubs, the tradespeople, the hairdressers, the start-ups—they are all hard-working people, yet this Government think that employers in those small independent businesses are not workers. They put out that narrative as if those employers need to be taxed more. Let me tell the House about one of those businesses, which I visited just yesterday. The Turkey Inn in Goose Eye is a pub that is much loved by locals and visitors alike, and I called in there last night to have a meal. The owners of that pub are grafters. They produce excellent food that is second to none and they support our local community with many local activities. They do everything right, working day in, day out to support the community, but yesterday, on the back of this Budget, they announced that they were cutting their opening hours from seven days a week to just four, and they were clear about why. In their own words, they said: “With no measures in the budget to help small hospitality businesses and local pubs like ours, we must take this step”. That is the verdict not of a politician or of a Labour think-tank but of hard-working people in my constituency who have been impacted by this third Labour Budget. The Turkey Inn is not alone. I speak to pubs and small independent businesses every single week in my constituency and they are telling me the same thing. Labour is not on the side of our hard-working businesses, and that is impacting them. This Labour Budget has not provided any breathing space at all. This Government must wake up and listen to our small and medium-sized businesses, who are the backbone of our communities and our local economies, because they are pushing them to breaking point. If the Government do not wake up and listen, I fear for all of them. A simple policy of tax, tax, tax on our businesses with more regulation is stifling those businesses, not helping them thrive.

For most people in Wolverhampton and Willenhall, the real test of a Budget is simple: does it make life a little easier? I hear about and absolutely understand the pressure of household bills, the cost of raising a family and the challenges facing our local businesses. That is why I will continue to raise their concerns right here in Parliament and make sure that their voices are heard at every level of Government, at every opportunity that I get. Of course, everyone would like more giveaways in a Budget, but many people also understand that the Government have a responsibility for the state of our public finances. We have seen the consequences of getting the balance wrong. The wider energy and cost of living support package during the 2022 energy crisis cost taxpayers around £51 billion net in one year alone. That required extraordinary borrowing, adding to our national debt and the interest payments that taxpayers, including future generations, will continue to carry. This Budget takes a very different approach to providing immediate support. Around 44,900 properties in Wolverhampton North East—almost 99%—are in council tax bands A to D, and that means a large number of local households will benefit from the £100 household energy payment from January. Alongside the extension of 0% VAT on electricity, which is expected to take around £50 off the annual Ofgem price cap, that means around £150 in combined support. Martin Lewis, the famous consumer champion, has highlighted that the £100 payment could broadly cover the forecast increase in energy costs for a typical household over the three winter months. I am also pleased to see the end of gas standing charges, especially for low gas usage households. Importantly, the Government are asking banks to contribute more to help to pay for that support, rather than relying on borrowing. I particularly welcome the help for our high street. Raising the small business rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 means that many more independent shops, cafés and restaurants will pay no business rates at all. For some owners, that could mean a saving of around £300 a month. Across the west midlands, around 52% of retail, hospitality and leisure properties will pay no business rates. For qualifying businesses that still have a bill, there will be a real-terms freeze in the business rates multiplier. In Wolverhampton North East, around 975 premises will benefit. I am also pleased that 10 schools in Wolverhampton North East have now secured free breakfast club funding. That means more children starting the school day with a good breakfast, ready to learn, and parents having a little more help with the pressures of family life. People are still feeling the pressure, and no one pretends otherwise, but we have to be able to afford the support that we offer and pay for it responsibly. There is more to do, and I will keep making that case in Parliament.

The Chancellor called this a “breathing space” Budget, but it seems only to be breathing space for the Government to put off the hard decisions. It is not a breathing space for my constituents, with frozen tax and student loan repayment thresholds. It is not a breathing space for my local businesses: the rise in employer national insurance contributions has not been reversed, there is no emergency VAT cut for hospitality to help our high streets, and on business rates, which I have repeatedly raised in this House, the Budget just tinkers with a system that needs wholesale reform. The Budget is not a breathing space for farmers. There is no change in the family farm tax. The cut to fertiliser tariffs will make little difference when, as the NFU has pointed out, much already arrives tariff-free. I am disappointed that the Budget does not treat food security as national security. The Budget is not a breathing space for local transport users. In a Budget that mentions the north repeatedly, the west barely gets a look in. South Gloucestershire is mentioned once—a brief reference to a mass transit system that we have been hearing about for decades and that is unlikely to touch our rural villages. A £1 bus fare cap and discounted rail fares would have helped families in the short term, and investment in rural transport would help them in the longer term. The west of England is a growth engine outside of London. It deserves more ambition than that. The Budget is not a breathing space for energy bill payers. Suppliers forecast that the price cap will rise by around a quarter in January. Although welcome, the £100 for this winter and the promise of scrapping gas standing charges in the future do not touch the sides. Scrapping the standing charge will save people just £45 on average—and only those who actually use gas. One in five properties in Thornbury and Yate is heated by oil. Those households have no price cap at all, and there is nothing to ensure that the removal of import tariffs on kerosene is passed to consumers. The surest way to bring down bills is to insulate homes and move people off volatile oil and gas, so why is there a £1 billion cut in the warm homes plan? What of the promised growth? When will we hear about plans for new nuclear at Oldbury? The outcome of Great British Energy Nuclear’s review was promised this autumn. If data centres that meet the new British data centre covenant are to get priority grid connections, then, given the problem with providing nuclear connections, where is the grid capacity for new homes to meet the Government’s own housing targets? Where is the investment in skills in the rural west of England so that our local young people can access the technical jobs available? This Budget is a missed opportunity to provide real breathing space for our constituents, our businesses and our economy.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker, for giving us breathing space with a little bit more time. It is a pleasure to respond to this Budget by talking about growth in every postcode. North West Leicestershire is a former mining area, so I welcome the progress made on the miners’ pension. I welcome the confirmation that surplus sharing and the standstill will be abolished to protect bonus pensions, helping members to benefit from the success of their pensions. No Government have ever done more on pensions for former mineworkers than this one, but as the Chancellor said himself, the job is not finished. It is clear that more work is needed to resolve the substantial undistributed guarantor fund surplus currently held within the mineworkers’ pension scheme. The miners who powered our country and our homes and who supported us deserve our support now, and I want to reassure my constituents that I will do just that. North West Leicestershire is home to one of the three sites in the only inland freeport in the UK. The site in Leicestershire has created considerable concern, which I share, particularly for Diseworth—an 825-year-old village with heritage status. While the new data centre covenant is helpful, I worry that it will apply only to AI and not to the creation of new mega-sheds more broadly, which impacts communities such as mine. The other two sites in the freeport are covered by the Mayor of the East Midlands, so I welcome the Chancellor’s announcement on devolution and the settlement for Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland—something I have long called for. I look forward to continuing the discussions on how devolution will deliver greater benefits and strategic powers to ensure that the freeport site for Leicestershire has a mayor fighting its corner. The powers offered to mayors on transport could be transformational for Leicestershire. Transport connectivity is a significant barrier to growth locally. My constituent Eli spoke to me recently about the impact that poor public transport has on their access to further education. They said: “I wake up before six in the morning to catch a 7 am bus to college, which is always packed, standing room only due to there being too many students for the capacity of the public bus services. Even if I do everything right, the buses are unreliable—either being late or completely absent—which is treated as my responsibility by my college”. A lot is said about demand in rural areas. In fact, Arriva increased its patronage by 30% for one of my local routes because it started one bus stop earlier, connecting the route to another village and allowing more kids to get to college. Just think about what we could achieve if we want to grow even more. North West Leicestershire still has no passenger rail service anywhere in the constituency, making it home to the two largest towns in the country without any access to rail, which restricts growth and investment. If we want growth in every postcode, transport has to be a priority. North West Leicestershire has so much potential, including in our SME sector. I know that this will surprise you, Madam Deputy Speaker, but nearly 30 years ago I wrote my dissertation on small business support, so I know how much we limit our growth if we fail to invest in small businesses. I have always advocated for dedicated business support, just like we saw in the universal offer we had from Business Link. We now have a patchwork that is devolution dependent—another reason why devolution for Leicestershire is so vital.

I thank my hon. Friend for giving way—we are neighbours and friends in our neck of the woods, but I benefit from being part of a mayoralty that can have money devolved to my region, and she does not. Does she agree that, as well as we work together now, it would be even better if we could be part of the same funding pot and overall leadership?

I thank my hon. Friend for making that incredibly important point. The Mayor of the East Midlands does not cover the whole of the east midlands, and I think that gives us the opportunity to continue to talk. Because I now have a bit of time left, I note that the Chancellor confirmed that land sold to social housing providers will now be VAT free. After two decades working in the social housing sector, I cannot express the difference that that will make to social homes and growth in our communities. House building is also a massive builder of growth; it helps brick manufacturers in my constituency, and it helps builders and local tradespeople to grow. We should not underestimate that important step forward.

It is a pleasure to speak in this debate; thank you for calling me, Madam Deputy Speaker. I wish to welcome some of the good things in the Budget, because it is not all bad news, by the way—[Interruption.] Members should not put their thumbs up just yet—I am coming to the parts about which I have important Northern Ireland-based concerns. I am concerned for the squeezed families of Strangford, who look at the Budget and have little cause for celebration. Look at the uncertainty facing the local business community in Northern Ireland. Standard small business rates relief is being permanently expanded in England, yet there is zero certainty that our small and medium-sized enterprises back home will see an equivalent benefit. Our highly capable SMEs, which form the bedrock of the Northern Irish economy, need iron-clad guarantees, not vague hopes. The working middle class go to work and pay their taxes. They try to build something for their children, yet they are treated like a bottomless well of revenue by the Treasury. Take, for example, a hard-working family in my constituency of Strangford—a schoolteacher and a mid-level nurse. They have managed to put away a modest amount of savings to help fund their children’s university education. They will get no help for their children’s education and future, yet they will be forced to work on past retirement to ensure that their child has a chance at a future. Nowhere is that clearer than in the cruel and punitive approach to family inheritance tax. Our agricultural sector in Northern Ireland is in a state of absolute panic. I have spoken with the Ulster Farmers’ Union, which tells me that generations of family farms—the very lifeblood of our rural communities—are now halting investment decisions because of inheritance tax fears. Passing a family business or a family farm down to the next generation is not a luxury; it is a way of life, and the Budget threatens to dismantle that. On the Barnett formula, let us be realistic: the Barnett consequentials are totally inadequate. Why is that the case? Throwing a general lump sum at the Northern Ireland Executive and hoping that it covers police, health and education is a failure of governance. We need an allocation method equivalent to that for Wales, not a funding system that is not fit for purpose. That must be sorted out. Funding must be based on genuine local need, not a rigid, detached mathematical formula. We must protect our middle class, safeguard our family farms, and give Northern Ireland the specific, targeted support that it desperately needs. Our hard-working middle class see no benefit for themselves, and even less for their children. When a parent works 50 hours a week, pays their taxes—big taxes—plays by the rules and still cannot see a path to a better future or a stable inheritance for the next generation, the social contract is broken. If the Government continue to bleed the middle class dry to paper over the cracks of their own fiscal failures, they will destroy the very aspiration that keeps this nation, this great United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, moving forward. The Budget offers no security on defence, and no reason to build a business and to work hard. It relies on the ethic of some to make up for the lack of ethic in too many. The Government must look closely at the people it punishes, because they need to breathe, and I do not believe the Budget provides that.

I start by thanking my right hon. Friend the Chancellor for the measures that he laid out in his Budget last week, and for his focus on giving my constituents breathing space as we navigate through tough global headwinds. Like him, I pay tribute and offer my thanks to the former Chancellor, my right hon. Friend the Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves). It is clear that through her work and clear focus on fiscal discipline, she helped to stabilise the economy, despite the significant headwinds, and to create the headroom that has enabled us to take the positive actions set out in this Budget. I am lucky to have my office on Leigh Road in Leigh-on-Sea. Along with Leigh Broadway, it is a thriving high street, full of small independent shops and hospitality businesses, including Tiny, a sandwich shop, Juice Bay, which does fantastic smoothies and juices, and Float On Records. They are all new businesses and it is great to see so many new businesses opening despite the challenges we have faced of late. That shows me that there is confidence in our economy and belief in our country. And it is not just in Leigh: Mez, a delicious Turkish restaurant, recently opened in Westcliff—I can vouch for that as I had my dinner there on Saturday. However, I have listened to businesses in my constituency that tell me that sometimes things can be challenging. That is why I am delighted by the Government’s announcement that more retail, hospitality and leisure businesses will be completely exempt from business rates, meaning that around 52% of those types of business in the east of England will pay absolutely no business rates whatsoever. That is help for businesses. An additional 484 businesses in my constituency will have their business rates frozen in real terms until 2029, giving business owners time to plan ahead, while many others will see their business rates reduced. When my constituents get home from their days out shopping, they will know that they have support with paying their bills. In addition to extending the 0% rate of VAT on electricity, an enormous 39,520 households in my constituency will benefit from the £100 payment to combat rising energy costs. I know that will help many people, from young families through to pensioners. Speaking of pensioners, I welcome the excellent news that pensioners on low incomes will not have to pay income tax on their state pension. I am glad to hear the announcement that pensioners who rely solely on their state pension income will get to keep all of it. The Budget also provides the security that comes with knowing that pensions will continue to rise in line with earnings, while the adjusted triple lock will mean we can focus on providing a high-quality national care service. Finally, I was really glad to hear that self-employed fathers and partners will now get statutory paternity pay. I have personally championed that, alongside many colleagues, and I pay particular tribute to my hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) for her work in this area and in championing this cause. This Budget shows that the Government are listening to people in my constituency and taking action to fix the issues they have raised. The constituents I spoke to at the weekend know that the times that we are in and that we face are difficult, and they are grateful for everything this Government are doing to support them.

I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. This country faces fundamental problems: the faces at the top may have changed, but once again Labour has shown itself incapable of making the tough calls. This morning, I hosted a post-Budget roundtable for local employers in my constituency. I regret to report that the business community in Wimbledon shares my concern about this short-term, lacklustre Budget. By kicking the can down the road, this mañana Budget has failed the businesses that are critical to growing the economy. Rather than providing businesses with breathing space, the Chancellor has many of them drowning in crippling taxes and excessive regulation. Raising the business rates relief threshold to £18,000 is, of course, welcome, but high streets across my constituency, in Wimbledon, Raynes Park, New Malden and Morden, will see little benefit. Craig Hurring, the chief executive officer of Love Wimbledon, informed me today that the change will benefit an estimated 1% of the businesses in his business improvement district. Other changes that are in the pipeline are making matters worse. A company that manages fantastic serviced office space for new businesses in Wimbledon tells me that new restrictions on business rates relief mean that it will have to increase rents by up to 25%—a huge cost to start-ups. Business rates are crippling my local businesses. Gina Conway runs an award-winning hair and beauty salon in Wimbledon. She employs 38 people and trains up to 20 apprentices every year, but she tells me that “the pressure for most salon owners is too much to bear”. The long shadow of covid, soaring energy bills, VAT and crippling business rates are killing high street businesses. I was honoured to be present for the excellent maiden speech by the hon. Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Sagal Abdi-Wali). I own a bar in Covent Garden in her constituency, so it feels a bit like she is my MP—I will invite her to it one day. That means that I know at first hand how the night-time economy is suffering. Since 2020, the UK has lost almost three in 10 late-night venues, and across the sector we continue to lose the equivalent of 13 businesses every week. The changes for self-assessment taxpayers are just as worrying. The Chancellor said that he would champion “the small British firms that give character to our communities”.—[Official Report, 28 October 2026; Vol. 792, c. 305.] Instead, 2029 risks becoming a brutal cash crunch, with 18 months of tax squeezed into 12 months. Increasing the tax on rental income is misguided. As the OBR has outlined, it will inevitably result in fewer homes to rent and higher rents. I fear that the new Prime Minister is repeating his predecessor’s mistakes. His only plan is to have a plan. The Budget makes no substantive progress on addressing welfare spending, social care or defence readiness. The only glimmer of hope is the Prime Minister’s recent comments on Europe, but even here my constituents still do not know what he really intends. According to Goldman Sachs, a close relationship with the EU could boost our economy by at least £60 billion per year. The Prime Minister must be bold. He must tear up his predecessor’s red lines, seek unfettered access to the world’s largest market and let British business realise its full potential.

In this third day of the Budget debate, I worry about repeating what has already been said, so I will focus on two issues of particular importance to my communities in Cannock Chase. Before I do so, briefly, I welcome the cost of living support in this Budget—£100 back on council tax, VAT kept off electricity bills for longer, standing charges taken off gas and the continuation of the fuel duty freeze. Those measures will not solve every financial pressure, but they will provide welcome relief at a time when it is needed most. Let me turn to my beautiful home county of Staffordshire, which, thanks to this Government, will soon be able to catch up with the likes of Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire with the announcement of a mayoral strategic authority. That is a massive opportunity, particularly for our towns, which, as my hon. Friend the Member for Stafford (Leigh Ingham) always says, must be at the heart of the national growth and renewal that this Government stand for. Our big cities have done well, but it is the turn of the towns, and having those powers and the funding that comes with devolution gives us the tools we need to turn our potential into reality. Perhaps surprisingly to many, our towns have, on average, more than twice the proportion of their workforce employed in manufacturing as our cities, at around 9% compared with 4%, yet employment growth over the past decade has been almost twice as high in cities, at 10.7%, compared with just 5.4% in our towns. We cannot seriously talk about rebalancing our economy while allowing that gap to persist, but that requires investment and, crucially, proper transport connections. For too many people, particularly young people and those without access to a car, getting to work, college or an apprenticeship remains unnecessarily difficult. That is where devolution matters, because a mayoral authority with meaningful powers over transport, skills and economic development gives Staffordshire the opportunity to join those things up and be the masters of our own destiny. I hope that it will also bring some much-needed stability to our county’s leadership. Since last May, Staffordshire county council has had not one, not two, not three, but four leaders, courtesy of the chaos of Reform UK. Staffordshire needs a little less political musical chairs and a lot more long-term focus on the priorities of our communities. Let me turn to the second issue: the mineworkers’ pension scheme. As the proud representative of nearly 1,000 MPS members, I will always raise my voice in support of those who risked their lives to power our nation. Alongside them and my fellow coalfield Labour MPs, we pressed the Government to release the £1.2 billion guarantor’s fund, end the standstill mechanism and ensure that all future surpluses go to those who earned that money in the first place. The MPS investment reserve was returned to members by this Labour Government two years ago, and the Chancellor’s decision in this Budget to end surplus sharing and the standstill are major steps forward. However, we are deeply disappointed that the Budget did not include the transfer of the guarantor’s fund—a measure that would have put money back into the pockets of our retired miners. There was a clear expectation that this would be done, finally righting the wrongs of the past 32 years. I welcome the Chancellor saying from the Dispatch Box that it will be done, but we must never forget that this money came from the graft of our miners —it is their deferred wages, and it belongs in their bank accounts. With 100 MPS members passing away every week, we must move as quickly as possible, and we certainly cannot wait for next year’s Budget. This Budget brought forward support with the cost of living, and it is allowing Staffordshire to take control of its own destiny. I wish it had sealed full justice for our MPS members, but we are now so close to ending their fight, and they can count me as an ally right until the very end.

The cost of living is the No. 1 issue that is raised with me on the doorstep by constituents across Paisley and Renfrewshire South, so there is much to welcome in this Budget, which gives much-needed breathing space for many working households. We Labour Members do not think that the increase in the national minimum wage is a bad thing—it is a good thing. The increase in the mileage rate will help working people, and I am glad that the Chancellor has extended the VAT cut for energy bills and will look to abolish gas standing charges. I also welcome the £100 household energy payment for households in council tax bands A to D, and I am hopeful that the SNP will pass this on to people across my constituency.

Does my hon. Friend also call on the SNP to extend the business rates relief that our Labour Government have provided, especially considering that they have historically maintained a stricter system for high streets such as those in Paisley and Falkirk?

I absolutely agree with my hon. Friend that the SNP should pass on that much-needed change. I also note that the Budget provides an additional £600 million for the Scottish Government, and I hope that they will actually spend it on improving our public services. Today’s debate focuses on achieving good growth in every postcode, an ambition I wholeheartedly support. One route to growth in postcodes PA1, PA2, PA3 and PA4—I could go on, but Members get my drift—is revitalising our high street in Paisley. Paisley is Scotland’s largest town, and we have a shovel-ready project in the middle of our high street that received planning permission four years ago, which is regenerating the Paisley Centre. Realising that ambition needs Governments to come together, but it could bring 330 jobs to our area and breathe life into our high street. If Treasury colleagues would like to see that potential for themselves, I would be very happy to show them around the area. Our Government were elected on a clear manifesto commitment to end the need for emergency food parcels. As chair of the all-party parliamentary group on ending the need for food banks, I know that food banks provide a lifeline when people have nowhere else to turn, but emergency food provision should never become a normal part of life in Britain. A report published last week by the Trussell Trust laid out the scale of the challenge. Some 9 million people across the UK—more than the entire populations of Wales and Scotland combined—are at severe risk of hardship and needing to turn to a food bank. Hardship does not happen in isolation; it is driven by inadequate incomes, the high cost of essentials, and a lack of the support that people need in their communities. We also know that some groups of people are at higher risk of hunger and hardship than others. People who have disabilities, those who are in low-paid or insecure work, and children remain disproportionately affected by severe hardship. As such, I hope that my right hon. Friend the Chancellor will reaffirm this Government’s commitment to end the need for emergency food parcels, and ensure that the upcoming 10-year plan sets out a clear path towards tackling the severe hardship that blights our communities. The Government are rightly steadfast in our support for Ukraine. This House will be aware that I have campaigned extensively on the forcible deportation of Ukrainian children by Russia, and it was a pleasure to work with my hon. Friend the Member for Cardiff South and Penarth (Stephen Doughty) when he was the Minister responsible for that issue. We worked on establishing a tracing pilot that provided vital intelligence on the whereabouts of thousands of Ukrainian children who had been taken by Russia. Save Ukraine is the leading non-governmental organisation working on the return and rehabilitation of Ukrainian children. When I met Save Ukraine representatives in September, they told me that the UK has been a leading partner. As of this morning, that practical support has helped them return 1,887 children. I therefore warmly welcome the announcement in the Budget that the Government have committed an additional £3 million to support the tracing programme until at least 2028, because the defence of Ukraine must also ensure the defence of its future. By committing to this vital work, we are doing just that. I thank the Chancellor for those measures.

This Labour Government are helping families in Cornwall with their energy and fuel bills. Nearly 37,500 households in Truro and Falmouth will get £100 directly into their bank accounts. The drop in VAT and standing charges going will also help. In a rural and coastal constituency, where a car is not a luxury, the extension of the 5p fuel duty cut will help, as will the rise in travel rates, and the extension of the red diesel cut will help our farmers. We are also tackling the specific challenges facing rural, off-grid communities. Some 14% of Cornish households rely on heating oil, including 5,000 families in Truro and Falmouth, which is well above the national average. Suspending those tariffs alongside more than £50 million of support for low-income households that use heating oil will make a real difference to those homes, as will regulating the market. By pairing that short-term relief with the warm homes plan, this Government are helping rural families to move towards cleaner, cheaper heating on their own terms. I have been working with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero on a medium-term solution to license hydrotreated vegetable oil for use in heating. It has been trialled in Kehelland village in Cornwall with great success, and I hope to engage with DESNZ to get that rolled out further. On devolution, Cornwall will be designated a single strategic authority. That will hopefully bring growth, funding and further devolution on top of the £30 million Kernow industrial growth fund announced last year. A delivery plan will now be worked up, and I look forward to seeing the further devolution of powers to unlock housing, skills and economic growth. Truro and Falmouth enjoys a vibrant local tourist economy, with independent shops, bakeries, cafés and pubs. Raising small business rate relief to £18,000 means that 56% of retail, hospitality and leisure properties in the south-west will pay no business rates at all. Together with that real-terms business rates freeze, 6,500 hospitality, retail and leisure properties in Cornwall will benefit. Crucially for Truro and Falmouth, the right to buy community assets scheme, support for co-ops and high street rental auctions will give local people the tools to take back vacant units and bring empty shops back into use. I would like to see those powers rolled out to our town and city councils. The unitary authority has limited resources and our town councils have grown to fill that gap. They are very capable and they could run those schemes in the absence of appetite from the unitary, and they know their high streets far better. We have many towns of approximately 20,000 people, each with an expanded town council. In Cornwall, only 11% of our housing is social housing, against a national average of 18%. We have 26,000 households on the social housing waiting list. I therefore welcome extending preferential borrowing rates for councils. But Cornwall’s housing revenue account is struggling to put more investment into repairs, and rents are low in Cornwall, so rent convergence will take time. It means that the HRA has had to reduce the annual funds available for new homes. One of the barriers is the £90 million debt from the self-financing arrangements dating back to 2012. If that debt was reduced, Cornwall could do more. HRA and debt reform would allow council houses to be built once again in Cornwall. There are root causes of our housing crisis in Truro and Falmouth. We have many holiday lets, which are a good thing for Cornwall, but I welcome the Government’s plans for a registration system. We need to go further to look at licensing, too, to check that insurance and fire safety documents are seen and that local authorities can inspect properties.

I know that people in Worcester will be looking for two things: some let-up in the endless pressure on bills and the public services that keep letting us down, and a genuine sense that there is a plan for things to improve— that there is hope. Let me start by recognising that those two aims have been front and centre as the Chancellor and the Prime Minister have developed this Budget. I believe in politics that is focused on people, and I believe that the Budget aims to focus on people. However, the challenges that we face require a deeper shift—not just adjustments to budgets, but something far more fundamental: an approach that recognises people’s real lived experiences, and puts them at the heart of our decisions and systems. Digital technology is reshaping our world, and we need a fresh approach to digital safety. The Chancellor is right to say that we should build the data centres and artificial intelligence models that keep us secure, but we should also be insisting on safety by design for AI and online social platforms, and should be holding providers responsible. We need an answer that matches the desperate urgency of the climate crisis. The Budget starts to recognise gaps in our energy policy, but it also risks creating new ones.
