I am engaging all the time with farmers across the country and their representatives. They are at the heart of our redesign of the scheme for next year. Workshops are starting today, and I have already met with representatives from the NFU and been on farms listening to farmers’ views—both from those who applied and those who were unable to do so. I absolutely understand the frustrations that people feel, but I am committed to improving the process for the future.

The Minister knows, because I wrote to him the day after this latest SFI shambles, that farmers in North Herefordshire are livid about the problem. Farmers in Ocle Pychard, Pudleston, Linley Green, Kimbolton, Dilwyn and more have all written to tell me that they are not only hopping mad; they are distressed and depressed at the devastating impact that this situation is having on their livelihoods and the prospect of them continuing to run their farms. Will the Minister recognise that farmers need to hear “sorry”? They need support, sustainability and certainty, not a lottery of fingers on buzzers. Fundamentally, they need direct answers to the following questions. Why is there less money available under the scheme than there was previously? Why did the Government not learn the lessons from the failure last year? And what are they going to do to genuinely own the problem?

I do not accept that we have not learned lessons from the past. That is why we made a number of changes for SFI26, as I set out at the outset of my statement. Of course I am sorry if people applied for this scheme and were unsuccessful, and I understand people’s frustrations, and that is why I am working hard to put it right.

Many farms in Wiltshire are marginal at best, and now that they are having to divert investment into a pot to pay future inheritance taxes, they are being pushed over the edge, to be honest. What does the Minister think this latest will do for those businesses, and what assessment has he made, regardless of the attribution of blame, of how many farms will actually be sold up—families packing up and going away—as a result of this latest round of DEFRA incompetence?

I thank the right hon. Member for his question. As I said at the outset, it is worth noting that £2.3 billion has been made available for the farming budget this year, with £11.8 billion for sustainable farming throughout the lifetime of this Parliament. If he has particular examples of farmers who have been unable to apply for SFI26, I encourage him to share those with me. For the first time since the second world war, a Government have published a farming road map to bring certainty to the sector, and I am busy getting on delivering that, working in partnership with the sector to ensure a profitable, productive and more resilient farming sector for the future.

Food security is national security. Without playing the blame game, the ineptness of the scheme is causing British farms to close and, in extreme circumstances, farmers to commit suicide. I wonder whether the Minister agrees with the principle that food security is national security, and could he explain to the House how he takes that principle forwards in his work when administering schemes such as this?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his question. I absolutely appreciate the difficulties that farmers have faced and the challenges that many have faced in applying for the scheme this year. As our manifesto says, food security is national security, and we are working through what that looks like in the Department. We have set out a clear vision through the road map for the future to bring certainty and consistency to the sector.

At a time when the Government really should be supporting the producers of our food and the guardians of our countryside, they saw fit to open the new SFI scheme offer and then close it down after just six hours. Will the Minister acknowledge that his Government got this wrong, provide a road map—a forward look for the farmers—detailing what the next scheme will be, give them more notice and assure both farmers and this House that they will have more time next time round?

I thank the right hon. Lady for her question. As I mentioned at the outset, it was her Government who introduced the “first come, first served” approach. We are absolutely keen to ensure that we make changes and improvements for future years, and if she has practical ideas about how we make that happen, I would be delighted to hear from her.

I wanted to point out to the Minister that a lot of farmers in my area have terrible difficulties with buffering broadband, as internet access is poor. I had actually thought that those who had agents were the lucky ones, but I was informed quite neatly after I had said something about this that most agents actually only managed to get in eight, nine or 10 applications in the very short window that was available, so that was not the case. The Minister has mentioned that he is going to be running workshops with farmers, but has he actually asked the Rural Payments Agency to do a high-speed review, as he does not have very much time before 2027, so that the barriers to applicants, particularly those who had expiring agreements and those who do use agents—
Order. Marvellous, fantastic question. I call the Minister.

I thank the hon. Member for her question, and I can assure her that I have met the RPA on the lessons learned from the scheme and what worked well this year, and we will analyse what the applications tell us.

Farmers across Somerset have been left without certainty and support by this latest DEFRA snafu, and they will not be consoled by the thought of a workshop. How does the Minister envisage farmers being able to plan financially for the year ahead if they do not know when the next round is or how the funds will be allocated?

We will publish more information about future rounds in due course. The hon. Gentleman will have heard my message that we are keen to open SFI27 as early as possible into the new year. There are lots of ways that farmers can feed in their thoughts and views on the scheme for the future, and there are other funding schemes available for farmers, so I encourage him to check the DEFRA blog for that information.

A dozen farmers I was with out on the levels last week from North Curry, Stoke St Gregory and the surrounding areas were visibly shaken by the economic impacts that they are facing and the price of diesel. This latest debacle has been disastrous for farmers. They are considering ripping out the trees and margins that were planted under previous funding initiatives because they simply will not be able to continue without funding being provided under this initiative, which seems to have only gone to around 10% to 12% of farms in the country. Can the Minister tell me what he would have me say to those farmers about the loss of the wildlife that they have already put in?
I am very happy to meet the hon. Gentleman to discuss those issues.

The NFU and farmers were a klaxon on the impending car crash that unravelled—those are the words of a local farmer. A debacle—those are the words of a Labour MP. Having had no decency to warn farmers that it was coming, today was an opportunity for humility rather than gaslighting them that only some of the technical complaints were legitimate. Will the Minister at least now publish a transparent breakdown of how the farming budget is being spent in its entirety? That is the least that farmers deserve after this debacle.

Our annual report obviously sets out how the farming budget is spent. When we announce future rounds of schemes, we set out the overall budget available. I mentioned earlier the amount available for SFI this year. We will continue to be as transparent as we can beyond the figures available for farmers.
With the final question, I call Jim Shannon.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. While the sustainable farming incentive applies specifically to England, the allocation underpinning it directly impacts devolved regions. Given that the Ulster Farmers Union—I declare an interest as a member —has expressed severe concern over the long-term stability of the multi-year agricultural budget and the transition away from direct support, what discussions has the Minister had with the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs Minister and the Northern Ireland Assembly to ensure that the unique family farm structure in Northern Ireland is strengthened and protected within the Barnett consequentials and the UK-wide funding envelope in order to help towards soaring costs?

I always appreciate a question from the hon. Gentleman. We will certainly look into the issues that he describes. Farming is a devolved matter, but he knows my commitment to working in partnership with the Northern Ireland Government. I have already met with my counterparts in Northern Ireland.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. Earlier the shadow Minister may have inadvertently misled the House by stating that for the first time this scheme was changed to operate on a first come, first served basis. That is simply not the case. A first come, first served scheme was set up under the Conservatives. Madam Deputy Speaker, can you advise how the record may be corrected?

I thank the hon. Member for his point of order. Members themselves, not the Chair, are responsible for what they say in the Chamber. If the shadow Minister wishes to clarify his earlier remarks, that is for him, but he needs to keep it short, because I do not want to continue the debate.

Further to that point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. As a matter of fact, when the SFI window was closed under this Labour Government in March 2025, that process in itself led to the huge demand that came up in September this time, therefore making it competitive and first come, first served. That is exactly the scenario that happened. [Interruption.]
Order. We are not going to continue the debate. The urgent question is over.

title: School Transport: Safety and Accessibility
turns: What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to ensure safe and accessible transport to school for pupils.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education

Local authorities must make safe, suitable and free travel arrangements for eligible children. Buses and coaches are regulated as public services vehicles and are expected to meet high safety standards. Licensing authorities are also expected to ensure that taxis and private hire vehicles are safe and roadworthy, and that their drivers are fit and proper.

It is the 33rd anniversary of the M40 school minibus tragedy, in which 12 children and their teacher lost their lives. I extend my condolences to all those affected. Exemptions remain in the law that allow unqualified and untrained staff or teachers to drive a school minibus, when other drivers would normally be required to have a D1 licence. Despite assurances in February from Department for Education and Department for Transport Ministers that they would meet to address the licensing exemption, no action has so far been taken, and these section 19 permits continue to put the safety of children at risk. I recently heard a report of a school minibus leaking brake fluid for weeks, because there is no set minibus inspection for schools. The official guidance for minibuses is 13 years out of date. Will the Minister please take action on this matter, or do we need to wait for another tragedy?

May I, too, extend my condolences to all those marking that anniversary? I commend the tireless campaigning by my hon. Friend and by Liz and Steve Fitzgerald, who have done so much to raise the public profile of this important matter. What happened to their daughter and the other children involved was, indeed, a terrible tragedy. I know my hon. Friend has met the Minister for School Standards who agreed to work with the Department for Transport to understand the impacts of changing the regulations. I will of course be happy to meet my hon. Friend to update her on how those conversations are progressing, but she can rest assured that the Government are fully engaged with the campaign and her calls for changes to minibus driver licensing.

Those who attended my recent school and college transport roundtable with Cornwall council and colleges across Cornwall were absolutely exasperated with the rising costs. SEND children in Cornwall have to travel double the distance of their peers in England, and Cornwall council has said that its transport budget will hit £44 million by 2028-29. Will the Minister consider introducing rural adjusted funding formulas to offset these higher transport costs in rural areas?

As my hon. Friend the Minister has already set out, the entire purpose of this Government’s SEND reforms is to make sure that we address the situation for every child with every need, and that includes transport. We can get those bills down, particularly where there is mainstream education and an education closer to where parents want, rather than having to send children out of the area.

title: Fly-tipping
turns: What steps she is taking to help tackle fly-tipping.
What steps she is taking to help tackle fly-tipping.
What steps she is taking to help tackle fly-tipping.
The Minister of State, Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs

Fly-tipping is unacceptable. It blights communities, harms the environment and imposes significant costs on taxpayers and businesses. Those responsible should be cleaning it up and paying for it. That is why we have strengthened the powers and penalties available to councils, to ensure that vandals face real consequences, and we are consulting on making them clean up their own mess.

I thank the Minister for that response. Fly-tipping is a real scourge for my Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes constituents. Whether it is in alleyways or local beauty spots, it is so disappointing, especially when so many members of the community are involved in doing community clean-ups. As the Minister said, the Government have done a huge amount of work, increasing fines to £5,000 and giving powers to scrap vehicles once they are seized, but those powers are only effective if they are used. Will she join me in urging my Reform-led North East Lincolnshire council to make greater use of these enforcement powers?

My hon. Friend is right to raise that. Her constituents are, understandably, frustrated, and I share her confusion as to why her council does not want to use the powers it has been given to fine fly-tippers, seize their vans and prosecute them. I join her in urging her council to do the job it has been elected to do, and I hope her residents remember this lack of action when it comes to the next election.

Trafalgar Square—not the one down the road, but the much smaller one back home in Erewash—is a private road with a persistent fly-tipping problem. There are signs up that ask people to stop doing it. I have reported it loads of times to the council, and so do local people all the time, but if the piles of bulky waste in the area get cleared, they come back almost immediately, so today I am escalating this. Could the Minister elaborate on how the Government are working to get a grip on fly-tipping, particularly in hotspots like Trafalgar Square in Long Eaton?

I completely understand the frustration of my hon. Friend’s constituents at repeated fly-tipping on private roads. We are taking this seriously. We have increased the maximum fine for offenders to £5,000, and we are working on advising the owners of private land on land security through the National Fly-Tipping Prevention Group. We are happy to give that advice to private landowners, but where we find out who is responsible, we will not hesitate in going after them.

Like many other MPs, I am often reporting the worst examples of fly-tipping to our local councils. My most recent case is on Marymead Drive, with boards and tarpaulin thrown under trees and walls graffitied. I expect that Stevenage borough council staff will be on to this as quickly as possible, but they should not have to do it in the first place. What assurances can the Minister give me and the House about the Government’s war on waste crime and whether it will extend to graffiti and reduce these instances of fly-tipping?

It is good to hear about a council being proactive and cleaning up some of this mess. I agree that graffiti and fly-tipping offences are unacceptable. Graffiti is a separate offence from fly-tipping, but local councils can issue fixed penalties of up to £500 for graffiti offences, and we are consulting on powers for councils to use conditional cautions, requiring offenders to clean up their mess and cover the clean-up costs, instead of simply walking away from the damage they cause.

A constituent got in touch with me last week to point out that farmers are often the ones who are left to deal with fly-tipping, but I note in the Government’s response on Tuesday that insurance is one option that could be available. What progress is the Minister making in talking to insurance companies about making fly-tipping part of a routine farm policy that farmers could take out against this scourge?

The right hon. Gentleman raises an important point. I absolutely sympathise with farmers, who, as he rightly highlighted, often see repeated dumping on their private land. As I mentioned, there is the National Fly-Tipping Prevention Group. I meet insurers regularly—in fact, I met them all last week—and I will certainly raise the issue of how we can ensure that farmers get the support they need in having to deal with a problem that is simply not of their making.

Local authorities will be looking to the Environment Agency to set standards as far as enforcement action is concerned. Trevoole Moor in my constituency is the fifth largest illegal dump in the country, affecting a nature reserve, but the Environment Agency has decided not to take enforcement action. When I discussed this with the Environment Agency, it said that it deals with these matters on a case-by-case basis. Will the Minister ensure that the guidance the Environment Agency uses is published, so that we can properly understand where and why it makes these decisions?

The hon. Gentleman raises an important issue. We have these illegal sites around the country; we are focusing heavily on the prevention side, before crimes are committed. We have already published the toughest ever waste crime action plan, given £45 million extra to the Environment Agency for frontline enforcement, granted new powers and expanded the joint unit for waste crime. We are going after prevention and are trying to clean up as many sites as possible, but fundamentally, we believe it is the polluter and not the taxpayer who should pay for the clean-up, and that is always the first route that we will pursue.

Waste crime and fly-tipping affect rural communities across Somerset. While I welcome the action that the Government are taking, does the Minister agree that the very substantial increases that we have seen in landfill tax enable rogue waste operators to undercut legitimate businesses? Does she accept that those substantial tax increases are fuelling waste crime, and will she join me in asking the Chancellor to cut those taxes?

The main problem that we have in the country is the serious organised crime behind some of these criminal activities, and that is exactly what we are going after through the new crackdown group, on which we are working with the National Crime Agency. We are escalating this issue and taking it extremely seriously because, as the hon. Gentleman said, we want to support legitimate businesses that are doing the right thing and get the criminals out of this industry.

title: Grassroots Sports: Facilities for Girls
turns: What assessment she has made of the adequacy of facilities for girls’ grassroots sports.
The Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport

This Government are more committed than ever to championing women’s sport and inspiring girls to get involved. One of the great pleasures I have had in recent years is being presented with the challenge of a whole generation of girls coming forward to play sports such as football and rugby, inspired by the stunning success of the Lionesses and the Red Roses. That is why we have removed many of the restrictions on what grassroots facilities we are prepared to fund. The one restriction we have put in place is that women and girls must have equal access to priority slots when we invest in grassroots sports facilities. I would be delighted to discuss with the hon. Member what more we can do.

At Westminster Park in my constituency, girls want to play football and cricket, but there is nowhere suitable for them to change. For the Leopards, Westminster Park’s girls football team, that becomes a real barrier as the girls get older and move up to the adult pitches. Councillor Razia Daniels and I have been campaigning with local residents to get better facilities, and the council has commissioned a feasibility study, but it has no capital budget for this, and without proper funding the girls risk another season without being able to play. I would like to take up the Secretary of State’s offer, so will she meet me to discuss how we can work with the Department to ensure that the council, the Football Foundation and Sport England secure the funding so that no more girls miss out?

I would be very happy to ensure that officials follow up with the hon. Member to resolve that issue. She is right to point to changing facilities as one of the key reasons why girls do not stay involved in sport. We really have pushed hard to ensure that this is a priority for funding from the Football Foundation and others. A number of Members across the House have raised with me as Culture Secretary over the past couple of years the significant challenge of navigating these funding systems and the conditions attached to them. We are looking at how to make it much easier for councils and Members of Parliament to access that funding to solve the local problems that she describes, but I would be very happy to follow this up.

Will the Secretary of State please join me in thanking the volunteers at Junior Parkrun at Parc Bryn Bach in Tredegar. It has good facilities, but their hard work has doubled the number of girls and boys getting out to run on a Sunday morning. Having said that, research from Sky shows that girls in my constituency still do an hour and 16 minutes less sport each week than boys. Can she give us the wider picture of the steps that she is taking to close that gap and get more girls to be active?

I thank my hon. Friend for his advocacy for Parkrun, which has been one of the real bright spots on the sport landscape in recent years—I am a keen participant in my local Parkrun at Haigh Hall and across the borough. I take this opportunity to congratulate all the volunteers at Junior Parkrun, because without them these amazing events would not happen. He is right to point to the challenges we still have with women and girls’ participation. There is no single solution, but I can assure him that I and my hon. Friend the Minister for Sport are treating this as one of the top priorities in the Department.

title: UK Nationals Detained Abroad
turns: What diplomatic steps he is taking to support UK nationals arbitrarily detained abroad.
The Minister of State, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office

We take all allegations of arbitrary detention very seriously, considering all available information and any opinions issued by the UN working group on arbitrary detention. Our support is tailored to each individual, and may include raising welfare or concerns about process, where needed. Reflecting our commitment to supporting British nationals detained overseas, we have appointed the right hon. Alistair Burt as our first envoy for complex consular detentions to work on these matters, and I am working with him very closely on this.

My West Dunbartonshire constituent Jagtar Singh Johal was released on bail 26 days ago, but Jagtar is by no means free. While he may have walked out of Tihar jail, having endured 3,254 days of illegal detention, torture and abuse, he still cannot return home to his family in Dumbarton, and still faces eight outstanding cases and the death penalty. Over the last 26 days, has the Minister escalated Jagtar’s case to the highest diplomatic level?

I can confirm that, most recently, the Foreign Secretary raised Mr Johal’s case with his Indian counterpart on 24 September at the UN General Assembly. I will be very clear: we recognise the immense toll that nine years in detention have taken on Mr Johal and his family, and I thank my hon. Friend for his advocacy for his constituent. His release on bail is a welcome development, but we recognise that eight cases remain outstanding, and it is crucial that those processes are resolved as quickly as possible within India’s independent legal system. We consistently raise concerns about his case at every appropriate opportunity.

British citizens Ryan Cornelius and his partner have now been detained for 18—nearly 19—years, without due process, by the United Arab Emirates. The reality is that the UAE supports a huge amount of terrorism in Sudan, where it is responsible for huge loss of life. To make matters worse, it has nominated Lana Nusseibeh of the UAE to be UN Secretary-General. Apart from demanding the release of Ryan Cornelius and his partner, will the hon. Gentleman condemn the UAE for its brutal involvement in Sudan, and block its nominee for Secretary-General, who should never be allowed to take over the UN?

As the right hon. Member knows, I take the case of Ryan Cornelius and Charles Ridley very seriously, as I do any of the other related cases. I have raised that case with the UAE at a high level, and I will continue to do so. Indeed, I have discussed it with our envoy, Alistair Burt, and I am very happy to discuss it further with him. On Sudan, as the right hon. Member knows, the international community, including this country, must do more to tackle that crisis. Yesterday, my hon. Friend the Member for Bridgend announced further sanctions against suspected perpetrators of sexual violence and other atrocities, including in El-Fasher. We continue to raise concerns with all the countries that are in any way involved in that conflict to urge them to de-escalate, stop arms supplies and bring peace to Sudan.

When President Trump met Xi Jinping last month, the US President raised with the Chairman the case of imprisoned British citizen Jimmy Lai. Has the Minister had a readout from that conversation, and what can he tell us about his own efforts to bring about Jimmy Lai’s release?

The Foreign Secretary and I take this case incredibly seriously, and the Prime Minister also raised it with President Trump. As I have said on a number of occasions, we condemn in the strongest terms the politically motivated prosecution of Jimmy Lai. The national security law was imposed on Hong Kong to silence China’s critics. For someone who is 78, a 20-year sentence is tantamount to a life sentence. We are deeply concerned for his health. This is a priority for the Government, and we raise the case at every possible opportunity, both directly with China and with other partners.

title: Sexual Offending by Healthcare Professionals
turns: What discussions he has had with the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care on the handling of sexual offences committed by healthcare professionals in the criminal justice system.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Justice

I thank my hon. Friend for asking that very important question. I want to reassure her, the House and anyone else who is listening that the Government take sexual offending extremely seriously, no matter who the perpetrator may be—a physician, a celebrity, or anyone else—and it must be dealt with appropriately by the criminal justice system. In our strategy to tackle violence against women and girls, we have committed to preventing these awful crimes, pursuing perpetrators and supporting the victims. We have signed up to this commitment across Government, and that includes the Health Secretary.

My constituent Sarah Johnson showed remarkable courage in helping to convict a physiotherapist who sexually assaulted her and other women in his care. Her case raised serious questions about how a practitioner who was subject to regulatory restrictions and was later suspended from practice was able to remain employed by the NHS and in contact with patients. Will the Minister work with the Department of Health and Social Care to strengthen the regulations, so that those who are under investigation for sexual offences cannot continue to have contact with patients, and will she meet the survivors and me to discuss the matter further?

I will gladly meet my hon. Friend and the survivors, and let me put on record my thanks to Sarah for her remarkable courage in coming forward to describe her horrific experience. We will of course continue to engage with colleagues across Government, particularly those in the Department of Health and Social Care, to ensure that anyone who abuses his or her position of trust and influence is held to account, and I look forward to meeting my hon. Friend and Sarah.

An issue that crops up regularly in Northern Ireland is the searching of the £400 million digital patient record system by healthcare staff, some 30 of whom have been able to gain access to information and data through the system. What discussions has the Minister had, or will she have, with the Northern Ireland Assembly—and, in particular, with the relevant Minister—to ensure that appropriate penalties are in place to deter healthcare staff from accessing confidential patient records without authorisation?

This issue is of grave concern to the Government, in England and Wales but more broadly across the United Kingdom. Anyone accessing records without the appropriate permission and level of security should be held accountable. As the hon. Gentleman will know, the Public Office (Accountability) Bill is in the other place, and although the new offence of misconduct in public office does not apply to frontline NHS workers, I have had conversations with the Health Secretary about how we can apply nuance in the case of people accessing records without permission. It causes immense distress to victims and bereaved families, and I will be sure to raise the matter with my counterparts across the United Kingdom.

title: Special Schools: Funding
turns: Whether she plans to provide additional funding for special schools.

Special schools are vital for many children with the most complex needs and will remain essential as we bring in SEND reforms. This is why we are investing £3.7 billion of high needs capital funding to create 60,000 specialist places nationwide, with £860 million allocated to councils this year.

I appreciate that answer, but the reality is that since taking office, this Government have scrapped plans for a 152-place SEND school in Buckinghamshire. That school would have been no magic bullet and it would not have solved all our problems, but it would have helped the huge number of families that write to me and come to my surgeries desperate to get their children into that specialist support that they need and deserve. It often ends up costing tens of thousands of pounds in taxes to take those children out of county. Will the Minister reconsider the position that the Government have taken on the new school for Buckinghamshire, and give us the school that we need?

When we looked at the pipeline of some of the later special schools, none of which were funded, we knew that we needed to get more money into the system quicker. My understanding is that the council will have got equivalent money to create specialist places quicker and order to meet the urgent need that we are seeing in communities around the country.

Too many young people have been held back by decades of under-investment in specialist provision in my communities, so I was delighted, after our campaigning, to secure a record increase in high needs funding for Hertfordshire council and Central Bedfordshire council, including the biggest increase in the country for Herts. This is already making a difference, with the new SEND unit at Hitchin Boys’ school and the expansion of Ivel Valley school in Biggleswade finally confirmed. We know, though, that we need to go further and that, historically, local authorities have not always done a great job of commissioning the places their communities need, so how will the Department for Education hold both my councils to account to ensure they are doing right by the young people in my community?

We have asked every local authority and integrated care board to develop a SEND reform plan that sets out how they should improve services, including their commissioning, and we will be holding them to account regularly. We are getting quarterly data back from those plans, and in our proposals for the new system we want to develop specialist provision packages, which will be really clear on the specialist provision we expect to see available in every part of the country for the young people who need it.

There is huge concern among parents with SEND children that the Government are pressing ahead with their SEND reforms while underdelivering special school places. New modelling that I have seen suggests that 41,600 additional special school places will be needed by the end of the decade. The Minister mentioned 60,000 places, but I am talking only about special school places, not mainstream provision. Will she confirm how many children her analysis shows will need special school places, and how many places the Government expect to deliver, by the end of the decade?

Our reforms are trying to do two things. First, we are making the mainstream genuinely inclusive; so many children could have thrived in mainstream but are not able to. We are rolling out new teacher training and Experts at Hand, and extra funding is going into mainstream schools to ensure that they are genuinely inclusive. We also recognise that we need new specialist places. The £3.7 billion is to create 60,000 new specialist places, which can be in inclusion bases linked to mainstream schools or in new special schools. We are investing heavily: we are putting £4 billion into early intervention and £3.7 billion into capital. We just did not see that investment under the previous Government.

title: Rogue Traders
turns: What steps he is taking to help protect consumers from rogue traders.
The Minister for the Future of Work

I know all too well the devastating impact that rogue traders can have on constituents, having had similar discussions in my own constituency and with many colleagues across the House too. That is why my Department supported the independent furniture and home improvement ombudsman’s new approved code and payment protection scheme, backed by independent dispute resolution, to help hard-working families identify trusted traders and ensure that people can spend their money with greater confidence and security. We remain committed to supporting the Competition and Markets Authority and local trading standards in their ability to impose penalties via the courts. This Labour Government are delivering everyday fixes to protect families and give them room to breathe.
Order. We need to move a bit faster, so questions and answers must be shorter.

My constituent Joanne paid £11,000 for a new kitchen. Her house was left in a terrible state and she was unable to get the builder to return to rectify the substandard work. It also turned out that he was associated with 21 other companies mostly in the building trade, many of which have been dissolved. The Minister mentioned quite rightly the new code for the home improvement sector, which will give confidence to consumers and support to reputable traders. Is more not needed to go after the cowboy builders to ensure that constituents such as Joanne can get the remedy that they so need?

I am sorry about that incident with my hon. Friend’s constituent. The damaging impact that that can have, making people who have saved their entire lives for home improvements feel robbed and unsafe in their homes, is dreadful. That is why we are taking action, starting with the backing of the furniture and home improvement ombudsman scheme. I am not complacent in this space: we are determined to ensure that customers know what protections are available and that they can use them with confidence. I look forward to working further in this area.

Rogue traders operate with impunity in the park homes sector, yet the Government have refused to supply sufficient money to National Trading Standards to enable it to carry out a national investigation and bring those rogues to book. What is the Minister going to do about it?

Regrettably, trading standards has faced a real-terms funding cut of more than 50% since 2010, under the previous Government. The system is therefore under severe strain. I back the incredible work that it does across the country and know how much support it needs. That is why we are committed to backing it and those longer-terms plans to overhaul the wider consumer protection landscape and particularly trading standards to help it continue cracking on with its brilliant job.

title: Business of the House
turns: Will the Leader of the House give us the forthcoming business?
The Leader of the House of Commons

The business for next week is as follows: Monday 23 November—Second Reading of the Finance Bill. Tuesday 24 November—Consideration of Lords amendments to the Armed Forces Bill, followed by consideration of Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill. Wednesday 25 November—Opposition day (seventh allotted day). Debate on a motion in the name of the official Opposition, subject to be announced. Thursday 26 November—General debate on inequalities in cancer care, followed by a general debate on lifelong sex education. The subjects for these debates were determined by the Backbench Business Committee. Friday 27 November—Private Members’ Bills. The provisional business for the following week will include: Monday 30 November—Committee of the whole House on the Finance Bill (day one). Tuesday 1 December—Committee of the whole House on the Finance Bill (day two). Wednesday 2 December—Opposition day (eighth allotted day). Debate on a motion in the name of the Liberal Democrats, subject to be announced, followed by, if necessary, consideration of a Lords message.

I thank the Leader of the House for updating the House. I know that the House will want to join me in paying tribute to two great stalwarts of this place who have died this week: David Evennett and John Pardoe. David, in particular, will be remembered with huge affection by many colleagues, he having stepped down only in 2024. We send all good wishes to his family and loved ones. In other news, I am pleased to report that the Scottish Government have now responded to public concern about the annual cost of their hundreds of jobless employee ghost workers. Their position, formally set out this week by Ivan McKee, the SNP Minister for Public Sector Reform, is that they have no idea how much they cost, no plans to find out, and no intention of changing the policy. There is hardly a more hallowed convention of this House than the code of omertà—the vow of silence—that binds the Whips Offices. Don Corleone himself would pale to think of the methods deployed over the years to enforce it. When Gyles Brandreth published a book, aptly named “Breaking the Code”, about his time as a Whip, he received a letter with a black spot the following day. So I was rather surprised to hear about an interview given to none other than Vogue magazine this month, by the new Labour Chief Whip. In it we learned that she loves to collect clothes from the Paris fashion houses Courrèges and Pierre Cardin—brilliant, one might think, and in no way a parody of socialism. The Chief Whip ran off to the left bank when she was 17, in order to become, as she put it, André Breton of the surrealists. Breton’s mantra was, of course: “The simplest Surrealist act consists of dashing down the street, revolver in hand, and firing blindly…into the crowd” —which explains rather a lot. But after a year of living on cheese and wine in France, the Chief Whip said she felt ill—perhaps not surprisingly—which she attributes to “never looking at a vegetable.” Some might say—I couldn’t possibly comment—that she addressed that problem when she joined the Labour party shortly thereafter. It can hardly by coincidental, but it was not quite the cure that she needed. Faithful to André Breton’s mantra, she had barely become an MP, just two years ago, before she decapitated the last Prime Minister. Why? Because, in her words, “After a couple of years, people came away thinking, ‘Well, what is happening for us? We’re just more skint.’” As she says, “the Labour party needed to be saved”. I could hardly have put it better myself, except I would say that the country needs to be saved from the Labour party. The Chief Whip ends her interview in Vogue by saying: “I said all of that stuff before about team-building…But…I’m not going to take any”— expletive deleted— “and I don’t”— expletive deleted— “about.” A bit panicky, one might think, but at least a bit more on message for the Whips Office. The modern art of spinning was invented by a vastly lesser A. Campbell—Alastair Campbell, under Tony Blair —but given the Leader of the House’s 15 years as Deputy Chief Whip and then Chief Whip, I am bound to ask for his views on this topic. Does this interview mark a new direction of spin from the Labour party? Instead of the dark arts, can we now expect some salacious titbits from the Deputy Chief Whip in Cosmo or Grazia, or perhaps a pearl-clutching confessional from the Leader of the House himself in the pages of Hello! magazine? Instead of my asking for a debate, Mr Speaker, perhaps we could all ask the Labour Chief Whip for what she might call an—expletive deleted—period of silence.

Before I respond to the comments of the shadow Leader of the House, I want to welcome home the crew of HMS Vengeance following their record-breaking 217-day submerged deployment. To put that into context, if the crew were to undertake the same deployment today, they would not return until 24 June 2027. Spending seven months beneath the surface as a submariner takes extraordinary professionalism, quiet resilience and personal sacrifice, as well as the silent sacrifice of their families. I just want to place on the record my thanks—and, I am sure, the thanks of every Member of the House—to the members of the 140-strong crew and their families for enduring to keep the UK safe. I join the shadow Leader of the House in paying tribute to Sir David Evennett, who passed away on Tuesday after a short retirement from this House. He served as a Conservative Whip in opposition and in government, in addition to being vice-chairman of the party. I found him a worthy adversary as a Whip, and he was always good company. He was, in my view and that of many others, a genuine and caring man. My thoughts are with his loved ones during this difficult time. In that vein, I know that the whole House will also wish to join me in paying tribute to the former Cornwall North MP John Pardoe and to Lord Davies of Oldham, who both passed away recently. My thoughts are with their loved ones, to whom I send my sincere condolences. An issue frequently raised with me during business questions is access to banking services. Following the review conducted by Richard Lloyd, we have this week announced that we are bringing forward new legal protections through the Financial Services and Markets Bill to protect access to the essential face-to-face banking services that many of our constituents rely on. Another matter often raised with me is the feudal leasehold system. Last week we acted to protect leaseholders by introducing regulations that will improve the fairness and transparency of service charges. Today we are introducing the commonhold and leasehold reform Bill, which will deliver a revitalised commonhold model, much-needed leasehold reform and fairer rules for estate rentcharges. I will turn now to the comments of the shadow Leader of the House. He talked at length about the Chief Whip’s interview in Vogue, which I thought was rather good, actually, and set out not simply what a thoroughly decent person she is, but what a fantastic politician she is. I understand what he says about the role of Chief Whips and what might have happened in the past, but the world does move on. It is not for me to stand here and answer every point the right hon. Gentleman made, because the Chief Whip is more than capable of fighting her own corner. If he is suggesting that these interviews should extend from the Chief Whip to the Leader of the House, then I await offers with keenness, Mr Speaker—although in my case, I think it will probably be less Vogue and more Exchange and Mart.

This is national Road Safety Week. It is 11 months since the Government launched their excellent road safety strategy and I launched my last road safety campaign in Rossendale and Darwen. We have made progress in Darwin with a forward-thinking council, but I am sorry to say that Lancashire county council has completely failed to act in Rossendale. Despite near misses, extensive evidence and harrowing accounts from residents, the council continues to refuse road safety measures where we need them most. For Burnley Road, Rochdale Road, Burnley Road East and Newchurch Road, there is nothing. The repeated excuse is that not enough people have yet been killed or injured to justify action. This is unacceptable, outdated and out of line with the road safety strategy, and it rightly infuriates my residents. Will the Leader of the House join me in calling on the Reform leadership of Lancashire county council to think again?

This Government introduced the road safety strategy and we take these matters seriously. Road safety should be a top priority for all local authorities, so I am concerned to hear about the lack of action from the Reform administration at Lancashire county council. It should be proactively improving safety, not waiting for tragedy to strike. Reform councillors in that part of the world, but also across local government, need to stop making excuses. They need to start listening to calls from my hon. Friend and his constituents and get on with it.
I welcome Lee Dillon as the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

Thank you, Mr Speaker. May I associate the Liberal Democrats with the Leader of the House’s comments on our brave submariners and on the passing of Sir David and John Pardoe? I also disassociate myself with the approach just taken by the shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire (Jesse Norman). I am sure that if the Chief Whip was not a woman, he might not have raised the issue of how she dresses. I have two issues to raise this morning, and I start with the much-awaited EU summit tomorrow. The Bill following tomorrow’s summit will be of major significance, and it is vital that Members are given time to scrutinise and debate the legislation in detail. Can the Leader of the House please confirm when the Bill will receive its First Reading and be published, and how will he ensure that parliamentarians can scrutinise it in this House and the other place? We Liberal Democrats are clear that joining the single market is the biggest lever that the Government can pull to grow our economy, cut taxes and invest in our nation’s defence. Can the Leader of the House please indicate whether the Government will ensure that Members can debate and vote on options to further improve our relationship with Europe and bring growth to our economy? The Leader of the House will also be aware that Cornwall Insight yesterday published its final forecast for the January 2027 default tariff cap. It predicts that energy bills will rise by 26%, taking a typical household bill over £2,000 for the first time. That is an increase of £443 on the current cap. The Government’s current measures will not stop this increase, as the forecast already includes the removal of VAT on electricity bills. The rise will be catastrophic, hitting households in the coldest months of the year. Will the Leader of the House ask the Chancellor to address the House directly on this issue as soon as possible, so that Members have the opportunity to question the Government’s response?

On the hon. Gentleman’s first point, we await the outcome of the summit keenly. The Government’s intention if things go well, as we anticipate they will, is to bring forward a Bill, which we will introduce in the normal way. I assure him that there will be plenty of time for the House to debate these important matters. He asks how he and his party may be able to amend the Bill, or give options to the House. We will be looking at amendments, which will come forward in the usual way. The hon. Gentleman raised the important matter of energy bills. He will know that we have taken action with the warm home discount allowance, with £150 more off bills until 2031. There is also a household energy payment for houses in council tax bands A to D, which will come into bank accounts in January. He acknowledges that we have cut VAT on electricity bills and extended that until 30 June. However, the Government are not complacent on these matters. As we approach what is already looking like a cold winter, his constituents and mine will still be concerned, but the Government are doing everything we can at present. If the Chancellor needs to announce anything further, I am sure he will come to the House in the usual way.

The UK Youth Parliament was established over 25 years ago to give young people a stronger voice in decisions affecting their lives. Elected members campaign on issues such as knife crime, mental health, education and the cost of living. However, its future is uncertain, as its funding is to be stopped. Given that the Government want to introduce votes at 16, does the Leader of the House agree that we should be encouraging our young people to engage with democracy? Will he please arrange for me to meet urgently the Under-Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, my hon. Friend the Member for Lewisham North (Vicky Foxcroft), to discuss the future of the UK Youth Parliament?

My hon. Friend is right to champion inclusion in our democratic process; I pay tribute to him for that. The current funding settlement runs until March 2027, and the Government will take a decision in due course on what happens past that point. It is important that we encourage young people to engage with democracy. His question is timely, given that Parliament Week is next week. I will ensure that he gets a meeting with the relevant Minister to get the answers he seeks.
I call Martin Vickers, who is representing the Backbench Business Committee.

The Chairman of the Committee sends his apologies. I have come off the subs’ bench to stand in for him. In addition to the business announced by the Leader for next Thursday, there will be Select Committee statements from the Transport and Justice Committees. In Westminster Hall, next Tuesday morning, the debate will be on the role of an MP; the afternoon debates will be on access to stroke services in remote areas and on Islamophobia Awareness Month. I hope that the Leader of the House can indicate whether we have been allocated time in the week beginning 3 December, because we have provisionally allocated some debates for days in that week. There is still a long wait for hon. Members who want debates in the Chamber, but we are making good progress with the Westminster Hall debates, and would welcome further applications. As the Leader of the House will know, Samaritans provides a vital service. I appreciate that it is a charity, and that the Government are not directly responsible for it—although of course they do provide some taxpayers’ funding—but 200 branches across the country are due for closure. I have met volunteers from my constituency who work in the Scunthorpe and Grimsby branches, and we have been seeking a meeting with the chief executive of Samaritans, without success so far. I hope that raising this here—and perhaps a nudge from the Leader of the House—might prove helpful.

I thank the hon. Gentleman for that. He is a more than admirable substitute; in fact, he is such a good substitute that I am sure that he would be worthy of being on the bench for Bridlington Town, in anticipation of the hon. Member for Bridlington and The Wolds (Charlie Dewhirst), if it required his services in playing against South Shields.

Indeed. On the future business, I try to give as much notice as I can to the Backbench Business Committee. I cannot confirm the business for the week beginning 3 December yet, but we will do all we can to ensure that the Committee gets all the time it needs and has as early notice as possible of it. The hon. Gentleman raised the important question of what is happening with Samaritans. He was right to praise it for the fantastic work that it does in not just his constituency but all our constituencies; I am sure that the House joins him in his praise. The Government cannot intervene in an independent organisation’s restructuring, but we recognise the valuable contribution made by volunteers. I encourage Samaritans to continue engaging with the volunteers in every part of the country affected during the process. I hope that the chief executive heard him this morning, and will do him the courtesy of giving him a meeting.

Following on from the comments of the hon. Member for Brigg and Immingham (Martin Vickers), Samaritans is an essential national charity that is there for us at our times of greatest need. Unfortunately, the Worthing branch is one of those at risk of closure. It has 100 dedicated volunteers available, day and night, to listen to anyone calling in. Those people have dedicated many years of their life to the service, and we risk losing not only their listening skills but the invaluable community networking and outreach that they undertake. I recognise that, as the Leader of the House said in response to the hon. Member, the Government cannot intervene directly, but I ask him to join me in praising the Worthing volunteers, and to encourage the national charity to engage with local MPs on this issue.

I certainly do that. I will not repeat what I said to the hon. Member for Brigg and Immingham (Martin Vickers), but the Samaritans provide a vital service. My hon. Friend is absolutely right to raise what is happening in Worthing. The Government cannot intervene, as I have said, but I think the Samaritans owe it to MPs to respond in a positive way, and at least explain what they are doing. I think a number of MPs have the same view. If the chief exec is not keen for MPs to go to them, I am sure that Parliament will give a great welcome to the chief exec, if the Samaritans wish to come here and explain what they are doing to MPs.

Road safety, which we heard about earlier, is a major issue in Skipton and Ripon and north Yorkshire. We have 5,000 miles of road, and there have been many deaths and many injured constituents. What more can the Government do to help the council with communications and strategies to reduce injuries and deaths during this Road Safety Week?

I agree with the right hon. Gentleman that this is a dark side to the absolutely beautiful constituency of Skipton and Ripon. The Government have brought forward a road safety strategy, but he makes a good point on communications, and I will take that to Transport Ministers. If he seeks a meeting with them to see what assistance local authorities can get, I am sure that those Ministers will be keen to meet him.

I have been proud to lead the campaign to protect the title of “nurse”. I have worked with the NHS, doctors and the #ProtectNurse campaign to ensure that if someone says they are a nurse, they are actually qualified as one. The Government’s consultation ended last month. Will the Leader of the House give a lovely Christmas present to the NHS and ensure that the Government implement this important legislation soon?

I join my hon. Friend in praising nurses and healthcare professionals in general for their work in what is often a busy period for them. The consultation has closed, and I am sure that Ministers will be poring over the contributions. I cannot guarantee when the response will come forward, but I expect that there will be a response, and that it will be made to this House.

Mr Speaker, may I first join your remarks yesterday, and the remarks made by the Front Benchers this morning, about our late colleague David Evennett? As one of the three, I think, surviving members of the ’83 intake still in the House, I know David to have been a good man, a wonderful constituency MP, a great father and a dear friend, with a very laconic sense of humour. Our thoughts are with Marilyn, his two boys and their family at a very sad time for them. Mr Speaker, may I try your patience just a little, with what might seem to be a parochial issue, though I believe it to be of national importance? For three weeks, a road in my constituency has been closed to school transport, public transport, emergency vehicles and domestic vehicles at the behest of the South African company Trooli, which is licensed by Ofcom to install yet another fibre optic cable. Six businesses—three pubs, one village shop, one butcher, and one tea shop—are all losing money as a result of the activities of this commercial enterprise, which has to be authorised by Kent county council because Ofcom has licensed it. It has to be wrong that a wholly commercial company can disadvantage other businesses without giving them any compensation. Will the Leader of the House talk to the appropriate Ministers to see whether either primary or secondary legislation is needed to address this issue?

The right hon. Gentleman is expressing a frustration that many of us feel in our constituency when we see roadworks that do not appear to be necessary, and that seem to take longer than was envisioned, as is often the case. They seem to happen in an unplanned way. I hope that the company that he refers to, but also Ofcom and anybody else who has a hand in this, has heard what he has said. It is hard to overestimate the effect on businesses, families and children going to school, so I hope that those involved have heard his words. I will certainly take this away and talk to Ministers to see what more can be done—to the point that if this requires legislation, there is a legislative response.

Today is World Toilet Day. It sounds quite amusing, but this is not an amusing issue for the train drivers and other transport workers who are required to work for 11 hours with only one 20-minute break, with a total lack of clean, accessible toilets. Unbelievably, train drivers have had to resort to extreme measures: changing sanitary products in the cab; leaving the train to urinate alongside the railway; or using bottles and lunchboxes. Despite ASLEF’s campaign and the Office of Rail and Road charter, the industry is still not meeting the required standards. Will my right hon. Friend use his offices to secure a meeting with the relevant Ministers to discuss what can be done to provide the dignity that those workers so rightly deserve?

My hon. Friend is a powerful advocate for workers’ rights and he raises an important matter. Welfare provision across the rail network is a vital principle, not least as railways come back under public control. I will be happy, on his behalf, to raise the matter with Transport Ministers and the Office of Rail and Road, and if he seeks a meeting, I will help him to arrange one.

Like many in this House, I welcomed the Prime Minister announcing in his Labour party conference speech the formulation of a national commission on electoral reform. This is the most disproportionate Parliament in history; the Labour party got about a third of the votes, two thirds of the seats and 100% of the power. Despite submitting several written questions, we have not seen the commission’s remit, the membership, the chair or the timescale. My constituents, particularly the 14-year-olds at schools such as Marple Hall and Harrytown who might be able to vote at the next election, are keen to know if the outdated first-past-the-post system will be used at the next general election or beyond. Will the Leader of the House ask the relevant Minister to make a statement to this House on a national commission? We need to fix our politics, so that we can get on with fixing our country. I urge the Government to crack on.

This is a priority for the Prime Minister, and work is in progress on the matter. I am not sure, with due respect, that it is the top priority for all our constituents in the way it seems to be for the hon. Lady’s party, but it is important; I accept that. When progress has been made—we want to make sure, as we change politics, that it is done in a way that changes our country for the better—I am sure that Ministers will want to come to this place and update the House on that.

Meur ras, Mr Speaker. Earlier this week, I met Surfers Against Sewage, who are based in St Agnes in my constituency of Camborne, Redruth and Hayle. Since the clean water White Paper was announced in the King’s Speech, they and many constituents have been eagerly awaiting its publication. Will the Leader of the House update Members and our constituents on when the Government plan to publish that and introduce the Bill to Parliament?

My hon. Friend is right to raise that. In our water system, shareholders appear never to lose and customers never to win. As a coastal constituency Member of Parliament, I know the importance of this issue, not just to those who surf, but to everyone who cares about the state of our waters. We have announced a series of measures to go further in implementing public control. In September, the Prime Minister announced that we would bring forward a strengthened water Bill when parliamentary time allows. I do not think my hon. Friend will have long to wait before that can be confirmed.

I am currently assisting 28 constituents—the number goes up and down—with civil service pension problems. There is a particular irony in the fact that the people affected are civil servants, who have given their career to the bureaucracy that is now so badly letting them down. Capita recently demonstrated that there is not even uniformity in the level and manner of its incompetence: it seems to be finding new ways to let civil servants down all the time. Can we have a debate in Government time to allow right hon. and hon. Members to bear witness to this utter disaster on behalf of their constituents, and allow the Cabinet Office to explain away why there is such institutional lack of grip on the issue?

I do not agree with the final point, because Ministers are working very hard to ensure that the situation improves, but I do understand, because I have similar cases, that it is extraordinarily frustrating for people—in fact, more than frustrating—who are waiting for their pensions. The Government have been clear that Capita’s performance has been unacceptable. It is a complex issue, but it has taken too long to resolve. There have been a number of debates on these matters, and there was an opportunity to raise them at Cabinet Office questions, which we have just had. Ministers have updated the House, and I am sure that they will continue to do so.

The Milburn review rightly identifies that young people lack neither resilience nor ambition, but opportunity on their doorstep. That is particularly stark in Portsmouth, which is joint worst in England for the availability of post-16 provision. I welcome the proposals for early intervention and a new system of support that will help young people to fulfil their potential and will reduce the benefit bill. Will the Leader of the House, who is also a coastal MP, make time for a debate on the unique challenges faced in coastal communities by young people not in education, employment or training?

My hon. Friend is a powerful advocate for her area. As she said, I am a fellow coastal MP, and I am aware of the particular challenges that communities like ours face. I agree that this Government will give hope to young people across all our constituencies, including in coastal areas, and help them to reach their potential. I am sure that the Milburn review will continue to be hotly debated; I encourage her to apply for a Westminster Hall debate so that she can put her questions directly to Ministers and hear answers about how we intend to take it forward.

Stockton’s Labour borough council has turned parts of our town into a free-for-all for houses in multiple occupation, bedsits and bail accommodation, and has volunteered for us to take a disproportionate share of the country’s asylum seekers. Residents see groups of lone men hanging around the town centre, and shoplifting is up 168%. Residents now face plans for a 229-bed HMO near the town centre, which is opposed in the strongest possible terms by Cleveland police, but under Labour’s new rules, councillors might not even get a vote. Can we have a debate on stopping councils cramming ever more HMOs into communities that have already had enough?

Local authorities do have planning powers to limit the proliferation of HMOs, and we will keep the regulation of HMOs under review. I understand the frustration of the hon. Gentleman’s constituents. I am not sure that people would necessarily jump to some of the conclusions that he jumps to in these matters, but we keep these matters under review.

This year, Steve at the Neptune, volunteers and Derby punters have pulled together and raised a whopping £36,744 for the poppy appeal. They are a credit to our city, and their efforts remind us that no community is complete without its local pub. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating everybody at the Neptune on their brilliant fundraising work? Does he agree that we must protect our local pubs, which are the heartbeat of our communities?

Yes, I do. I join my hon. Friend in congratulating Steve and all the volunteers and customers of the Neptune on raising an extraordinary amount of money for the poppy appeal. As my hon. Friend says, great community pubs are the cornerstone of our towns. They bring people together to tackle isolation and serve as hubs for local communities—and long may they continue to do so. The Government are not just praising them; we have brought forward support for hospitality in the Budget, and I am sure that we will look at what further actions we can take to ensure that pubs continue to flourish in the future.

It is Restorative Justice Week, which has the theme of rebuilding communities, repairing connections and building peace. In my experience, restorative justice is a powerful tool that helped my family heal after I was attacked in my home. It puts the victim at the heart of the criminal justice process. Does the Leader of the House agree that restorative justice should be available to every victim of crime, where deemed appropriate, and can he assist me in pushing for a cross-Government review to maximise its potential to help victims and cut reoffending?

The Government agree with the hon. Member that victims should be at the heart of the criminal justice system. If he wishes to raise those points directly with Ministers, I will help to arrange a meeting with them.

I greatly welcome the Prime Minister’s ambition of devolving by default the powers and investment that this Labour Government are spreading out from Whitehall and Westminster into local communities, where they should be, but can the Leader of the House give a gentle nudge to departmental colleagues to ensure that non-mayoral strategic authorities receive those powers as the rule and not the exception?

My hon. Friend and all his Cornish colleagues are powerful advocates for their region, and I pay tribute to him and each and every one of them for that. We are seeing the biggest transfer of power, funding and responsibility away from Westminster in a generation to ensure that local decisions are made by local people. But this is a process, and it will continue. Not every part of the country is in the same place, as he suggests. In the meantime, I am sure that Departments will want to ensure they give due regard to where resources should be spent, not least in areas like his. I hope that Ministers have heard what my hon. Friend has said.

I will give the Leader of the House a brief respite from Brid Town—perhaps we can return to their heroics at a later date. I want to cover an altogether more serious subject—something I hope the Leader of the House will agree with me on—which is that it is now over five years since Sir Chris Whitty’s report on health in coastal communities. Its implementation was delayed by covid. I know that the Leader of the House’s constituency shares the same challenges as mine in towns such as Bridlington and Hornsea, so could he persuade the Health Secretary to give a statement to the House updating us on the implementation of the recommendations of that incredibly important report?

I will do that. I will go away and talk to colleagues about what might be said in response to that. But I gently point out that at the end of covid, the then Government commissioned the Collins report, which suggested that £6 billion should be spent to tackle the real problems that face young people in particular. Not a penny was spent on that, so I think we need to be clear about the promises that were made, and the Milburn report addresses that directly.

Collette Gallacher was murdered in 1986 on her way to school. Her murderer is due for parole again next year. Since being in prison, he has changed his name. The family will not be advised of the name change as the presumption is not to inform them to protect the rights of the murderer. Would the Leader of the House agree with me and my campaign for Collette’s law that families of victims should automatically be advised of a name change of a convicted criminal to protect the rights of the victims and not those of the perpetrator?

My hon. Friend raises a very concerning case on behalf of his constituents. He is right that we need to do everything we can to protect victims of violence against women and girls, which is why we introduced a requirement for registered sex offenders to notify the police in advance of any intended change of name. I accept that that is not exactly what he is referring to. I understand that the family are meeting the relevant Minister in the new year, but I will make sure that the Minister has heard his representations made here today.

Yesterday I tabled early-day motion 1226, calling for a national register of asylum accommodation. [That this House believes that the use of public money to provide asylum accommodation must be subject to proper transparency and scrutiny; recognises the need for accurate information about houses in multiple occupation and other residential properties used for this purpose; calls on the Government to establish and maintain a comprehensive national register of such properties, recording their addresses, ownership, accommodation providers, occupancy, public cost, planning status and compliance with applicable licensing requirements; further calls for accommodation providers to be required to keep those records up to date; urges the Government to ensure that relevant local authorities and constituency hon. Members have access to the register and are notified before properties are brought into use; and also calls for the publication of quarterly figures by ward and local authority area showing the number of properties, residents accommodated and associated expenditure.] In Runcorn and Helsby and across the country, homes that local families could otherwise live in are being used to house asylum seekers. When I asked the Home Office over a year ago how many HMOs in my constituency were being used for this purpose, I was told that it would cost too much to give me that figure. My constituents deserve to know, ward by ward, how many homes are being used to house asylum seekers and how much it is costing them. Will the Leader of the House ask the Home Secretary to make a statement on whether the Government will establish this register?

There have been opportunities to raise this directly with the Home Secretary, not least during the remaining stages of the Immigration and Asylum Bill. I will take away what the hon. Lady says, because I understand that there is often concern in communities and a need for as much clarity as possible. But as an MP representing a constituency where rumour of HMOs very recently caused violence that made the national headlines, I think there is an element of public safety here. We have to balance what information local people have against the need to keep the community safe, because there are people out there who, once they get information, will stir it up, cause trouble and put people’s lives at risk, and that is not acceptable.

Understanding, not division; light, not darkness. Last Sunday, I was proud to again join the Sunderland Inter Faith Forum’s walk of friendship, featuring Christian, Muslim, Buddhist, Sikh, Hindu and Quaker contributions. They say that hope happens when we walk together in peace, so will the Leader of the House join me in thanking the organisers for their important work, and will he consider a debate on the importance of interfaith work in supporting community cohesion?

With some irony, my hon. Friend follows the previous question with one that offers hope. He is a strong advocate for community cohesion not just in his area but across the country, and I pay tribute to him for that. I join him in thanking all those involved in the Sunderland Inter Faith Forum’s walk of friendship for the important work they do in encouraging interfaith dialogue. Should he seek an Adjournment debate or a Westminster Hall debate, I am sure that he and other Members will be able to share stories of hope from their own constituencies.

The Prime Minister has rightly talked about growth in every postcode, but the people of Peasedown St John are not feeling that at the moment because the West of England combined authority has cut a key local bus route, which means they are struggling to get to their jobs and to the Sulis hospital. Will the Leader of the House help me to secure a meeting with the relevant Minister to discuss how we can ensure that the funding the Government have given to combined authorities reaches people who do not necessarily live in the big cities of those areas, like those living in the Somer valley?

The hon. Lady raises a very important point—it is one that is referred to in the Milburn review—about people getting into work but also ensuring that the transport is there. She will know that my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister is, quite rightly, somewhat obsessed with this. I will take that back to the relevant Minister, but I hope the local authority that she refers to has heard what she said and can restore services to people who need them in her area.

I welcome the news that the Government have called on Google to take down Russell Brand’s YouTube account in the wake of his conviction, but that simply does not go far enough, because his podcast can still be seen on other streaming platforms such as Spotify, Amazon and Rumble, which is deeply disturbing for his victims. This issue also extends to the likes of LinkedIn, as in the case of Naomi Timperley and Brad Burton, who were victims of a convicted criminal who used LinkedIn and other methods to stalk them and try to make their life a living hell. Will the Leader of the House work with me to urge Ministers to bring in regulation and perhaps legislation to ensure that these tech platforms are acting based on not just how they feel about something but what the law dictates they must do, so that victims see justice when criminals are locked away?

To be clear, the request was to take down the specific video, which is clearly appalling. The matter is being investigated urgently, and we expect further action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules. We have taken some steps on online safety, but my hon. Friend raises a perfectly legitimate concern. Should she wish to speak to Ministers about it, I will help to arrange a meeting.

It is reported today that the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero is encouraging her Labour colleagues to lobby against the Rosebank oilfield development. We are constantly being told that the decision on Rosebank is quasi-judicial, so there should be no lobbying. Does the Leader of the House believe it is still appropriate for the Secretary of State to make the decision if she is behind attempts to lobby against the proposal?

The hon. Gentleman should not believe all the rumours that may swirl on these matters. It is a quasi-judicial decision, and I am sure that my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State will make it in the right way.

My residents still face huge challenges getting driving tests. One constituent, Andrew, logged on to the booking system at 6 am on Monday only to find 12,500 people ahead of him in a 70-minute queue. When he finally got to the front of the queue, there was no availability for tests within a 50-mile radius. The Government are rightly determined to help young people into education, training and employment, but in areas like Aylesbury and the villages, where we have very limited public transport, that often depends on young people being able to drive to college or work. Will the Leader of the House make time for us to further debate the issue and progress it?

My hon. Friend has been an assiduous campaigner on this matter, and I absolutely sympathise with those affected by the long wait for tests. As she said, we are taking action—we are stamping out test reselling and limiting changes to bookings and locations to stop bots—but there is further work to be done, and I will make sure that she gets an update from the relevant Minister on what further steps are planned.

As we have heard, it is national Road Safety Week. One of the worst accident blackspots in the midlands is the Llynclys crossroads in my constituency, on the A483 between Welshpool and Oswestry. I am pleased to say that a complete redesign of the junction to create a roundabout, which I fully support, has been included in the national safety programme as part of road investment strategy 3, but the certainty of that funding has been put into question by changes to defence investment. The safety programme is critical, so will the Leader of the House ask the Transport Secretary to make a statement, or perhaps arrange a meeting for me with the relevant Minister to impress upon him the importance of this change?

The hon. Lady is right to press the case for her constituents in the way that she does. I will take it up with the relevant Minister and see whether we can get that meeting so she can make the case that she wants to make.
