I warmly welcome the Government’s £2.5 billion youth guarantee package. However, discussions of youth employment and financial independence must not exclude those affected by the student loans system. Student loans remain one of the greatest barriers to young people achieving financial security, imposing a seemingly insurmountable financial burden on them for the majority of their working lives. Will the Leader of the House help to ensure that appropriate attention is given to that unfair system, which so desperately needs reform?

My hon. Friend is right to praise the Government’s youth guarantee package, and I join him in doing so. We are taking action by capping maximum interest rates at 6% for plan 2 and plan 3 loans, and reintroducing maintenance grants. However, we continue to look for ways to make the system even fairer for students, who I have to say were let down in a big way by the previous Government. We want to make the system fairer for students, graduates and, indeed, taxpayers, in a financially sustainable way, but I will make sure that Ministers have heard his concerns.

Will the Leader of the House join me in paying tribute to Lady Elizabeth Godsal MBE, who sadly passed away last week? Lady Elizabeth gave decades of service to local institutions, including 26 years as the high steward of Wokingham. She was a vice-lord lieutenant of the Royal County of Berkshire, high sheriff of Berkshire in 1990, chief president of St John Ambulance, chairman of the board of visitors of Reading Prison, patron of Girlguiding Royal Berkshire, and a former president of the Wokingham Society. Lady Elizabeth made an exceptional contribution to Wokingham and will be greatly missed.

I certainly join the hon. Gentleman in paying tribute to Lady Elizabeth. She sounds like one of those very busy people who we meet as we go about our civic roles. They are not only busy but live exceptional lives, and we should pay particular tribute to the contribution that they make to society. I join him in paying tribute to Lady Elizabeth and all the other people out there who are making a similar contribution.

I declare an interest as a member of GMB. Recently, Jo Taylor, in my High Peak office, celebrated 25 years of working for Labour Members, which is a tremendous achievement. Jo has dedicated her career to making the everyday lives of people better and protecting their rights. Now is a good time for us to look to protect the rights of all staff like Jo, which is why I am backing GMB’s “One Parliament One Employer” campaign. The Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority writes the contracts, sets the job descriptions and the pay bands, and pays the salaries, yet the legal liability sits with 650 individual MPs. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating Jo on her 25 years of public service, and make time in Government time for a debate on making Parliament the single employer for its staff?

My hon. Friend is right to recognise the incredible work done by our staff, both in Westminster and across the country. I join him in paying tribute to Jo and thank her for all her hard work over the years. There are a range of views on this topic. I note, Mr Speaker, that the Speaker’s Conference did a great deal of work on this matter in the last Parliament, and I am sure that the issue will continue to be a matter of debate. Should my hon. Friend want to press his case with House officials, then I will help him to arrange those meetings, and I will see what we can do about finding some time to arrange a debate on these matters, because it is an important question.

The Department for Education’s keeping children safe in education accreditation scheme is voluntary and does not automatically apply to permanent online-only schools. Ofsted visits only those providers who choose to join it as a quality assurance body, rather than under the usual inspection regime. As of August 2026, only 17 providers in England are accredited. Safeguarding children should not rely on whether their education provider opts in, so will the Leader of the House ask the Education Secretary to look again at bringing all full-time and part-time online education providers within a statutory framework?

The hon. Lady is absolutely right that safeguarding should never be an option. I have to confess that I do not know enough about this subject to give her any more of a response than that, except to say that I will take it up with the Secretary of State for Education and see what further plans there are to address what is a very important matter.

The Sair Inn is a characterful old pub in my constituency and has been a great asset to the local community for many years. I recently visited after it was recognised as one of the best pubs in the UK by The Daily Telegraph, and enjoyed an excellent pint with Jim, the landlord and owner. It is not the only pub that has been recognised in my constituency: the Royal Oak in Upperthong was given the same accolade. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating both the Sair Inn and the Royal Oak, and recognise the great work of the landlords and excellent staff at both pubs?

I will indeed join my hon. Friend in congratulating Jim and the Sair Inn, as well as the Royal Oak and its publican, on being recognised as among the best pubs in the United Kingdom. I have said it before and I will say it again: local pubs are the beating heart of our towns and villages. We are committed to supporting them, including through cutting business rates, and there was help in the Budget. They have gone through a tough time—7,000 closed during the period of the last Government. We are doing everything we can and looking at what more we can do to ensure our pubs thrive, because if they thrive, it helps our communities to thrive.

The wonderful Evington Road in my constituency already has two gambling shops, and a third gambling arcade has been proposed. Families are already feeling the financial squeeze, and there is practically nothing for young people to do, yet the gambling outlets keep coming. Will the Leader of the House make time for a debate on the spread of gambling premises in communities that are the hardest hit financially?

The hon. Gentleman is right to raise the state of our high streets because this Government care very deeply about that and share his concern about the proliferation of gambling shops. The Chancellor referred to this matter in his Budget and the action that we intend to take. This sounds to me like the sort of issue that the hon. Gentleman might want to raise in an Adjournment debate or a Westminster Hall debate, because I am sure that colleagues on both sides of the House will want to express similar concerns and hear from the Government on what more we intend to do about it.

Ayrshire Cancer Support, based in my constituency, delivers essential transport for people affected by cancer. Alongside that, it has dedicated support for children living with the disease and supports parents through treatment. Next year, I will be doing a 23-mile kilt walk as a way of raising awareness of its vital work. Will the Leader of the House join me in commending the staff and volunteers at Ayrshire Cancer Support on all their hard work? Will he consider donning a kilt and joining me on the walk?

I certainly join my hon. Friend in thanking Ayrshire Cancer Support for all its hard work, and I wish her every success in her kilt walk. I will certainly give her suggestion some consideration, but I would be hard pushed to decide which Campbell tartan kilt I would wear—there are so many. On a serious point, she will know that the Government are committed to taking action on cancer, and we have published our national cancer plan to end the cancer postcode lottery. At a local level, it is so important that she pays tribute to local people and gets involved in that work, and I wish her well on her kilt walk.

As it stands, China projects itself as a country of great freedom, but the fact of the matter is that the truth is very different. Back home, we would say that butter would not melt in his mouth, but the fact is that President Xi is involved in suppressing human rights, denying religious liberty and ensuring that people are tortured and killed because of their faith. I want to ask the Leader of the House about one example. Will he ask the Foreign Secretary to make a statement on the reported death of Rahile Omer? She was a Uyghur Muslim who was detained at the age of 14 and later sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment after reportedly being punished for praying during her detention in Konasheher in Xinjiang province. What representations are the Government making to urge the Chinese authorities to clarify the circumstances of her death, release medical evidence and prison records, and protect Uyghur Muslims from detention and punishment for peacefully practising their faith and praying?

The reports of Rahile Omer’s death in custody are very distressing, to say the least. We stand firm on human rights, including standing against China’s repression of people in Xinjiang and Tibet. We continue to raise these issues directly with the Chinese authorities and other international partners. I will ensure that the Foreign Secretary hears the hon. Gentleman’s concerns. As ever, he makes a very important point in a very responsible way, and I will ensure that he gets an update on what this Government are doing to hold the Chinese authorities to account.

I recently visited Hednesford nursery school to toast its success, because a recent Ofsted inspection saw it achieve an incredible three areas at “strong” standard and three areas at “exceptional” standard. That makes it the highest-rated school in Staffordshire, the highest-rated nursery school in the country and, we believe, one of the highest-rated schools overall across the UK. Having seen the incredible work done by nursery manager Dawn Freeman and her team, that feels correct. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating the team at Hednesford nursery school? Can we have a debate on the vital importance of high-quality early education?

I join my hon. Friend in congratulating Dawn Freeman and the entire team at Hednesford nursery school on their exceptional achievement, which is certainly something to be proud of. I hope that the whole House will join me in paying tribute not only to their work, but to all the teachers, educational support staff and nursery workers across our constituencies. We truly appreciate their hard work.

At the weekend, it was announced that Lomond Radio in my constituency is to be awarded the King’s award for voluntary service. What started as a small lockdown project in 2020 has grown into a brilliant local radio station powered by more than 50 volunteers who provide local news, support charities and community groups, and give a platform to local talent across West Dunbartonshire and beyond. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating everyone involved—both on air and behind the scenes—on receiving the highest award presented to voluntary groups in the UK, and in wishing Lomond Radio every success for the future?

I certainly join my hon. Friend in congratulating the team at Lomond Radio on their vital work and all the volunteers who provide the services he describes. As he says, the King’s award is a considerable achievement, and I congratulate them on that. We are committed to supporting local radio and have launched our local media strategy, increasing community radio funding. At the end of the day, however, local radio depends on volunteers and the fantastic service they provide.

This week, the BBC released a podcast called “Chasing Mr Sunshine”, which is a deep dive into how a dodgy grifter called Liam Kavanagh managed to siphon vital public funds away from Thurrock council, aided and abetted by Sean Clark, the then finance director. It cannot be right that the closest these people have ever come to answering questions about putting my constituency in such dire straits is through BBC reporters’ efforts in chasing them down at their homes. Will the Leader of the House allow a debate in Government time about how we can hold to account public officials who so diabolically fail in their duty to the people they serve, so that we might finally be able to hold them to account?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right to raise that matter. As she says, it cannot be right that this information has to be dragged out by others; it should be out in the open for all to see. That debate is going on in government, and if my hon. Friend wants to know where our thinking on that has got to—or to raise this matter further, if necessary—I suggest that an Adjournment debate or Westminster Hall debate would be the way to do so.

Constituents in Truro and Falmouth who live on a park home site have reached out to me because the owner has not allowed them to have individual water meters. During the drought over the summer, they have been trying to conserve water, and they do not feel this is fair. Would the Leader of the House be able to either make space for a debate in Government time on this issue, or ask the relevant Minister to speak with me about whether they plan to review the rights of park home residents in relation to billing arrangements for water and other utilities on residential park home sites?

I am sure that situation must be very frustrating for my hon. Friend’s constituents. I understand that the rules around park homes and their residents are quite complex, but one of the Ministers responsible for these matters, the Minister for Housing and Planning, is sitting on the Front Bench and has heard what my hon. Friend has said. I am sure that if she catches him outside the Chamber, he would be more than happy to meet her.

Businesses at Lancing’s Chartwell business centre are losing customers after hundreds of them have received unfair fines of £100 due to poorly rolled-out automatic number plate recognition enforcement by One Parking Solution. As well as damaging those businesses, it has had a dangerous knock-on effect, with children at risk of injury from heavy goods vehicles on the neighbouring road. Will the Leader of the House join me in calling on One Parking Solution to work with me and the affected businesses to fix this problem as soon as possible, and will he grant time in this place for Members to debate how we can more effectively hold parking management companies to account?

My hon. Friend is a great advocate for businesses in his constituency, which will undoubtedly have been negatively impacted by what he describes. We are cracking down on unfair private parking charges through our new strengthened private parking code of practice, giving drivers the right to challenge those unfair charges. However, I hope One Parking Solution has heard his words today and that a swift solution can be found. I hope it respects my hon. Friend’s position as a Member of Parliament and offers him a meeting to work on how it can put this right. He is doing his best on behalf of his constituents, and One Parking Solution should listen to what he says.
Saving the best till last, I call Josh Dean.

The Holy Trinity night shelter in Bishop’s Stortford provides much-needed support and stability to those who are most in need in our community. It is no exaggeration to say that its work changes lives. I was delighted to see those who run the shelter awarded a King’s award for voluntary service last week. Will the Leader of the House, and the whole House, join me in congratulating Dave, Michelle and all the volunteers at the night shelter, and in thanking them for their hard work?

I am sure that the whole House will join me in congratulating Dave, Michelle and all the volunteers at the Holy Trinity night shelter on a very well-deserved King’s award, which, as I have said, is a very high and prestigious award. I am sure that it means a great deal to them and to the whole community. As my hon. Friend will know, ending rough sleeping is a top priority for the Government and the Prime Minister, and the valuable work of such shelters does not go unnoticed. I pay tribute to the work of people in my hon. Friend’s constituency and across the country, as we bear down on that intolerable problem.

title: Procurement Policy Note 024
turns: What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to prepare for the commencement of procurement policy note 024.

This Government are committed to delivering good jobs and the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation. The First Secretary of State recently established an insourcing and market-shaping unit. The unit will identify insourcing opportunities, scrutinise departmental insourcing strategies and be a centre of expertise. We recently announced that 2,700 universal credit case workers will be brought into the Department for Work and Pensions. This Government will turn the tide and drive up insourcing.

My constituents want taxpayer money spent on the state delivering where possible, not spent needlessly hiving off capacity to private contractors, so I welcome the public interest test and insourcing strategy coming into force from 1 April next year. However, 120 jobs in Scotland at the Student Loans Company are threatened following the workforce being notified last month that their roles are being outsourced to Capgemini by 1 March next year. Where outsourcing decisions appear to have been accelerated prior to PPN 024 coming into force, will my hon. Friend require in-scope bodies, like the Student Loans Company, to evidence that their decisions are compliant with the public interest test?

I thank my hon. Friend for his engagement on this subject. The insourcing unit is already working across the public sector to support contracting authorities and prepare for the introduction of our public interest test. I declare an interest: I was proud as a trade unionist to have fought for the public interest test, and I am proud as a Minister in this Government to deliver the public interest test. In addition, Departments will set out and publish their five-year insourcing strategies, but that is the start, not the end of our ambition. Delivering that insourcing will benefit those in his Falkirk constituency, my Gateshead Central and Whickham constituency and the constituencies of hon. Members throughout the House. On his specific question, all procurements are subject to a robust set of approvals and we have no evidence that Departments are accelerating any of their decision-making processes.

When considering insourcing, Northern Ireland must be very much part of the process. I hope the Minister will confirm that shortly, but will he ensure that Northern Ireland departments, wherever they may be, can be a part of the policy as we move forward, so that we, as part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, can benefit from the policy?

On devolved matters, we would encourage the Northern Ireland Assembly to take the same insourcing moves we seek to take as a Government. Where matters are not devolved, of course Northern Ireland will be fully involved in the process.

title: Peatland: Energy Infrastructure
turns: What assessment she has made of the potential impact of constructing energy infrastructure on peatland on the climate.

I pay tribute to my hon. Friend, who has been a champion for Yorkshire and for climate change mitigation and adaptation. We recognise that our peatlands are vital habitats for biodiversity, storing carbon and water. We have strong protections in national planning policy that guide developers to avoid peatland and, where that is not possible, to mitigate. We are working with the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs to strengthen and collaborate on both climate and nature policies.

We cannot strengthen one part of our climate response by weakening another. Peatland stores 50% of the country’s soil carbon—3 billion tonnes of the stuff. That is the equivalent of all the carbon stored by forests in the UK, Germany, and France combined. Building on peatland releases that carbon. That is why there are rules against doing so for development or farming. Will the Minister please look at cases of siting wind farms and other energy projects on peatland, so that there is consistency across the board?

My hon. Friend is right to highlight the hugely valuable role of peat in storing carbon and water, and in ensuring biodiversity. That is why the Government announced £47 million to restore our peatlands in June. As I said, there is national policy guidance, but we are working with DEFRA and Natural England to improve the interaction that he mentions. I will follow up with the Department to ensure that we are reviewing policy options, so that we deliver clean energy while protecting our natural environment. I am happy to keep him in the loop on that.
We do not have an abundance of peatland in east Kent, but we do have acres of wonderful marshland and sites of special scientific interest. On that land—[Interruption.]

Order. Mr Farron is shaking his head at me. There is some peatland in Kent, so there is a link to the question. I do not need any help, and you shaking your head so violently will not change Sir Roger’s question.

I am most grateful, Mr Speaker. Let me go back to the beginning: we do not have acres of peatland in east Kent, but we do have acres of wonderful marshland and sites of scientific interest. On that marshland, National Grid is proposing to build a 90-foot-high converter station the size of five football pitches, floated on concrete 2 metres deep. The Secretary of State is due to determine the planning application in short order. When she takes that decision, will she give an assurance that she will take into account the irreparable environmental damage that that ill-conceived project will do to the environment?
It sounds like the marshlands will be pushed on to the peatland.

Thank you for the clarification, Mr Speaker, and I thank the right hon. Member for his question. Everything we do has an environmental impact, but clearly we want to make sure that we minimise the environmental impact of any infrastructure that we build. I cannot comment on any individual planning application, as the right hon. Member will well know, but I take his wider point on looking to minimise, in all places, the environmental impacts of any of our clean energy infrastructure.

title: Topical Questions
turns: T1. If she will make a statement on her departmental responsibilities.
The Secretary of State for Transport

I am sure I speak for the whole House when I say that our thoughts are with those affected by yesterday’s horrific train crash in Spain. Our Rail Accident Investigation Branch has reached out to offer assistance, and I have written to my counterpart, Minister Puente, to formally offer my condolences. Yesterday’s Budget gave families the breathing space that they need, and transport is no exception. By extending the 5p fuel duty cut to July next year and lowering the cost of using local public electric vehicle chargers, we are putting money back in the pockets of Britain’s drivers. The Budget also confirmed a total investment of £300 million to upgrade Leeds station: breathing space today backed by investment for the future. This builds on the everyday fixes that we are already making to improve people’s journeys, whether that is the 7,000 miles of road resurfaced this year, the ending of unfair charges for air passengers, the cracking down on antisocial behaviour on public transport or the £2 bus fare cap coming back in January. Those are just some of the ways we are making everyday journeys better, safer and easier.

I associate myself with the Secretary of State’s remarks concerning the Spanish rail disaster. Research from Common Wealth estimates that £129 billion was spent on outsourcing public services in 2024-25, generating billions in private profits. I welcome the announcement from the First Secretary of State of a dedicated insourcing unit. Will the Secretary of State meet with recognised trade unions to develop a Department for Transport insourcing strategy, including across rail and other transport services, to improve value for money, rebuild public capacity and protect workers?

My hon. Friend is entirely right to raise the opportunity presented by the work being led by the First Secretary of State. I meet with the leadership of the trade unions regularly, and I know that this issue has already been raised at the Rail Engagement Group. Our lifting of the ban on new municipal bus companies in the Bus Services Act 2025 also presents opportunities. Where insourcing drives better outcomes for passengers and better value for the taxpayer, we should undoubtedly look at it.
I call the shadow Secretary of State.

I associate myself with the comments of the Secretary of State about the Spanish rail crash. On 18 June, the Secretary of State said in a statement that the Heathrow expansion is “critical to national growth”. On 27 September the Prime Minister said, however: “Principally, it’s a matter for London and Londoners”. And last week, in response to a written parliamentary question, the Under-Secretary of State for Transport, the hon. Member for Selby (Keir Mather), said that the Government will consider the Transport Committee’s recommendations before deciding next steps. Does she agree with herself, the Prime Minister or her junior Minister?

The Government’s position on Heathrow expansion was set out in the draft Heathrow expansion national policy statement that we consulted on in the summer. We are working through the responses to it very carefully. The right hon. Gentleman will know that this is a very significant, privately financed infrastructure project, and it is right that we look thoroughly at all the evidence, including the independent economic analysis and the really strict tests on climate, noise and air quality. It is entirely right that the Prime Minister wants to look closely at the detail of such a nationally significant project.

I thank the Secretary of State for that clarification. Last week, Chancellor Merz set out his plans to scrap the ban on petrol and diesel cars across the EU, saying, “We stand by drivers. We stand with our industry. We stand with open innovation in technology…the internal combustion ban is off the table.” When will this Transport Secretary listen to British business, the unions and British drivers and scrap the zero emission vehicle mandate that is costing British jobs and costing British taxpayers?

I say gently to the right hon. Gentleman that the ZEV mandate is the rarest of things: a policy brought in by his Government that I agree with. Sadly, after a good start, even they managed to mess that up. When we came into office, we had to reinstate the 2030 phase-out date for petrol and diesel cars. It is important that we provide certainty to consumers and industry. I believe that approach is working: nearly a third of new cars sold are electric vehicles, up from around a quarter a year ago.

T4. The recent announcement that 7 Steel will supply Heathrow expansion with low-carbon steel production will be essential both to decarbonise our transport infrastructure and to protect Welsh workers. What steps are the Government taking to ensure that lower-carbon Welsh steel is used in all major rail and transport infrastructure projects?
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Transport

Welsh steelmaking remains a key part of the UK Government’s steel strategy, with Wales expected to account for around half of future UK steelmaking capacity. We are committed to a sustainable UK steel sector and encourage the use of lower-carbon materials, recognising that electric arc furnace steel can provide a lower-carbon alternative in infrastructure projects across the country.

T2. Unlike my constituents, Mr Speaker, you are lucky enough not to have to suffer the weekly misery of South Western Railway. I surveyed my constituents recently and asked them what they wanted from the first nationalised rail service, now that we are paying for it. Their priorities were clear: they want more services from Liphook, more carriages at Haslemere, faster journeys from Farnham and any access at all from Whitehill and Bordon. Will the Minister commit to meeting me to get those four rather simple things done soon?

As the hon. Member has referenced, SWR is developing proposals for a refreshed timetable, which focuses on improving reliability and the resilience of services. Plans will be shared through public consultation with passengers and stakeholders later this year, and I encourage his constituents to contribute to that. In the meantime, I will ensure that I facilitate a meeting with the Rail Minister on the topic he raises.

T5. The Department is aware of my increasing frustration at balaclava-clad yobs tearing up and down on dirtbikes in Darlington. Indeed, the rest of the House is increasingly frustrated and we need action. Will the Minister and the Department commit to licensing or registration at the point of sale to aid the valiant effort of our police forces in the north-east?
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Transport

I commend my hon. Friend for her work in this area. She is right that these yobbos are causing misery for many communities. We are determined to see retailers cleaning up their act, and I am keen to explore how we tackle the issue. I am happy to meet my hon. Friend, through my cross-departmental ministerial group, to see how we can take the matter further.

T3. Harpenden Thameslink services are facing Luton airport expansion, the Bedford Universal studios development and 9,000 more houses coming down the line from this Government, following a local plan. All the while, passengers such as Emma are facing expensive, cramped and unreliable services. What are the Government doing to improve capacity, services and pricing?

GTR is working with Network Rail and local partners to explore potential timetable, rolling stock and infrastructure improvements to increase capacity through Harpenden. That follows long-term demand forecasting, which indicates continued passenger growth driven by planned housing development and the expansion of Luton airport, which the hon. Lady references. I will be glad to continue working with her to ensure we get the capacity improvements that we need over time to meet the needs of her constituents.

T6. Most of us in Monmouthshire have to rely on our cars for every single journey, so I am over the moon that, following meetings with National Express, it will bring services back to the Monmouth area next week, with coaches stopping at Raglan services, so passengers can travel from Haverfordwest to Birmingham. Will the Minister come with me on a journey on the coach so that he can see how important the route is for my constituents?
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Transport

I am delighted to join my hon. Friend in welcoming that new coach service to her constituency. This Government are supporting operators by extending the 5p fuel duty cut until next July. I will of course check my diary, but I encourage all hon. Members to get on and book their seat; there are nine castles and some fantastic countryside to visit.

T8. I think it is fair to say that there is disappointment on both sides of the House, following Wrexham, Shropshire and Midlands Railway’s open-access application being rejected because of concerns about capacity and reliability on the west coast main line. Is the Secretary of State confident that nationalising Avanti will result in the punctuality improvements and extra pathways needed to accommodate new services, which I hope can result in WSMR stopping at Aldridge railway station?

I share the right hon. Lady’s disappointment in the decision of the Office of Rail and Road. It can independently make that decision. My had supported the application for that new direct service, which would also have served places such as Shrewsbury. I will work with Network Rail, train operators and Great British Railways, when it is established, to consider all options for new direct services to London, as well as for that part of the route. Some of the investment coming in future years could enable that to happen, because I know how important that is to her constituents and other travellers in the region.

T7. As the Government prepare their taxi and private hire vehicle Bill, will the Minister ensure that local authorities such as Sunderland have the enforcement powers and resources that they need to regulate all vehicles operating in their area, regardless of where those vehicles are registered?

I fully recognise my hon. Friend’s concerns. Taxis and private hire vehicles are regulated through an outdated and fragmented framework, and this Government intend to bring forward a draft Bill to address that. My officials are also working hard to commence the powers from the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 that will let enforcement officers suspend any licence used in their area if there are immediate safety concerns.

My constituents have suffered delays, cancellations, and trains that are meant to go from London to Ely or King’s Lynn terminating early at Cambridge. Will the Secretary of State meet me to discuss how we can take forward the Ely junction improvements, which will increase capacity and make our railway more reliable?

We of course recognise the strategic importance of the Ely area capacity enhancement programme, and the significant benefits that it could deliver for passengers, freight and economic growth, both in the hon. Lady’s constituency and across the region. We will actively consider this scheme as further funding opportunities become available, and I will do my level best to ensure that she is involved in those conversations.

T9. A second runway at Gatwick airport will be a lightning rod for our economy. It will bring £1 billion in economic benefits and 14,000 new jobs, many of which will benefit the south Londoners I serve. Now that it has the green light and work is about to begin, what support are the Government giving this important infrastructure project?

The Government recognise the importance of this project, which is why we approved the development consent order. It is now for Gatwick airport to progress with this privately funded project. My officials continue to engage with the airport to understand how Government can help with the project’s delivery, and I encourage my hon. Friend to continue to work with me on how we can best support that process.

In May, the Government announced £57 million in nationwide funding for wi-fi on trains. Some other parts of the country have had many rail upgrades, but the south-west has terrible rail lines, and delays due to the High Speed 2 works at Old Oak Common. Will the Minister commit to a minimum fair share of £12 million for the south-west, to cover the entire Great Western Railway network of 93 inter-city express trains?

The fact that Great Western Railways will come into public ownership on 13 December presents an opportunity. The hon. Gentleman talks about the importance of wi-fi; I hope to have more to say on that in the months ahead, because I know how important good connectivity is for people who use our railways.

T10. The extension of the fuel duty cut to July 2027 will be welcomed by my Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes constituents, many of whom rely on their cars for work purposes. What more are the Government doing to help reduce the cost of motoring for those who use their vehicles for work purposes?

My hon. Friend is completely right to raise the subject of the pressures that motorists and businesses face. In addition to the extension of the temporary 5p cut to fuel duty, we are also maintaining the road tax holiday for heavy goods vehicles until summer next year. We are making public charging cheaper for those who have already made the switch to an electric vehicle, but do not have a driveway to charge at home, and we continue to offer money off the purchase price of more than 60 models of electric car.

The village of Isham in my constituency is sandwiched between Wellingborough and Kettering, and for 40 years it has been battling to get a bypass. The situation has now got worse because of a huge development of warehousing, yet the bypass has been refused funding. May I invite the Minister to Isham, where I would give him a warm welcome? It is only when people see it for themselves that they can understand how desperately we need this bypass.

I am happy to do that; I think it would probably be on my way home one weekend. We have invested a record amount of money in our networks, and there is only a finite amount, but I am happy to discuss the issue further with the right hon. Member.

This month, there has been a series of serious road accidents in Bracknell, Warfield and Crowthorne in my constituency. In one incident, a young man, Shayan, very tragically lost his life at the scene. Will the roads Minister meet me to discuss these incidents, and listen to Shayan’s family’s plea for more action on road safety?

First, can I extend my sympathies to Shayan’s family? I am happy to meet them. I commend my predecessor, my hon. Friend the Member for Nottingham South (Lilian Greenwood), on the excellent work she did on the road safety strategy, on which I am privileged to be able to build. Part of that will be engaging with bereaved families.

Greedy corporate interests have stripped out more than £200 million from our Isle of Wight ferry services in the past 10 years. I am grateful to the Minister for setting up local roundtable meetings, but they are at risk of becoming a talking shop, and the ferry companies do not appear to be taking them seriously. Can he give us an assurance locally that if the ferry companies do not take this opportunity to improve services and reduce prices, the Government will consider taking steps to force their hand?

The hon. Member is determined to achieve better ferry services for his constituents, and I am pleased that he reflects on the cross-Solent group, the work it has done and the progress it is making. I am keeping a close watch on its proceedings. I expect all its members to contribute in meaningful ways to find practical, local solutions to these challenges, and we will of course keep options under advisement. For ferry services, the Government believe that locally led solutions are often best in matters such as the one that he describes.
Cowbar Lane in my constituency is at serious risk of collapse into the sea. We have a plan in place for relocating it and making it safe. Will Ministers meet me to discuss it?

We recognise the impact of coastal erosion on Cowbar Lane, and we aware of the plans set out by Redcar and Cleveland council to move the road further inland. The Government have already provided more than £300 million of city region sustainable transport settlement funding to the Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen to deliver on that, but we are clearly not seeing anything happening on the ground. I am happy to meet my hon. Friend to see what more we can do to encourage the mayor to deliver on this issue.

Residents of Holton Heath and Sandford are being blighted every weekend by racing vehicles, motorcycles and modified small cars causing nuisance and loud noises. What progress is being made on the acoustic devices that enable police to act on these illegal vehicles?

I am sorry to hear that the hon. Lady’s constituents are having to endure these issues. There have been a number of trials, which have found that it is not that straightforward to isolate the noise. Police forces have powers to tackle this issue, and I am happy to write to her with further information about what they can do.

The A259 coast road runs the entire southern length of my constituency, but daily delays on it are a huge frustration, particularly for constituents in Rottingdean, Telscombe and Saltdean. What more can the Minister do to unlock long-promised upgrades to this road, and to finally get Reform-led East Sussex county council to put in the funding and focus needed to get those upgrades over the line?

The Department recognises the importance of that particular road, and we are ready to crack on with this. I join my hon. Friend in encouraging the Reform-led county council to release the funding necessary and get on with the job.

My constituents are not demanding a multibillion-pound, high-speed answer to the five-and-a-half-hour journey time from Penzance to London, for example; they want just a fraction of that amount, to improve the comfort, reliability and punctuality of the service. My hon. Friend the Member for North Cornwall (Ben Maguire) mentioned that £57 million has been allocated for wi-fi on trains. That is a fraction of the money spent on high speed policies. We understand that the money is being held by the Treasury at the moment; when will it be rolled out? It is desperately needed now.

As I said to the hon. Member for North Cornwall (Ben Maguire), we are very keen to make progress on better wi-fi connectivity on Great Western services, and I hope to say more on that in the coming months.
I call the Chair of the Transport Committee.

First, may I associate myself with the condolences expressed by the Transport Secretary and others about the terrible tragedy in Spain yesterday? There are many bottlenecks on the national rail system that are holding back rail freight growth. I welcome the Government’s announcement of the interim rail freight growth target of 40% by 2040, but without a clear and deliverable strategy, the Government risk falling behind on the expansion of rail freight, which is such an important sector for us all. When will we see a rail freight growth strategy, or will we have to wait for the overall rail enhancement strategy?

The Chair of the Transport Committee is completely right to highlight the need to increase the amount of freight that we transport by rail. That is why we have set a target of growing rail freight by 75% by 2050, and an interim target of 40% by 2040. We are not publishing a separate rail freight strategy, as I will put that target in the long-term rail strategy when it is published, and I expect Great British Railways to set out in its first business plan how it will achieve that.

Earlier this week, the all-party parliamentary group on rail had presentations from representatives about access to both airports and seaports. They made the suggestion that modest electrification projects linking seaports such as Immingham to the main line would greatly improve rail freight distribution. Do the Government have plans for such schemes?

It was a pleasure to visit the port of Immingham a few months ago. Rail connectivity to our ports, encouraging modal shift, and electrification’s role in increasing the efficiency of the growth in the amount of freight taken to our seaports are of real personal interest to me. I will therefore happily take this conversation forward with the hon. Member and think about how we can facilitate better connectivity to our ports through electrification of our railways.

Meur ras ha myttin da, Mr Speaker. I declare an interest as the chair of the electric vehicle APPG. After more record EV sales, the Government’s consultation on the zero-emission vehicles mandate closed last Friday. The mandate affects only 8% of all registrations of new cars manufactured in the UK. Has the consultation considered the billions of pounds in private sector investment in domestic lithium extraction, battery manufacturing and charge point infrastructure?

I can assure my hon. Friend that we look at these issues in the round. He mentions charge point infrastructure. Only this week, I had a roundtable with the main operators of charge point infrastructure, as well as a meeting with the car manufacturers. We have held a review of the ZEV mandate, on which we consulted this summer. The Chancellor has set out the Government’s intention to respond to that by Christmas, so that we can provide certainty to everyone who is contributing to the EV transition.

The decision in July to abandon plans for changes to the remuneration of coastguards was widely welcomed, but that was over three months ago. Coastguards around the coastline tell me that there has been radio silence in the Maritime and Coastguard Agency since then. There are a number of whistleblowing complaints about the senior executive team that have simply not been addressed. When will we hear what the Government will do to fix our coastguards?

I thank the right hon. Member for his work in representing the coastguard service in his constituency and across the country. I reassure him that work progressed over the summer both on questions relating to backdated liabilities and on future workforce arrangements as they apply to His Majesty’s Coastguard. I hope to have more to say in the future, but I will maintain my obligation to keep him and hon. Members across the House updated as closely as I can on developments as they unfold.

Not a single rail service has run from Clitheroe on a Sunday for a very long time. I know that the Secretary of State and her team of Ministers have heard many representations from me on this issue, but can they reassure me that they are doing everything they can to get those Sunday services back up and running?

I agree with my hon. Friend that his constituents are right to expect a good service every day of the week, including Sundays. I assure him that the management of Northern is around the table with the RMT to work together on a way forward, and I hope to be able to say more soon.

Community transport minibuses, such as Mendip Community Transport, are a lifeline for rural communities, but the minibus driving test is costly—it costs up to £2,000 per volunteer—hard to access and pretty unrealistic for volunteers, and drivers who qualified before 1997, and therefore have the D1 classification on their driving licence, are retiring. Will the Minister meet me and representatives of the industry, and recognise officially the sector’s own minibus driver awareness scheme as a route for car drivers to gain a minibus licence?

The Government recognise the vital role that community transport plays in connecting people with communities, enabling access to employment, education and essential services such as healthcare. I am happy to meet the hon. Lady.

The last train from London to Newcastle tonight is at 11.08 pm, but the last train from London to Carlisle is at 7.30 pm. Now that the experiment with train privatisation is coming to an end, is it possibly time for a new experiment where the west coast gets the same level of service as the east coast?

Avanti West Coast is due to come into public ownership in March next year, and there is an opportunity to look again at the timetable over the course of the next few years. I recognise the importance of later services going direct to my hon. Friend’s constituency as well as to constituencies on the other side of the country.

The derailment in the summer between Haywards Heath and Lewes caused great concern to my constituents. It happened during a period of very hot, dry weather that caused the ground to dry out and crack. I understand that Network Rail is looking at ways to change how it maintains embankments and cuttings, but there was no money in yesterday’s Budget for railway services in the south-east. Do the Government have a plan to ensure that our services are punctual and safe?

I completely understand why that incident will have been of huge concern to the hon. Member’s constituents. In this control period, we are spending over £2.5 billion on the railways to address climate change mitigation and adaptation. We are awaiting the final report of the Rail Accident Investigation Branch as to the causes of that incident. Network Rail took immediate steps to increase inspections across the network to ensure safety, and the events in Spain yesterday serve as a reminder of why safety must always be paramount on our railways.

Consideration of eastern access at Hitchin station has been stalled for far too long. I am delighted that, having worked with Ministers and our councils, we have finally been able to get it moving forward, and yesterday’s announcement of £5.6 million in new growth funding for Hertfordshire provides a fantastic opportunity to go further and finally make it happen. Will Ministers meet me to discuss how we can lobby Hertfordshire county council to make the most of this opportunity for my town?
In the interests of speed, yes.

Aura Mobility is a company in Falkirk that designs assistive mobility products for disabled people. It and its customers need certainty that any reforms to light zero emission vehicles regulation will protect access to pavements and roads, not reduce it. Six months after the consultation on powered mobility devices closed, when will the Government provide that certainty and publish their response?
I am grateful to Aura Mobility for engaging with the Department’s consultation, which we will respond to very shortly.

I am aware that the Secretary of State has already answered two questions about Peninsula Transport’s fantastic wi-fi pilot on GWR trains, but if we are to go ahead with rolling it out for nationalisation on 13 December, I gently ask whether there is a way to nudge the Treasury to make that money available.

My hon. Friend has been a tireless campaigner on this issue, and I know that she depends on GWR services, as do I in my constituency. Having good mobile connectivity is something that people feel strongly about, and it could improve satisfaction with journeys. I will continue my discussions with colleagues across Government to make that happen.

title: Local Policing
turns: What steps her Department is taking to support the provision of local policing.
The Minister for Policing and Crime
Our police reform plans will embed highly localised policing. We have already delivered 3,800 extra neighbourhood police to our communities, and in Avon and Somerset we have delivered 71 since 2025.

In recent years shoplifting has become an increasing issue for many of the high streets in my constituency, and our shop workers are having to deal with increasingly frightening and dangerous situations. In the light of that, we look forward to seeing meaningful progress towards the Government’s ambitious targets for the expansion of neighbourhood policing. What practical steps are the Government taking to boost local police numbers and neighbourhood policing in the Bristol area?

As I have said, neighbourhood police numbers in Avon and Somerset have risen by 71 since 2025. We are also introducing a raft of measures to deal with shop theft, such as the removal of the £200 threshold, and investment in new technology to help the police and retailers to work together so that crime can be reported and people can then be charged. There has been huge progress in many parts of the country where retailers and police are working together. During the two years in the run-up to the general election, shop theft went up by 60%, but it is now on the turn, falling by 2% this year. We are making progress with those extra police, but there is still a great deal more to do.

West Mercia police have changed the hours of police community support officers, introducing an 8 pm finish in order to save money. Unsurprisingly, that has led to an increase in antisocial behaviour in my constituency after 8 pm. The police are very thin on the ground: Ellesmere’s safer neighbourhood team consists of one police officer—who I do not think works 24/7—and just two PCSOs. Our officers and PCSOs do a fantastic job, but they are far too thinly spread. Will the Minister meet me so that she can understand the challenges facing rural policing and the resources that are required in places such as Shropshire?

We are delivering more neighbourhood police to our communities, and we are encouraging the police to use data as much as they can to determine where they go, which means that, as often as possible, they go to the areas where crime is occurring. The purpose of our police reforms is to answer some of the challenges that the hon. Lady has raised. At present we have 43 forces who are having to look up towards serious and organised crime, international and national fraud and online crime, and having to look down towards their local communities, and they are doing neither very well at the moment.

title: Oil and Gas Sector: Jobs
turns: What discussions he has had with Cabinet colleagues on support for jobs in the oil and gas sector in Scotland.
What discussions he has had with Cabinet colleagues on levels of employment in the oil and gas sector in Scotland.
What discussions he has had with Cabinet colleagues on levels of employment in the oil and gas sector in Scotland.
What discussions he has had with Cabinet colleagues on levels of employment in the oil and gas sector in Scotland.
The Secretary of State for Scotland

As shown by our decision last week to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, the United Kingdom Government are committed to a pragmatic approach to the North sea. We recognise that domestic oil and gas will continue to play an important part in our energy mix for decades to come.

In 2024 the Scottish oil and gas industry supported 118,000 direct and indirect jobs, and after much dither and delay, thankfully the Government have approved Jackdaw, which will safeguard jobs that otherwise would have been lost, and create more. The Government need to do more to support Scottish oil and gas, so what steps is the Secretary of State taking?

Conservative Members are experts in dither and delay, and over the decade preceding July 2024 and the election of the Labour Government, alas 70,000 jobs were lost. Of course, we hit peak production in the North sea more than 20 years ago. That is why we need a credible plan for transition, and that is what we are putting in place.

The Government are accelerating the decline of an industry that supports thousands of jobs across Scotland, while promising replacement jobs that are not materialising quickly enough. Scotland’s oil and gas workers are paying the price for the Government’s ideological opposition to the oil and gas sector. Will the Secretary of State confirm now whether he supports Labour’s ban on new licences?

There is a certain irony in the Conservative party lecturing the Government on deindustrialisation in Scotland. In reality, it left an energy system in 2024 that was less secure, more exposed to international shocks, and slower to invest. The hon. Lady’s question might have more credibility had we not agreed Jackdaw just last week.

The Government spent two and a half years virtue signalling about the North sea. They said there was no future for oil and gas and had a ban on licences, as well as increasing taxation. The result has been 25,000 job losses—1,000 every month and counting—not because of an external shock, but because of a crisis 100% caused by Government policy. When will this Government leave their student politics behind, back British business and get us drilling again?

The Conservative party’s policy towards the North sea was a study in incompetence. The reason we took the decision on Jackdaw last week was that the Conservative Government so messed up the process that we ended up in court.

For many of my constituents in rural Stirling and Strathallan, energy security also means being able to afford the heating oil they rely on to live and to run businesses from home. What discussions has the Secretary of State had with Cabinet colleagues about ensuring that support for jobs in the oil and gas sector is mindful of the need to deliver the affordable and secure energy that many rural homes and jobs rely on?

The point that my hon. Friend makes is well taken. The supply chain supporting oil and gas, and the energy sector more generally, is not limited to the north-east but stretches right across Scotland, including in his Stirling constituency. I hope that he will listen with interest to the words of the Chancellor in just a few minutes’ time.

It is fair to say that there was a muted response from the First Minister at the good news from the UK Government on Jackdaw. Will the Secretary of State help to inspire and animate Mr Swinney by telling him more about the new energy wealth fund and how it will support jobs in Scotland?

The SNP-led Government in Edinburgh are not short of opinions on anything, apart from their view on the Jackdaw decision that we reached last week. The First Minister opposed the decision in recent months and the former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon said that she wanted the “fastest possible just transition” away from oil and gas in the North sea—the SNP seems to have more positions than she has coffee machines.

I commend the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero for the decision to approve Jackdaw. It takes courage to lead, and the same logic applies to Rosebank. Does the Secretary of State agree that the £2 billion fund set up to transfer jobs from oil, gas and carbon into renewables sends a signal to workers that we are with them in the North sea, today and for years to come?

My hon. Friend speaks with great authority because a number of North sea workers are based in the Western Isles. For many years, people have argued for the establishment of an energy wealth fund. Alas, we did not get much gratitude from the party in power in Edinburgh that failed to deliver a publicly owned energy company, and we have now delivered this energy wealth fund.

Last week, the Government finally approved Jackdaw. The Secretary of State called that “a win for Aberdeen, a win for Scottish workers and a win for Britain’s energy security.” But there can be many more wins: Rosebank and other fields can also protect jobs and supply chains, secure investment and tax returns, and boost our energy security. Based on his own logic from last week, will he confirm that he fully supports approving Rosebank and ending Labour’s ban on new licensing?

The shadow Ministers are like the Bourbons: they have forgotten nothing and learned nothing. The reason we took the decision about Jackdaw last week and the reason that I am appropriately cautious in relation to Rosebank, is that there is a process that needs to be followed, following the evidence and reaching a determination. Alas, that was not a process that the Conservatives chose to follow.

Oil and gas workers are fed up with the Government skirting around this. Some 25,000 linked oil and gas jobs have been lost since the general election. The Government know that new fields support jobs—they said that last week—and they know that UK production supports UK businesses. Last month, they signed off on new oil in the Falklands, but are too squeamish to do it in UK waters. The Secretary of State knows more is needed. When are the Government going to wake up to the damage they are doing to our crucial oil and gas industry?
I get the impression that that question was drafted before the Jackdaw decision was issued just last week.

title: Welfare Budget
turns: What estimate he has made of what the total welfare budget will be at the end of this Parliament.
The Minister for Social Security and Disability

In March, the Office for Budget Responsibility published its official forecast, predicting that at the end of the current Parliament, in 2029-30, UK welfare spending will be about £390 billion. The OBR will update that forecast in the Budget, which will take place on Wednesday fortnight.

The Minister has just confirmed that the benefits bill will continue to grow. He also seems to have confirmed the Prime Minister’s position that national security “cannot come at the expense of social security.”—[Official Report, 9 September 2026; Vol. 790, c. 1036.] Is that correct?

The hon. Member will be relieved to know that spending on working-age adults’ and children’s welfare is forecast to be 4.9% of GDP at the end of the current Parliament, as it is now. Overall welfare spending is forecast to rise by less than half as much in this Parliament as in the last, by just over 0.3 percentage points by 2030-31 compared with 0.7 percentage points in the last Parliament. This Government are putting right the problems that they inherited.

According to a recent report from the Good Growth Foundation, 50% of disability claimants would swap up to £1,000 of benefits for help such as employment support, therapy and physical aids. Does the Minister agree that giving disabled people tailored support could both reduce the welfare bill and stop those who want to work being written off by the system?

I do agree with my hon. Friend, and, as she has said, we inherited a system that wrote people off. We are pleased with the early results emerging from our Connect to Work programme, which is providing exactly that kind of tailored support for disabled people and others faced with complex barriers to work. We recently published the second set of quarterly outcome statistics, and the news is very encouraging.

The number of children between the ages of six and 11 with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder has grown sixfold, which means that in the years ahead there will be a surge in the number of applications for personal independence payment as children become adults. Even the Secretary of State accepts that owing to the growing number of children receiving disability living allowance, most will be transferred to PIP. Does the Minister agree that it is time to end a cash payments benefit system for people with more minor conditions, and ensure that those with genuine needs receive the therapeutic support that will enable them to learn, work and contribute to the economy?

The hon. Gentleman will have seen Professor Peter Fonagy’s recent report about the incidence of ADHD, autism and other conditions. He will also know that I am co-chairing a review of PIP which is looking into how we can ensure that the system meets the very real needs of many disabled people, and that the benefit is on a sustainable financial footing for the future. The report of my review will be published before the end of the year.

title: SEND Services:  Joint Commissioning Statutory Requirement
turns: What discussions she has had with Cabinet colleagues on introducing a statutory requirement for local authorities and integrated care boards to jointly commission SEND services.

Joint commissioning between local authorities and integrated care boards is key to the successful delivery of special educational needs and disabilities services. I recently met the Minister for Social Care and Mental Health to discuss strengthening the role of health partners across the SEND system, and we are committed to achieving that.

It is so important that partners jointly commission services such as speech and language therapy. However, despite the requirements set out in the Children and Families Act 2014, families tell me that joint commissioning is often inconsistent and insufficient to meet need, and that they often feel like they are being passed from pillar to post. Will the Minister therefore introduce a stronger statutory requirement for local areas to jointly commission services for young people with SEND issues across universal, targeted and specialist layers of support?

My hon. Friend is right: it is essential that we have greater integration between health, social care and education. That is why we are putting £1.8 billion into Experts at Hand. That is about the joint commissioning of speech and language therapists, educational psychologists, occupational therapists and other specialist support, but he is absolutely right that we need to strengthen joint commissioning, and we will set out more on that in due course.

Like the constituents of the hon. Member for Stoke-on-Trent North (David Williams), Guildford families tell me that their children with SEND can end up with fragmented care, and that parents are left with no co-ordination between health and education. As the Surrey SEND reforms are implemented, and the new West Surrey council prepares to take on responsibilities following the local government reorganisation, how will the Government ensure that joint commissioning leads to earlier support and better outcomes for children, with clear accountability when those outcomes are not achieved?

That is exactly why we are putting the new investment into the system, including £4 billion into early intervention. Through the SEND reform plans, we are asking ICBs and local authorities to come together with clear plans for implementation. In the new system, we are proposing national inclusion standards that set out really clearly our expectations on early intervention, and new duties for schools to recognise need and put in place individual support plans. It is so important that we are wrapping that wider support around schools. Families should not have to fight for it; it should just be available.

title: Waste Crime
turns: What steps she is taking to help tackle waste crime.
The Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs

Waste crime is fuelled by serious organised crime, and it is blighting our communities. We are tackling it: since April, we have made 21 arrests and shut down 339 illegal waste sites. Police operations have triggered more than 30 criminal investigations, and we are strengthening enforcement and disrupting those who are profiting from waste crime.

Illegal waste dumping at the Simonswood industrial estate in my constituency has long blighted the residents in West Lancashire and Kirkby. My right hon. Friend the Member for Knowsley (Anneliese Midgley) and I have worked together on tackling the Simonswood stink, and we welcomed the Environment Agency’s permit revocation earlier this year, but the mound remains, as do the odour and dust. What assurances can the Government give that Simonswood will be considered in the next phase of the illegal waste site clearance scheme?

I know how tirelessly my hon. Friend and her neighbour, my right hon. Friend the Member for Knowsley, have campaigned on this issue. Waste crime blights local communities, and the Government are committed to tackling it. The Environment Agency continues to investigate activity at Simonswood, and the site will be considered for clearance alongside other illegal waste sites.

Waste crime and fly-tipping are a blight on rural communities and, as the Secretary of State said, are increasingly linked to organised crime, so I commend Ministers for building on the work of the previous Government to increase penalties, tighten up restrictions on carriers and speed up the digital tracking of waste. Communities play their part, too, so will the Secretary of State join me in praising the work of the Wombles of Hambleton, whose volunteers do an excellent job of organising monthly litter picks, collecting hundreds of bags of rubbish and ensuring that North Yorkshire remains the most beautiful part of the country?

As a Yorkshirewoman myself, I will not disagree about the beauty of Yorkshire, though it might get me into trouble. I am happy to join the right hon. Member in praising the Wombles of Hambleton. I need him to show me a photograph of them out doing this job next time we bump into each other. Many community-organised litter picks and clean-ups are going on in all our communities, including one at Seacombe in my own constituency a couple of weekends ago. Much litter is picked up, but we have a lot of work to do to persuade people to be more responsible by not dropping it in the first place.

title: Strengthening the Union
turns: What steps he is taking with Cabinet colleagues to strengthen Wales’s place in the Union.
The Secretary of State for Wales

Whether it is through Wales’s role in bolstering the UK’s defence and steel production, or leading the way in industries such as compound semiconductors and the life sciences, our Union of nations is hugely strengthened by Wales. We cannot put a ceiling on the awesome talent and ambition of the Welsh people, and I simply cannot understand why Plaid Cymru is hellbent on doing so.

I was shocked to see the front page of the Western Mail last week, which said: “Free milk scheme for pupils could be scrapped”. I thought we had gone back in time to the infamous milk snatcher, Margaret Thatcher, but no, it was the modern-day Plaid Cymru Welsh Government. Does the Secretary of State agree with me that scrapping free school milk would be a backward step, and will he commit to working with Cabinet colleagues to ensure that the Union means more opportunities for our children in Wales, not fewer?

Well, I have to say that when Plaid won in May, I did not have Thatcherism 2.0 on my bingo card. First, Plaid dragged its feet on additional learning needs funding; then it refused to commit to Flying Start; and now it may be targeting free school milk. My hon. Friend is right: the Plaid Welsh Government should be supporting children and families, just as this UK Labour Government have by scrapping the two-child cap, which will be hugely beneficial for nearly 70,000 Welsh children.

One would hope that any Union would be a Union of equals, in which equal partners listen to each other with mutual respect. May I respectfully ask the Secretary of State to check his facts, as he has asked Plaid Members to check theirs? Can he confirm that the UK Government have listened to the Welsh Government on the Cynnal child payment pilot? Will he ensure that His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs will not count this payment as income, so that families do not lose out on the other benefit support that they need?

We have a shared priority with devolved Governments to tackle child poverty, so that no child living in poverty in the UK is left behind. Child poverty is a significant challenge, and reducing it over the next 10 years will require ongoing commitment and collaboration, particularly through the implementation phase. We are open to exploring the Welsh Government’s Cynnal pilot and we will continue to engage with them on the details.

title: Gaza: Humanitarian Situation
turns: The Minister of State, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office

With permission, I would like to make a statement on the humanitarian situation in Gaza and the wider region. With Gaza entering its fourth winter of conflict, last weekend’s heavy rain and strong winds have made the intolerable humanitarian situation even worse for Palestinian civilians. Like so many others, I was horrified by the scenes. Flooding has damaged displacement sites, tents and buildings, including hospitals and schools. According to our humanitarian partners on the ground, more than 152,000 people have been affected, with over 6,000 shelters destroyed, 17,400 damaged and nearly 4,000 households left without shelter. Three children and their mother were killed when a sand embankment collapsed on their tents. The cumulative impact, as well as the immediate impact, is appalling. For more than three years, families have lost loved ones, homes and livelihoods, and many have had to move again and again in search of safety. Meanwhile, civilian deaths continue, with more than 1,600 killed since the so-called ceasefire alone, and Gazans have been kettled into around 30% of their territory. The reality on the ground is heartbreaking, yet we knew this was coming. The UN and non-governmental organisations have raised the alarm for months. Donors, including ourselves, geared up for it and put in support for aid agencies ahead of time, but restrictions on access to vital supplies and machinery have hampered preparations for winter. According to the UN, over 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins that humanitarian partners and donors purchased are outside Gaza, ready to go in, yet the Israeli authorities have prevented these items from entering. They also continue to block timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza. This is shameful. The problem is not simply whether the international community can provide help; it is whether that help can reach the people who need it. I have a very simple and direct message to the Israeli authorities: let the aid in. This is only the first storm of winter, and there will be more. The UN has said that new tents alone will not protect people from flooding. Gaza urgently needs machinery and tools for drainage and rubble removal, and this is unilaterally in the Government of Israel’s control. As the occupying power, there are strict legal obligations that Israel must obey. We have repeatedly pressed it to prepare for winter and to allow humanitarian aid into Gaza, in line with international law. At the UN General Assembly, the UK brought international partners together behind a call to action on humanitarian access and healthcare. Today, again in New York, we will bring together multiple international partners once again to reinforce that pressure. Our immediate asks of the Government of Israel are clear: open crossing points, starting with Erez in northern Gaza; allow additional days for dual-use items to enter; and reduce the list of those items, so that vital medicines, medical equipment, and materials for tents and shelter can reach the people who need them. I saw with my own eyes items for which I could see no reasonable ground for refusing entry. The Israeli Government must also allow access for journalists, diplomats and Foreign Ministers, so that the world can see the scale of what is happening. I am shocked by reports overnight that an Israeli airstrike on the Nasser hospital in southern Gaza has killed at least six people. So many healthcare workers and humanitarians have lost their lives and faced peril trying to alleviate suffering in Gaza. I am thinking in particular of those, including the brave British nationals, who lost their lives in the World Central Kitchen attack. In recent months, officials at the British embassy in Tel Aviv have pressed the Israeli authorities to take the action needed to prepare Gaza for winter. On Monday, officials again met those at the Israeli embassy in London to reinforce the urgent need for action. We call on all parties to the conflict to allow aid to enter Gaza and get to the people who need it. I am sorry to say that in recent weeks, the flow of aid and essential goods into Gaza has been repeatedly disrupted. Commercial deliveries were temporarily suspended in September following reports of Hamas taxation. On 3 November, the Israeli authorities closed the Egypt corridor for six days over allegations of smuggling, cutting off an essential lifeline to Gazans. I have been to the Egypt warehouses myself and seen the stockpiles of essential aid waiting to get in. The UN chief for humanitarian affairs, Tom Fletcher, and other international counterparts have said that there is no excuse for this. The law is clear that civilians should get the aid they need and should not be punished, and that that should not be subject to political negotiations. The UK Government will not stand by, but will keep working with our partners to press for the restrictions to be lifted. I am proud that our Government and our support have already made a difference. We provided UNICEF with £14 million this year to support nutrition, child protection, health, water and sanitation, and preparation for winter, but we must do more. Today, I can announce that we are releasing a further £5 million from our bilateral budget to UNICEF, which will be focused on the winter response, including the impact of flooding over the weekend. Overall, UK support will make a tangible difference to the people of Gaza, aiming to provide winter clothing for 100,000 children, tarpaulins for 62,500 people, family tents for 1,250 households and blankets for 150,000 people. Last month, the Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs’ pooled fund, to which the UK is a significant contributor, provided $45 million for winter supplies, and when the flooding hit, OCHA was able to respond quickly and help families in displacement sites. Through our £88 million of humanitarian funding this financial year, we expect to provide healthcare for up to 900,000 people, safe water for 150,000 people, and rehabilitation and prosthetic care for 1,000 children with blast injuries. At the G7 this week, the Foreign Secretary was clear that Israel must ensure humanitarian access, humane treatment and basic welfare for civilians in Gaza. So we are acting, and we will continue to act, to alleviate the suffering. Let me repeat that we recognise Israel’s legitimate security concerns and of course condemn Hamas’s 7 October terrorist attack, the worst antisemitic massacre since the Holocaust. I stood in resolute solidarity with Israelis and Jews at the memorial event and exhibition organised with the Israeli embassy just a few weeks ago. Let me also be clear that the United Kingdom remains committed—fully committed—to resolution 2803 and the 20-point peace plan. We are resolute and clear that Hamas must decommission their weapons, dismantle their terrorist infrastructure and relinquish control of Gaza. Ultimately, we need a lasting answer to this conflict. Our north star remains the two-state solution as the only route to lasting peace, security and prosperity for Israelis and Palestinians. With your permission, Madam Deputy Speaker, let me add that while Gaza is rightly the immediate focus of my statement, it is not the only humanitarian crisis in the region that demands our attention. I want to say something about the appalling situation in Yemen, which is compounding the years of suffering, death and destruction faced by Yemenis. The Houthis’ decision to resume conflict has worsened an already desperate humanitarian situation. Since August, more than 330,000 people have fled their homes, there have been more than 1,000 civilian casualties and hundreds have been killed. The situation is particularly acute in Taiz, where the continued Houthi siege restricts the movement of people, aid and essential goods. Women and children are particularly vulnerable as supplies run low, and healthcare services have been drastically reduced. The recruitment and use of children in the conflict, widespread displacement and food insecurity are causing further suffering. In recent weeks, I have met senior representatives of the Government of Yemen, and listened directly to humanitarians working on the frontline. We cannot turn away, and donors and the world cannot turn away, in the face of such appalling suffering. We need to do more. I am also appalled by the continued detention of UN workers, and the deaths we have seen. I reiterate that international humanitarian law must be upheld by all. We are providing £104 million in humanitarian support to Yemen, including the recently announced £10 million to the UN’s emergency fund. We will continue to work with the Government of Yemen and other partners to protect and support civilians and return to a political process. Finally, I want to update the House on sanctions, which I know are a matter of keen interest. In September, the Foreign Secretary announced further action in relation to Gaza and the west bank, including a new sanctions regime targeting illegal settlement activity.
