It was an incredible privilege to bring HMS Vengeance home on Sunday. I attended the submarine with the Defence Secretary, and it was an extraordinary honour to welcome the crew home after their unfortunate record-breaking tour at sea—they have made an incredible sacrifice for the defence of our nation, and indeed the whole of NATO. As the Defence Secretary and the Chancellor have repeatedly set out, we are committed to reaching 3% of GDP on defence spending by 2030 and to all of our NATO commitments.

T2. Last month, I was proud to join my constituent Ness Abbess as she delivered to No. 10 a letter from bereaved families on the issue of preventable drownings. I welcome the Prime Minister’s response to that letter and his support for the Daily Mirror’s drowning prevention campaign, but the issue is that water safety sits between four different Government Departments. Will the First Secretary of State use her powers to bring those Departments together? Will she consider appointing a single Minister to drive this work forward, and will she meet me and bereaved families so that we can discuss the vital next steps to save lives?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for raising that important point in the way that he has. Like the Prime Minister, I warmly welcome the Save Lives at Sea campaign. I assure him that the Government take water safety very seriously, as was demonstrated by the recent roundtable chaired by the Minister with responsibility for water and flooding, my hon. Friend the Member for Kingston upon Hull West and Haltemprice (Emma Hardy). I have listened carefully to his point about deconflicting across Government Departments. I will reflect on it and come back to him with more detail.
I call the shadow Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster.

The Government’s sanitary and phytosanitary deal with the European Union will require UK farmers to take on thousands upon thousands of EU regulations, even if they do not trade with the EU. Have the Government estimated the dead cost of dynamic alignment for those farmers?
The Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations

I look forward to discussing the fine detail once we have an agreement over the line in the way that I hope we will tomorrow. On SPS, it is important to recognise that the previous Conservative Government, and indeed our Government, have not diverged a great deal from European food safety standards. Where we have, we have obviously made careful assessments of the impact on farmers.

The right hon. Gentleman will be aware that since we left the EU, it has gone through one of its most profound periods of regulation. There are now tens of thousands of regulations that the UK has never signed up to—that will be an additional burden. If he has done that work on the dead cost, will he publish it so that the House can consider it?

The hon. Gentleman is right to say both that we have assessed where we have chosen to diverge, and of course that there are areas where the EU has changed regulation without our being part of that process of change. I think his question was about farmers. We are, of course, in regular dialogue with farmers about the impact. It is quite difficult to quantify the impact on either precision breeding or the approach to bovine tuberculosis, for example, without the detail. Once the detail is agreed at the summit, we are very happy to come back to this place and talk about the full impacts.

T3. As work is undertaken across Government to improve national resilience and the public’s preparedness for emergencies, what consideration have Ministers given to broadcasting an expert-led national emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis?

The Government are taking urgent action to tackle the climate crisis and to raise awareness among the public. The Be Ready public awareness campaign provides simple and effective advice on practical steps that individuals, households and communities can take to improve their resilience to a range of risks, including those presented by climate change. Not only are the Government acting to prepare people for the threats that climate change poses, but, through our commitment to net zero, we are acting to address climate change.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

Back in September, the Government promised a cross-Government task and finish group on mega-donors that would work at pace. However, 11 weeks and several written questions later, we have seen no terms of reference and no start date. No one should be able to buy the keys to No. 10, so will the First Secretary of State tell us how they are getting on with the task and when they expect to finish?

The Representation of the People Bill is still making its way through the other place. We will be considering work through that piece of legislation. I have asked the group to meet the hon. Lady to brief her on their work, as I did for the shadow Minister. I will ensure that that takes place.

T4. The Government recently delivered almost £16 billion in efficiency savings across Whitehall. However, up to £45 billion more can be found in productivity gains and efficiency savings, so will the Minister ensure that ambitious artificial intelligence and technology adoption plans are at the very heart of next year’s spending review?

Both the 10-year plan and the spending review offer us the chance to put into practice my hon. Friend’s belief that technology should not be the preserve of a few but, through our public services, the driver of opportunity and dignity for the many.

The Minister was asked earlier about digital resilience. Rural areas across North Yorkshire are stressed and concerned, because communities coming off analogue that do not have a mobile signal are stuffed. The commitments from BT and others, to which the Minister referred, are not worth the paper they are written on. The move to digital is happening in January. I urge the Minister to take a look at it.

As the House can see, given the nature of those concerns, which have been raised twice now, there is enthusiasm on the Front Bench to take them deeply seriously. We will do exactly that by responding swifty.

T5. Following the devastating wildfires in High Peak and across the UK this summer and the National Resilience Committee’s warning this week that Britain is “seriously underprepared” for major emergencies, will the Minister accept the recommendation to put local resilience forums on a statutory footing, with clear responsibilities and accountability, so that partnerships such as the Derbyshire LRF have the authority they need to protect our communities?

Let me place on record my profound thanks for the important work that local resilience forums do, not least the vital work they did over the summer and the supporting role they are playing in our Be Ready campaign, including in my hon. Friend’s constituency. The Government are currently leading a post-implementation review of the Civil Contingencies Act 2004, which is considering the merits of putting local resilience forums on a statutory footing. A decision will be taken through the review, and we will present that to Parliament early next year.

People do not have to be white to be English, but the census currently disagrees when it asks for their ethnicity, as do the 10,000 different accounts that have sent me racist messages and death threats since I raised this matter in the Chamber last week. [Hon. Members: “Shame!”] Ahead of my meeting with the Prime Minister to discuss it, will the Cabinet Office reaffirm that Englishness cannot be boiled down to ethnicity and that the census must reflect this?

It was a pleasure to sit on the Front Bench for the introduction of the hon. Member’s recent ten-minute rule Bill. I must say that he gave an absolutely tremendous speech and set out his case incredibly well. To be frank, it was one of the better speeches I have heard in this Chamber. I know he looks forward to meeting the Prime Minister, and I will not prejudge that, but I think and hope that we all, from all parts of the House, agree that Englishness is not a matter of race or ethnicity. Englishness is about the shared culture we share together in this country.

T6. Further to the Government’s commitment to devolution by default, a month ago Cornish MPs met officials at No. 10 North to discuss the powers we need devolved to Cornwall, including economic development funding, housing, transport, post-14 skills and culture. Since then, Cornwall has been formally designated a single foundation strategic authority. Will the Minister meet Cornish MPs to discuss the progress made since that meeting towards devolution in each of those five specific areas?

I was delighted to see Cornish MPs and leaders attend No. 10 North recently to discuss the deal that they want in Cornwall. We are considering all the points they made in that meeting as part of the “Rewiring the State” delivery plan more widely. That work is still ongoing, but we will keep Cornish Members and, indeed, leaders updated.

Following my exchange with the Prime Minister in this place, No. 10 North wrote to offer a meeting to discuss regulating the Isle of Wight ferries. The offer was for a meeting within weeks, but that was two months ago, and we still have no date in the diary. Will the Minister ensure that I get that meeting with No. 10 North without any further delay?
I will ensure that is looked at and the meeting is arranged, and we look forward to welcoming the hon. Member to No. 10 North.

T7. I was delighted that, at the Budget, the Government set out their intention to move ahead with a devolution deal for the Thames valley. I am very determined to get this over the line, so that residents in Bracknell Forest and the wider region can enjoy the benefits that devolution will bring. Will my hon. Friend commit to continuing to work with local MPs and leaders to unlock devolution in the Thames valley?

I agree with my hon. Friend that the opportunities for the Thames valley will be fantastic. Devolution will mean greater powers and funding to maximise economic opportunities across the whole area, including, but not limited to, the measures announced in the fiscal devolution road map as well as those in the forthcoming delivery plan. We are considering all the responses and thoughts given to us so far. The delivery plan will be coming soon, and I look forward to sharing it with Members in this House, people across the country and, most importantly for my hon. Friend, those in the Thames valley.
The removal of peerages Bill was in the King’s Speech. When will it be introduced?
We will provide a further update to the House on our plans in due course.

T8. The Government’s fiscal devolution road map recognises that London has a unique governance arrangement. It is the oldest mayoral model and is out of step with newer combined authority models. If new powers are to work for all of London, which is such a large city, we need decision making to tie directly to local borough delivery. As part of the rewiring the state plans, will the Minister consider reviewing London’s historic devolution powers and ensuring that strategic decision making is fully linked to local delivery?

The delivery plan will not include changes to the London governance structure. I am happy to meet my hon. Friend and other London MPs to discuss their concerns and what change they would perhaps like to see in London, but it will not be included in the delivery plan itself.

Leicester is one of the most vulnerable cities in Britain and is projected to rise fast up the ranking. This summer saw record-breaking heat, and thousands of people up and down the country died. London has its own heat resilience strategy, but Leicester does not. Will the Minister publish a national heat resilience strategy and put adequate funding behind it?
I visited Leicestershire over the summer to engage with local communities and the local resilience forum. Let me look more closely at what the hon. Gentleman has said and I will write to him.

T9. The Minister will be aware that by 2028, London will be the only mayoral authority in the country that is not a combined authority. That means that, unlike Greater Manchester for example, there is no requirement for the Mayor of London to work with the councils that actually deliver services. Will the Minister tell us how she will ensure London is not left behind in the Government’s very welcome drive to devolve power from Whitehall?

As my hon. Friend will know, London has one of the longest standing devolution settlements. The mayor is accountable to voters in every borough. He is scrutinised by the London Assembly and works in partnership with boroughs where responsibilities might overlap. As I said in a previous answer, I am happy to meet London MPs to discuss their thoughts about this issue further. Through “Rewiring the State”, we will work with London partners so that the settlement keeps pace with the changes we are making and, of course, London’s role as a global city, building on the package agreed at the Budget.

The Government have asked the public to prepare for a black sky event. Many people with very severe ME— myalgic encephalomyelitis—are bedbound and rely on electric pumps for nutrition. If we experience a prolonged national or even regional power outage, they would be at very grave risk. What specific provision is in place for them? Will the Minister ensure that national resilience planning fully accounts for people who are dependent on powered medical equipment?

I think the hon. Lady is referring to the recent Be Ready campaign that we launched. This is about raising awareness of simple steps that households can take in their everyday lives to prepare for everyday emergencies. It is part of a process by which we ensure that our country is as resilient as possible, because we cannot have national resilience and national security without resilience at the most localised levels. These are issues that the Government take incredibly seriously. That is why we invested £1 billion in pandemic preparedness and launched the home defence programme. We are doing work in Government now that we have not been doing for almost 25 years. We are determined to ensure that our country is as resilient as it can be, given the nature of the world we are living in.

I support the calls for a reversal of the Tory and coalition-era outsourcing of the civil service pension scheme. The Minister committed to me last month that she would look at publishing a smaller version of the remedial adviser’s report, which I believe would help Members to scrutinise progress of the new rectification plan on behalf of our many constituents affected by Capita’s significant failures. What progress has my hon. Friend made in determining whether that can be published?

I thank my hon. Friend for his question and for the tireless championing and campaigning he does for his constituents on the issue of the Capita civil service pension scheme. On the remedial adviser’s report, my officials are working with the Clerks of the Public Accounts Committee and the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee on sharing a copy with them. There are a number of market-sensitive issues that need to be considered, but that work is ongoing and hopefully will be resolved soon.

Northern Ireland has an international reputation as a region of expertise and knowledge in tech development. World-leading tech companies such as Fujitsu, WhiteHat Security and Microsoft have chosen to establish their operations in Northern Ireland in recognition of the talent and innovation we hold. What steps will the Minister take to use Northern Ireland-based firms to support the strengthening of the UK’s digital infrastructure?

I have personally witnessed the strength of Northern Ireland’s digital and technology sectors on multiple visits to Belfast. I will take the hon. Member’s points to heart and ensure that we make the most of that strength in the opportunities for digital resilience.

title: Emerging Renewable Technology
turns: What steps her Department is taking to support the development of emerging renewable technology.

We will need a range of technologies to build the clean power system that will get us off fossil fuels. We are backing emerging renewable technology through innovation and investments via our publicly owned energy company, Great British Energy, which will create skilled jobs and strengthen domestic supply chains. That includes investing in floating offshore wind projects including Pentland in Scotland and Erebus in the Celtic sea.

The success of offshore wind is proof that early Government investment in emerging technologies can achieve cost reductions, create viable technology for energy generation and help to reindustrialise the UK. Recent comments suggest that future contracts for difference rounds will be focused on the lowest cost possible, which is understandable, but will my hon. Friend confirm that the Government will continue to support all emerging technologies, and will he commit to using money from the new North sea energy wealth fund for that purpose?

My hon. Friend is right to say that affordability will be absolutely central to the decisions that we make in allocation round 8 and to other decisions we make when it comes to investing in technologies. We have also said that through the National Wealth Fund and Great British Energy, we will continue to support the deployment of clean energy, because it is the only answer that will get us off fossil fuels, and protect bill payers in the long term and the industrialisation that is so important in communities across the country. By taking that funding alongside our continued commitment to deploy clean power, we will make sure that we have jobs in every single part of the country and the power that will get us off fossil fuels.

The east of England has a strong record in delivering renewable energy projects; the Minister will be very familiar with the offshore programmes and turbines. Will he review the merits of developing an offshore grid to get the electricity generated into the grid without the need for more than 100 miles of pylons, which would devastate the east of England, the constituencies of Essex and our countryside?

I am really glad to hear Conservative Members championing renewables; it is really good to hear that. I hope that we can rebuild that consensus across the House. I agree with the right hon. Lady that renewables are hugely important. Of course, the great grid upgrade was started by the Conservatives, including the important transmission infrastructure that we need. The problem was that they left it too late, and that is why important projects off the east of England are not connected and delivering cheaper power to homes and businesses across the country. I am really interested in the idea of offshore co-ordinated assets. We agreed with European neighbours to look at much more offshore co-ordination—I think it is the long-term answer—but we also have to build the grid here in the UK to get the power to where it is needed.

In my constituency, there is so much innovation going on in floating offshore wind in the Celtic sea that could add to the energy mix and provide security. However, our offshore wind projects are all in the east of the country. Developers and investors are ripe to invest in the Celtic sea, but they need certainty to do so, because emerging technology needs to be tested. The contracts for difference AR8 will be crucial to supporting those test and demonstration models for offshore wind in the Celtic sea. Will the Minister commit to floating offshore wind in the Celtic sea as part of AR8 and future auction rounds?

My hon. Friend is a great champion for her constituency and for the Celtic sea more generally, as she is for the important role that technologies will play in reindustrialisation and in the energy mix. I will not be drawn on what will or will not come in AR8. We will say more on the budget later this week and then the process will have to run its course. Of course, in AR7 we got the first Welsh project through in more than decade. The Erebus project is also one of the first test and demo projects of floating offshore wind in the country, and it is in the Celtic sea. We remain committed to deploying those technologies, but I will say what I have said frequently before: that technology has to come at an affordable price to make sure that we are also bringing down bills for consumers.

Last week, the Prime Minister responded to me from the Dispatch Box, saying that £1 billion was being invested in a project off the east coast of Scotland. That was backed up later in the day by the Under-Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, the hon. Member for Inverclyde and Renfrewshire West (Martin McCluskey), who stated it in a post on X. Will the Minister confirm exactly which project off the east coast of Scotland is getting that £1 billion?

I am disappointed that the hon. Gentleman has not come here to welcome the investment decision in Berwick Bank, off the coast of Scotland, with £33 billion going to SSE across the next five years, including investment in Berwick Bank—a hugely important project. We are driving forward investment not just in building those projects but in the supply chains and industrialisation in Scotland. If the Scottish Government moved forward faster with some of the consenting decisions, we might see even more being built.

title: Passenger Rail Services
turns: What steps she is taking to improve passenger rail services.
What steps she is taking to improve passenger rail services.
The Secretary of State for Transport

For too long, our railways have not been run in the service of passengers. We are turning this around, with six operators already brought into public ownership under this Government and the renationalisation of Great Western Railway on 13 December. Next year, the creation of Great British Railways will bring the management of track and train together, ending decades of fragmentation, and delivering better and more reliable services for passengers.

My constituents rely on the Cross-City line to get them in and out of Birmingham, but the last train back from Birmingham in the evening does not run as far as Lichfield, meaning that we cannot make the most of the nightlife there. As Christmas approaches, does the Secretary of State agree that it is time to change that and boost the evening service from New Street to Lichfield City, so that my constituents can make the best of Birmingham’s Frankfurt Christmas market?

I thank my hon. Friend for his tireless campaigning on rail issues, and I know these services would make a real difference for his constituents over the Christmas period. I welcome the work done by West Midlands Trains and the local community on developing proposals for this trial. I think our publicly owned railways should work in the service of passengers, and these extra trains would be a great example of that. I very much back his call for this trial to take place.

I thank my right hon. Friend, because my Cardiff East constituents were absolutely delighted with the announcement yesterday of £30 million for Cardiff Parkway station. Mine is the only constituency in the capital city without a train station, so this will be transformational for growth, jobs and travel. Before the Senedd election, the Welsh Labour Government agreed to a funding contribution, alongside private investors, to ensure that this project is delivered. Can she please confirm whether, in the five months since that election, the minority Plaid Government have said they will honour that intergovernmental agreement?

It is for the new Welsh Government to confirm their own contribution to this project, so that we can get on and deliver it as quickly as possible. To my knowledge, no such confirmation has been provided to date. I am really pleased that we confirmed our contribution in the Budget yesterday, and I congratulate my right hon. Friend on her campaigning on this issue for her constituents. She was an excellent Welsh Secretary, and it was an absolute delight to work alongside her and start to put right the historical wrongs of under-investment in the Welsh railways.

May I constructively suggest a way in which the Secretary of State could help three Cabinet colleagues—the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Secretary, who is building a major reservoir in my constituency; the Housing Secretary, who has big plans within Cambridgeshire; and the Chancellor, who often talks about the Oxford-Cambridge arc? Securing a light rail link to the reservoir will shape the public response to it, but the Department for Transport currently does not seem to be involved at all with the other Departments. I do not expect her to be familiar with the scheme—it is primarily for one of her colleagues—but could she write to me setting out what her Department might do to help those other Departments deliver on their aims?

This Government are investing considerably in improving rail services and public transport connections in Cambridgeshire. I would be happy to follow up on the detail of the right hon. Member’s proposal. I would just say that, with the East West Rail proposals linking Oxford to Cambridgeshire and the opening of the new station at Cambridge South, significant investment is going into this part of the country, but I will come back to him with the detail on his point.

In yesterday’s Budget, there was one mention of Northern Powerhouse Rail. One of the easiest ways to deliver benefit for passengers would be to unlock the indefinitely paused York area capacity scheme. Will the Secretary of State commit to continuing to look at this, and make sure that passengers in Harrogate and Knaresborough, and along that line, get trains when they need them with the service they would expect?

As part of Northern Powerhouse Rail, we are prioritising improvements in the Yorkshire region, such as services from York to Leeds, and between Sheffield, Bradford and Leeds. Indeed, I was in Bradford just last week to make the announcement about a brand-new station at Bradford, which is much needed. I know the hon. Member continues to champion the case for the York area capacity study. We will continue to keep all of this under review, because we must provide the right number of trains, where people need them and when they need them.

The Penistone line, which runs through my constituency, serves over half a million people, eight constituencies, six hospitals, four universities and a network of colleges, schools and GP surgeries, but it has only one train an hour. Our Government are funding phase 1 of upgrading the line, but further funding is needed to deliver phase 2 to enable two trains an hour along our line—the spine that connects south and west Yorkshire. Does the Secretary of State agree with me that delivering both phases of the upgrade together will most effectively secure two trains an hour, and will she meet me ahead of the next spending review to discuss delivering the full upgrade and two trains an hour to ensure growth in every postcode along the line?

My hon. Friend and I have met on this issue, and she is right to say that the Government are making that investment in phase 1. I remember discussing it with her when I was at Sheffield station for the Northern Powerhouse Rail announcement earlier this year. I would be happy to continue those conversations about phase 2 as we head into the next spending review.

My London constituency does not have a tube service. My residents are entirely reliant on South Western Railway services to get to work, school and elsewhere. Stations such as Hampton and Whitton have seen passenger footfall close to or exceeding half a million in the last year, yet the services are infrequent and less reliable since nationalisation. Will the Secretary of State back my call, supported by thousands of local residents with the timetable review under way, for far more frequent and reliable services for such stations?

The hon. Lady is right to mention the timetable review that is under way. I would be happy to discuss with South Western the options with regard to Hampton and Whitton. I would just note that one of the benefits of renationalising South Western Railways has been the roll-out of the new Arterio fleet of air-conditioned trains that are providing more capacity. I also recognise the important work that South Western has done to reduce the number of cancellations that come about as a consequence of the unavailability of staff. We need to get the basics right on South Western to provide the service that she and her constituents deserve.

Labour promised that nationalisation would deliver a more reliable railway. Two years on, it is getting worse. Between April and June, all Government-run operators saw cancellations rise or punctuality fall. Ministers say that Great British Railways will turn that around when it launches next year. They promised its implementation timetable and draft licence consultation this autumn. On this last sitting day of October, neither has yet appeared. When will they, and when will passengers see the improvements they were promised?

May I start by congratulating the hon. Lady on her appointment to the Opposition Front Bench? I think this is the first opportunity that I have had a chance to do so from the Dispatch Box. She is right in some respects. We do need to make more progress on improving punctuality and reliability, and I cannot pretend that I am happy with performance across the entirety of the rail network at the moment. However, I would gently point out to her that at the last reporting period, cancellations across publicly-owned operators were 3.9% compared to 4.9% for operators yet to transfer and still in private ownership. On punctuality, 82.6% of stops by publicly-owned operators were within three minutes of their scheduled arrival time, compared with just 73.8% for operators yet to transfer.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

A £1 billion order for 29 new five-car, battery-electric trains for TransPennine Express was recently announced. While welcome, it has raised some eyebrows, with Modern Railways magazine estimating that the cost is nearly double that of conventional electric-only trains. It would cost a staggering £25.2 billion for similar deals to replace England’s passenger trains that have diesel engines. Are we on the right value-for-money track with this approach to rolling stock specification and procurement?

I was delighted to be in Derby a few weeks ago to announce the new fleet of battery-electric trains for TransPennine Express. It is a £1.2 billion investment. Included in that are hundreds of millions of pounds of maintenance costs for the duration of that contract. We are working on procurements for both Southeastern trains and Northern trains at the moment. Value for money and affordability will be central to the decisions we make on those procurements.

title: Personal Statement
turns: With your permission, Madam Deputy Speaker, I wish to make a personal statement. Following a complaint to Parliament’s Independent Complaints and Grievance Scheme by a former member of my constituency staff, the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards and the Independent Expert Panel have found that, on three occasions in February 2025, I breached Parliament’s bullying and harassment policy. I accept those findings in full. At a small gathering to thank my former colleague for her work establishing the constituency office, I initiated a hug. I assumed that she was content to be hugged, but I did not ask, and the hug was unwelcome to her. Later that month, while out of the office, intending to join an online meeting that was not in my diary, I took my former colleague’s phone from her hand without her consent to join that meeting. She immediately challenged me and took the phone back. It was not mine to take. The next day, two calls between my former colleague and me were ended abruptly while I was trying to find the venue for a constituency appointment—one of them deliberately by me, after I entered a live church service. Regrettably, I never explained why these calls had ended, as I ought to have done. As a result of these behaviours, my former colleague was upset and humiliated. My behaviour had a real and continuing impact on her and her family, and I am truly sorry for this. I was the employer of my former colleague. There was an imbalance of power between us, and I was not sufficiently alert to it, as the behaviour code requires. The responsibility for behaving in a way that was mindful of that imbalance was mine, not hers. I also recognise that behaviour like this could well impact on somebody who is vulnerable, whether or not it is known that they are vulnerable. That is why respect and courtesy must come first in every interaction I have with others. Since these events, my approach has changed. I am more alert to the need for sensitivity to those I work with. I have undertaken further training, including one-to-one training. Going forwards, I will be mindful of the need for both courtesy in my dealings with staff, including in times of stress, and for my personal attention when staffing problems arise. I made mistakes, and I breached the policy. I apologise unreservedly to my former colleague and to this House.

title: Knife Crime
turns: What progress her Department has made on reducing levels of knife crime.
The Secretary of State for the Home Department

Since the general election, knife crime is down by 11%, knife homicides are down by 25% and knife-enabled robberies are down by 18%. That is huge progress, but we must do more. That is why I recently launched crackdowns in more than 230 of the areas most affected by knife crime. We will be tough on knife crime, through increased patrols, but also tough on the causes of knife crime, by undertaking prevention work to prevent these crimes.

I am concerned about young people and knife crime in my home city of Glasgow. Victim Support Scotland has asked the Scottish Government to carry out a comprehensive review of why young people become involved in knife crime and how effective Scottish programmes are at preventing it. This is backed by my constituent, Neil McCrimmon, and his family. Their beloved son Kory was stabbed to death, and the family has campaigned with great courage against knife crime. I fully support Victim Support Scotland’s call for a comprehensive review. Will the Home Secretary confirm that she would support the Scottish Government, were they to carry out such a review?

My hon. Friend has told me how much he admires the family for their campaigning efforts. We know from our own work how powerful it is when those who have suffered because of knife crime join in the effort to tackle it. As he knows, policing is a devolved matter and the question of a review is therefore one for the Scottish Government, but this Government stand ready to support them where we can.

I thank the Home Secretary for her answers and for her commitment to trying to stop knife crime. One of the greatest ways of stopping knife crime across this United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is to ensure that people cannot buy knives. What is she doing to ensure that access to knives, whether through sections of the media or industry, is stopped? If we stop the knives, we stop the crime.

The hon. Gentleman is absolutely right. It is imperative that we get knives off our streets, and he will know that we have already taken 63,000 knives off our streets and banned ninja swords. We will make more progress, including on a consultation that we have recently carried out looking at a wider regime for the sale of knives, and we will update the House on that in due course.

title: Nolan Principles
turns: What steps she is taking to ensure local authorities uphold the Nolan principles.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government

Standards in local government are important. The Localism Act 2011 requires every local authority in England to adopt a code of conduct that conforms to the Nolan principles. The Government are committed to a whole system reform of the local government standards framework to make it stronger and more efficient, including with stronger sanctions, and we will legislate when parliamentary time allows.

Despite concerns, Reform rushed through the appointment of Norfolk county council’s new CEO, Dennis Bacon. Thanks to Councillor Ben Weston, we now know that Mr Bacon hosted senior Reform councillors at his luxury B&B the day before job applications opened. Norfolk Reform has failed on three Nolan principles: selflessness, integrity and objectivity. Does my hon. Friend agree that a slap-up meal should not get someone a £215,000 job?

My hon. Friend raises concerning point. I thank my hon. Friend and Councillor Ben Weston too for highlighting the issue. I obviously cannot get into the specifics of the case—local authorities are independent employers, so individual employment decisions are a matter for them—but I am concerned that there is a pattern of conduct and behaviour in Reform councils that we would not usually find acceptable, and we should not allow it to be normalised.

Kinver Business Solutions has secured more than £1 million in project management fees from Ashfield district council. It now turns out that one of the project managers is actually the son of the chief executive of Ashfield district council. I thank the Department for arranging an appointment this week, but does the Minister agree that it is time to send the commissioners in to Ashfield district council? There is not a minute to spare.

I know that the hon. Gentleman raised the same point at Prime Minister’s questions last week, and it is clearly concerning. There should not be that type of conflict. I have written to him today, and he should have a copy of the letter in his office. We take such matters seriously. I have asked the Department to conduct an urgent best-value assessment of the local authority. Meetings are taking place with officials and the council’s chief executive to find out exactly what is going on.

I thank the Minister for the intervention that his Department has made with the rapid best-value assessment at Ashfield district council, in response to my representations over the past two months. These are extremely serious allegations, and my constituents in Hucknall have been let down badly by the council. Will the Minister confirm that urgent action is being taken? Can he say what more can be done to prevent further inappropriate decisions, especially on planning? Does he agree that the severity of the allegations warrants a referral to the police for an independent investigation?

My hon. Friend has raised this matter on a number of occasions, and I hope she received a copy of my letter on Friday after raising it further. The issue is very serious. In addition to the points I have made about the rapid best-value review and the conversations taking place with the council’s chief executive, I can also say that our officials will be contacting the external auditor to understand more details of the case.

The Prime Minister has made it clear that Labour councils should end their power-sharing agreements with local Green parties, following the disgracefully antisemitic motion passed by the national Green party that Zionism is racism. However, the Labour leader of Havant borough council has refused to condemn her Green party coalition partners for supporting that motion and has refused to withdraw from the coalition. Does the Minister agree that that is a breach of the Nolan principles, and will he clarify who is right: the Prime Minister, or the Labour leader of Havant borough council?

For the avoidance of doubt, I should point out that the Prime Minister is always right. I will take no lectures from Reform on standards and conduct in local government. We hear repeated complaints about the conduct of Reform-led councils across the country—about the way in which they treat their staff, the way in which they treat each other, and the way in which, quite often, the toxicity that we see online is brought into council chambers.

The first of the Nolan principles is selflessness—acting solely in the public interest—but, according to feedback from councillors throughout the country, during the botched local government reorganisation process they felt that they were under pressure to put political considerations first: pressure that came from the previous Secretary of State, the right hon. Member for Streatham and Croydon North (Steve Reed). The new Secretary of State told the House recently that she could not say whether his decision making was even lawful. Can she now tell the House whether the pressure that was put on those councillors to submit to his reorganisation agenda left them at risk of breaching the Nolan principles as well as the law?

The only pressure on us is the pressure that we place on ourselves to do the job well. As I said in my statement last week, there are no easy decisions on local reorganisation, and there is no perfect solution for most counties in England. What the Government have to do is balance competing interests and ensure that we assess the evidence base objectively, that we challenge when there may be gaps in the information provided, and, ultimately, that we make the best possible decision, and that is what we are getting on with doing.

title: Children's Commissioner for England Report
turns: What steps her Department is taking to respond to the Children's Commissioner for England’s report entitled “The Childhood Lottery: The hardest places to grow up in England”, published in October 2026.
The Secretary of State for Education

We will ensure that no child is left behind and no child is held back by where they grow up. The report was right to focus on stronger local leadership, and we are bringing together local leaders to help shape the future of childhood in their areas. We are taking cross-Government action, bringing together public services through our rewiring of the state programme, and our 10-year plan will focus on childhood.

Medway was one of the lowest-scoring areas in the Children’s Commissioner’s recent report, but, on closer inspection, we see that ranking was heavily based on its 2024 survey, which identified Medway as one of the local authorities whose sample was not representative, with just a few hundred respondents. A lot of good work is happening in Medway to create a brighter future for our young people, as is reflected in a more recent children and young people survey, which had thousands of young respondents, 81% of whom said they “liked” or “strongly liked” their area, up from 68% in 2021. Does the Secretary of State agree that it is much better for us to work with places to build better services around children and family rather than to criticise them? Will she consider visiting Medway to see the good work being done?

I agree with my hon. Friend that we need to be talking areas up, not putting them down. She is also right to say that Medway is offering many of its young people a brighter future and has some fantastic local leaders who are working really hard for young people in their area. She has four Best Start family hubs in Medway, to take just one example. I look forward to us working together and I am sure I will be visiting Medway very soon.

The report by the Children’s Commissioner is a damning indictment of the Liberal Democrats’ record of running Somerset council. To be ranked among the worst places in England for children to grow up is appalling. At the time of the report, Somerset was the third worst out of 148 local authorities for issuing education, health and care plans within the statutory 20-week framework, with just 6% completed on time. I am now told that figure has fallen to 0%. What steps will the Secretary of State take to ensure that the Liberal Democrats do not continue to fail children in Somerset?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for raising issues relating to his constituency. I might add that the report also reflects on previous Governments, in terms of the support they brought in for children, but he is right to say that we need to take further action on supporting children with special educational needs. We are bringing forward our generational reform plans so that we can get more support in earlier, for more children. It is also why we are working with local authorities to ensure that they have a SEND plan that they are able to deliver, and that we can hold them to account for that.

title: Engagements
turns: Q1. If he will list his official engagements for Wednesday 18 November.

May I add my condolences to the family, friends and colleagues of Sir David Evennett? He was a kind and generous friend to me when I was in this House before, and to many on all sides, particularly those on the Conservative Benches. He will be much missed. This morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others, and—according to ChatGPT—I shall have further such meetings later today.

Sir David Evennett was a member of the Education Committee with me when I was first elected. He was a really kind man and I was very fond of him. I send my heartfelt condolences to his family. May I add that we should pay our condolences to the family of John Pardoe, who passed away this week? He served North Cornwall and the Liberal movement so proudly for many years. Every year, more than 600 people with cancer in south Cumbria have to make debilitating round trips of nearly four hours, every day for weeks on end, to the nearest radiotherapy centre in Preston. We have the worst access to radiotherapy in the whole of England, and therefore tragically many of my constituents die before their time. The answer is obvious: we need to open a satellite radiotherapy unit at the Westmorland general hospital in Kendal. Will the Prime Minister agree to meet me, local cancer patients and clinicians to help us achieve that long overdue investment, so that people who suffer from cancer in south Cumbria can have shorter journeys, but longer lives?

I want to see the end of the postcode lottery in cancer care. I am going to agree with the hon. Gentleman—he and I used to talk about this very issue 15 or so years ago, when I was Health Secretary. I would like to see cancer care more in the community and more satellite units, exactly as he says. I will arrange for a Minister to meet him to discuss this issue. We are investing in new cutting-edge radiotherapy machines in hospitals across England. Perhaps there is an opportunity to do more in his area, and we will look into it.

Q3. I was really proud to organise recently the first ever South West Norfolk farming conference, with more than 70 rural stakeholders meeting near Downham Market. It has been a difficult year for farmers, with rising input costs, wildfires and water scarcity. That has led to food productivity being increasingly unprofitable, and alternative uses for land being proposed, such as AI data centres and ground-mounted solar, tragically on some of the most productive farmland. So with the EU reset and the 10-year plan on the horizon, will my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister commit to tackling those fundamental challenges around farm profitability and commit to domestic UK food production?

I have an idea of how difficult this year has been for our farmers. I visited a farm myself in Truro at the height of the summer. At the time, we confirmed funding for reservoirs on farms to support them with the changing climate that they face. I will be fighting in Brussels on Friday for a new arrangement to improve the Tory Brexit deal that actually will support our farmers and our food producers, but I recognise that we can do more to support farmers and farming, and I will work with my hon. Friend to that end.
I call the Leader of the Opposition.

May I, too, start by paying tribute to Sir David Evennett? He passed away suddenly yesterday after a short illness. He was a good friend of mine, a good Whip and a great constituency MP, and he will be very much missed. I am sure that the whole House will join me in offering our condolences to his wife Marilyn, his two sons, and all his family and friends. Will the Prime Minister cut welfare in this Parliament?

I will do everything I can as quickly as possible to get the welfare bill down. We received the landmark report yesterday from Alan Milburn, and I say a huge thank you to him, because he has done a great service to this country and particularly to its young people. Finally—a landmark report that will change the way we think about the coming generation and give them the support that they need to get on in life. I hope that all sides of the House will get behind it. Specifically, I have asked the Cabinet to reprioritise spending plans for ’27-28 to put the beginnings of a fund together to support the youth opportunity service, initially delivering 25,000 quality work placements for 16 and 17-year-olds. We are making progress immediately to get the welfare bill down.

I asked the Prime Minister if he was going to cut the welfare bill in this Parliament; it sounds very clearly like he is not. He talks about a landmark report, but he is not planning any savings for 10 years. Those young people are not going to be young in 10 years’ time. Everything that he wants to do takes 10 years. He wants a 10-year plan—which is still not ready, by the way. The NATO defence plan will take 10 years. Now it is going to take him 10 years to make any welfare savings. We cannot wait 10 years: those young people need those jobs now. Working-age welfare alone costs £180 billion a year and is set to rise to more than £220 billion a year because of this Government. As the welfare Secretary told us, every Labour MP just wants to know who they can tax to pay for more benefits. Keir Starmer failed to make welfare cuts, because this Chief Whip, the right hon. Member for Knowsley (Anneliese Midgley), and that First Secretary of State, the right hon. Member for Sheffield Heeley (Louise Haigh), led the rebellion on welfare. Now they are in charge of the Labour party. Is that not more proof that the Labour party is just the welfare party?

The right hon. Lady reveals time and time again, when she comes to that Dispatch Box, why she does not understand this issue, because she only ever stands at that Dispatch Box asking for cuts. That is all she ever asks for. Her shadow Work and Pensions Secretary confirmed on the television that hundreds of thousands of disabled children would lose funding under her proposals. The Milburn report says that, in order to reduce the welfare bill, we have to improve support. Here is where the Opposition really do not understand it: the report also says that the biggest rise in NEETs came between 2022 and 2024. That is because a report by Sir Kevan Collins, commissioned by the Conservatives, recommended major investment in support for young people coming out of the pandemic to prevent them becoming NEET. Some 250,000 people became NEET because the Conservatives failed to provide that support. We will give hope to young people, and we will oppose the cuts-only approach of the Conservatives.

The Prime Minister says that I do not understand—the only person who does not understand is him. He talks about NEETs, but let me clear his confusion up. When we were in government, between 2011 and 2021, the NEETs rate actually fell by 7%. It then went up because of covid. That 7% is more than all of the savings that the Government are going to find to help young people from the Milburn review. We did more during our time in government than the Prime Minister is proposing now. That is a fact. The Prime Minister wants to pretend that he actually understands. What he wants is the vibes of welfare reform without actually doing any welfare reform. We need to bring down the welfare bill because we cannot afford it, but he does not understand. On Sky News yesterday, the Prime Minister actually said that no one would lose money as a result of his welfare changes. Also on Sky News yesterday, Alan Milburn said that there will be some young people “who…get less”, so there seems to be some confusion here. Can the Prime Minister clear it up for us? Who is right?

We are about helping young people into work. We are about giving young people hope and a better life. That is what this whole reform is about, and I need to hear from the Leader of the Opposition today whether she and her party are going to back the opportunity and support guarantee—a legal guarantee—so that young people in this country can have a better life and can have hope. There needs to be some humility from the Conservatives. They left government with almost 1 million young people without any hope for their future; we want to give them a better life. Yes, we do want people to accept the support that is on offer. That is clear and it is in the report, but we will not accept the Conservatives coming to this House time and again saying, “We are going to bring down the welfare bill”, but failing to support our young people. They slashed youth services when they were in government, they cut the education maintenance allowance, and they trebled tuition fees. They took hope from a generation; we will give it back to them.

I am going to cut through all this waffle. The Prime Minister says that he wants to give young people a better life; all he is offering them is false hope, because none of the things he is saying are going to work. He keeps talking about all of the schemes that the Government have. The youth guarantee scheme is a complete and total failure—everyone out there knows it. The Government destroy jobs, they kill businesses, and then they offer the businesses a little money to give young people work placements. It makes no sense at all. We are not offering young people false hope; we are the ones who are offering them a better plan. Yesterday, I spoke to a café owner in Waterloo. He said to me: “I can’t believe the Government thinks I’m not a working person because I employ people.” Earlier, I asked the Prime Minister to clear up the confusion about who would lose out, and he could not do so. Let me tell him who is really losing out: it is people like that man, every single hard-working taxpayer out there struggling with the cost of living who is going to have to pay higher taxes because of Labour’s welfare bill. That café owner did not blame the last Government; he blamed this Government. Since Labour came into office, the cost of hiring a young person has gone up by almost £5,000. The best thing the Prime Minister could do to solve this crisis is to cut the jobs tax for young people. Why will he not do it?

The Leader of the Opposition comes to the Dispatch Box time and again with her selective facts. Did she see in the news yesterday that unemployment is down? There are hundreds of thousands more people in work in this country, and that includes young people. Did she see last Thursday that growth is up over the last three quarters? Actually, they are the best growth figures for a 10-year period if you exclude the bounce back after the pandemic. The fundamentals of the British economy are strong, and they are getting stronger. We will consider the Milburn report in the round. We will look at all of its proposals in detail and bring forward our response next month, but if the Leader of the Opposition is arguing for a cuts-only approach, we will stand against that, because we know that that will not help a generation to move on. We will bring forward an approach based on support and opportunity—that will always be the approach of the Labour party. We know that our approach will work, and we also have evidence that the Conservatives’ approach failed comprehensively.

I think the Prime Minister said the quiet part out loud when he said he will consider the report in the round. That will probably take another 10 years as well. The Government want to have reviews, to consult and to create reports, and then they come here and say, “It’s a landmark report.” No—it is yet more kicking things into the long grass. We do not have 10 years; we need to get jobs now. The cheek of him to say that unemployment has gone down! He does not know why. It is because people have stopped looking for work; they cannot get jobs, so they have moved into claiming benefits and are no longer classified as unemployed, and that is because of this Labour Government. Across Britain, we are watching a lost generation of young people going straight on to welfare because jobs are disappearing. There are nearly 200,000 fewer vacancies under this Labour Government, and the Prime Minister is congratulating himself that unemployment has gone down. Then on Friday, he will, as he said, go to Brussels and sign up to 100,000 more young people coming to our country to compete for those jobs. Where are those jobs supposed to come from?

We do need jobs now, and that requires growth in the economy. We know that over the last decade, when the Conservatives were in government, we had a decade of low growth. Those are the facts; they go quiet, because they know that is a fact. The deal that is on the table will bring growth to the British economy; it will reduce red tape for businesses; it will cut the cost of exporting to Europe; and, critically, it will bring food prices down. M&S says that it will ease pressure on the price of the weekly shop. Asda says that it will reduce costs. Morrisons says the same thing. Right now, when families across Britain are struggling with the cost of the weekly shop, what are those families to make of a Conservative party that used to back business in reducing red tape and to back working families with their costs, but that is now so split over this issue that it cannot stand up for this country and support a deal that will bring growth to the British economy?

Again, I am just going to clear up some confusion for the Prime Minister. [Interruption.] Yes, I have to. He said that we do need jobs and that that requires growth. No, the growth is created by the businesses that create the jobs. It is business that creates growth, not Government. Growth comes after the jobs. It does not just happen. After all these years, Labour still does not understand that there is only one way to reduce youth unemployment, and that is to make it easier for firms to hire people. All the Government have done is make it harder and harder for firms to hire people. They are in a mess on welfare, because the same people who led the welfare rebellion against Keir Starmer are now in charge—the same people who think social security is more important than national security. Let us see how they are doing. Today, we learn that energy bills are going up by 26%. Inflation is up, interest rates are up and young people aren’t working. Isn’t the truth that it is the Labour party—and this Labour Government—that isn’t working?

As I said, growth is up and unemployment is down. The right hon. Lady can ask all the self-serving questions that she likes, and she can take a patronising tone, if she wants to, at that Dispatch Box, but this Government are leading on the big issues. We will not let a lost generation be the let-down generation. We are acting to deal with these issues and to face them. And we will—yes, we will—lead on Europe and bring growth to the British economy. This side of the House believes in the next generation; that side wants to throw them on the scrapheap again with more cuts. This side of the House has a vision for growth and a positive working relationship with our biggest market; that side is still stuck in the politics of the past and cannot accept that the status quo that they negotiated is not working. They gave us a decade of drift and division; this side of the House is letting Britain believe again and bringing back hope.

Q5. Tomorrow is International Men’s Day. May I, as someone who is doing his rather small bit for Movember, ask whether the Prime Minister agrees that, as three out of four suicides are by men, we must challenge the idea that men should simply man up and keep worries to themselves without asking for help? Will he join me in paying tribute to the fantastic organisations in High Peak that are working to change that, from Mentell in Glossop and Buxton to Andy’s Man Club in Whaley Bridge, and will he commit himself to taking further action to support these efforts so that we can save more lives in the years to come?

I certainly pay tribute to all those organisations, and I look forward to welcoming Andy’s Man Club into 10 Downing Street later today. We know that suicide is the leading cause of death for men under 50, and we know that the sessions that those organisations put on make all the difference, connecting men of all backgrounds so that they can talk openly in a way that they could not do in the family home or at work. We are launching the first ever men’s health strategy, which will put more funding into the kind of projects that my hon. Friend has mentioned. May I also compliment him on his Movember efforts? He has 12 days to go—it might even turn into a moustache at some point. [Laughter.]
I call the leader of the Liberal Democrats.

May I join others in sending our condolences to the family of Sir David Evennett and to the family of John Pardoe? Halloween may be over, but the Vote Leave zombies are out in force: Boris Johnson, staggering back, denying the enormous damage to our economy and the cost of living caused by the Conservatives’ Brexit deal; and Dominic Cummings and Lord Gove, trying to scare us with a new made-up number, no doubt coming soon to the side of a bus. But British people now see the true Brexit horror—higher taxes and higher bills—and they want change now, so will the Prime Minister ditch the whole trade and co-operation agreement, and get a new deal that works for the British people?

Well, I think we heard from some of those zombies a few moments ago—they were shouting at me. The truth is that they do not like it when we say the truth in this House. The truth is that the Brexit deal that they negotiated was not good enough for Britain. It is just a fact, and the vast majority of the public know that as well. It is really important that we face up to that. They burned bridges with our largest market—old friends and neighbours. They just destroyed all those relationships. Exports are down from their constituencies, and they know that as well. There will be a deal in front of us on Friday, and I am looking for support across the Floor of this House for what we are trying to negotiate. [Interruption.] Yes, I am, because it can bring growth to the British economy. It can lower the cost of the weekly shop. It can get greater collaboration back on immigration. It is time that they faced up to these facts, and I am hoping that the right hon. Gentleman will back us in our efforts on Friday.

I thank the Prime Minister for his answer, but I hope that he will absolutely ditch the trade and co-operation agreement, because it is bad from start to finish. If the cost of living crisis does not convince him that a totally new deal with Europe is needed, surely the security implications of Trump, Putin and Xi cosying up should. Lurking behind their talks in China is the scandal of Nvidia, the US firm accused of shipping $12 billion of advanced AI chips to China. With Donald Trump investing millions in Nvidia and selling shares before news of Jensen Huang’s affair broke, White House corruption is once more in plain sight. Does the Prime Minister accept that the Nvidia scandal is not just a major US security threat but a threat to the whole world, and given that corrupt President Trump will not, can he tell us what steps he is taking to keep Britain safe?

I think we have to have our eyes open to all the threats that are out there, particularly in relation to the issue that the right hon. Gentleman has raised in relation to Nvidia. We have to establish all those facts, and act on them. Can I say where I will be tomorrow when that meeting is taking place in China? I will be in Berlin for a meeting of the coalition of the willing. The thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine, and that is what this Government will do. On this issue, I pay tribute to both sides of the House, because that is what we have managed to do in the years since the conflict began, and that is the right thing to do. On this issue, let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in Beijing: this country is squarely with Ukraine. We know who the aggressor is in this situation, and we will not in any way deflect from continuing that support.

Q9. There are currently 35 brain tumour drug trials in the UK. Of these, about 10 relate to glioblastoma, which has an average life expectancy of just nine months and has seen no improvement in treatment for 30 years. Astonishingly, as of today, nobody appears to know how many people are on those trials. The Department of Health and Social Care does not know, and the National Institute for Health and Care Research does not know, or is at least not telling the Department, so may I ask the Prime Minister if he can find out? I suspect that it is less than 1%, or less than 30 of the 3,000 people diagnosed with this terrible illness in the UK in the last year.

My hon. Friend has been a formidable campaigner on this issue, and rightly so. We all remember her sister Margaret with love and affection, and we all support Margaret’s final campaign. My hon. Friend is asking the right questions in this House, and many people are asking the same questions up and down the country. I recently met Archie Goodburn, who is campaigning on these issues, and we all know that Tessa Jowell’s family are campaigning on the same issues as well. As well as understanding how many people are on those trials, we need to galvanise a change here and get a breakthrough, so that more people can access them. The Health Secretary and I, in that meeting with Archie, agreed to appoint a new national brain cancer clinical lead—that is No. 1—and we have said that we will use the G20 next year to see if we can bring a catalyst for change in respect of cutting-edge research on this terrible issue. I look forward to involving my hon. Friend in all of that work.

The Prime Minister has already acknowledged that Brexit has been an unbridled disaster for businesses and communities up and down these islands, but let me contrast the ruthlessness with which he dispatched his predecessor with the queasiness with which he now prevaricates over Keir Starmer’s red lines on the European Union. Rejoining is something that his Back Benchers, in their greater number, would support. It is also something that the more progressive members of his Cabinet, all the Liberal Democrats and even the SNP would support him on. With the parliamentary arithmetic and public opinion behind him, why does he continue to kick this can even further down the road? Why does he not just set out when we are rejoining the EU?

Well, I am leading on Europe, as I have said today, but I will also stick by what I said at the recent by-election, where I said that I would honour the red lines in the Labour manifesto. That is the answer to the hon. Gentleman’s question. We made a clear commitment. That is a contract with the people, and I will honour it.

Q10. With new skilled jobs in manufacturing and aerospace to the left of us, and new nuclear to the right, there are more opportunities within reach of our young people in Clwyd North than ever before, thanks to record investment in north Wales by this Government. But without decent transport links to key sites, our young people are at risk of being stuck in the middle on the north Wales coast. Funding for the new Deeside Parkway station is an excellent start, but does the Prime Minister agree that we must continue investing in Welsh rail so that young people can be connected to good work, wherever they live?

I completely agree that north Wales needs better transport; it is so connected to the north-west of England. The Welsh Labour Government, when in power, created Transport for Wales, which I believe is one of the better rail operators under public control, but the infrastructure is not good enough, and that often leads to delays. I can commit to work with my hon. Friend and her colleagues to improve transport infrastructure across Wales, but particularly in north Wales, where it does need to be better.

Q2. The war in Ukraine has demonstrated that space is an increasingly critical domain—one where operational control is all-important—so can the Prime Minister assure the House that, when procuring future military satellites, he will prioritise British manufacturing jobs, and will he give a guarantee today that any contract will ensure British sovereign control over this vital capability?

The hon. Gentleman is raising a live public procurement, and in the circumstances, I think it is best that I do not comment in detail on what he has said, but I heard the important points that he raised.

Q12. It was the devastating cuts to youth provision by the coalition Government that led me to join the Labour party, yet today the Opposition have proven that they have learned nothing; their only idea is to take more things away from our young people. Whether born in Chelsea or Clayton-le-Moors, every young person deserves the opportunity to thrive. That is why I am driving forward a youth opportunity hub in Hyndburn. Can the Prime Minister please tell me how this Government will ensure that every young person in Hyndburn has the opportunity to earn or learn?

I pay tribute to my hon. Friend, because her youth hub in Hyndburn sounds to me like a forerunner of the Milburn report. I have agreed with the Work and Pensions Secretary that we need to see a much more devolved approach to employment support, and this is exactly the type of facility that we need—a place that people do not fear walking into, as they sometimes do when it comes to Jobcentre Plus, and a place that is going to support them. This is entirely in keeping with what we are trying to do, and I will ensure that she gets support for the youth hub in Hyndburn.

Q4. Brixham is the highest-value fishing port in England, yet local fishers tell me that they can hardly afford to go out to sea any more because of the extraordinarily high cost of fuel. One is spending an extra £18,000 a week for his three vessels. The smaller inshore fleet is being particularly hard hit. Governments across Europe are supporting their fishers. If the Prime Minister wants growth in every postcode, that means growth for our fishing communities, too, in the places that are literally at the end of the road, where job opportunities are scarce and the fishing industry is crucial. Will his Government commit to supporting the fishing industry, so that our inshore fleet can survive this existential crisis due to the high price of fuel?

I was talking about farming before, but I am going to make the same commitment to the hon. Lady: I will also support our fishing industry, and I look forward to having that conversation with it. We have taken action on fuel duty; obviously, it was frozen in the Budget. I know that there is probably more that can be done, but again, it is really important that we focus on what we can do in the here and now. The Budget did provide help for businesses up and down the country, but we know we need to do more.

Q14. I begin by asking the Prime Minister and, indeed, the whole House to join me in congratulating the Welsh rugby team on beating the All Blacks on Saturday, for the first time in 73 years.In Wrexham, the communities of Coedpoeth and Minera have for months had to put up with illegal waste dumping and non-permitted development. There are 16 similar sites across Wrexham county and hundreds across Wales and the UK. Over 1,000 people have already signed my petition to the Senedd calling for action. Those tipping waste simply ignore Natural Resources Wales notices, and the Plaid Cymru Welsh Government have yet to respond. As a former mayor, the Prime Minister knows that when councils, the police and regulators work together, crime does not pay. Will the Prime Minister urge the Welsh Government to give Wrexham council and NRW the stronger powers that they need?

Yes, certainly, I will congratulate Wales on a genuinely historic victory. Perhaps, in return, the Welsh parliamentary Labour party will congratulate England on their fantastic victory in Spain. On the question of powers, I am talking to the First Minister of Wales about pushing power further down in Wales, in a similar way to what we see happening in England. It has to be a model that is right for Wales, but the offer is on the table to work to put power right down into the communities of Wales. I look forward to working with my hon. Friend on that, and with Welsh colleagues across the House.

Q6. The hundreds of my constituents who work at British Steel Scunthorpe greatly appreciate the support that the Government are giving. Looking to the future, though, the 2,000 acre site, which stretches across the Brigg and Immingham and Scunthorpe constituencies, offers great opportunities for investment and future jobs. Could the Government reaffirm that they consider it a priority location for the strategic sites accelerator programme?

I am very keen to pay tribute to the hon. Gentleman, because I know that he has done a really good job on this issue. I hear that from my Parliamentary Private Secretary, my hon. Friend the Member for Scunthorpe (Sir Nicholas Dakin), who has also worked hard on it. We have common cause here, I believe. The hon. Gentleman mentions the strategic sites accelerator, which is backed by £700 million and is open for applications. We would absolutely encourage an application from his area.

My constituent Keaton Slater was just 12 years old when he was killed by a dangerous driver, who then fled to Latvia. His family spent more than two years seeking an extradition. Does the Prime Minister agree that when offenders flee the country and extradition is required before they can face justice, that should be taken into account in sentencing guidance and sentencing decisions?

I understand that this case has been referred to the Attorney General’s Office, and I will ask for an update on it myself. If appropriate, I will raise this with the Latvian Prime Minister when I next see him. I credit my hon. Friend for raising this issue, and if she would like to discuss it further, I would be available for that.

Q7. In August, it was reported that Leicestershire police have been issuing dual identity warrant cards for gender-fluid officers. At a time when women in Leicester East and across the country are rightly demanding basic common-sense protections and single-sex safeguards, this sends entirely the wrong message about operational priorities and public trust. The Government were built on a pledge to halve violence against women and girls, so can the Prime Minister explain why he is yet to reaffirm that commitment, and will he ban these absurd dual identity warrant cards today?

I have said repeatedly that the Government I lead will be relentless in tackling violence against women and girls in every single respect, and the everyday harassment that people are on the receiving end of. I am not aware of the case the hon. Lady raises, but I will look into it.

It was a pleasure to welcome my right hon. Friend to my constituency recently. We sat down with the Single Homeless Project, a wonderful and vital service. We spoke to women with lived experience, and heard about the difficulty identifying women who are rough sleeping, as often their homelessness is out of sight and hidden away. Will the Prime Minister support a dedicated women’s census, so that we can understand the full scale of the issue and ensure that support reaches those who need it most?

Credit to my hon. Friend for the work that she does on this issue and on homelessness. I remember well the meeting we had at the Single Homeless Project. It is an amazing organisation that made the point that women’s homelessness can often go missed and does not get the same attention, so I support what she is saying on a local census. We have a drive to end rough sleeping; that is a personal priority for me. I will make sure that there is the right focus in councils across the country on women’s homelessness as well.

Q8. Meur ras, Mr Speaker. Although I was disappointed that my private Member’s Bill, which puts first homes before second homes, was postponed last week, the campaign for housing justice will continue. Will the Prime Minister meet me and the supporters of the Bill to consider the extreme housing challenges in places like my west Cornwall and Isles of Scilly constituency, and in particular the unintended risk of the recent Budget further rewarding second home owners who holiday-let their properties to obtain multimillion-pound tax benefits—tax benefits, of course, that the Tories do not take into consideration? This is public money that could be far better spent, not least on helping those in particular housing need.

I did ask officials to look seriously at the hon. Gentleman’s private Member’s Bill. It was felt that it was not the best way to address the issue, but we do not disagree with what he is trying to do. I will ensure that the Housing Minister meets campaigners, as the hon. Gentleman requests. We will see if we can come back to the issue with a workable solution.

Further to the very important points made by my hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce), the last few weeks have shown us that there is a critical need to hold powerful men to account when they abuse their position, and to tackle the manosphere, but also to create and support alternative places for our young men and boys, with humour and love. Will the Prime Minister therefore join me in thanking Suggs from Madness, Rowan Williams, Ella Vaday from “Drag Race”, Richard Herring and Sanjeev Bhaskar for being willing to start that conversation on International Men’s Day, this Sunday, at the Soho Theatre Walthamstow? It will show that it must be love, not hate, that leads the relationship between men and women in the future.

I am more than happy to send that message to all those people, who are brave for stepping forward. We must address this issue of power imbalances in workplaces; in the media industry, as the Culture Secretary is doing; and in our own workplace. There is an obligation on every single Member of this House, as I said, to be relentless in tackling violence and sexual crime against women and girls.

Q11. Habibi is the pseudonym used by a troll on the internet. This individual has been identified as Ben Tait, who has deep connections in the House of Lords. He has smeared and attacked Members in both Houses, as well as prominent public figures. We all enjoy freedoms afforded to us by democracy, but when those freedoms stray into inciting religious hatred against Muslims and Jews, or inciting violence, such as driving a van into a serving MP’s constituency office, every Member should condemn such abhorrent behaviour.
