Marriages within prohibited degrees, including incestuous ones between uncle and niece or aunt and nephew, were made automatically void by the Marriage Act 1835, nearly two centuries ago. Our modern legislation explicitly outlaws incestuous sexual activity between uncles and nieces or aunts and nephews. When Parliament has rightly drawn those boundaries, surely it is right that our welfare system should uphold them. I have brought to the House this Bill, backed by the Leader of the Opposition and the shadow Work and Pensions Secretary, my hon. Friend the Member for Faversham and Mid Kent (Helen Whately), to end recognition of polygamous marriages and put it beyond doubt that overseas incestuous marriages cannot and should not be recognised in our welfare system for social security purposes. How did we get here, when such marriages are illegal in our country? How did it come about that we recognise them if they were conducted overseas? The situation developed as a result of common-law rules and decisions made by courts. As in so many other areas, these decisions were probably well meaning, but this situation is completely inimical to a cohesive society and a coherent polity, and anathema to the values of our country. The beautiful thing about our country and Parliament is that we are sovereign; Parliament can legislate to remove uncertainty and revoke common law where it is wrong. Parliament must take responsibility. We decide what our welfare system recognises, and that is the signal that this House should send, clearly and explicitly, through the law of this country. Time and again, I meet constituents in Basildon and Billericay who need support, or those on the other side, who are being squeezed more and more by higher taxes—people who work long hours, but who see their bills rise as they try to support their family. Why are my constituents not more deserving of our attention? Instead, we are bundling cash, first class, to men with multiple wives, and to those who made an uncle-niece marriage overseas. Let us take a sensible step to address the issue in a way that recognises the values behind our benefit system, which is rooted in compassion and the principle of contribution, and in the values of our country. It is not there to pay for cultural practices that are illegal here. Surely it is insane that our welfare rules make special provision for men with many wives. I believe that Parliament should put the matter beyond doubt. I hope that the House supports the Bill, and that the Government do not back away from it, but instead support it on its Second Reading on Friday 13 November. Question put and agreed to. Ordered, That Mr Richard Holden, Mrs Kemi Badenoch, Helen Whateley, Claire Coutinho, Laura Trott, Tom Tugendhat, Katie Lam, Dame Rebecca Harris, Joy Morrissey, Andrew Griffith, Nick Timothy and Neil O’Brien present the Bill. Mr Richard Holden accordingly presented the Bill. Bill read the First time; to be read a Second time on Friday 13 November, and to be printed (Bill 163).

title: Topical Questions
turns: T1. If he will make a statement on his departmental responsibilities.
The Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice

Since the last Justice orals, I have sworn my oath as Lord Chancellor to uphold the independence of the judiciary and mark the opening of the legal year. We continue to clear up the mess left by the previous Conservative Government as we build a modern justice system, delivering the fast and fair justice that victims deserve. Our landmark Courts and Tribunals Bill has had its Third Reading in this place and is progressing in the other place, and we continue our action for victims by rolling out specialist rape and sexual offence courts to improve their experience of the justice process. We are launching Respond, the latest phase of our Enough campaign, and we have announced legislation that will help thousands of young adults who lack mental capacity to benefit from their child trust fund savings. I had the honour of representing the UK at the United Nations General Assembly, reaffirming our commitment to the international rule of law. Let me also take this opportunity to congratulate the UK’s candidate for the International Court of Justice, Professor Dapo Akande, who has been elected to the Court; the UK is back on the world stage and I wish him well in his new role.

Despite the Planning Inspectorate recommending refusal, a third prison is under construction at Ulnes Walton in my South Ribble constituency. Unfortunately, the local community has been hugely impacted by issues around access, highway safety and vehicle movements—the very reasons refusal was originally recommended. Will the Minister please meet me as a matter of urgency to discuss how we can develop solutions for the benefit of the Ulnes Walton community?

The importance of new prison places in this country has been well rehearsed over the last 45 minutes. Nevertheless, I believe strongly that we must be good neighbours, both in the operation of prisons and in their construction, and I also feel very strongly about our liability through our contractors. I believe that I am already planning to meet my hon. Friend on another important matter, and I will ensure that we talk about this point too, because I want to make sure that we are good neighbours with his constituents.

The ability of powerful men to exert control over and exploit women is again at the forefront of our minds. But it is not just rich and powerful men: we recently debated in this place a petition by Paris Shears, who campaigns against coercive and controlling behaviour. During the debate, the Minister refused to give Paris the common courtesy of explaining whether those convicted of coercive and controlling behaviour are eligible for Labour’s early release programme. Can the Justice Secretary show proper respect to Paris and other victims and at least answer that question now?

I am slightly surprised that the hon. Member has taken this tack. He will know that, alongside the announcements we made in the summer, we published precisely which offences were in scope and not in scope for the progression model, so all I can suggest is that he refers to that, as he could have done for the last six weeks.

It is obvious that the Minister does not want to put on record and own up to the fact that those convicted of coercive and controlling behaviour are, according to our understanding, eligible for early release. [Interruption.] The Minister says from a sedentary position that I should read; I will pass it on to Paris that he feels she should have just read. The public want clarity from Ministers on these complex matters, and it is right for me to ask this question. How can the Minister justify releasing those convicted of coercive and controlling behaviour early when we know that perpetrators who go on to commit offences like rape often start out with lower offences, like common assault, coercive and controlling behaviour and grooming. We know the patterns that emerge over time. Surely we should tackle this at the first instance and not let these people out early.

I am slightly surprised that the hon. Gentleman thinks that making a commencement order for legislation in this place is not putting something on the record. I find that hard to understand. He asks how we got into this situation. I gently point him towards the hon. Member for West Suffolk (Nick Timothy), the Leader of the Opposition and the shadow Minister for policy development, the hon. Member for Harborough, Oadby and Wigston (Neil O’Brien), all of whom admitted that they did not build enough places. He talks about exemptions, but I note that their early release schemes have no exemptions.

T2. Members across the House will remember the desperate prison capacity situation back in July 2024, when fewer than 100 prison places were left on the whole estate and the whole justice system was on the brink of collapse thanks to the shocking incompetence of the Conservative party. Will the Minister update the House on the progress made on fixing that Tory mess through the Government’s prison rebuilding programme?
The Minister for Prisons, Probation and Reducing Reoffending

We are making good progress. Around 3,300 places out of our target of 14,000 have been delivered since we took office, including a 170-place refurbished wing at HMP Norwich, which opened in June this year, bringing these places into the 21st century. We are also bringing forward £110 million from existing budgets to deliver additional prison places even faster. We are determined to clean up the mess that the previous Government left us and to build a criminal justice system that is fit for today.

T4. Two months ago, I wrote to the Secretary of State asking him to confirm how many prisoners will be released under the Government’s early release scheme untagged because they cited homelessness or mental health issues. I got a reply from his Minister saying that she could not answer the question because the scheme did not start till 1 October, but her letter was dated 4 November—five weeks later. Will Secretary of State tell me today how many have been released early untagged for those reasons?

The hon. Lady will have heard me say two things in this session: first, that there is for the first time a presumption on tagging and, secondly, that we will release full data so that Parliament can scrutinise it in the normal way. I suggest that she waits for that release.

T3. In response to written questions last month, Ministers claimed that Serco has met every single key performance indicator since March, yet the Department’s figures from 30 September show that 15% of those with a monitoring order had no tag fitted, and that 1,309 had been out of contact for 28 days or more. The Department will not disclose what penalties Serco has paid, but has agreed £48 million in extra payments. With up to 22,000 more people due to be tagged next year, how is that value for money? When will the Department do away with its poorer performing contractors?

As my hon. Friend will know, the contract with Serco was entered into by the previous Government. Serco’s KPI measures include whether installation visits take place within contractual timescales, but being recorded without a tag does not necessarily indicate failure; it may be that the individual has returned to prison, or they may still remain within the installation window. That is why we regularly publish the statistics to ensure that they accurately reflect the situation. I will take her other points on board.

T5. We were all disgusted by the shocking details of the Russell Brand court case this week, and we had all seen reporting of the famous man who lost his appeal to remain anonymous, who was today named as David Walliams. One of the most common lawfare tactics used to shut down investigations and block accountability are SLAPP—strategic lawsuit against public participation—orders, which have a chilling effect on media scrutiny and faith in the legal process overall. Will the Minister therefore confirm whether the Government plan to finally listen to the Lib Dems and introduce a comprehensive anti-SLAPP law to stop this harmful practice?

Order. The last question was very long. This is topicals. I have to get all colleagues in, and I am struggling. To help me get through, the questions have to be short, as do the responses from Front Benchers.
The Minister for Courts and Legal Services

The Government recognise the profound financial and psychological impact that SLAPPs have on individuals, and their corrosive effect on our democracy and public discourse. As the hon. Gentleman will know, we commenced the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, and we remain committed to introducing legislation. I recently met the right hon. Member for Maldon (Sir John Whittingdale), and am grateful to him for the constructive discussions that we are having. I will set out the Government’s position on Second Reading of his private Member’s Bill on 27 November.

T6. Twenty-year-old Sophie Brimble was killed when a car driven by her boyfriend crashed into a lamp post at three times the speed limit. I applaud her family, who have worked incredibly hard through their grief, and have put out a petition, which has been signed by more than 100,000 people, to change the law on “unfit to plead”. The driver was deemed unfit to plead at the time because of his injuries; earlier this year, a judge gave him an absolute discharge, deeming him unfit to stand trial again. Will the Minister meet me and the family, and update me on the progress towards changing the law?

I would be glad to meet my hon. Friend to discuss Sophie’s tragic case. The Government agree that the law and procedure on unfitness to plead require updating. We are actively considering how best to take forward the Law Commission’s proposed changes, including modernising the legal test for unfitness to plead and the issue of whether courts should have a broader, more flexible range of disposals when dealing with such cases.

T7. Last week the Government announced their Visitor Levy (England) Bill, which will create a number of new offences, including a 14-year maximum prison sentence for deliberate evasion of a tourist tax, all while the Government are still releasing prisoners early. Has the Department carried out a justice impact test, and when will the impact assessments be published? What assessment has the Department made of the additional prison spaces that would be needed?

The hon. Gentleman will not be surprised to hear that when any decision is taken across Government, it is done in the round and we have those conversations with our colleagues in other Departments. Giving local leaders the power to make that decision, if they want it, is important and, of course, if people do not follow it, there ought to be sanctions.

T8. The number of C51 parental order applications has more than doubled in the past decade, and with more applications involving international surrogacy arrangements, the complexity of these cases has increased. Can the Minister confirm whether His Majesty’s Courts and Tribunals Service has raised concerns with the Department on these increased numbers, and will the Minister meet me and campaigners to discuss the growing concerns?
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Justice

These applications and surrogacy issues raise complex issues around ethics, law and medicine. We have not had those concerns raised by HMCTS, but I am happy to meet my hon. Friend and campaigners to discuss it in more detail.

Last week the Justice Committee heard harrowing testimony about the tragic deaths of 14-year-old Ruth Szymankiewicz, 15-year-old Gabriel Santer and 23-year-old Matthew Caseby from their parents. These are all utterly tragic cases, but only one of them led to a prevention of future deaths case, and even then there is no enforcement of them. Will the Minister commit to reviewing the situation so that when the words “lessons learned” are said, families actually believe them?
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Justice

I welcome this question and the important point raised by the hon. Lady. I welcome the work that the Justice Committee is doing in this space to look at the prevention of future deaths reports to see what more we can do to ensure they are enforceable, responded to and acted upon. The Government are determined to ensure accountability at all levels on prevention of future deaths reports, and I look forward to laying out my position to the Committee soon.

T9. Probation officers like those who work at Harlow probation office do crucial work rehabilitating those who are released from prison and ensuring that our communities are safe. What is the Minister doing to ensure that we recruit more probation officers and to ensure that they have the skills needed to do that vital work?

I pay tribute to our hard-working and dedicated probation staff, including those who bravely intervened yesterday at Manchester magistrates court to tackle an individual with a knife. Probation staff perform vital work in our communities, we owe them a debt of gratitude, and we need more to come and join the team. While we continue to exceed our recruitment targets with almost 1,400 recruited last year and a target of 1,300 in 2026-27, my message is, “Come and join this important service to protect the public and keep communities safe.”

After the sexual predator Russell Brand was convicted last week, the newspapers reported on an injunction brought by him and Jemima Goldsmith against Miss Berki, aimed at stopping antisemitic harassment by Miss Berki. It included a clause, however, that suppressed free speech. Jemima Goldsmith tried to relax that in December, and Brand stopped her. He is still stopping her from doing that. She is a victim of his violence. Can the Secretary of State look at how a convicted criminal can suppress free speech and continue to embarrass his victims?

I want to place on the record my thanks to all the victims of Russell Brand for speaking out so bravely, some of them at huge personal cost as well—that is important for this House to recognise. The right hon. Gentleman is right to raise the issue of super-injunctions, injunctions and SLAPPs, as we have previously heard, being used by powerful perpetrators to hide their abuse in plain sight. I am keen to work with him and anyone else in this House to ensure that these are not abused or taken for granted. He will know, however, that some of these injunctions are independently assessed; it is not for the Government to comment on them. However, I am clear that any action we can take to prevent violence against women and girls should be taken.

T10. Many victims of domestic abuse are unfortunately still falling through the cracks of our justice system as a result of capital means-testing of legal aid. Will the Justice Secretary look to move forward with the recommendation of the Domestic Abuse Commissioner to remove capital means-testing for all victims of domestic abuse going through family court proceedings?

I understand that my hon. Friend is due to meet the Secretary of State to discuss this very issue. It is vital that we support domestic abuse victims with legal aid through the court process. We have already taken steps to extend the equity disregard in the legal aid means test, which means that £100,000-worth of the value of a victim’s home is not considered as part of that eligibility test. It is also the case that the Legal Aid Agency can discount the value of capital that cannot realistically be accessed because of that very abuse. I look forward to discussing this matter with him further.

There is a close association between domestic violence and animal cruelty. My constituent Annette Bramley’s daughter Holly was murdered by a wicked husband. The Government are working on this, but may I ask them to meet me, Annette and others to look at what further steps can be taken to establish that link and do something about it?

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for raising this. Along with my good friend the Member for Newport West and Islwyn (Ruth Jones), I have been looking at what more we can do here. He is right that there is a correlation between animal abuse and domestic abuse, and abuse of individuals in general, and I would happily meet him to see what more we can do to tackle this.

Probation services play a vital role in protecting the public, reducing reoffending and supporting rehabilitation. As the UK and Welsh Governments review probation governance in Wales, can the Lord Chancellor update the House on how he is working with the Welsh Government to better integrate probation with devolved services, to strengthen public safety in communities such as mine in Pembrokeshire?

I met with the Welsh Government yesterday, and we discussed probation. My strong view is that if we are to get the best outcomes for individuals when they leave prison, we need those local services. That might be probation services in this case, but it is also about local authority services, health services and education, to get the best outcomes in exactly the spirit my hon. Friend talks about.

Birmingham and Solihull coroner’s service is still not meeting the expectations of its residents. Will the Minister meet me to see how we could improve the service, which is impacting so many communities?

I am aware of issues with coronial services across England and Wales. I regularly meet the chief coroner to discuss this and what more we can do to reduce the backlog. Our coroners perform vital services in their communities, and I want to reassure the hon. Member that the Government are committed to reducing this backlog and giving coroners the support and guidance they need to carry out their vital work.

My constituent Tom Hughes, the owner of Red Dragon’s Vault in Wrexham, has repeatedly had his shop targeted by antisocial behaviour, with objects thrown at the window and customers being subjected to abuse. Rather than responding with anger, he is responding with hope, working with local youth organisations to support young people and provide them with more activities and opportunities. Does the Minister agree that while we must be tough on those committing antisocial behaviour, we must also be tough on its causes, such as the lack of youth opportunity?

I am old enough, just, to remember a former Labour Prime Minister talk about being tough on crime and tough on the causes of crime. That informs our approach to youth justice. We set it out in the White Paper published earlier this year, and we will be making progress on that issue in due course.

Mr Speaker, ask any legal practitioner and they will tell you about the parlous state of our court estate. Can the Minister set out the estimated number of sitting days that have been lost since the last election as a result of emergency repairs across the HMCTS estate?

As the hon. Member will know, we have uncapped the number of sitting days, and it is very rare for sitting days to be lost due to disrepair. But he is absolutely right: the crumbling courts that we inherited were a symbol of a justice system very much degraded by the Conservatives. I am glad that we are reinvesting £287 million in the capital budget, with brand new courts in Blackpool, London and Reading, and we are starting to see our justice system restored to health.

It is not right that children who were once in foster care, children’s homes or semi-independent living accommodation find themselves at the hands of the criminal justice system. In fact, over 50% of children in prison were once being cared for by the local authority. What are the Government doing to identify care leavers and care-experienced people in prison, and how are they working to reduce their reoffending and offending in the first place?

My hon. Friend has raised this issue consistently and has done some really important work on it, both from the Back Benches and in government. In the next few weeks we will publish a protocol on exactly this issue. Before we do so, I should meet her to discuss it in more detail, and I will do so.

Last year the British Horse Society recorded nearly 3,000 road incidents involving horses. However, because horses are classed as property, judges and courts cannot reflect the emotional distress that horse riders have when they lose their animal. Will the Secretary of State meet me to discuss how we can change the law to better reflect the needs of victims?

The hon. Member raises a really important issue. I have taken part in the Dead Slow campaign with the British Horse Society on two occasions. We are a nation of animal lovers, and I do not think that people would see things quite in the spirit that the law always does, so I am interested in having a conversation with him and the BHS to see what might be done.

I strongly welcome the steps that this Government are taking to help young people who lack the capacity to access their child trust funds. Can the Minister outline how many people he thinks that will benefit? What value will that have to families?

We simply would not have got to this point without the almost constant championing of this cause by my hon. Friend, so I am very grateful to her. We estimate that up to 120,000 families will benefit from the changes that we are bringing about with my hon. Friend the Exchequer Secretary to the Treasury. The average amount is £2,600, which will have a transformative effect for many families—I know that for one family in my constituency it means that they can go on holiday for the first time in three years. This is a really important step that this Labour Government are taking.
Victims of crime have asked the Lord Chancellor to publish criminal conviction data by nationality. Will he do so?

The hon. Gentleman knows that that has been a point of discussion in this place on multiple occasions. We are looking very closely at the data to ensure that we are getting it right. In conjunction with the Home Office, we want the fullest amount of data to be available so that we can have a proper political conversation about what it tells us.

When 73% of those released from prison with no home to go to go on to reoffend, the system is clearly setting people up to fail. It is vital that we attack the social and economic causes of reoffending and help people to rebuild their lives. What cross-departmental discussions have Ministers had about improving access to social housing, mental health support and drug and alcohol dependency support?

Many discussions are ongoing. Ending rough sleeping and tackling homelessness is a key priority for the Prime Minister, as he has said. Those who are homeless on release from custody have reoffending rates that are nearly double those of people released into accommodation. We are already working on the national plan to end homelessness, but we are working at pace on a cross-Government basis to ensure that we can legislate for a duty to collaborate and that we tackle the scourge that is homelessness both for those leaving prison and re-entering the community and across the board.

Will the Minister meet me to discuss the possible addition of assault in cases of grievous bodily harm to schedule 5 to the Criminal Justice Act 2003? That seems to be the only pathway to justice for a constituent of mine who, despite being the victim of a brutal attack, saw the case against their alleged assailant withdrawn just days before trial because of the erroneous decision of the Crown Prosecution Service not to offer any evidence in support of prosecution.

I am so sorry to hear of the situation that the hon. Gentleman’s constituent finds themselves in. I would be delighted to meet him to discuss this issue and to see what more we can do to support victims in that situation.

I recently visited Central Jamia mosque in Southall Green, where I heard about delays in the coroners courts system. In particular, the lack of post-mortem scanning machines locally means that people need to drive to Oxford, causing further delays. What work is the Minister doing with the Muslim community and other faiths to allow them to bury family members according to their religion?

I thank my hon. Friend for raising this very important issue. I know that this matter concerns Members across the House and outside this place. I have met representatives from the Muslim and Jewish communities to see what more we can do to help them to bury their loved ones in a timely manner while working with coroners to expedite inquests, and I am happy to work across parties and across faiths to see what more we can do to make that a reality.

The sentencing of Russell Brand yesterday for his terrible violence against women has had people reflecting on a book he wrote several years ago, in which he said that he repeatedly lured his dog upstairs and kicked it down the stairs again. That is just the latest high-profile example of violence against animals being an indicator of someone who will go on to commit violence against women and children. I know that the Minister cares very much about this issue, so will she meet me and relevant stakeholders and researchers to discuss it?

I happily extend to the hon. Gentleman the invitation I gave previously to the right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes), and the commitment I made to look at what more we can do regarding the correlation between animal abuse and physical abuse.

Over 60% of people in prison have speech, language or communication needs. Effective rehabilitation must be holistic. To prevent reoffending and provide support, it is paramount that we address not only the offending behaviour, but the underlying communication, health, education and social needs. What steps is my hon. Friend the Minister taking to ensure that access to speech and language therapists and other allied health professionals is available in prison?

My hon. Friend is an avid campaigner, and with her health background, she is well placed to understand the value of the allied health professionals right across our society. That applies to prison in the same way. Obviously, there is a commitment that any person in prison will have the same access to treatment as they would if they were on the outside, which is vital if we are going to achieve the outcomes we want: reducing reoffending by giving people purposeful activity, education opportunities and the ability to gain skills, so that they can lead a more fulfilling life on the outside. I will certainly take away my hon. Friend’s suggestion about what more we can do.

Earlier today, I heard from the head of the Prisoners’ Education Trust about the chaos and cuts caused by new education contracts. In Scotland, scandalously, all prison education is delivered by a private company owned by a US-based venture capitalist. Surely it is time that we take that service in-house for prisons across the United Kingdom and prioritise rehabilitation, not private sector profits.

My hon. Friend is right that education in prison is vital to rehabilitation; it provides hope for an alternative future, and engagement with education is proven to reduce reoffending by up to nine percentage points. We are determined to modernise the prison education, skills and work system. We want a joined-up system that maximises opportunities to support prisoners to progress. We recognise that there have been challenges with rising costs, and we are working at pace to ensure we deliver an education system that works for all.

title: Reading for Pleasure
turns: We now come to the Select Committee statement on behalf of the Education Committee. Helen Hayes will speak for up to 10 minutes, during which no interventions may be taken. At the conclusion of the statement, Members may ask questions on the subject of the statement; they should be brief questions, not full speeches.

I am grateful to the Backbench Business Committee for granting time for this statement on the Education Committee’s fifth special report, “Reading for Pleasure: Government Response”. Select Committee work is a privilege. We hear hard evidence about systems that have failed and opportunities that have been lost. However, scrutiny is not only about finding fault, but about finding what works and ensuring it travels further. This inquiry gave us that chance, and it offered something that is rarer than it should be in public policy: joy. Witness after witness in our inquiry described reading as something that brings joy to life. Former children’s laureate Frank Cottrell-Boyce told us that in education, we can teach children all the steps, “but the important thing is that they dance.” He urged us to encourage policymakers to “prioritise the pleasure before you get into the learning”. The children we spoke to, including at our World Book Day roundtable, told us that reading helps them “escape from stress”, lets them “enter a whole new world full of new adventures”, and makes them feel “free”. I am sure that every one of us in this Chamber can remember a first book that did that, a torchlight under the covers, a library card, or a character who inspired us or made us feel less alone. Matilda found her refuge in the village library; Alice followed a rabbit down a hole and never looked back. Millions of children have since picked up a book and found a whole world that they had not known existed. That is what our report is about. Reading for pleasure is not an optional extra to be squeezed in once the serious business of education is done. The evidence was remarkably consistent: children who read for pleasure do better at school, develop stronger language and communication skills, enjoy better wellbeing, build empathy and understand the world more deeply. One witness described it as a form of preventive medicine. When we published, I said that if a miracle medicine that improved educational outcomes, built empathy and widened horizons existed, we would want every child to have it. Reading for pleasure comes remarkably close and costs a fraction of the price of any medicine. Yet too many children are missing out—and not at random. Children from disadvantaged backgrounds, children with special education needs and disabilities, and teenage boys are the least likely to fall in love with reading. A child’s chance of finding a book they love should never depend on how many books are on the shelves at home, or on the postcode of the nearest library. That is why, in the early years, joy must lead the way. As Frank Cottrell-Boyce put it, no parent says to a child, “When you’ve learned the offside rule, then I’ll play football with you.” We should not make children earn the pleasure of a story. Our report asked for a national reading guarantee: regular opportunities for every child, whatever their background, to enjoy books, stories and shared reading from birth through to adulthood. We called for stronger support for libraries, better access to books and a long-term strategy to reverse the decline in reading for pleasure. We were clear that that cannot rest on schools alone; it would take families, communities, libraries, charities and Government pulling in the same direction. In the Government response, Ministers have embraced the central importance of reading for pleasure and accepted our underlying ambition. I welcome the support for local areas through Best Start family hubs, and I welcome the National Year of Reading and its encouragement for schools to share best practice. I pay tribute to all the organisations involved in the National Year of Reading. I also welcome the work to explore how successful primary school reading culture programmes might be taken into secondary schools, and I welcome the early results. More than 2 million children have taken part in National Year of Reading activities, and there are encouraging signs that children’s enjoyment of reading may at last be starting to recover after years of decline. The Government deserve every credit for that. However, if I may stretch a literary metaphor a little further, this should not be the final chapter. It should be the opening volume of a much longer series, because on the structural questions—the things that would make the change last—the Government have so far closed the book. They have not accepted a national reading guarantee, they have not committed to making libraries in secondary schools a statutory requirement, and they have not agreed to restore funding for public libraries or to provide dedicated outreach officers for library services. I understand, as does my Committee, that the Government have many hard choices to make. Our report was written in a constructive spirit, and I am pleased that the response was too, but there is a difference between a campaign and a commitment. A year of reading is a wonderful thing, but a generation of readers needs infrastructure, with books in every school, a library in every community that is open and staffed, and someone whose job it is to bring a reluctant reader through the door. Oliver Twist famously stood up with his empty bowl and asked for more. Today, I am asking the Government to be even bolder. We are not asking for a handout, but for the things that will make the gains of this year stick. Nowhere is that more important than in secondary school. The Government have spoken rightly about a richer and more engaging educational experience for young people in their teens. Reading for pleasure should sit at the heart of that promise. We know what happens otherwise: children who leave primary school as enthusiastic readers drift away in adolescence, just when they need books most to understand themselves, to understand other people and to find their place in the world. Every parent in this House, including me, knows the child who stops reading at 12. We cannot afford to let the good work of primary schools be lost between years 6 and 9. A school without a library is a story with its middle chapters torn out. The National Year of Reading has generated real momentum. Schools, libraries, charities, authors and publishers have rallied behind a common cause. Teachers have adapted their practice, families have engaged and young people have taken part. The challenge now is to stop that momentum fading when the year ends. Campaigns end; commitments last. This is about far more than books. Reading for pleasure can be a golden ticket for young people who have become disengaged from education, or who struggle to see themselves in our traditional measures of success. It is about literacy and communication, about mental wellbeing, about empathy and understanding, and about social mobility and life chances. The witnesses reminded us again and again that children cannot fall in love with books they have never held. Access matters, opportunity matters, encouragement matters and, above all, joy matters. To become lifelong readers, children must first discover that reading can be enjoyable, exciting, comforting, challenging, inspiring and fun. That is why reading for pleasure deserves a sustained national commitment long after the National Year of Reading has ended. Finally, I thank everyone who contributed to our inquiry, particularly the children and young people who shared their experiences so openly. The Committee will continue to work constructively with Ministers, educators, librarians, charities and the wider literary sector. There is still more of this story to write. The Government have turned the page, and the early signs in the early years and primary schools are good, but if Ministers are serious about reversing the decline in reading for pleasure, they must have the boldness to carry that momentum into secondary schools, libraries and the structures that will sustain it. Let us not end on a cliffhanger, but give every child in this country the joy of reading and the lifetime of benefits that comes with it.
Mr Swallow, you seem to have some special privileges. [Laughter.]

I thank Mr Speaker for delivering my opening speech for the International Men’s Day debate that is to follow this statement. It is testament to how important he knows the issue is. On reading for pleasure, will my hon. Friend join me in paying tribute to the immense legacy of Dolly Parton and all she did to support children’s literacy? Our report highlighted the work of the Imagination Library. I am sure that she will join me in welcoming the funding for charities, including the Imagination Library, in the Budget.

I thank my hon. Friend for his question and for the contribution he made as a member of the Select Committee to our inquiry on reading for pleasure. I join him in paying tribute to the late, great Dolly Parton. It is due to her work that every child in my constituency has access to books from birth through her Imagination Library. It has been a transformative programme for millions of children. All of us owe her a great debt of gratitude for that work.

I thank the Education Committee and its Chair for their contribution. As the grandfather of six children, I am very aware of the importance of books. When I was small, we had maybe one or two books, whereas today’s child has maybe a dozen or 20 books. The hon. Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) referred to Dolly Parton. In the world we live in, partnership and how we can do things together is incredibly important. Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library has donated 7 million books to the United Kingdom, and I think almost 300,000 to London alone and 300 million across the world. Is there not an opportunity here to work with the Imagination Library to collectively and collaboratively do something that can benefit all our children? Dolly Parton wanted that, the hon. Member for Dulwich and West Norwood (Helen Hayes) wants that, and so do I.

The hon. Member is right about the need for partnership. Books and literature are the product of creativity. It takes creativity across the whole infrastructure of reading to get the best out of it for every child, and that does involve partnership working. It also involves infrastructure and frameworks from the Government into which that creativity can flow. We called for both of those things in our report.

I want to take this opportunity to welcome the Select Committee’s report and to draw attention and give thanks to Cheshire’s school library service. Not every area still has access to such a service, but my area does. I had the great pleasure of visiting it recently, so I just wanted to highlight for my local schools that it is still there and we absolutely must make use of it. Lastly, I would just like to say a huge thank you to my father, on International Men’s Day, because he took me to the library when I was child, as I take my children now. Truly, reading has been one of the greatest pleasures of my life and that is thanks primarily to him.

I thank my hon. Friend for that lovely tribute to her father. I take this opportunity to extend that tribute to every parent who opens up for their children the whole universe through books. One of the things we call for in our report—we are delighted that the Government have accepted this recommendation—is a real focus on making reading for pleasure an essential strand of the work of Best Start family hubs, so that parents and carers, from the earliest stages of a child’s life, understand just how precious that gift is and also how accessible it is. As Frank Cottrell-Boyce told us, you can read with your child in a book that does not have words in it. Literacy need not be an automatic barrier to sharing the pleasure of bonding with your child in the earliest stages. I join her in paying tribute to school library services, where they still exist. They are a precious resource and play an important role in unlocking the pleasure of reading for so many children.

I thank my hon. Friend and the Committee for their work, and all who contributed to the report. As a former teacher, I have campaigned for decades for children to discover the joy of reading. In Portsmouth we have our very own Dolly Parton in James Ralls from the Victorious Festival. Alongside his wife Terri, he like Dolly has championed children’s love of books, even paying anonymously all children’s overdue library fines—he believes that if you love a book that much, you should keep it. Will my hon. Friend thank James and Terri for all their work not only on the Victorious Festival but in doing what they do for the children in our city? Will she let me know how the Committee will ensure that reading for pleasure becomes a lasting priority, so that every child has the chance to fall in love with books?

I thank my hon. Friend for her question and for her tribute to James and Terri for everything they do—it is a huge and generous gift to my hon. Friend’s city, and a great blessing, I am sure, to so many children in Portsmouth. Through our report, we set out, based on the evidence, what we believe the infrastructure looks like to ensure that that love of reading can be extended to every child across the country. I think for all members of the Committee who were a part of the inquiry, that became a burning passion—if it was not already, it certainly was by the end of our inquiry. This is certainly an area the Committee will continue to pursue and we will continue to hold the Government to account on going even further than they are already.
I call Harlow’s top teacher, Chris Vince.

My hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) might be Mr Speaker’s favourite, but—[Laughter.] I’m just saying. I thank the Education Committee and its Chair for all their work on this really important issue. Books teach us so much. I have recently learnt that you should not invite a tiger in for tea, however polite that tiger might be, that you should never feed chocolate cake to a hungry caterpillar, and more importantly, that a stickman is definitely not a stick. I have not got Harlow into this question, so I apologise. Does the Chair of the Education Committee agree that reading to our children can and should start from day one, and that we also need to encourage parents to get off their phones and into a good book?

My hon. Friend is right that reading for pleasure should start from the earliest days, weeks and months of life, because it is also a precious opportunity for parents, grandparents and carers to bond with their children—the evidence is really clear on that. Everybody can enjoy the pleasure of those children’s stories, which help all of us to unwind and connect with our babies and children. It is a precious thing. My hon. Friend is also right to say that this is an effort that involves everybody, and that it is for parents to model good behaviour to their children with regard to phones.

title: International Men’s Day
turns: I call Peter Swallow, who will speak for up to 15 minutes.

I beg to move, That this House has considered International Men’s Day 2026. I thank all colleagues for being here today on International Men’s Day for this important debate, I thank the Backbench Business Committee for granting it, and I thank Mr Speaker for helping to get my speech into my hands. I am honoured to be opening the 11th Backbench Business debate to mark IMD. Since 2015, Members across the House have used this debate to highlight persistent issues facing men and boys in this country in the spirit of bipartisanship, from mental health to parental leave, missing only a single year—2019 —because of a general election. This might be International Men’s Day, but what we talk about in today’s debate affects each and every one of us. We still see gender disparities in almost every walk of life, whether that be in outcomes at school, progression in the workplace, or caregiving and responsibilities at home. When fathers are unable to take more than two weeks of paternity leave, it is not only men who suffer, but their partner, who has to shoulder the lion’s share of caregiving while, in many cases, recovering from the physical challenge of giving birth, and their child, who is deprived of vital time with their father in those crucial first weeks of life. When boys, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds, leave school without the qualifications they need to get on in life because the education system has failed to meet their needs, the impact is not confined to their future, but shows up in the welfare system, in our mental health system and, too often, in our criminal justice system.

I commend the hon. Gentleman for introducing this debate. He is absolutely right to underline the issue of mental health. The stats in Northern Ireland are incredible: we face a devastating mental health crisis among our men, with official figures showing that nearly eight in every 10 suicide deaths are male. Suicide remains the leading cause of death for men under 50; too often, stigma and silence prevent our young men from reaching out before it is too late. Does the hon. Member agree that the Government must work closely with the Northern Ireland Executive and grassroots community groups to deliver accessible, targeted mental health support so that no young man feels he has to suffer alone?

I do. I thank the hon. Member in particular for raising the important role of community groups, such as Andy’s Man Club, which works tirelessly in Bracknell and across the country to provide an opportunity for men to share their mental health challenges in a way that works for them. I also pay tribute to the fantastic men’s shed in my constituency, which again works to provide men with a place to share how they are feeling that day, often in a way that does not centre and focus on mental health, but that still includes it as an important part of its function. The voluntary sector does so much to support the health services in this country, and we can never thank them enough for that. When men feel that they are not being heard and disengage from seeking help, the tragic impacts of that disengagement can, and all too often do, reverberate out, affecting and impacting those around them. Confronting what it means to be a man in this world means confronting issues that go right to the heart of some of the most serious and difficult challenges we are grappling with as a society. I want to acknowledge that we are having this debate at a time when we are again asking questions about how cultures of misogyny and violence against women and girls continue to be perpetrated, particularly among those with power and influence in our society, but also behind closed doors in households across the country and, as we are increasingly seeing, online. International Men’s Day gives us an important opportunity to be very clear: a world in which we do not seriously reckon with both what it currently means and what we want it to mean to be a man or a boy today is a world that fails us all. We should not be mealy-mouthed in calling out violence against women and girls and sex-based crimes. We can, and should, tackle these issues head-on. Of course, we should also recognise and commit to supporting the male victims of domestic violence and sexual assault; these are men’s issues, too, and we need to be honest about that. But whatever difficult topics we discuss in today’s debate, International Men’s Day is also an opportunity to celebrate the many positive contributions that the men in our lives make. Last year’s debate saw many Members doing so with that purest of things: the dad joke. Not to be outdone, I have asked my own dad for his very best, or should I say worst, examples. I stand ready to take an intervention on this one, if anyone happens to know the answer. Can anyone tell me why the French have only one egg for breakfast?

Absolutely. I will let the Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations know that he can use that at tomorrow’s summit. I know personally the importance that a male role model can have. Like many men, my dad worked long hours to support our family, but when my mum died when I was a teenager, he took time away from work to finish raising me, and to support me through that loss. That is something for which I will always be grateful. I recognise the privilege we had as a family that allowed him to do that. Not all fathers can be there for their families in times of need, even if they want to be. That is especially true at birth. We know that a father’s presence in the first few months after childbirth is indispensable. Greater involvement by a father in a child’s life improves a child’s cognitive and emotional outcomes, and it is linked to lower levels of post-partum depression in partners and better mental health for fathers. That is without mentioning the wider benefits for the economy and improvements to gender equality in the workplace. Why, therefore, do around a third of men take no leave at all when their baby arrives? Statutory paternity leave is not long enough and does not pay enough. By failing to give men the security that they need to be with their family at the start of a child’s life, we are locking them out of the most important job they will ever have. We are also reinforcing gender roles that we claim to have left in the past, and the inequalities that they entrench. This is a question of equality. Office for National Statistics analysis shows that mothers lose around £65,000 in earnings in the five years after the first birth. Let us be completely clear: what locks men out of care-giving locks women out of the workplace. We cannot expect to make progress on one without recognising its relationship to the other. I pay tribute to the many people who are campaigning on this issue for their tireless work, including many Members across this House, the Dad Shift, and many other organisations. I also welcome the Government’s announcement of a new paternity allowance for self-employed dads. With the parental leave review due to conclude soon, I urge the Government to go further and set out a clear route to improving statutory paternity leave and delivering real equality. Empowering men to take the time to be active, present fathers is a structural issue that affects us all and, crucially, we can change it. Young people do not look only to their parents for role models, and I welcome the Government’s national youth strategy, which recognises that every young person should have a trusted adult outside their home. It sets out steps to make that a reality, including by embedding youth workers and professionals in new young futures hubs, and empowering local leaders to provide the support that the young people they work with might need. I take this opportunity to thank all the adult volunteers across Bracknell Forest and the country who work so hard to provide opportunities and support for our young people, including in the cadets, scouting groups and sports clubs. I pay particular tribute to one youth worker in Bracknell Forest for his years of dedication to boys and girls in our community. Gareth runs The Wayz, a youth club that recently celebrated its 60th year supporting young people in Bracknell, making it almost as old as our town. Gareth actually went to The Wayz as a young person, and he has dedicated his life to supporting some of the most vulnerable, hard-to-reach young people in our community. Every time I see him, he tells me about a new project to reach more kids and offer them support. There are Gareths in every town in Britain, working tirelessly to support young people and to be that trusted adult.

The hon. Gentleman has referred to a number of organisations, and we congratulate them all, but there are a couple that he has not spoken of: the Boys’ Brigade and the Campaigners, which are found in my constituency of Strangford and across Northern Ireland. Those Church-oriented and faith-based groups ensure that young people are given the leadership and encouragement that they need. Does the hon. Member recognise that, too?

I am happy to recognise that; it is so important. I have frequently made the point that we need a range of opportunities for young people to engage with youth services, because what is right for one will not be right for another. It is so important that we take a holistic approach. That is why it is so fantastic to see the Government’s enrichment entitlement for young people. Not everyone will be lucky enough to have a man at home whom they can trust and turn to, but they should be able to look to someone like Gareth, or other inspiring leaders in the wider community.

As my hon. Friend knows, like him, I used to be a teacher. I will not comment on where I ranked among teachers in Harlow, but Madam Deputy Speaker was kind about that earlier. I was 22 years old when I became a teacher, and I found it daunting that young men in my class saw me as a father figure; I certainly did not feel ready to be that. Does he agree that it is important that as well as having male teachers as role models, we have role models in the community? I will quickly plug groups in Harlow, including the sea cadets and the air cadets, that provide that leadership—that parental substitution, I might say, but perhaps that is unnecessary—in the community.

My hon. Friend is so right. I want to focus a little on teachers, because they have an important part to play. Only about 24% of teachers in England are men. The shortfall is particularly acute in early years and primary education, which is a time when growing numbers of boys and young men turn to social media and the manosphere for role models. If we do not want young, often vulnerable, men turning to the Andrew Tates of this world when they are feeling isolated, we need male role models in schools, youth services and the community—leaders who can give them a different perspective on what it really means to be a successful man. With Alan Milburn’s report fresh in my mind, it is important to highlight that more young men than women are not in education, employment or training, and that outcomes at school for boys, particularly white boys, continue to lag behind those of girls. Boys are also more likely to be excluded from school, and the review’s interim report found that exclusion was a strong predictor of becoming NEET. These are complex issues, but if we do not want young men who are feeling vulnerable or isolated to disengage from their education or turn away from the world and towards the seductive and easy answers of the manosphere, we must face up to these challenges and do whatever it takes to ensure that school speaks to and engages boys. Between family, schools and local youth groups and clubs, we can build a safety net that ensures that every young man has somewhere to turn and someone to look up to. Landmark longitudinal research by the Australian Institute of Family Studies found that more than one in three Australian men commit intimate partner violence in their lifetime. It also found that men who felt strongly that they had a quality relationship, marked with affection, with a father or a father figure during childhood were 48% less likely to report ever having used intimate partner violence. Men who reported high levels of social support were also less likely to report using intimate partner violence. Men with moderate or severe depressive symptoms were 62% more likely to use it than those without such symptoms. Violence against women and girls is a men’s issue, a health issue, and something that we as men, and as politicians, can prevent, but not if we do not have the right role models for young men, and the right support to enable men to be those role models. There is another difficult truth that we have to confront: suicide remains the leading cause of death for men under 50 years old. While the suicide rate for women has almost halved since 1985, for men it has reduced by only 7%. There is a wider context, too: men in the UK have a lower life expectancy than those in many OECD countries, and are more at risk of heart disease, cancer and substance abuse. I welcome the men’s health strategy—the first of its kind. It is a real step forward in recognising that there are issues in men’s health that require attention, and in setting out a clear plan to address them. It is important to highlight that the strategy explicitly recognises the relationship between challenges for men’s mental health and their physical health, and the impact that can have on those around them. It draws wider connections to ongoing plans and projects across Departments, including the NHS 10-year plan and the national youth strategy, as well as legislative changes, including the Employment Rights Act 2025. In this context, I welcome the announcement this morning that the Government will convene a summit on men and boys in the new year, which will ensure that we continue to draw together the work being done across Departments to deliver on this important mission. That is exactly the holistic view we need to take, so I thank the Government for their work up to this point, and urge them to outline a comprehensive men and boys strategy as quickly as possible. Preparing for this debate was complex, in part because of the wide range of issues that I wanted to touch on and do justice to, but also because pitching this conversation can, at times, feel difficult. It is a conversation about men, yes, but not just about men. It is a conversation in which we say clearly that men must take responsibility for their part in ending the cycle of violence, and for being there for one another, but we must also recognise that we all play a role in building a world that makes that more possible. These are not contradictions, but they are complexities. My hope for today is that we have a conversation that confronts them bravely and paves the way for a fairer world for us all. Just before I wrap up, I want to share one more terrible joke, courtesy of my dad. Can anyone tell me what is yellow and dangerous?

I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing this debate, and commend him on his fantastic speech. International Men’s Day is an opportunity to celebrate men and recognise the contribution they make to our families, workplaces and communities, but also to confront some uncomfortable truths about men’s health. Speaking of uncomfortable truths, my eldest daughter recently broke and asked me to stop telling dad jokes. I told her that I completely understood where she was coming from, that it was an important issue that I was determined to do something about, and that I therefore asked for a judge-led statutory inquiry, which I fully expect to report at some point after her 18th birthday. In the meantime, I am attempting to do my bit for Movember. At Prime Minister’s questions yesterday, the Prime Minister offered hope: I still had 12 days to grow a proper moustache. As he delivers growth in every postcode, I will do my best to deliver a little bit more growth in mine. While the ’tache may be failing to live up to expectations, it is at least achieving its purpose of getting people to talk about men’s health. As I said yesterday at PMQs, three in four people who take their own lives are men. Suicide remains the leading cause of death for men under 50. We cannot and should not accept this. Last International Men’s Day, the Government took the important step of publishing a men’s health strategy for the first time. It is important recognition that men’s health needs a proper, co-ordinated response. The £3.6 million investment in neighbourhood-based suicide prevention for middle-aged men is particularly welcome. Support does not always begin in a doctor’s surgery or mental health clinic; sometimes it begins in a room where men feel comfortable and able to talk. Sometimes it begins on a football pitch, and sometimes it begins over a cup of tea. We are very fortunate in High Peak to have some fantastic organisations that allow for exactly that. Mentell in Glossop and Buxton provides safe, confidential spaces for men to talk. I have seen for myself that the men’s shed in Whaley Bridge provides another way of tackling isolation and bringing people together. I am also particularly pleased that the Minister and the Prime Minister this morning took Andy’s Man Club into 10 Downing Street. I saw this support for myself when I joined one of Buxton FC’s mental health kickabouts last year. Men of all ages and abilities get together for a game of football before heading to the clubhouse for a cup of tea, a biscuit and a chat. Thanks to some very charitable defending, I was even kindly allowed to score a couple of goals. There are many stresses and strains, changes and turning points in our lives that can affect our mental health—debt, insecure work, relationship breakdown, gambling, alcohol, loneliness and housing insecurity, to name but a few. I want to focus on one change that is particularly personal to me: becoming a dad. I remember how overwhelming it was when we had our first daughter. Of course, you want to be there, be involved and do your bit, but you are also trying to work out how to be a dad, how to support your family, and how to navigate all the changes that come with that. If I were asked, I would say that becoming a dad is the best thing I have done and will ever do. But I will be honest, if I were to be asked the same question most nights at 2 am when my two-year-old is point-blank refusing to accept that night time is when we sleep, I might give a rather unparliamentary reply. Whether it is your first child or third child, becoming a dad brings enormous joy, but it can also feel like an overwhelming responsibility. Suddenly there is a little person who depends on you for absolutely everything. Priorities change overnight, and new things have to be learned that are not always easy. Finances come under pressure, which is all the more difficult during a cost of living crisis. What I have found is that every time I think I have cracked it, my children immediately come up with a new ruse to snap me out of my complacency. Despite all that, the evidence is clear that dads do want to be there—they want to be present and involved. Polling for the Dad Shift found that 90% of fathers want to play a bigger part in their children’s lives. That support cuts across political parties, geography and class. This is not some niche middle-class dads thing; it is something that fathers right across the country want. But wanting to be there and being able to be there are two different things. We have a system that too often makes it difficult for dads to take the time that they need—a system that embeds traditional gender roles right from the outset. We have the worst paternity leave provision in Europe: just two weeks of statutory paternity leave paid at a rate less than half the minimum wage. For many families, particularly those struggling with the cost of living, taking more time off just is not financially possible. The figures show the consequences. Government research has found that only 59% of fathers take paternity leave. All too often, that means that mum becomes the primary carer and dads become, like a sous chef, the sous parent who plays a supporting role, not knowing where the nappies are kept or when nap time is. That is no joke. These roles can become entrenched very quickly, and they can create tensions within the home, putting additional pressures on mothers and leaving fathers disconnected from family life. The consequences go beyond who changes the nappies. Research cited by the Dad Shift and Movember found that 45% of new fathers experience multiple symptoms of depression during their baby’s first year. Nearly two thirds of recent fathers said they had not felt mentally ready for fatherhood. We also know that 10 to 15 mothers in every 100 experience post-natal depression, with many recovering from childbirth—sometimes major surgery—at precisely the point that their partners have to return to work. The impact can extend to relationships. A survey commissioned by the Dad Shift and Movember found that more than one in three separated parents felt that the UK’s paternity leave arrangements had contributed to their relationship breakdown. These figures should make us stop and think. Of course, paternity leave alone will not solve the mental health challenges facing men and mothers, but it can make a difference at one of the most important and vulnerable points in family life. It gives dads time to find their feet, build a bond with their children and support their partners through one of the biggest changes in their lives. It gives families a better chance of sharing the responsibilities of parenthood from the beginning, and it gives fathers the opportunity to establish the kind of relationship with their children that we know they want. I welcome the steps that the Government have already taken. From April, paternity leave became a day-one right as a result of the Employment Rights Act 2025, removing the requirement for fathers to have worked for their employer for six months before qualifying for the leave. In the Budget, the Government announced that eligible self-employed dads will receive paternity pay for the first time. It is shocking that it has taken until now for self-employed dads to have that. Around 80 dads in High Peak could benefit from that provision each year. That is real progress and something we should be proud of, but there is more to do. Two weeks is not enough, and I will continue to campaign for six weeks of statutory paternity leave, properly paid, so that dads are not forced to choose between spending time with their new family and keeping the bills paid. The Government’s parental leave review gives us the opportunity to make that change. Supporting fathers is not just about employment rights; it is about men’s health. It is about giving men the opportunity to be the fathers they want to be, to look after their families and to look after themselves. We should not be setting fathers and families up to fail; we should be backing them to succeed. That means recognising that being a good dad is not just about providing for your family; it is about being there, being present and being involved. When we give dads the time and support to be there from the very beginning, we are not just investing in fathers; we are investing in mothers, in children, in stronger families and in healthier communities. That is something worth doing, not just on International Men’s Day, but every day.

I thank both of the speakers so far, particularly my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow), who gave such a great big overview of International Men’s Day. To start, I will say that, probably like a lot of men, this is a day that has passed me by throughout most of my life. This is not a day that necessarily has the same degree of awareness around it as International Women’s Day. I do not mean that in the way that some very annoying reply guys on the internet say, every International Women’s Day, “When is International Men’s Day?”—it is today; it just passes us by and does not have the same amount of awareness around it. Since becoming an MP, however, the issues facing men in our communities—in my community in Sittingbourne and Sheppey and across every constituency in the country—have really come to the fore. On the Women and Equalities Committee, we have also looked into things such as the manosphere, and the roles, responsibilities and part that men play in violence against women and girls, in the perceptions of women and men online, and in our communities. We have also done some work looking at parental leave around the world and how that impacts. This year has also given me the opportunity to reflect a bit on myself: what it means for me to be a man, the experience of that and how, in the end, being a man is something you just are—if you are a man. You just have it, but it is also something you have to work at. There are challenges to understanding what it is to be a man in the world and what it is to be a man for you. That is true for any adult of any gender: you have to work out who you are and not take on everyone else’s definitions of who you are and who you might be. For men, there are other people’s definitions of masculinity and what that looks like, and other people’s definitions of how you should respond and behave in a society. The core point of that came when I realised I was gay at the age of 11. It hit me as a bit of a bolt from the blue—an instant realisation—and several things flowed from that straightaway. One was about fatherhood. As the eldest child in a large Catholic family, I had always expected to be someone who had kids of my own. Suddenly, there was a realisation: I will not have a female partner, I will not marry a woman and it is very unlikely that I will have children of my own. There was no expectation at the time that gay people would be able to adopt. That came a lot later in my life, at a point when neither I nor my husband were able to take that on. That was quite a big blow; it was quite a big shock. I absorbed it at the time, like a lot of teenagers—well, some teenagers—would, but it has had impacts and it has affected the whole of my life. It has also affected the way that I approach manhood and what being a man is. The other thing that came with that experience was that, at that time, most of the social expectation for gay men was about being effeminate—the sort of Larry Grayson-type presentation of what a gay man would be. That is a great and a fantastic way to be, but it is not quite me. Although I was useless at football and a lot of those sorts of boys’ activities, I was a very geeky boy and I loved stuff like science fiction and transport—other boy activities. Those are all things you have to work out. What does it mean to you as you approach manhood and, as you then progress into adulthood, what are the responsibilities that you take on? How do you avoid the toxicities of manhood that are out there? My response was: I am just me, but I am a bloke and I will be a bloke. On an incidental note, that is why I very much understand how trans people know that they are trans. I know that I am not trans; I am a gay man. It really is just automatic; it does not even take any thinking. If we reflected a little on that in the whole debate around trans and non-binary people, most of us would think, “I never even thought of that.” I had to think of that at that age and that gives me my insights—limited though they are—into some of the challenges that trans people face when they have to identify what they are. Because of the strong expectation at the time around being effeminate, a lot of my generation of gay men totally rebelled and then probably overcompensated. I went slightly to the butch side at a point in my life, which is not something hon. Members would recognise now, but at a point in my 20s, when I was at work, I realised that people kept coming up to me and being shocked that I was gay. That was really quite insulting—in a nice way—but I would say, “I really am. I talk about my boyfriend, but you have not heard that.” Then I realised that no, part of the evolution is about relaxing into yourself and just being the person you want or aim to be. That is all we can ever ask for ourselves. The question for us as Members of Parliament, and therefore as leaders in our communities and societies and as setters of the laws and rules that the country operates within, is: are we creating the right space for our young men to find out who they are? We have seen all the problems. With Alan Milburn’s report this week into NEETs, we see that the world of work is potentially empowering for everyone. Have we set the right framework for that? The barriers that have been there, preventing people from getting to jobs and employment when they are young, have an impact on the type of men that young guys will evolve into. As has been raised a lot already, the issue of paternity pay and parental leave is vital and something we can do to help shape that experience for young men as they come into themselves. As I have said, I do not have kids. I am married to my husband and we still do not have kids. We recently adopted a dog, and that is as close as we have got so far to addressing some of our mutual broodiness. The dog is a retired greyhound and is definitely a teenager: he spends most of his time sleeping, he has learned to get on the bed and now we do not get the bed back, and he spends a lot of time being very surly and boundary testing. That is my little insight into what being a father of a human being might be like. There are some inspirational people I have met in my life—men and women in same-sex relationships—who have children. In my constituency, on the Isle of Sheppey, there is an amazing place called Curly’s Farm, which is a farm school set up by two dads, Garry and Kyle, who have adopted four children, some of whom have disabilities. They recognised that their son, Curly, who did not have a school place that would suit him, really liked being outdoors and engaging with animals, so they bought a farm and they set up an educational space for other children to come to. It is about that level of leadership. When I talk to Garry and Kyle, I can see that they have insights from the challenges they have faced and their unusual route, compared with many people, into parenthood. They have taken that and are helping so many other families with disabilities. In fact, Garry has gone on to be the chair of our local Pride in Place board and we can see all the insights from the lives he has led, from being a father and from coming to fatherhood through that route, and he approaches being chair in a slightly paternal way—in a good way. Those are great ways to look at how to be a man in the world. The options around parental leave are vital, and the Women and Equalities Committee has looked into those. We visited Iceland, where I think they have six months of shared parental leave, and Spain, where they have 19 weeks. They are way ahead of us. There is a strong evidence base for the positive impact that that has on women and mothers, as my hon. Friend the Member for Basingstoke (Luke Murphy) has talked about—sorry, he is my hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce). I apologise; the moustache has thrown me. There is strong evidence from those countries that parental leave has a wider social impact, in particular in helping women, but it also helps fathers on the journey of learning to be a good man. It gives them the space to be a different type of man—the sort of man that I am so glad my father was, a very nurturing man. I therefore very much endorse the campaign for better parental leave in this country. We are not pushing for as much as Spain or Iceland, so it should not be impossible for Ministers to take this on board. Six weeks at 90% pay would be a big step forward. I heartily endorse that. I am very aware that everyone else has done dad jokes, but it seems completely wrong to do one, particularly since I am not a father—a dog dad is not enough. The people who have been asking me to do that are totally barking up the wrong tree. [Laughter.]

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) on securing this important debate. My hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) mentioned people who complain about International Women’s Day. They say, “When’s International Men’s Day?” That happens so often, especially in this House. We are always getting criticised. Where are they? There is not one person on the Opposition Benches for International Men’s Day. [Interruption.] I mean on the Back Benches, not the Front Bench. They complain about International Women’s Day and other things for women. They talk about men as though they care about them, but they do not care enough to come to the Chamber and participate in this debate. That is a disgrace, and I hope that their constituents are watching. International Men’s Day was formally inaugurated by a lecturer, Dr Jerome Teelucksingh, in Trinidad and Tobago. Dr Teelucksingh was driven to promote positive role models. The theme for 2026 is supporting men and boys, and there is nothing more important than ensuring that we are leading on that. Men, especially young men, sometimes feel isolated—as though the world does not belong to them or they are lost in the world.
