It is important for us, as politicians, not to use the insecurity of young men to get them angry. That is the playbook of Reform Members especially: getting young men angry. What do they do with that anger? They use it for their own personal gain. They do not accept or acknowledge that they are having an effect on young men’s mental health. It is important that we set the political agenda, and doing so through this debate is fundamental. Being a man includes protecting women and girls. Real men protect women and girls, and we should teach that. Real men cry. There is all this stuff about keeping calm and carrying on, not accepting that real men cry. Men are criticised or called wusses and all sorts of other things. Real men cry, and that is okay.

My hon. Friend is giving a powerful speech; it is important that we hear voices like hers in debates such as this. My constituent, Leo Shepherd, is a victim of domestic violence, and he has a powerful one-man show that talks about that. Does she recognise the importance of role models, such as Leo, talking about their experiences and encouraging other young men who have been victims of violence to come forward?
Oh, of course—it is just that you did not mention Harlow.
Order. The hon. Member is so experienced that she knows better than to use the words “you” or “your”, because she is speaking through the Chair.

I apologise, Madam Deputy Speaker. I congratulate Leo on the work that he is doing. We must recognise that men also suffer from domestic abuse and domestic violence. Real men wear pink. I have seen some say online that real men do not wear pink. Real men can wear whatever colour they please. Real men talk about their feelings. Real men are woke. I read an article about a Member saying that the new James Bond is going to be all woke. Who cares? Woke is a good thing. When I was a child, my dad was 8 feet tall to me, and when I became an adult, he was still 8 feet tall. I would fix cars with him. He would take me to A&E when I was suffering from period pains, and was being sick and having cramps. He explain to the doctors and nurses, “My daughter is suffering from really bad period pains.” He was not ashamed to talk about periods. That is a real man. On 1 June 2026, the Mayor of London launched a £1 million fund to call on society to act on a lost generation of young men. That is an important fund, and we need to ensure that we activate it. We cannot afford to lose a generation of young men. We need them to be participants, good participants, in society. Research has shown that 15% of Londoners think that young men and boys do not have enough positive role models, and 55% of men say that they face pressure to meet societal expectations related to being a man. That rises to 71% among men aged 18 to 24. Londoners are nine times more likely to say that social media is harmful and harmful to their mental health. We have to get a grip on social media. The algorithms are there to promote an environment of continuous scrolling and of bubbles, such that if someone hates women, they will be put in circles where other people hate women and will think that that is the norm. We have to get a grip on social media and algorithms. In Brent, we have several men’s clubs that tackle how to parent. We have a scheme in which barbers have positive conversations—they have a captive audience when they are cutting hair. That is an innovative way to interject positivity into everyday life. We have heard about suicide in men. In 2022 to 2024, 73% of suicides were, very sadly, men, and suicide remains the leading cause of death in men under 50 years old. These are men who say that they do not know what to do, or that they do not know how to carry on. That is something of an emergency. This Government have done a great deal to acknowledge men and to ensure that we have legislation that showcases the role that men play. That is important. Women live longer than men—it is a fact. We sometimes make light of that when we see some of the stuff that men get up to, especially on social media—we think, “No wonder women live longer.” But it is not just about living longer. Older men often have worse health outcomes, and we have to tackle that. This goes back to men being told to suffer in silence. They do not have to suffer in silence. If they are ill, they should go to the GP. If they have a pain, they should go to the GP. Because men are sometimes reluctant to go to the GP, they get diagnosed later, and so they have worse health outcomes. In Brent, male life expectancy at birth is 80 years old, and for women it is 85 years old. Across London, men do slightly better, at 80.5 years old, and women do slightly worse, at 84.7 years old. The charity Mind reports that 33% of men say that their job has a negative impact on their mental health, that 43% of men regularly feel worried or low, and that young black men are around three times more likely to present as a suicide risk than young white men. The Government’s men’s health strategy is vital when it comes to cancer. The incidence of cancer is higher in males than in females. We have to say to men, “It’s okay to talk about your mental health and your physical health.” It is still a fact—it has not changed—that a woman is killed every three days by a male partner or male former partner. We need men to call this out. These are men in the company of other men. I cannot believe that the statistic has not changed. We have to be in a position where we do not excuse bad behaviour and where we call it out. That is vital if we are to change that statistic and catch these violent men early. I will end, as is customary on International Men’s Day, with a joke. Madam Deputy Speaker, why should you not be friends with a prawn?
Because they are shellfish. I am available for after-dinner speeches.
Real men do wear pink, as the hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler) can attest to. I call Samantha Niblett.

Thank you for calling me, Madam Deputy Speaker, as I furiously update my speech with the latest names suggested to me of brilliant men in my constituency who deserve recognition, but I will start at the beginning. I rise to mark International Men’s Day and, in particular, to pay tribute to some of the remarkable men and groups that have been nominated by people across South Derbyshire for the positive difference they make to our communities. A personal mention for me is Ian Bottrill, who we sadly lost earlier this year. He was my agent in the general election, but he was also my friend. I and many across our community miss him dearly every day, especially those at Sharpe’s Pottery where he was a trustee and those at Swad in Bloom where his personal contribution was so valued. Before moving to south Derbyshire, he dedicated years of his life as a teacher inspiring many and as a councillor, including as leader of Warwickshire county council. I want to give a special mention to the wonderful Antony and Roger Cobley. They have spent a lifetime caring for others, and they still do. They dedicated their lives and careers to nursing and were the first gay couple to foster and change the lives and fortunes of boys whose future was not hopeful based on their start in life. Their ongoing commitment to their sons and their families is wonderful, as we would expect from all good fathers, but they are not just good fathers; they are amazing fathers. Back to some of the people who were recommended by my community, I asked local people to put forward the names of men who they felt deserved recognition, and this is just the tip of the iceberg—it really is. The response was a powerful reminder that across our towns and villages, there are men quietly doing extraordinary things, men who give their time, compassion and energy, and often their own personal experiences, to help others. One name that came up time and again was Alex Garner, who co-founded and runs Our Little Angels. Alex provides invaluable support to families experiencing miscarriage and the devastating loss of a baby or child. His personal compassion, alongside his fundraising efforts, has touched many lives. Supporting families through unimaginable grief requires a special kind of strength, and Alex deserves enormous recognition. Adam Foster, the owner of Nomad Tattoo & Co in Swadlincote, was also nominated repeatedly. Adam uses his business and influence to raise money for good causes, including fundraising connected with hospital dermatology services in Birmingham children’s hospital. He demonstrates how local businesses can be a force for good. I want to recognise Adam Stretton, a military veteran and the head coach and owner of Fight Station in Church Gresley. Through his work supporting men’s mental health, veterans and those facing serious personal challenges, including through a men’s release and recharge programme, Adam is helping men find connection, support and a way forward when life becomes difficult. There are many others whose contributions deserve to be acknowledged. Stephen Morley—I know Stephen personally; he is such a lovely man—owns Swadlincote Electrical and Solar Supplies and will frequently send me a message on LinkedIn just checking that I am okay. He was praised for his work supporting our local community, including frequent and generous donations to South Derbyshire CVS food bank. Graham Knight, who I know personally, too, as a fellow Labour party member, has dedicated nearly 40 years to running Moira Replan. Moira is just outside my constituency, but has certainly served those who live in it. He has served his local community. People have a lot of time and love for Andy Dawson because of the time he has dedicated to parish council work, rugby and charity fundraising, but he is one of those people who does not make a fuss about it, rolls up his sleeves and just gets on with it. Andy Heathfield had a shout-out as well. Loads of people were disappointed when he stepped down from running Melbourne Assembly Rooms because he did such a brilliant job attracting major names to our small and gorgeous market town. Jarno, or Joe, Ward was recognised for establishing ManClub in Melbourne, which provides support for men experiencing mental health difficulties. Matthew Gotheridge, a local councillor, is chair of Kings Newton bowls club and also a fellow director of ManClub. He is another example of a younger man making a substantial contribution to community life. Groups such as GRIT, a men’s talking group founded by Matt Cooke, who I had the great pleasure of meeting earlier this year, also deserve recognition. GRIT provides something vital: a safe space where men can talk openly, connect with others and realise that they are not alone. I must mention Swadlincote Round Table, whose fundraising and volunteering, including their much-loved Santa and Rudolph activities that everybody looks forward to at Christmas, have raised money for local charities and brought communities together. I was particularly moved by the nomination of Jimmy, a 13-year-old volunteer at the Circle Swadlincote family support centre. He is living with autism and ADHD, but it is not stopping him. Jimmy gives his time to breakfast clubs and family walks, while also fundraising for a future volunteering trip to Kenya. He is a wonderful example of compassion and community spirit in the next generation. I want to mention Andrew Gamon at St Helen’s church in Etwall. He organises men’s breakfasts every month between September and March and arranges speakers. Around 30 to 35 men turn up to the safe space that he has created to talk on a whole range of topics. It would be remiss of me not to mention the bean man—this might not be the first time I have mentioned him in the Chamber—Neil Potter, who dresses up as a can of beans and goes collecting food donations in all weathers for food banks. He is locally beloved, and one of his biggest champions is Officer Bob, who is not technically a constituent but is much loved. He was significantly responsible for the creation of a youth club in Repton, and I believe he also has a hand in creating a soup kitchen in Willington, which I think opens in December and which I am very much hoping to dip in to. There are, of course, many ordinary men who simply get on with life while dealing with grief, financial pressures, relationship difficulties and challenges to their mental health. It is impossible for me to mention them all, but I hope that they know that in their Member of Parliament they have someone who cares deeply for them and that if they ever have troubles I could help them with as a Member of Parliament, my office is there for them. I want to give a special mention to something absolutely wonderful. On Sunday I went to the first screening of “Tales from the Magic Attic”. The Magic Attic was created by Graham Nutt back in the ’80s. Burton Mail was going to throw away its archive, and Graham stepped in and said, “You can’t do that! This is our local history. Once that information is gone, it’s gone.” Ever since then, he has built this incredible archive, supported by a raft of volunteers. This tender film is a glorious celebration of the wonderful work done by Graham and the volunteers who help to conserve our local history. I hope to have a screening of it here in Parliament. I want to end by saying that International Men’s Day is not about suggesting that men deserve special recognition at the expense of anyone else—it is not a competition. It is about celebrating positive role models, encouraging men to speak about their mental health, challenging harmful stereotypes and recognising the value of kindness, responsibility and community service. To every man nominated and to the many others whose names may never appear on this list, I say thank you. South Derbyshire is a stronger, kinder place because of what they do, and I hope this House will join me in recognising and celebrating the men of South Derbyshire on this International Men’s Day.

I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for initiating the debate. I stand once more to raise the topic of improvements we could make to paternity leave in this country. This has been spoken about in the Chamber, so I am not going to do the topic to death, but we have made massive improvements by making two weeks of statutory paternity leave a day-one right under this Government, and I am glad that we will be bringing self-employed people within that regime from 2029 onwards. I absolutely want to support and reiterate the calls for six weeks of shared parental leave at 90% of pay. I have long been an advocate for discrimination to cease, and I do not understand why women get 90% of pay for six weeks as standard within a heterosexual couple and men do not. It is not fair or right, and it is time that we resolved it, so please can we look at that again as a Government as soon as possible? Moving on to slightly sadder topics, we have a huge problem with avoidable deaths in this country, particularly in respect of men. Three quarters of deaths on UK roads happen to men and boys; three quarters of suicides, unfortunately, occur among men; and 85% of drownings happen to men. Lots and lots of men are losing their lives in circumstances that should and could be prevented. Road deaths are a huge issue in my constituency. The latest Brake statistics, from 2025, suggest that in my constituency one person is either killed or seriously injured on the roads every single week—every week. This is a massive public health issue that is not being treated with the urgency it warrants. I have a number of suggestions about how this could be improved. We should definitely be looking at average speed checks, and there are plenty of other statistics I could cite to support that, but we also know that rural roads are six times more fatal than motorways—this is a massive problem. The Government published a road safety strategy last year with really challenging targets for reducing the number of deaths on our roads, but I would like to encourage everyone in my community: please get black boxes for young people when you first insure them, whether or not you financially need to, because they train really good driving, and please put young people through advanced driving skills classes. Congleton and Macclesfield Advanced Drivers and Riders will provide that, and we could reduce deaths significantly. I will continue to work with the local authority, the police and literally anyone who will listen, because I consider this to be one of the biggest emergencies in my community. As I said, 85% of drownings happen to men. It is not something that is talked about much, but with the rise in hot weather we saw really large numbers of people drowning this summer. I do not live in a coastal community, but actually the large majority of drownings occur inland. Reservoirs are particularly fatal. We have beautiful meres near me, and we need to ensure that our young people learn to swim. I know there is real pressure on national curriculum time and on resources, but I encourage all my local schools to continue their swimming programmes, and I encourage everyone to think very carefully about the risks before they enter water. We all need to think about how the Government can help more with this. We are encouraging more open water swimming, which lots of people love and is fantastic, but it is in many respects very high-risk, particularly for men. Lastly, I want to talk about online safety. We talk a lot about online safety in respect of children, and I do that a great deal too, but men face particular risks online. The algorithms are pushing videos of people dying towards young men. The Children’s Commissioner has found that young men and boys see, on average, two real-life deaths a month online. We need to better regulate this, but we also need to look at suicide forums. Ofcom recently found that it could take no further steps against a suicide forum that has repeatedly turned on and off its geo-blocking for the UK. There are steps we could be taking, but the current law is not sufficient to enable us to prevent access to some of these forums. Of course, there is a free speech point around any sort of restriction on online matters, but we have forums that are clearly promoting people doing serious harm to themselves. We have to acknowledge that there is a degree of vulnerability in our society, particularly among men, and we have an obligation to look after one another, and not just children. I would like to encourage any men in my community who are suffering with their mental health to seek help, because there is help out there. As we await the publication of the mental health strategy before Christmas, I want to highlight that we need to address the gender imbalances in how problems with men’s and women’s mental health occur. The strategy needs to be alive to that. It must also be alive to the fact that, in my local area, waiting lists for mental health services are simply being shut for significant periods because there is not the capacity to deal with them, and neurodiversity services are simply shut because there is not the capacity to take more people on. I desperately want to encourage men who need help to seek it, because at some point it will become available, but we must not pretend that the services we have are meeting the level of need when they are not. Shutting waiting lists does not make people’s need go away; it just means we do not have an accurate understanding of it. I met with the Samaritans yesterday, and I want to salute their fantastic work. We have multiple mental health groups for men in my community, and I want to encourage men to reach out to those groups but also to contact the Samaritans if they feel they need to. I thank the Samaritans hugely for their work. We have a suicide prevention strategy, which was produced under the last Government; we have a men’s health strategy, which also addresses suicide; and we are going to develop a mental health strategy. All those things need to look through a gendered lens at how we can better support men in our communities. I know that it is now the done thing on International Men’s Day to tell a joke. I think that might land quite badly when I have just been discussing such serious issues, but I know that we do it in support of the paternity leave campaign that the Dad Shift, Pregnant Then Screwed and many others have been running. I want to salute those campaigns once more. We can do better by men in this country in a multitude of areas. We need to recognise that their preventable deaths should be prevented, we need to ensure that men who want to be fathers are fully supported in doing that, and we need to generally recognise the huge amount that men contribute to our society.

I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing this incredibly important debate. I had the honour of leading the debate last year, so I know how much there is to cover. He made a powerful speech and we are all very proud of him. Once again, this is such a powerful debate, and I consider myself very fortunate to be among the Members who have spoken. I would like to begin with the greatest joy of my life: fatherhood. Like others who have spoken, I will give my attempt at a dad joke. Why did the bicycle fall over? Because it was two-tyred! I thought I would get that in early in my speech, to give Members a chance to recover. As we have heard, paternity leave becoming a day-one right and finally being extended to the self-employed are massive steps forward for dads, but fathers are still entitled to just two weeks, on £194.32 a week for those who qualify. A fortnight is simply not enough time to adjust to a huge life event like becoming a parent. Those first days matter for bonding, for mothers recovering from childbirth and for families finding their feet. We talk about parenting being 50/50, but our system makes that incredibly difficult. The physical recovery from childbirth is not shared; the initial burden of childcare is not shared; and when one parent has two weeks away from work while the other may have to put their career on hold for months or even years, the impact on pay and progression is not shared either. Our current paternity leave system risks treating active fatherhood as a “nice to have” and motherhood as an obligation. Office for National Statistics research estimates that women lose an average of £65,618 in earnings over the five years following the birth of their first child. Properly paid, extended paternity leave would give fathers the chance to share responsibility and mothers a fairer chance to return to work and progress. It is about genuine equality, and it shows boys that fatherhood means more than being the breadwinner; it means caring, sharing responsibility and being there. Moving on to boys in education and the online world, 60% of boys are meeting the expected standard in reading, writing and maths at the end of primary school, compared with 67% of girls. In writing, the gap was 11%. It is clear that we need earlier literacy support, targeted catch-up for children falling behind, and better support for pupils with additional needs and many of our white working-class boys, who seem to be at the sharp end of so many statistics. We should also value apprenticeships, technical education and vocational routes as ambitious pathways to success. I welcome the attention that the Government have given to all of the above. We also need to ask ourselves why some of the divisive and reductive voices we are hearing online are finding an audience. If a boy is struggling at school, does not feel that he has a future, does not have positive male role models around him and is looking for somewhere to belong, we should not be surprised when someone online comes along offering him answers. The problem is that those answers can be deeply damaging, and we cannot blame boys for listening to them if we have not done enough to give them a positive and compelling alternative. A report by the Centre for Countering Digital Hate entitled “The Looks Trap” describes the growing world of looksmaxxing—influencers encouraging boys and young men to obsess over their appearance. The report describes boys as young as 13 taking steroids and illegal growth hormones. Others have injured themselves through “bone smashing”—hitting their own faces with hammers in the hope of changing their jawline or cheekbones. We have got to a point where it is easier for boys to find people telling them to take a hammer to their face than to find people telling them to read for pleasure and strive for educational achievement. If that does not ring alarm bells for us as a society, I do not know what will. I wanted to understand this world better, so I set up a TikTok account using the date of birth 10 August 2013. Within four minutes and 38 seconds, without interacting with anything, I was shown a video of someone laying money across a table. I then engaged with similar videos about money, appearance and “bettering yourself”. Quickly, I was shown promises of making $50,000 a month. I came across a term I had never heard before: peniaphobia—the constant fear of being poor or unsuccessful. After about 10 minutes, I searched for “looksmaxxing men” and interacted with the first 20 videos. I then refreshed my “For you” feed. One video asked: “Fraud cases rarely get solved, so what are you scared of?” Others insisted that looks do matter, or offered advice on how to “glow up” using Vaseline or ginger for acne. But then the content became much darker. I came across what I now believe is a trend, in which a post has five photos to swipe through. In each, the first photo reads, “How to clear your mind,” and the first four contain advice such as “Take a walk” or “Have a shower,” but the fifth suggests starvation, self-harm or even suicide. I logged back on after a couple of hours. Immediately, I saw a video asking: “They told you: go to school, get good grades and you’ll be successful. But is that really how it works?” I came across a whole vocabulary: “Chad”, “Stacy”, “alpha”, “beta”, “blackpill”, “geomaxxing” and “statusmaxxing”—a language built on looks, dominance, status and the belief that someone’s appearance or genetics determine their future. I am no Louis Theroux, Madam Deputy Speaker, and this was one very small experiment in the scale of things, but it showed me how quickly a young man can be drawn into a world that offers dangerous answers to some very real and typical teenage insecurities. We need to give boys a sense of purpose, opportunity and belonging. We need to show them that they can be ambitious without being cruel, and successful without having to dominate anyone else. I was honoured to lead last year’s debate on International Men’s Day. Colleagues may recall that I spoke about rape and sexual assault, and in particular about the acute stigma and shame that male survivors often feel. The gravity of sharing my experience publicly for the first time in this House only really hit me after I made my speech. That is probably just as well; otherwise, I might have kept it to myself for a bit longer. In the days, weeks and months following last year’s debate, my eyes were truly opened to so much. I have found that positivity and kindness far outweigh anything else. From the colleagues who gave me a hug after the debate to the hundreds of messages I received from people from all parts of my life, I certainly felt the love, support and validation that I would want every survivor of these vile crimes to feel. We are often told not to read the social media comments, but I admit that I did read some on the news reports that followed. I was blown away by how overwhelmingly positive they were. That should remind us that there are far more people in our society who want to see stigma smashed than there are people who want to see taboos persist. My office received 186 emails from people from across the world, many of them men. Many shared their harrowing experiences of rape, sexual assault and harassment. Some told me that they had never spoken to anyone about these things before, but they trusted me, a complete stranger, simply because I had spoken out. I was moved by every single one. I wish I could have replied to each of them individually, but I thank all of them for their courage, kindness and trust. I have also had conversations with people in my life, including some I have known for many years, who I never knew had endured horrific experiences. Some of those conversations were extremely painful, because they opened my eyes to the sheer number of people who are going through life silently carrying the immense weight of what happened to them. What I have heard over the last year has brought it home to me that the statistics on rape and sexual assault, horrific though they are, are the tip of the iceberg. Many people I spoke to have never reported what happened to them. I say all this not to seek a profile for myself—trust me, on an issue like this, that is the last thing I would want—but to remind us all of three clear truths. The first is that we must continue to break down stigma and barriers to speaking out and reporting, because we must see the true scale of the issue, particularly among men, who often feel a greater pressure, internal or external, to stay silent. The second is that for survivors, simply sharing what happened to them can lift a huge weight; we should make sure that as individuals, and through families, friendship circles, charities and public bodies, we make a non-judgmental space for those conversations. The third is that we must continue to push towards a society in which this evil is prevented, rooted out and exposed to the light of justice. I am proud to be part of a Government who are investing £550 million in victim support over three years, and who have a landmark commitment to halving violence against women and girls, but in recognition of the stigma that men can feel around rape and sexual assault, I hope that we can also recommit to gender-specific support for male survivors. In March last year, the £250,000-a-year funding that the Ministry of Justice gave to the charity Safeline to run the national male survivor helpline—which the Conservatives, to their credit, had funded since 2016—was withdrawn. Although there are fantastic services available elsewhere for all survivors, I know from speaking to some men who have been through this that gender-specific support and advice for men can make all the difference to them speaking out and moving forward. I hope the Minister will be willing at least to discuss that in coming months. International Men’s Day is a chance for us to show up for men and boys—for dads wanting to spend those precious first weeks with their newborn, for young men trying to find their place in a confusing and shifting world, for survivors of some of the most horrendous experiences anyone can endure—and to commit once again to making a real difference to their lives. I thank all hon. Members who have done that today; it is an honour to work alongside them all.
I thank the hon. Member for another powerful speech.

I pay tribute to my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) for his advocacy, his bravery and his continued positivity. It is a real privilege to speak in this debate; I am genuinely proud to be here. I want to give a shout-out to my fellow hon. Members who are men, who make this a very welcoming place for me. I am a proud colleague, partner, daughter, auntie, niece and sister—and, above all, a very proud mum to three fabulous young men. I want to say happy International Men’s Day and “Thank you, and I love you” to all the men in my life and in my city of Portsmouth. I know how important the men in our lives are. I know the difference a good dad, brother, partner, friend or role model can make, and I know that behind every statistic is somebody’s son, dad, brother or friend. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing the debate and for his continued advocacy for men and boys. In honour of the good people of the Dad Shift and all dads across the country—including mine—who remain absolutely convinced that they are funny, I will start with a dad joke. Knock, knock. [Hon. Members: “Who’s there?”] Isabelle. [Hon. Members: “Isabelle who?”] Isabelle necessary on a bicycle? Madam Deputy Speaker, I should warn the House that the quality of these jokes may not improve.

I want to start by reflecting on last year’s debate. Last year I spoke about men feeling forgotten —men who felt that their struggles were not recognised, that they were not being listened to, and that there was not a space for them to talk openly. Something happened after that speech that really stayed with me. I was contacted by men in my constituency who wanted to share their experiences, their worries and, in some cases, things they had not felt able to talk about before. I want to say a genuine thank you to every single one of them: thank you for getting in touch, for being honest, and for trusting me with your experiences and to bring your voices here every day. I listened, and I have not forgotten those conversations. As a Labour MP, I am proud that my Government are listening to me, and standing up for men and boys by enacting policies and legislation that back British men, and men in my city. That is why I wanted to speak in this year’s debate. We cannot simply keep saying that men feel forgotten and leave it there. We have to ask ourselves what we are going to do differently; how we can make men feel heard, supported and valued; how we can make it easier to ask for help; and how we can make sure that our boys grow up knowing that they have someone in their corner. For me, International Men’s Day this year must be about moving the conversation forward—not just recognising the challenges, but doing something about them. Let me be clear: supporting men and boys does not mean taking anything away from women and girls. It is not a competition. I agree with my colleagues who have spoken about sex-based crimes, violence against women and girls, and the vile men who use their positions of power to abuse. I also agree with my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase, who spoke about his dive into the online world: we must challenge all these things all the time. When men are healthier and happier, families are stronger, children do better and communities thrive. As one of the proud co-chairs of the Labour group for men and boys, I have been incredibly proud to help put those issues on the agenda, particularly those around health and work. I recognise the progress that this Government have made. Last year, England’s first men’s health strategy was published, and it was launched at a building site. It marked a really important step in recognising that men’s health is not just about what happens in a GP’s surgery, but about work, housing, relationships, family life and feeling part of the community. However, the statistics remain stark. As we have heard, men in the UK live for an average of four years less than women. In my own city of Portsmouth, suicide is a leading cause of death for men aged 20 to 49, with 24 people taking their own lives every year, 78% of whom are men. Behind those figures are families who have lost someone they love, mums who have lost sons, children who have lost dads, and partners who have lost someone they thought they had their whole life ahead of them with. They are not numbers; they are people. At Movember’s reception at the Labour party conference, I was delighted to hear the Minister announce that the Government will appoint a men’s health ambassador to turn the strategy into real change, and today I was delighted by the announcement that there will be a men’s summit, but we must ensure that men feel the difference in our communities. It is all very well telling men to ask for help, but we need to ensure that the help is accessible, and that they feel comfortable using it. Some of the biggest improvements in men’s health may not necessarily come from policies labelled as health policies. Paternity leave, which we have already heard about during the debate, is a perfect example. Nearly one in 15 new dads experience suicidal thoughts during the first years of fatherhood, and 82% of fathers say that improving paternity leave is the single biggest action the Government could take to support their mental health. Those first few weeks can be wonderful, but they can also be exhausting and overwhelming. There are sleepless nights, financial worries and a huge new responsibility. For too long, our system has effectively told dads to enjoy a few days at home and then go back to work. That is not good enough—for dads, mums or babies. I warmly welcome the Chancellor’s Budget announcement about self-employed fathers. In fact, I did more than warmly welcome it: I might have said a few expletives and then burst out crying when the Chancellor first told me that self-employed fathers will, for the first time, be bought into paternity provision. The reason I was so emotional is that over the past 18 months, tradies have told me their stories about how they cannot be with their families. For me, the announcement was a win. I particularly welcome the change for the people of Portsmouth. We have so many brilliant tradespeople, self-employed workers and small business owners in my city. Electricians, plumbers, builders and taxi drivers should not have to choose between being there for their newborn baby and putting food on the table. It is an important step forward, but leave must be long enough to make a difference and paid well enough for families to afford to take it, because a right that you cannot afford is not much use at all. Talking of tradespeople, it is only fair to include a construction-themed joke: what do you call a man with a spade on his head? [Hon. Members: “Doug.”] What do you call a man without a spade on his head? [Hon. Members: “Douglas.”] I promise there is a serious point behind the jokes. Humour often opens the door to talking about our feelings. We need to talk about what it means to grow up as a boy today. For generations, many men have been brought up to believe that they must be tough, keep their feelings to themselves, earn the money and never ask for help, but that does not make men stronger. Too often, it leaves them isolated. The answer is not to tell boys that masculinity in itself is bad—far from it. There are so many qualities we should celebrate—courage, loyalty, kindness, resilience, responsibility and standing up for others. A good man can be strong and gentle, and confident without being dominating. He can admit that he is struggling without feeling any less of a man. That is the message that I hope my lads have grown up with, but boys need to see those qualities lived. In England, over 600,000—nearly one in five—teenagers say that they do not have a trusted adult they can turn to, and boys without guidance are 50% more likely to drop out of school, enter cycles of crime and be in long-term unemployment. A trusted adult does not have to be perfect or have all the answers; they just need to care, to turn up, to listen, and be there when things go wrong. Sometimes that is a dad, a grandad, an uncle, a teacher, a football coach or a family friend. In Portsmouth, I know how important communities are and how much brilliant work is done by those supporting young people. We need to celebrate them and invest in them. When youth services disappear, they leave a gap, and it is hardly surprising that online influencers can step into that. The so-called manosphere can appeal to boys who feel lonely, frustrated or lost. It offers belonging and answers, but often those answers blame women, promote control and domination, and are unhealthy. We must challenge the platforms, not the lads, but we also need to understand why those boys and young men are listening. If the first time we show an interest in a boy is when we disapprove of something they have watched online, we have probably left it too late. We need to listen to boys about loneliness, relationships, rejection, body image and the pressures they face. We can challenge harmful attitudes while giving them something positive to believe in. Being a good man is not about having the most money or being the loudest person in the room; it is about treating people with kindness and respect, and being somebody others can rely on. International Men’s Day should recognise the challenges men and boys face, but it should also celebrate the enormous contribution they make to this country. I think of the dads getting up for work early, the grandads helping with childcare, the brothers looking out for their sisters, and the men quietly supporting their friends and family. I think of my own sons and the positive relationships they have with their Gramps, whose life is changing right now, and how they concentrate and love each other and their friends. I think of the men in Portsmouth working on building sites and in our port, our naval base, our hospitals, our schools, our shops and our small businesses—good men who work hard, care about their families and want the same things we all want: security, opportunities and a happy life. In last year’s debate, I spoke about men feeling forgotten. This year, I ask us to go further. I want men to feel listened to, boys to feel supported and fathers to be valued. I want every man who contacted me after last year’s debate to know that those conversations mattered, that I heard them and that I continue to hear them. We must turn those conversations into action so men never feel that they have to face challenges alone. Madam Deputy Speaker, I have one final joke: my children asked me once whether I could explain what a solar eclipse was. I said, “No, sun.” [Hon. Members: “Ah!”] Before I finish, I want to say a thank you to Matt and the team at the Portsmouth-based Dadzclub, organised in collaboration with the Forge, for the International Men’s Day awards they are hosting this weekend, which I look forward to attending. I must give a shout-out to my youngest son, who I am proud to say is one of the nominees, and to all of those men in Portsmouth who make our city a better place—you should be proud to be the good men in our lives, you should be celebrated and you should be listened to and supported. I know that every boy growing up in Portsmouth needs to know that he matters, that he has people in his corner and that he never has to face life challenges alone.

You have been practising my name, Madam Deputy Speaker. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing and introducing the debate. It was an excellent contribution, as all contributions from hon. Members have been. I would like to speak about something that weighs heavily on my mind. I am not originally from Clackmannanshire—I first started working in the area in 2012—but not long after arriving, it struck me that it has some of the highest recorded suicide rates in Scotland. As we have heard from my hon. Friends, it is typically men who make up the majority of that figure, and Clackmannanshire is no different. Like many working-class communities, Clackmannanshire has seen a lot of industry leave. Alloa was once Scotland’s brewery capital: there used to be many mills along the Hillfoots and, once upon a time, we had seven coal mines. As we all know, when big industrial employers close, wealth and prosperity leave. With that, we see unemployment, meaning low economic activity. Low income obviously then means shops closing and boarded-up high streets, with the local economy devastated. That all leads to dreadful societal issues. For example, people sometimes end up making life choices that lead them to spiral into addictions, such as drink or drugs. People are looking for an escape route, trying to find some way to cope. With all that, poor health outcomes become almost inevitable—depression and anxiety become more common, and as people battle to survive as they live in deprivation, we can see that the male life expectancy in Clackmannanshire is lower than the Scottish average. Young people in Clackmannanshire are highly likely to look away from the area for what comes next in their lives. Something that shows the deterioration of living standards is the parlous state of Scottish public education. The way that our colleges in Scotland are funded is totally broke—it is just not fit for purpose. As part of the three-campus model across Forth Valley, the Alloa campus is under threat. Everyone knows that colleges transform people’s lives. The Alloa campus is essential to the life chances of young people from across Clackmannanshire. I was proud of my Labour Government just a fortnight ago when I went to the opening of the Alloa youth hub, based in the Alloa campus, which will provide a wide range of support for young people all under one roof. Local partners such as Skills Development Scotland, Clacks Works and Clackmannanshire council will provide education, training and employability support to 16 to 24-year-olds. Career advice, skills training, housing advice and mental health services will be of incredible help to my local people. A Labour Government giving people confidence and, crucially, access to employment opportunities will be worth their weight in gold to people who feel disengaged or disenfranchised, or who are living their life in despair. That is the sort of intervention and action that makes great changes for people, and they are the sorts of actions that make me proud to be a Labour MP. I thank the many organisations across Alloa and Grangemouth that do so much for people’s mental health. They do lifesaving work. Let me mention a meeting that I had with a constituent just a couple of weeks ago. Craig Hunter shares my dismay at the suicide rate that we have in our area. He quite rightly highlighted that people who are at their lowest go to the Clackmannanshire bridge to commit suicide. In representing Craig’s concerns, I have written to the Scottish Government Minister for Mental Wellbeing and the Cabinet Secretary for Transport to see if the Scottish Government will look into the possibility of suicide prevention measures being installed at the bridge, as well as increasing the mental health support available in my constituency. I thank Craig for his compassion. Everything that we do in this job has to be geared towards making people’s lives better—that seems like such an obvious thing to say, but so many people in our constituencies are wrestling with incredible emotional turmoil and despair that sometimes it needs to be said out loud. I am about to finish, but I was not aware that it is customary to finish on a joke, and neither were my constituency office staff—I have to say that the work group chat has exploded in the last hour. They are panicking, and I can understand that, because they know that the sorts of jokes I repeat at Christmas parties and birthday celebrations would probably see me in front of the Standards Committee. Let me say to comrades on the Labour Benches and across the House that I have been suspended for four months before, and I am not going to jeopardise myself today, so I will finish on this joke. Madam Deputy Speaker, did you hear about the actor who fell through the floorboards? [Hon. Members: “No.”] Don’t worry; he was only going through a stage.
A point of order would help, but here we are. I call Laura Kyrke-Smith—I hope your joke is going to be funny.

Just you wait, Madam Deputy Speaker. I admit that Members are generally more likely to see me in a debate about women than a debate about men, but it is absolutely right that we mark International Men’s Day in this place. One of its themes this year—the focus on men’s wellbeing—is absolutely spot on, and I will focus my contribution on men’s mental health. I see in my own residents in Aylesbury and the villages how tough it can be, and I want everyone to know that mental health challenges are normal and help is out there. I cannot put it better than Scott Grover, who runs a lovely group called Men Walking and Talking in my constituency. As he puts it, his group offers “friendship, brotherhood and a shoulder to cry on if needed”. They are out walking once a week. The group is completely free to join, and anyone can show up. As Scott says: “We believe it’s ok to say you’re not ok, that big boys do cry, but as men we’re too often told otherwise.” That is exactly the point. Life can be tough for all of us, and it is okay to admit that. There are so many issues that affect the men in Scott’s group, whether it is struggling to find work, being unable to get hospital appointments locally, or being stuck for hours in the traffic that so often clogs up our town, and they can add up to a feeling that our area is being left behind, that those men are being left behind and that they somehow do not matter. As Scott says: “When people feel they don’t matter, their self-worth drops and this adds to mental health issues.” Things are doubly difficult when they also face other barriers, as one deaf member of the group has pointed out to me. For example, he struggles to access healthcare with British Sign Language support. We are still a long way off breaking the stigma so that men feel they can freely admit that they are not well—perhaps even to themselves, let alone when talking about it to others. Even if they do admit it, the question is whether the support that they need then flows. We have another great mental health group in Aylesbury called Talk Club, which is there to offer support and help men build mental fitness, as their captain Steve puts it, but I bet too many people have not heard of the group. It is run by volunteers who do not have the budget or the time to advertise or get media coverage. We need to build webs of awareness and support across our communities. We need people to know about Steve’s group, Scott’s group and the other support groups out there, whether it is Space—a support group for older adults that meets in St Mary’s church—or fantastic charities such as Youth Concern for younger people. I can play a part in that, and so can our local council, our health services and our local employers. For those with serious mental health challenges, we need the professional help to be there too. If people go to their GP practice or the hospital, they need to know that their mental health issues will be taken seriously. The Government are making really good progress with more mental health support for boys in school and the expansion of mental health services nationally, including a new mental health centre in town in Aylesbury, where Bucks Talking Therapies is running services. There is much more to do, however, and I look forward to the Government’s upcoming mental health strategy, which I am sure will be firm in its commitments, including to men’s mental health. In the rest of my speech, as others have done powerfully, I will talk about one specific group of men who can struggle with their mental health: new dads. I have spoken many times before about the one in four pregnant and new mums who struggle with post-natal depression, anxiety, obsessive compulsive disorder, post-partum psychosis and other conditions, and I have also spoken about the high risk of suicide at that time of life. But it is not just the mums who can struggle: that period can be so difficult for partners and dads too, and we are only just starting to get a grip on that fact. Recent studies show that perinatal depression can affect one in 10 men, with one study from Nottingham Trent University showing changes in the hormone levels of new fathers, which could be a contributing factor. Full credit goes to men who have spoken out about their experiences, such as Mat Lewis-Carter, co-host of “The Secret Life of Dads” podcast. Whether it is post-traumatic stress disorder from being alongside their partner going through a traumatic birth, difficulties in bonding with the new baby, financial challenges or an idealised version of fatherhood that just does not materialise in reality, there is a lot to process and adjust to. Other hon. Members have made that point powerfully, including my hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce). As Mat points out, the tools that are used to identify mental health challenges in women in this period of life, such as the Edinburgh post-natal depression scale, may not pick up the different ways in which men experience mental health challenges. The risks can be incredibly serious, as they are for women. We have heard from other hon. Members that suicide is the biggest killer of men under the age of 50, and we know that men are more likely to die by suicide than women, but research this year from Swansea University, commissioned by the 1001 Critical Days Foundation, homes in on the time in a man’s life from the conception of their child to two years after the birth. That research shows that men face a higher risk of suicide during that period. Across the UK, a shocking two to three babies every week lose their dad to suicide—let that sink in. As ever, inequalities are rife, as the number of suicides is twice as high among fathers living in the most-deprived areas of the country as it is among those in the least-deprived areas. Too often, women still struggle to access mental health support in that period, but that research suggests that it is time to think about more support for men too, including routine mental health screening and clear referral pathways during their partner’s pregnancy and after the birth of their child. That should be underpinned by a better understanding among healthcare professionals of how paternal mental health challenges can present themselves differently from how they show up for mums in that period. Will the Minister pick up that issue with ministerial counterparts in the Department of Health and Social Care, and work with me to push for progress? There is so much more to do for men’s mental health, but it always starts with breaking the stigma and raising awareness. That is why today’s debate is an important step. Finally, since my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) tempted us to talk about dad jokes, I will share a scene that happens in my home most days. One of the kids walks into the kitchen and says, “Hi, Dad. I’m hungry.” My husband replies, “Hi, Hungry. I’m Dad.” Cue intense frustration from the kids at best and tears at worst, and a mad scramble as they take matters into their own hands and raid any snack cupboard that they can find. Perhaps now that I have publicly shamed my husband in this way, he may stop doing that, but we will see.
I call Chris Vince to make the final Back-Bench contribution.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I particularly thank you for encouraging me to participate in this debate—you have done your bit to support men today. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for bringing this debate forward and for his powerful opening speech. A huge number of powerful speeches have been made by hon. Friends throughout this debate, so it is a real pleasure to go last, because I get the opportunity to talk about some of them. My hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) challenged us as men to think about what being a man means to us. The way he described it was really personal—it is a personal question that we have to ask ourselves. I probably did not know that until a few years ago. When young men are asked to consider what it means to be a man—effectively, what it means to be them, whether that is questioning their sexuality or trying to deal with the fact that their sexuality might not be what they thought it was—it is okay to have questions. We do not need to have all the answers at a young age. I certainly did not; until I had a row at the age of 27 with my friend who was a Tory, I did not know that I had any particular ambition to become a Member of Parliament, let alone a Member of Parliament who mentions Harlow on a regular basis. It is okay for young men to not know where they are and to discover that, and it is important that they should not be scared of that. My hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce) spoke about the challenges of being a father. I found his words particularly relevant; as you will be aware, Madam Deputy Speaker, I am a fairly new father, and always feel guilty about being an absent one. Representing the constituency of Harlow is the third greatest honour of my life—as I am talking about being a father, I should be careful how I word this—after marrying my wife and having my son. Being in this place and representing the town and the community that I love so much—and mention quite regularly—is a huge honour, but I am aware that it comes with some sacrifices. It was interesting to hear from the Chair of the Education Select Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Dulwich and West Norwood (Helen Hayes), about the importance of reading for pleasure, because since my son was born, I have read more books than ever before, because I am determined that he should see the value of books and not of my mobile phone. I have to say to hon. Members—[Interruption.]
Order. Mr Lavery, just as the hon. Member was talking about mobile phones, yours goes off.

It was perfect timing for my hon. Friend’s phone to go off—not a problem on the Opposition Benches—as I was about to say that if any Members lose their mobile phone, my son will find it for them, which is terrifying. It is really important to me that he also sees the value of reading. On International Men’s Day, I also reflect on my experience of being a teacher. Earlier, I briefly mentioned in my usual haphazard way my experience of being a young teacher, and finding myself very early on in my career having to be a male role model for young men in my class. I reflect on what happens to young men whose father figures are absent from their lives, and what impact that has on them. There can be some really positive substitutes for that father figure—I have spoken about the wonderful volunteers at Harlow Sea Cadets, Harlow Air Cadets and Harlow Scouts, and I pay tribute to Matt Brace, who is the district leader of Harlow Scouts. I always forget to shake his left hand whenever I see him, so I apologise to him now. However, there are also some really bad substitutes. My hon. Friend the Member for Lowestoft (Jess Asato), who I can see hiding in the wings, is very aware of the huge danger that the internet—especially social media—will provide negative substitutes for that missing father figure. This debate is, therefore, as timely as it has ever been. I will take the opportunity to mention Harlow a few more times. I pay tribute again to Leo Shephed, who I mentioned in a previous intervention; he is a young man who has been a victim of domestic violence and does a one-man show on that topic. I always say to Leo that the reason his one-man show is so powerful is that, unlike me, he is really cool. I know that that sounds like a silly thing to say, but it is important that someone like Leo, who is cool—he is into his music and his drama—can tell that story, so that young men who may have been victims of domestic violence do not think there is something wrong with them because of it. It is important to make it clear that if you are a victim of any crime, you are not the problem. I also pay tribute to some other men in Harlow. I cannot fail to mention Vic Goddard—anyone who remembers “Educating Essex” will know that he was, and still is, the headteacher of Passmores school. I did not watch it myself, because I was a teacher at the time, and the idea of watching a programme about teaching horrified me. Vic is someone who cares passionately about every young person in his school. There is a brilliant story I tell about him. One boy who was not normally the best behaved student, had done something really well in class, and Vic was so excited to hear that this boy had written a fantastic essay in whatever subject it was, that he ran out of his office down to the classroom to congratulate that young boy in person, and then realised he had not put his shoes on. That gives Members some idea of the commitment and passion that Vic Goddard has for supporting his students in his school, whoever they are. I pay tribute, too, to Rod Wainwright, who I mention regularly. My hon. Friend the Member for Kensington and Bayswater (Joe Powell) will know who I am taking about, as Rod was one of the first responders at the terrible Grenfell Tower disaster. Subsequently, he has had some huge issues with his mental health and has been medically retired. I will not go into the details—I have shared them in this place before—but Rod has really been on a journey. He has been forced to confront his own mental health challenges, and I think he has found that really hard. He has been very open with me about how he does not want his children to see that side of him, but as one of my hon. Friends said earlier, it is okay to cry. It is okay to show your children that you can be upset and you can cry as well; it is not a weakness. There are many things that Rod should be proud of, but I think he should also be really proud of his ability to open up about his own mental health challenges and still be a man—still be what we would describe as a man.

Listening to my hon. Friend speak made me reflect on the surgeries I have held as a Member of Parliament, where I have had far more men break down in tears than women. I do not know whether other hon. Members have had that experience—[Interruption.] I see nodding and agreement. I wonder whether that demonstrates the lack of safe spaces for men, and whether speaking with their Member of Parliament in a confidential setting feels like the only place they have to go. As other hon. Members have said in their contributions, it is important to get the message out there that first, it is okay to cry, and secondly, we need more of those spaces and we need to promote them. We need to create safe spaces for men to let that emotion out, so that they do not feel that their Member of Parliament’s surgery is the only place left for them to go, much as it will always be my privilege to try to support men in those situations.

I thank my hon. Friend for that powerful intervention. I was not going to talk about my own experiences growing up, because they are quite difficult for me to talk about, but I grew up in a military family, and crying was seen very much as something that men did not do—“Men don’t cry.” My hon. Friend is right; if men do not feel comfortable opening up about their mental health and sometimes having a good cry, that can have a long-term negative effect on their mental health. Whenever I have suffered a personal tragedy such as the loss of a family member—when both my grandads died—I went into a corner and had a good cry for 15 minutes. It did me a hell of a lot of good, so my hon. Friend is right to say that. I pay tribute to some of the safe spaces in Harlow, and I thank Rory at Harlow Playhouse. When I worked for a homeless charity in Harlow, Streets2Homes, Rory was very helpful in providing safe spaces for some of my clients who suffered from mental health issues in the way that my hon. Friend the Member for Hyndburn (Sarah Smith) has talked about, and sometimes even more severely. I also pay tribute to Harlow men’s shed, which provides a safe space for men to talk and have a cup of tea. It is currently making me something out of wood—it does that sort of thing. It is really important to have those safe spaces. I do not know any dad jokes to finish on, I am afraid. [Hon. Members: “Oh!”] Well, maybe later. My son is very little, and although I am confident that I will get at least two terms as the MP for Harlow—obviously—it is not very likely that I will still be an MP when he is an adult. I am taking this opportunity—although he will look back on his dad in Hansard in 20 or 30 years’ time and go, “Oh my God, he is so embarrassing!”, because that is what kids do—to send him a message. I want him to be happy, I want him to be healthy, but above all, I want him to be kind. That is really important. You have tempted me into this, Madam Deputy Speaker. What is the favourite wine of the Whips Office and the shadow Whips Office?
“Oh my God, will you stop going on about Harlow?”
That was actually quite funny. I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

I am the proud father for four daughters. Until they started leaving home, I lived in a house with five women, and I soon learned where I was in the pecking order. This dad joke is for them: I advised my wife to embrace her mistakes, so she gave me a hug. It is a privilege to contribute to this debate on International Men’s Day on behalf of my party and my constituents. I commend the hon. Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing this important debate, and thank Members for their important and moving speeches. In a changing world, we are asking men to redefine their traditional roles and responsibilities. This debate is an opportunity to highlight men’s health, celebrate positive role models and address issues affecting men, such as loneliness, abuse and mental health. Positive male role models play a vital role in supporting that redefinition and fighting outdated and rigid stereotypes. However, I share concerns that so many boys are spending more time alone and online, and less time at youth centres, sports facilities and community events. The result is less opportunity to engage directly with positive male role models—the team coach, the youth worker, the teacher. Instead, far too many are victims of a social media barrage of hyper-masculinity. Men and boys are made to feel that they are not enough. Algorithms seize on their insecurities, and they are too often confronted by poisonous role models such as Andrew Tate and Russell Brand, who promote and glory in a deeply unpleasant and damaging misogyny. Is it any surprise, then, that the crisis in male mental health is acute? Some 74% of all suicides are male. Appallingly, suicide is the biggest killer of men under 50, as we have heard. In 2022, the all-party parliamentary group on men and boys’ issues identified the sad truth that many men view suicide as a rational solution to the various challenges life inevitably throws at us—loneliness, relationship difficulties, trouble in the workplace or financial pressures. Men and boys all too often, suffer in silence, disengaging from those around them when they face challenges. When we do reach out for support, it is often at crisis point. Consequently, the role of suicide prevention charities is vital; that phone call might be the only time men in severe distress ask for help. As has been mentioned, it is disappointing that, in the face of that reality, the Government withdrew the national grant scheme for suicide prevention in March 2025. Organisations such as the Samaritans are stretched to breaking point in the wake of soaring demand. Such charities need more funding, not less. They provide essential lifesaving support day in, day out. The Government must recognise their importance, and I hope that the Minister will take that thought away. I ask the Government to consider supporting Liberal Democrat policies in this area, including better resourced local hubs, and mental health MOTs to check in and check up at crucial points in people’s lives. Stronger online protections and education to empower children to stay safe online are also essential. Support cannot be focused on the moment of crisis alone. Earlier engagement in schools, workplaces and with friends prevents the destructive culture of silence that is so pervasive among men. National campaigns like Movember, which aim to break down stigmas and get us talking, are an example of how much can be achieved. The earlier boys learn that asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness, the better the outcomes will be. As one great role model, Sir Gareth Southgate, said: “The culture we create today will shape the kind of men that we inherit tomorrow.” Men must feel that they have a place and a role in the world. That is why I fear that the rising numbers of 18 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education, or training is so dangerous. Without routine—a job, school, university or college—young people are left adrift. I do not doubt that that is central to the mental health travails of younger generations, and I welcome the Government’s increased scrutiny of the issue, as evidenced in Alan Milburn’s recent report. I feel strongly that investment in sport has to be part of the answer to the NEET crisis, for the transformative role that it can play in our lives. It teaches teamwork, discipline, perseverance, resilience; the importance of hard work, rules, respect and etiquette; and the ability to deal with the twin imposters of success and failure. Skills that are essential to future careers are instilled in an environment that encourages teammates to talk to each other and to their coaches. Sadly, sport received only passing reference in the Milburn review. That is a disappointing omission, because school sports are critically underfunded, and that is set to get even worse through further cuts to school funding. That is another thing that I would like the Minister to take back and discuss with the Government. Local football team such as AFC Wimbledon, a truly grassroots club in my constituency, are stepping up and supporting boys and young men. They take part in the Premier League Kicks programme, performing outreach and intervention in schools across the community. Just this weekend, the Dons welcomed charities focused on men’s mental health, and launched their new mental health campaign, with calls before kick-off and at full time for fans to open up and speak to their mates when in need. I will take this opportunity to mention a number of other organisations in my constituency that are doing so much in the field of men’s health and wellbeing. Man & Boy is a charity that works with families, schools and referral partners to support boys aged eight to 12 through mentoring and positive male role models. It takes children struggling with family separation, social isolation or difficulties building positive relationships and offers them the chance to take part in activities that they might never otherwise have enjoyed. I am pleased that, over the years, Kingston council and organisations like the All England Lawn Tennis Club’s Wimbledon Foundation have supported that important work through grant funding. Charities such as the Wimbledon Guild men’s space; the Gentlemen of Value Club, which meets in Wimbledon Chase; and Oxygen in New Malden, which runs the “What’s The Point?” anti-knife crime campaign, play a vital role in our community by supporting men to tackle the challenges of the modern world. Finally, I will reflect on the difference we can all make. To echo the mental health campaign at AFC Wimbledon’s match against Blackpool last weekend, “Half time is 15 minutes long. You can use this time to check in on a friend or speak to the person next to you. You are not alone.” Sometimes a simple question can make all the difference.
I call my constituency neighbour, the shadow Minister.

It is always a pleasure to respond on behalf of His Majesty’s loyal Opposition, especially on a subject that is very close to my heart. I am grateful to the Backbench Business Committee for granting the debate, to hon. Members for supporting it with their thoughtful, interesting and wide-ranging speeches, and to the hon. Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing it. I absolutely agree about the strength of local charities and organisations that support men, and about the opportunity to celebrate the men in our lives. The theme for this year’s International Men’s Day is “The Future is Everyone”, as we have heard. As we look at the challenges facing young men in particular, we must not underestimate the importance of a good-quality job, genuine career prospects and the opportunity to build a secure and fulfilling future to help families and communities such as yours and mine to thrive, Madam Deputy Speaker. I agree with the Liberal Democrat spokesperson, the hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler), about the power of sport. I remind hon. Members that from January to March this year, 14.4% of young men were NEET, but perhaps most shockingly of all, an additional 89,000 young people have been added to this category. As we have heard from many Members, this is about real lives. I have an interest in this area, and it is a pleasure to co-chair the all-party group on men and boys’ issues alongside the hon. Member for Bishop Auckland (Dr Rushworth). I am very grateful to Mark Brooks for all the work that he and the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys do. We in the all-party group are doing wide-ranging work, and seeing the interest here, I ask Members—I know we always have competing diaries—to please get involved. We are currently looking at the manosphere, looksmaxxing, the impact of gambling and much more. As we have heard, each year International Men’s Day has grown—from just 11 organisations taking part in 2010 to more than 800 being involved every year. There is widespread recognition of the challenges that men and boys face, not least the growing pressures of the online world, and how they can shape how men and boys approach relationships. Many of the groups we have heard about today help our young men and boys to be seen, heard, understood and supported, which is important. I thought the hon. Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin), who is clearly very engaged in this sector, made a great speech. Financial wellbeing, body pressures and emotional concerns all matter. Many men want and need to be in their children’s lives, and this world and our processes need to work better to support both women and men. Like many people in this place, I focus on women’s issues, but I have been brought to this sector by the challenges our men face. I agree with the hon. Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith) about birth trauma, which I think has a real impact on men’s lives. I thank the hon. Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) for an insightful speech about the toxicities of manhood and the shape of families. He spoke with no notes and from the heart, and I really appreciated that. What he said pointed to the question: why do we still need an adjective when it comes to masculinity? That is still a challenge that I think we should seek to answer. The hon. Member for Congleton (Sarah Russell) spoke about the threat on our roads. As somebody who used to work in the Sussex safer roads partnership, I know that the threat of death and trauma to young men is huge. As ever, I loved the contribution from the hon. Member for Brent East (Dawn Butler). She spoke about men speaking up for women in pain, whether it is period pain or on hospital visits. I remember my dad buying me 96 Anadin and saying, “That will keep you going, love,” so there you go. The hon. Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) spoke about the groups in her area. Our Lions and Rotary clubs are full of fabulous men working with women, and often contain men giving directly back to the community, which I think shows the power of role models. There is the Greenaway Foundation in my patch, and I have the pleasure of being one of its patrons. Darren Greenaway used his childhood trauma to shape young children’s futures by making sure that they have the Christmas they deserve, and I will be proud to be part of that again this year. So many men are working tirelessly in our areas as leaders, such as scout leaders and leaders of sea, air or army cadets—to name but a few. There is a range of opportunities, and we saw many of them in the Armistice Day services, parades and processions on Remembrance Day. It filled my heart with pride—I am sure this is the case for many Members—to see so many people out doing their bit once again in East Grinstead, Uckfield and the villages. It was a particular pleasure to see how those role models are shaping young people’s futures, and this is happening daily. I will briefly do the dad joke, because I was like, “Do I do it? Don’t I do it? Okay, I’m doing it.” One great dad joke teller, formerly of this parish and of the Whips Office, is Chris Heaton-Harris—a very great man. With Christmas nearly around the corner, I thought I would use this one: what is the best tube line for leftover turkey?

The Piccalilli line, obviously—come on! That one is courtesy of Chris Heaton-Harris. We have spoken about the great work happening in our communities at men’s sheds and community groups. This year, I had the opportunity to celebrate losing a million pounds, and that is rare in this House. That was because MAN v FAT came to Parliament and celebrated how it promotes men’s health and weight loss, including the fact that men have lost a million pounds, got fitter and healthier, had people to talk to and had football and rugby to play. I have seen the valiant attempts at moustaches. I will be honest: I am a woman of a certain age, and I could get competitive, but I am not going to. [Laughter.] I always value the opportunity to speak up for men and boys, and I could not resist that one, but well done to everyone taking part. To be serious, the hon. Member for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) raised domestic abuse and his personal experience. I have spoken out about my spiking experience, and that issue affects men as well. I thank all those who are sharing their experience of male domestic abuse. I agree that we very often see men at their lowest ebb in our constituency surgeries. The Menshare Listening Group in East Grinstead meets at St Swithun’s parish hall, and when I was in its circle of trust earlier this year, I saw men sharing fears, successes, hopes and dreams, and knowing that that was needed. There is a serious point to all this. This week, we have had the Milburn report, and when I was a Work and Pensions Minister I worked on the kickstart partnerships with businesses and sectors, focusing on additional jobs. We need the report to turn into action, because this is a daily concern for people. I have covered the number of NEET men, but we must not continue to make disastrous policy decisions like that on national insurance contributions that increase the cost of employing young people and remove the first rung from the employment ladder. We must reverse that increase, and our policy is to halve NICs. I am delighted to see the Labour Government building on youth hubs, as I did as Employment Minister, because it is crucial for young men and boys to have a space where they can get extra support. It is very concerning that the economy is struggling. Parental leave is important, but hospitality and tourism businesses as well as the builders, the creators, the leaders and the self-employed—we have talked today about those one-man bands—are struggling with business costs and the cost of living. All of us, but particularly Labour Members, like to talk about a compelling alternative, but we need an economic approach that does not squeeze jobs and put pressure on men as providers and care givers. As the hon. Member for Portsmouth North said, this debate has to be about more than just what we talked about last year. The hon.
