Member for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman) spoke about deindustrialisation, and the impact of the use of drink and drugs as a coping method. The reality of the energy situation in Scotland has to be taken on. It is a little disappointing that there are areas on which we need to do more, such as prostate cancer screening. My right hon. Friend the Member for Richmond and Northallerton (Rishi Sunak) has been working with Sir Chris Hoy on that, so let us focus on what we can do there. As we have heard, the summit on men and boys is of considerable interest. Hon. Members may have heard my hon. Friend the Member for Huntingdon (Ben Obese-Jecty) talk about it, as has my hon. Friend the Member for Hinckley and Bosworth (Dr Evans), whom I congratulate on becoming a new father himself. We need this summit, but we need to know when it will happen, what action it will take and how it will make the lives of men and boys better, so that the House can be assured that we are fully addressing men’s health and online misogyny, and that we have a fully cross-Government agenda. Strategies sat on shelves have to be turned into action in our communities, and I have covered the actions that some of our men are already taking. We want to see real progress for all our men and boys. I have never viewed support for men or women as being in opposition to each other, and it is great that many of us have said that today. Let us see positive progress by next year, let us get involved in this summit and let us see the men’s health strategy deliver for our men in the same way that we want our women’s health strategy and our work on birth trauma to deliver for women. If we support men and boys—our dads, partners, uncles, brothers, sons, pops, gramps and friends—to be safer and happier, it will be all the better for the lives of our girls and young women, as well as for our communities and constituencies.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Justice

It is a real honour to speak on behalf of the Government as the first ever Minister for men and boys. It is a huge responsibility, but what is clear from today’s debate and my time in this role is that the solutions to many of the challenges that men and boys face will not be solved by the Government alone; they will be solved by parliamentarians across the House; they will be solved by partnerships with business, charities, the third sector and campaigners. International Men’s Day is an opportunity to galvanise that sector and that movement, and to begin to talk about the challenges that men and boys face and how we as a society are going to meet them. I am very grateful to my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for opening today’s debate, for speaking so powerfully about his experience, and for campaigning on parental leave—and for starting the debate with some truly awful dad jokes, which set the bar so low that some, later in the debate, became rather amusing. The attempt at a moustache by my hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce) is just so silly that it was hard to take his contribution seriously, but I commend him for his admirable campaigning on parental leave. Without him, the progress made at the Budget might not have happened and the progress the Government hope to make early next year may not have happened either, so he deserves great credit. As has already been said, my hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna), once again without notes, spoke from the heart about really complex personal issues for us as a society, around notions and concepts of masculinity, especially in the gay community. I thank him for his contribution. My hon. Friend the Member for Brent East (Dawn Butler) is right about the concern that if we fail to act on the anger that men and boys feel, the toxic influences in our politics will only gain from that failure. I do not want to be partisan on a day like today, but she was also right to point out that on the Labour Benches we get a lot of stick for perhaps not talking about issues to do with men and boys. We are called weak and we are called woke. Well, today I did not see a single Tory Back Bencher in the debate, so we will take no lectures on those issues going forward. My hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) talked with characteristic warmth and humour about incredible men in her constituency and in her life, and about incredible organisations. Importantly, she said that this is not a competition between women’s rights and men’s rights—a theme that others mentioned. They are two sides of the same coin. When we approach both themes, we should do so in a mature way that does not try to pit the differences against one another, but that comes together for the benefit of all.

I am very grateful to the Minister for giving way. Obviously, I do not speak for Members on the Opposition Benches, but because he mentioned it and because he referenced his own role as the first Minister for men, I congratulate him on that. I want to pay tribute to my colleague Nick Fletcher, the former MP for Don Valley, who spoke every year in this debate when he was in this House campaigning for the creation of exactly the role that the hon. Gentleman now has, which is a Minister for men. I just wanted to remember him with gratitude for his work.

Yes, I am sure that Nick Fletcher will be on social media later praising the Labour Government for appointing a Minister for men and boys, and perhaps lambasting his Tory colleagues for not turning up and contributing. No, the hon. Member makes a fair point. I do not pretend for a moment to be the first politician—indeed, there is a wave of them behind me—to raise these issues. They have been raising them for a long time. My hon. Friend the Member for Congleton (Sarah Russell) raised two very interesting issues relating to road safety and drownings, which particularly affect men and boys. I am always struck in my day job at the Ministry of Justice by road safety, boy racers and online activity that seems almost to encourage that dangerous activity. She is absolutely right that we really need to clamp down on it. I should mention, with regard to drownings, that in my constituency Sam’s Army’s Mission 1 Life is a brilliant charity that works to try to educate children about the dangers of drowning. Simon is a constituent of mine. His son sadly drowned in Ulley reservoir some years ago and he has turned his grief into trying to educate children across the country about the dangers of cold-water swimming. He does incredible work. This time last year, my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) made one of the most powerful speeches that I have heard in this Parliament. He spoke again on a similar theme, but he also raised important and substantive issues around literacy—in particular for white working-class boys, something that is very alive to me in my constituency—and looksmaxxing. I remember listening to a podcast about that over the summer and being completely bamboozled, but if we do not talk about these issues, especially in this place, then we will never confront them. My hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) has done perhaps more than most to champion this issue and these causes since she came to this place. Again, with characteristic good humour—her dad jokes were about middle level, I would say—she talked about moving the conversation forward. She has been talking about these issues for a long time and now wants action. I have no doubt that she will be holding my feet and the Government’s feet to the fire to ensure that words turn into action in the coming months. My hon. Friend the Member for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman) spoke about the importance of education in his constituency. When he spoke about the dad jokes he makes in private, I saw the Whip look incredibly nervous about what was about to come out and any future disciplinary action. Alas, his joke was at the high end as well, I think. My hon. Friend the Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith) started her speech in modest fashion, saying that she is usually a women’s issues champion and that is why it is important for her to be here today. Going back to what my hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire said, these are two sides of the same coin, so it is so important that women’s champions and men’s champions come together to talk about the different issues we face. Ultimately, we need to work together to overcome them. She also made a point about social disadvantage. All the evidence is that the challenges men and boys face are far more acute when facing social and economic deprivation. As a Government, we need to be alive to that. I was not sure whether my hon. Friend the Member for Harlow (Chris Vince) was going to speak in the debate, but no, he did. He is an hon. Friend and a friend, and I have seen him become a dad in a similar timeframe to me. He talked about reading to his son. As someone who has spent many, many hours reading “The Gruffalo”, I can empathise, but they are some of the most enjoyable hours that we will probably have in our lives and we need to remember that. The hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler) spoke about the power of sport, and I totally concur. He knows that I am a sports fan—in fact, we were talking about sport earlier today. He challenged us on some of the Government’s policies in this area. I would just gently push back and talk about the men’s health strategy, which was a really important step forward. We have invested more in community suicide prevention projects, working with the Samaritans and the Premier League. This cannot be done by Government alone, so we need to support the organisations on the ground, but of course he is right to press us to do more and we will look to doing that. The shadow Minister, the hon. Member for East Grinstead and Uckfield (Mims Davies), gave a characteristically amusing and thoughtful speech. For a lot of these themes, we need to work on a cross-party basis. Of course there will be politics and of course there will be debates about exactly the right means, but we all want to get to the right ends on the many issues we face. I hope, as we lead into the summit I will be speaking about shortly, that we can enter into that on a cross-party basis as much as possible. I want to work with her and other Members—I have had conversations privately with many Opposition Back Benchers to see how we can do that—and I am determined to try my best. Today I announced that early next year we will be holding the first ever national men and boys summit. The summit aims to do two things. One is what I call hard policy: drawing together the different agendas across Departments—whether in the Department of Health and Social Care, the Ministry of Justice, the Treasury or the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs; whatever it may be—where there is an issue that that Department is working on that can change outcomes for men and boys. We want to use this as a hard-hitting opportunity, with the Lord Chancellor leading at Cabinet level, to draw that agenda together and to begin to build a charter for men and boys, going into the summer. This is not a comms exercise. This is not an opportunity to make dad jokes. This is a hard-headed policy that will change lives. At the same time, we know that we have a role as the Government—indeed, Parliament and parliamentarians have a role—as leaders, convenors and beginners of conversations. We want, in the build-up to the summit, to have millions of conversations with men and boys about the issues that matter to them. I want MPs on all sides of the House to play their role in that, and shape what the discussions should look like and what the issues should be. Over the coming weeks, we will be consulting widely. Consulting sounds like a dry word, but we will be having conversations with as many people as possible to make sure we get it right. This week I have tried to begin in my own very small way by undertaking a number of visits across the country. I was in Tottenham on Monday, working with Football Beyond Borders, which does incredible work in the Duke’s Aldridge Academy. It works with children who are just on the edge of potentially getting excluded from school. We all know that once you are excluded from school it can be very difficult, especially for boys, who are grossly disproportionately represented in those figures. It has a mentoring scheme, working with those young lads, and the effects are absolutely brilliant. We need to do much more of that in schools and outside schools, offering male role models when they might not be there in the home, to make sure that we can help turn those young lives around. The second thing that stayed with me is the importance of fatherhood. I am not going to comment on the paternity leave campaign, which is ongoing. The review will come back early next year, and I hope there will be good news that we can announce in this place. I met with Future Dads, organised by the brilliant Movember campaign, to look at what more we can do. As a relatively new dad myself, the process of fatherhood is often secondary—sometimes rightly—to ensuring that the mother is well, both health-wise and emotionally, before, during and after labour. That is right; I am not suggesting that we should compromise that in any way—in fact we need to go much further—but we also need to consider how we support men. That is not just an issue of paternity rights; it is an issue of wellbeing, relationship and peer support, and looking at what more we can do. I saw some brilliant work at Future Dads. The final thing is the importance of having someone to talk to. Yesterday I had genuinely one of the most privileged and humbling experiences when I held an Andy’s Man Club session in 10 Downing Street with the Prime Minister. I went to my first Andy’s Man Club in Maltby in South Yorkshire in 2023. I admit that I went slightly cynically. I was standing to be the Member of Parliament, and someone asked me to go—when you are asked, you go. But I was completely blown away by how much it actually helped me during a relatively tough period in my career, and by the fact that these blokes were turning up at 7 pm on a Monday night with problems big and small, sharing them together, and coming out with a weight lifted from their shoulders. Yesterday, even in the more sterile environment of the Cabinet Room, with cameras following the Prime Minister around, we again had a discussion in which members broke down in tears. There was real support; it is such a simple format—of asking how someone’s week has been, what do they want to get off their chest, and what are they looking forward to—but it can really help blokes who sometimes do not have the opportunity to do that. I am aware of time; I have a lot more to say, but I will not today.

I was going to make a speech about Lancashire cheese, but I thought no, that’s a crumbly basis for a speech—maybe that was a joke better suited to Mr Speaker himself. In the Minister’s preparations for this important summit, is he considering what we can do around online spaces and social media? The evidence is there that algorithms are turning our young boys into perpetrators, when in fact they are victims of those algorithms. I would be interested to hear the Minister’s view on that.

My hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase raised his experience of exploring that, which is something that we absolutely must do. There is a lot of good work going on in Government to tackle the causes of some of the toxicity that we see in masculine spaces. The Secretary of State for Women and Equalities has launched a misogyny taskforce, which is going to do important work in this space. There is the Online Safety Act 2023, and there is a debate straight after this one on some aspects of how we can protect young and vulnerable people from online spaces. The other side of that coin—rebalancing that debate—is ensuring that we give people opportunities, purpose, connection and belonging in the real world. We cannot expect young boys to turn their phones off and get out of their rooms unless we are offering them real, purposeful activity in their community. My hon. Friend the Member for Hyndburn (Sarah Smith) is right to raise the issue, and it is going to be part of the summit, but I want the summit to be a more positive moment for our country to say, “Men and boys face these challenges. Let’s give them the opportunities to get over them. Let’s empower them to move away from the online space that can be so harmful.” My hon. Friend is right to raise the issue, and it will be part of the summit, as no doubt she will be too. I thank everyone across the House for this debate. It has been incredibly emotional at times, and quite funny at others. I am looking forward to working with everyone in the build-up to the summit so that we can deliver for men and boys across the country.

Today’s debate has not just been about sharing terrible dad jokes and having the Minister review them bluntly; we have also raised some really important issues. With my hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce), hopes for a good dad joke were high, but it was his ’tache that piqued our interest. He shared a deeply personal reflection on being a dad. My hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) touched on being a gay man. I agree with him that there is no one way to navigate that, and I also agree that the myth that trans people are just confused gay men or lesbians is deeply harmful. My hon. Friend the Member for Brent East (Dawn Butler) reminded us that real men are about love, not anger. My hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) paid tribute to some of the incredible men who have impacted her community, including—improbably—bean man. My hon. Friends the Members for Congleton (Sarah Russell) and for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) added their voices to the call for better paternity leave, and raised other serious issues, including male suicide and looksmaxxing. And I will say that my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase is one of bravest men I know. My hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) is a terrible joke teller, but a powerful campaigner for trainees and self-employed dads. My hon. Friends the Members for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman), and for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith), highlighted some really alarming health disparities. My hon. Friend the Member for Harlow (Chris Vince) revealed that he has a friend who is a Tory, but more importantly, spoke about his guilt because the nature of this job sometimes makes him feel absent; I know that many hon. Members will relate to that. The Lib Dem spokesperson, hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler), resplendent in pink, is right to highlight the importance of sport—up the Dons! The shadow Secretary of State, the hon. Member for East Grinstead and Uckfield (Mims Davies), is a long-standing campaigner on these issues as the co-chair of the APPG on men and boys’ issues. As ever, she gave a thoughtful contribution. Finally, I thank the Minister for announcing the first ever men and boys summit and committing to a men and boys charter. He is right that Government cannot tackle all these issues alone, but there is a lot that we can do—and, I hope, a lot that this Government will do. Question put and agreed to. Resolved, That this House has considered International Men’s Day 2026.

title: Milburn Report
turns: What recent progress Alan Milburn has made on producing the final “Young People and Work” report.
The Secretary of State for Work and Pensions

Alan Milburn delivered his interim report a few months ago and will deliver his final report in a few weeks’ time. I thank Alan Milburn for his tremendous work highlighting the issue of youth inactivity. I look forward to his final report.

Ahead of Alan Milburn’s report, in Gloucester there are over 2,500 young people not in employment, education or training. I have spoken with many of them across the last two years who want an opportunity but have been let down by the system. Something needs to change. At the end of November, I am hosting the Gloucestershire Futures summit with Gloucestershire county council. We have invited schools and colleges, local employers, healthcare providers, local government and the third sector in an effort to get everyone in the room to discuss how we can solve the problem together. I know the Secretary of State has a long list of constituencies to visit after today’s questions, but he also shares my determination to give every young person the opportunity to fulfil their potential, so will he or one of his team join us for the summit at the end of November?

I will add the summit to the list of places to go. I would dearly love to visit my hon. Friend’s constituency, and if I cannot, I will ensure that one of my colleagues does. On the point of substance that he raises, the problem of youth inactivity in the country has built up over many years, and not enough has been done about it in the past. We now have the youth guarantee, which is investing in the issue. We know that there is more that we must do, which is why we are looking forward to the final report from Alan Milburn in a few weeks’ time.

When it comes to youth unemployment, it sounds like the Secretary of State has his head very firmly in the sand. Did he not hear Member after Member from across this House stand up and quote how the number of young people who are not in education, employment or training has gone up under this Government? The Secretary of State quotes back to us the national figures for people in employment overall, but that is because the population has gone up. What are the NEET figures? In Gosport, the number of young people not in education, employment or training has gone up by 23% under this Government. That is all because of the number of taxes that are being put on the businesses there to employ them, particularly the small businesses that provide the Saturday jobs and apprenticeships: hair and beauty, adult social care and care. What will Alan Milburn’s report say, and what is the Secretary of State actually going to do about it?

The truth is that it has been a problem for a long time. I repeat what I said to the shadow Secretary of State: under the Government that the hon. Lady supported, the number of NEETs went up by a quarter of a million between 2021 and 2024. She asks me what we will do, and in addition to the programmes I have announced, we recently announced a partnership with the British Retail Consortium to hire 100,000 young people not in education, employment or training over the next few years. The hon. Lady will be pleased to know that the latest Recruitment and Employment Confederation survey showed the strongest hiring sentiment in four years.
We welcome the new shadow Minister, Andrew Snowden.

Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. Labour has been talking up the Milburn report for months, and the Treasury is so pleased with the report that it has delayed it until after the Budget, which means it is not going to be good news for taxpayers or the bond market. While the Government dither and delay, we have published our plan for tough love on youth unemployment: support from day one to get back into work, and after six months, those who can work but won’t work will have their benefits cut. I am sure the Chancellor of the Exchequer would welcome our cost-cutting plan in the Budget, so can the Secretary of State explain why the Treasury does not want his plan in the Budget?

I refer the hon. Gentleman to the Chancellor’s speech at our party conference a couple of weeks ago, in which he was quite clear that we owe young people not just an income, but a future too. That is why the Government are behind the agenda I am setting out. I look forward to reading Alan Milburn’s final report in a few weeks’ time, and I remind the shadow Minister and everyone on the Opposition Benches that Alan Milburn was clear in his interim report that the problems we are talking about are deep-seated, long-term and have existed in this country for a great many years.

title: Employment Support: Young People
turns: What steps he is taking to support young people into employment.
What steps he is taking to support young people into employment.
What steps he is taking to support young people into employment.
What steps he is taking to support young people into employment.
The Secretary of State for Work and Pensions

We have announced an additional £2.5 billion, as part of the youth guarantee, to create up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn over the next few years, and we have begun to roll this out across Great Britain. The gateway to the youth guarantee is available in jobcentres. We are expanding youth hubs, we have launched the £3,000 youth jobs grant, and we are rolling out the jobs guarantee for young people who are long-term unemployed. I recently met the first beneficiaries of the jobs guarantee at Boots headquarters in Nottingham and saw the huge difference that having a job made to the young people taking part.

I thank the Minister for Employment for joining me to mark the opening of the Uxbridge job hub a few weeks ago, and I am sure he will join me in thanking the college, the jobcentre, the chamber of commerce and the many others who made it a reality. One group who still experience the biggest employment gap are young people with special educational needs. What steps are the Government taking to ensure that the job hubs, and the youth guarantee offer more broadly, are inclusive of young people with SEND and that they also see the benefits?

I thank my hon. Friend for the campaigning that he has done on this issue, and the Minister for Employment enjoyed cutting the ribbon at the Future Start youth hub a few weeks ago. My hon. Friend is absolutely right in what he says. We need to end the culture of “signed off and written off”, and we want all young people, including those with special educational needs, to benefit from the youth guarantee. That is why youth hubs work closely with our work coaches and disability employment advisers, as well as local partners. The idea is that whatever condition people have, we try to give them the opportunities that are available and help them to live the fullest life.

Just last week, I had the privilege of visiting Derwentside college in my constituency to see the amazing work it does in linking to employers in a range of sectors across the region, ensuring that every qualification offered can lead to real employment opportunities across Durham and the region. From care to construction, there are real opportunities to tackle the issues for young people currently not in education, employment or training. Will the Secretary of State join me in congratulating the college on the work it does, and will he join me on a visit to see that incredible work in practice?

I am very happy to echo my hon. Friend’s congratulations to Derwentside college on all the work it is doing. With regard to a visit, I will do the best I can. I know that she is a passionate advocate for the college, and if I get an opportunity to visit, I most certainly will.

The Prime Minister hit the nail on the head when he said that too many young people have been failed by a schools system that focused too much “on the university route, and not enough on technical education.” It is not surprising that the number of young people on benefits has grown so significantly when the education system has failed to equip them with the skills they need for today’s jobs market. When I speak to unemployed young people in my constituency, they tell me that they are desperate to find work not just for the pay, but for a sense of purpose and the independence to shape their own future. The choice before us is clear: invest in young people’s success or create a lifetime of dependency, carrying a huge price for the taxpayer. Does the Secretary of State agree with me that we need to invest in young people’s success rather than leave them to languish on benefits?

Yes, I do agree with my hon. Friend. She is absolutely right to say that we need to invest in opportunity and success, and she has spoken admirably about her own life experiences in this House. As I have said, we are putting forward an additional £2.5 billion of investment in the youth guarantee and the growth and skills levy. We have recently announced that we are expanding the jobs guarantee to help eligible young people receiving health-related benefits. They should not be signed off and written off. Another point raised in her question is that too often in these debates, young people are attacked in a negative narrative in which they are described as “snowflakes” and “shirkers”. She is right to say that, given the chance, young people want to work, want to have a full life and do not want to spend it on benefits.

Youth hubs such as that based in Inclusion Education in Basingstoke provide fantastic opportunities for young people, including those with special educational needs and disabilities, to learn and to work. Could the Secretary of State say a bit more about how youth hubs are helping to deliver the youth guarantee so that young people can realise their potential? Having heard that the Minister for Employment opened the youth hub in Uxbridge, may I ask whether the Secretary of State or the Minister might consider a visit to Basingstoke youth hub to discuss young people’s challenges and opportunities?

When I get back from Derwentside, I will see whether a visit to Basingstoke is popular. Youth hubs are a crucial part of the youth guarantee. They bring together employment and skills, with wider support that often involves housing and health advice. They are an important feature of the Dutch system, where the NEET rate is one third of ours. We are expanding the network to over 360 locations across Great Britain, and the whole idea is to get the help that a jobcentre can provide out of the jobcentre and into the community. There are also other important parts of the youth guarantee, such as hiring bonuses, an extra 300,000 work experience places and a jobs guarantee for the long-term young unemployed.

I recently visited Portugal to observe a NATO exercise using maritime uncrewed systems, and the young man who drove our safety boat had done his apprenticeship at SeaRegs in Plymouth. However, it came to light over the recess that Skills England is consulting to axe the small commercial vessel crewmember level 3 apprenticeship. This 18-year-old did that apprenticeship for the Plymouth Cattewater harbour authority, but he would not have been able to qualify if it had been scrapped. The small enrolment numbers for this course reflect the specialist nature of the industry, not a lack of value. The apprenticeship gives young people in coastal communities such as mine a direct route into skilled jobs that support our national defence. So will the Secretary of State step in and stop this apprenticeship, and others like it that are also being consulted on, being scrapped?

I am grateful to the hon. Lady for her question. Skills England plays an important role in accrediting approved apprenticeships, looking at demand and quality, and I am sure it has heard the representations she has made. The overall direction of travel that we have given to Skills England is intended to ensure that we have more youth apprenticeship starts in future, because that is where the need is greatest and where the public expect us to be investing the growth and skills levy to create the most opportunity that can change the most lives.

Last week I visited several successful marine businesses at Noss on Dart. They are struggling to find the crew needed for work boats that support the wider maritime sector. Following on from the question by my neighbour, the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith), with the funding for commercial vessel apprenticeships now threatened, the route for young people to enter this sector and find well-paid, year-round permanent employment in coastal communities will potentially be closed off. Will the Secretary of State commit to continue that funding? These specialised apprenticeships may not have the same take-up as nationwide apprenticeships, but they are vital to economic growth in coastal communities such as South Devon.

I am grateful to the hon. Lady for her question. As I said to the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) a moment ago, Skills England will always look at the range of courses available and will always consider accreditation. I am sure it will have heard the representations that she has made.

The Secretary of State talks about jobs hubs. May I gently say to him that the best jobs hub of all is a business that is expanding and that the best youth hub of all is a business taking on apprentices? He mentions a wide range of schemes to try to get young people back into work. In The Wrekin, youth unemployment has risen by 27.8% in the last 12 months alone. A lot of the schemes are in urban areas. What is he going to do for my young constituents who live in rural and semi-rural counties such as Shropshire?

The right hon. Gentleman is right to emphasise the importance of jobs. That is why he will be pleased to know that there are 243,000 more people in work than at this time last year. He will also be pleased to know that the employment rate in the UK is higher today than in all but one of the 14 years when his party was in power.[Official Report, 10 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 2WC.] (Correction) He will be pleased a third time to know that economic inactivity is down by 367,000 since the last election.

If we want to support young people into employment, we must address the barriers they face long before they enter the workplace. One is child poverty, which is why the Plaid Cymru Government will pilot the Cynnal payment. Will the Secretary of State confirm that the £10 a week payment for children in households receiving universal credit will be disregarded for benefit purposes?

We made a major change on this front last year, when we abolished the two-child limit. That, together with other elements in the child poverty strategy, is estimated to bring down child poverty by about half a million over the course of this Parliament. That is an important step towards children being able to live the fullest life possible. Children who are poor can also suffer from worse education results and worse mental health later in life, so this is not just an anti-poverty measure; it is a pro-opportunity measure too.
I call the shadow Secretary of State.

Every DWP Question Time, Labour Members dutifully line up to give the welfare Secretary a chance to make it look like he is doing something about the youth unemployment crisis—a crisis of their own making. Their jobs tax and their unemployment Act have killed 300,000 jobs, hitting young people hardest. We have had enough talk about hubs and schemes. Young people tell me they want real jobs. That is why we will halve national insurance for 21 to 24-year-olds, so it is cheaper for businesses to hire them. Under the Conservatives, there will be thousands more jobs for young people. Will the Secretary of State get the Chancellor to use his Budget to do the same?

I remind the hon. Lady that, under her Government, the number of young people not in employment, education or training went up by a quarter of a million in the two years before the last election. As I said to the right hon. Member for The Wrekin (Mark Pritchard), there are now 243,000 more people in work than at this time last year. The employment rate in the UK today is higher than in every year but one of the Conservatives’ 14 years in power.[Official Report, 10 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 2WC.] (Correction) The UK had the fastest growing economy in the G7 in the first half of this year. I will tell the hon. Lady what could threaten that: a bunch of unfunded tax cuts from the Opposition. We know where that ends up—we saw the movie a few years ago—so I advise her not to repeat it.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

The Government recently announced funding for apprenticeships through areas where there are elected mayors. However, almost half of England does not have an elected mayor. Will the Secretary of State acknowledge that young people in communities such as Torbay, and across Devon and Cornwall, will feel that the Government have turned their backs on them?

The hon. Member is right to say that the devolution map in England is uneven. I urge him to wait for the White Paper later this year, when we will have more to say about that. However, we believe that locally delivered services in employment support can break down the departmental barriers that have too often dogged getting the right help to people at the right time. People are human beings, not departmental clients, and it is time we treated them as such. Delivering more services locally can help us do that.

title: Afghanistan: Support for Women and Girls
turns: What support his Department is providing to Afghan women and girls.
The Minister of State, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office

We are all deeply alarmed by the systematic discrimination and exclusion of women and girls from public life, education, employment and decision making in Afghanistan. That is why we are providing £105 million a year to support the Afghan people, and our aid reached 5 million Afghans last year, including 3 million women and girls. We continue to press the Taliban directly on women’s rights, and we work through our international partnerships to raise these important issues.

During Evidence Week, I met Dr Sara Polo to discuss violence against women and girls in conflict areas, including Afghanistan. Although many aspects of the national action plan on women, peace and security are encouraging, academics such as Dr Polo have pointed out that there are areas for improvement, such as including victims of non-sexual violence in NAP initiatives. What discussions has the Minister had with academics about the NAP, and how can academics engage further?

We engage with a wide range of experts on these issues, and I would certainly welcome a chance to discuss these matters with the academics the hon. Lady references, but I can absolutely assure her that the Department engages with a huge range of civil society and expert organisations. That is very important in informing our work on these issues.
I call the Chair of the International Development Committee.

It is not just Afghanistan where we see a rollback in the protection of women and girls. Last week, I was in Sierra Leone, working with parliamentarians there to try to prevent sexual-based violence. As part of that trip, we went to the maternal health unit in Freetown, where the UK has been supporting the health industry for the last 20 years. We cut all of our funding to that last year, which means there is now no money for procurement or for any healthcare in that country. What are we going to do for countries where we have cut all our funding to help them transition in a meaningful way, rather than presenting them, basically, with a death sentence?

The Chair of the Select Committee is a long-standing champion on these issues, even before her time chairing the Committee, and she and I have discussed these issues on many occasions. We always welcome a conversation with her about these matters, and I am sure that the Minister for International Development, who has responsibility for Africa, and indeed the Under-Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs, my hon. Friend the Member for Bridgend (Chris Elmore), who works on preventing sexual violence, would be happy to sit down and discuss these issues with her.

title: NHS Dentists
turns: What assessment her Department has made of the adequacy of access to NHS dentists.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Health and Social Care

This Government have been working to rebuild the NHS dental service since we came to office. The latest data shows that 37.6 million courses of dental treatment were delivered last year—nearly 3 million more than at the time of the general election.

Access to NHS dentistry is a major problem in my constituency, with 86% of the respondents to my dentistry survey being unable to access one. Some told me that they still travel back to their old NHS dentist after moving home and, in one case, someone took a trip of more than 130 miles because no local practice would take them as a patient. Unlike GP surgeries, NHS dentists have no catchment areas. Will the Minister please look at whether that is making it harder for local people to get an appointment?

The hon. Member raises an important point—that is a theme in the work I am doing. Last year, 81% of those who wanted to get an NHS dentist were able to, but I recognise that too often people have to have an existing relationship with an NHS dentist to access that. Since the general election, the Government’s effort to tackle dental deserts has seen us ringfence £4 billion for NHS dentistry. Huge amounts have been done, but there is even more to do, and he has the Government’s and my attention on this matter.

Since being elected, I have campaigned for a new dental school in the east of England. I thank the Government for backing that at the University of East Anglia with 25 new funded places. However, Norfolk is still a dental desert where people struggle to get an appointment. I have just returned from maternity leave and I could not get one when I was pregnant, and I am not alone in that, pregnant or otherwise. Can the Minister set out what the Government will do to ensure that constituents can get a dental appointment, and give a timetable for the reform of the dentistry contract?

I thank my hon. Friend and welcome her back from maternity leave—what a time that is. I know that she has been campaigning relentlessly on the issue of dental schools, but also on addressing the dental deserts that we speak about so frequently. The east of England and south-east dental schools are incoming and will start to take on new students in September 2027. I look forward to their playing a part in strengthening dental provision locally.

title: Pelvic Mesh and Sodium Valproate: Redress
turns: Whether she plans to implement a redress scheme for people harmed by pelvic mesh and sodium valproate.
The Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety

I am aware that a number of right hon. and hon. Members are very interested in this issue, and as the new Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety, I am driving the work and giving the report by the Patient Safety Commissioner the urgent and thorough consideration that it requires. As has been stated, the Government are committed to making meaningful progress in this Parliament, and we are advancing non-financial redress to improve health service support for those affected.

In 2006 my constituent, Ruth, had pelvic mesh implanted. It has corroded and caused her severe pain. She has been desperate for me to raise this issue with the Government. Three years ago, she paid for surgery to remove it but that has left her tens of thousands of pounds out of pocket and she requires more surgery. What steps is the Minister taking to implement the recommendations of the 2024 Hughes report, particularly if we are to give justice to pelvic mesh patients and support to those who cannot access the NHS compensation scheme?

I am very sorry to hear about Ruth’s experience and what she has gone through. Just last night, I watched the film that has been produced about the experience of a number of women—my hon. Friend the Member for Washington and Gateshead South (Mrs Hodgson) provided a screening of it in Parliament last week—and the stories in it are harrowing. As I have said, I am looking at the issue. I am conscious that right hon. and hon. Members are interested in what the Government are going to do. The previous Secretary of State had made it clear that progress would be made by the end of this Parliament. That is as far as I can go today, but I am personally looking at this issue.

From pelvic mesh to diethylstilbestrol, women have been harmed by a health system that has not and still does not listen to them, as starkly illustrated in Mumsnet’s recent report, “Medical Misogyny: A Lifetime of Failure”. Does the Minister agree that tackling medical misogyny must be at the heart of how we rebuild the NHS?

My hon. Friend makes a very important point. That is why we have revised the women’s health strategy. It makes it very clear that medical misogyny is not acceptable and that women’s voices must be heard.

title: High North: British Interests
turns: What steps he is taking to protect British interests in the High North.
The Minister for the Armed Forces

The UK is stepping up its defence of the High North. This year, our carrier strike group operated in the region, alongside 19 NATO allies, and 1,500 of our Royal Marines have trained in Arctic conditions. We are also doubling our military presence in Norway, investing in key anti-submarine warfare and undersea surveillance capabilities, and our carrier strike group will be returning shortly to NATO’s northern flank.

The North Atlantic, High North and Baltic are the frontline of the UK’s security, which is why British leadership of the joint expeditionary force is so vital to our defence. Will the Minister update the House on the recent meetings of the joint expeditionary force counterparts in Iceland, and on the major exercises that have taken place across the region?

We are rightly proud of the work that we are doing with partner nations in the JEF. In July this year, the carrier strike group deployed to the High North, working alongside 19 NATO allies, and is due back this autumn. The UK has recently taken command of NATO’s Joint Force Command Norfolk, which oversees all NATO operations across the High North, and the Royal Marines took part in Exercise Cold Response, alongside approximately 25,000 personnel from 14 allied nations.

Last weekend I was in Iceland for the Arctic Circle Assembly, where I heard a great deal of support for greater co-operation with the United Kingdom in the High North, but also an excitement about the impending Arctic policy framework that was published on Thursday. That document recognised the great strategic importance of the High North to the United Kingdom. Given that, will the Minister say more about when a new icebreaker will be brought online, which is clearly critical to our polar strategy and posture? What other resources will the United Kingdom need in the short term to deliver that strategy?
The hon. Gentleman is right to highlight the importance of our icebreaking capability. Project Shackleton is looking at the longer-term options for the capability.

I was pleased to see the Defence Readiness and Industry Minister welcoming HMS Protector home to Devonport, although judging by the three tugboats, I suspect she was rather less enthusiastic about the reunion than he was. With growing Russian activity in the High North and renewed chest beating from Argentina over the Falklands, Britain’s only naval ice patrol ship faces an uncertain future. How can a single replacement sustain a credible presence at both poles, while allowing for maintenance and refits, and how will the Minister prevent a gap in capability?

We have recently launched Project Shackleton, which is looking at some of the very questions that the hon. Gentleman raises. It is a very important capability, and we will look at the options to ensure we are mitigating the risks that we know we all face.

title: Cold Homes Plan
turns: Whether her Department is taking steps to implement a cold homes plan.

We all felt the impacts of climate change this summer, whether in our schools and classrooms or in our homes. The warm homes plan and the measures within it to ensure cooling as well as heating are available for the most vulnerable homes. In England and Wales, all eligible households can benefit from the expanded boiler upgrade scheme, which now includes air-to-air heat pumps that can heat and cool our homes.

This summer, extreme heat was responsible for thousands of excess deaths across the United Kingdom. Though I commend the Department’s mission to tackle climate change and the root causes of extreme heat, does the Minister recognise that we must go faster and further in adapting and supporting households, especially vulnerable ones, with regard to extreme heat, and does she recognise that we need a cold homes plan across the country?

I thank my hon. Friend for her excellent question. As we have mentioned a few times today, the intention to introduce some passive cooling measures, whether that be shading, shutters, reflective windows or cooler building materials, in the warm homes plan has already been announced. The delivery of the warm homes plan, which has been devolved to mayors, local government and communities, presents an opportunity to shape that in the most appropriate ways locally. We want to go faster to make sure that new homes are built to resilient standards. That is why we have committed to the net zero standards and why we are reviewing the overheating building regulations to ensure that our homes are fit for the future. I want to make sure that we build together heating and cooling options, so that we are thinking about the integration of climate mitigation and adaptation at the same time.

Twenty-five per cent of the properties in my constituency were built before 1900. They are very hard to retrofit; they are solid-wall properties. It is therefore important that there should be a bespoke scheme to ensure that homes that are hard to retrofit, particularly in rural communities such as mine, can be made cooler or warmer in these times of more extreme temperatures.

The hon. Member is right that some properties are more challenging to retrofit. That is why we are working with many heritage organisations to determine the best way to do that. We are constantly learning to make sure that there is mitigation and adaptation at the same time. I am happy to keep the hon. Member in the loop on the progress on that.

title: Science and Research Investment
turns: What steps his Department has taken to support investment in science and research.
The Minister for Science, Innovation and Investment

As this is my first run-out in my new brief, I thought it might be nice to just take a moment to recognise the work of Lord Vallance as Science Minister and Lord Stockwood as Investment Minister, and thank them very much for their work. As we have just heard from the Secretary of State, the Government are making record investments in science and technology to keep the UK at the forefront of global research and innovation. We are committing £86 billion to R&D between 2026-27 and 2029-30, including £38.6 billion for UK research and innovation. These investments are translating into jobs, innovation and economic opportunity across the UK, including in the east midlands.

I welcome the new Minister to his new place. Despite the Government’s significant funding increases to science generally, the Science and Technology Facilities Council is facing significant cost pressures. I met recently with some STFC-funded former colleagues who fear an exodus of professional talent from the UK because of those pressures. Given the importance of STFC-funded facilities in the UK’s scientific capability, will the Minister set out what he is doing to ensure that the council’s financial position is put on a sustainable footing, without undermining the long-term pipeline of researchers and the UK’s ability to participate in major international science programmes?

It is important to recognise that the changes have an impact on the staff that work for the STFC. I have been in the unfortunate position of working in a company undertaking such a restructure—and of having to do such restructures in the past—and I appreciate how difficult that is for staff. I have spoken to the executive chair of STFC, and at the core of the programme —exactly as my hon. Friend has described—is a desire to get STFC into a position where it has appropriate financial management, while also increasing productivity and modernising in response to new technology. The Government are supporting that with an increase in STFC’s funding to £842 million by 2029-30, from the £835 million of 2025-26.

Harpenden is home to Rothamsted Research and our universities lead the world, yet too much of that brilliance never leaves the lab. Will the Minister look at Lib Dem proposals to bring in a standard national framework for spin-out IP, and quintuple proof-of-concept funding, so Britain’s discoveries scale here and not abroad?

I agree with the hon. Member’s point about the need for Britain’s discoveries to be scaled at home rather than abroad. I am taking an end-to-end approach on that, starting with scientific discovery and hopefully ending with large companies listed on the London stock exchange, supporting businesses throughout that process. UKRI and Innovate UK are doing great work in that area, supported by the increased role of the British Business Bank.
I call the Chair of the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee.

I welcome the Minister to his new role as well as this Government’s emphasis on driving growth through innovation in every region of our country, as recommended by my Committee’s recent report, “Flying Blind”. It was called that because it identified a lack of data and information about the factors that drive growth and how to measure success in our regions and across clusters. The report called for a dashboard. Will the Minister tell me what progress has been made on that dashboard, and has he looked at the Cambridge x Manchester Partnership baseline report, which identified a number of indicators, including company stock, funded count, and disclosed funding by employee band?

My hon. Friend and I share a great confidence in data and a desire to make decisions based on it. With the regional disparities that she is describing, I have looked at the data and there is a clear distinction between the proportion of UKRI funding and UKRI spin-outs, for instance, and then the ability of those companies to attract investment. In fact, the level of funding they received is based on their proximity to London. I share her concern, we are looking at the data on that, and I am happy to work with her and the Committee on how we ensure that regional funding is more appropriately spread.

Universal Quantum, born out of the University of Sussex, is based in my constituency. It is developing a unique trapped-ion modular technology for quantum computing at scale. It received $77 million from the German Government in 2022, and last week secured $100 million of Series A funding from investors, including the Singaporean Government. However, it has been unsuccessful in getting any funding from our own Government. Can the Minister explain how that tallies with their Department’s commitment to investing in exceptional home-grown companies?

The situation that the hon. Member described about the loss of UK quantum companies, largely under the previous Government, is exactly why my predecessor was determined to set up the ProQure programme, to ensure that the UK is leading the procurement of quantum computing and enabling the growth of UK businesses to do that. In March 2026, the Government announced a landmark commitment of up to £2 billion for the next stage of the national programme, and our ambition is to see UK quantum companies scale and stay in the UK.

title: Serious Fraud Office
turns: What assessment she has made of the effectiveness of the Serious Fraud Office.

The Serious Fraud Office is delivering results. Over the past five years, the SFO has secured over half a billion pounds for the taxpayer, investigations announced in the last year included suspected criminality worth over £350 million, and two recently charged cases involved potentially 50,000 victims. I know that the right hon. Gentleman takes a legitimate and forensic interest in the important work of the SFO, and I am very happy to talk to him about this any time.

Last week, the Court of Appeal recommended that six victims of the miscarriage of justice in the Libor scandal should have money that was wrongfully taken from them returned with compound interest, yet the Serious Fraud Office appears unwilling to do that. The SFO is not just being ineffective in this; it is being immoral, piling injustice upon injustice. With a strict court deadline this Friday, will the Minister now direct the SFO to follow the express wish of the Court of Appeal, rather than wasting further public money in the courts?

I do not think it is for me to direct the SFO in this matter. As the right hon. Member says, the Court of Appeal handed down its judgment last week—last Friday, I think. It is therefore reasonable, notwithstanding any timetable, that the SFO is still considering the matter. The court declined, as he says, to make a ruling on interest, but there are a number of elements to the case.
I call the Chair of the Justice Committee.

Fraud makes up nearly 50% of overall crime, and the Serious Fraud Office is the UK’s agency dedicated to tackling serious economic crime. But it needs powers comparable to those of the National Crime Agency to conduct surveillance and accompany police on searches to keep pace with increasingly complex economic crime and corruption at home and abroad. Its work protects people’s savings and the honest businesses on which jobs and prosperity depend. Will the Attorney General bring forward legislation to give the SFO the powers it needs to investigate these crimes more quickly and efficiently?

This is the first opportunity I have had to answer a question from the new Chair of the Justice Committee, so may I begin by congratulating her on her new position—and on the fact that she is doing a much better job than her predecessor? [Laughter.] As evidenced by this question, she is absolutely right that the SFO needs more effective powers to investigate serious economic crime swiftly and effectively. We do keep those powers under review, and we will seek a suitable legislative vehicle to strengthen them for complex investigations in the future.

title: Child Sexual Abuse: Duty to Report
turns: What steps the Church of England is taking to ensure compliance with the duty to report child sexual abuse introduced in the Crime and Policing Act 2026.

The national Church institutions have reviewed the duty to report in the Crime and Policing Act 2026 and consider that the Church’s existing policies and code of practice reporting expectations regarding safeguarding are compliant with the new duty. The Church will continue to keep its guidance under review as the new statutory duty is implemented. Since 2016, all Church officers have a mandatory requirement to promptly report safeguarding concerns, allegations and disclosures of abuse to the appropriate safeguarding authorities.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his reply. General Synod papers from June claim that “it is now clear” that the duty to report child sexual abuse in the Crime and Policing Act does not apply to religious confessionals. That comes despite many reassurances from the Home Office to me and the hon. Member for Wells and Mendip Hills (Tessa Munt) during the passage of the Act that confessionals would not be exempted. What discussions has the Church had with the Home Office to inform its current position?

I thank my hon. Friend for that question. He has spoken very powerfully, over a period of time since joining the House, on the importance of safeguarding and I thank him for that. It is the role of this Chamber to scrutinise the Church and I am sure that the Second Church Estates Commissioner welcomes his continued scrutiny of this aspect of the Church. We all need to continue to do better to address safeguarding. The protection of children and vulnerable adults remains the Church’s first priority. It is committed to preventing abuse and ensuring survivors are heard with compassion and care. He asks a question on a specific point about discussions between the Home Office and the Church. I am not across that, for fairly obvious reasons, but I will ensure that he gets an update from the Second Church Estates Commissioner, which I hope will answer the points he raises.

The Church’s lead safeguarding bishop has said that mandatory reporting should take precedence over confidences passed under the seal of confession, which is to be lauded. Confession is not a regulated activity, as defined under the Crime and Policing Act 2026, so does the right hon. Gentleman agree with the Bishop of Tewkesbury when he says: “the responsibility is firmly in our court”? Can the right hon. Gentleman set out what steps the Church will take to ensure that that happens?

In line with what I just said to my hon. Friend the Member for North West Cambridgeshire (Sam Carling), if the hon. Lady—who speaks powerfully on those matters—puts what she is saying in writing to the Second Church Estates Commissioner, I am sure that she will take it up with the Church to ensure that that view is heard and her question is answered.

title: Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act 2023: Replacement
turns: What steps he is taking to replace the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act 2023.
The Secretary of State for Northern Ireland
The hon. Lady asks what steps we are taking to replace the legacy Act of 2023. I refer her to the debates of yesterday and the day before.

Yesterday’s vote on Third Reading on the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill has reopened the door to continual vexatious cases against Northern Ireland veterans, including Alan, Ewen and Ivar from my constituency. Will the Secretary of State continue to work on the Bill, which many agree is not perfect, to ensure that there are adequate protections against lawfare?

It is important to say, not only after we have we completed our processes here but now that the Bill will go to the House of Lords, that I am happy, as I said to the hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler), to work with all the different associations, including veterans in the hon. Lady’s constituency if she has people who want to meet me, to make sure that we end up with a Bill that really works. I urge her and all hon. Members to say to veterans in their constituencies: first, there will be answers for veterans’ families because many lost loved ones; and secondly, no veteran will be cold called, no veteran will be approached unless there is compelling new evidence and no process will be repeated unless it is essential. Those are guarantees for all, but in particular for our veterans.
I call the Chair of the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee.

The previous Government’s legacy Act failed to command the confidence of victims, survivors and many veterans. Will the Secretary of State join me in thanking the organisations that represent them that have engaged with my Committee, with Members across this House and with him?

I am really grateful to my hon. Friend, because she is absolutely right. Although sometimes I think our debates have felt as though the Bill was an armed forces Bill, it is actually a Bill that is primarily about families, including the families of veterans, of course. Joe McVey, who brought several members of his group here earlier this week, has very much informed the debate that we have had, but in the end, the most important thing is getting answers for families, and my hon. Friend’s Committee has led the way on that.

The Government have united the SAS Regimental Association, the Special Boat Service Association and the Special Reconnaissance Regimental Association against the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, with the SAS Regimental Association dismissing the legislation as “incoherent, contradictory, imprecise and muddled”. They are rightly concerned about the potential impact of the Bill on special forces recruitment and retention, and yesterday the Government voted down the Opposition amendment that would have given Parliament proper oversight of this. As the Bill begins its passage through the other place, will the Secretary of State work with the Ministry of Defence to ensure that Parliament has sufficient oversight of special forces recruitment and retention?

As I said yesterday, it would be false to make a direct equation between special forces recruitment and our Bill. As I pointed out, recruitment to the armed forces is 7% up at the moment, for the first time. It is true, of course, that we want to ensure that confidence and morale in the armed forces are upheld, and I think our Bill will help to achieve that. I would just push back on one point. The hon. Gentleman says that everybody is united, but actually there are many different views on the Bill in the veterans community. I am very happy to work with all the different associations to make sure that we get to the right answers at the end of the process.

title: High Streets and Town Centres
turns: What fiscal steps he is taking to support high streets and town centres.
What fiscal steps he is taking to support high streets and town centres.
What fiscal steps he is taking to support high streets and town centres.
The Financial Secretary to the Treasury and Paymaster General

At the Budget, we announced a two-year real-terms freeze to business rates bills for all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England; cut bills by an extra 20% for pubs and all but the largest live music venues; and removed 70,000 smaller properties from business rates altogether. Taken together, these measures show how the Government are backing our high streets: all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England are seeing their business rates frozen in real terms, reduced, or cut to zero.

My constituents and I welcome the Budget measures to support small businesses in Ilford South, including the business rates freeze for retail, hospitality and leisure properties, which will benefit more than a thousand businesses across my constituency. Will the Chancellor outline what further fiscal steps the Government are taking to support high street businesses, such as those in my constituency, to encourage investment and ensure that our town centres remain vibrant, thriving places for generations to come?

I am very glad to hear that more than a thousand retail, hospitality and leisure properties in Redbridge may benefit from a real-terms freeze in their business rates bills, giving them real breathing space over the next two years. We are also helping high street businesses through our new high streets strategy, which was published at the Budget, providing £210 million to transform derelict buildings into the new anchors of our high streets across the country.

The changes to business rates announced in last week’s Budget will provide some much-needed breathing space for many businesses in Weston-super-Mare, Worle and the villages. However, thriving high streets and coastal communities such as mine depend on businesses being able to take on new staff, particularly local young people. At a roundtable I held with small businesses last week, the cost and difficulty of employing young people were raised repeatedly as a major concern. What more can the Treasury do to ease those financial pressures, and will the Minister provide more information about the new high streets strategy and how the Treasury will ensure that vision is matched with funding?

The Government want to support businesses in Weston-super-Mare and across the country to take on young people in particular, which is why our youth jobs grant offers businesses £3,000 for every young person they hire aged 18 to 24 who has been on universal credit and looking for work for six months. Businesses also benefit from targeted employer national insurance contribution reliefs for young people, meaning that employers pay no employer NICs on earnings up to just over £50,000 for employees up to the age of 21 and for apprentices under 25—a saving of nearly £7,000 per eligible employee per year.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his answer. I welcome last week’s Budget and its efforts to create breathing space for people and businesses—[Interruption.] It does indeed. Watford has a popular high street. I have met local business owners post Budget, and they are keen to see the Government cut red tape and stimulate growth. Will my right hon. Friend outline some of the specific measures the Government are taking to help our high streets?

As my hon. Friend points out, the Government are working to reduce red tape for businesses in Watford and right across the country by making progress towards our target of cutting the annual admin burden of regulation for businesses by 25% by the end of this Parliament. As I have mentioned, we published our high streets strategy at the Budget, which is backed by £210 million of new funding that will bring vacant and derelict properties back into use, support the growth of co-ops and mutuals and help more communities to take ownership of valued local assets.

I recently received an email from a publican in my constituency, who said: “I cannot find people willing to work minimum wage because they earn more on benefits, I cannot give my experienced staff a pay rise because minimum wage increases eat into my budget, and often people will turn up for interviews only to demonstrate that they are ‘looking for work’ at the Jobcentre before bunking off on their first day.” Can the Minister explain why he has used the Budget to compound the problems of an unaffordable minimum wage and an out-of-control welfare system?

It is important that people get paid for the work that they do in a fair way. It is also important that we support our pubs, which are much loved in communities across the country. That is why one of the first announcements that the Prime Minister made when he came into office in July was an extra 20% cut in business rates bills for pubs and live music venues. That was confirmed at the Budget and will be implemented from next year. It will help pubs across our country to thrive, including those in the hon. Gentleman’s constituency.

While the Budget provides some welcome support for high streets, so many businesses in Tiverton and Minehead tell me that excessive costs, regulation and red tape remain a drag on growth. Does the Minister agree that lasting economic growth will require not just short-term support but fundamental reform of business rates and tax administration so that businesses can invest, expand and create jobs with confidence?

I agree with some of the principles behind the hon. Lady’s comments. In addition to the breathing space that the Budget delivered, we are beginning work to help businesses and the economy to grow in the long run. She mentioned the importance of us cutting red tape and bureaucracy. Indeed, as I mentioned just a moment ago, we are cutting the regulatory admin burden on businesses by 25% by the end of this Parliament, which is critical to taking some of the pressures off businesses to allow them to invest, grow and succeed in their local communities.

At my business club in my constituency last week—before the Budget—businesses on the high street, including ones that will be well known to the Minister, told me about their concerns. They have not been assuaged by this Budget. What will the Government do to reduce the tax burdens on the hospitality and tourism industry, and when will that happen?

April 2027, as we announced at the Budget. As I set out in my earlier responses, to help businesses on high streets across the country we are making sure that all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England get a real-terms two-year freeze in their business rates bills or see them reduced or cut to zero.

I have been sitting here listening to the Minister give some sort of victory lap on business rates. It is like the Government have broken the high street’s leg, given it a crutch and are now asking for a thank you. The British Retail Consortium called the Chancellor’s business rates package a “smoke and mirrors announcement”. I call it a missed opportunity to fix their cut in business rates relief from 75% to 40%. Why does he not just back the Conservatives’ plan to abolish business rates for 250,000 businesses on high streets across our country?

The hon. Gentleman talks about missed opportunities. When the Conservatives were in government they missed the opportunity for 14 years to support high streets properly. This Government are giving real support to businesses on high streets across the country from April next year, starting with the 20% saving for pubs that the Prime Minister announced in July. Added to that, we are taking 70,000 small RHL businesses out of paying business rates altogether and giving a real-terms two-year freeze to all other RHL businesses in England. That is real help for businesses, helping them to succeed.

title: Topical Questions
turns: T1. If he will make a statement on his departmental responsibilities.
The Secretary of State for Defence

Last week in Washington, I met my US counterpart in person for the first time to discuss a range of issues including Ukraine, Russian aggression and Iran’s state-sponsored terrorism. In recent weeks, we have seen threats to our airbases here at home and deadly attacks on civilians in Saudi Arabia. The first responsibility of any Government is to defend the nation, and this Government are stepping up to meet the challenge with the largest sustained increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war. We are building a country ready to fight and a Britain worth fighting for.

Since 2020, the Royal Navy has lost more than half of its frigates, its entire landing craft capability and its only icebreaker, and all of its attack submarines are now inoperable. I fear that our ability to protect the Falkland Islands is now in doubt, so will the Secretary of State take the defence of His Majesty’s overseas territories seriously and rebuild our naval capability?

It is simply irresponsible, not to mention inaccurate, to suggest that the UK is incapable of defending the Falkland Islands. We are perfectly capable of doing so, and we had a very visible demonstration of that only recently. Maybe if Reform had a defence spokesperson, they might have noticed.

T2. I am proud that my constituency is home to one of the largest numbers of military family housing in the country, and that last year, this Labour Government improved 100 of those homes. Does the Minister agree that we must go further and give all our military heroes the good homes that they deserve, and when I have the findings of my military housing survey, will he meet me to hear what they would like to improve?
The Minister for Veterans and People

We are rapidly improving defence housing; we have already upgraded 1,250 homes, with a further 1,000 brought back into use this year. We have introduced customer commitments for service families, including clear pledges on housing standards, customer service and listening to families’ experiences. I will find the time to meet those people who live in service housing in my hon. Friend’s constituency.
I call the shadow Secretary of State.

As it is the first time we have debated, may I begin by welcoming the new Secretary of State to his position? On 26 July, he appeared on the Camilla Tominey show on GB News and was asked, “If the Chancellor of the Exchequer does not stump up enough defence spending, will he resign?” The Secretary of State replied, “Absolutely.” Is that still the case?

Absolutely. My answer is the same as it was before, and the reason I could give that answer so confidently in my first week in office was because this Government are already delivering the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war. The Chancellor resigned from the previous Government on a matter of principle. He is committed to invest more at the Budget, and he will set out the path to 3% and 3.5% at next year’s spending review. I trust the Chancellor a hell of a lot more than I trust the record of the previous Government, who under-invested in defence for more than a decade.

The Chancellor resigned then to go to 3% on defence. Bearing that in mind, on the same day, the Secretary of State also appeared on Times Radio and was asked by Adam Boulton if a failure to deliver on defence spending would be a resignation issue for him, as it had been for the now Chancellor. The Secretary of State replied: “It is. It is absolutely, for me, a matter of principle.” It begs a simple question. If the Budget does not deliver 3% for defence by 2030, will he resign?

This is what happens when the shadow Secretary of State writes his question before listening to the answer to his first question. The Chancellor has been very clear. I do not think repetition is a crime in the Commons, so I will repeat what I said just a moment ago: at next year’s spending review, the Chancellor will set out the path to 3% and 3.5%.

T3. Dorset Innovation Park has rapidly become a hub for defence companies, but we now need a college on site to ensure that more young people can gain the qualifications they need to stay and work locally. Will the Minister work with Yeovil college, the innovation park, the Department for Education and me to establish a satellite college on site, which will give more young people a direct pathway into high-skilled, well-paid defence jobs?
The Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry

I was hugely impressed by what I saw when I visited Dorset Innovation Park. Awarding Yeovil college status as one of the five defence technical excellence colleges was good news not only for Yeovil and Leonardo and its helicopter business, but for the wider region. I would be happy to meet my hon. Friend to discuss how we can operate more of the hub-and-spoke models that the DTECs deliver up and down the country.

T5. Leuchars station in North East Fife has seen investment as an Army base recently, and it is home to a significant military airfield, too. I welcome service families to the community in North East Fife, but there is always pressure on local services, particularly in areas such as education. Can I be advised as to what engagement takes place, so that we can ensure we are as welcoming a community as possible?

There are two aspects in answering this question. The first is the provision that we provide to our veterans; we are pleased to be rolling out the Valour network, with announcements for further centres soon. The second is the roll-out of the armed forces covenant and making sure that all local service providers play their part in delivering for our service families and their communities.

T4. North-east MPs and business leaders are very keen for an update on procurement for Skynet, the Ministry of Defence’s secure satellite communications system. That is because, were Lockheed Martin UK successful, 500 jobs would be created in Sedgefield in my constituency, and it would be a huge boost to the north-east’s growing satellite industry. The Minister cannot comment on the outcome, but can we get an update on when we might expect this important decision?
