I thank my hon. Friend for the work he does in raising defence business opportunities in his patch. This is an ongoing procurement, and no final decisions have been made. Both the UK-based bidders are subject to full evaluation of their proposals and must offer satellites that are assembled, integrated and tested in the UK. We hope to make an announcement shortly.

T6. Last month, our oldest allies, the Portuguese, hosted NATO’s REPMUS—robotic experimentation and prototyping with maritime unmanned systems—event, and I had the privilege of attending for a couple of days. Over three weeks, member nations worked together to test the interoperability of autonomous drones, submersibles and surface vessels. Will the Secretary of State join me in thanking the Portuguese navy for hosting this important event again? Will he commit to exploring why the 2022 defence agreement between our two nations has not yet been finalised?

I think I was the only Plymouth MP not at REPMUS, given that the hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) and my hon. Friend the Member for Plymouth Moor View (Fred Thomas) attended. I support the work that the hon. Member for South West Devon is doing. We have a huge opportunity in marine autonomy to create more jobs and increase the lethality and deterrence of our Royal Navy. I am very happy to pick up the points that she raised.

T7. How food reaches us is important, and 40% of British food is imported, almost all of it by sea. The combined value of British imports and exports by sea is around £1 trillion. During a crisis, it will be the role of the Royal Navy to protect that essential trade and ensure that imports reach Britain. What is the Minister doing to ensure that the Royal Navy is ready for that role, should we need it?
The Minister for the Armed Forces

I thank my hon. Friend for raising such an important topic. Protecting the vital sea routes on which Britain depends is a fundamental task of the Royal Navy. We are strengthening these capabilities through the strategic defence review and defence investment plan, including through investment in the hybrid Navy, which will bring together crewed warships, submarines and uncrewed systems.

T9. The Wall Street Journal reported yesterday that Putin has proposed a meeting with President Xi and President Trump to agree a deal to end the war in Ukraine. Will the Secretary of State take this opportunity to confirm that Britain’s support for Ukraine to win this war is unwavering, no matter what dodgy deals are done by autocrats behind closed doors?

We support the diplomatic track that is being promoted by the Americans, which aims to bring together the Ukrainians and negotiators from Russia to bring an end to the war. Our position is clear, and I relayed this directly in Washington last week: there can be no decision about the Ukrainians without the Ukrainians; the peace would have to be acceptable to them. We will back Ukraine to the hilt.

T8. Last month, I visited Ukraine with colleagues from across the House. It was clear that Putin’s tactic of terrorising Ukrainian civilians is putting a huge strain on air defence, so I thank the Secretary of State and his Department for all we are doing on that front. We also saw the reckless damage done at Chernobyl, so I was pleased to see last week’s announcement of support for repairs there. Could the Secretary of State update the House on the timeline for that project, and the importance of securing that really sensitive site?

Notwithstanding the challenges posed by the fact that Ukraine continues to be subject to bombardment by Russia, which is targeting its energy facilities, we are working closely with our Ukrainian friends on this, delivering £17 million to support repairs to the site. We want those repairs to be undertaken as quickly and safely as possible, while recognising the challenging planning environment in which we are operating.

Support for defence bonds now reaches far beyond political divides; it has spread from the Liberal Democrat Benches to former Conservative Defence Secretaries and many Labour Members. Given that broad support, can the Secretary of State confirm that he will make representations to the Chancellor about including defence bonds in his Budget next week?

I thank the hon. Member for his continuing support for defence. There are a variety of methods for increasing support for defence. I am grateful for the work he is doing, and I am always happy to have a conversation with him. In the meantime, the Government will continue to increase defence spending for our armed forces.

Across Scotland, including in my constituency, innovative companies are helping to develop the UK’s space capabilities. Innovation in the sector, however, comes with considerable up-front costs, as new technologies require extensive research and development and rigorous testing to the point of destruction. What steps is the Ministry of Defence taking to support research and development, overcome these financial barriers and help businesses in the space sector to grow and thrive?

I thank my hon. Friend for her interest in championing space. As a space nerd myself, the subject is close to my heart. In fact, I have had two brilliant small ministerial group meetings on space in the last week alone. I direct the House’s attention to the new UK space strategy, which was published only a few weeks ago. It sets out how we will grow the space sector, creating more jobs and providing more testing, more launch capability and more resilience for our space assets.

Veterans injured serving our country can see their pension credit cut because their military compensation is counted as income. How is that consistent with the armed forces covenant? Will the Minister commit to working with the Department for Work and Pensions to end this deduction?
I recognise the challenge raised by the right hon. Member. That is something I am looking at.

Businesses such as Cairnhill Structures in Coatbridge play a critical role in supporting infrastructure repairs in Ukraine, including the rebuilding of bridges destroyed by Russian forces, to help reconnect Ukrainian communities. Does my right hon. Friend agree that our continued support for Ukraine can go hand in hand with strengthening Scottish industry, supporting skilled employment and driving economic growth? If he gets the opportunity, will he visit Cairnhill to see the work it is doing?

I would be delighted to visit, diary permitting, at the first available opportunity. My hon. Friend is absolutely right that investing in the UK’s defence and in Ukraine’s defence can also have a positive impact on jobs and growth here in the United Kingdom. We are determined to deliver that benefit for our country.

A moment ago, the Secretary of State for Defence said that the Government would set out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence, but he forgot to say by which year that would happen. Will he take this opportunity to confirm that this is 3% defence spending by 2030?

I refer the hon. Gentleman to page 11 of “The Defence Investment Plan”. I also urge him to understand why, after the catastrophic misconduct of the Government of Liz Truss, we take a rather more prudent approach to the management of the public finances, and do not set out spending commitments without showing how we will pay for them.

The north-east has the highest rate of NEETs—those not in education, employment or training—and remains the region with the lowest level of Government defence investment. As the defence youth participation and employment pledge is signed by primes, and the north-east defence industry is largely based on small and medium-sized enterprises, can my right hon. Friend assure me that we will see some tangible support from that pledge for our region?

I can give my hon. Friend that commitment. Indeed, in front of the House of Lords Industry and Regulators Committee last week, I highlighted my dissatisfaction with investment in the north-east. The Government have already taken steps since the general election to increase defence spending in the north-east, as the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry reported, but we can and will do more, including through the employment pledge.

Scotland is on the frontline of defending the High North, yet despite the very real threats we face, the UK Government spend seven times more on defence in south-east England than in the whole of Scotland combined. Given the very real threats that we face, and given that our coastland is currently undefended by the Royal Navy, will the Secretary of State commit to placing a surface-level vessel permanently on the north coast of Scotland?

Can I just say gently to the hon. Member that I think it is both inaccurate and irresponsible to suggest that Scotland’s coast is undefended? In the same spirit, I underscore that I am very willing to work with the Scottish Government in defence of the United Kingdom, regardless of our constitutional differences. It is important that we work together, and I hope we can do so, in the spirit in which I answered her question.

Drones are changing the way we fight and the structures used to fight. America is creating the robotic uncrewed systems combatant command; Germany is creating an uncrewed regiment; and the Ukrainians have created the Unmanned Systems Force. What projects are we moving forward with, to revolutionise the approach used in the Army, Navy and Air Force?

May I first thank my hon. Friend for the leadership he showed in this space as a Minister in the Department, the work he is now championing, and the support and advice he provides to me? As he will know, whether we are talking about initiatives like the hybrid Navy, the collaborative combat aircraft programme or the heavy investment we are making in innovation and drone technology, we have to be ready for the fight ahead. That means innovating—not just out-producing, but out-innovating and building new systems and new platforms, rather than relying on old ones. I look forward to working with him closely on developing those.

During the Hillsborough law debate, the Prime Minister pledged his support for the families of the 1994 Chinook tragedy. I have since written to him, alongside my hon. Friends the Members for Lagan Valley (Sorcha Eastwood) and for Wells and Mendip Hills (Tessa Munt). Sadly, our meeting has been pushed over to the Ministry of Defence. As we come up to the Prime Minister’s 100th day in his role, will the Secretary of State facilitate that meeting between the families and the Prime Minister?
I will certainly make sure that a meeting is arranged with my Department to discuss the issue.

In the last few days, Ukraine’s satellite intelligence has been badly disrupted. Nobody’s defence should be dependent on someone else’s decision on whether to provide that support. What can the Secretary of State and the Government do to ensure that our defence intelligence is kept secure and sovereign?

I can give my hon. Friend an assurance on that. I can also reassure him that over the weekend, I was in contact with both the Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, in the United States and Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara in Ukraine to try to improve the coverage and the capability of that intelligence.
I call the Father of the House.

For all intents and purposes, Diego Garcia is an American military base, but the Government claim that to protect it, we must basically sell it to Mauritius at vast cost. There is one country in the world that does not acknowledge the International Court of Justice: the United States. Why do we not create a virtuous circle and sell the base to President Trump for £6 billion, and use that £6 billion to start the process of raising our defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030?

With great respect to the Father of the House, I do not think that is the right solution. I think we can reach an agreement with the United States and Mauritius—and before Opposition Front Benchers become too animated, let me just delicately point out that they were accused only last week by the United States of playing politics with national security. I could not agree more, and I hope that they can work in a more constructive spirit.

My great-aunt was one of the thousands of Canary Girls who did vital but dangerous work in Britain’s munitions factories during both world wars. Those women have no national memorial. Does the Minister agree, as we approach our national day of remembrance, that that is a historical omission, and will he meet me to discuss a national memorial for the Canary Girls?

As a proud east Londoner, I learned as a child about the Woolwich Canaries, and the difficult conditions to which they were exposed in support of our war effort and to keep our armed forces equipped. The contribution of the Canary Girls, along with that of all civilian and military women, is recognised on the “Women of World War II” memorial in Whitehall. Because the responsibility for matters involving civilian wartime workers sits outside the Ministry of Defence, I direct my hon. Friend to the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, but as an east London MP who knows very well of the great sacrifices of the Canaries, I would like to meet her and support her campaign.
Nowhere were those sacrifices greater than in Chorley. I call Sir Roger Gale.

Mr. Trump’s disgraceful show of support for Putin has clearly raised the stakes, not only in Ukraine but in the Baltic states and Poland. Given the perfidious nature of the current incumbent of the White House, will the Secretary of State reaffirm our commitment to NATO, and indicate very clearly that an attack on one NATO state is an attack on all of us, and that this country stands by its friends?

I can wholeheartedly give that commitment to the right hon. Member. This is a principle, but also a conviction that is held across the entire NATO alliance. Putin should be in no doubt that NATO stands ready to defend every inch of NATO territory. Let me place on record again that when I was in Washington last week, the United States, through the Secretary of War, thanked us for our leadership in Ukraine. It has not been an easy week for US-Ukraine relations—I would not pretend otherwise—but I think that we should recognise the support that the United States provides, and will continue to provide, for Ukraine. This country will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes.

My hon. Friend is aware of the unique case involving my constituent Rachel Gallagher, a former MOD civil servant who was released from her role under civil service nationality rules. While I accept that my constituent was not legally employable, I simply cannot accept that, after a decade of dedicated service, her accrued pension contributions have been declared void. Will the Minister meet me, so that we can ensure that an equitable resolution is found, and my constituent receives the full pension contributions that she earned in service to this country?
My hon. Friend is making a passionate case about a very complex and tragic issue. I agree to meet him, and I hope that we can find an equitable outcome for his constituent.

title: Oil-fired Heating
turns: What steps she is taking to support off-grid homes using oil-fired heating systems.
What steps she is taking to support off-grid homes using oil-fired heating systems.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero

Off-grid homes in council tax bands A to D are eligible for the £100 household energy payment and will also benefit from the zero rate of VAT on electricity bills that we have extended to July 2027. In the Glastonbury and Somerton constituency, around 33,000 households will receive the energy payment. In the Chichester constituency, around 37,000 households will receive payment. This is on top of the £53 million of targeted support for low-income heating oil users via the crisis and resilience fund, announced in March.

One Henstridge household now pays more than double for 500 litres of heating oil compared with this time last year. They are not alone. The way off of oil is by switching to a heat pump, powered by clean, home-grown renewables, but some older homes are harder to switch. The off-grid grant uplift ends in March, adding around £2,200 to the cost of switching. Will the Minister extend the uplift and back alternatives for homes where heat pumps will not work?

We have talked at length in this place and elsewhere about the challenges around heating oil. I am keen to make sure that the maximum number of people possible take up the £9,000 boiler upgrade scheme. We have already seen a 120% increase in the number of people applying to that scheme since the outbreak of the war in Iran. That is precisely because, unlike the Tories, those people understand that the best thing to do is wean themselves off the exposure to global fossil fuel prices.

More than 8,000 households in my constituency, because of their reliance on heating oil, have been left exposed to the price volatility that the Minister talks about. A specific issue is the minimum order requirement, which currently stands at 500 litres. It means that households are having to stump up hundreds of pounds at a time when they cannot afford to, especially those that do not receive financial support. The Competition and Markets Authority report into the heating oil market recognised this specific issue and called for a review. Will the Minister outline what steps the Government are taking to reduce the required minimum order volume?

The hon. Lady is right. I am delighted that the Government decided to respond to the Competition and Markets Authority recommendations and to finally regulate the heating oil market. It is appalling that people have been so exposed to those prices and that behaviour for so long. We will explore how minimum payments will fit into regulation. In the interim—we need to ensure that regulation is right—I am talking to the UK and Ireland Fuel Distributors Association and other trade bodies to ensure that the voluntary standards and codes of conduct are enforced and upheld this winter, including on minimum payments. I am concerned about people ending up out of pocket. It is also worth while pointing out that heating oil users in council tax bands A to D will benefit from the household energy payment, which will give people some of the breathing space they are looking for.

In Scotland, the SNP Government run the heating oil fund centrally, but despite boasting that they would double the fund to £10 million, only 7,028 households out of 169,000 in Scotland that rely on heating oil have had approval from the heating oil fund. Of over 12,000 households in my constituency, half of which use heating oil, only 324 have been able to claim the £300. Will the Minister meet Scottish Ministers and urge them to get that money out the door, take the rurality and insularity of islands into account, and widen the eligibility so that more people can get support?

I am disappointed to see that the Scottish Government, despite claiming they have allocated more money, are not managing to get that money out the door. I am really determined to ensure that anybody who has allocations given to them—be they local authorities in England, the Welsh Government or the Scottish Government—gets the money to the people who really need it as fast as possible.

With Government support for those struggling with the cost of liquefied petroleum gas and heating oil heavily reliant on councils distributing the money quickly and fairly, would the Minister consider instructing the Department to publish performance data for councils allocated money, so that, where needed, local Members and councillors could hold underperforming local authorities to account?

I know that my hon. Friend has been diligent in pursuing issues around the crisis and resilience fund. I and the Under-Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, my hon. Friend the Member for Suffolk Coastal (Jenny Riddell-Carpenter), met Baroness Sherlock from the Department for Work and Pensions to understand what more can be done to ensure that support reaches those households that need it. Indeed, although the crisis and resilience fund was the choice back when the war broke out—it was pretty much the only option we had—with the household energy payment, we will be looking at a new discretionary fund with better ways of targeting the people who really need help.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

The Liberal Democrats welcome the Minister’s work in this area and her recognition that rural households off the gas grid that rely on expensive heating oil and LPG are already particularly exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices. However, from next April, they face a double blow: the end of the enhanced boiler upgrade scheme grant and the reintroduction of VAT on energy-saving materials such as heat pumps, batteries and solar panels. Our analysis shows that a household installing a heat pump, 4 kW solar array and battery could face an additional £1,530 in costs. It seems bonkers that the Government are reintroducing a solar and heat pump tax at the same time as paying households to adopt the technology. Does the Minister agree with the Liberal Democrats that, to help rural off-gas-grid homes to get off volatile fossil fuel prices, we should reverse those measures?

The hon. Lady will be aware that the key means of improving the fabric of people’s homes—not only in rural areas—will be delivered through our warm homes plan and in particular the warm homes loan that the Under-Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, my hon. Friend the Member for Inverclyde and Renfrewshire West (Martin McCluskey), outlined earlier. Funding for the boiler upgrade scheme will also continue. We are working with the heat pump industry to drive down costs, ensure consumer protections, and reduce as much as possible the regulatory barriers so that people can get what they need installed.

title: Topical Questions
turns: T1. If she will make a statement on her departmental responsibilities.
The Secretary of State for Education

Alan Milburn’s final report on youth opportunities is soon to be published, and the issues that he has already identified are hugely impactful. As the Prime Minister says, this is a watershed moment. We are embarking on wide education reforms to ensure that no child is left behind, and that we truly offer education for all.

Surrey county council’s special educational needs and disabilities reform plan includes funding for only 12,000 out of 20,000 children with education, health and care plans. Will the Secretary of State explain how West Surrey council, which will serve my constituency from next year, is expected to meet its legal duties to children and families without the funding to do so?

Following the approval of Surrey’s local SEND reform plan, we have confirmed that the local authority will receive a grant allocation of more than £205 million, to be paid on 30 November. The hon. Gentleman highlights why we need to embark on generational reforms to special educational needs: so that we can help local authorities to support their local children.

T2. Every week, I hear more stories of children with special educational needs being failed by Lib Dem-run Hertfordshire county council. My constituents are tired of hearing excuses from HCC, so will the Secretary of State provide an update on the investment from the Labour Government to help us to tackle the SEND crisis?
My hon. Friend might be aware that this Labour Government are allocating Hertfordshire county council more than £221 million for special educational needs through the high-needs funding block.
I call the shadow Secretary of State.

In June, in response to data from Safe Screens, which found that almost 1 million children are spending most lessons learning from a screen, a Department for Education spokesperson said: “Personal and educational screen time are not the same thing—what matters is what children are using their screens for.” Does that remain the Department’s position?

These issues are important, and we should be debating and discussing them, but I find it a bit irresponsible of the Conservatives to use baseless claims for party political point scoring. The evidence actually shows the opposite; some 95% of teachers in primary schools say that less than an hour a day is spent on screens in schools. However, more needs to be done, and that is why we have taken steps, in relation to statutory guidance on phones in schools. We are bringing in ed tech guidance, so that safety comes first. We have a social media ban for under-16s, and there is more to come.

I am absolutely astonished by that response. Either more needs to be done, or I am scaremongering—the Secretary of State needs to make up her mind. The point is that looking at a screen for hours a day is harmful to children, regardless of the content on it. I have little hope of this now, but will she back the guidance from Health Professionals for Safer Screens—from doctors—that was published today? It would limit screen time to two hours a day at secondary school, and would ensure minimal screen time at primary schools.

The shadow Secretary of State said over the weekend that no action had been taken on this issue over the past 10 years. I wonder who was in government over those 10 years. The Conservatives were responsible for the Online Safety Act 2023, which they watered down at the last minute. How much screen time guidance did they introduce when they were in government? None at all. Were they the Government who used artificial intelligence to give children their GCSE and A-level results during covid? Yes, I think they were. Labour will take action to keep children safe, put child development first and make sure that no child is left behind.

T3. I am pleased that my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State is acting on the recommendation of the curriculum and assessment review, and is considering introducing a national curriculum for religious education, having commissioned a task-and-finish group to produce a draft. I gather that that draft will be fully inclusive of humanism, which I strongly welcome. Can she say when the consultation on that draft will be published?

We are grateful to all those who have been involved in developing the RE curriculum. This historic consensus will help every child to receive a great RE education. We will consult on the draft RE curriculum later this year, as part of our consultation on curriculum and assessment reform.
I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that spending on schools will fall by 2% between 2028 and 2032 as pupil numbers decline. Many schools already struggle to afford basic classroom supplies and are cutting back on teaching assistants, so will the Education Secretary promise to go in to bat against the Treasury, to make sure that every penny saved from falling pupil numbers is reinvested in our schools and colleges?

As the hon. Lady knows, school funding is a protected area. She is right to point out that where pupil rolls are falling, that will have an impact on school budgets, but she can be assured that this Government are committed to supporting our schools. We are also reforming special educational needs funding, to make sure that we get teachers doing what they do best: being in the classroom, improving outcomes for all our children.

T4. Last week, Calderdale’s Reform-led council announced a consultation on the closure of Colden junior and infant school. It compounded the distress by throwing parents out of the cabinet meeting at which that decision was made. Does my hon. Friend agree that parents’ voices and opinions must be central when it comes to the future of their children’s education?
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education

I do agree with my hon. Friend, who I know is a champion of schools in his community. When a local authority proposes the closure of a maintained school, it must follow the relevant statutory process, which includes careful consultation before any final decisions are made.

T7. The Secretary of State has rightly set out the importance of using evidence to determine policy about schools and the national curriculum. Could she set out the evidence that has been used to give oracy equivalence with writing and reading in the curriculum?

The right hon. Gentleman is absolutely right—our new national curriculum is led by experts, by the evidence, and by our desire to ensure great outcomes for all our children, and that no child is left behind. He will be aware that there is a huge amount of evidence regarding oracy, and there is a lot of support for our policy in this area. He will also be well aware that oracy is hugely valued, particularly by private schools; young people leave those schools as confident speakers who can advocate for themselves. I want every child to have those skills, no matter what school they go to.

T5. The Government inherited a broken student loan system that was introduced by the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition. Too many young people—especially from low-income families like those in my constituency—feel that going to university is beyond their means and those of their family. What are the Government doing to address the barriers to going to university?

Going to university provides a really good opportunity for many young people, and I encourage young people in my hon. Friend’s constituency and elsewhere to think about going to university. She is right that we inherited the plan 2 student loan system, which is putting some strain on graduates, but going to university does improve young people’s outcomes.

On Friday, I met with parents who had lost their children to suicide. They are worried that with the demise of Papyrus and its hotline, there is a real gap in suicide intervention. It is a Department of Health and Social Care area, but I urge the Secretary of State to work with that Department on the provision being put in place for schools and for young children with regard to suicide.

I was not aware of Papyrus discontinuing its phone line. I know from many parents what a valuable service it has provided over many years in the terrible circumstance where a young person takes their own life. I will definitely take that issue up with the Department of Health and Social Care.

T6. The failure of tuition fees to cover increasing costs and an over-reliance on international students to plug the gap, coupled with weak governance and poor financial decisions by some universities, have led to a spiralling funding crisis. The current model is broken. What action are the Government taking to deliver sustainable public funding to our universities?

I know that this is a particular issue for my hon. Friend in Nottingham at the moment. Universities are autonomous, but we want to ensure that they have sustainable funding, are well led and make good decisions. We are supporting our universities in a number of ways to attract more students and to make sure that they are healthy and sustainable.

Will the Secretary of State launch an inquiry into the sudden closure of Leweston school, an independent Roman Catholic faith school in Dorset? It is becoming a scandal. It was done suddenly with no warning, and various excuses were given about the school not being viable, although it has 600 pupils. It was closed by Concept Education, which took on the school recently. There is a belief that either there was financial mismanagement by Concept Education or, worse, that this was asset-stripping of a valuable site with a large acreage. This is an important school for the Catholic community. Will she launch an inquiry?

I am sorry to hear of that case in the right hon. Gentleman’s constituency. I am happy to arrange a meeting for him with a Minister to discuss it. It sounds like there are more questions to be answered about that particular case.

T8. Our universities have long welcomed international students, but a recent survey shows that this autumn, enrolment at postgrad level has fallen by one fifth. Will the Minister engage with universities and their representatives to address this costly and concerning decline?

We engage regularly with universities. My noble Friend the Minister for Skills regularly engages with universities on exactly these topics. As a Government, we have taken steps to strengthen university finance. Our international education strategy confirms that international students are an important part of the future of universities, but we need to make sure that there is balance in our immigration system.

Teachers, education unions, parents and governors have all voiced serious alarm about the Government’s draft conversion therapy ban, because it clearly exposes teachers, staff and pupils to the risk of prosecution and prison time of up to five years, simply for questioning a child’s desire to change gender or preventing them from using the toilets meant for a member of the opposite sex. The ban is riddled with unintended consequences and itself poses a child safety risk. Will the Secretary of State listen to these important voices, put biological sex as upheld in the Supreme Court first, and scrap the draft Conversion Practices Bill?

As the right hon. and learned Lady knows, that is a draft Bill that is going through intensive pre-legislative scrutiny. I am sure that the issues she raises can be looked at, but they are not in any way the intention of the Bill. Members from all parts of the House have been calling for such a Bill for a very long time.

T9. Freezing the plan 2 student loan repayment threshold from April 2027 means that my constituent George Alliott and millions more like him will lose more of their earnings at a time when many are already struggling with the cost of living, but to change the terms promised to borrowers also feels somewhat unfair. Will the Secretary of State look again at this decision?

My hon. Friend is right to raise this matter. The threshold was frozen a considerable number of times by the Conservatives, and they introduced the plan 2 loan, which has high interest rates associated with it. We took immediate steps to cap the interest rates, and we have introduced new maintenance loans and other measures. However, as my hon. Friend says, we need to keep these issues under constant review, and when it is affordable we will look at them again.

Breakwater academy in Newhaven has been forced to relocate its pupils because its ageing buildings are considered dangerous. Families face considerable disruption, and there is uncertainty about whether their children can return to the school that they love. Will the Minister meet me to discuss the situation, and will he fund the new buildings that those pupils need so that they can return to their school?
I will gladly meet the hon. Member. This case underlines the importance of the estates renewal that we have under way, with record investment.

I warmly welcome the Government’s roll-out of free school meals expansion, but entitlement on paper is not a meal on a plate, and eligibility is now more complicated. Gateshead council has nearly doubled take-up by automatically enrolling families that it already knew about. The Minister’s colleagues in the Department for Work and Pensions already know which families are receiving universal credit; will the Minister use that data so that no child misses out on a meal because a parent has not filled in a form?
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education

I thank my hon. Friend for the campaigning work that she has done to bring about the historic expansion of free school meals to children whose families are receiving universal credit. Like me, she was on free school meals herself, and we both have personal knowledge of the impact that that can have on a family’s finances. She can be reassured that, along with the DWP, we are looking closely at the whole idea of auto-enrolment. Some councils, including Gateshead, have made it work, but there is much more to be discussed with the DWP.

In West Sussex, nearly one in 10 young people are either not in education, employment or training or have an unknown destination. Meanwhile, our local university, the University of Chichester, and local employers are telling me how difficult it is to employ young people. When will the Secretary of State accept that this Government have simply got it wrong?

Oh dear. It is this Government who are taking action to ensure that all young people have a pathway to success, that no child is left behind, and that children are at school and are not excluded from schools and left home-schooled or off-rolled and elsewhere, as was the case under the Conservatives. They cancelled the covid catch-up plan, they scrapped Sure Start, they got rid of all the youth services that support people, and they embarked on a narrower and narrower education system that left far too many behind.

Last week I was contacted by the head of East Leake academy in my constituency, who told me that owing to delays over the new progress 8 and attainment 8 measures, schools are having to advise pupils about GCSE options without knowing the full rules. When will the Department publish the response, and will the Secretary of State confirm that the final model will not narrow pupils’ options?
It will be out very soon, and I can assure my hon. Friend that it will be not narrowing but broadening.

Teachers at Beckley Church of England primary school in my constituency, as well as parents of pupils, have contacted me to talk about the severe impact of the Government’s reforms of the way in which physical education is funded in schools on the school’s provision, in which there has been a massive drop. I am sure that that is not the intention of the reforms, but will the Minister agree to meet me to discuss what is happening in Beckley and at other schools?

I should be delighted to meet the hon. Gentleman. We are investing £1 billion in the new PE partnerships. We are procuring a partner, and we want to bring together all the expertise from the governing bodies and elsewhere to link with local sports organisations and schools to improve matters for children.

As the Secretary of State will know, I have repeatedly raised the appalling condition of Forest high school in my constituency, where surveys have identified significant safety risks. I welcome the Government’s commitment to rebuilding schools through the school rebuilding programme, but time is of the essence for Forest high school, especially because concerns about the condition of the site extend beyond the school itself to the leisure facilities used by the wider public. Will the Secretary of State commit herself to visiting the school with me to see the condition of the buildings at first hand and to discuss how we can secure, as a matter of urgency, the rebuilding that pupils, staff and the wider community so desperately need?

My hon. Friend has done much to drawn attention to the issues at Forest high school, and I can assure him that the nomination is in for that secondary school. The process of selecting the next schools to be covered by the school rebuilding programme is under way. We are obviously looking at the condition need throughout the estate, and we will make that decision as soon as possible.

I should declare an interest as a plan 2 and postgrad student loan holder. We know that there is a really tough jobs market out there for graduates, and we now see many postgraduates having to take up minimum-wage jobs. The terms and conditions of their repayments mean that they pay back 6% on any earnings over £21,000. That effectively means that postgraduates on the minimum wage are taking home less than the minimum wage. Will the Secretary of State agree to meet me and look at how we can rectify the situation as a matter of urgency?

I am aware that the situation is particularly difficult for postgraduates, and I am happy to have a conversation with the hon. Gentleman about that. We are trying to make sure that there are job opportunities for more of our young people, including graduates and postgraduates. We are supporting them in the housing market, and with childcare and other things, so that they can go on and lead a successful life.

Given that only 5% of children on EHCPs end up in the world of work, it is clear that our education system is failing far too many young people. Does the Minister agree that we need to open the doors to employers, get them into our schools, and give more children the opportunity to learn about the work of work and the opportunities that it creates? What else will we do to improve work experience and get more children on EHCPs into the world of work afterwards?

I wholly agree with my hon. Friend, and he is absolutely right to raise this issue, especially on the day before we are due to have the full publication of the Milburn review. Sixteen areas are currently being supported by the Department for Education in providing supported internships. They have huge potential for the future, and we will look at what more we can do to support those programmes.

A particular concern in York is the number of children with SEND who are not in school. We have seen a sharp rise in the use of section 19 of the Education Act 1996, and we also see many children who are not able to access their education. When the Secretary of State publishes the SEND review, will she ensure that there is a section on EOTIS—education otherwise than in school—children?

I recently visited York and saw some of the brilliant work being done there. We had a separate consultation on EOTIS, because we heard parents’ huge concern about this issue. It is something that we are looking at carefully, and we will respond as we bring out the reform plans.

In Dudley, the number of home-educated children is rising due to the lack of alternative provision for SEND children who are not managing in mainstream schools, and parents are crying out for support. Will the Secretary of State back Dudley Academies Trust’s proposal for alternative provision for under-16s, and meet us to discuss giving every child the best start in life?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. We want to see more schools have strong inclusion policies for all their children. That is what our SEND reforms and our education reforms are about: no child left behind and children supported in school, where they can get the best outcomes.

On Friday I had the pleasure of visiting the Downs primary school in Harlow and meeting its newly elected school council. What was fascinating was that students as young as those in year 4 were talking about the challenges of online security and disinformation online. What would the Secretary of State say to young people at the Downs primary school about what this Government are doing to keep them safe online, both now and in the future?

My hon. Friend might be the last, but he is never the least, and he is absolutely right. This Government are determined to keep our young people safe online, which is why we are bringing in the measures on phones in schools, the social media ban and the rest. It is really important that we equip young people with the know-how and skills that they need in media literacy, digital literacy and the rest, so that they can discern disinformation and misinformation and self-regulate.

title: Defence in the High North
turns: We now come to the Select Committee statement on behalf of the Defence Committee. Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi will speak for up to 10 minutes, during which there will be no interventions, and there will be questions for 10 minutes at the end.

I thank the Backbench Business Committee for granting this statement on the Defence Committee’s report, “Defence in the High North”. The High North is a priority theatre for the UK, as well as a particularly challenging and hostile environment in which to operate. Russia is seeking to dominate and exploit the High North, potentially turning the region into a major vulnerability for the UK. The UK is a near neighbour of the High North. Indeed, parts of northern Scotland are closer to the Arctic circle than to the channel, while the strategically important GIUK gap spans Greenland, Iceland and the UK. The region is changing rapidly. As temperatures rise and ice melts, new access routes are opening up, making the High North more congested and contested. Most critically, the High North is home to much of Russia’s strategic nuclear, naval and undersea sabotage capability and provides a base from which Russia can project military power into adjacent regions. That extends to UK territorial waters, where there has been a significant increase in hybrid threats to subsea critical infrastructure. In recent weeks, the Royal Navy has intercepted a Russian intelligence ship off the coast of Scotland. Our report concluded that the UK has glaring capability gaps in the High North that leave us vulnerable. Without intervention, those gaps are set to widen, further weakening the UK along its northern flank. Evidence of low availability among frigates, destroyers and attack submarines raises serious questions about whether the UK can meet its High North commitments before new capabilities enter service. The Ministry of Defence also has a serious gap in its anti-submarine warfare capability measured against its own military requirements. Currently, there are 11 frigates and destroyers in service. That is just over half of the requirement for 19 vessels. Of the required 13 frigates, eight should be fitted with towed array sonar for anti-submarine warfare. At present, this capability is limited to the remaining five Type 23s. That weakens the UK’s ability to respond to Russian submarines and underwater sabotage. It is a worrying picture. The Royal Marines’ Arctic experience is a significant national strength, but it cannot compensate for shortfalls in the naval platforms needed to deploy, protect and sustain operations in the region. The Government are already rightly investing in the hybrid Navy and Atlantic Bastion, including the £90 million investment announced this week in new drones and sensors to counter undersea threats. We know that the Government are aware of the growing threat in the High North. Our concern is not that nothing is being done, but that the necessary capabilities will not be available fast enough. Given the critical role of anti-submarine operations in the High North, the Committee called on the Government to ensure that no further towed array-equipped Type 23 frigates leave service until they are replaced one for one by the new Type 26 vessels. Addressing our own capability gaps is fundamental, but the UK must also be able to deploy flexibly to the High North, whether acting alone, with partners such as Norway, or through the joint expeditionary force or NATO. That brings me to the joint expeditionary force—the JEF—a UK-led force of 10 like-minded northern European nations. Although the JEF was originally conceived as capable of operating across the full spectrum of conflict, its role has become increasingly focused on countering sub-threshold and hybrid threats, on the assumption that NATO would deter any escalation to warfighting. But with less certainty about the US commitment to collective NATO defence, the JEF’s comparatively limited capabilities could be seen as less of a deterrent. That could leave it exposed if an incident threatens to escalate. We heard from some during our inquiry that the JEF was a “jack of all trades” and therefore master of no military tasks. The Government should therefore reassess the JEF’s contribution to European security. We welcome this week’s northern navies initiative as a step towards strengthening the JEF and aligning it more closely with NATO. The Government should also consider whether the JEF should focus more closely on the High North, particularly if Canada joins. It is clear that Russia is not a future threat but a present danger. Failure to deter Russia in the High North would put subsea data cables and energy pipelines at risk in peacetime. In the event of hostilities, it would threaten the UK and its critical national infrastructure, including the nuclear deterrent. Atlantic resupply routes from the US would also be at risk. In conclusion, our report sets out the threat that Russia poses in the High North, and what the Ministry of Defence needs to do in response. It is now time for the Government to act with urgency to address those capability gaps and strengthen the UK’s defence of that critical region.

I congratulate the Committee and its Chairman on the production of such an important report. One section that most struck me was that beginning at paragraph 84 on submarine under-ice capability. I was surprised to learn that Astute-class submarines do not have the capability that their predecessors, the Trafalgar-class submarines, used to have. Can the hon. Gentleman tell us a little more about when that capability might be acquired, and can he throw any light on the fact that, as has become painfully clear over recent weeks and months, the existing Astute-class submarines, some of them very new, are not at sea? Is that a manning problem, is it a technical problem, or is it both?

I thank the right hon. Gentleman, a former Chair of the Defence and Intelligence and Security Committees, for his perceptive and incisive remarks. Under-ice capability is key for the UK to effectively deter and defend in the High North. Unfortunately, we have allowed our under-ice capabilities to lapse precisely at the time when they are most needed. That is why a previous Defence Committee report advocated for the hardening of hulls. This report recommends that we rapidly re-establish those under-ice capabilities, because if we do not, Russia will not be deterred from its activities. In fact, it will be further emboldened, because we will not be able to protect those transatlantic supply routes.

I thank the Committee Chair for presenting this report on the High North to the Chamber. Does he agree that it underscores how acutely important our submarine programme is, and the value of what we do in Barrow-in-Furness? Does he also agree that we need a massive increase in funding to help deliver those changes rapidly?

I thank my hon. Friend, a fellow member of the Defence Committee, for her strong and positive contributions to this report, and her other work. Indeed, it was a pleasure to visit Barrow-in-Furness and to see some of those submarine capabilities. She is right: as a nation, we need to invest at pace because of the lack of availability of those submarines, and that is portrayed strongly in our report.

I thank the Chair of the Defence Committee for his remarks, and I very much enjoyed going with him on our various visits to make this report. Did he feel, as I did, slightly awkward when we were visiting the Nordic states? We know what we are spending on defence. We know that Norway is spending 3.35% of GDP, Denmark 3.5%, Sweden 2.8% and reaching 3.5% by 2028, and Finland 2.85% and reaching 3.3% by 2032, yet we have not yet committed to the Committee’s preferred 3% by the end of this Parliament. That created a certain unease. Does the hon. Gentleman remember that when we visited Norway, we were told by its Chief of Defence that every time the Prime Minister of Norway makes a speech, he mentions the threat from Russia? Does he agree that we must advance the so-called national conversation if we are to take the British public with us, and explain the threat to them, as well as the capability and investment that we need to counter it?

I thank the hon. Gentleman, a fellow member of the Defence Committee. I very much enjoyed going with him on various visits to increase our knowledge and understanding of what is happening out there, and to get that perspective from our allies. He rightly highlights the significant increases in defence spending among our European allies, which is why some of us have been vocal in our advocacy for the position that the UK must not be left behind, and that we need to reach defence spending of 3% of GDP by the end of this Parliament. Indeed, as Committee members will be more than aware, we made a joint statement to ensure that the Government focus their attention on that issue. I could not agree more with the hon. Gentleman.

I thank the Chair of the Committee for his magnificent statement. As the Arctic becomes increasingly contested, with growing Russian and Chinese activity, does he believe that the UK armed forces are adequately equipped, trained and prepared to operate effectively in extreme Arctic conditions, or are there significant gaps in capability and readiness?

I congratulate the hon. Gentleman, a fellow member of the Defence Committee, on his recent elevation to Lib Dem defence spokesperson for veterans and people. No doubt he will give our former Committee member, now the Minister for Veterans and People, good scrutiny in the future. The hon. Gentleman rightly highlights that there are significant capability gaps, and those need to be addressed. As I said earlier, while we can be proud of the expertise and capabilities of the Royal Marines, those are no substitute for naval vessels or for having the platforms through which they can project that expertise.

Unlike the Secretary of State for Defence, Conservative Members listen to the Chair of the Defence Committee, and indeed to his colleagues who have produced an excellent report, “Defence in the High North”. As I must be brief, I wish to ask about the report’s warnings about the lack of operationally available assets in the Royal Navy, both surface escorts and attack submarines. As the report states on page 29: “According to several media sources, all five Astute Class nuclear attack submarines have recently all been tied up in dockyards at the same time, with none deployed.” That point has been mentioned by several Members this afternoon. The Astute class was once described to me by a naval officer as being like a Formula 1 racing car—great on the track, but a bitch when it gets into the pits. The hon. Gentleman mentioned serious capability gaps, so when does he think Ministers will finally come clean about why all five of our nuclear attack submarines have been tied up for months?

I thank the shadow Minister for his kind words about the work of the Committee. Capability gaps, particularly with regard to submarines, were mentioned by the Committee at length, and my hon. Friend the Member for Barrow and Furness (Michelle Scrogham) was also forthright in making that point. The capability gaps in the delivery of future subs must be addressed urgently. For example, we received evidence suggesting that the production of certain assets was advancing at a “leisurely” pace. That needs to be addressed. Ultimately, as the Committee’s report on AUKUS highlighted, the next-generation SSN-AUKUS is incredibly important and we must ensure that we are investing at pace so that our Australian friends also have that capability at pace. For much of the time at present, we are left in a situation where many of our assets, including submarines, are in either maintenance or deep maintenance.

I commend the Chair of the Defence Committee and his colleagues for a tremendous report. As he rightly mentioned, Scotland is effectively on the frontline of the new potential battleground of the High North. Will the Chair be circling back to the report to see whether there has been progress? Scotland is critical to closing the frigate gap; BAE Systems on the Clyde and Babcock in Rosyth on the east coast are building warships even as we speak. I am concerned by recent comments made by Scotland’s First Minister, John Swinney, who claimed that Britain is in some way abandoning Scotland to the Russian threat, when in fact one of the real threats to national security in this country is the Scottish National party’s separatist agenda: it is not sure whether it wants to be in NATO or out of NATO, and it wants the nuclear submarines out of Faslane. It is a strange picture, so I wonder whether the hon. Gentleman might go back to that?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his incisive comments. He will be pleased to note that Scotland had several mentions in our report, as well as in the wall-to-wall coverage that the hard-hitting report attracted. There was much mention of the need to strengthen our capabilities in Scotland. Obviously, the Scottish Government need to make sure that they are aligned with some of the investments that are being made by the UK Government. That is really important, because during our visits to Scotland we saw that many of those working in the industry, as well as those serving, are very much looking to the UK Government and the Scottish Government to work in partnership. The hon. Gentleman mentioned NATO. Let nobody be in any doubt that NATO is a cornerstone of British defence. I therefore fully concur with his views on that question.

I thank the Chair of the Defence Committee and the Committee for all they have done. The Chair outlined the training that the Royal Marines receive to carry out their duties in the High North. If there is a war—we hope there will not be—the Royal Marines will not fight that war on their own, because the Royal Irish Regiment, along with all the other regiments in the British Army, will fight alongside them. What has been done to ensure that the Royal Irish Regiment and other regiments have the same training as the Royal Marines in the High North?
You have 40 seconds or less to answer, Mr Dhesi

Thank you for that steer, Madam Deputy Speaker. I thank the hon. Gentleman, who is ever present in the Chamber, for his question. The Committee did not look into the capabilities offered by the Royal Irish Regiment, but it is true that it needs to be strengthening their capabilities and training because Britain can only succeed if all regiments are fighting together, just as we can only succeed more widely if we are fighting alongside our NATO allies. We need to deter the threat before there is any conflict or crisis.
I thank the Chair of the Defence Committee for his statement and his excellent timekeeping.

title: International Law: UK Obligations
turns: What steps she is taking to help ensure that the UK upholds international law.

We remain completely committed to upholding international law. That commitment reflects our values, but also the real benefits that international law brings to our everyday lives. It underpins the global rules that allow us to travel on holiday more easily and UK businesses to sell their goods abroad, and it enables greater co-operation between international law enforcement agencies, keeping our streets safer at home.

President Trump’s Administration stated that they would dismantle the International Criminal Court “brick by brick”, and have imposed sanctions following ICC judge Navi Pillay being awarded the 2026 Nobel peace prize. The International Criminal Court’s chief prosecutor has had access to emails and bank accounts removed, following sanctions by President Trump. What steps are the Government taking with European allies to uphold international law and human rights in the face of threats to the ICC by the US Administration?

The hon. Gentleman raises an incredibly important point. The UK stands with the International Criminal Court, and we stand united with our partners in strongly disagreeing with the sanctions imposed on the Court. The ICC must be permitted to continue its critical work of holding perpetrators of the most horrific international crimes to account. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office is in close contact with the Court and individuals impacted, to support them during this period.

Sometimes, this topic can seem abstract to residents in my constituency of Harlow, so could the Attorney General talk about the practical ways in which obeying international law can benefit my residents in Harlow?

My hon. Friend is a fantastic champion for the people of Harlow, including on the topic of international law, which brings real benefits to us. For example, when his constituents set off for their summer holidays—presumably from Stansted airport—the Chicago convention, which governs flights, enables them to do so safely and securely.
I call the shadow Attorney General.

I think I am in the slightly novel position of being fresh to the Dispatch Box myself, but also able to welcome both the Attorney General and the Solicitor General to their new places, which I do with gusto. Last month, the Attorney General published her new “Attorney General’s Legal Guidance”, a direction to all Government lawyers on how to advise Ministers on lawfulness and legal risk, which replaced the advice of Lord Hermer. Across the board, she has removed references to international law. She has removed Lord Hermer’s demand that “the rule of law requires compliance by the state with its obligations in international law as in national law”; she has removed Lord Hermer’s direction that the Government “should not invite Parliament to legislate contrary to international obligations”; and she has removed the whole paragraph in which Lord Hermer instructed Government lawyers that compliance and respect for international law must be a critical factor in legal advice. She served as Solicitor General under Lord Hermer for a year. What persuaded her that his guidance to Government lawyers was wrong, and that the Conservatives were right all along that his guidance needed to be replaced?

I welcome the hon. Gentleman to his post, and I am pleased that he has raised the updated legal risk guidance. This is a Government committed to getting things done, and I make it clear in the revised guidance that, where there is a tenable legal argument, we can take action. On international law, my new guidance makes it clear that domestic law and international law should be treated in the same way. It is important that we adhere to both, and that is set out in the guidance.

Having removed Lord Hermer’s focus on the importance of international law, the Attorney General has in fact added a new consideration: whether an international court has jurisdiction. This could have Chagos written all over it. Without express United Kingdom consent, there is no international court with binding jurisdiction over the sovereignty of the Chagos islands. Applying her own legal guidance, does the Attorney General now agree that the decision to cede sovereignty of the Chagos islands has never been a legal imperative forced on the Government, but is instead a political decision, taken by Labour?

The military base at Diego Garcia is critical for our national security, and for keeping people safe here in Britain. Our priority has always been clear: to secure the long-term, effective operation of that base. Since its creation, there have been challenges relating to the base in various international courts and tribunals, threatening its long-term, secure operation. That is why we continue to work closely with the US and with Mauritius to find a way forward that is in the UK’s best interests, and that continues to protect our national security.

title: Prisons: Rehabilitative Programmes
turns: What steps he is taking to improve rehabilitative programmes in prisons.
The Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice

Education, skills and work are central to rehabilitation. We are modernising prison education and creating a joined-up system that supports prisoners in progressing from basic literacy to skills training and work experience. We are also tackling the root causes of offending through offender behaviour programmes and substance misuse treatment.

Many ex-prisoners experience challenges after prison, particularly when trying to reintegrate into society, which is really difficult to do. We know that 40% of prisoners reoffend within one year, and that reoffending costs £22.7 billion per year; at the same time, 97% of prison capacity is taken. Will the Secretary of State ensure that ex-prisoners are properly supported, so that they can positively integrate into society, and reoffending can be reduced?

That is an important point. It is great to start Question Time on a note of unanimity, and I am sure that one view that we all hold in common in this place is that when people leave prison, we do not want them to return and reoffend. The key to that is a multi-agency approach locally, starting before individuals leave prison. We are working closely with local government partners to ensure more effective pre-release planning work.
I call the Chair of the Justice Committee.

The public are safer when people leave prisons with the skills to find work and stay out of crime. Despite the Coates review calling for education to be put “at the heart of the prison regime”, a decade later, cuts have halved the number of education hours in some of our prisons. Today, Ofsted and the chief inspector of prisons have both published a letter calling on Ministers to act on the review’s recommendations, and to tackle poor performance on purposeful activity in prisons. What is being done to ensure that prisoners receive the education that they need to find work and stay out of prison?

I am grateful for that question from the Chair of the Justice Committee, because that too is a crucial point. We are in a self-defeating cycle: the capacity problems in our prisons, which have been talked about in this Chamber for months, impair governors’ ability to move individuals around and get them to the right place, be it to substance abuse treatment, mental health treatment, educational classes or work training. That is why the steps that we have taken are so important. However, I recognise the vigour with which the Chair and the Committee make their comments, and I certainly intend to work closely with them to deliver on this.

Diolch yn fawr iawn, Lefarydd. Tackling reoffending requires rehabilitation, but the Wales Governance Centre’s latest report shows that that is not happening well enough in Wales. Recall numbers are up 27%; rough sleeping on release is becoming the norm; and the rate of death by drug poisoning while under community supervision is considerably higher than in England. Addressing those issues requires a holistic approach, which is impossible when Westminster controls the levers when it comes to justice. Following the Secretary of State’s meeting with Welsh Government Ministers yesterday, does he agree that devolving justice is key to making justice work in Wales?

As the right hon. Lady says, I was in Wales yesterday, meeting the Welsh Government and talking about exactly these issues. As I said in my answer to the original question, we have to use all organisations—yes, His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service, but also others, including local authorities, local health services and charities—effectively at a place-based level. That is what we said in the conversations that we had yesterday, and I very much look forward to building on them.

I welcome the Government focusing prisons on rehabilitation, and on better education, training and support to help people turn their life around. I am particularly concerned about pregnant women leaving prison, many of whom have no secure accommodation, are vulnerable to being targeted by drug dealers and could even feel safer in prison than on the outside. How can we provide better support for pregnant women leaving prison?

My hon. Friend touches on an important question for his community and the country more generally. For anybody—particularly pregnant women—to leave prison with security, they must have access to housing; that is the anchor. We are taking incredible steps forward in this place to ensure that everybody is offered somewhere to be from night one, and through our emergency accommodation, we can offer up to 84 days of support. There is much to do, particularly with pregnant women, to make sure that the other support systems then wrap around them, to give them the best possible chance of staying out of prison.

title: Youth Hubs
turns: What recent progress he has made on the expansion of youth hubs.
What steps he is taking to help support the establishment of youth hubs.

We are making strong progress expanding youth hubs across Great Britain, with delivery ahead of schedule, bringing the total number of youth hubs to 160. These hubs provide a single, community-based front door to joined-up employment, skills and wider support for young people. We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners to maintain momentum and support further expansion.

In August, Falkirk became one of the first towns in Scotland to have a youth hub. Opened at the Falkirk campus of Forth Valley college—our primary local further education institute—it is visible evidence of our Labour Government’s investment in young people’s futures. Will the Minister join me on a visit to the youth hub and Forth Valley college, and will the Department re-engage with the Falkirk-based local training provider Powering Futures, whose model could deliver a preventive solution to youth unemployment but currently falls between the cracks of reserved and devolved competency?

I thank my hon. Friend for his invitation and for highlighting the work of the Falkirk youth hub and its partners. My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State has met with Powering Futures and is aware of the issues that he raises. My hon. Friend has been relentless in seeking support for this organisation, and I hope that the Scottish Government will think again and consider supporting the good work of Powering Futures with funding.

For many of our young people, the hardest step towards obtaining work is the first one: walking into a jobcentre or youth hub and asking for support. Does the Minister agree that part of the approach of youth hubs, including the new hub in Wrexham, must be to reach those young people where they are, rather than waiting for them to come through the door?

My hon. Friend is right. The whole purpose of youth hubs is to take support out of traditional settings and into communities, meeting young people where they are rather than expecting them to come to us. Through partnerships with local authorities, charities, colleges and other organisations, youth hubs such as the upcoming Wrexham youth hub will help us reach young people in their local communities who might otherwise miss out on support. We will continue to encourage all youth hubs to undertake proactive outreach and work with local partners to reach young people. I have seen excellent examples of that in the hubs I have visited thus far.

Over the last two years, the Government have increased the cost of employing young people with higher national insurance charges on employers and imposed the 350 pages of additional regulation contained in their “unemployment rights Act”. Does the Minister agree that the best way of reducing youth unemployment is to cut the cost of employing young people rather than an endless array of hubs, grants, schemes and guarantees?

I would agree with the hon. Gentleman, but then we would both be wrong. I attended a recent parliamentary event hosted by the Resolution Foundation, chaired by the former Tory Minister Lord Willetts, and the research it had undertaken was clear that cutting taxes was not as effective in delivering opportunities to get young people into work—[Interruption.] It was very clear that the targeting of employment support was much more effective than the approach the hon. Gentleman is suggesting. The shadow Secretary of State was there; she saw that. She may not have agreed with it—maybe that was because she did not stay until the end of the event—but none the less it was very clear that the best way to support young people into work is through employment support schemes, youth hubs and the routes that we are taking.
Every local area should have a youth hub—the benefits are so very clear. The Minister is promising an expansion of youth hubs, so when can we see one in Bath?

I would be happy to write to the hon. Lady to confirm specific timings in individual localities. We are ahead of projected delivery at the moment, having already hit more than 160 youth hubs, but we have a target of reaching more than 300 in the coming months and years. I will set out to her in writing plans for the youth hub that will serve her local area.

title: Topical Questions
turns: T1. If she will make a statement on her departmental responsibilities.
The Minister for Women and Equalities

Women and girls should never have to shrink our lives or ambitions because of outdated misogynistic attitudes. The appalling testimonies we have heard in recent days underline how much further we have to go. I pay tribute to all the women who have shown such bravery in coming forward and sharing their experiences. The misogyny taskforce will help to tackle misogyny in workplaces, communities and online. It is backed by £15 million, which we are working with businesses and philanthropists to grow. The Government are clear that misogyny has no place in our society and it is time to consign those attitudes to history.

A report in July by the Women and Equalities Committee found that black people are four times more likely to experience homelessness than people who are white. In 2025-26, black people made up 2% of households in Liverpool, with 12% of those recorded homeless, or at risk of being so. Despite the Government’s welcome commitment to end rough sleeping, they are still to respond to the Committee’s report. Will the Minister chase that urgently and set out what steps the Office for Equality and Opportunity is taking to ensure that the rough sleeping programme addresses the specific challenges facing black people experiencing homelessness?

The Committee’s report provides important evidence on the experiences of black people facing homelessness, and I can assure my hon. Friend that the Government will respond shortly. Last month, I visited Liverpool with Baroness Lawrence and the race equality engagement group, and we heard about how real efforts are being made to build stronger communities and tackle racism, and how important it is that there is safe and secure housing for ethnic minority communities across our country.

The Secretary of State has made class a central theme of her equalities agenda, but before she can tackle class-based disadvantage, she must surely be able to define it, so what is her definition of class and how will her Department identify who is and who is not working class?

It is important that we take action on the disadvantage that holds people back by virtue of family background and income. We intend to enact the socioeconomic duty, which will ensure that all public authorities take seriously their responsibility in how they design and deliver public services. I am grateful for the shadow Minister’s interest in this area and look forward to working with her to ensure that we finally take class seriously as a country.

T3. There is a clear distinction between discussion and disagreement, and harmful conversion practices. The Government’s draft Bill is clear in using the existing definition of abusive conduct in criminal law. Does the Minister agree with me that the protections in the Bill are urgently needed, and that before the end of this Session we should pass the comprehensive, trans-inclusive conversion practices ban that our manifesto called for?

Abusive conversion practices have no place in our country, and no one should face abuse because of who they are or who they love. We have brought forward a draft Bill for pre-legislative scrutiny because we want to get it right. I look forward to the Joint Committee’s recommendations and to working across the House to finally deliver that long-overdue ban.
T5. Will the Minister set out what steps she is taking to ensure compliance with the legal framework around single-sex spaces for all public bodies?

The Equality and Human Rights Commission is responsible for ensuring that public bodies honour their responsibilities and provide appropriate single-sex spaces, as well as ensuring that we have services available for everyone in our country. Government Departments have also published guidance so that we can be clear about how we will deliver on our responsibilities, but we recognise and will uphold the ruling of the Supreme Court.

T4. For nearly a decade, Dunfermline Athletic football club has made Samaritans its main charity partner. Through matchday messages, pitch-side advertising and an annual awareness day at East End Park, the Pars tell fans that it is always good to talk, reaching people who might never walk into a GP surgery. Will the Minister join me in congratulating the Pars on the work they do, and will she ensure that the Government’s own work on mental health learns from such community partnerships?

I commend Dunfermline Athletic for a powerful example of what can be achieved in that kind of partnership with Samaritans. It is important that we are all able to seek help when we are experiencing mental health challenges. Suicide is one of the biggest killers of men in our country, which is why the work that the Minister for men and boys, my hon. Friend the Member for Rother Valley (Jake Richards), is leading is incredibly important in ensuring that everyone can access timely support, so that we do not see a single person lost to suicide wherever we can prevent it.

T6. The Prime Minister has said that it is important that rape and sexual assault victims do not feel like they are the ones being put on trial in cases, yet the mother of a rape victim who came to see me last week said that her daughter felt exactly that way when her abuser was put on trial. Does the Minister agree with the Victims’ Commissioner that juries in those cases need to be directed in the myths and misconceptions around rape?

As the Prime Minister has set out, we believe that it is important that that recognition is there. I am very sorry to hear about the experiences of the hon. Lady’s constituent, and if she would like to discuss that further with a Minister, I can certainly ensure that takes place. In recent times we have seen shameful comments that trivialise the experiences of women, and we must all be clear, right across society, that violence against women and girls is abhorrent, there can be no excuses and those who commit acts of violence and sexual violence against women should face the full force of the law.

Thank you, Mr Speaker—[Interruption.] On behalf of menopausal women around the world, I thank the House for that warm welcome. According to the big Menopause Mandate 2026 survey, 90% of working women say that symptoms affect them at work, yet only 39% of their employers have a menopause policy. How will the Government ensure that the menopause action plans set to be introduced next year will be implemented and monitored to support women through that very important stage of their life?

My hon. Friend has been an incredible campaigner on this issue and has done so much to help women across our country. We are taking action as a Government, ensuring that big employers have to produce action plans to say how they will support women going through the menopause, which many already do, because they know it is an incredible waste of talent to see women leaving brilliant jobs and careers just when they are getting into their stride.
